いい.etymology: Colloquial modern Tokyo/standard form of the adjective よい (良い 'good'), arising in Edo-period eastern Japanese via vowel assimilation (*yoi* > *ii*). Conjugated inflections (よく, よかった, etc.) still retain the historical よ- stem.

history.meaning: good; fine
good
good; fine; acceptable

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — いい

いいえ.etymology: Polite negative response interjection ('no') that emerged in Early Modern Japanese by lengthening and compounding earlier negative/corrective exclamations いや / いえ.

history.meaning: no; by no means
polite 'no'; 'not at all'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — いいえ

cognates.meaning: addition and subtraction; more or less

いいかげん.etymology: Hybrid Yamato-Sino (wago-kango) compound joining native いい (ii, Early Modern Edo vowel-assimilated variant of よい yoi < Classical よし 良し 'good, proper') with Sino-Japanese 加減 (kagen: 加 ka < Middle Chinese *kæ 'add, increase' + 減 gen < Middle Chinese *hɛmX 'subtract, reduce'). Originally meant adjusting seasoning, bathwater, or medicine to 'just the right balance', before ironic understatement flipped it into 'half-baked, irresponsible' and exasperated 'know when to stop!'.

history.meaning: adding and subtracting; adjusting medicinal dosage or seasoning
just the right moderation; (ironically) lukewarm, perfunctory
irresponsible, sloppy, half-baked; moderate (in fixed phrases); enough already

morphemes.meaning: good, suitable (colloquial variant of native yoi < yoshi)
add, increase (Sino-Japanese kango from Middle Chinese *kæ)
subtract, diminish (Sino-Japanese kango from Middle Chinese *hɛmX)

いいかげん.notes: Classic contronym: いい加減な奴 means 'a flaky, irresponsible guy' and いい加減にしろ！ means 'Cut it out / Enough already!', yet いい加減のお湯 preserves the older positive sense 'bathwater at just the right temperature'.

いう.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb descending from Old and Classical Japanese いふ (言ふ, ifu, from Proto-Japonic *ipu 'to speak, utter, call by name'). Regular medial labial lenition (*-p- > *-f- > *-w-) and loss of *w before u yielded dictionary spelling いう (iu), while spoken Japanese coalesces the vowel hiatus iu into palatalized long yū [jɯː] specifically in the non-past form.

history.meaning: to speak, utter, call by name
to say, recite, declare, be named
to say, tell, call, mean

いう.notes: Though spelled いう in kana, its dictionary form is naturally pronounced [jɯː] (ゆう) in everyday speech, whereas conjugated stems retain crisp [i] (言わない iwanai, 言った itta).

いえ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) polite negative response word and discourse conjunction, functioning as a brisker shortened variant of いいえ (iie). Developed in Early Modern Japanese via palatal vowel fronting (*iya > *iye > ie / iie) from the Old and Classical Japanese negative exclamation いや (否, iya, 'no, unwelcome, disagreeable'), softening refusal or modestly deflecting praise and thanks.

history.meaning: no! unwelcome, reluctant
no (polite negative reply via vowel fronting iya > iye > ie)
no; on the contrary; not at all (concise polite discourse marker)

いえ.notes: Much smoother and more natural in real workplace conversation than textbook いいえ (which can sound stiffly contradictory); do not confuse in kana with homographic 家 (いえ, ie, 'house', pronounced with LH pitch vs. HL for 'no').

rootFamily.gloss: no, no; don't mention it (modest reduplication)

いえいえ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) reduplicated interjection (jōgo 畳語) doubling the polite negative particle いえ (ie < いいえ iie < Classical 否 iya 'no'). In Japanese conversational pragmatics, rapid reduplication strips away confrontational contradiction and turns the negative into warm social modesty when waving off compliments, apologies, or gratitude.

history.meaning: exclamation of refusal or aversion
polite negative response 'no'
no, no; not at all; think nothing of it (modest deflection)

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated element softening refusal into polite modesty

いえいえ.notes: Often a far more natural everyday response to 'thank you' or 'sorry' than textbook どういたしまして, frequently paired with とんでもないです ('Not at all!').

いかが.etymology: Phonological development in Heian-period Early Middle Japanese from Old Japanese *ikani ka* (いかにか 'in what manner?, how?'), via nasalization and voicing (*ikanika* > *ikaga*).

history.meaning: in what way?; how?
how; in what way
polite 'how?; how about?'

いく.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb emerging via palatal glide loss (*yu- > i- before a velar) alongside older ゆく (行く, yuku, from Old Japanese yuku < Proto-Japonic *yuku 'to move away from a reference point, pass on'). Colloquial speech generalized iku and innovated an irregular geminate te-form 行って (itte rather than expected *iite) for phonological distinctness, while retaining yuku in literary compounds.

rootFamily.gloss: to go, pass on (literary and poetic doublet)

いくつ.etymology: Interrogative number word formed in Old Japanese from the interrogative root いく- ('how many, what extent') and the native numeral classifier suffix -つ.

how many; how old

いける.etymology: Potential verb derived from いく (行く 'to go, proceed well'), attested from the Edo period onward in the idiomatic senses 'can go', 'works well', 'tastes good', or 'can handle alcohol'. Also writes 生ける / 活ける ('to arrange flowers') from the transitive verb meaning 'keep alive'.

いずれ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) indeterminate pronoun and temporal adverb descending from Old and Classical Japanese いづれ (何れ / 孰れ, idure). Built transparently within the Proto-Japonic interrogative system from the wh-root いづ- (idu- < Proto-Japonic *intu 'which/where', also seen in iduko > doko) plus the pronominal suffix -re (shared by kore, sore, are, tare), shifting from 'which one' to 'either way' and 'sooner or later'.

history.meaning: which one (of two or more choices)
whichever, in either case; at some unspecified future point
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: sooner or later, eventually; either way; which (formal)

morphemes.meaning: pronominal nominalizing suffix (parallel to kore, sore, dare)

いずれ.notes: Used adverbially in drama (いずれ分かる, 'You'll find out sooner or later'), いずれ projects calm or ominous inevitability; in formal prose, いずれにせよ means 'in any event / either way'.

rootFamily.gloss: any and all, both, every one of them
who (< Classical tare, sharing pronominal suffix -re)

いたす.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *itasu* (致す), originally meaning 'to cause to arrive, bring about, carry through to the end' (causative counterpart of 至る *itaru* 'to reach'). From medieval Japanese onward it grammaticalized into the humble verb for 'to do'.

history.meaning: bring to a destination; bring about
humbly do / perform

いただきます.etymology: Polite mealtime and receiving formula, the *-masu* form of いただく (頂く 'to place on top of one's head; humbly receive'). Originally referring to the gesture of raising a gift or bowl toward the crown of the head (頂 *itadaki*) in gratitude before partaking.

いただく.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) humble (kenjōgo) godan verb derived from Old Japanese いただく (頂 / 戴く, itadaku, 'to place or hold high upon the crown of the head'), denominal from いただき (頂, itadaki, 'summit, crown of the head'). Because gifts or awards from a social superior were reverently bowed over and raised toward one's forehead upon acceptance, this physical gesture grammaticalized into 'to humbly receive, eat, drink' and benefactive -te itadaku.

history.meaning: to place upon or carry on the crown of the head
to reverently lift and accept a gift from a superior
to humbly receive, eat, or drink; polite benefactive auxiliary

morphemes.meaning: crown of the head, summit, peak

rootFamily.gloss: summit, mountain peak, crown of the head
mealtime expression of gratitude ('I humbly partake')
Sino-Japanese semantic parallel ('lifting to the crown' -> please give me)

いただける.etymology: Potential form of the humble verb いただく (頂く 'to humbly receive'), used in polite modern Japanese to ask or state whether one 'can receive' a favor or action ('could I have you do...').

be able to humbly receive; could you please

いちゃもん.etymology: Early Modern Edo slang and underworld (gambler and street-stall tekiya) argot whose exact phonological origin remains disputed among Japanese philologists. Major hypotheses derive it either from a slangy distortion of 一文 (ichimon, 'a single mon copper coin'—quibbling or picking a fight over a petty trifle), or from the expressive stem いちゃ- (seen in ichatsuku, originally 'to pester, get entangled obstinately with' before narrowing to 'flirt') + colloquial もん (< 物 mono 'thing, matter').

history.meaning: petty cavil or quarrel picked in Edo pleasure quarters and gambling dens
bogus complaint, groundless nitpicking, or pretext for a shakedown

morphemes.meaning: expressive slang stem suggesting pestering entanglement or altered ichi- ('one/petty')
colloquial reduced form of 物 (mono 'thing, matter') or 文 (mon 'coin')

いちゃもん.notes: Virtually locked into the collocation いちゃもんをつける (ichamon o tsukeru, 'to pick a bogus quarrel / trump up a complaint'), classic Shōwa yakuza and nightlife parlance for extortionate nitpicking.

rootFamily.gloss: to flirt openly; (older) to pester or tangle with

いっか.etymology: In hiragana dialogue, native Yamato (wago) colloquial contraction of いいか (ii ka, 'is it fine? -> oh well, good enough'), combining colloquial いい (< よい yoi < Classical よし 良し 'good, acceptable') with the self-directed deliberative particle か (ka) via expressive consonant gemination (ii ka > ikka). Note that Japanese morphological taggers frequently classify kana いっか as a noun by matching its Sino-Japanese homophone 一家 (ikka, from Middle Chinese *ʔjit 一 'one' + *kæ 家 'household, clan').

history.meaning: good, proper, acceptable

history.form: よいか > いいか (yoi ka > ii ka)
history.meaning: is it acceptable or good enough?
oh well, fine then, let it go (resigned self-directed colloquialism)

morphemes.meaning: good, fine, acceptable (geminated colloquial stem of native adjective ii < yoi)
self-directed deliberative/interrogative final particle ('is it? -> I suppose so')

いっか.notes: Ubiquitous in conversational まあ、いっか ('Oh well, whatever / good enough') when shrugging off a minor issue; when written in kanji as a Sino-Japanese noun, homophonous 一家 (ikka) means a family household or a yakuza syndicate clan.

rootFamily.gloss: good; alright! (classical form preserved as interjection)

いってきます.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) ritualized departure formula uniting 行って (itte, the sokuonbin geminated te-form of 行く iku < yuku 'to go', from earlier ikite) with 来ます (kimasu, polite -masu conjugation of subsidiary directional verb 来る kuru < Old Japanese ku 'to come back to the deictic center'). Literally 'I will go and come back', encoding an auspicious pledge of safe return to the household or workplace.

history.form: ゆきてく (行きて来, yukite ku)
history.meaning: to go somewhere and return here

history.form: いってきます (行って来ます, itte kimasu)
history.meaning: I am stepping out and will return (polite domestic formula)
I'm off! See you later! (standard departure greeting)

morphemes.meaning: going (geminated onbin stem of native verb iku 行く)
coming back (continuative stem of native verb kuru 来る)

いってきます.notes: Say いってきます only when leaving a home base or office to which you intend to return; using it when checking out of a hotel or leaving permanently sounds unnatural because 来ます promises a return.

rootFamily.gloss: have a safe trip / see you later (paired response)

いってらっしゃい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) contracted send-off greeting reduced via vowel elision from 行っていらっしゃい (itte irasshai). Combines 行って (itte, geminated te-form of 行く iku 'to go') with いらっしゃい (irasshai, imperative of the sonkeigo honorific directional verb いらっしゃる irassharu, evolved in Edo Japanese from Late Middle Japanese 入らせらる iraseraru—stem of 入る iru 'to enter, go/come' + causative-honorific -seraru). Literally 'go and honorably return!'.

history.form: いらせらる (入らせらる, iraseraru)
history.meaning: to honorably enter, go, or be present

history.form: いっていらっしゃい (行っていらっしゃい, itte irasshai)
history.meaning: please go and honorably return
have a good day; see you later (contracted send-off greeting)

morphemes.meaning: going (geminated stem of native verb iku 行く)
elided imperative of honorific auxiliary irassharu ('go and return safely')

いってらっしゃい.notes: Standard warm reply from the person staying behind when someone says いってきます at home or the office; hotel and cafe staff also say いってらっしゃいませ to morning commuters.

いっぱい.etymology: Sino-Japanese numeral-classifier compound 一杯 (いっぱい), from 一 ('one') + 杯 ('cup, vessel, bowlful'). From 'one full cup', it broadened in Early Modern Japanese to 'filled to capacity' and colloquially 'a lot, many'.

history.meaning: one cupful; one vessel
full to the brim; a lot; many

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一杯

いつ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *itu* ('when, what time'), built on the interrogative root *i-* (shared with いずこ, いかに, いく) plus temporal suffix *-tu*.

history.meaning: when; what time
when; at what time

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 何時

いつか.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) compound adverb いつか (何時か), formed from the interrogative temporal noun いつ (itsu, 'when', from Old Japanese itu) + the indefinite/question particle か (ka). A homophonous native word 五日 (itsuka, 'fifth day of the month; five days') derives from Old Japanese itu- ('five') + the day-counter suffix -ka ('day').

history.meaning: when, what time
at some time, when?
someday, one day, sooner or later

いつか.notes: Pitch accent distinguishes the two senses in standard Tokyo speech: いつか (LHH or HLL) for 'someday', versus 五日 (LHH) for 'the fifth day'. Used with future reference ('someday') or past reference ('at some point previously').

いつでも.etymology: Compound adverb formed in Early Modern Japanese by combining the interrogative temporal pronoun いつ (itsu, 'when', from Old Japanese itu) with the concessive-inclusive particle compound でも (demo, 'even; any'). The particle sequence でも grammaticalized from the copular gerund で (de) plus the inclusive particle も (mo), turning interrogatives into universal free-choice expressions. In modern spoken and written Japanese, いつでも functions both as a welcoming invitation ('whenever you like') and as a habitual temporal adverb ('at all times').

history.meaning: interrogative temporal pronoun 'when'
free-choice temporal adverb 'at any time; whenever'
anytime; whenever; always

いつでも.notes: Frequently paired with どうぞ (いつでもどうぞ, 'whenever you are ready / anytime at all') in hospitality registers.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — いつでも

いつまでも.etymology: Compound native Yamato adverbial expression built from the interrogative temporal pronoun いつ (itsu, 'when', from Old Japanese いづ idu), the terminative limit particle まで (made, 'until, as far as'), and the inclusive topic/concessive particle も (mo, 'even, no matter'). Together, 'even until when' grammaticalized into a universal temporal quantifier meaning 'forever, indefinitely, or for as long as one wishes'.

history.meaning: when, at what time
until any time whatsoever, without end
forever, indefinitely, as long as one likes

いつまでも.notes: Frequently paired with polite hospitality invitations (いつまでもお使いください) or warm wishes for lasting health and friendship.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — いつまでも

いつも.etymology: Compound adverb formed from the temporal interrogative いつ ('when') and the inclusive particle も ('even, every'), literally 'at every when' -> 'always, usually'.

always; usually; habitually

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 何時も

いとこ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *itoko* (従兄弟 / 従姉妹), attested in the Man'yōshū as a term of endearment ('beloved person, dear one', likely from *ito* 'very, dearly' + *ko* 'child/person') and kinship term for a cousin.

cousin

いま.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) temporal noun いま (今), inherited from Old Japanese ima ('now, this moment') and Proto-Japonic *ima. now, presently, immediately
now, the present time; just now

いや.etymology: Conversational negative or corrective interjection/conjunction ('no, wait, well') continuing earlier Japanese いや (否 'no'), alongside the homophonous adjective/noun 嫌 (いや 'disagreeable, reluctant', from Old Japanese *iya*).

おとなしい.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) i-adjective おとなしい (大人しい, otonashii, 'quiet, docile, gentle, well-behaved, obedient'), derived from the noun おとな (大人, otona, 'adult, grown-up; headman/elder') + the adjectival suffix -しい (-shii, '-like, characteristic of'). Historically, おとな derives from 音無し (otonashi, 'without making a fussy noise' or 'composed'), or from 老い (oi 'mature') + とな (person/companion). Originally meaning 'mature, sensible, and composed like a grown-up', the adjective shifted in Early Modern Japanese to 'quiet, mild-mannered, docile, obedient'.

Formed from the honorific prefix お- (o-, 御) + なか (中, naka, 'inside, middle, interior of the body', from Old Japanese naka). Later assigned the jukujikun kanji spelling お腹.

おふくろ.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) noun おふくろ (お袋, ofukuro, 'one's own mother, mom'), formed from the honorific prefix お- (o-, 御) + ふくろ (袋, fukuro, 'bag, sack, pouch', from Old Japanese pukuro). Several classical etymologies are attested in Edo-period scholarship: (1) reference to the womb/placenta (胞衣, ena / fukuro) that holds the child; (2) the matriarch's role as keeper of the household storage bags and purse strings (袋を預かる); or (3) wrapping and sheltering children as inside a protective bag.

おめえ.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) second-person pronoun おめえ (omee, 'you'), a colloquial Eastern Japanese and Tokyo (shitamachi) phonological contraction of おまえ (お前, omae) via regular /ae/ > /ee/ vowel coalescence. Etymologically, お前 consists of the honorific prefix お- (o-, 御) + 前 (mae, 'front, presence', from Old Japanese mape₁ < 目 ma 'eye' + へ pe 'direction/side'). Originally a high-respect noun meaning 'the honorable presence before a noble or deity', it underwent severe pronominal pejoration (depreciation) by the late Edo period into a rough or intimate second-person pronoun.

The underlying adjective めでたし derives from the Old Japanese verb めづ (medu, modern 愛でる mederu, 'to admire, cherish, prize') plus the desiderative/intensive adjectival suffix -たし (-tashi). Over the Edo period, the literal sense 'it is most auspicious' grammaticalized into the universal standard greeting for any joyous occasion or success.

おる.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) verb おる (居る, oru, 'to be [animate], to exist, to stay; [humble] to be'), inherited from Old Japanese woru ('to sit, be seated, exist in a place'). Etymologically, Old Japanese woru arose as a lexicalized stative contraction of *wi-aru, combining the continuative stem wi of 居る (wiru > modern iru, 'to sit down, settle') + the existential verb 有る (aru, 'to be, exist'). In Western Japanese (Kansai, Chūgoku, Kyūshū), おる remains the everyday verb for animate existence, whereas in standard Tokyo Japanese it specializes as a humble (kenjōgo) or pompous/literary counterpart of いる. (Homophonous with 折る oru 'to fold, break' and 織る oru 'to weave'.)

In turn, 世話 combines 世 (se, go-on reading from Middle Chinese sjejH, 'world, society, everyday life') + 話 (wa, kan-on reading from Middle Chinese hwaejH, 'talk, speech, dealings'). Originally a Buddhist and Muromachi term for 'everyday vernacular talk or worldly dealings', 世話 evolved into 'mediating, looking after someone's everyday needs, rendering assistance'.

お世話.notes: Forms the backbone of Japanese workplace and social etiquette: お世話になっております (osewa ni natte orimasu, 'Thank you for your ongoing support/patronage') opens nearly every business email and phone call, while お世話になりました expresses gratitude when parting ways. (Ironically, 大きなお世話だ！ means 'Mind your own business! / None of your concern!')

お供.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) honorific noun お供 (otomo, 'accompanying a superior, attendant, retinue, companion'), composed of the honorific/humble prefix お- (o-, 御) + 供 (tomo, 'companion, follower, attendant', from Old Japanese tomo₂ 'companion, suite, group following a lord'). Popularized in urban Early Modern and Meiji bourgeois households for the unmarried daughter of a respectable family, it became the standard respectful term for another person's daughter or a well-bred young lady.

お宅.etymology: Hybrid Yamato–Sino-Japanese (wago–kango) polite noun and pronoun joining native honorific prefix お- (o-) with Sino-Japanese 宅 (taku, Kan'on reading of Middle Chinese draek 宅 'chosen dwelling, residence, house'). Following Japanese deference norms that avoid direct pronouns by naming a person's location or household, 'your honorable residence' metonymically extended to 'your family', 'your company/firm' in business speech, and a polite yet socially distanced 'you'.

お宅.notes: A staple of Shōwa B2B negotiation meaning 'your company/outfit' (less stiff than 御社); in late-1970s/1980s sci-fi and anime clubs, fans addressing acquaintances at arm's length as お宅 gave birth to global loanword otaku ('geek').

rootFamily.gloss: obsessive fan, geek (1980s subcultural offshoot of the pronoun)

お客.etymology: Hybrid Yamato–Sino-Japanese (wago–kango) noun combining native polite/honorific prefix お- (o-) with Sino-Japanese 客 (kyaku, Kan'on reading of Middle Chinese khaek 客 'traveler, stranger from afar, visiting guest'; compare older Go-on kaku in 旅客 ryokaku). In medieval and Edo merchant society, the household 'guest' sense expanded seamlessly to commercial patrons, clients, and theatergoers, framing commerce in terms of hospitality.

guest, caller; customer, client, or audience member

お客.notes: Staff say お客 among themselves backstage ('we have customers'), but when speaking to or in front of clientele, adding -さん or -さま (お客さま) is mandatory etiquette.

お客さま.etymology: High-respect hospitality term ('honored guest, customer'), formed from honorific prefix お- + Sino-Japanese 客 (きゃく 'guest, visitor, customer') + honorific suffix -さま (様).

honored guest; customer; client

お客さん.etymology: Everyday polite term for 'guest, visitor, customer', formed from prefix お- + Sino-Japanese 客 (きゃく 'guest') + polite suffix -さん (derived from -さま).

guest; customer (polite conversational)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — お客さん

お客様.etymology: Honorific tripartite compound consisting of the polite prefix お- (o-), the Sino-Japanese noun 客 (kyaku, 'guest, visitor, client', from Middle Chinese *kʰˠæk), and the deferential title suffix 様 (sama, originally denoting 'appearance, direction'). While 客 entered Japanese during the Nara and Heian periods for official visitors and travelers, framing it as お客様 became the hallmark of Edo and modern Japanese hospitality (おもてなし) in inns, shops, and tea houses.

お客様.notes: Standard hospitality form used by staff at a 旅館 (ryokan) or café when speaking to or about guests.

お巡りさん.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound coined by Tokyo townspeople in the early Meiji era (1870s) upon the creation of the modern uniformed beat-patrol police: polite prefix お- (o-) + 巡り (mawari, nominalized ren'yōkei stem of 巡る/回る mawaru 'to go around, make rounds, patrol', from Old Japanese maparu 'to turn, circle') + friendly polite suffix -さん (-san < 様 -sama). Literally 'Mr. Make-the-Rounds', capturing the sight of constables walking neighborhood beats.

police officer, beat cop (warm, everyday register)

お巡りさん.notes: Far warmer than English 'cop': お巡りさん is taught to children and can be used politely to address a uniformed neighborhood kōban officer directly, whereas 警察官 is institutional and サツ is crime-drama slang.

police constable (official Sino-Japanese rank sharing kanji 巡)

お布施.etymology: Hybrid Buddhist term combining native polite prefix お- (o-) with Sino-Japanese 布施 (fuse, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese puH sje 布施 'spreading wide and bestowing'). Chinese Buddhist translators coined 布施 to render Sanskrit dāna ('giving, charity, almsgiving', from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- 'to give'), the first of the six pāramitās. In Japan it specialized into the monetary offering presented to a Buddhist priest or temple for sutra chanting and memorial rites.

お布施.notes: Because お布施 is doctrinally a voluntary religious donation rather than a fee for service, funeral etiquette avoids asking 'How much does it cost?' directly; in secular slang, fans or crooks jokingly call pricey merch spending or kickbacks お布施.

rootFamily.gloss: to give in charity, bestow, perform (native verb written with 施)
chief mourner or patron sponsoring a Buddhist rite

お帰りなさい.etymology: Standard domestic and hospitality greeting grammaticalized from the honourific prefix お- (o-), the continuative stem 帰り (kaeri) of the native Yamato verb 帰る (kaeru, 'to return home, come back'), and なさい (nasai), the polite imperative of the honourific auxiliary なさる (nasaru, 'to deign to do'). Literally meaning 'please honourably return', it became the universal reply to ただいま ('I am back') when welcoming someone home.

history.meaning: to return, go back to one's starting point
polite household and inn greeting to a returning person
welcome home; welcome back

morphemes.meaning: stem of 帰る (kaeru, 'to return home')
polite imperative of honourific verb なさる (nasaru)

お帰りなさい.notes: In traditional ryokan hospitality, staff greet guests returning from an evening walk with お帰りなさいませ to make the inn feel like a second home.

shop; store; establishment (polite)

お待たせ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) elliptical humble expression clipped from お待たせいたしました / お待たせしました (omatase shimashita 'I have caused you to wait'). Built from polite prefix お- (o-) + 待たせ (matase), the nominalized ren'yōkei stem of causative verb 待たせる (mataseru 'to make or keep someone waiting'), derived from root verb 待つ (matsu, Old Japanese matu 'to wait, await') + causative auxiliary -せる (-seru, from classical -su).

history.meaning: to wait for, await, watch expectantly for

keeping someone waiting; casual exclamation 'Sorry to keep you waiting!'

irrealis stem mata- of matsu 'to wait'

rootFamily.gloss: meeting up at an appointed place and time

お待ち.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) honorific verbal noun formed from prefix お- (o-) and 待ち (machi), the continuative ren'yōkei stem of 待つ (matsu, Old Japanese matu 'to wait, await, anticipate'). Grammatically it anchors respectful sonkeigo expressions elevating the listener's act of waiting (such as お待ちになる and お待ちください 'please wait'), and also survives as a brisk Edo-style diner/merchant call (お待ち! 'order up / sorry for the wait!'), clipped from お待ち遠さま.

courteous merchant phrase: 'waiting must have felt long for you'
honorific stem for waiting (in omachi kudasai); lively eatery call upon serving

nominalized ren'yōkei stem machi of matsu 'to wait'

お待ち.notes: Never mix up causative vs. base stems: お待ちください asks the listener to wait ('please wait'), while *お待たせください would absurdly beg 'please keep me waiting!'

rootFamily.gloss: sorry to have kept you waiting (traditional shop/restaurant phrase)

お忙しい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) respectful i-adjective combining honorific prefix お- (o-) with 忙しい (isogashii 'busy, pressed for time'). Classical Japanese いそがし (isogasi) derives via the state/emotive adjectival suffix -si (modern -shii) from the verbal root preserved in 急ぐ (isogu, Old Japanese isogu 'to hurry, hasten, press forward urgently'). Semantically it shifted from an agitated, hurried state of spirit to having one's time heavily occupied.

history.meaning: hurried, restless, urgently pressed in mind or action

busy, tied up with work or engagements (polite/honorific)

morphemes.meaning: honorific prefix (o-) attributing the state to a respected interlocutor
native adjectival stem isogashi- (< verbal root isog- 'to hurry, bustle')

お忙しい.notes: Strictly honorific—never say お忙しい about your own schedule; it shines in the classic business cushion お忙しいところ恐れ入りますが ('I am sorry to trouble you while you are busy, but...').

お持ちする.etymology: Productive humble (kenjōgo) verbal construction built from the prefix お- (o-), the continuative stem 持ち (mochi) of the native Yamato verb 持つ (motsu, 'to hold, carry, bring'), and the light verb する (suru, 'to do'). By framing the speaker's act of carrying or bringing as a humble service directed toward the recipient, お持ちする serves as the standard polite equivalent of 持つ or 持っていく in customer service and hospitality.

history.meaning: to hold in the hand, carry

to humbly bring or carry (for a guest)

morphemes.meaning: stem of 持つ (motsu, 'to hold, carry')

お持ちする.notes: Waitstaff and hosts constantly use すぐお持ちします ('I will bring it right out to you') after taking an order.

お昼.etymology: Polite everyday noun for 'noon, midday' or 'lunch', formed from prefix お- + 昼 (ひる 'daytime, noon', inherited from Old Japanese *piru*). The lunch sense arose from court ladies' speech (*nyōbō kotoba*) shortening お昼飯.

お気.etymology: Polite noun formed from honorific prefix お- + Sino-Japanese 気 (き 'spirit, mind, attention, care'), used in set polite expressions such as お気をつけて ('please take care') and お気に召す ('to please one's fancy').

history.meaning: one who pleases a master; favorite
favorite item, place, or person

お気遣い.notes: Indispensable in polite social lubrication, especially お気遣いなく ('please don't trouble yourself on my account') and お気遣いありがとうございます ('thank you for your thoughtfulness').

warm thoughtfulness, solicitude (native synonym with 心)
attentiveness to everyone's needs in a room

お水.etymology: Polite everyday word for '(cold/drinking) water', formed from beautifying prefix お- + 水 (みず, inherited from Old Japanese *midu* 'water'). Originating in court ladies' speech (*nyōbō kotoba* おひや / おみず), it is now universal in dining and hospitality.

お疲れさま.notes: In film, TV, and entertainment crews (heard constantly in The Naked Director), お疲れさまです serves as an all-day hallway 'hello' at any hour, while お疲れさまでした! marks wrapping a shoot or leaving work.

お疲れさん.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) colloquial phrase derived by phonetic reduction from お疲れさま (otsukaresama): honorific prefix お- (o-) + 疲れ (tsukare, nominalized ren'yōkei stem of 疲れる tsukareru 'to become tired, labor', Classical Japanese tukaru) + familiar suffix -さん (-san, contracted in Early Modern Japanese from 様 -sama). お疲れさん.notes: Mind workplace hierarchy: directors and bosses say お疲れさん downward to crew or juniors, or peers say it jokingly, but saying お疲れさん upward to a superior sounds presumptuous—use お疲れさまです instead.

to be utterly exhausted, worn out

お皿.etymology: Polite everyday noun formed by adding the beautifying prefix お- (o-, bikago) to the native Yamato noun 皿 (sara, 'plate, shallow dish'), which is attested since the Nara period in wooden tally strips (mokkan) and the Man'yōshū. plate, dish, saucer

お祈り.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) polite noun formed from honorific/beautifying prefix お- (o-) and 祈り (inori, nominalized ren'yōkei stem of 祈る inoru 'to pray, invoke divine blessing', Old Japanese inoru). お祈り.notes: Because Japanese HR rejection emails invariably close with 今後のご活躍をお祈り申し上げます ('we pray for your future success'), job-hunters wryly call getting rejected お祈りメール ('a prayer email').

お祝い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) polite noun joining prefix お- (o-) with 祝い (iwai, nominalized ren'yōkei stem of 祝う iwau < Classical ifafu < Old Japanese ipapu 'to observe ritual abstinence, purify, consecrate for good fortune'). Old Japanese ipapu is the iterative/continuative -apu derivative of 斎ふ (ipu 'to keep ritually pure, ward off pollution', built on sacred root 斎 i-). Solemn Shinto purification for auspiciousness gradually broadened into festive celebration and gift-giving.

お祝い.notes: お祝い denotes not just the celebratory party or sentiment, but concretely the congratulatory gift or crisp bills inside a mizuhiki envelope given for weddings, births, or store openings (お祝い返し is the obligatory return gift).

お紅茶.etymology: Hybrid bikago (speech-beautification) noun attaching native prefix お- (o-) to Sino-Japanese (kango) 紅茶 (kōcha 'black tea'), composed of 紅 (kō, Kan'on of Middle Chinese huwng 紅 'crimson, red') + 茶 (cha, Middle Chinese dra 茶 'tea'). Like Chinese 紅茶, East Asian terminology names oxidized tea 'red tea' after the coppery-crimson color of the brewed liquid rather than the dark dry leaves (English 'black tea'). Adding お- by analogy with お茶 marks genteel, salon, or feminine register.

お腹.etymology: Polite everyday word for 'stomach, belly', originating in Muromachi court ladies' speech (*nyōbō kotoba*) おなか, which attached prefix お- to 中 (なか 'middle, inside of the body') as a refined avoidance term for 腹 (はら 'belly'). お茶.etymology: Polite everyday word for 'tea' (especially Japanese green tea), formed from beautifying prefix お- + Sino-Japanese 茶 (ちゃ 'tea', borrowed from Middle Chinese *drae*). Used both for the beverage and for taking a break over tea.

history.meaning: tea
tea; green tea; tea break

history.meaning: genitive and subordinate-subject particle
nominative subject particle; conjunctive 'but'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — が

がたつき.etymology: Verbal noun derived from the continuative stem of がたつく ('to rattle, wobble, be loose'), itself built on the onomatopoeic root がた- (from がたがた 'rattling, shaking') + verbalizing suffix -つく.

history.meaning: rattle; wobble; shake
rattling; wobble; looseness

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — がたつく

がっかり.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) mimetic/ideophonic adverb (擬態語) attested from the Edo period, formed from an expressive root *gaka-* evoking the sudden collapse of tension, energy, or structural support, amplified by the intensive geminate *-kk-* and the adverbial suffix *-ri*. Originally used both for physical exhaustion and the sudden sinking of one's spirits upon disappointment.

history.meaning: suddenly losing strength or tension
exhausted; dejected, disappointed

morphemes.meaning: sudden drop in tension or spirit

がっかり.notes: Frequently takes the light verb する (がっかりする 'to be disappointed') or functions adverbially before verbs of emotional letdown. Pitch accent is typically [3] (がっか↓り).

がる.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) verbalizing suffix derived in the Heian period via phonetic contraction of げ (ge, 'appearance, sign', from Old Japanese *ke*) + ある (aru, 'to exist, to have'), literally meaning 'to have the appearance of' or 'to outwardly display signs of feeling'. In the pejorative auxiliary やがる (yagaru), it stems from the verb 上がる (agaru, 'to rise up, get carried away') fused onto a preceding verb's continuative stem.

history.meaning: to have the air or outward sign of
to display feelings of (third-person psychological state)

がる.notes: In Japanese grammar, subjective adjectives like 欲しい (want) or 怖い (afraid) cannot directly describe third-person inner states in unmarked prose; attaching -がる (欲しがる, 怖がる) shifts the meaning to observable behavior ('acts like they want').

rootFamily.gloss: to want (visibly, of a third person)
to show off, to act pretentious

きちんとした.etymology: The term 'きちんとした' (meaning 'neat') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: neat
neat

きちんとした.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — きちんとした

きっちり.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) mimetic adverb built on the sound-symbolic root *kichi-* (expressing tightness, exactness, or a snug fit with zero slack), intensified by consonant gemination (*-tt-*) and the adverbial suffix *-ri*. Closely related to きちんと (kichinto) and きっかり (kikkari) within the *ki-* precision ideophone family.

history.meaning: tightly packed, leaving no gap
tightly, precisely, punctually, without discrepancy

きっちり.notes: Often used in business and colloquial registers alike for paying exact amounts, meeting strict deadlines, or doing a job thoroughly without cutting corners.

rootFamily.gloss: exactly, on the dot (especially of time or numbers)

きっと.etymology: Mimetic and modal adverb attested from Late Heian and Kamakura tales as きと / きっと, originally describing a sharp, tense, or decisive action ('tightly, sternly, without fail'). In Modern Japanese its epistemic sense 'surely, undoubtedly' predominates.

history.meaning: sharply; sternly; unfailingly
surely; certainly; without fail

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 屹度

きつい.etymology: The term 'きつい' (meaning 'tight') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: tight
tight

きつい.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — きつい

きゃ.etymology: Native Japanese colloquial phonetic contraction of the conditional ending -ければ (-kereba, the provisional/realis conditional form of i-adjectives and the negative auxiliary -ない) or the verb conditional -けば (-keba). Through rapid speech palatalization and elision (*-kereba > -kerya > -kya*, or *-keba > -kya*), it became standard in casual Tokyo speech, especially in obligation idioms like なきゃ (from なければ).

history.meaning: if / when (conditional inflection)
if (colloquial contracted conditional)

きゃ.notes: In spoken Japanese, negative conditionals like 行かなきゃ (ikanakya) routinely drop the trailing ならない / いけない, functioning as a standalone sentence meaning 'I have to go!'.

rootFamily.gloss: must, have to (contracted from なければならない)
if one goes (contracted from 行けば)

きる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb 切る (kiru, 'to cut, sever'), attested since Old Japanese *kiru* (from Proto-Japonic *kira- 'to cut'). When attached as an auxiliary verb to the continuative stem (連用形, ren'yōkei) of another verb, the literal sense of 'cutting off at the boundary' grammaticalized into a telic/completive aspect marker meaning 'to do completely, to exhaust, to carry through to the very end'.

history.meaning: to cut, sever, divide with a blade
to finish doing, do to completion or excess

きる.notes: As a compound verb suffix (e.g., 言い切る 'declare definitively', 使い切る 'use up completely', 疲れ切る 'be utterly exhausted'), it emphasizes reaching an absolute limit.

rootFamily.gloss: a cut, slice; end, bounds, limit

きれい.etymology: Sino-Japanese adjectival noun 綺麗 (きれい), borrowed from Middle Chinese *khjeX lejH* (綺麗 'fine patterned silk; splendid and graceful'). In Japanese it broadened from 'splendid, beautiful' to include 'clean, neat, tidy, pure'.

history.meaning: resplendent; finely adorned; beautiful
pretty; beautiful; clean; neat

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 綺麗

きれいだ.etymology: The term 'きれいだ' (meaning 'cleanly') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: cleanly
cleanly

きれいだ.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — きれいだ

ぎ.etymology: Voiced bound morpheme (via rendaku or Sino-Japanese reading) appearing across key compounds in colloquial Japanese transcripts: most notably as the Sino-Japanese reading *gi* of 義 (Middle Chinese *ngjɨH*, 'righteousness, duty, sworn bond', as in 義理 giri) or 技 (Middle Chinese *gjeX*, 'skill, technique'), or as the voiced *rendaku* form of native 木 (*ki > -gi*, 'tree, wood') and 着 (*ki > -gi*, 'wearing, clothes', from 着る kiru).

history.meaning: moral duty, principle / wood, tree; garment
duty, principle; skill; (bound suffix) wear, wood

ぎ.notes: When encountered as a segmented token in subtitle corpora, ぎ typically represents either a rendaku suffix like 水着 (mizugi, 'swimwear') or a Sino-Japanese morpheme like 義 (gi, 'honor/principle').

rootFamily.gloss: swimsuit (water + wear, with rendaku ki > gi)

く.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) inflectional suffix -く (-ku) forming the continuative and adverbial stem (連用形, ren'yōkei) of *i*-adjectives (形容詞), attested directly in Old Japanese as *-ku* (e.g., 高く takaku 'highly', 良く yoku 'well') from Proto-Japonic *-ku*. In casual dialogue, a trailing く token can also represent a truncated or phonetically contracted syllable in rapid speech.

history.meaning: adverbial and conjunctive marker on adjectival roots
adverbializer and predicate-linking stem for i-adjectives

く.notes: Besides turning adjectives into adverbs (早い 'fast' → 早く 'quickly'), the -く form is the required stem before negative ない (高くない) and the te-form て (高くて).

rootFamily.gloss: early, quickly (adverbial form of 早い)
well, often (adverbial form of 良い)

くさい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) adjective 臭い (kusai), derived from the Old Japanese nominal root *kusa* ('foul odor, excrement, filth') + the adjectival suffix *-si* (modern *-i*), attested in the *Nihon Shoki* and *Man'yōshū* as 臭し (*kusasi*, 'foul-smelling'). By metaphorical extension, 'smelling of something' evolved into a productive suffix (-くさい) meaning 'reeking of, suspiciously like, or smack of' (e.g., うさんくさい 'shady/fishy', 素人くさい 'amateurish').

history.meaning: foul-smelling, stinking
smelly; suspicious, fishy, reeking of a quality

くさい.notes: Standalone 臭い! means 'It stinks!' or 'That's fishy/suspicious!' (e.g., of a cover-up or bad acting: 臭い芝居 'hammy/cheesy acting'). When suffixed to nouns, it often resists rendaku (素人くさい, 面倒くさい) though lexicalized pairs like 胡散臭い also keep -kusai.

rootFamily.gloss: to rot, decay, spoil (verbal derivative of *kusa-)

rootFamily.word: 面倒くさい (めんどうくさい)
胡散臭い (うさんくさい)

くじける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive verb 挫ける (kujikeru), the mediopassive/intransitive counterpart of transitive 挫く (kujiku, 'to sprain, crush, break by force'). Attested in Old and Early Middle Japanese as *kudiku / kudikuru* ('to sprain a joint; to break down'), it underwent regular shift of *di > ji* and broadened metaphorically from physical spraining or fracturing to emotional and mental collapse ('to have one's spirit broken, to get discouraged').

history.meaning: to crush, sprain, break by twisting or pressure
to be sprained; to lose heart, be disheartened, falter

くじける.notes: Most commonly heard in encouraging imperatives like 挫けるな! (Kujikeru na! 'Don't lose heart! / Don't give up!') or 挫けずに頑張る ('persevere without getting discouraged').

rootFamily.gloss: to crush, sprain, break someone's spirit (transitive)
setback, frustration, discouragement (Sino-Japanese compound using 挫)

くすねる.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) colloquial verb attested from the Edo period meaning 'to pilfer, pocket, or skim off on the sly'. Likely derived from the root of 潜る (kuguru, archaic *kukuru*, 'to slip under, pass through covertly') or 薬 (kusuri) / 楠 (kusu, associated with camphor/concealment slang) combined with a verbalizing suffix *-neru* (compare 抓ねる tsuneru, 捻る hineru), expressing a covert twisting or slipping motion of the hand into one's pocket.

history.meaning: to pilfer, pocket secretly, skim money or goods

くすねる.notes: Unlike 盗む (nusumu, general theft/robbery), くすねる specifically implies petty, sneaky pilfering, skimming cash from a register, or pocketing small items when no one is looking.

rootFamily.gloss: to tickle; to stir up secretly (phonetically parallel *kusu- verb)
to twist, pinch, contort (sharing the *-neru manipulative suffix)

くせ.etymology: Inherited from Old/Early Middle Japanese *kuse* (癖 'habit, peculiarity, crease, flaw in posture or behavior'). Also used grammatically in 〜くせに ('despite, even though') from 'with the peculiarity of'.

history.meaning: peculiar habit; flaw; tendency
habit; quirk; curl/crease in hair

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 癖

くせに.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) grammaticalized conjunctive phrase composed of the noun 癖 (kuse, 'habit, peculiarity, flaw, characteristic', attested since Old/Early Middle Japanese) + the locative/copular case particle に (ni). Literally meaning 'in the habit/characteristic of [X]', by the Late Middle Japanese (Muromachi) period it grammaticalized into a concessive conjunction meaning 'even though, despite being [X]', carrying a strong tone of reproach or contempt.

history.meaning: behavioral quirk, bodily or personal habit, flaw
despite, even though (with speaker annoyance or criticism)

くせに.notes: Unlike neutral のに ('although'), くせに always implies blame, hypocrisy, or irritation toward a second or third person (e.g., 知らないくせに 'Even though you don't know anything [you act like you do]!'). Never use it for your own actions.

rootFamily.gloss: foul-mouthed habit, verbal tic or insult
having strong peculiarities; quirky or shady

ください.etymology: Polite request form ('please give me; please do'), arisen in Early Modern Japanese by phonological reduction of くだされ (*kudasare*, imperative of the honorific verb くださる 下さる 'to bestow from above').

history.meaning: pray bestow / grant
please give me; please do (~てください)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 下さい

くださる.etymology: Honorific verb 下さる ('for a respected person to give'), evolved in Late Middle Japanese from 下さる (*kudasaru*, originally the passive/honorific form of 下す *kudasu* 'to hand down from above, bestow').

history.meaning: be handed down from a superior; deign to bestow
give (honorific)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 下さる

くだる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb 下る / 降る (kudaru, 'to descend, go down, be handed down'), attested in Old Japanese as *kudaru* (from Proto-Japonic *kunta-ra-). Historically, goods of high quality traveled 'down' (下る) from the imperial capital Kyoto to Edo; goods so shoddy that they were not worth transporting down to Edo—or words that did not 'go down' the throat smoothly—gave rise to the Edo-period negative adjective 下らない (kudaranai, 'worthless, trivial, nonsense').

history.meaning: to descend from a height or from the capital to the provinces

history.form: 下らぬ / 下らない (kudaranu / kudaranai)
history.meaning: not coming down from Kyoto; shoddy, worthless, trivial nonsense

くだる.notes: While standalone 下る means 'to go down / descend' (or 'have diarrhea' in お腹が下る), in everyday speech it is overwhelmingly encountered in its lexicalized negative くだらない ('stupid, pointless, trivial').

rootFamily.gloss: to hand down, pass judgment, lower (transitive counterpart)

くらい.etymology: Inherited from Old/Early Middle Japanese *kurawi* (位 'court rank, station, seat'), literally 'the place where one sits' (座 *kura* 'seat, platform' + 居 *wi* 'sitting'). From 'rank, grade, level', it grammaticalized into a particle indicating approximate degree ('about, approximately, to the extent of').

history.meaning: seat of rank; social station; grade
approximate degree ('about, around')

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 位
Wiktionary — くらい / ぐらい (Japanese)

くる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) irregular (*ka-gyō henkaku*) verb 来る (kuru, 'to come'), descending from Old Japanese *ku* (attributive *kuru*, stem *kə-* / *ki-*), from Proto-Japonic *kə- ('to come toward the speaker'). When following the *-te* form of another verb (〜てくる), it functions as an aspectual/directional auxiliary indicating movement toward the speaker, the onset/emergence of a change, or doing an action and returning ('go and come back').

history.meaning: to come, approach the deictic center
to come; to begin to, to come to (up to now), to go do and return

くる.notes: One of only two core irregular verbs in modern Japanese (alongside する): its stem shifts vowels across こな-い (negative ko-), き-ます (polite ki-), and く-る (dictionary ku-). In ちょっと買ってくる, it means 'I'll go buy it and come right back.'

rootFamily.gloss: going and coming back, round trip, social intercourse

くるみ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *kurumi* (胡桃 'walnut'), attested in tenth-century lexicons such as the *Wamyō Ruijushō*; often analyzed as combining *kuro-* ('dark') + *mi* ('nut, fruit') from the dark stain of walnut husks.

history.meaning: walnut
walnut

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 胡桃

くれぐれも.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) reduplicated adverb 呉れ呉れも (kuregure mo), formed by reduplicating the continuative stem of the Old Japanese verb 暮る / 暗る (*kuru* > modern 暮れる *kureru*, 'to grow dark, come to an end, be overwhelmed with emotion') with rendaku (*kure-gure*) plus the inclusive/emphatic particle も (*mo*). In Heian literature, くれぐれ expressed one's heart darkening with deep emotion or doing something over and over until dusk, evolving into 'repeatedly, earnestly, sincerely'.

history.meaning: as dusk falls; with darkened/overwhelmed heart; repeatedly
earnestly, repeatedly, by all means (in cautions and regards)

morphemes.meaning: grow dark, repeat to the end (reduplicated stem of 暮れる)

くれぐれも.notes: Used almost exclusively in earnest warnings, requests, or polite closing regards, such as くれぐれも気をつけて ('Please take the utmost care') or くれぐれもよろしくお伝えください ('Please give them my warmest regards').

rootFamily.gloss: to grow dark, to end (of a day or year)

くれる.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) verb 呉れる, continuing Old Japanese *kuru* ('to give to the speaker or an inferior'). Also used after a *-te* verb (〜てくれる) as the benefactive auxiliary indicating someone does a favor for the speaker.

history.meaning: give; hand over
give (to me/in-group); do as a favor

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 呉れる

くん.etymology: Familiar honorific title suffix 君 (-くん), using the Sino-Japanese *on'yomi* of 君 ('lord, prince, gentleman'). Popularized among late Edo and Meiji students and officials as a camaraderie address term, and now used for boys, male peers, or juniors.

history.meaning: fellow student/statesman address title
familiar title suffix

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 君

ぐ.etymology: Bound Japanese syllable and inflectional ending -ぐ (-gu), primarily representing the dictionary/attributive ending of *ga*-row consonant-stem (*godan*) native Yamato verbs (such as 稼ぐ kasegu 'to earn', 急ぐ isogu 'to hurry', 泳ぐ oyogu 'to swim', 繋ぐ tsunagu 'to connect'), descending from Old Japanese *-gu* (Proto-Japonic prenasalized *-nku*), or the Sino-Japanese morpheme 具 (Middle Chinese *gjuH*, 'tool, implement, furnish').

history.meaning: godan verb stem-final velar / tool, implement, ingredient
verbal termination; tool, gear, ingredient in soup/sushi

ぐ.notes: In morphological segmentation of Japanese subtitles, a standalone ぐ most often arises from verb-stem splitting on *-gu* verbs (whose *-te* form undergoes *i-onbin* nasal voicing to -いで, e.g., 稼ぐ → 稼いで) or the noun 具 ('tool; filling/ingredient').

rootFamily.gloss: to earn money, work for a living

ぐっすり.etymology: Mimetic adverb attested from the Edo period onward, built on the voiced sound-symbolic root *gusu-* + intensive gemination and *-ri* suffix, describing deep, sound, undisturbed sleep ('soundly, fast asleep').

history.meaning: fast asleep; thoroughly
soundly (of sleeping)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ぐっすり

ぐらい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) approximative and degree particle derived via *rendaku* voicing from the noun 位 (kurai, 'rank, court grade, throne, position, degree'), which in turn derives from 座 (kura, 'seat, raised platform, storehouse') + 居 (i, continuative stem of 居る iru 'to sit, occupy'). From 'occupying a specific rank or grade', it grammaticalized into a postpositional particle indicating an approximate quantity, degree, or baseline comparison ('to the degree of, about, at least').

history.meaning: seat occupied; court rank, station, dignity
degree, extent; approximately, about, at least

ぐらい.notes: ぐらい and くらい are largely interchangeable in modern Japanese, though ぐらい with voiced *g-* is slightly more colloquial and heavily favored after demonstratives (これぐらい, それぐらい) and numbers in casual speech. Often expresses 'at least (something that easy/small)': 電話ぐらいしてよ ('At least give me a call!').

rootFamily.gloss: rank, social standing; about, approximately (unvoiced variant)

け.etymology: Polysemous Japanese morpheme: (1) Native Yamato noun and prefix/suffix 気 (ke, from Old Japanese *ke* 'spirit, air, sign, trace, symptom', fused with the Sino-Japanese *kan'on* reading *ke* of 気, Middle Chinese *khjɨjH* 'vital breath, vapor'); and (2) the colloquial sentence-final recollection or question particle け / っけ (from Classical Japanese retrospective auxiliary verb けり *keri*, reduced via *keri > kere > kke / ke*), used when trying to recall something previously known.

history.meaning: visible sign, vapor, spirit / retrospective auxiliary ('it turned out that')
sign, trace, touch of; colloquial recollection particle ('was it...?')

け.notes: As a noun/suffix, 気 (ke) appears in phrases like 火の気 (hi no ke, 'sign of fire/heat') or 味気ない (ajikenai, 'dreary, charmless'); as a sentence-final particle (だっけ / け), it signals trying to jog one's memory ('Wait, what was his name again?').

rootFamily.gloss: dreary, wearisome, lacking charm or flavor
spirit, mind, energy, mood (go-on reading of 気)

けど.etymology: Colloquial conjunctive particle ('but, although, however'), formed in Early Modern Japanese by shortening けれど (itself from the concessive inflection *-keredo* of the classical past/retrospective auxiliary けり).

history.meaning: although it is the case that
but; although; and (topic-framing)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — けど

けやき通り.etymology: Compound street name ('Keyaki Avenue / Zelkova Street'), combining けやき (欅 'Japanese zelkova tree', *Zelkova serrata*, related to けやけし 'conspicuous, striking' for its stately grain and canopy) + 通り (とおり 'street, avenue', stem of 通る 'to pass through').

history.form: けやき (欅) + 通り (とおり)
history.meaning: zelkova-lined avenue
Keyaki Street / Zelkova Avenue

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 欅

けれど.etymology: Conjunctive particle and conjunction ('however, although'), grammaticalized in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese by detaching the concessive form (*izenkei* けれ + concessive particle ど) of classical adjectival and auxiliary inflections.

history.meaning: concessive inflection ('although...')
although; but; however

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — けれど

cognates.meaning: to tow, pull, draw along (牽引)

けん引.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound 牽引 (ken'in), spelled in mixed *mazegaki* script as けん引 because 牽 ('to pull, lead an ox by a rope', Middle Chinese *khen*) was historically outside the Jōyō Kanji list, paired with 引 ('to draw a bow, pull, attract, lead', Middle Chinese *ywinX*). Originally denoting physical traction (towing vehicles or orthopedic traction), it broadened metaphorically into 'pulling an industry or economy forward, acting as the driving force'.

history.meaning: to lead by a rope and pull along
mechanical towing, medical traction; driving/leading a market or movement

morphemes.meaning: pull, haul, lead an ox by a halter (牽, MC *khen)

けん引.notes: Written けん引 in newspapers and subtitles due to press kanji restrictions on 牽. Extremely common in business journalism: 業界をけん引する ('to spearhead/drive the industry'). Pitch accent is flat [0] (けんいん).

rootFamily.gloss: to pull, draw, attract (native wago reading of 引)
leadership, guidance, pulling someone along (shares 引)

げ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) suffix and bound noun 気 (ge, 'seeming, air, appearance, sign'), derived via *rendaku* voicing from Old Japanese *ke* ('outward sign, atmosphere, spirit') and orthographically merged with the voiced *kan'on* reading of 気 (Middle Chinese *khjɨjH*). Attached to adjective stems or verb continuative stems, it creates *na*-adjectives and nouns describing an observable demeanor or impression (e.g., 楽しげ tanoshige 'seeming happy', 怪しげ ayashige 'shady-looking', 意味ありげ imi-arige 'meaningful-looking').

history.meaning: visible sign, outward air or demeanor
seeming, giving the impression of; sign, trace (as in 人気 hitoke/hitoge)

げ.notes: Unlike -そう (which can express pure conjecture or imminent action), -げ specifically describes an outward visual or behavioral vibe projected by a person or thing (e.g., 自信ありげな顔 'a self-assured-looking face').

rootFamily.gloss: meaningful, suggestive, loaded with hidden meaning
rootFamily.word: 意味ありげ (いみありげ)

rootFamily.gloss: what kind of, how (derived from 何 + 気 nanige)

げんまん.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) Edo-period compound 拳万 (genman), formed from 拳 (gen, *kan'on* reading of Middle Chinese *gjwen*, 'fist') + 万 (man, Middle Chinese *mjonH*, 'ten thousand'). Originating in the children's pinky-swear rhyme 指切りげんまん (yubikiri genman, 'finger-cutting and ten thousand fist-punches'), it originally meant 'if you break this promise, you will be struck ten thousand times with a fist', later reanalyzed as a gesture of sealing a pinky promise by bumping fists together.

history.meaning: punishment of ten thousand blows with a fist for breaking a vow
fist-pledge seal accompanying a pinky swear (指切りげんまん)

げんまん.notes: Almost always heard in the famous chant: 指切りげんまん、嘘ついたら針千本飲ます ('Pinky swear, ten thousand punches—if you lie, I'll make you swallow a thousand needles!'). The red-light district version of 指切り involved courtesans literally cutting off a fingertip as proof of devotion.

rootFamily.gloss: fist, clenched hand (native + Sino-Japanese reading of 拳)
martial art of the fist, kung fu / kenpō

こう.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) proximal manner adverb 斯う (kō, 'in this way, thus, like this'), derived via regular historical sound changes from Old Japanese proximal demonstrative root *kə* / *ko* ('this') + adverbial suffix *-ku* (or *-u*): *kaku > ka-u > kau > kō* during the Late Middle Japanese coalescence of *au* to long *ō*. Forms the proximal member of the *ko-so-a-do* manner adverb paradigm alongside そう (sō), ああ (ā), and どう (dō).

history.meaning: in this manner, thus (proximal manner adverb)
like this, in this way, so

こう.notes: Besides literal 'in this way' (こうやって 'doing it like this'), こう is frequently used as a conversational discourse filler when gesturing or searching for the right description ('you know, kind of like...'). Pitch accent is [0] or [1].

rootFamily.gloss: in that way, so (mesial counterpart in ko-so-a-do)
thus, in this way (literary retention of the uncontracted Old Japanese form)
