ご堪能.notes: A classic reading trap: 堪能 is read たんのう when meaning 'enjoy to the fullest' (ご堪能ください, 'please enjoy!'), whereas the conservative reading かんのう survives for 'fluent/proficient' (英語に堪能だ), though たんのう increasingly encroaches there too.

ご夫婦.etymology: Polite noun ('married couple, husband and wife'), formed from honorific prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 夫婦 (ふうふ, from 夫 'husband' + 婦 'wife').

history.meaning: husband and wife
married couple (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご夫婦

ご存じ.etymology: Honorific noun ('knowing, being aware'), formed from prefix ご- + 存じ (continuative stem of the hybrid Sino-Japanese verb 存ずる / 存じる 'to think, know, keep in mind', from Sino-Japanese 存 *zon* 'exist, hold in mind' + する).

history.form: ごぞんじ (御存知・御存じ)
history.meaning: honorable knowledge or awareness
knowing (honorific, in ご存じですか / ご存じの通り)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 御存じ

ご安心.etymology: Polite verbal noun ('peace of mind, relief'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 安心 (あんしん, originally a Buddhist term meaning 'resting the mind in faith', from 安 'peaceful, calm' + 心 'heart, mind').

history.form: 安心 (あんじん / あんしん)
history.meaning: calming the heart; peace of mind
relief; peace of mind (polite, e.g. ご安心ください)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 安心

ご家族.etymology: Polite noun ('someone's family'), formed from honorific prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 家族 (かぞく 'family, household members', from 家 'house, home' + 族 'clan, kin').

history.meaning: family; household
family (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご家族

ご尽力.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) honorific noun combining ご- (御) with じんりょく (尽力, traditional kanji 盡力): 尽 (go-on *zin, Middle Chinese *dzinX, 'to empty a vessel, exhaust completely' — originally depicting a brush scrubbing a dish clean) + 力 (kan-on *ryoku, Middle Chinese *lik, 'sinew, strength, exertion'). Literally 'expending one's entire strength,' prefixed with ご- to honor another party's tireless assistance or advocacy.

history.meaning: to expend the entirety of one's strength
strenuous exertion on behalf of a cause or person
another's dedicated efforts or assistance (formal honorific)

morphemes.meaning: exhaust, use up completely (go-on of 尽/盡, MC *dzinX)
strength, power, effort (kan-on of 力, MC *lik)

ご尽力.notes: Strictly elevate others' efforts with ご尽力 (e.g. ご尽力いただき感謝申し上げます); when pledging your own efforts humbly in business Japanese, use 微力ながら尽くします or 力添え rather than ご尽力.

ご恩.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of honorific ご- (御) and おん (恩, Middle Chinese *?on, 'grace, benevolence, kindness' — phono-semantic character combining 因 'cause/rely upon' over 心 'heart'). Deeply shaped by both Buddhist ethics (四恩, the four great debts of gratitude) and medieval samurai feudalism (御恩と奉公, a lord's grant of land and protection reciprocated by a vassal's loyal service), denoting an enduring moral obligation for kindness received.

history.meaning: benevolence, grace, compassionate favor from above
feudal lord's land grant and patronage owed vassal service
profound debt of gratitude owed to a benefactor

ご恩.notes: Carries far heavier moral weight than casual English 'thanks'—idioms like このご恩は一生忘れません ('I will never forget this debt of gratitude as long as I live') evoke lifelong loyalty in drama and formal speech.

rootFamily.gloss: repaying a kindness or moral debt

cognates.meaning: paying a visit, calling on someone

ご来訪.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) formal honorific combining ご- (御) with らいほう (来訪, traditional 來訪): 来 (on'yomi *rai, Middle Chinese *loj, 'to come, arrive') + 訪 (kan-on *hou, Middle Chinese *phjangH, 'to inquire after, call upon, visit'). Adopted from Literary Chinese epistolary prose, ご来訪 honors the perspective of the host receiving an esteemed guest or client who has taken the trouble to come in person.

history.meaning: to come and call upon someone
formal visit by a guest to one's residence or office
another's visit to one's home, office, or site (honorific)

ご来訪.notes: Directional perspective matters: 来訪 means someone visits *here* (your office/home/website), whereas 訪問 means going *out* to visit someone else—so you thank a guest for ご来訪, never ご訪問, when they come to you.

rootFamily.gloss: coming to a store or restaurant

ご案内.etymology: Polite noun and verbal noun ('guidance, showing around, announcement'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 案内 (あんない, from 案 'desk, document, plan' + 内 'inside contents', which evolved in Heian Japanese from 'contents of a document' to 'prior knowledge of a place' and 'guiding someone').

history.meaning: contents of a matter; inside familiarity; guidance
guiding; showing around; information (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご案内

cognates.meaning: attentive listening of an esteemed audience

ご清聴.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) rhetorical honorific composed of ご- (御) + せいちょう (清聴, traditional 清聽): 清 (kan-on *sei, Middle Chinese *tshjeng, 'pure, clear, unclouded' — used in Classical Chinese courtesy compounds like 清覧 and 清鑑 to treat an addressee's senses as pure and exalted) + 聴 (kan-on *tyou, Middle Chinese *thjeng, 'to listen attentively'). Standardized in modern public speaking as the closing formula thanking an audience for their attention.

history.meaning: the pure, noble hearing of a respected listener
respectful term for an audience's attentive listening
kind attention to a speech or presentation (oratorical formula)

morphemes.meaning: pure, clear — Chinese honorific modifier (清, MC *tshjeng)

ご清聴.notes: Virtually restricted to closing a formal speech or presentation: ご清聴ありがとうございました ('Thank you for your kind attention'). Because 清 already honors the listener, never use 清聴 for your own listening (use 拝聴 instead).

ご無沙汰.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of honorific ご- (御), negative prefix ぶ- (無, go-on variant *bu alongside *mu, Middle Chinese *mju, 'without, lack of'), and さた (沙汰: 沙 *sa, Middle Chinese *srae 'sand' + 汰 *ta, Middle Chinese *thajH 'wash, scour, sift'). In Tang–Song Chinese, 沙汰 meant washing sand to separate gold or grain, hence 'sorting out, selecting'; in medieval Japan 沙汰 came to mean 'official ruling, directive, or tidings,' so ご無沙汰 evolved from 'sending no instructions or word' into a polite apology for being out of touch.

history.meaning: washing away sand to sift out gold or clean grain
neglect of official directives, duties, or correspondence
failing to write, call, or visit for a long time

morphemes.meaning: without, lack of (go-on ぶ of 無, MC *mju)

ご無沙汰.notes: ご無沙汰しております is the gold-standard polite greeting when reconnecting after a long silence; colloquially, 〜はご無沙汰だ can also playfully mean 'it has been ages since I last did X (e.g. dating or drinking).'

rootFamily.gloss: rudeness, lack of courtesy (sharing go-on ぶ-)

ご用意.etymology: Polite noun and verbal noun ('preparation, readiness'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 用意 (ようい, from 用 'use, employ' + 意 'mind, attention', shifting from 'mental attentiveness' to 'preparing in advance').

history.meaning: mental precaution; preparation
preparation; provision (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご用意

ご自分.etymology: Polite reflexive pronoun ('yourself, oneself'), formed from honorific prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 自分 (じぶん 'oneself', from 自 'self' + 分 'portion, status').

history.meaning: oneself; one's own share
yourself; himself/herself (polite reflexive)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご自分

ご苦労さま.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato expression combining honorific ご- (御), Sino-Japanese くろう (苦労: 苦 *ku, Middle Chinese *khuX 'bitter, painful' + 労 *rou, Middle Chinese *law 'toil, labor, exertion'), and native honorific suffix -さま (様 *sama, grammaticalized from the Yamato noun meaning 'appearance, state, direction'). Formed in Early Modern Japanese to acknowledge the hardship and trouble endured by someone carrying out a task or errand.

history.meaning: painful toil and weariness
polite acknowledgment of trouble taken on another's behalf
appreciative formula thanking someone for completing hard work

morphemes.meaning: honorific suffix from native noun 'appearance, state' (様)

ご苦労さま.notes: Crucial workplace etiquette trap: ご苦労さま sounds patronizing (top-down, boss-to-subordinate or customer-to-delivery-driver) and must NEVER be said to a superior—use お疲れさまです with bosses and colleagues instead.

rootFamily.gloss: thank you for your hard work (safe for superiors/peers)
rootFamily.word: お疲れさま (おつかれさま)

ご褒美.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of honorific ご- (御) and ほうび (褒美): 褒 (kan-on *hou, Middle Chinese *paw, 'to praise, commend; wide ceremonial robe bestowed in honor') + 美 (kan-on *bi, Middle Chinese *mijX, 'admirable, fine, extol'). Originally denoting verbal commendation of merit in Chinese and medieval Japanese chronicles, it underwent metonymic shift in Muromachi–Edo samurai administration to denote a tangible grant, money, or gift bestowed alongside praise.

history.meaning: to praise and extol admirable conduct
official commendation, shifting to a material reward from a lord
reward, prize, or indulgent treat for good work

morphemes.meaning: admirable, fine, extol (kan-on of 美, MC *mijX)

ご褒美.notes: Here ご- functions as beautifying speech (美化語) rather than pure deference; modern speakers frequently use 自分へのご褒美 ('a little reward/treat for myself') after finishing hard work.

rootFamily.gloss: to praise, commend (native verb written with 褒)

ご覧.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) honorific noun combining ご- (御) with らん (覧, traditional 覽, Middle Chinese *lamX, 'to survey from above, inspect, behold', composed of 臣 + 見 'eyes looking closely' + 監). Borrowed in Heian court Japanese as the verbal noun base of 御覧ず (goranzu), the suppletive honorific equivalent of 見る ('to see') reserved for emperors and high nobility, and preserved today in ご覧になる ('to look [respectful]') and the gentle directive 〜てごらん ('try looking/doing').

history.meaning: to survey broadly, inspect, peruse
to behold or inspect (imperial/noble honorific verb)
looking, viewing (respectful noun and auxiliary 〜てごらん)

ご覧.notes: Notice the split register: ご覧ください and ご覧になる are high formal keigo for clients and audiences, whereas standalone 〜てごらん (やってごらん, 'give it a try') is warm, parent-to-child or senior-to-junior encouragement.

rootFamily.gloss: a glance; summary list or catalog

ご親切.etymology: Polite adjectival noun ('kindness, goodwill'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 親切 (しんせつ, from 親 'intimate, close' + 切 'earnest, keen,切実', originally meaning 'keenly close and earnest').

history.meaning: keenly close; earnest kindness
kindness; thoughtfulness (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 親切

cognates.meaning: to approve of, endorse, agree with

ご賛同.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) formal honorific formed from ご- (御) + さんどう (賛同, traditional 贊同): 賛 (on'yomi *san, Middle Chinese *tsanH, 'to step forward with shell-money gifts to assist or commend — 先/兟 over 貝') + 同 (go-on *dou, Middle Chinese *duwng, 'same, join together, concur'). Popularized in Meiji parliamentary and civic prose to denote aligning oneself in support of a cause or motion, prefixed with ご- when soliciting or thanking others for endorsement.

history.meaning: to join in assisting or concurring with a view
formal endorsement or concurrence with a proposal
another's approval, endorsement, or backing (respectful)

morphemes.meaning: same, unite, concur (go-on of 同, MC *duwng)

ご賛同.notes: More empathetic and alignment-focused than 賛成 (which can be a dry yes/no vote): ご賛同いただける方 denotes people who genuinely share and rally behind a vision or fundraising appeal.

ご購入.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) commercial honorific combining ご- (御) with こうにゅう (購入): 購 (kan-on *kou, Middle Chinese *kuwH, 'to seek and buy with cowrie/money — 貝 wealth radical + 冓 interlocking frame') + 入 (go-on *nyuu, Middle Chinese *nyip, 'to enter, take in, bring into possession'). Adopted in Meiji commercial and legal usage for formal procurement, with ご- honoring a customer's act of buying.

history.meaning: to buy and bring goods into one's possession
formal acquisition of goods or property by purchase
a customer's purchase (polite commercial honorific)

morphemes.meaning: enter, take in, acquire (go-on of 入, MC *nyip)

ご購入.notes: Standard in written commerce, e-commerce checkouts, and sales pitches (ご購入ありがとうございます), whereas spoken retail clerks at a counter often prefer the softer native-based お買い上げありがとうございます.

ご近所.etymology: Polite noun ('neighborhood, neighbors'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 近所 (きんじょ 'nearby place, neighborhood', from 近 'near' + 所 'place').

history.meaning: nearby place; neighborhood
neighborhood; neighbors (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご近所

ご近所さん.etymology: Warm conversational compound built from the Sino-Japanese prefix ご- (go-, 御), the Sino-Japanese noun 近所 (kinjo, 'neighbourhood, nearby place', from 近 'near' + 所 'place'), and the native polite personal suffix -さん (-san). By wrapping 'neighbourhood' in both an honourific prefix and a personalizing title, the word shifts from an abstract location ('the area nearby') to the friendly people who live next door.

history.meaning: nearby place, vicinity
polite reference to one's neighbourhood
neighbour, folks from the neighbourhood

ご近所さん.notes: Parallel to お隣さん ('next-door neighbour'), ご近所さん evokes warm traditional street-level community life.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご近所

ご迷惑.etymology: Polite noun ('trouble, inconvenience, annoyance'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 迷惑 (めいわく, originally a Buddhist/Chinese compound of 迷 'go astray' + 惑 'be bewildered', which shifted in Early Modern Japanese to 'being troubled or inconvenienced by someone').

history.meaning: bewilderment; perplexity
trouble; inconvenience caused to someone (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ご迷惑

ご選択.etymology: Polite verbal noun ('selection, choice'), formed from prefix ご- + Sino-Japanese 選択 (せんたく, from 選 'choose, select' + 択 'pick out').

history.meaning: choosing; selection
your choice / selection (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 選択

ご都合.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound prefixing honorific ご- (御) to つごう (都合), formed from go-on readings of 都 (*tu, Middle Chinese *tu, 'capital city; gather together, all, in total') and 合 (*gou, Middle Chinese *hop, 'to join, combine, fit together'). In Kamakura–Muromachi documents 都合 was an accounting adverb meaning 'summing up, altogether'; in the Edo period it shifted semantically to 'how matters come together—circumstances, arrangement, convenience,' taking ご- when inquiring respectfully about another's availability.

history.meaning: summing up figures; grand total, altogether
the way circumstances fit together; arrangement or convenience
another's schedule, circumstances, or convenience (respectful)

morphemes.meaning: gather together, in all (go-on of 都, MC *tu)
join, combine, match (go-on of 合, MC *hop)

ご都合.notes: Essential polite scheduling phrase: ご都合はいかがでしょうか ('How does that fit your schedule?'). Note that unprefixed 都合 still retains its medieval 'in total' sense (都合三回, 'three times in all') and the ironic ご都合主義 means 'self-serving opportunism / convenient plot armor.'

rootFamily.word: ご都合主義 (ごつごうしゅぎ)

さ.etymology: Colloquial sentence-final and interjectional particle ('you know, of course, well') that emerged in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese, generally derived from the distal/anaphoric demonstrative adverb さ (然 'so, like that', asserting 'that is how it is').

history.meaning: so; thus
sentence-final particle of light assertion; filler particle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — さ

さあ.etymology: Native Japanese interjection used either to prompt action ('come on!, well now, here we go') or to express hesitant uncertainty ('well..., I'm not sure'), formed by lengthening the deictic/exclamatory syllable さ.

history.meaning: interjection urging action or expressing hesitation
come now!; well, let's see...

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — さあ

さえ.etymology: Focus particle inherited from Old Japanese *sape* (さへ, spelled さへ in historical kana). Originally meaning 'in addition, furthermore' (linked to 添ふ *sopu* 'to add to, accompany'), in Late Middle and Modern Japanese it absorbed the extreme-example function of classical だに ('even').

history.meaning: in addition; on top of that
even; as long as (with conditional)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — さえ

ささげる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb descending from Old and Classical Japanese shimo-nidan ささぐ (捧ぐ, sasagu), phonologically contracted from さし (差し, continuative of 差す sasu, 'to thrust outward, hold out') + あぐ (上ぐ, agu, ancestor of 上げる ageru, 'to lift, raise on high' — via *sasi-agu > *sasagu). Originally describing the physical gesture of lifting an object reverently above eye level with both hands before a kami or sovereign, it broadened to dedicating one's life, heart, or labor to a higher cause.

history.meaning: to hold high overhead with both hands
to present reverently as an offering to a deity or sovereign
to offer up, consecrate, or devote one's life or effort

morphemes.meaning: hold out, extend upward (contracted from 差し)
raise, lift high (from Classical 上ぐ / 上げる)

ささげる.notes: High, solemn register compared to あげる: used for prayers (祈りをささげる), tributes to the deceased, military salutes (捧げ銃), or devoting one's entire life/career to a passion (人生をささげる).

rootFamily.gloss: to lift up; humble verb 'to give'
rootFamily.word: 差し上げる (さしあげる)

さすが.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) adverb and interjection contracted from Old Japanese しかすがに (sikasuga ni, 'even though things are thus; nonetheless'), composed of mesial demonstrative adverb しか ('thus, so') + verb す ('do, be') + adversative/concessive particle がに (*sikasuga > Heian sasuga). Its famous kanji spelling 流石 ('flowing stones') is a witty literary jukujikun/ateji alluding to the Jin Shu (Book of Jin) anecdote of Sun Chu (孫楚), who misspoke 'pillow on streams and rinse one's mouth with stones' (漱石枕流) for 'rinse with streams and pillow on stones' and resourcefully defended the slip—making readers marvel, 'True to his reputation!'

history.meaning: even though it is thus; all the same, nonetheless
admittedly; living up to expectations despite circumstances
as expected; true to one's reputation; indeed!

morphemes.meaning: thus, in that manner (contracted from しか)

さすが.notes: Bare さすが (e.g. さすが社長！ 'Classic boss—just what you'd expect!') is admiring praise, whereas さすがに with a negative or limit (さすがに無理だ, 'Even so, that's going too far') preserves the ancient concessive sense. This same Sun Chu anecdote also inspired Natsume Soseki's pen name 漱石!

rootFamily.gloss: indeed, as expected; even so, admittedly
however, nevertheless (sharing demonstrative root しか)

させる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) causative verb and productive causative auxiliary, representing the modern ichidan outcome of Classical Japanese shimo-nidan causative-honorific -さす (-sasu, attached to vowel-stem and irregular verbs) and specifically the causative of する ('to do': Classical せさす sesasu > Late Middle Japanese さする sasuru > させる saseru). Built on the causative formant *-s- doubled onto the irrealis stem, expressing either coercion ('make someone do') or permission/non-intervention ('let someone do').

history.meaning: cause to do; high court honorific auxiliary (shimo-nidan)

history.form: さする / させる (sasuru / saseru)
history.meaning: make or allow someone to perform an action (shifting to ichidan)
causative of する ('make/let do') and vowel-stem causative suffix

morphemes.meaning: causative/irrealis stem of する ('to do') or thematic *-s-
ichidan causative auxiliary (< Classical せさす / さす)

させる.notes: Context and case particles disambiguate coercion vs. permission, and in polite speech させていただく ('humbly allow oneself to do') is ubiquitous—watch out for 'さ入れ言葉' (inserting an extra さ after consonant-stem verbs like 行かさせる instead of standard 行かせる).

さっき.etymology: Temporal noun and adverb ('a little while ago, just now'), arisen by consonant gemination from さき (先 'earlier, before, a moment ago', inherited from Old Japanese *saki*).

history.meaning: ahead; earlier; previously
a short while ago; just now

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — さっき

さっさと.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) mimetic/ideophonic adverb (gitaigo) formed from the reduplicated and geminated sound-symbolic root さっさ (sassa, depicting crisp, rustling, unhesitating movement—an intensive expansion of the swift-motion mimetic さっと satto) followed by the adverbial quotative particle と (to). Attested widely in Edo-period vernacular fiction and kabuki dialogue for brisk walking or unhesitating execution of an action.

history.meaning: in a sudden gust, swift sweep, or flash of motion
history.stage: Early Middle to Late Middle Japanese

history.meaning: walking or acting briskly without looking back
promptly, briskly, right away without dawdling

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated/geminated mimetic base for brisk, swift motion

さっさと.notes: When directed at someone else in commands (さっさと行け！ 'Get moving already!'), it sounds blunt, impatient, or bossy; when describing your own actions (さっさと終わらせよう, 'Let's knock this out quickly'), it simply conveys efficient briskness.

rootFamily.gloss: quickly, swiftly, in a single stroke
cleanly, refreshingly; not at all (with negative)

さっと.etymology: Mimetic adverb with gemination and quotative/adverbial particle と on a sibilant root *sa-* (attested in Heian/Kamakura texts as さと / さっと), evoking a swift, light, brisk movement, gust, or glance ('quickly, briskly, in a flash').

history.meaning: suddenly; swiftly; with a light rush
quickly; briskly; lightly

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — さっと

さま.etymology: Inherited from Old/Early Middle Japanese *sama* (様 'manner, state, appearance, direction'). From respectful indirect reference to 'the direction or manner of a high personage', it grammaticalized in Late Middle Japanese into the polite honorific title suffix -さま (様).

history.meaning: appearance; manner; direction
way/state; honorific title suffix

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 様

さみしんぼう.etymology: Hybrid native Yamato (wago) and Sino-Japanese colloquialism combining the stem of さみしい (寂しい, an Early Modern labialized *b > *m variant of さびしい sabisii, from Old Japanese さぶし sabusi, 'desolate, cheerless, yearning for company'), a reduced nasal liaison -ん- (< adjectival/genitive particle), and the Sino-Japanese personifying suffix -ぼう (坊, go-on *bou, Middle Chinese *bjang, originally 'monk's cell' -> 'monk' -> 'little boy / fellow characterized by a trait'). Literally 'little lonely-heart fellow.'

history.meaning: desolate, faded, wistfully yearning in solitude
lonely, lonesome (colloquial b > m shift from さびしい)
lonely soul; person who cannot bear being alone

morphemes.meaning: lonely, lonesome (labialized variant of 寂し < OJ さぶし)
nasal liaison connecting adjectival stem to -坊
personifying suffix 'little fellow / one prone to X' (坊, MC *bjang)

さみしんぼう.notes: Choosing さみしんぼう (with み) over さびしんぼう sounds softer, warmer, and more intimate—part of a productive affectionate/teasing -ん坊 family alongside 甘えん坊 ('clingy/spoiled one') and 食いしん坊 ('foodie/glutton').

rootFamily.word: 寂しい (さびしい / さみしい)

rootFamily.gloss: spoiled or clingy person (parallel -ん坊 noun)
rootFamily.word: 甘えん坊 (あまえんぼう)
食いしん坊 (くいしんぼう)

さようなら.etymology: Standard parting greeting ('goodbye, farewell'), shortened in Early Modern Japanese from the conditional transition phrase 左様ならば (*sayō naraba* 'if that is so, that being the case, [I shall take my leave]').

history.form: さやうならば (左様ならば)
history.meaning: if it be so; in that case
farewell; goodbye

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 左様なら

さらけ出す.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) emphatic compound verb joining さらけ (continuative stem of さらける sarakeru, 'to lay bare, empty out completely' — derived within Early Modern vernacular Japanese from the root *sara- shared by 晒す/曝す sarasu 'to bleach in sun and air, expose openly' and さらう sarau 'to sweep clean to the bottom') with the directional auxiliary 出す (だす dasu, 'to bring forth, thrust out'). Conveys flinging hidden secrets, shame, or raw desire completely into the open.

history.meaning: to bleach cloth in water and sun; expose to open air
to empty out completely, turn inside out, lay bare
to bare everything unreservedly—secrets, flaws, or raw truth

morphemes.meaning: lay bare, empty out completely (continuative of さらける)
put out, bring forth into the open (出す)

さらけ出す.notes: A signature thematic verb of *The Naked Director* (全裸監督): 自分をさらけ出す means stripping away social masks and hypocrisy to expose one's unvarnished, vulnerable self on camera or in life.

rootFamily.gloss: to bleach; to expose to the elements or public view
public spectacle, object of public exposure
everything completely, holding nothing back (sharing root さら-)
rootFamily.word: 洗いざらい (あらいざらい)

さらし合う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) reciprocal compound verb formed from さらし (continuative *ren'youkei stem of 晒す / 曝す sarasu, Old Japanese sarasu, 'to wash and bleach cloth under open sun and wind; to expose unshielded to public view') + the reciprocal auxiliary 合う (あう au, Old Japanese apu, 'to meet, join together, act mutually upon one another'). Signifies two or more people mutually exposing their nakedness, secrets, or inner vulnerabilities to each other.

history.meaning: to bleach/expose in open sun + to meet or act together
to expose unshielded to public gaze or shame
to bare or expose things mutually to one another

morphemes.meaning: bleach, weather, expose openly (continuative of 晒す/曝す)
reciprocal auxiliary verb 'do to each other' (合う < OJ あふ)

さらし合う.notes: Productively built with -合う (V-stem + 合う = 'do V to each other'): whereas unilateral 晒す often implies public shaming or doxxing online, reciprocal さらし合う emphasizes mutual vulnerability and holding nothing back from each other.

rootFamily.gloss: to bleach; to expose to the elements or public eye

rootFamily.word: さらけ出す (さらけだす)

rootFamily.gloss: to talk together, discuss mutually (parallel -合う verb)

さらに.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) adverb composed of the Old Japanese nominal root さら (更, sara, 'something new, fresh, untouched, anew' — preserved in まっさら 'brand-new' and さら地 'unbuilt land') + the dative-locative/adverbial particle に (ni). Originally meaning 'in a fresh manner, all over again,' it developed both its dominant additive/comparative sense ('furthermore, even more') and, when paired with a negative predicate, an emphatic negative-polarity sense ('not at all').

history.meaning: anew, afresh, starting over again
all over again; moreover; (with negative) not in the least
furthermore, even more, to a still greater degree

morphemes.meaning: new, fresh, anew (native Yamato root written 更)

さらに.notes: Watch for its two faces: before positives it means 'even more / furthermore' (さらに良くなる), while in formal negative idioms like さらさら〜ない or 驚くにはさらに及ばない it retains its classical 'not in the slightest' sense.

rootFamily.gloss: now after all this time; too late now

される.etymology: Passive voice form of the irregular verb する (suru, 'to do'). Formed by attaching the passive suffix れる (reru) to the irrealis (mizenkei) stem さ (sa) of する.

history.meaning: to do
to be done

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — される

さわる.etymology: Inherited from Early Middle Japanese *sawaru* (触る 'to touch, come into contact with'), originally overlapping with 障る (*sawaru* 'to bump into, hinder, affect'). In Modern Japanese 触る denotes physical touching or feeling with the hand.

history.meaning: come into contact with; brush against
touch; feel

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 触る

さん.etymology: Standard polite title suffix (-さん 'Mr., Ms.') that arose in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese via phonological wear and nasalization of the honorific suffix -さま (様 *sama* > *san*).

polite title suffix

さんしょう漬け.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato culinary compound joining さんしょう (山椒, 'Japanese pepper, Zanthoxylum piperitum' — composed of 山 *san, Middle Chinese *srean 'mountain' + 椒 *syou < *syau, Middle Chinese *tsjew 'prickly-ash peppercorn plant') with づけ (漬け, rendaku-voiced nominalization of native verb 漬ける tukeru, 'to steep, soak, pickle'). Denotes regional preserved dishes (such as福島/Tohoku herring ニシンの山椒漬け or vegetables) pickled in soy-mirin-vinegar brine layered with fragrant sansho leaves or berries.

history.meaning: wild mountain prickly-ash pepper plant
Japanese pepper (Zanthoxylum piperitum), prized spice and preservative
fish or vegetables pickled with aromatic sansho leaves or berries

morphemes.meaning: prickly ash, aromatic peppercorn plant (椒, MC *tsjew)
pickled dish; rendaku nominalization of 漬ける ('soak, pickle')

さんしょう漬け.notes: Notice rendaku voicing (つけ -> づけ) in culinary compounds, and cultural context: ニシンの山椒漬け (herring pickled with sansho leaves) is a famous specialty of Fukushima Prefecture (Aizu), evoking regional home cooking and sake accompaniments.

ざ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) colloquial coalesced particle originating in Early Modern (Edo) vernacular Japanese through phonological fusion (*o + *wa > *a) of the emphatic/deprecatory particle ぞ (zo) + topic particle は (wa, Old Japanese *pa), most commonly appearing after なん (< なんぞは nanzo wa > なんざ nanza / なんざあ nanzaa, 'as for the likes of...'), alongside parallel Edo contractions of negative continuative ず + は (ずは zu wa > ざ / ざあ, 'if not...'). Tokenized in morphological analyzers as a distinct colloquial particle lemma ざ.

history.form: ぞは / ずは (zo wa / zu wa)
history.meaning: emphatic or negative particle sequence followed by topic/conditional は
coalesced Edo vernacular particle ('as for the likes of...' / 'if not...')
rough/colloquial particle bound in なんざ ('the likes of') or dialectal endings

morphemes.meaning: emphatic particle ぞ (or negative ず) fused with following vowel
topic/contrastive particle (< OJ *pa), triggering coalescence to -a

ざ.notes: In gritty Tokyo/working-class dialogue (like *The Naked Director*), you hear this constantly inside なんざ (俺なんざ 'a guy like me', てめえなんざ 'the likes of you'), giving speech a punchy, streetwise Edokko edge compared to textbook なんか or などは.

rootFamily.gloss: the likes of, such a thing as (< なんぞは)
as for this guy (parallel Edo は coalescence < こいつは)

ざっと.etymology: Mimetic and manner adverb with voiced initial *za-* (contrasting with lighter さっと), attested from Late Middle Japanese for the rushing sound of water/wind and by extension doing something roughly, briskly, or in broad strokes ('roughly, briefly, approximately').

history.meaning: with a rush; roughly; in brief
roughly; briefly; approximately

し.etymology: Conjunctive particle ('and, what's more, besides') listing non-exhaustive reasons or qualities. Evolved from the classical continuative/conclusive inflection *-si* (originally the past/perfective auxiliary き's attributive form or adjective stem), grammaticalized as a clause linker by Late Middle Japanese.

history.meaning: emphatic/clause-linking particle
and besides; not only... but also

しか.etymology: Restrictive focus particle used with a negative predicate ('only, nothing but'), evolved in Early Modern Japanese from the comparative particle し (emphatic) + か (question/focus), or from しか ('thus, to that extent', cf. しかじ 'nothing is better than').

history.meaning: nothing beyond; only
only; nothing but (with negative verb)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — しか

しかし.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) adversative conjunction derived by Early Modern clipping from しかしながら (然しながら, sikanagara), itself built on the Old Japanese mesial demonstrative adverb しか (sika, 'thus, like that', from *si- + adverbial *-ka), the emphatic particle し (si), and the concurrent suffix ながら (nagara). Originally meaning 'just as things stand, altogether,' しかしながら shifted via concessive bridging contexts ('while that remains so, nonetheless') to 'however,' and its clipped form しかし became the standard modern conjunction.

history.meaning: just as things are; in their entirety, altogether
while that is true, even so, nevertheless
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: however, but; (interjectionally) still, I must say!

morphemes.meaning: thus, in that way (mesial demonstrative 然 *sika)
emphatic adverbial particle (clipped from 然しながら)

しかし.notes: Neutral-to-formal between Demo/でも (casual) and しかしながら (stiff written/oratorical); in spoken dialogue, sentence-initial しかし… followed by a pause often expresses astonished musing ('Still, I gotta say...!') rather than logical contrast.

rootFamily.gloss: as expected (< しかすがに, sharing demonstrative root しか)
so it is, indeed (literary verb from しか + あり)

しかも.etymology: Conjunctive adverb ('moreover, furthermore, and yet'), formed in Old and Early Middle Japanese from the anaphoric adverb しか (然 'so, thus') + inclusive/concessive particle も ('even, also'), literally 'even while being so'.

history.meaning: even so; and furthermore
moreover; what is more; and yet

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 然も

しすぎる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb uniting し (continuative *ren'youkei stem of irregular verb する suru, Classical す su, 'to do') with the auxiliary verb すぎる (過ぎる sugiru, modern ichidan descendant of Old and Classical Japanese kami-nidan すぐ sugu, 'to pass through, cross beyond, exceed a boundary'). Exemplifies Japanese's productive V-stem + 過ぎる construction denoting action carried beyond proper or healthy limits.

history.meaning: to pass by, cross over, exceed a proper measure (kami-nidan)

history.form: し過ぐ / し過ぎる (sisugu / sisugiru)

to overdo, do too much

auxiliary verb 'exceed, go too far' (過ぎる < Classical すぐ)

rootFamily.gloss: to go too far, overdo (colloquial counterpart)
to say too much, go too far in speaking
rootFamily.word: 言いすぎる (いいすぎる)

しっかり.etymology: Mimetic adverb formed on the root *shika-* (seen in しかと 'firmly, certainly', attested since Early Middle Japanese) with consonant gemination and the adverbial suffix *-ri*, meaning 'firmly, tightly, reliably, steadily'.

history.meaning: firmly; reliably; clearly
firmly; tightly; reliably; soundly

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — しっかり

している.etymology: The term 'している' (meaning 'doing') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: doing
doing

している.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — している

してやる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) directional-benefactive verbal expression combining して (continuative し of する 'to do' + conjunctive particle て te) with the auxiliary verb やる (遣る yaru, Old Japanese yaru, 'to send away, dispatch outward, bestow downward'). Grammaticalized in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese as the outward/downward benefactive auxiliary ('do for an inferior, child, or animal'), and by pragmatic extension developed a defiant or triumphant malefactive nuance ('do something *to* someone / show them what I can do!').

history.meaning: to send off, dispatch outward, propel away
to perform an action directed toward a recipient or subordinate
to do for a subordinate/intimate, or defiantly pull off against a rival

morphemes.meaning: continuative stem of する ('to do')
conjunctive particle linking action and auxiliary
outward/downward benefactive or defiant auxiliary (遣る)

してやる.notes: Dual-edged pragmatics: 餌をしてやる / やってやる can be rough affection toward pets or kids, while 絶対成功してやる！ ('I'll pull it off and show them!') expresses fierce underdog determination, and the passive してやられた！ idiomatically means 'They totally outsmarted/got me!'

rootFamily.gloss: to do for someone (polite upward/equal counterpart)
to be outwitted, tricked, or gotten the better of

しばらく.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) temporal adverb attested in Old Japanese as *simasi* and *simaraku*, derived from an ancient temporal root *sima* ("brief interval, short span") extended with the adverbializing nominal suffix *-raku* (compare *osoraku*). During the Heian and Kamakura periods, bilabial nasal assimilation shifted intervocalic *-m-* to *-b-* (*simaraku* > *sibaraku*), yielding modern *shibaraku* (orthographically matched via *kundoku* to kanji 暫く).

history.meaning: for a brief interval, for a little while
for a short time, temporarily; after some delay
for a while, for the time being; a good while (in greetings)

しばらく.notes: Exhibits polar temporal nuance depending on context: "just a moment" in requests (*shibaraku omachi kudasai*) versus "a long time" in reunion greetings (*shibaraku desu ne*, "it's been a while!").

しまう.etymology: Inherited from Late Middle / Early Modern Japanese 仕舞う・終う (*simapu* 'to bring to an end, finish, put away'), originally derived from 仕舞 (*simai* 'performing a dance / finishing a task'). After a *-te* verb (〜てしまう), it functions as an aspectual auxiliary of completion or regrettable outcome.

history.meaning: finish; put away in storage
finish; put away; end up doing (~てしまう)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 仕舞う

しゃ.etymology: Colloquial native (*wago*) particle contraction arising via palatalization (*拗音化*) of the sequence *shi* + topic/emphatic coefficient particle *wa* (*しは* > *shiwa* > *sha*), especially before negative predicates as in *ありはしない* / *しはしない* > *しゃしない*, and in rapid casual speech as a voiceless sibilant fusion parallel to *-ては* > *-ちゃ*. It condenses emphatic contrast or conditional framing into a single clipped syllable.

history.meaning: doing (at least) [emphatic verbal stem + topic particle]
emphatic/conditional contracted particle (as in しゃしない)

morphemes.meaning: continuative ending -shi (from する or s-stem verbs)

しゃ.notes: Most commonly heard in gritty spoken idioms like *ありゃしない* / *できゃしない* / *ししゃしない* ("not a chance I'd do it") or rough dialectal conditionals; distinctly informal and blunt.

しょ.etymology: Colloquial sentence-final particle formed by aphetic clipping of the polite presumptive copula *でしょう* (*deshō* > *desho* > *sho* / *-ssho*). Popularized originally in Hokkaido regional speech (*北海道方言*) during the twentieth century and subsequently diffused nationwide through Tokyo youth, nightlife, and media slang as a breezy tag seeking confirmation.

history.meaning: it probably is; right? (polite conjectural copula)
right?, isn't it? (shortened conversational tag)
right?, yeah? (casual confirmation particle)

morphemes.meaning: aphetic clipped form of でしょ (< でしょう)

しょ.notes: Frequently preceded by a geminate glottal stop (*いいっしょ*, *そうっしょ*); conveys casual camaraderie or playful insistence, heavily favored in informal street, industry, and youth dialogue.

しょうが.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) botanical and culinary noun しょうが (生姜), borrowed from Middle Chinese *sˠæŋ kɨɐŋ* (生 "raw, fresh, undried" + 薑/姜 "ginger rhizome", originally distinguishing fresh root from 乾薑 "dried medicinal ginger"). Attested in Heian herbal glossaries as *seikau* / *shōkau*, whose final velar nasal/diphthong underwent irregular phonological erosion and vowel lowering (*shōkau* > *shōga*), obscuring its Sino-Japanese origin.

history.meaning: fresh, undried ginger root (contrasted with dried medicinal ginger)

history.form: せうかう / しゃうが (shōkau > shōga)
history.meaning: fresh ginger root used in medicine and seasoning
ginger (Zingiber officinale)

しょうが.notes: Do not confuse the culinary noun 生姜 (*shōga*, accentless/heiban) with the homophonous sequence 仕様が (*shō ga*, "way/method + subject marker") inside *shō ga nai* ("it can't be helped").

rootFamily.word: 生姜焼き (しょうがやき)

cognates.meaning: soy (borrowed via Dutch soya from Japanese shōyu)

しょう油.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound 醤油 (partially rendered as *まぜ書き* しょう油), combining 醤 (MC *tɕɨɐŋH*, "fermented grain, bean, or meat paste", Japanese *hishio*) + 油 (MC *jɨu*, "oil, liquid extract"). Coined or popularized in Late Muromachi Japan (first recorded in the 1597 *Ekirinbon Setsuyōshū*) for the dark savory liquid pressed from fermented soybean-wheat mash (*moromi*), likened in sheen and viscosity to oil. Through VOC Dutch *soya*, Japanese *shōyu* also gave English the word *soy*.

history.meaning: fermented soybean or grain paste seasoning

history.form: しゃうゆ (醬油, shauyu > shōyu)
history.meaning: liquid condiment pressed from fermented soy-wheat mash
soy sauce

しょう油.notes: Written しょう油 in everyday menus and subtitles because 醤 was historically outside the core *Jōyō kanji* table until 2010; Japanese *shōyu* is the ultimate ancestor of English *soy*.

しょっぱい.etymology: Eastern and standard colloquial adjective ('salty'), contracted in Early Modern Japanese from 塩っぱい (*shioppai*), a compound of 塩 (しお 'salt') + adjectival suffix -っぱい ('full of the taste/quality of', from 一杯 *ippai*).

history.meaning: tasting strongly of salt
salty; briny

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 塩っぱい

しれない.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for might; may. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: might; may

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — しれない

しれる.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) verb 知れる, continuing Early Middle Japanese *siru* ('to become known, come to light'), the spontaneous/potential counterpart of 知る ('to know'). Preserved in modern expressions like かもしれない ('might be').

history.meaning: become known; be recognized
become known; be possible to know

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 知れる

じ.etymology: Continuative stem (*連用形*) and morphological base of the voiced verbalizing verb *-じる* (*-jiru*, classical *sa*-row irregular *-ずる* *-zuru*), derived via *rendaku* (sequential voicing) from the native Yamato light verb *す* (*su*, modern *suru*, "to do"). Attached to single-kanji Sino-Japanese (*kango*) roots ending in nasal *-n* or long vowels (e.g., 信じる, 感じる, 演じる, 応じる), *su* voiced to *zu* in Heian Japanese and reanalyzed into a regular *kami-ichidan* verb *jiru* (stem *ji*) from the Muromachi–Edo periods onward.

history.meaning: to enact or feel [voiced verbalizer after nasal/long kango stems]
shift from irregular z-conjugation to upper-monograde ichidan verb
productive bound verb stem forming Sino-Japanese verbs

morphemes.meaning: voiced ichidan verbalizer (< ずる < す 'to do')

じ.notes: Tokenizers frequently isolate *じ* (lemma *じる* / *じ*) in compounds like *応じ* (*ōji*, "responding") or *演じ* (*enji*, "performing"); literary style occasionally retains classical *-ずる* (e.g., *信ずる*).

じっと.etymology: Mimetic adverb attested from Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese, describing unmoving concentration, stillness, or patient endurance ('motionlessly, fixedly, patiently').

history.meaning: fixedly; without moving; steadily
still; fixedly (staring or waiting)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — じっと

じゃ.etymology: Colloquial discourse conjunction contracted from *では* (*de wa*, locative/instrumental particle *で* + topic particle *は*, literally "in [that] case / with [that] being so"). history.meaning: being in that situation; as for therein
if that is the case; well then
well then, alright then, see you (casual conjunction)

じゃ.notes: Ubiquitous in spoken Japanese to pivot into action ("Alright then...") or wrap up a conversation (*ja, mata*, "well, see ya"); switch to *de wa* or *sore de wa* in formal speeches and business writing.

じゃあ.etymology: Colloquial conjunction and discourse transition marker ('well then, in that case, if so'), contracted in Edo-period eastern Japanese from では (*de wa* > *jaa*), itself composed of copular/locative で + topic particle は.

history.meaning: in that case; well then
well then; if so; bye then

じゃあね.etymology: Casual parting greeting ('see you, bye then'), formed from the conversational transition marker じゃあ ('well then') + sentence-final rapport particle ね.

history.meaning: see you!; bye for now

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — じゃあ

じゅう.etymology: Sino-Japanese suffix 中 (-じゅう 'throughout, all over, during the entire'), voiced via rendaku from ちゅう (Middle Chinese *trjuwng* 'middle, inside, throughout'). Also represents the Sino-Japanese numeral 十 (じゅう 'ten').

throughout (all day, all over town)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中

short causative/verbal ending

すいません.etymology: Colloquial phonological reduction of *すみません* (*sumimasen*, polite negative of native Yamato *済む* *sumu*, "to be settled, come to a clean end", plus polite auxiliary *-ます* + negative *-ん* < *-ぬ*). Originating in Edo merchant phrasing meaning "my debt/imposition toward you is not settled," rapid casual speech elided the bilabial nasal between high vowels (*sumimasen* > *suimasen*), establishing Japan's everyday spoken formula for apologies, requests, and gratitude.

history.form: すまぬ / すみませぬ (sumanu / sumimasenu)
history.meaning: (my obligation/account) is not yet settled or cleared
I am sorry; excuse me; thank you for the trouble
excuse me; sorry; thanks (colloquial spoken variant)

morphemes.meaning: reduced stem of 済む (sumi- > sui-, 'to be settled')

すいません.notes: Extremely natural in everyday conversation across all ages, though strict business etiquette and formal written correspondence require restoring the unreduced spelling *すみません* (or *申し訳ありません*).

rootFamily.word: すみません (済みません)

すか.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) colloquial and underworld slang noun スカ (*suka*), derived from the verbal root *すく* (*suku*, 透く / 空く, "to have a gap, be empty, let air pass through") plus the nominalizing state suffix *-a* (compare *すかす* *sukasu*, "to whiff, dodge, leave empty-handed"). Originally referring to missing a strike or drawing a blank lottery slip, it flourished in Shōwa street, gambling, and adult-video industry jargon for a "dud," "rip-off," or hyped product devoid of promised substance.

history.meaning: to leave a gap; to make someone miss their mark or whiff
missing a blow; a blank ticket in a draw or gamble
dud, flop, disappointment, rip-off (especially hyped media/bets)

morphemes.meaning: empty, hollow, gapped (stem of 空く/透く)

すか.notes: Central to 1980s Shōwa adult-entertainment and gambling slang: *スカを食う* ("to get burned by a dud / draw a blank") describes paying for hyped goods that fail to deliver.

rootFamily.gloss: to whiff, dodge, give someone the slip

すぎる.etymology: Upper bigrade (now ichidan) verb 過ぎる, continuing Old Japanese *sugu* ('to pass by, pass through, elapse, exceed'). Attached to verb stems and adjective roots, it functions as the productive suffix meaning 'too much, excessively'.

history.meaning: pass by; elapse; exceed
pass by; exceed; be too ...

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 過ぎる

cognates.meaning: to become empty, hungry; to like

すく.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) *godan* verb attested since Old Japanese (*Man'yōshū*) along two major semantic tracks: (1) 空く / 透く (*suku*, "for spaces to open up, become sparse, uncrowded, or empty," whence *おなかがすく* "stomach becomes empty/hungry"), and (2) 好く (*suku*, "to incline strongly toward, fancy, feel attraction for"). Both descend from Old Japanese consonantal stem *suk-*, with some philologists linking 好く to a heart opening space toward an object of desire, though synchronically distinct.
