たらふく.etymology: Early Modern Edo colloquial adverb meaning 'to full satiety, to one's heart's content'. Most plausibly reanalyzed from the native verb stem tarafu (足らふ, 'to be fully sufficient, be sated', iterative of taru 足る 'to suffice') blended with or reshaped via popular etymology into the ateji compound 鱈腹: native tara (鱈, 'codfish', notorious for its gluttonous appetite and bulging stomach) + Sino-Japanese fuku (腹, Middle Chinese *pjuwk, 'belly, abdomen').

history.meaning: to be completely sufficient, abundant, or satisfied
until one's belly is stuffed; to one's heart's content

morphemes.meaning: sufficiency (< 足らふ) reanalyzed as codfish (鱈)

たらふく.notes: Predominantly collocates with eating and drinking (たらふく食う / 飲む 'eat/drink till stuffed'), carrying a hearty, earthy register suited to celebratory feasts or tavern talk.

たり.etymology: The term 'たり' (meaning 'even') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: even
even

たり.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — たり

だ.etymology: Plain copula formed by phonological contraction of である to であ and then だ during the Muromachi period, especially in eastern Japanese speech (with cited examples from 1473 onward).

history.meaning: to be (copular phrase)
to be
plain copula

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だ

だい.etymology: Colloquial interrogative sentence-final particle ('what is it?, who is it?'), contracted in Early Modern eastern Japanese from だ ('copula') + い (emphatic sentence-final particle); or the Sino-Japanese noun 台 (だい 'stand, platform, counter for machines').

history.form: だい (だ + い) / 台 (だい)
history.meaning: emphatic question copula; stand/base
colloquial question marker; stand/counter

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だい

だから.etymology: Causal conjunction ('therefore, so, that's why'), formed in Early Modern Japanese by combining the plain copula だ ('it is') + causal conjunctive particle から ('because, since').

history.meaning: because it is so; therefore; so

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だから

だけ.etymology: Restrictive and degree particle ('only, just, as much as'), grammaticalized in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese from the native noun 丈 (たけ 'stature, height, full measure, length'). From 'to the full height/extent of', it came to mark a bounded limit ('only').

history.meaning: height; stature; full extent
to the extent of; only; just

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 丈

だけど.etymology: Colloquial Japanese adversative conjunction formed by fusing the plain non-past copula da (だ, an Eastern Japanese contraction of de aru である < Classical ni te ari にてあり) with the concessive conjunctive particle kedo (けど, truncated from keredomo けれども, which originally joined the realis izenkei ending -kere of adjectival auxiliaries with concessive domo ども). Used sentence-initially as an independent connector ('however; even so').

history.form: にてありけれども (nite arikeredomo)
history.meaning: although it is the case that

history.form: だけれども > だけど (dakedo)
history.meaning: however; though; be that as it may

だけど.notes: More conversational than しかし and slightly softer than でも; placed between clauses (好きだけど高い) or at the start of a new turn to gently pivot or push back.

rootFamily.gloss: fuller, slightly more formal variant: however

だし.etymology: Deverbal noun from the continuative stem (出し dashi) of the native transitive verb 出す (dasu, 'to draw out, extract, bring forth'), an abbreviation of 出し汁 (dashijiru, 'extracted broth'). In Japanese culinary history from the Muromachi period onward, だし referred to simmering kelp (昆布), dried bonito (鰹節), or dried mushrooms in hot water to draw out their savory umami compounds into a clear cooking stock.

history.meaning: broth obtained by extracting flavor in hot water
culinary soup stock
dashi; savory broth or soup stock

morphemes.meaning: extraction; drawing out (stem of 出す)

だし.notes: Often written in hiragana (だし) or with the ateji compound 出汁 ('extracted broth').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だし

だったら.etymology: Colloquial Japanese conditional conjunction representing the lexicalized -tara conditional form of the plain copula da (だ). Historically contracted from de attara (であったら < Classical ni te aritaraba にてありたらば, 'if it has come to be the case'), where de aru syncopated to datt- before the conditional suffix -tara. Bridges a partner's statement to a logical consequence ('if that's the case; then').

history.meaning: if it should be the case that

history.form: であったら > だったら (dattara)
history.meaning: if so; in that case; well then

morphemes.meaning: past/geminate stem of copula da (< de att-)

だったら.notes: Often opens a snappy counter-proposal in dialogue (だったら俺が行くよ 'In that case, I'll go!'), directly picking up on whatever premise the other speaker just stated.

rootFamily.gloss: more formal conditional: if that is the case

だって.etymology: Colloquial conjunction ('but, because, after all') and concessive focus particle ('even, too'), contracted in Edo-period Japanese from だとて (*da tote* 'even if you say it is so'), combining copula だ + quotative-concessive とて.

history.meaning: even if one says it is
but; after all; even; also

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だって

だと.etymology: Combination of copula だ (da) and particle と (to). Can function conditionally ('if it is...') or quotatively ('[says/thinks] that it is...').

history.meaning: is + that/if

だと.notes: Context determines if it is the conditional 'to' or quotative 'to'.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だと

だめ.etymology: Originated as the Go board-game term 駄目 (だめ 'neutral intersections between territories that yield no points for either player', combining 駄 'worthless, mere' + 目 'board intersection/point'). In Edo-period colloquial speech it generalized to 'useless, no good, forbidden'.

history.meaning: neutral/pointless intersection on a Go board
no good; useless; not allowed

morphemes.meaning: grid point on a Go board

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 駄目

だよ.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for it is (emphatic).

history.meaning: it is (emphatic)

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だよ

だらけ.etymology: Suffix (-だらけ 'covered in, full of, riddled with [something unwanted]'), attested from Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese (e.g. 血だらけ 'covered in blood'); often linked to a nominalization of *daraku / darakeru* ('to drip, sprawl messily') or classical *tare-* ('dripping').

history.meaning: smeared or covered all over with
full of; covered with (dust, mistakes, etc.)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だらけ

ちくしょう.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed via Buddhist Chinese 畜生 (Middle Chinese *thriwk sraeng), uniting 畜 (*thriwk, 'domesticated animal, livestock raised by humans') and 生 (*sraeng, 'living creature, birth'). Originally a Buddhist technical term translating Sanskrit tiryagyoni ('the realm of beasts', one of the Three Evil Paths of rebirth characterized by ignorance and base instinct), it underwent pragmatic bleaching in Edo-period vernacular into a general cry of frustration ('damn it!; son of a bitch!').

history.meaning: beasts; rebirth in the subhuman animal realm
brute, bastard; 'damn it!' (expletive of rage or regret)

ちくしょう.notes: Frequently intensified with prefix こん- (< この 'this') as こんちくしょう! ('Goddamn it!'); unlike English profanity, it vents frustration at fate as readily as hostility at a person.

ちまう.etymology: Colloquial spoken auxiliary verb contracted from the native conjunctive sequence -te shimau (てしまう, conjunctive particle -te + aspectual auxiliary shimau 仕舞う 'to finish completely, do irrevocably or regrettably'). Through syncope of the vowel -e- and affrication/palatalization of t + sh into ch, -te shimau fused into -chimau (and after voiced -de into -jimau), preserving the labial nasal -m- lost in the softer variant -chau.

history.meaning: to bring an action to completion
to end up doing; to get something over and done with

morphemes.meaning: coalesced conjunctive -te + initial sh- of shimau

ちまう.notes: Carries a rougher, streetwise, traditionally masculine Kantō flavor compared to gender-neutral ちゃう (e.g., 忘れちまった 'I clean forgot' vs. 忘れちゃった); voices to じまう after ん/ग/b/m stems (死んじまう).

rootFamily.gloss: uncontracted auxiliary: to finish; to end up doing

ちゃ.etymology: Colloquial contracted particle combo resulting from the rapid-speech coalescence of the native conjunctive particle -te (て) with the topic/conditional particle wa (は): -te wa > -tya > -cha (parallel to voiced -de wa > -ja じゃ). Primarily introduces an undesirable condition before a negative or evaluative predicate (e.g., 言っちゃだめ 'you mustn't say it'), where -te wa grammaticalized as a negative-conditional topic marker.

history.meaning: if/when doing (as topic of evaluation)
colloquial conditional-topic fusion ('if one does...')

ちゃ.notes: Mandatory in natural spoken deontic expressions: 食べちゃいけない ('mustn't eat') and なくちゃ (< なくては 'have to'); voices to じゃ after -de (飲んじゃだめ).

ちゃう.etymology: Ubiquitous colloquial Japanese aspectual auxiliary verb arising via two-stage phonological reduction of -te shimau (てしまう, conjunctive -te + completive/regrettable auxiliary shimau 仕舞う 'to put away, conclude'). Following affrication of t + sh (-te shimau > -chimau), intervocalic -m- elided and the resulting hiatus coalesced (-chimau > -chau), yielding a fully regular godan auxiliary paradigm (ちゃった, ちゃおう, ちゃえば).

history.meaning: to finish doing; to put an end to
to do completely, inadvertently, or regrettably

morphemes.meaning: fused conjunctive -te + palatalized sh- of shimau

ちゃう.notes: Expresses either total completion (全部食べちゃった 'ate it all up!') or unintended/regrettable outcome (壊れちゃった 'it broke on me'); voices to じゃう after voiced -de forms (飲んじゃう).

rootFamily.gloss: full auxiliary verb: to finish, end up doing

ちゃん.etymology: Affectionate diminutive title suffix (-ちゃん), which arose in Edo-period children's and familial speech by palatalization of the polite suffix -さん (*-san* > *-chan*).

history.meaning: affectionate childish pronunciation of -san
endearing title suffix

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ちゃん

ちゃんと.etymology: Mimetic and manner adverb attested from the Edo period, originally imitating the crisp metallic chime or click of objects fitting into place, and hence meaning 'properly, neatly, punctual and in good order'.

history.meaning: promptly; neatly in place; properly
properly; neatly; reliably

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ちゃんと

ちゅ.etymology: Colloquial spoken quotative/attributive particle shortened from chū (ちゅう), itself the palatalized phonological fusion of the native quotative phrase to iu (という, quotative particle to と + verb iu 言う 'to say, call': to iu > tiu > chū > chu). Common in fast, earthy regional and working-class dialogue (often geminated as っちゅ / っちゅう) to link clauses or gloss a noun ('called; meaning; that').

history.meaning: which is called; saying that
colloquial quotative/attributive linker ('that; so-called')

morphemes.meaning: to say, call (< iu, coalesced via palatalization)

ちゅ.notes: In rapid dialogue, ちゅ / ちゅう (e.g., ちゅうか 'or rather; I mean') competes with Kantō depalatalized つー; homophonous in casual speech with the mimetic particle ちゅっ ('smooch/kiss').

ちょうだい.etymology: Colloquial request word ('please give me; please do') and humble verbal noun 頂戴 (ちょうだい), a Sino-Japanese compound of 頂 ('crown of the head') + 戴 ('carry on the head'), calquing the native gesture いただく ('raise a gift to the forehead when receiving').

history.meaning: humbly receiving on the crown of the head
humbly receive; 'please give me / please do'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 頂戴

ちょうちん.etymology: Borrowed in the Muromachi period from late Middle / early Mandarin Chinese *tiāodēng* (提灯 'portable hanging paper lantern', combining 提 'carry in the hand' + 灯 'lamp, lantern'), using the *tō-on* (Tang/Song–Ming) pronunciation.

history.meaning: portable collapsible paper lantern
paper lantern

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 提灯

ちょうど.etymology: Originally a Late Heian / Kamakura mimetic adverb ちやうど / ちやうと imitating the solid impact of a blow or two objects meeting squarely ('squarely, right on target'). By Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese it shifted to 'precisely, exactly, just'.

history.meaning: squarely; with a direct hit
exactly; just; right on time

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 丁度

ちょっと.etymology: Evolved in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese by palatalization and consonant gemination from ちと ('a little bit, briefly', cf. ちっと), describing a small amount, a brief moment, or a polite attention-getter ('just a moment, a little').

history.meaning: slightly; a little; briefly
a little; for a moment; excuse me

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一寸

ちょっとした.etymology: Lexicalized prenominal determiner (rentaishi) formed from the Early Modern colloquial degree adverb chotto (ちょっと, 'a little, briefly', geminated and palatalized from Late Middle Japanese chito ちと / chitto ちっと 'slightly') plus shita (した), the adnominal past/stative form of suru (する, 'to do, possess an attribute'). Literally 'slightly-styled', it developed an intriguing dual sense: both 'minor, casual' and via litotes 'quite impressive, not half bad'.

history.meaning: a tiny bit; momentarily
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: slight, trifling; conversely, fairly notable or decent

morphemes.meaning: having the quality of (past adnominal of suru)

ちょっとした.notes: Context flips its polarity via understatement: ちょっとしたミス means 'a minor slip-up', whereas ちょっとした有名人 means 'something of a local celebrity / quite famous'.

rootFamily.gloss: a little, for a moment; hey!

ちる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive godan verb inherited directly from Old Japanese tiru (< Proto-Japonic *tiru), designating the dispersal or falling away of clustered small entities—paradigmatically cherry blossoms, autumn leaves, sparks, clouds, or concentrated attention. Forms a classic transitivity pair with transitive chirasu (散らす, 'to scatter, strew') and stative-resultative chirakaru (散らかる, 'to lie cluttered').

history.meaning: to fall and scatter (of blossoms, leaves, crowds)
to scatter, disperse, fade away, die nobly

ちる.notes: Central to classical Japanese aesthetics of impermanence (桜が散る 'cherry blossoms fall'), while 気が散る ('one's mind scatters') is the everyday idiom for getting distracted.

っけ.etymology: Colloquial retrospective and recall sentence-final particle (-っけ 'wasn't it?, what was it again?'), descended from the classical past/retrospective auxiliary けり (*-keri*, via eastern/colloquial *-kke*).

history.meaning: retrospective and realization auxiliary
particle of trying to recall ('what was it again?')

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — っけ

っす.etymology: Colloquial polite sentence-final copula and suffix produced by apheresis and consonantal gemination of the standard polite copula desu (です): loss of initial de- leaves a moraic sibilant onset (-ssu), attaching directly to nouns, adjectives, and plain verb forms (e.g., そうっす < そうです, 行くっす). Popularized in athletic hierarchies (taiikukai-kei) and working-class male speech to blend casual camaraderie with deferential politeness.

history.meaning: polite declarative copula
casual-deferential contracted copula/politeness marker

っす.notes: Hallmark of junior-to-senior male banter (了解っす! 'Got it, boss!'); unlike standard です, speakers casually attach っす directly after plain verbs (やるっす), though prescriptivists frown on it in formal business.

って.etymology: Colloquial quotative and topic-introducing particle ('that, called, speaking of'), contracted in Early Modern Japanese from とて (*tote* 'saying that') and といって (*to itte* 'saying that').

history.meaning: saying that; called
quotative and topic particle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — って

っと.etymology: Colloquial expressive particle formed by prefixing a glottal stop (sokuon っ) to the native quotative/manner particle to (と, Old Japanese tö). Used at the end of a brief self-directed utterance, physical heave, or mental checklist item, framing one's own movement or fleeting thought as a brisk, self-contained action ('there we go; alrighty; let's see now').

history.meaning: quotative and manner-marking particle
brisk self-addressed particle accompanying an action or pause

morphemes.meaning: expressive glottal catch adding crisp closure

っと.notes: Constantly heard in involuntary vocalizations like よいしょっと (grunting while sitting/lifting), さてっと ('well then, let's get to it'), or えーっと ('let's see, umm').

つ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *-tu*, the native Japanese numeral classifier suffix attached to the native numbers 1 through 9 (ひとつ, ふたつ ... ここのつ) and いくつ; also an archaic genitive particle ('of', preserved in まつげ 'eyelash', みなと 'harbor').

history.meaning: native general counter suffix; archaic genitive particle
counter suffix in ひとつ–ここのつ

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — つ

ついに.etymology: Inherited from Early Middle Japanese *tupini* (遂に・終に 'in the end, at last; (with negative) never'), formed from the noun つひ (*tupi* 'end, final limit, completion', related to 潰ゆ / 尽く) + adverbial particle に.

history.meaning: until the end; finally; (with negative) never
finally; at last; in the end

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 遂に

cognates.meaning: to pass through; expert, authority (e.g. 日本通)
passing through; expert conversant in a field

つう.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) single-character noun from 通 (Middle Chinese *thuwng, 'to pass all the way through, penetrate unobstructed, communicate, know thoroughly'). During the mid-to-late Edo period (18th century), urban townspeople elevated 通 (tsū) into an aesthetic ideal denoting a worldly aficionado or connoisseur possessing effortless insider mastery of pleasure-quarter manners, gastronomy, or specialized arts.

history.meaning: penetration; unimpeded passage; mastery of doctrine
refined Edo connoisseur; aficionado or insider expert

つう.notes: Works both standalone (あの人は通だ 'he's a true connoisseur') and as a productive suffix (映画通 'film buff', 事情通 'well-informed insider'); contrast 半可通 ('pretentious know-it-all').

rootFamily.gloss: well-informed insider privy to behind-the-scenes facts
native reading of 通: to commute, frequent, pass through

つかまる.etymology: Intransitive verb 捕まる・掴まる ('to be caught; to hold on tightly to'), paired with 掴む (*tukamu* 'to grasp, seize') and 捕まえる (*tukamaeru* 'to catch, arrest'), attested from Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese.

history.form: つかまる (捕まる・掴まる)
history.meaning: be caught; cling/hold fast to
hold on to; be caught

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 捕まる

つきあう.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan compound verb joining tsuki- (付き), the conjunctive (ren'yōkei) stem of tsuku (付く, Old Japanese tuku 'to adhere, attach oneself to, accompany'), with the reciprocal/mutual verb au (合う, Old Japanese apu 'to meet, do together'). From literally 'attaching to one another / accompanying reciprocally', its senses broadened to socializing over drinks,humoring someone's errands, doing business together, and romantic dating.

history.meaning: to come into contact; to associate or keep company with
to socialize, go along with someone, or date romantically

morphemes.meaning: attach, stick close to, accompany (ren'yōkei of 付く)

つきあう.notes: Crucial cultural keyword: 付き合いで飲む means drinking out of social obligation to colleagues, whereas 彼女と付き合っている means 'going out / in a relationship with her'.

rootFamily.gloss: to attach, stick to, attend upon
to talk things over mutually (stem + au)

つぎ込む.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan compound verb formed from tsugi- (注ぎ), the conjunctive (ren'yōkei) stem of tsugu (注ぐ, 'to pour liquid into a receptacle', cognate with or reinforced by 継ぐ 'to add continuously'), plus the directional-intensive auxiliary verb komu (込む, 'to enter deeply, pack inward'). Extended metaphorically from pouring liquid into a vessel to funneling massive capital, labor, or obsession into an enterprise.

history.meaning: to pour liquid or material continuously into a container
to pour in; to sink vast money, resources, or passion into

morphemes.meaning: pour into, replenish (ren'yōkei of 注ぐ)
go deeply inward, pack into (込む)

つぎ込む.notes: Frequently carries a high-stakes or reckless undertone in financial contexts (全財産をつぎ込む 'sink one's entire fortune into a venture'), central to 1980s bubble-era entrepreneurial drama.

rootFamily.gloss: to pour (drinks/liquid) into a cup or vessel
to throw/invest resources into (投げ + 込む)
to pour/channel effort or water into (sosogi-komu)

つく.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tuku*, representing several core verbs including 付く・着く ('to attach, stick to, arrive at, turn on [of lights]') and 突く ('to thrust, poke, strike a bell').

history.form: つく (付く・着く / 突く)
history.meaning: make contact; arrive; thrust
attach; arrive; come on (lights); poke

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 付く

つける.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) transitive verb 付ける・着ける ('to attach, apply, put on, turn on a light, season/soak 漬ける'), continuing Old Japanese *tuku* (transitive counterpart of four-grade *tuku* 'to stick, arrive').

history.form: つく (付く・着く, lower bigrade)
history.meaning: attach; apply; put on
attach; put on; turn on; keep (a record)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 付ける

つじつま合わせ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun built from tsujitsuma (辻褄, 'logical consistency') + awase (合わせ, nominalized ren'yōkei of transitive awaseru 合わせる 'to bring into alignment'). Tsujitsuma originated in traditional kimono tailoring, compounding tsuji (辻, 'cross-shaped intersection of seams, crossroads', a kokuji) and tsuma (褄, 'lower front corner/hem of a kimono skirt'). Making garment seams line up smoothly became a vivid metaphor for doctoring accounts or stories so everything appears consistent.

history.meaning: aligning cross-seams and skirt edges neatly in sewing
making stories add up; cooking or balancing the books post hoc

morphemes.meaning: skirt hem corner of a kimono (褄)
matching, aligning together (stem of 合わせる)

つじつま合わせ.notes: Whereas intransitive つじつまが合う neutral-positively means 'the story adds up', nominal つじつま合わせ almost always implies contrived, after-the-fact rationalization or creative accounting.

rootFamily.gloss: for a story or figures to make sense / add up
to match, combine, adjust to fit

つながる.etymology: Intransitive verb 繋がる ('to be connected, linked, tied together, get through by phone'), derived in Middle Japanese from つなぐ (繋ぐ 'to tie, tether') + intransitive suffix -ある (*-aru*).

history.meaning: be tied together; form a continuous link
be connected; be linked; lead to

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 繋がる

つなぎ.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem (連用形) of the native verb つなぐ (tsunagu, Old Japanese tunagu, 'to tie, link, tether, join together', related to 綱 tsuna, 'rope, cord'). Because it names 'that which links two parts together', つなぎ developed versatile specialized senses across Japanese crafts: in music and theater, a bridging passage or interlude between two sections; in architecture, a tie-beam; and in cooking, a binding ingredient (such as wheat flour in soba noodles or egg in fillings).

history.meaning: to tie; to tether; to link
connecting link, musical/theatrical interlude, or culinary binder
transition; bridge; link; binder

つなぎ.notes: In music, つなぎ specifically denotes a short transitional bridge linking two themes or bars.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — つなぎ

つなぐ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tunagu* (繋ぐ 'to tie with a rope, tether, connect, join'), verbalized from the noun 綱 (つな *tuna* 'rope, cord, tether').

history.meaning: fasten with a tether; tie; link
connect; join; hold hands; tether

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 繋ぐ

つまずく.etymology: The term 'つまずく' (meaning 'trip') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: trip
trip

つまずく.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — つまずく

つもり.etymology: Verbal noun 積もり ('intention, plan, expectation'), nominalized from the continuative stem of 積もる (*tumoru* 'to pile up, accumulate; estimate/calculate by piling up'). From 'mental estimate or calculation', it shifted in Early Modern Japanese to 'one's intention or plan'.

history.meaning: accumulation; calculation; estimate
intention; plan; supposition

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 積もり

つややか.etymology: Native descriptive na-adjective derived by attaching the classical adjectival suffix -やか (-yaka, indicating vivid visual appearance or full quality, as in 鮮やか azayaka and 穏やか odayaka) to the noun 艶 (tsuya, 'luster, gloss, sheen'). Attested since Heian literature for the healthy sheen of dark hair, silk, or blossoms, つややか in modern Japanese describes anything with a warm, smooth, inviting luster—from emulsified lemon curd and glazed pastries to polished walnut wood.

history.meaning: lustrous; blooming with sheen and charm
glossy; lustrous; sleek

つややか.notes: Takes な before nouns (つややかな色) and に as an adverbial/resultative complement (つややかになる, 'to turn glossy').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — つややか

つる草.etymology: Native Japanese botanical compound 蔓草 (つるくさ 'climbing vine, creeper'), combining つる (蔓 'vine, tendril, runner', from Old Japanese *turu*, cognate with 弦 'bowstring') + 草 (くさ 'grass, herbaceous plant').

history.meaning: trailing or climbing vine plant

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 蔓草

つー.etymology: Colloquial Kantō/Tokyo spoken quotative and attributive particle contracted from the native phrase to iu (という, quotative particle to と + verb iu 言う 'to say, call'). Through rapid-speech syncope and alveolar affrication without palatalization (to iu > tiu > tsū, often geminated post-vocalically as っつー), it serves as a blunt, working-class equivalent of という ('called; meaning; the fact that').

history.meaning: which is called; saying that
blunt colloquial quotative/attributive particle ('that; called')

morphemes.meaning: to say, call (< iu, fused into alveolar affricate + long u)

つー.notes: quintessential rough Tokyo banter: つーか (< というか 'I mean / rather') and なんつーか ('how should I put it') instantly signal unvarnished, street-level informality.

rootFamily.gloss: or rather; I mean (< to iu ka)

て.etymology: Conjunctive particle (-て) linking sequential actions, means, or states, inherited from Old Japanese *-te*, which grammaticalized from the continuative stem (*-te*) of the perfective auxiliary つ (*-tu* 'to finish doing').

history.meaning: having done; and then
clause-linking, request, and aspectual particle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — て

てめえ.etymology: Vulgar, confrontational second-person pronoun derived via regular Kantō monophthongization (-ae > -ē) from native Yamato compound temae (手前, te 手 'hand' + mae 前 'area in front', literally 'the space right before one's own hands'). Originally a polite, self-effacing first-person noun ('this side; I, your humble servant'), it shifted in the Edo period to address an interlocutor and split stylistically: uncontracted temae remained formal/humble 'I/we', while contracted temē underwent sharp pejoration into 'you bastard'.

history.meaning: right in front of one's hands; humble first-person 'I'
second-person pronoun shifting from casual 'you' to hostile 'you bastard'

morphemes.meaning: front, space before (< mae, coalesced to mē)

てめえ.notes: A textbook case of Japanese pronoun pejoration (like 貴様 kisama, once 'noble lord'): uncontracted 手前ども is still used humbly by shopkeepers ('we'), while てめえ is fighting words unless clearly joking among close buddies.

rootFamily.gloss: in front of; humble 'I'; tea/craft ceremony form

ても.etymology: Concessive conjunctive particle ('even if, although'), formed by combining the conjunctive particle て (-て) + the inclusive/concessive focus particle も ('even').

history.meaning: even after doing; even if

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ても

てる.etymology: Colloquial progressive and resultative auxiliary verb formed by apheresis (i-dropping) of the animate existential verb iru (いる, 'to be, exist', from Classical Japanese wiru ゐる 'to sit, stay') immediately following the conjunctive particle -te (て): -te iru > -teru (and after voiced -de: -de iru > -deru). Inflects as a regular ichidan verb (てない, てた, てて).

history.form: てゐる (te wiru) > ている (te iru)
history.meaning: to remain in the state of having done; to be doing
colloquial progressive/resultative auxiliary ('is doing; has done')

morphemes.meaning: apheresized stem/ending of existential iru (< wiru)

てる.notes: Standard in virtually all everyday conversation regardless of politeness level (知ってる / 知ってます 'I know'), though omitted in formal prose where full ている is required.

rootFamily.gloss: uncontracted aspectual construction: is doing / has done
voiced counterpart after nasal/voiced stems (< -de iru)

てん.etymology: Colloquial contracted aspectual sequence formed when progressive/stative -te iru (ている > -teru てる) undergoes regressive nasal assimilation of final -ru to moraic nasal -n before nasal- or dental-initial particles such as explanatory no (の), copula da (だ), or topic/question endings (e.g., 何してんの < 何しているの 'what are you doing?', やってんだ < やっているんだ). Also surfaces in Kansai speech as -te + explanatory/past -n (< -te yoru / -ta no).

history.form: ているの / ているんだ (te iru no / te iru n da)
history.meaning: it is that one is doing / has done

history.form: てん (ten, e.g. てんの / てんだ)
history.meaning: nasal-assimilated colloquial progressive ('is doing [explanatory]')

morphemes.meaning: apheresized and nasal-assimilated iru (< -ru before n/d)

てん.notes: Extremely frequent in rapid spoken questions and assertions: 何見てんだよ ('What the hell are you looking at?') compresses 見ているのだよ by three moras for punchy immediacy.

rootFamily.gloss: voiced counterpart (< -de iru before no/da, e.g. 飲んでんの)

で.etymology: Case particle marking location of action, instrument/means, cause, or material ('at, in, by, with'), which arose in Late Heian and Kamakura Japanese via phonetic fusion of にて (*ni te*, locative particle に + conjunctive て). Also serves as the continuative (*-te*) form of the copula だ.

history.meaning: at; in; by means of (being at)
at; by; with; and (copula te-form)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — で

でかい.etymology: Colloquial Yamato i-adjective first attested in Early Modern Edo vernacular (alongside adverbial dekadeka and Edo variant dekachi) meaning 'huge, colossal, outsized'. Most widely derived in Japanese philology from the stem of the compound verb dekasu (出かす, 'to bring forth impressively, pull off something grand', from de- 出 'come out, protrude' + transitive suffix -kasu), shifting from 'outstandingly turned out' to sheer physical or metaphorical magnitude.

history.form: でかす (dekasu) > でかし / でかい (dekai)
history.meaning: brought forth conspicuously; impressively grand in scale
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: huge, massive, loud (voice), major (achievement/impact)

morphemes.meaning: protrude, come forth impressively (< 出かす dekasu)

でかい.notes: Punchier and more visceral than neutral 大きい; extends readily to loud voices (声がでかい), grand ambitions (話がでかい 'big talk / grand scheme'), and big wins (これはでかいぞ! 'This is huge!').

rootFamily.gloss: to pull off admirably; well done! (出かした!)

できる.etymology: Upper bigrade/ichidan verb 出来る ('to come into existence, be completed, be able to do'), contracted in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese from 出で来る (*idekuru* 'to come forth, appear, emerge', combining 出づ 'come out' + 来る 'come').

history.form: いでく / いでくる (出で来)
history.meaning: come out; appear; happen
be made/ready; be able to do

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 出来る

でしょう.etymology: Polite presumptive copula and confirmation-seeking auxiliary representing the volitional/conjectural inflection of the polite copula desu (です, consolidated in late Edo Tokyo speech from de sōrō で候 / de gozarimasu でございます). Attaching the Classical conjectural suffix -u (う < -mu む) to the irrealis stem dese- yielded historical kana でせう (deseu), which regularly palatalized and coalesced into modern でしょう (deshō), serving as the polite counterpart to plain だろう.

history.meaning: polite conjecture: 'it would probably be'
probably (falling pitch); 'right?, don't you think?' (rising pitch)

morphemes.meaning: irrealis stem of polite copula desu

でしょう.notes: Intonation completely transforms its pragmatic force: falling pitch expresses polite probability ('it will probably rain'), whereas sharp rising pitch (でしょ↗?) seeks agreement or nudges ('I told you so, right?').

rootFamily.gloss: casual shortened tag question: right?, you know?

です.etymology: Polite copula documented from the Muromachi period onward that spread across general polite speech in the late Edo and Meiji periods. Reference dictionaries list several proposed contractions—including で候 (de sōrō), でおはす, でございます, and であります—without consensus on a single source.

history.meaning: stylized copular ending in dramatic and social registers
standard polite copula

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — です

でないと.etymology: Conditional connective ('otherwise, if not, unless'), formed from でない ('is not', composed of copular で + negative ない) + conditional particle と ('when, if').

history.meaning: if it is not so; otherwise

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — でないと

では.etymology: Conjunction ('well then, in that case') and compound particle, formed from the locative/copular particle で + topic/contrastive particle は. Source of colloquial じゃあ.

history.meaning: in/at (with contrast); well then; if so

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — では

でも.etymology: Concessive conjunction ('but, however, even so') and focus particle ('even, or something like'), formed from the copular/case particle で + inclusive particle も ('even').

history.meaning: even being; however; or something

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — でも

でる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) verb, written 出る. Evolved via apheresis (loss of initial *i-*) from Classical and Old Japanese *idu* (出づ, lower bigrade verb), from Proto-Japonic *\*intə-* ('to go out, emerge'). It forms a classic transitivity pair with transitive *dasu* (出す, from *idasu*, 'to put out, take out').

history.meaning: to go out, emerge
to go out, come forth, appear
to go out, to appear, to leave, to be served

morphemes.meaning: go out, emerge (from Old Japanese id-)

でる.notes: One of the most versatile verbs in Japanese: beyond physical exiting, it means 'to attend' (会議に出る), 'to answer the phone' (電話に出る), 'to be served' (料理が出る), and 'to appear in media' (テレビに出る). Pitch accent is [1] (頭高型: で↓る).

rootFamily.gloss: to take out, to put out, to submit (transitive counterpart)

と.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *to*, serving since eighth-century texts as the comitative and coordinating particle ('with, and'), the quotative particle ('that, thus'), and the natural-consequence conditional particle ('when, whenever').

history.meaning: with; and; quotative marker
and; with; quotative 'that'; conditional 'when'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — と

という.etymology: Appositive and clause-linking expression ('called, that, namely'), composed of the quotative particle と + the verb いう (言う 'to say, call').

history.meaning: called; saying that
called; that (content clause marker)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — と言う

とおり.etymology: Verbal noun 通り ('street, passage; manner, just as'), nominalized from the continuative stem of 通る (*tooru* 'to pass through, go along', from Old Japanese *toporu*).

history.meaning: passing through; way; street
street; avenue; in accordance with; just as

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 通り

とか.etymology: Non-exhaustive listing and quotative uncertainty particle ('things like ... and ...; I hear that'), formed from the quotative/coordinating particle と + question/indefinite particle か.

history.meaning: something to the effect of; things like ... and ...

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — とか

とかいう.etymology: Compound adnominal phrase ('called something like..., someone by the name of...'), combining the indefinite quotative particle とか ('something like') + いう (言う 'to say, call').

history.meaning: called something like; or whatever it is called

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — とか言う
Wiktionary — とかいう (とか言う) (Japanese)

とき.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *toki* (時 'time, hour, season, occasion, when'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; used both as a standalone noun and as a temporal clause head ('when...').

history.meaning: time; season; occasion
time; moment; when

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 時

とく.etymology: Colloquial phonological contraction of the conjunctive particle *te* (て) plus the subsidiary verb *oku* (置く, 'to put, to place; to do in advance for future readiness'), via vowel coalescence (*-te oku* > *-toku*). After nasal or voiced gerunds (*-nde*), the voiced allomorph *doku* (どく, from *de oku*) occurs. Note that homophonous standalone verbs *toku* (解く 'to untie, solve' and 溶く 'to dissolve') come from Old Japanese *toku* (< Proto-Japonic *\*təka-*).

history.meaning: to do and leave in place; to do in advance for future preparation
to do in advance, to leave in a certain state (colloquial contraction)

morphemes.meaning: to place, to do in advance for future use (置く)

とく.notes: Ubiquitous in casual speech: 買っとく (from 買っておく, 'I'll buy it in advance') or 置いとく (from 置いておく, 'I'll leave it there'). After ん or んだ stems, it voices to どく, as in 飲んどく (from 飲んでおく).

rootFamily.gloss: to put, to place; to do in advance (full auxiliary form)
voiced colloquial contraction of でおく after nasal/voiced stems
leaving a thing as it is, neglect (noun from 置きっ放し)
rootFamily.word: 置きっ放し (おきっぱなし)

sources.title: Wiktionary — とく (toku) / ておく (te oku)

とこ.etymology: Colloquial apocopated (clipped) form of native Yamato (*wago*) noun *tokoro* (所 / 処, 'place, spot, scene'), which experienced loss of the final syllable *-ro* in casual speech from the Late Middle Japanese period onward. *Tokoro* itself is attested in Old Japanese as *tökörö* (with *kö*₂ vowels), from Proto-Japonic *\*təkərə* ('place').

history.meaning: place, locality
place, physical spot, abstract situation or point
place, spot, someone's home/house (colloquial apocope)

とこ.notes: Very common in conversational Japanese both for physical locations (俺んとこ 'my place') and abstract aspects (いいとこあるじゃん 'he has his good points'). In formal writing, always restore the full form ところ (所).

rootFamily.gloss: place, spot, scene, point (full standard form)

ところ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tokoro* (所・処 'place, spot, locality'), likely built on the spatial root *to* ('place', as in あと, そと) + extended suffix *-koro*. Grammaticalized also to mark temporal aspect ('just about to, in the midst of, just finished').

history.meaning: place; locality
place; point; aspectual 'just now / about to'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 所

として.etymology: Compound particle ('as, in the capacity of, taking as'), formed from the quotative/essives particle と + して (the *-te* form of する 'to treat as, make').

history.meaning: treating as; in the role/capacity of

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — として

とっても.etymology: Emphatic geminated variant of the adverb *totemo* (とても, 'very, exceedingly'), derived from the verb *toru* (取る, 'to take') in its concessive gerund phrase *toritemo* (取りても, 'even if one takes/tries') > *totemo*. Historically in Classical and Early Modern Japanese, *totemo* (and *totemo kakutemo*) was a negative polarity item meaning 'by no means, (not) at all' when paired with a negative predicate; during the Meiji–Taisho era it underwent semantic extension to a positive degree intensifier ('impossibly so' > 'extremely, very'), with internal consonant gemination (*tottemo*) adding expressive emotional emphasis.

history.meaning: even if one takes it; no matter how one tries
by no means, cannot possibly (with negative verb)
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: very, awfully, really (emphatic geminated positive intensifier)

とっても.notes: The geminated っ in とっても gives it a warmer, more expressive, and more conversational feel than standard とても. Note that the older negative polarity sense survives in phrases like とてもじゃないが無理だ ('there is no way at all I can do it').

rootFamily.gloss: very, exceedingly; (with negative) cannot possibly (standard form)
to take, to pick up (verbal source)
all the more, above all (related tori- adverbial)

sources.title: Wiktionary — とっても (tottemo) / とても (totemo)

とても.etymology: Originally an Early and Late Middle Japanese adverb とて (with inclusive も) shortened from とてもかくても ('whether this way or that way, no matter how'), used with negative predicates to mean 'by no means, cannot possibly'. In the Meiji–Taishō era it generalized to affirmative sentences as 'very, awfully, extremely'.

history.meaning: either way; (with negative) by no means
very; extremely; (with negative) cannot possibly

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 迚も

とにかく.etymology: Idiomatic adverb 兎に角 ('anyway, at any rate, first of all'), shortened from the classical phrase とにもかくにも ('whether this way [と] or that way [かく]'). The kanji 兎に角 are Edo/Meiji playful phonetic ateji.

history.meaning: whether that way or this way
anyway; in any case; at any rate

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 兎に角

とも.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tomo*, functioning both as a concessive conjunctive particle ('even if, no matter') and as a noun/suffix 共 ('both, together, including; humble plural'). Also combines quotative と + も ('certainly, of course').

history.meaning: together/both; even if
both; even if; certainly (empatic response)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 共

とろっと.etymology: Native Japanese tactile/visual mimetic adverb formed from the root *toro- (seen in the verb とろける torokeru, 'to melt down into a soft liquid', and the reduplicated adverb とろとろ torotoro, 'syrupy, simmering softly') plus the intensive-punctual quotative suffix -っと (-tto). Adding -っと captures the exact moment a sauce, custard, or honeyed glaze reaches a cohesive, velvety, spoon-coating thickness.

history.meaning: slowly melting or syrupy state
turning thickly and silkily smooth

とろっと.notes: Frequently paired with する (とろっとしたスープ, 'a velvety thick soup') or なる (とろっとなる, 'to thicken silkily').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — とろっと

とんでもない.etymology: Emphatic adjective ('unthinkable, outrageous, by no means, don't mention it!'), formed in Early Modern Japanese from 途方もない (*tohō mo nai* 'without rhyme, reason, or direction') or 飛んでもない ('not even by a wild leap'), expressing strong denial or astonishment.

history.meaning: extraordinary; unthinkable; out of the question
unthinkable; outrageous; 'not at all / don't mention it'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — とんでもない

どう.etymology: Interrogative manner adverb ('how, in what way'), which evolved in Late Middle Japanese via *u*-onbin (*dau* > *dō*) from ど- (the interrogative root seen in どこ, どれ, どの, which replaced older いづ-) + adverbial ending -う (patterned after こう, そう, ああ).

history.meaning: in what manner; how
how; in what way; how about

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 如何

どういう.etymology: Native Japanese compound pre-nominal determiner (*rentaishi*) formed from the interrogative manner adverb *dō* (どう, 'how, in what way', itself a long-vowel contraction of Early Middle Japanese *ikaga* / *ika ni* or more directly from demonstrative-interrogative *idu-* + *-u* parallel to *kō* < *kaku* and *sō* < *sa-u*) plus the attributive verb *iu* (言う / 云う, 'to say, to call', from Old Japanese *ipu* < Proto-Japonic *\*ip-*). Literally 'called how' or 'said in what way', hence 'what kind of, what sort of'.

history.form: いかにいふ (ika ni ipu) / どういふ (dou ipu)
history.meaning: how called, said in what manner
what kind of, what sort of

morphemes.meaning: how, in what way (interrogative manner adverb)
to say, to call, to name (言う)

どういう.notes: Part of the regular *ko-so-a-do* (こそあど) paradigm alongside こういう ('this kind of'), そういう ('that kind of'), and ああいう ('that kind of over there'). Very common in どういうこと？ ('What does that mean? / What's going on?').

rootFamily.gloss: this kind of, like this (proximal counterpart)
that kind of, like that (medial counterpart)

どうして.etymology: Interrogative adverb ('why, how, by what means'), formed from the manner interrogative どう ('how') + して (the *-te* form of する 'to do'), literally 'doing how?'.

history.meaning: how; why; for what reason

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 如何して

どうしても.etymology: Lexicalized adverbial phrase composed of the interrogative adverb *dō* (どう, 'how, in what way'), the continuative stem *shi* (し) of the verb *suru* (する, 'to do', from Old Japanese *su*), the conjunctive particle *te* (て), and the inclusive/concessive particle *mo* (も, 'even'). Literally 'even doing it how(ever) / no matter how one does it', evolving into both 'by all means, at any cost' (with affirmative or desiderative predicates) and 'no matter how hard one tries, simply (cannot)' (with negative predicates).

history.meaning: even if one does it in whatever way; no matter how one acts
no matter what, by all means, inevitably, cannot help but

どうしても.notes: Has two main contextual senses: strong determination ('by all means / no matter what', e.g., どうしても行きたい 'I desperately want to go') and inevitability ('no matter how one tries', e.g., どうしても思い出せない 'I just can't remember no matter what').

rootFamily.gloss: how, in what way; why (interrogative adverb)
somehow or other, one way or another

どうする.etymology: Phrase: adverb どう (dō, how) + verb する (suru, to do). This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: what to do

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — どうする

どうせ.etymology: Modal adverb ('anyway, in any case, after all'), shortened in Edo-period Japanese from どうせうとも ('no matter how one may do it') or どうせう ('how shall we do -> either way').

history.meaning: no matter what; in any event; after all
anyway; after all; at any rate

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — どうせ

どうぞ.etymology: Polite adverb of request or invitation ('please, go ahead, by all means'), formed in Late Middle / Early Modern Japanese from どう ('how, in some way') + emphatic particle ぞ. Originally meaning 'somehow or other, by all means', it specialized into a polite invitation ('please').

history.meaning: by all means; somehow; earnestly
please; go right ahead; here you are

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 何卒

どうも.etymology: Adverb and versatile conversational greeting ('somehow, very much, thanks, hello'), formed in Early Modern Japanese from どう ('how') + inclusive particle も ('even/in every way'). From 'no matter how one tries [to express thanks/apology]', it became a polite all-purpose acknowledgement.

history.meaning: no matter how; somehow; indeed
thank you; very much; somehow

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — どうも

どうやって.etymology: Interrogative manner phrase ('how, by doing what'), composed of どう ('how') + やって (the *-te* form of やる 'to do, perform').

history.meaning: by doing how; in what way

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — どう

どおり.etymology: Sequential voiced (*rendaku*) suffixal form of the native Yamato (*wago*) deverbal noun *tōri* (通り, 'passage, street, way, manner'), derived from the continuative stem (*ren'yōkei*) of the verb *tōru* (通る, 'to pass through, go along', Old Japanese *töporu* < Proto-Japonic *\*təpər-*). When attached directly to a noun without *no* (e.g., *keikaku-dōri* 計画通り 'according to plan'), initial *t-* voices to *d-* (*dōri*). When preceded by the genitive particle *no* or a verb (e.g., *omotta tōri* 思った通り, *watashi no iu tōri* 私の言う通り), it normally remains unvoiced *tōri*, though colloquial post-*no* *dōri* also occurs.

history.meaning: passing through, passage, pathway
way, street; in the exact manner of, in accordance with

morphemes.meaning: pass through, follow a path (verb stem tōr- with rendaku d-)

どおり.notes: Watch the voicing rule: directly after a noun, use どおり with rendaku (予想どおり 'just as expected', 約束どおり 'as promised'); after の or a verb in plain form, use unvoiced とおり (そのとおり 'exactly right', 言ったとおり 'just as I said').

rootFamily.gloss: street, avenue; manner, way (unvoiced standalone form)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — に

におい.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *nipopi* (匂い・臭い), nominalized from the verb *nipopu* (匂ふ). In Old Japanese (Man'yōshū), *nipopu* meant 'to shine with warm, vivid color (especially red)'; in Heian court culture (famous for incense blending) it shifted to 'fragrance, aroma', and later to any 'smell, scent, odor'.

history.meaning: radiant color; warm glow

にぎやか.etymology: Adjectival noun 賑やか ('lively, bustling, cheerful'), formed from the root *nigi-* (seen in Old Japanese *nigipapu* / 賑わう 'to flourish, be abundant and prosperous', related to 和 *nigi* 'gentle, harmonious, plentiful') + adjectival suffix -やか.

history.meaning: prosperous; bustling with people; lively
lively; bustling; cheerful

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 賑やか

にこにこ.etymology: Reduplicated mimetic adverb attested from Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese (built on the ancient root *niko-* 'soft, gentle, smiling', seen in Old Japanese *nikoyaka* and *nikoniko*), describing a warm, cheerful smile.

history.form: にこやか / にこにこ
history.meaning: softly; with a gentle smile
smilingly; beaming happily

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — にこにこ

にっこり.etymology: Native Japanese mimetic adverb (擬態語) built on the root *niko- (attested in Old and Classical Japanese にこやか nikoyaka, 'soft, gentle-faced, amiable', and reduplicated にこにこ nikoniko, 'smiling cheerfully'). The geminated pattern にっこり (*niko- + emphatic gemination + -ri) highlights a single, warm smile blooming on the face, distinguishing silent facial smiling (にっこり笑う, 'to beam a smile') from audible laughter (声を立てて笑う).

history.meaning: gentle, soft, and smiling in expression
breaking into a single bright smile
beamingly; with a warm smile

にっこり.notes: Because 笑う covers both 'laugh' and 'smile', adding にっこり (にっこり笑う) unambiguously specifies 'to smile warmly'.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — にっこり

について.etymology: Grammaticalized compound postpositional particle derived from the target particle に (ni) followed by ついて (tsuite), the te-form of the native verb つく (tsuku, written 就く / 付く, 'to attach to, follow along, pertain to'). Originally meaning 'attaching to [a topic]' in Late Middle Japanese prose, に就いて bleached into a general-purpose compound particle marking the topic of speech, inquiry, thought, or writing ('about, concerning').

history.meaning: following upon; in connection with
compound particle 'concerning; about'
about; regarding

morphemes.meaning: te-form of 就く/付く ('to pertain to')

について.notes: When modifying a following noun rather than a verb, it takes の: 九号室についての質問 ('a question about Room Nine').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — について

にとって.etymology: Compound postpositional particle ('for, from the standpoint of, to'), grammaticalized from dative particle に + とって (the *-te* form of 取る *toru* 'to take, adopt as a viewpoint').

history.form: にとりて → にとって

にんじん.etymology: Originally the Sino-Japanese name 人参 (にんじん 'ginseng', literally 'human-shaped root', fromの人 'person' + 参 'ginseng'). When the culinary carrot (*Daucus carota*) entered Japan in the 16th–17th centuries, it was called せりにんじん ('parsley-ginseng') for its similar root and foliage, soon shortening to にんじん.

history.meaning: ginseng root
carrot

history.meaning: conversational confirmation or shared feeling

ねえ.etymology: Lengthened form of the sentence-final and interjectional particle ね (derived from earlier な / なあ), used either to call someone's attention ('hey, say, listen') or to seek warm agreement ('isn't it?, right?').

history.meaning: hey; listen; isn't it so?

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ねえ

ねじ.etymology: Noun 螺子・捻じ ('screw, spiral thread, clockwork spring'), nominalized from the continuative stem (*nedi* > *neji*) of the Old/Middle Japanese verb ねづ / ねじる (捻じる 'to twist, wrench, turn spirally').

history.meaning: twisting; torsion
screw; threaded fastener; winding key

cognates.word: にーん (nīn) / にんじゅん (ninjun)

ねる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) verb, written 寝る ('to lie down, go to bed, sleep'), which evolved from the Old and Classical Japanese lower bigrade (*shimo nidan*) verb *nu* (寝, stem *ne-*, attributive *nuru*), from Proto-Japonic *\*na-* ('to lie down, sleep'). Historically, Old Japanese distinguished *nu* (寝, 'to lie down, share a bed') from *i nu* (眠ぬ, 'to sleep a sleep'); in Modern Japanese, *neru* covers both 'to go to bed / lie down' and 'to sleep', as well as 'to ferment/mature' (of dough, curry, or plans) and 'to lie unsold'. Note: in tokenized subtitle transcripts, *nette* (ねって) is sometimes lemmatized under *neru* when representing the particle *ne* (ね) + quotative *tte* (って, 'right?, I tell you').

history.meaning: to lie down, to sleep
to lie down, go to bed, sleep (lower bigrade verb)
to sleep, to go to bed, to lie down; to mature/ferment (ichidan verb)

ねる.notes: Crucial distinction: 寝る (ねる) means 'to go to bed, lie down, or go to sleep' (including sleeping with someone sexually), whereas 眠る (ねむる) specifically means 'to be asleep / fall into slumber'. Thus 昨日何時に寝た？ asks 'What time did you go to bed yesterday?'. Pitch accent is [0] (平板型: ねる￣).

rootFamily.gloss: to fall asleep, to slumber (derived from the same *na- / ne- root)
to put to sleep, to lay down; to let dough/plans rest (transitive/causative)

ねん.etymology: The term 'ねん' (meaning 'explanatory') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: explanatory
explanatory

ねん.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ねん

の.etymology: Native Japanese genitive and noun-linking particle already attested in the Kojiki (712). Over time it also developed a nominalizing function turning clauses into noun-like statements; in modern spoken Japanese, explanatory の before です or だ frequently contracts to ん.

history.meaning: links a modifying noun to a following noun
contracted explanatory nominalizer

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — の

のか.etymology: Compound sentence-final particle expressing an explanatory question or realization ('is it that...?, oh, so...!'), formed from the explanatory nominalizer の + question particle か.

history.meaning: is it the case that...?; oh, so that's why

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — のか

のぞく.etymology: Inherited from Early Middle Japanese *nozoku* (覗く・臨く 'to peer into, peek through a gap, look down from an edge'), alongside homophonous 除く (*nozoku* 'to remove, exclude, omit').

history.meaning: lean over to look in; peek / remove
peek; peer in; exclude

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 覗く

のだ.etymology: Compound explanatory sentence-ending construction (*no da*, colloquial *nda* んだ, polite *no desu* のです / *ndesu* んです) formed from the formal nominalizer particle *no* (の, originally the genitive/attributive particle *nö* in Old Japanese < Proto-Japonic *\*nə*, which developed a clause-nominalizing function 'the fact/one that...' in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese, replacing Classical attributive nominalization) plus the plain copula *da* (だ, contracted from *de aru* である < *nite aru* にてある). Literally 'it is the fact that...', used to provide or seek an explanation, reason, background context, or emphatic assertion.

history.form: にてある (nite aru) > である (de aru) > だ (da)
history.meaning: to exist at / to be (copula development)
history.stage: Early Middle to Late Middle Japanese

history.form: のだ (no da) / んだ (n da)
history.meaning: it is the case that... (explanatory nominalizer + copula construction)

morphemes.meaning: plain declarative copula ('is', from de aru)

のだ.notes: In spoken conversation, のだ almost always contracts to んだ (or polite んです), while bare のだ belongs to written prose, essays, or dramatic inner monologue. Remember that after a noun or *na*-adjective, you must insert な before のだ/んだ (e.g., 静かなんだ, 病気なのだ).

rootFamily.gloss: polite explanatory ending (no + polite copula desu)
casual spoken contraction of のだ
explanatory sentence-final particle (omitting copula da in questions/soft speech)

ので.etymology: Causal conjunctive particle ('because, since'), formed in Early Modern Japanese by combining the clause-nominalizing particle の + the instrumental/causal copular particle で ('it being the fact that...').

history.meaning: because of the fact that; since
because; since (objective/polite reason)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ので

のに.etymology: Concessive conjunctive particle ('although, even though, despite') and purpose/context marker ('for doing'), formed in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese from the nominalizing particle の + dative/locative particle に ('in the situation where...').

history.meaning: in the circumstance that -> even though; in order to
although; despite; for the purpose of

は.etymology: Topic and contrastive particle (pronounced *wa*, spelled は), inherited from Old Japanese *pa*. By the Heian–Kamakura periods, intervocalic *-p-* lenited to *-w-* (*pa* > *wa*), while classical orthography retained the kana は for the particle.

history.meaning: topic and contrastive focus particle
topic marker ('as for')

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — は

はあ.etymology: Lengthened native Japanese interjection representing either a polite/tentative acknowledgment ('yes, I see'), puzzled wonder ('huh?'), or an audible sigh/exhalation ('ah, phew').

history.meaning: polite acknowledgment; sigh; puzzled 'huh?'

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — はあ

はい.etymology: Standard polite affirmative response ('yes, here, present'), which arose in Edo-period Japanese from earlier はい / はあ (possibly linked to 拝 *hai* 'bowing in respect' or a vocalic shift from medieval affirmative へい / おう).

history.meaning: polite 'yes' or response when called
yes; certainly; here you go

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — はい

はいはい.etymology: Reduplication of the interjection *hai* (はい, 'yes, okay, I hear you'). *Hai* itself emerged during the Early Modern (Edo) period—originally in Edo/Kamigata merchant and courtesan speech—most likely via diphthongization or palatalization from earlier Late Middle Japanese *hei* (へい) or *ai* (あい), or from Classical Sino-Japanese *hai* (拝, 'humbly acknowledging'). Repeating *hai* twice (*haihai* はいはい) shifts the pragmatic nuance from respectful acknowledgment to brisk, placating, or slightly dismissive compliance ('yes, yes; alright, alright, I get it').

history.form: へい (hei) / あい (ai) > はい (hai)
history.meaning: yes, I hear and acknowledge you
yes, yes; alright, alright; coming! (reduplicated response)

morphemes.meaning: repeated interjection indicating brisk or dismissive compliance

はいはい.notes: Classic learner trap: in Japanese, saying はいはい twice when a boss or elder gives you instructions sounds dismissive and perfunctory ('Yeah, yeah, whatever, I heard you!'). Always answer with a single crisp はい！ in polite or professional situations; reserve はいはい for soothing children or joking with close peers.

rootFamily.gloss: yes, okay, present!, here you go (single standard response)
okay!, coming right up! (cheerful lengthened variant)
yes, right, uh-huh (humble/old-fashioned merchant variant from the same root)

sources.title: Wiktionary — はいはい (haihai) / はい (hai)

はがき.etymology: Native Japanese compound 葉書 (はがき), from 葉 (は, 'leaf, small slip') and 書き (かき -> -がき by rendaku, 'writing').
はがき.notes: Originally referred to brief notes jotted on single slips of paper (端書き / 葉書き), standardized for postal cards in modern Japan.

はき違える.etymology: Idiomatic native Yamato (*wago*) compound verb, written 履き違える ('to misunderstand, to get the wrong idea, to confuse one concept for another'). Formed from the continuative stem *haki* (履き) of *haku* (履く, 'to put on footwear or lower-body garments', Old Japanese *paku* < Proto-Japonic *\*pak-*) plus the compound-forming verb *chigaeru* (違える, 'to mistake, to alter, to do wrongly', transitive counterpart of *chigau* 違う < Old Japanese *tigapu* 'to cross, differ'). Literally 'to put on the wrong pair of shoes/sandals (at an entranceway)', which metaphorically came to mean 'to confuse two fundamentally different principles (such as freedom vs. selfishness) or misjudge one's own standing'.

history.form: はきちがふ (pakitigapu > hakichigau) / はきちがへる (hakichigaeru)
history.meaning: literally to put on someone else's or the wrong footwear; figuratively to mistake one thing for another
to misunderstand fundamentally, to get the wrong idea, to confuse concepts

morphemes.meaning: to put on footwear (履き, stem of haku)
to mistake, to confuse, to get wrong (違える)

はき違える.notes: Almost always used in the figurative sense of confusing two moral/social concepts or overstepping one's bounds: e.g., 自由とわがままをはき違える ('to confuse freedom with selfishness') or 立場をはき違えるな ('Don't forget your place / Don't get the wrong idea about who's boss'). Rarely written 吐き違える by folk-etymology ('to say/spit out wrongly'), though 履き違える ('putting on the wrong shoes') is the historically primary image.

rootFamily.gloss: to put on shoes, pants, or skirts (first component verb)
to mistake, to make an error (related compound with ma-)
to misunderstand, to hear/take wrongly (synonymous compound verb)
rootFamily.word: 取り違える (とりちがえる)

はじめまして.etymology: Standard greeting on meeting someone for the first time ('nice to meet you, how do you do'), literally the polite *-masu* + *-te* form of 始める (*hajimeru* 'to begin'): 'beginning [our acquaintance] for the first time, [I greet you]'.

history.form: はじめまして (始めまして)
history.meaning: for the first time [we meet]...
how do you do; nice to meet you

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 始めまして

はず.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *padu* (筈 'the nock at the end of an arrow that fits onto the bowstring, or the tip of a bow where the string notches'). Because the arrow nock and bowstring must fit together precisely, in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese はず came to mean 'natural fit, logical expectation, supposed to be'.

history.meaning: notch of an arrow or bow tip
fitting expectation; supposed to be; bound to

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 筈

はっきり.etymology: Mimetic adverb attested from the Edo period, formed on a root *haki-* (related to はきはき 'briskly, clearly' and 明く *aku* 'to open, grow bright/clear') with gemination and *-ri* suffix, meaning 'clearly, distinctly, definitely'.

history.meaning: distinctly; clearly; plainly
clearly; distinctly; definitely

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — はっきり

はは.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection representing light, open-mouthed laughter ('haha'), alongside the homophonous kinship noun 母 (はは 'mother', inherited from Old Japanese *papa*).

history.meaning: mother; sound of laughing
haha (laughing interjection); mother

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — はは

はまる.etymology: Inherited from Early Middle Japanese *pamaru* (嵌まる・填まる 'to plunge into, fit snugly into a groove or socket, fall into a trap'), intransitive counterpart of はめる (*hameru*). In modern colloquial Japanese it also means 'to get hooked on, be absorbed in'.

history.meaning: plunge into; fall in; fit inside
fit snugly into; get stuck in; be hooked on

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 嵌まる

はやる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) intransitive verb, written 流行る ('to be popular, be in fashion, flourish, be going around [of an illness]'). Derived from the adjective root *haya-* seen in *hayai* (早い / 速い, 'fast, rapid, early, vigorous', Old Japanese *payasi* < Proto-Japonic *\*paya-*) plus the verbalizing suffix *-ru* (る). Originally in Late Middle Japanese (*hayaru* 逸る / 早る), it meant 'to be impetuous, to surge forward with rapid momentum, to flourish vigorously'; from 'spreading rapidly and thriving', it specialized into 'to be in vogue, to be popular, to be prevalent (of trends or epidemics)', written with the semantic Sino-Japanese compound 流行 ('flow and go/spread') as *jukujikun*.

history.meaning: to be impetuous, to surge rapidly, to flourish vigorously (from stem haya- 'fast')
to be popular, to be in fashion, to be widespread (of trends, businesses, or diseases)

morphemes.meaning: fast, rapid, vigorous (from adjective root haya-)

はやる.notes: Used both for positive trends/fashions (この曲が今流行っている 'This song is trending right now', 流行っている店 'a thriving, popular shop') and for contagious illnesses (インフルエンザが流行っている 'The flu is going around'). Note that the homophonous 逸る ('to be impatient/eager', as in 気が逸る) is the exact same etymological word! Pitch accent is [2] (はや↓る).

rootFamily.gloss: trend, fashion, craze, epidemic (deverbal noun from hayaru)
to popularize, to make trendy, to spread (transitive/causative counterpart)
rootFamily.word: 流行らせる (はやらせる)

はーい.etymology: Expressive vowel-lengthened variant of the native/Early Modern Japanese affirmative interjection *hai* (はい, 'yes, okay, present, coming!'). As with *hai* (attested from the Edo period via *hei* / *ai*), drawing out the first vowel (*hāi* はーい) softens the sharp, formal crispness of *hai* into a cheerful, sing-song, approachable call—typically used when answering the door or someone calling one's name ('Coming! / Here!'), handing something over casually, or calling for attention ('Okay everyone!').

history.meaning: yes, I acknowledge (standard Edo-period affirmative response)
all right!, okay!, coming! (cheerful lengthened spoken variant)

はーい.notes: Tone and length matter: a short, crisp はい！ is respectful and businesslike, whereas a drawn-out はーい！ with rising-falling melody sounds warm, cheerful, or playful (like answering when mom calls you for dinner or answering the intercom at home), though too casual for formal superiors.

ば.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) conditional conjunctive particle ('if, when, provided that'), attested in Old Japanese as *ba* (ば), which emerged via intervocalic voicing after a nasalized or vocalic verbal inflection from the topic/contrastive particle *pa* (は, Old Japanese *pa* < Proto-Japonic *\*pa*, modern *wa*). In Old and Classical Japanese, attaching *ba* to the irrealis stem (*mizenkei*, e.g., *yukaba* 行かば) expressed a hypothetical condition ('if one goes'), whereas attaching it to the realis stem (*izenkei*, e.g., *yukeba* 行けば) expressed an actualized cause or general temporal 'when/since'. During Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese, the *izenkei* + *ba* (*-eba*) form took over the general hypothetical conditional function ('if'). Also occurs as the voiced *rendaku* form of the counter *ha* / *wa* (羽 'birds' or 把 'bundles') after *n* or certain numerals (e.g., *sanba* 三羽).

history.meaning: conditional/topicalizing conjunctive particle after verb stems
if (after mizenkei); since, when, whenever (after izenkei)
if, provided that (general conditional particle attached to kateikei)

ば.notes: The ば conditional (e.g., 行けば, 安ければ, なら[ば]) highlights a general, logical, or desirable condition ('if A happens, then naturally B follows'), and is indispensable in idioms like ～ばいい ('should / it would be good if') and ～なければならない ('must do, lit. if not, it won't do').

rootFamily.gloss: topic marker particle (unvoiced source particle from Old Japanese pa)
if it is the case that (copular conditional from nare + ba / nara + ba)
the more... the more... (idiomatic correlative pattern using ba + hodo)

ばあちゃん.etymology: Affectionate/familiar kinship noun ('grandma, granny; old woman'), formed from *bā* (ばあ, 婆, 'grandmother, old woman') plus the diminutive/familiar title suffix *-chan* (ちゃん, which evolved in Early Modern Edo child/family speech via palatalization of *-san* さん < *sama* 様). The stem *bā* (also *baba* ばば) is a native Yamato word attested since Early Middle Japanese (*baba* / *uba* 姥, Old Japanese *ömö* / *uba* 'old woman, wet nurse', reinforced by universal nursery bilabial reduplication *ba-ba* parallel to *jī* / *jiji* 'grandpa'), later written with the Sino-Japanese character 婆 (Middle Chinese *ba*, 'old woman'). Often preceded by honorific *o-* (おばあちゃん).

history.form: うば (uba) / ばば (baba) > ばあ (baa)
history.meaning: old woman, grandmother, elderly female relative
history.stage: Early Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.form: ばあちゃん (baachan) / おばあちゃん (obaachan)
history.meaning: grandma, granny, affectionate address for an elderly woman (bā + diminutive -chan < -san)

ばあちゃん.notes: ばあちゃん (without お) feels rustic, boyish, or warmly working-class (very common in *The Naked Director* and Showa-era family speech), while おばあちゃん is standard polite-affectionate 'grandma'. Be careful: bare ばばあ (婆あ) without ちゃん or さん is a harsh, derogatory slur ('old hag'). Pitch accent is [1] (ば↓あちゃん).

rootFamily.gloss: grandma, granny (standard polite-affectionate form with honorific o-)
rootFamily.word: おばあちゃん (お婆ちゃん)

sources.title: Wiktionary — ばあちゃん (bāchan) / おばあちゃん (obāchan)

ばい.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) noun and numeric suffix, written 倍 ('double, twice; -fold, times'), borrowed from Middle Chinese *bwojX* (倍, rising tone, originally 'to turn the back on' > 'to fold back on itself, double, multiply', Old Chinese *\*[b]ˤəʔ*). Used standalone (*bai* 倍), it specifically means 'double, twice as much (2x)'; placed after a number (e.g., *sanbai* 三倍 'three times'), it means '-fold'. Note: in spoken subtitle segmentation, *bai* can also represent a rapid contraction of the conditional advice pattern *-ba ii* (～ばいい, 'it would be good if / should', e.g., *sureba ii* > *surya ii* / *sura bai*) or Kyushu (Hakata/Kumamoto) dialect sentence-final particle *bai* (ばい, emphatic assertion).

ぱ.etymology: Phonological *handakuten* (*p-*) variant arising in three distinct contexts in Japanese: (1) as the geminated *rendaku* / *handakuon* form *-ppa* (っぱ) of the noun/counter *ha* (葉 'leaf', 派 'faction', 波 'wave', or 端 'edge'), or of the colloquial suffix *-ppanashi* (っ放し, 'leaving in a state', often clipped to *-ppa* as in *ake-ppa* 開けっぱ 'left open') and conditional particle *ba* after a glottal stop (*-ppa*); (2) as the explosive mimetic/onomatopoeic adverb *pa'* / *patto* (ぱっ / ぱっと, 'with a sudden flash, popping open, bursting brightly'), preserving archaic Proto-Japonic voiceless bilabial *\*p-*; or (3) in subtitle tokenization, as a split fragment of words like *yappa* (やっぱ, 'as expected') or *ippai* (いっぱい, 'full'). Historically, all native Japanese *h-* words had initial *\*p-* in Proto-Japonic, which shifted to *\*ɸ-* in Old Japanese and *h-* in Modern Japanese, except after geminate *っ* or nasal *ん* and in mimetics where *p-* was preserved or restored.

ぼ.etymology: Voiced (dakuten) bilabial kana syllable bo (ぼ), corresponding to unvoiced ほ (ho < Old Japanese po). In Japanese historical phonology and morphological segmentation, ぼ arises via three pathways: (1) sequential voicing (rendaku) of native Yamato roots beginning with ho < *po, such as ho 穂 ('ear of grain, tip') or ho 帆 ('sail'); (2) native mimetic and expressive roots beginning with bo- that evoke haziness, dazedness, or dullness (e.g., bon'yari ぼんやり, bōtto ぼーっと); and (3) Sino-Japanese readings such as 母 (bo 'mother', Middle Chinese muwX) or 坊 (bō > bo 'monk's quarters, boy, chap', Middle Chinese pjang).

む.etymology: Native kana syllable mu (む) and multifunctional bound morpheme. In modern morphological segmentation, む surfaces either as the Sino-Japanese morpheme 無 (mu 'nothingness, without, non-', Middle Chinese mju, go-on reading), as a closed-lip humming/grunting interjection (むっ), or as the final syllable of godan verbs in -mu.

From 'eye / point of view', it extended to 'experience or ordeal one undergoes' (as in ひどい目に遭う 'suffer a terrible experience'). As a pejorative or humbling nominal suffix -me (め, attached to people or animals to express contempt, as in あいつめ 'that bastard', or self-deprecation in 私め 'wretched little me'), it grammaticalized in Middle Japanese from a deprecatory sense of 目/群れ ('creature, specimen'). Universally abbreviated as AV (ēbui).

The Old French noun arose through univerbation of the phrase ce m'est a vis ("it seems to me"), from Vulgar Latin *ad visum ("according to what is seen, in one's view"), composed of Latin ad ("to, according to") + visum (neuter past participle of videre "to see", from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- "to see, know"). In Japanese, it functions both as a countable/uncountable noun ("a piece of advice") and as a verbal noun with する (アドバイスする "to advise").

Inside Japan, アニメ encompasses all animated works regardless of country of origin, whereas internationally it was reborrowed to denote specifically Japanese animation.

The English term comes from Middle French apointement ("arrangement, settlement"), from apointer ("to arrange, settle, bring to a point"), ultimately from Medieval Latin appunctare (ad- + punctum "point"). アングル.etymology: A gairaigo loanword borrowed from English angle, which came via Anglo-Norman and Old French angle from Latin angulus ("corner, bend, niche"), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éngulos ("joint, bend, corner"). While geometric angles are expressed in Japanese by the kango 角度 (kakudo), アングル was adopted specifically in photography, cinema, and journalism for the positioning of a camera lens or conceptual perspective.

history.meaning: corner, geometric angle; perspective or viewpoint
camera angle in film/photography or editorial slant in media

アングル.notes: Do not use アングル for mathematical or geometric angles (which require 角度 kakudo); アングル is reserved for camera framing, photography, journalism angles, and L-shaped structural steel brackets.

アンテナ.etymology: A gairaigo borrowing from English antenna (or directly via international radio terminology), which goes back to Latin antenna / antemna ("wooden sail yard of a ship"). Italian physicist Guglielmo Marconi applied antenna to wireless radio aerial poles in 1895 because the tent-pole-like wire masts resembled ship sail yards. In 1980s Japan, the word also became central to the satellite television boom (パラボラアンテナ, parabolic dish).

history.meaning: horizontal wooden yardarm supporting a ship sail
metallic aerial rod or dish for transmitting/receiving radio waves
radio/TV aerial, satellite dish, or figurative sensitivity to trends

morphemes.meaning: antenna, aerial, satellite dish (from English/Latin antenna)

history.meaning: present plural indicative form of the verb to be

Etymologically linked either to the squirming, wriggling motion of maggots (蛆 uji, which cluster and writhe in one spot without moving forward) or to the Late Middle Japanese root seen in うじむし (ujimushi, "maggot; spineless moping person") and うぢうぢ (udiudi), evoking someone squirming indecisively and hesitating timidly.

rootFamily.gloss: maggot, fly larva; metaphorically a spineless or wretched person (蛆虫)

Most philologists (following Yanagita Kunio and *Nihon Kokugo Daijiten*) trace it to Old Japanese うそ / をそ (uso / woso, "whistling, blowing breath lightly", seen in うそぶく usobuku "to whistle, roar, boast"), or to Classical Japanese をそ (woso, "frivolous, rash, false"). From "empty whistling / tall talk" it solidified as the primary word for a lie.

クスリ.notes: Japanese orthography creates a sharp semantic split: written in kanji as 薬 (kusuri), it means legitimate pharmacy medicine; written in katakana as クスリ (or read in reverse/on'yomi as ヤク yaku), it almost always means illegal street drugs or stimulants.

rootFamily.gloss: ring finger (literally 'medicine finger', used historically to stir/apply ointment)
illicit drugs, narcotics (slang using the Sino-Japanese reading yaku of 薬)
