クズ.etymology: Native Yamato noun 屑 (kuzu, attested since the Heian period for 'wood shavings, scraps, sawdust, dregs, waste left over from cutting or processing'). Probably related within Japonic to verbs of breaking down or crumbling, such as 崩す / 崩れる (kuzusu / kuzureru, Old Japanese kuduru 'to crumble, collapse, break into small fragments'). From physical scraps of paper, thread, or metal, it developed a harsh derogatory metaphorical sense (typically written in katakana as クズ) for a 'scumbag, lowlife, or worthless human being'.

history.meaning: wood shavings, scraps, dregs, refuse left over after cutting or crafting
waste scraps, rubbish, defective offcuts; worthless person
scum, lowlife, trashy or good-for-nothing person (derogatory katakana usage)

クズ.notes: When written in kanji or hiragana in compounds like 紙くず (kamikuzu, 'scrap paper') or 星くず (hoshikuzu, 'stardust'), it is neutral or even poetic; alone in katakana (クズ or 人間のクズ ningen no kuzu 'human scum'), it is one of the strongest everyday Japanese insults.

sources.title: Wiktionary: 屑 / くず / クズ

クソ.etymology: Native Yamato word 糞 (kuso, attested in Old Japanese as kuso 'feces, excrement, bodily discharge, dregs', already found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki of the early eighth century). Cognate across Ryukyuan languages (Proto-Japonic *kuso 'excrement, filth') and etymologically linked to the adjective 臭い (kusai, Old Japanese kusasi 'foul-smelling, stinking') and 腐る (kusaru 'to rot, putrefy'). Used both as an interjection ('Shit! / Damn!'), a derogatory adjectival noun, and an intensifying prefix meaning 'lousy, fucking, insanely'.

history.meaning: feces, excrement, bodily waste (earwax, nasal mucus, eye discharge)
excrement; vulgar exclamation of anger or contempt; disparaging prefix
lousy, damn, crap; vulgar intensifier ('extremely / fucking')

クソ.notes: Besides meaning 'crap/lousy' (e.g., クソ野郎 kusoyarō 'asshole/bastard' or クソ真面目 kusomajime 'deadly/excessively serious'), modern youth slang uses クソ as a pure degree intensifier even with positive adjectives (e.g., クソうまい kuso umai 'insanely delicious').

rootFamily.gloss: foul-smelling, stinking, fishy (derived from the same *kuso-/kusa- root)
bastard, asshole, son of a bitch (vulgar compound)
deadly serious, humorlessly earnest (pejorative intensifier compound)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 糞 / くそ / クソ

クッション.etymology: Borrowed from English cushion, which entered Middle English from Old French coissin / coussin (ultimately traced to Vulgar Latin *coxīnus, a pad for the hip or thigh, from Classical Latin coxa 'hip').

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Kotobank — クッション

クッション.notes: Distinguished from bed pillows (枕 まくら) and traditional floor cushions (座布団 ざぶとん); used for chair/sofa cushions and mechanical shock-absorbers.

クビ.etymology: Semantic extension of the native Yamato noun 首 (kubi, Old Japanese kubi 'neck, throat; severed head', from Proto-Japonic *kupi). In samurai warfare and feudal penal practice, losing one's life meant having one's head severed at the neck (首を切る kubi o kiru 'to behead' or 首が飛ぶ kubi ga tobu 'one's head flies off'). During the Meiji modernization era, this vivid decapitation imagery was transferred metaphorically to modern bureaucracy and wage labor to mean 'dismissal from employment, getting fired or sacked', now frequently written in katakana as クビ to distinguish the employment sense from the anatomical neck.

history.meaning: neck, throat; head (especially when severed in battle or execution)
to decapitate; figuratively, to dismiss a retainer or employee from service
getting fired, sacked, or dismissed from a job or position

クビ.notes: Used in core workplace idioms like クビになる ('to get fired'), クビにする ('to fire someone'), and 首が繋がる (kubi ga tsunagaru, literally 'one's neck stays attached' = 'to narrowly keep one's job').

クリア.etymology: Gairaigo loanword from English clear, borrowed in Middle English clere from Old French cler ('bright, shining, transparent, distinct'), from Classical Latin clarus ('bright, shining, loud, distinct, famous'), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh2-ro- ('sounding, bright, clear', from the root *kelh1- 'to call, shout', compare Latin calare and English claim). The Japanese verbal use クリアする ('to pass a regulatory hurdle, meet a target, or beat a video game stage') derives from the English athletic and nautical sense 'to leap over or pass an obstacle without touching it'.

history.meaning: loud, distinct; bright, shining, unclouded; renowned
transparent, unobstructed; to leap over a bar or pass an obstacle cleanly
clarity; clearing a legal/regulatory hurdle, meeting a quota, or completing a game stage

クリア.notes: In Japanese business and legal compliance (as in *The Naked Director*'s censorship battles), 条件をクリアする (jōken o kuria suru) or 審査をクリアする means 'to satisfy the conditions / pass regulatory review', not 'to erase or delete' them.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass a hurdle, satisfy a requirement, or complete a stage

rootFamily.gloss: beating a video game completely ('all clear')

クルーザー.etymology: Gairaigo loanword from English cruiser ('a fast naval warship or a large motor yacht equipped with a cabin for pleasure cruising'), borrowed in the seventeenth century from Dutch kruiser ('a ship that cruises or patrols back and forth'), an agent noun from kruisen ('to sail across, traverse zig-zag, make the sign of the cross'), derived from Middle Dutch cruce ('cross'), from Latin crux (stem cruc-, 'cross, stake'). In contemporary Japanese outside naval history, クルーザー primarily evokes a private luxury motor yacht.

history.meaning: cross (Latin) -> to sail crosswise / ship that patrols across the sea (17th-c. Dutch)
history.stage: Classical Latin to Early Modern Dutch

history.meaning: fast naval warship; cabin motorboat or yacht designed for pleasure cruising

クロス.etymology: Borrowed from two converging English words: (1) English *cloth* ('woven fabric, tablecloth', as in テーブルクロス), and (2) English *cross* ('intersecting lines, cross shape'). In café and interior contexts it commonly denotes a tablecloth or wiping cloth.

history.meaning: woven cloth (tablecloth) / cross

グ.etymology: In subtitle transcripts of The Naked Director, isolated katakana グ typically arises as a truncated stammer before a loanword (such as グッド or グループ), a guttural choke interjection (ぐっ), or a tokenizer split of the English participial suffix -ング (-ing); when used as a standalone Sino-Japanese bound noun, 具 (gu, from Middle Chinese gjuH) denotes equipment, a tool, or ingredients.

history.meaning: to prepare, furnish; utensil, implement
tool, means, ingredient; or truncated katakana speech particle/fragment

グ.notes: When encountered as a bare katakana token in raw Japanese drama subtitles, グ is almost always a cut-off syllable or a segmentation artifact rather than a true grammatical particle.

グッド.etymology: Borrowed from English good, which descends from Middle English good and Old English gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz ('fitting, suitable, good'), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʰedʰ- ('to unite, fit together, be associated'). In Japanese media and colloquial speech, it functions both as a punchy interjection of approval and as a prefixal modifier.

history.meaning: fitting, suitable, advantageous
virtuous, desirable, satisfactory
good, great, spot-on (interjection and modifier)

グッド.notes: Often paired with a thumbs-up gesture in showbiz and 1980s Japanese slang, or combined in pseudo-anglicisms and set phrases like グッドタイミング ('good timing').

cognates.meaning: glass (borrowed earlier into Japanese as ガラス)

グラス.etymology: Borrowed from English glass, from Middle English glas and Old English glæs ('glass, glass vessel'), from Proto-Germanic *glasą ('amber, glass'), derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʰel- ('to shine, gleam'). Modern Japanese distinguishes this Meiji-and-later English loan グラス ('drinking glass, stemware') from the earlier Edo-period Dutch loan ガラス (from Dutch glas), which refers to the raw material or windowpane glass.

history.meaning: shining substance, amber, glass
glass material; glass drinking vessel
drinking glass, tumbler, wineglass

グラス.notes: Be careful not to confuse グラス (a drinking glass or cup) with ガラス (glass as a material, such as a windowpane or broken glass): dropping a グラス scatters ガラス on the floor.

グラニュー糖.etymology: Hybrid Meiji culinary compound clipping English granulated (sugar) to グラニュー and attaching Sino-Japanese 糖 (とう, 'sugar').
グラニュー糖.notes: Refers to fine, dry, free-flowing white crystals prized in pastry baking.

グランドオープン.etymology: Modern Japanese commercial borrowing from English grand opening, clipped at the end from -ing to base オープン (ōpun) in accordance with standard Japanese loanword morphology (compare ハッピーエンド for 'happy ending'). It specifically designates the official public opening of a newly built or renovated shop, café, or inn, as distinct from a preview or soft opening (プレオープン).

history.meaning: official ceremonial opening of a business

history.form: グランドオープン (gurando ōpun)
history.meaning: official grand opening of a store or venue

グループ.etymology: Borrowed from English group (or French groupe), which entered English via French groupe from Italian gruppo ('knot, cluster, sculpted ensemble'), itself borrowed from a Germanic source akin to Proto-Germanic *kruppaz ('lump, round mass, crop'). In post-war Japanese corporate terminology, グループ acquired the specialized sense of an affiliated conglomerate or keiretsu network of companies.

cluster of figures in art; assemblage of people
group, clique; corporate conglomerate

グレーズ.etymology: The term 'グレーズ' (meaning 'glaze') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

ケガ人.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound written 怪我人 (keganin), combining 怪我 (kega, 'injury, wound, accident') with the suffix 人 (-nin, 'person', go-on reading of Middle Chinese nyin). Originally in medieval Japanese Buddhist and court usage, 怪我 (literally 'strange/blameworthy' + 'self') meant an unexpected spiritual defilement, blunder, or unintended fault, before narrowing during the Edo period to physical bodily injury.

history.meaning: unexpected fault, ritual defilement, accidental error
bodily wound, accidental injury
injured person, casualty

morphemes.meaning: unexpected fault, bodily injury (from 怪 'strange/fault' + 我 'self')

ケーキ.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English cake, itself borrowed in Middle English from Old Norse kaka ('flat round loaf or sweet cake', cognate with German Kuchen and Dutch koek).

history.meaning: baked loaf or sweetened pastry
Western-style sponge or cream cake

ケーキ.notes: Specifically denotes Western patisserie (洋菓子) cakes such as ショートケーキ and チーズケーキ, contrasting with traditional Japanese sweets (和菓子).

ケース.etymology: Borrowed from English case ('container, receptacle, protective box'), which entered Middle English from Anglo-Norman casse, ultimately from Latin capsa ('box, repository for scrolls', from capere 'to hold, take'). Note that English has two homophonous words 'case', and Japanese ケース borrowed both: this sense ('box, violin case, display case', from Latin capsa) and the sense 'instance, situation' (from Latin casus).

history.meaning: box, chest, container
protective container or glass cabinet
case, carrying box, display cabinet

ケース.notes: Common in compounds such as バイオリンのケース ('violin case'), ペンケース ('pencil case'), and ショーケース ('display case').

ゲス.etymology: Derived from the medieval Sino-Japanese administrative title 下司 (geshi or gesu, from 下 'lower' + 司 'official'), which designated a low-ranking steward on a Heian or Kamakura manor (shōen). Through folk association with 下種 ('low seed, base birth') and 下衆 ('common rabble'), the term shifted from low social rank to moral baseness, meaning a vulgar, greedy, or sleazy person.

history.meaning: subordinate manor steward or petty official
person of humble birth, menial servant
sleazy, vulgar, lowlife scum

ゲス.notes: Often written in katakana as ゲス (or expanded into the colloquial i-adjective ゲスい, 'sleazy, trashy') and preserved in the classic proverb 下衆の勘ぐり ('a lowlife always suspects others of base motives').

ゲーム.etymology: Borrowed from English game, from Middle English game, gamen and Old English gamen ('joy, mirth, sport, pastime'), descending from Proto-Germanic *gamaną ('fellowship, merriment, sport'). Adopted into Japanese initially for Western athletic matches and parlor games, it became the default term for arcade and home video games from the late 1970s onward, as well as figurative 'power games' in business.

history.meaning: joy, communal merriment, amusement
amusement, athletic contest, game of rules
athletic match, parlor game; video game; strategic contest

ゲーム.notes: By itself in modern Japanese, ゲーム defaults strongly to video or arcade games (originally called テレビゲーム), though in sports and business drama contexts it also means a match or high-stakes scheme.

コク.etymology: Culinary and sensory noun コク (originally written 濃く or 酷 'richness, body, depth of flavor'), derived from the Sino-Japanese noun 酷 (*koku* 'intense, ripe to the fullest degree', or the adverbial stem 濃く *koku* of 濃い 'thick, rich, strong'). Often written in katakana in modern food writing.

history.meaning: full-bodied ripeness and depth of taste in sake or broth
richness; body; depth of flavor

コケる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) Ichidan verb 転ける (kokeru), evolving from the classical Shimo-Nidan verb こく (koku, 'to fall over, tumble down'), which shares a common sound-symbolic root *koro- / *koko- with 転ぶ (korobu, 'to roll over, tumble') and 転がる (korogaru). Originally describing a physical stumble, it developed a vivid metaphorical sense in Kansai entertainment and showbiz slang for a joke, film, or venture 'falling flat on its face' or flopping commercially.

to trip, stumble, lose one's footing

コケる.notes: When written in katakana as コケる in entertainment or business dialogue, it almost always carries the figurative sense of a movie, product, or pitch bombing at the box office.

コップ.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch kop (or Portuguese copo) during the early modern trade era to name a tumbler or drinking cup without a handle.

コミュニケーション.etymology: Borrowed from English communication, which entered Middle English via Old French comunicacion from Latin commūnicātiō ('a sharing, imparting'), noun of action from commūnicāre ('to share, make common, impart'), itself derived from commūnis ('shared by all, common, public'). In Japanese, it denotes interpersonal rapport and mutual understanding rather than physical telecommunications infrastructure.

サイズ.etymology: Borrowed from English *size* ('dimensions, magnitude, garment/portion measurement'), shortened in Middle English from *assize* ('fixed standard or measure', from Old French *assise*).

サナギ.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) word 蛹 (sanagi, attested in Heian-period lexicons such as the Shinsen Jikyō and Wamyō Ruijushō). Traditional Japanese philology connects it either to the ancient word さなぎ (sanagi, an iron or bronze clapper/bell, due to the spindle-shaped cocoon or chrysalis resembling an archaic dōtaku bronze bell) or analyzes it as prefix さ- (sa-) + 成ぎ (nagi, related to 成る naru 'to become, transform into adult form'). The kanji 蛹 is a semantic-phonetic compound of 虫 ('insect') and 甬 ('cylindrical bell/sprouting').

Because Japanese lacks grammatical articles, ザ (za) was repurposed in showbiz titles and colloquial speech as an emphatic prefix meaning 'the quintessential, the ultimate, the classic'.

From the Edo period onward, tekiya (street peddlers), bakuto (gamblers), and modern yakuza adopted シマ to denote a gang's exclusive turf or protection-racket territory.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — スタイル

スタジオ.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century from English studio, which was itself borrowed from Italian studio ('study, workroom of an artist'), from Latin studium ('zeal, study, place of study', from studēre 'to be diligent'). In Japanese it denotes an artist's, designer's, or architect's workshop as well as a music, photography, or broadcast studio.

history.meaning: study room, artist's workshop
artist's workroom, recording or design room
studio, design or music workroom

スタジオ.notes: Used especially for creative, acoustic, photography, and architectural workspaces.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — スタジオ

cognates.meaning: artist's or filmmaker's workroom; recording facility

スタジオ代.etymology: A hybrid compound combining the gairaigo noun スタジオ (sutajio, from English studio, borrowed from Italian studio 'study, artist's workroom', from Latin studium 'zeal, eagerness, study', related to studēre 'to be diligent') with the Sino-Japanese (kango) suffix 代 (-dai, Middle Chinese *dojH, originally 'to substitute, replace', hence 'money paid in exchange for goods or services; fee, rental charge').

history.meaning: zeal, study → artist's workroom → film or recording studio
history.stage: Latin and Italian to Modern Japanese (first element)

history.meaning: generation, substitution → price, fee, charge paid in exchange
studio rental fee; cost of hiring a shooting or recording studio

morphemes.meaning: fee, charge, price paid in exchange (MC *dojH)

スタジオ代.notes: The suffix 〜代 (-dai) is highly productive with both native and loanword nouns to denote everyday bills and rental costs (e.g., 部屋代 room rent, タクシー代 taxi fare, スタジオ代 studio fee).

cognates.meaning: body of employees; rod or baton of office
rod, baton; military or organizational staff

スタッフ.etymology: Borrowed from English staff ('body of assistants or crew working under a director or manager'), a semantic extension from military usage ('group of officers assisting a commander'), which in turn derives from the concrete sense 'baton of office, walking stick, wooden pole' (Old English stæf, from Proto-Germanic *stabaz, PIE *stebh- 'post, pillar, to support').

history.meaning: wooden pole, walking stick → baton of authority → body of officers or personnel
history.stage: Proto-Germanic and Old English to Modern English

history.meaning: production crew, behind-the-scenes personnel, staff member

スタッフ.notes: Whereas English 'staff' is a collective noun (you cannot say 'a staff' for one person), Japanese スタッフ refers both to the collective crew and to an individual crew member, and on film sets contrasts directly with キャスト (kyasuto, 'cast/actors').

cognates.meaning: state of readiness to act; standing by

スタンバイ.etymology: Borrowed from the English noun and phrasal verb standby / stand by, originally a nautical command meaning 'to stand near a rope, sail, or station ready for immediate action', composed of stand (from Old English standan, Proto-Germanic *standaną, PIE *steh₂- 'to stand') and by (from Old English bī 'near, beside'). In Japanese broadcasting and film sets, it denotes positioning equipment and performers for immediate shooting.

history.meaning: to stand near → to remain ready for immediate action on ship or set
standing by on set; preparing cameras and actors to roll

morphemes.meaning: to stand, remain in position (from English stand)
near, ready at hand (from English by)

スタンバイ.notes: On Japanese film sets, スタンバイ (frequently shortened to スタンバる, sutanbaru, an inflecting godan verb meaning 'to get in position and wait ready') is the standard call before the director yells スタート (Action!).

rootFamily.gloss: to stand by, get ready in position (colloquial verb)

cognates.meaning: beginning of a race or action; sudden movement

スタート.etymology: Borrowed from English start ('beginning of a race, journey, or operation'), which developed in Middle English sterten ('to leap, bound, rush suddenly') from Old English styrtan ('to leap up, jerk'), from Proto-Germanic *sturtijaną ('to overturn, rush, dash'). In Japanese film and television directing, スタート! (or 本番スタート!) is the cue equivalent to English 'Action!'.

history.meaning: to rush or leap suddenly → beginning of a race or action
start, beginning; director's cue 'Action!' on a film set

スタート.notes: While Hollywood directors call 'Action!', Japanese directors traditionally call 「よーい、スタート！」 (Yōi, sutāto! — 'Ready, start!') or 「本番、スタート！」 to begin a take.

rootFamily.gloss: fresh start, restart (cutting a new start)

スタート地点.etymology: A hybrid compound joining the gairaigo noun スタート (sutāto, from English start 'beginning, commencement', Middle English sterten 'to leap, set out') with the Sino-Japanese (kango) noun 地点 (chiten, 'geographical spot, point, position'), which combines 地 (chi, Middle Chinese *dijH, 'earth, ground, place') and 点 (ten, Middle Chinese *temX, 'black fleck, dot, exact point').

history.meaning: beginning of a race or endeavor
specific point on the ground; location or spot
starting point, point of departure (literal or figurative)

スタート地点.notes: Frequently used figuratively in phrases like スタート地点に立つ ('to stand at the starting point') to describe finally qualifying or getting ready to begin a career or venture.

ステキ.etymology: Katakana rendering of 素敵 (suteki, 'lovely, wonderful, superb'), a late Edo-period colloquialism written with the ateji characters 素 ('bare, sheer') and 敵 ('rival, match, -like'). Etymologists generally derive it either from the native intensifying prefix す- (su-, 'utterly, extremely', or a clipping of すばらしい subarashii 'splendid') combined with the Sino-Japanese adjectival suffix -的 (-teki), or from すでき (su-deki, 'superb execution/workmanship'). Originally meaning 'extreme, outrageous, staggering in scale' in Edo vernacular, it narrowed in the Meiji era to positive aesthetic admiration ('lovely, charming, dashing').

history.meaning: extreme, staggering, beyond compare (often of scale or degree)
lovely, wonderful, charming, attractive

morphemes.meaning: target, -like; or matchless (ateji 敵 / 的)

ステキ.notes: Writing ステキ in katakana instead of kanji 素敵 is very common in scripts, magazines, and dialogue to convey a breezy, upbeat, or slightly theatrical conversational tone.

cognates.meaning: pace of the foot; stage in a process; dance movement

ステップ.etymology: Borrowed from English step ('movement of the foot in walking or dancing; stage in a graded progression'), from Middle English step, Old English stæpe / stepe ('pace, footprint, stair'), from Proto-Germanic *stapiz ('step, pace'), derived from the verb *stapjaną ('to tread, step'). In Japanese it encompasses physical dance steps, stairs/footrests, and developmental stages.

history.meaning: footstep, pace, stair → stage in a process or dance movement
dance step; stage or phase in a plan or career

morphemes.meaning: step, stage, dance pace (from English step)

ステップ.notes: Productive in the common wasei-eigo expression ステップアップ (suteppu-appu, 'advancing to the next stage, career progression, leveling up').

rootFamily.word: ステップバイステップ

cognates.meaning: thick slice of meat or fish for grilling or frying

ステーキ.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English steak ('thick slice of beef or other meat for broiling or frying'), which Middle English borrowed in the 15th century from Old Norse steik ('roast meat'), related to the Old Norse verb steikja ('to roast on a spit') and stikna ('to be roasted, scorched'), from Proto-Germanic *staikō (likely connected to *stikōną 'to stick, pierce with a spit').

history.meaning: meat roasted on a spit → thick slice of beef for grilling or frying
Western-style grilled beef steak (or thick-cut fish/pork steak)

ステーキ.notes: In Japan's postwar Rapid Economic Growth and 1980s Bubble eras, eating a thick beef ステーキ (or ビフテキ bifuteki, an older borrowing from French bifteck) was the ultimate culinary symbol of affluence, stamina, and celebratory success.

rootFamily.gloss: beefsteak (older Meiji/Shōwa loan from French bifteck)

cognates.meaning: raised platform for performance; phase or degree in a process
floor/story of a building; training period

ステージ.etymology: Borrowed from English stage ('raised platform for theatrical or musical performance; phase of development'), from Middle English stage, via Old French estage ('dwelling, story of a building, raised platform'), from Vulgar Latin *staticum ('standing place, station'), derived from Latin stāre ('to stand', from PIE *steh₂- 'to stand').

history.meaning: to stand → standing place → story of a building or raised platform
theatrical platform; phase or level in a progression
performance stage, show set; career or medical stage/level

ステージ.notes: In Japanese nightlife, cabaret, and strip theaters, ステージ refers both to the physical platform and to a single scheduled performance set (e.g., 1日4ステージ, 'four shows a day').

cognates.meaning: cessation of motion; to block or halt

ストップ.etymology: Borrowed from English stop ('halt, cessation of movement or operation'), from Middle English stoppen ('to block up, dam, bring to a halt'), from Old English *stoppian (attested in compounds like forstoppian 'to plug up, stifle'), an early West Germanic borrowing from Late Latin stuppāre ('to plug or caulk with tow'), from Latin stuppa ('coarse flax fiber, tow'), from Ancient Greek stúppē.

history.meaning: coarse flax tow → to plug a hole with tow → to block or dam up
to obstruct → to halt motion; cessation of activity
halt, stop, suspension of action or filming

ストップ.notes: Functions as a noun, an interjection ('Stop!'), and a suru-verb (ストップする, 'to come to a halt / be suspended'), as well as in idioms like ストップをかける ('to put a stop to, intervene to halt').

ストライキ状態.etymology: A hybrid compound combining the gairaigo noun ストライキ (sutoraiki, a Meiji-period borrowing of English strike 'organized labor walkout', which originated in 1768 London sailors 'striking' or lowering their ships' sails in refusal to go to sea, from Old English strīcan 'to stroke, rub, move') with the Sino-Japanese (kango) noun 状態 (jōtai, 'state, condition'), composed of 状 (jō, Middle Chinese *dzjangH, 'form, appearance, circumstance') and 態 (tai, Middle Chinese *thojH, 'posture, bearing, condition').

history.meaning: to stroke/lower sails → labor walkout (adapted with -ki vs baseball ストライク)
history.stage: Old English to Meiji Japanese (first element)

history.meaning: appearance and posture; current condition or state of affairs
state of being on strike; work stoppage or boycott condition

ストライキ状態.notes: Japanese splits English 'strike' into two distinct loanwords by meaning: ストライキ (sutoraiki, often clipped to スト) means a labor strike or walkout, whereas ストライク (sutoraiku) is used for a baseball or bowling strike!

rootFamily.gloss: labor strike (often abbreviated to スト)

ストリップ.etymology: Borrowed in the postwar Allied Occupation era as a clipping of American English striptease or strip show, from the English verb strip ('to remove clothing, lay bare'), from Middle English stripen, Old English *strīepan (attested in bestrīepan 'to plunder, despoil, strip of possessions'), from Proto-Germanic *straupijaną ('to pull off, skin, pluck'). In Japanese, ストリップ alone regularly denotes an erotic striptease performance or theater.

history.meaning: to pull off or plunder → to undress → erotic burlesque dance removing clothes
striptease, strip show, burlesque theater

morphemes.meaning: striptease, strip show (clipped from English striptease)

ストリップ.notes: Introduced to Tokyo in 1947 with the famous 'frame show' at the Teitoza in Shinjuku, ストリップ劇場 (strip theaters) became a major grass-roots entertainment circuit across postwar Shōwa Japan.

ストレート.etymology: Borrowed from English straight ('uncurved, direct, candid; undiluted liquor; straight fastball in baseball'), which originated in Middle English streight as the past participle of strecchen ('to stretch'), from Old English streht (past participle of streccan 'to stretch out at full length'), from Proto-Germanic *strakjaną ('to make taut or rigid').

history.meaning: stretched taut → uncurved, direct, frank, undiluted
direct, frank, straightforward; baseball fastball; neat/unmixed drink; straight-sets win

ストレート.notes: Besides functioning as a na-adjective (ストレートな表現, 'a blunt/direct expression'), ストレート is the standard Japanese baseball term for a four-seam fastball and the bar term for whisky served neat or tea without milk.

rootFamily.gloss: straight tea (black tea served without milk or lemon)

ストーリー.etymology: Borrowed from English story ('narrative account, plotline of a work'), which came via Anglo-Norman estorie and Old French estoire ('chronicle, narrative, picture') from Latin historia ('history, account, tale'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek historía ('inquiry, knowledge acquired by investigation, narrative'), from hístōr ('wise man, witness, judge', from PIE *weyd- 'to see, know').

history.meaning: inquiry, historical account → narrative tale or dramatic plotline
history.stage: Ancient Greek and Latin to Modern English

history.meaning: plot, storyline, narrative arc of a film, novel, or campaign

ストーリー.notes: In Japanese film and media criticism, ストーリー specifically emphasizes the plot structure or dramatic arc (as in ストーリー性がある, 'having a strong storyline/plot', a crucial point of debate in 1980s adult video production).

rootFamily.gloss: narrative quality, presence of a real plotline

スピーチ.etymology: Borrowed from English *speech* ('formal address or talk delivered to an audience'), from Old English *spǣċ*.

history.meaning: public talk or celebratory address
speech; formal address

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — スピーチ

スピード.etymology: Borrowed from English speed ('velocity, rapidity of movement or action'), which evolved from Middle English spede and Old English spēd ('success, prosperity, wealth, quickness'), from Proto-Germanic *spōdiz ('success, thriving'), derived from the verb *spōaną ('to succeed, prosper', from PIE *speh₁- 'to thrive, expand'). The semantic shift from 'good fortune/success' to 'swiftness' occurred in Middle English.

history.meaning: prosperity, success → quickness, rate of motion, velocity
history.stage: Proto-Germanic and Old English to Modern English

history.meaning: speed, velocity; rapid pace of execution

スピード.notes: Used as an attributive modifier in punchy Japanese media compounds to mean 'whirlwind' or 'rapid-fire', such as スピード結婚 ('whirlwind marriage'), スピード解決 ('rapid resolution'), and スピード違反 ('speeding violation').

rootFamily.gloss: speeding violation, exceeding the speed limit

スプーン.etymology: Borrowed from English *spoon* ('utensil with a shallow bowl on a handle'), from Old English *spōn* ('chip or sliver of wood').

history.meaning: eating and stirring utensil
spoon

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — スプーン

スペシャル.etymology: Borrowed from English special ('distinguished from what is ordinary, exceptional; special television broadcast or menu item'), from Middle English special, via Old French especial from Latin speciālis ('individual, particular, belonging to a specific kind'), derived from speciēs ('appearance, form, kind, sort'), from specere ('to look at, behold', PIE *spek- 'to observe').

history.meaning: appearance, kind → belonging to a particular sort → exceptional, extraordinary
history.stage: Latin and Old French to Modern English

history.meaning: special, deluxe; special edition or feature-length television broadcast

スペシャル.notes: Functions both as a na-adjective (スペシャルな体験, 'a special experience') and as a standalone noun for a feature-length TV broadcast (テレビスペシャル) or deluxe service package.

スポンジ.etymology: Borrowed from English sponge, descending through Old English spunge and Latin spongia from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá, 'sea sponge'). Earlier sixteenth-century Christian-century missionaries had also introduced Portuguese esponja as カステラ-related ボウロ vocabulary.

history.meaning: porous marine sponge
cleaning sponge; aerated sponge cake
washing sponge; sponge cake base

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Kotobank — スポンジ

スポンジ.notes: Does double duty in Japanese cafés and bakeries for both dishwashing/window sponges and airy cake layers (スポンジ生地).

cognates.meaning: matching set of garments (jacket and trousers)

スーツ.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji/Taishō era from English suit (specifically a suit of clothes, with final /-t/ adapted as ツ -tsu or reflecting plural suits), which derives from Middle English sute ('matching set, livery, retinue'), from Anglo-Norman siwte and Old French suite ('act of following, attendance, matching set of garments'), from Vulgar Latin *sequita, feminine past participle of *sequere (Classical Latin sequī 'to follow, accompany', PIE *sekʷ- 'to follow').

history.meaning: to follow → retinue of followers → uniform livery worn by a retinue
history.stage: Latin to Old French and Anglo-Norman

history.meaning: matching set of outer garments (jacket and trousers/skirt)
Western business suit or tailored two/three-piece outfit (singular or plural)

スーツ.notes: Although スーツ ends in ツ (-tsu) and looks like an English plural, it is completely singular in Japanese (one business suit is 一着のスーツ); the same French/Latin root entered Japanese separately as スイート (suīto, 'hotel suite').

rootFamily.gloss: wearing a business suit, dressed in a suit
job-hunting suit worn by university graduates (wasei-eigo)

スーツケース.etymology: Borrowed from English suitcase ('flat-sided Rectangular travel bag'), combining スーツ ('suit') and ケース ('case').

history.meaning: hinged travel case
suitcase

スープ.etymology: Borrowed from English *soup* (and French *soupe*), referring mainly to Western-style or Chinese-style soups in contrast to traditional Japanese 汁 (しる / みそ汁).

history.meaning: savory liquid dish
soup; broth

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — スープ

ズバリ.etymology: Katakana spelling of the native Japanese (wago) mimetic/ideophonic adverb ずばり (zubari), formed from the voiced onomatopoeic root zuba- (evoking the sound and sensation of slicing cleanly through an object in a single decisive stroke, the rendaku/voiced intensive counterpart of suba- as in すばやく subayaku 'swiftly') plus the adverbial suffix -ri (indicating a completed, crisp state). From 'cutting cleanly in one stroke', it developed the figurative sense 'hitting the nail on the head, speaking frankly and straight to the core'.

history.meaning: slicing cleanly through in a single decisive stroke
precisely on the mark; frankly, bluntly, straight to the point

morphemes.meaning: decisive, clean, single-stroke cut or strike (voiced intensive of suba-)
state or manner resulting from a crisp action

ズバリ.notes: Often printed in katakana (ズバリ!) in television titles, magazine headlines, and sales pitches (e.g., ズバリ言うわよ！ 'I'll tell you straight!') to project bold, no-nonsense candor.

rootFamily.gloss: repeatedly speaking bluntly or slashing cleanly (mimetic reduplication)
falling cleanly into place, fitting snugly and decisively
quick, nimble, swift (voiceless counterpart root suba-)

セクシー.etymology: Borrowed in the postwar Shōwa period from English sexy ('sexually attractive, alluring, glamorous'), which was coined in early 20th-century English (first attested around 1912–1925) from the noun sex (from Latin sexus 'male or female division') plus the adjectival suffix -y. In Japanese, it functions as a na-adjective covering a wide spectrum from mildly glamorous or alluring to overtly erotic.

history.meaning: preoccupied with sex → sexually attractive, glamorous, appealing
sexy, glamorous, seductive, alluring

セクシー.notes: In Japanese media and broadcasting, セクシー is frequently used as a polite or upbeat euphemism where English would use 'erotic' or 'adult' (for example, セクシー女優 sekushī joyū is the standard mainstream media term for an adult video actress).

rootFamily.gloss: adult video actress (lit. 'sexy actress', standard media euphemism)

セックス.etymology: Borrowed from English sex, which entered Middle English from Old French sexe and Latin sexus ('state of being either male or female, gender division'), traditionally connected to the Latin verb secāre ('to cut, divide', from PIE *sek- 'to cut', denoting the division of living beings into male and female halves). While early 20th-century Japanese academic usage occasionally used セックス for biological gender, in everyday modern Japanese it refers almost exclusively to sexual intercourse (clipped from English sexual intercourse).

history.meaning: division into male and female → sexual relations and intercourse (20th c.)
history.stage: Latin and Old French to Modern English

history.meaning: sexual intercourse, sexual relations (and in compounds, sex/gender)

セックス.notes: Important false friend of scope: in standalone Japanese conversation, セックス means 'sexual intercourse' (with セックスする meaning 'to have sex'), whereas 'biological sex/gender' on forms is expressed with the Sino-Japanese word 性別 (seibetsu).

cognates.meaning: sitting of an assembly; period of musical performance or recording
sitting, session of a court or assembly

セッション.etymology: Borrowed from English session ('period devoted to a particular activity', especially a musical jam session or recording session), from Middle English sessioun, via Old French session from Latin sessiō (stem sessiōn-, 'a sitting, seat, conference'), a action noun from sedēre ('to sit', past participle sessus, from PIE *sed- 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit → formal sitting of an assembly → collaborative musical or studio period
history.stage: Latin and Old French to Modern English

history.meaning: musical jam session, studio recording or photo session; parliamentary session

セッション.notes: In Japanese popular culture, セッション (and the verb セッションする) most commonly refers to musicians playing or improvising together in a jam session, or a photographer and model collaborating in a photo shoot.

rootFamily.word: レコーディングセッション

セット.etymology: Borrowed from English *set* ('matched group of items; setting up equipment or hair; fixed-menu combination').

history.meaning: matching collection; arrangement
set; combo meal; setting up

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — セット

セリフ.etymology: Native Edo-period theatrical noun 台詞・科白 (せりふ 'actor's spoken lines on stage, remark'), derived from 競り言ふ (*seri-iu* 'speaking in turn / vying in speech') or 世流布 (*serufu*). Often written in katakana セリフ in modern prose.

history.meaning: spoken dialogue on stage
lines (in a play/film); remark

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 台詞

cognates.meaning: faculty of perception; sound judgment or aesthetic flair

センス.etymology: Borrowed from English sense (or French sens), via Middle French sens from Latin sēnsus ('faculty of perception, feeling, understanding, frame of mind'), derived from the verb sentīre ('to feel, perceive', from PIE *sent- 'to head for, feel'). In Japanese, the word underwent semantic specialization from English phrases like good sense, fashion sense, and sense of humor to denote 'aesthetic taste, artistic flair, intuitive knack, or style'.

history.meaning: to feel/perceive → faculty of perception → sound judgment or aesthetic discernment
history.stage: Latin and French to Modern English

history.meaning: aesthetic taste, flair, style, intuitive knack for fashion, humor, or art

morphemes.meaning: aesthetic taste, flair, sense (from English sense)

センス.notes: A classic false friend for English speakers: センスがいい (sensu ga ii) does NOT mean 'sensible / practical', but rather 'stylish, tasteful, having great artistic or creative flair' (while the physical 'five senses' are 五感 gokan).

rootFamily.gloss: nonsense, absurd, lacking taste or logic

センチ.etymology: Clipped loanword from French *centimètre* / English *centimeter* (センチメートル 'centimeter, one-hundredth of a meter', from Latin *centum* 'hundred' + *mètre*). Also used as a clipping of センチメンタル (*sentimental*).

history.meaning: one-hundredth of a meter
centimeter (clipped form)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — センチ

セーター.etymology: Borrowed from English *sweater* ('knitted pullover garment', originally athletic wear designed to induce sweating, from *sweat* + *-er*), with simplification of the *sw-* cluster to *s-* in Japanese.

history.meaning: knitted upper-body garment
sweater; jumper

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — セーター

cognates.meaning: sale, handing over in exchange for payment

セールス.etymology: Borrowed from English sales (the plural of sale, used attributively in terms like sales department and sales representative), from Middle English sale, Late Old English sala ('act of selling'), borrowed from Old Norse sala ('sale, delivery of goods'), from Proto-Germanic *salō ('handing over, sale'), related to the verb *saljaną ('to hand over, deliver, sell'). In Japanese, セールス specifically denotes active commercial selling, canvassing, or door-to-door sales pitching.

history.meaning: handing over of goods → commercial selling and sales operations
history.stage: Proto-Germanic and Old Norse to Modern English

history.meaning: commercial selling, sales pitching, door-to-door canvassing

セールス.notes: Note the sharp distinction in Japanese between singular セール (sēru, 'a discount bargain sale at a store') and plural-derived セールス (sērusu, 'active selling, pitching to clients, or door-to-door sales').

cognates.meaning: persuasive speech used to sell a product; sales pitch

セールストーク.etymology: Borrowed from English sales talk ('persuasive speech or patter used by a salesperson to convince a prospective buyer'), a compound of sales (plural of sale, from Old Norse sala 'sale, transaction', Proto-Germanic *salō) and talk (from Middle English talken 'to speak, converse', a frequentative verb formed with -k- from Old English talian 'to reckon, recount' and talu 'tale, speech', Proto-Germanic *talō).

history.form: sala + talu → sales + talk → sales talk
history.meaning: transaction + speech → persuasive patter used by a salesperson
history.stage: Old Norse and Old English to Modern English

history.meaning: sales pitch, persuasive patter, smooth commercial spiel

セールストーク.notes: Used both literally for a salesperson's polished pitch (as in Toru Muranishi's legendary encyclopedia-selling patter) and figuratively for any smooth, self-promoting flattery or persuasive spiel.

rootFamily.gloss: talk show; conversational skill or patter
conversational skill, gift of gab (lit. 'talk power')

セールスマン.etymology: Borrowed from English salesman, a compound of sales (plural of sale, from Late Old English sala, borrowed from Old Norse sala, "sale, vending") and man (from Old English mann, "person, adult male", from Proto-Germanic *mann-). Adopted into Japanese during the post-WWII economic recovery to denote commission-based and door-to-door sales representatives.

history.meaning: transaction of goods + person
person whose occupation is selling goods
salesman, commercial sales representative

morphemes.meaning: sales, selling of goods (from English sales)

セールスマン.notes: In postwar Showa Japan, セールスマン strongly evoked door-to-door or quota-driven field sellers (like Toru Muranishi's early career selling English encyclopedias), whereas modern corporate contexts increasingly prefer 営業マン (eigyouman) or gender-neutral 営業担当 (eigyou tantou).

ゼロ.etymology: Borrowed from French *zéro* / English *zero* ('the number 0, nothing'), ultimately via Italian *zero* and Medieval Latin *zephirum* from Arabic صِفْر (*ṣifr* 'empty, zero').

history.meaning: naught; the numeral 0
zero; nothing

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ゼロ

タイトル.etymology: Borrowed from English title, from Middle English title, borrowed from Old French title ("inscription, heading, chapter"), from Latin titulus ("inscription on a tomb or altar, label, notice, title of honor"). In Japanese, it designates the name of a creative work (film, book, adult video release) as well as a sports or game championship.

history.meaning: inscription, label, notice, title of honor
name of a book or work; championship; rank
title of a work; championship title

タイトル.notes: While タイトル is used for books, movies, songs, and sports championships, a person's professional or aristocratic job title is never タイトル—use 肩書き (katagaki) or 役職 (yakushoku) instead.

タイプ.etymology: Borrowed from English type, from Middle French type, from Latin typus ("figure, image, form, kind"), from Ancient Greek tupos (τύπος, "impression, cast, die-mark, model, general form"), derived from the verb tupto (τύπτω, "to strike, beat"). In Japanese, besides "category" and "typewriter typing", it underwent colloquial narrowing to mean someone matching one's romantic or physical ideal.

history.meaning: impression struck by a die, figure, model
figure, image, representative form or class
category, model; one's romantic ideal; typing

morphemes.meaning: type, kind, romantic ideal (from English type)

タイプ.notes: Used predicatively in sentences like 彼女は僕のタイプだ ("She's my type"), タイプ alone without a qualifier almost always refers to romantic or aesthetic attraction in everyday conversation.

タイマー.etymology: Borrowed from English *timer* ('device that measures elapsed time and signals when a set interval ends', agent noun from *time*).

history.meaning: time-measuring and alarm device
timer (kitchen timer, automatic switch)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タイマー

cognates.meaning: limited space of time, season, occasion

タイミング.etymology: Borrowed from English timing, the verbal noun of time (from Middle English time, from Old English tima, "limited space of time, proper occasion", from Proto-Germanic *timo-, from PIE *di-mon-, suffixed form of root *da-, "to divide, cut up") + gerund suffix -ing. In Japanese, it broadened from sports/mechanical synchronization to mean any opportune moment or juncture in daily life.

history.meaning: measured period, season, proper occasion
selection or regulation of the exact moment for an action
timing, opportune moment, juncture

タイミング.notes: Japanese speakers use タイミング where English speakers would say "moment" or "time", as in どのタイミングで言えばいい？ ("When / At what moment should I bring it up?").

タイム.etymology: Borrowed from English thyme (/taɪm/), which descended via Old French thym and Latin thymus from Ancient Greek θύμον (thúmon, 'thyme', related to θύω thúō, 'to burn as fragrant incense'). Introduced into Japanese Western-style cooking (洋食) and kitchen gardening from the Meiji and Taishō eras onward alongside its native botanical name 立麝香草 (tachijakōsō, 'upright musk-herb').

history.meaning: fragrant Mediterranean culinary herb
aromatic herb Thymus vulgaris
culinary thyme

タイム.notes: Homophonous in Japanese with タイム from English 'time', but clear from culinary context.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タイム

タイムカプセル.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from American English time capsule, a compound coined in 1938 for the Westinghouse container buried at the 1939 New York World's Fair (from time + capsule, Latin capsula 'little box'). In Japan, the concept became extraordinarily popular after the Expo '70 time capsule was buried at Osaka Castle Park in 1970, making buried school and neighbourhood time capsules a beloved tradition.

history.meaning: sealed container of mementos buried for future opening
time capsule

cognates.meaning: container preserving items for a future date

タイムカプセル.notes: Osaka holds a special link to the word in Japan because the famous Expo '70 Time Capsule remains buried in front of Osaka Castle.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タイムカプセル

タイヤ.etymology: Borrowed from English *tire* / *tyre* ('rubber covering placed around a wheel rim').

history.meaning: rubber wheel tread
tire

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タイヤ

タイル.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for tile. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: tile

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タイル

タオル.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji period from English *towel* ('absorbent cloth for drying'), from Old French *toaille*. Primarily denotes Western-style looped cotton terrycloth towels in contrast to flat woven 手拭い (*tenugui*).

history.meaning: absorbent drying cloth
towel

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タオル

タクシー.etymology: Borrowed in the Taishō era from English taxi, itself clipped from taximeter cab.

history.meaning: taxicab
taxi

タバコ.etymology: An early Nanban (Southern Barbarian) loanword borrowed in the late 16th century (Azuchi-Momoyama period) from Portuguese tabaco ("tobacco plant, rolled tobacco leaves"), from Spanish tabaco, borrowed from Taino (Arawakan) tabako ("roll of dried tobacco leaves" or "Y-shaped sniffing pipe"). Historically written in Japanese with the semantic ateji 煙草 ("smoke-herb") or 莨.

history.meaning: roll of cured tobacco leaves; medicinal/smoking herb
cut tobacco smoked in a kiseru pipe
cigarette; tobacco products generally

タバコ.notes: Unlike modern katakana loanwords from English, タバコ is a 16th-century Portuguese borrowing that is so deeply naturalized it retains a flat (heiban, 0) pitch accent in standard Tokyo Japanese and collocates with the verb 吸う (suu, "to inhale/sip").

rootFamily.gloss: tobacconist, cigarette shop (with Sino-Japanese 屋 ya)

タブレット.etymology: Borrowed from English *tablet* ('flat portable touchscreen computer; compressed medicinal pill or lozenge'), from Old French *tablete* ('small table or writing slate').

history.meaning: writing slate; tablet computer; lozenge
tablet computer; compressed tablet

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タブレット

タルト.etymology: Borrowed from French *tarte* (and English *tart*), referring to a baked shortcrust pastry shell filled with fruit, custard, or cream; ultimately from Old French *tarte*.

history.meaning: open-faced fruit or custard pastry
tart; pastry tart

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — タルト

タルト生地.etymology: Hybrid baking compound タルト生地 ('tart dough, shortcrust pastry dough'), combining French loanword タルト (*tarte*) + native/Sino-Japanese 生地 (きじ 'unworked material, dough, fabric', from 生 *ki* 'raw, natural' + 地 *ji* 'ground, base material').

history.meaning: pastry dough for a tart shell

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 生地

タレこむ.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb (垂れ込む, tarekomu). In Classical Japanese (垂れ籠む), it meant "to lower bamboo blinds (sudare) and seclude oneself indoors" or "for heavy clouds to hang low". In modern underworld and police argot, it was reanalyzed from 垂れる (tareru, "to drip, let drop, spill information or bodily waste") + directional auxiliary 込む (komu, "inward, into"), meaning to secretly tip off the police or press ("snitch, rat out").

history.form: たれこむ (垂れ籠む, tarekomu)
history.meaning: to let down blinds and shut oneself inside; to hang low (of clouds)

history.form: たれこむ (垂れ込む, tarekomu)
history.meaning: to leak or drop secret information to authorities; to snitch
to snitch, tip off police or media (or in passive タレこまれる, get snitched on)

morphemes.meaning: to drip, hang down, spill secrets (stem of 垂れる tareru)
inward, deeply into (auxiliary verb 込む komu)

タレこむ.notes: When written with the first stem in katakana (タレこむ or タレコミ), it exclusively carries the gritty police/yakuza/tabloid slang sense of "snitching / tipping off", distinguishing it from meteorological 垂れ込める ("for dark clouds to hang low").

rootFamily.gloss: to drip, hang down; to spill or utter (slang)

sources.title: Kotobank: タレ込み / 垂れ込み

cognates.meaning: balance, scale, weight, monetary unit of silver/gold

タレント.etymology: Borrowed from English talent ("person of talent, radio/TV performer"), from Middle English talent, from Old French talent ("inclination, desire, disposition, sum of money"), from Latin talentum, from Ancient Greek talanton (τάλαντον, "balance, scale, weight, commercial monetary unit"). Its shift from "monetary weight" to "natural ability" stems from the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14–30); in postwar Japanese broadcasting, it narrowed to mean a television celebrity or variety-show regular.

history.meaning: weighing scale; standard weight of silver or gold
sum of money; figuratively God-given aptitude or skill (via Matthew 25)
TV personality, media celebrity appearing across variety and talk shows

タレント.notes: A classic false friend: in Japanese, タレント almost never means an abstract skill or gift (which is 才能 sainou); instead, it refers to a person—specifically a TV celebrity or variety-show personality.

rootFamily.gloss: multi-talent, entertainer active in acting, singing, and variety TV (wasei-eigo)
local/regional TV personality (with 地元 jimoto / ローカル)
politician or scholar who becomes a TV celebrity (文化人タレント)

ダシ.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun (出し, dashi), truncated from 出し汁 (dashijiru, "extracted broth") or 煮出し汁 (nidashijiru, "boiled-out broth"). It is the continuative stem (ren'youkei) of the transitive verb 出す (dasu, "to take out, draw out, extract", causative of 出る deru, Old Japanese idu, "to come out, emerge"), referring to extracting umami flavor into hot water from dried kelp (konbu), bonito flakes (katsuobushi), or dried sardines (niboshi).

history.meaning: to emerge / to cause to come out, draw forth

history.form: だしじる / だし (出し汁 / 出し, dashijiru / dashi)
history.meaning: broth made by boiling and extracting flavor from kelp or dried fish
umami soup stock; figuratively a pretext, pawn, or front

morphemes.meaning: extracting, drawing out (nominalized stem of 出す dasu)

ダシ.notes: Frequently written in katakana (ダシ) both in culinary contexts and in the common idiom ～をダシにする ("to use someone/something as a convenient excuse, pawn, or front for one's real agenda").

rootFamily.gloss: soup stock, extracted broth (full compound with 汁 shiru)
to take out, draw out, extract; to serve
japanese rolled omelette seasoned with dashi broth

sources.title: Kotobank: 出汁 / 出し (だし)

cognates.meaning: rattan cooling bolster; (nautical slang) sailor's masturbatory doll

ダッチワイフ.etymology: Borrowed and adapted as wasei-eigo (Japanese-coined English usage) from English Dutch wife. In colonial English, a "Dutch wife" originally denoted a hollow woven rattan or bamboo bolster used in the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia) to absorb sweat and keep limbs cool in bed (calque of Indonesian guling). In 20th-century maritime and postwar Japanese sex-industry parlance, it was conflated with sailors' leather/cloth dolls (French dame de voyage) and popularized in Showa Japan for full-sized inflatable or silicone love dolls.

history.meaning: open-weave rattan bolster used for cooling in tropical beds in the Dutch East Indies
full-sized rubber or vinyl inflatable adult doll marketed in postwar Japan

morphemes.meaning: Dutch (from English Dutch, from Middle Dutch duutsch)
wife, woman (from English wife, from Old English wif)

ダッチワイフ.notes: Although coined from English words, calling a sex doll a "Dutch wife" is virtually unknown to contemporary native English speakers (where "Dutch wife" means a tropical bamboo sleeping bolster); modern Japanese manufacturers now prefer ラブドール (rabu dooru, "love doll").

rootFamily.gloss: going Dutch, splitting the bill (wasei-eigo/idiom from English Dutch account)

cognates.meaning: dubbing, copying or mixing audio/video tracks
to double, duplicate, dub a film

ダビング.etymology: Borrowed from English dubbing, verbal noun of dub ("to copy a sound recording or transfer audio/video from a master tape to another"), itself a 1920s studio shortening of double ("to duplicate"), from Old French dobler, from Late Latin duplare ("to double"), from Latin duplus ("twofold"). In 1980s Japanese video culture (central to the VHS adult video industry), ダビング came to mean duplicating videotapes or audio cassettes.

history.meaning: to make twofold, duplicate
to duplicate a recording or combine sound tracks in film post-production
copying or duplicating VHS tapes, cassettes, or discs

morphemes.meaning: dub, duplicate a recording (from English dub < double)

ダビング.notes: Watch out for a subtle semantic divergence: in Japanese, ダビング primarily means "copying/duplicating a tape or disc", whereas voice-over translation of foreign films ("dubbing" in everyday English) is called 吹き替え (fukikae).

rootFamily.gloss: dubbing/duplication equipment (hybrid compound with 機材 kizai)
double, twofold; overlapping (from the same ultimate root double)
to overlap, be duplicated, be redundant (hybrid verb from double + -ru)

ダビング機材.etymology: A hybrid gairaigo–kango compound combining ダビング (from English dubbing, "tape duplication", ultimately from Latin duplare, "to double") + Sino-Japanese 機材 (kizai, "machinery and materials, technical equipment"), composed of 機 (ki, Middle Chinese *kj+j, originally "loom; clever mechanism, machine") and 材 (zai, Middle Chinese *dzoj, "timber, raw material, resource"). In 1980s Japan, banks of connected VCR decks (ダビング機材) enabled mass duplication of underground and commercial VHS tapes.

history.meaning: mechanical contrivance/loom + timber/working material
machinery, apparatus, and technical equipment (especially for film/broadcasting)
tape-duplicating equipment (VCR decks and signal splitters)

ダビング機材.notes: 機材 (kizai) specifically denotes portable or studio technical hardware—cameras, lighting rigs, audio mixers, and VCR decks—making it ubiquitous on film and video shoots.

rootFamily.gloss: filming equipment, camera and lighting gear

ダメ.etymology: Originated as a technical term in the board game Go (囲碁, igo), written 駄目 (dame): a hybrid compound of Sino-Japanese 駄 (da, Middle Chinese *da, "pack-horse load; trifling, worthless, in vain", used as a prefix for poor quality) + native Yamato 目 (me, Old Japanese me, "eye; grid intersection or point on a Go board"). In Go, dame denotes neutral intersection points between black and white territories that yield zero points to either player; in Edo-period vernacular, filling such points was seen as pointless effort, generalizing the word to mean "useless, no good, forbidden".

history.meaning: neutral, point-less intersection on a Go board belonging to neither player's territory
in vain, useless, ruined, hopeless
no good, useless, not allowed, forbidden

morphemes.meaning: pack-horse load; worthless, trifling, in vain (Sino-Japanese 駄 da, MC *da)
eye; grid intersection/point on a Go board (native Yamato 目 me)

ダメ.notes: One of several everyday Japanese words derived from the game of Go—alongside 布石 (fuseki, "laying the groundwork"), 一目置く (ichimoku oku, "to acknowledge someone's superiority"), and 八百長 (yaochou, "match-fixing").

rootFamily.gloss: making doubly sure; scoring insurance points (originally confirming neutral Go points)
good-for-nothing person, loser (colloquial compound with 人間 ningen)
giving up on something as hopeless (with 元 moto, "originally")

チェック.etymology: Borrowed from English check ("inspection, verification, mark of confirmation, plaid pattern"), from Middle English chek ("a call in chess warning that the king is under attack; a sudden stop or control"), from Old French eschec, via Arabic shah (شاه) from Persian shah (شاه, "king"). From the sense of "arresting or verifying a tally against a counterfoil", English developed the meaning "to inspect or examine", which entered Japanese as チェック (chekku).

history.meaning: king, monarch (used in chess to announce threat to the king)
check in chess; restraint, control, verification against a counterfoil
inspection, review, verification; checkered pattern; check-in/out

チェック.notes: While チェック covers "inspection/review", "checkered pattern", and hotel "check-in/out", a restaurant bill is called お会計 (okaikei) or チェック (in upscale bars), and a bank check is usually 小切手 (kogitte).

チェックイン.etymology: Borrowed from English *check-in* / *check in* ('registering one's arrival at a hotel, inn, or airport').

history.meaning: registration upon arrival at a hotel or airport
check-in

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — チェックイン

チェーン.etymology: Borrowed from English chain (and truncated from chain store, チェーンストア), from Middle English cheine, from Old French chaiene ("metal chain, fetter"), from Latin catena ("chain, fetter, connected series"). In Japanese commercial usage, チェーン denotes a network of retail shops, video rental stores, or restaurants operating under unified brand management.

history.meaning: metal chain, shackle, connected series
series of connected metal links; network of affiliated retail stores (from 1890s)
retail chain (clipped from チェーンストア); physical metal or tire chain

morphemes.meaning: chain, affiliated store network (from English chain)

チェーン.notes: In everyday Japanese, a branch of a retail or restaurant chain is almost always called a チェーン店 (cheen-ten, combining English chain + Sino-Japanese 店 ten, "shop").

rootFamily.gloss: chain store, branch of a retail/restaurant chain (with 店 ten)
keychain, key ring (wasei-eigo キーホルダー is common, alongside キーチェーン)

チキショー.etymology: Colloquial regressive vowel-assimilated pronunciation (chiku-shou > chikishou) of Sino-Japanese 畜生 (chikushou), borrowed from Middle Chinese *trhjuwk-srjaeng (畜生), a Buddhist translation of Sanskrit tiryagyoni ("horizontal-going womb/birth", i.e., the realm of animals, one of the Six Realms of rebirth, 六道 rokudou). Because Buddhism viewed animals as driven by blind instinct and incestuous taboo-breaking, 畜生 became an Edo-period curse meaning "Beast! Brute!" and an interjection of intense frustration ("Damn it!").

history.meaning: realm of rebirth as a non-human animal or beast in Buddhist cosmology
history.stage: Sanskrit to Middle Chinese Buddhist translation

history.meaning: beast, brute; expletive expressing anger or mortification
damn it! son of a bitch! (colloquial assimilated interjection)

morphemes.meaning: domesticated animal, beast, livestock (Sino-Japanese 畜 chiku > chiki, MC *trhjuwk)
living creature, birth, life (Sino-Japanese 生 shou, MC *srjaeng)

チキショー.notes: Often preceded by the emphatic prefix こん- (from この kono, "this") to form コンチキショー (konchikishou, "Goddamn it!"), a classic rough Tokyo/Edokko expletive.

rootFamily.gloss: beast, brute; damn it! (standard form of the word)
goddamn it! you bastard! (with emphatic この kono > こん kon)

sources.title: Wiktionary: ちくしょう / 畜生

cognates.meaning: challenge, summons to a contest, difficult task

チャレンジ.etymology: Borrowed from English challenge, from Middle English chalenge ("accusation, claim, summons to fight"), from Old French chalenge, inherited from Latin calumnia ("trickery, false accusation, malicious charge"). In Japanese, チャレンジ underwent an upbeat semantic shift: rather than "disputing someone" or "a daunting obstacle", it means "boldly attempting something new, taking on a goal".

history.meaning: false accusation, legal trickery, malicious claim
accusation; summons to a duel or contest; demanding task
taking on a new endeavor, giving something ambitious a try

チャレンジ.notes: In Japanese, チャレンジする is almost always positive and aspirational ("to try / have a go at something new", e.g., 新しい仕事にチャレンジする), whereas English "to challenge someone" (confront or dispute) translates to 挑む (idomu) or 異議を唱える (igi o tonaeru).

rootFamily.gloss: challenger (especially against a reigning champion; someone who tries boldly)
spirit of taking on new challenges, entrepreneurial boldness (wasei-eigo)

cognates.meaning: cadence (doublet via Italian from Latin cadentia)

チャンス.etymology: Borrowed from English chance (reinforced by French chance, "good luck"), from Middle English cheaunce, from Old French cheance ("the way the dice fall, luck, fortune, befalling"), from Late Latin cadentia ("a falling, the falling of dice"), neuter plural participle of Latin cadere ("to fall"). In Japanese, チャンス narrowed exclusively to the positive sense of a "favorable opportunity, golden moment, scoring chance".

history.meaning: a falling (especially the fall of dice in gaming)
fortune, luck, random occurrence, opportunity
favorable opportunity, big break, scoring chance

チャンス.notes: Unlike English "chance", Japanese チャンス is strictly positive ("a golden opportunity" = 好機 kouki); it cannot be used for neutral probability ("there is a 50% chance" is 可能性 kanousei or 確率 kakuritsu) or negative risk ("a chance of rain").

rootFamily.gloss: one more chance, a shot at something (slang ワンチャン, clipped from ワンチャンス)

チャンネル.etymology: Borrowed from English channel, from Middle English chanel ("riverbed, waterway, gutter"), from Old French chanel, inherited from Latin canalis ("water pipe, groove, trench, canal"), a derivative of canna ("reed, hollow cane"). Adopted into Japanese alongside the launch of television broadcasting in 1953 to denote broadcast frequency bands and television networks, while its learned doublet カナル (from English canal) was borrowed separately for man-made waterways.

history.meaning: reed-shaped water pipe, groove, open conduit
waterway, navigable strait; later (1920s–1940s) radio/TV frequency band
television broadcast channel; distribution channel

チャンネル.notes: In Japanese households, fighting over which TV station to watch is called チャンネル争い (channeru arasoi), and "Stay tuned / Don't touch that dial!" is チャンネルはそのまま (channeru wa sono mama).

rootFamily.gloss: dispute over which TV channel to watch (with 争い arasoi)
channel surfer, someone who constantly flips TV channels (with 権兵衛 gonbee)
canal, waterway (doublet borrowed from English canal)

チュウ.etymology: Has two converging origins in Japanese: (1) As a masculine nickname (such as the yakuza character Chu in The Naked Director), it is the Sino-Japanese on'yomi reading of 忠 (chuu, Middle Chinese *trjuwng, "loyalty, fidelity, devotion", composed of phonetic 中 *trjuwng "center" + semantic 心 "heart") or 宙/中, used hypocoristically for names like Chuji (忠治) or Chusuke (忠助); (2) As a colloquial noun meaning "a kiss, smooch", it derives from the native Japanese mimetic/onomatopoeic root ちゅう (chuu), imitating the puckered-lip sound of sucking or kissing (and historically the squeak of a mouse, 鼠鳴き nezuminaki, used since the Edo period as an amorous signal).

history.meaning: loyalty, centered heart (MC) / squeaking or sucking lip sound (Early Modern Japanese)
nickname Chu (from 忠 chuu); colloquial/childish word for a kiss or smooch

morphemes.meaning: Chu (from Sino-Japanese 忠 chuu, "loyalty"); mimetic sound of a kiss/smooch

チュウ.notes: In colloquial Japanese, チュウする ("to do a chuu") is the standard playful or affectionate everyday expression for giving a kiss (smooching), less formal or clinical than キスする or 口づけ (kuchizuke).

rootFamily.gloss: loyalty, devotion, faithfulness (Sino-Japanese 忠義 chuugi)
mouse, rat (childish/colloquial word from its squeak ちゅう)

sources.title: Wiktionary: ちゅう / チュウ

チョウチョウ.etymology: A reduplicated Sino-Japanese noun (蝶々 / 蝶蝶, chouchou, often shortened in speech to choucho), formed by doubling 蝶 (chou, historical kana orthography てふ tefu, borrowed from Middle Chinese *dep, "butterfly", literally "leaf-thin insect", composed of semantic 虫 "insect" + phonetic 枼 *yep / *dep, "thin wooden tablet, leaf, sheet"). Beginning in the Heian and Kamakura periods, Sino-Japanese tefu (> chou) displaced the indigenous Old Japanese word kawahirako (かはひらこ, "fluttering river-creature"). In traditional Hanafuda card games and yakuza gambling parlance, チョウチョウ specifically refers to the June peony-and-butterfly card or fluttering gestures.

history.meaning: butterfly (insect with thin, flat wings)

history.form: てふ / てふてふ (蝶 / 蝶々, tefu / tefutefu)
history.meaning: butterfly (replacing native Old Japanese kawahirako)
butterfly (also colloquial ちょうちょ choucho)

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated stem expressing fluttering or endearing familiarity (蝶 chou)

チョウチョウ.notes: Because the historical kana spelling of 蝶 was てふ (tefu), it became a famous symbol of the post-WWII 1946 orthography reform when it was respelled phonetically as ちょう (chou). In Hanafuda gambling (central to yakuza culture), チョウ represents the prized June 10-point "Peony and Butterflies" card, foundational to the winning hand 猪鹿蝶 (inoshikachou, "Boar-Deer-Butterfly").

rootFamily.gloss: bow tie ("butterfly tie", 蝶ネクタイ chou nekutai)
Boar-Deer-Butterfly (classic Hanafuda gambling combination; idiom for a trio)

sources.title: Wiktionary: ちょうちょう / 蝶々

チョーク.etymology: Borrowed from English *chalk* ('soft white limestone or calcium sulfate stick used for writing on blackboards'), from Old English *cealc* and Latin *calx* ('lime').

history.meaning: blackboard writing stick
chalk

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — チョーク

チーズ.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English cheese, which descends through Old English ċēse and West Germanic *kāsī from Classical Latin cāseus ('cheese', source also of Spanish queso and German Käse).

history.meaning: pressed curds, cheese
cheese
cheese

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Kotobank — チーズ

チーズ.notes: Largely superseded the early Meiji Sino-Japanese coinage 乾酪 (かんらく, 'dried dairy curd') in everyday Japanese.

チーム.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English team, which descends from Old English tēam ('set of draught animals harnessed together, family line, group pulling together'). Initially introduced through Western team sports such as baseball and rowing, チーム broadened in Japanese to mean any cooperative work crew, kitchen brigade, or project group.

history.meaning: set of draught animals pulling together
group working or playing together
team, cooperative crew

チーム.notes: Carries a warm, egalitarian ring when praising coworkers who pull together on a busy day.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — チーム

ツアー.etymology: Borrowed from English tour ("journey, guided trip, concert circuit"), from Middle English tour ("a turn, shift of duty, circular journey"), from Old French tour ("a turn, trick, circuit, circumference"), deverbal from Old French torner ("to turn"), from Latin tornare ("to turn on a lathe, round off"), from Ancient Greek tornos (τόρνος, "lathe, tool for drawing a circle"). In Japanese, ツアー denotes packaged travel excursions as well as concert or promotional tours.

history.meaning: lathe, compass -> to turn on a lathe, fashion round
circular movement, shift of duty; travelling circuit (from 17th-c. Grand Tour)
history.stage: Old French and Early Modern English

ニシン.notes: Because herring roe (数の子, kazunoko) contains thousands of eggs, folk etymology paired the parent fish ニシン with 二親 ("two parents") to make herring roe an essential New Year's (Osechi) fertility symbol.

rootFamily.gloss: herring buckwheat noodles (a specialty of Hokkaido and Kyoto)
herring roe (traditionally eaten at New Year's)

ニス.etymology: Edo-to-Meiji-period loanword from Dutch vernis ('varnish'), which was borrowed via Old French vernis and Medieval Latin veronix from Late Greek Berenikē. As happened with several Dutch technical terms adopted by Japanese craftsmen (such as メス mes and ペンキ pek), the unstressed initial syllable ver- was dropped by apheresis, leaving the crisp disyllabic noun ニス (nisu).

history.meaning: protective resinous wood coating, varnish
wood varnish
clear varnish for wood or musical instruments

ニス.notes: While ペンキ refers to opaque coloured paint, ニス specifically denotes a transparent protective finish that lets the wood grain show through.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ニス

ニュース.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji period from English *news* ('tidings, report of recent events', calqued on Old French *noveles* / Medieval Latin *nova* 'new things').

news

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ニュース

ニーズ.etymology: Gairaigo loanword borrowed from the English plural noun needs (from singular need, Middle English nede, Old English nied, neod, "compulsion, necessity, hardship, want", from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, "need, distress, fate"). ネクタイ.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era (attested by the 1880s as Western menswear spread) from English necktie, a compound of neck ('throat, collar area') + tie ('band or ribbon tied in a knot').

necktie, tie

ネジ.etymology: Katakana spelling of ねじ (螺子・捻じ 'screw, bolt, spiral thread'), nominalized from the continuative stem of the native verb 捻じる / 捻づ ('to twist, turn spirally').

screw; threaded fastener

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ねじ山

ネジ穴.etymology: Native Japanese carpentry compound combining ネジ (neji, 'screw', nominalized from the stem of the verb ねじる nejiru 'to twist, turn') with 穴 (ana, 'hole, cavity, aperture', attested from Old Japanese). Together, ネジ穴 names either the threaded hole drilled into wood or metal to receive a screw or the slotted recess on a screw head.

history.meaning: hole, opening, cavity
screw, spiral fastener (from 'twisting')
screw hole

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ねじ穴

ノコ.etymology: Clipped trade and colloquial form of 鋸 (nokogiri, "handsaw"), a native Yamato (wago) compound attested since Old Japanese (noko / nokogiri). The full noun nokogiri analyzes as noko ("serrated tooth, jagged blade edge", related to Old Japanese noko / hoko "point, tooth") + kiri (deverbal noun from kiru 切る, "to cut"), literally "tooth-cutter" or "serrated cutter"; truncation of the second element yielded standalone ノコ (noko).

history.meaning: serrated cutting blade, handsaw
clipped craftsman's term for a handsaw
handsaw, saw blade

ノコ.notes: Standard among carpenters, stagehands, and in crime dramas as the punchy shorthand for のこぎり, and used productively to form compounds like 電ノコ (den-noko, "electric power saw") and 鉄ノコ (tetsu-noko, "hacksaw").

cognates.meaning: factual prose literature and documentary media

ノンフィクション.etymology: Gairaigo loanword borrowed from English nonfiction (coined in early 20th-century American publishing and library classification from non-, via Old French from Latin non "not", + fiction, via Old French ficcion from Latin fictio, "a fashioning, feigning, invention", action noun of fingere, "to mold out of clay, shape, devise, feign", from Proto-Indo-European *dheigh- "to knead clay, build").

history.meaning: a shaping, molding, feigned supposition
prose literature based on factual events rather than invention
nonfiction literature, investigative journalism, documentary work

morphemes.meaning: not, non- (from Latin non via English)
fiction, invented narrative (from Latin fictio via English)

ノンフィクション.notes: In Japanese publishing (such as Nobuhiko Motohashi's biography Zenra Kantoku on which The Naked Director is based), ノンフィクション specifically connotes long-form investigative reportage and literary biography.

rootFamily.word: サイエンスフィクション

sources.title: Wiktionary: ノンフィクション

ノー.etymology: Gairaigo loanword from English no, from Middle English no, na, from Old English na ("no, never, not at all"), a compound of the negative particle ne ("not", from Proto-Germanic *ne, Proto-Indo-European *ne) + a ("ever, always", from Proto-Germanic *aiw, Proto-Indo-European *h2eyu- "vital force, age, eternity"). In Japanese, it serves both as an emphatic noun/interjection of refusal ("no") and as a highly productive prefix meaning "without, lacking".

history.meaning: never, not ever, by no means
negative particle and determiner meaning not any
explicit refusal ("no"); prefix meaning without or un-

ノー.notes: While Japanese speakers rarely answer everyday questions with standalone ノー (using いいえ or いや instead), ノー is preferred as a noun for "explicit refusal" (はっきりノーと言う, "to firmly say no") and forms many wasei-eigo compounds like ノーカット ("uncut/unedited") and ノーギャラ ("unpaid").

rootFamily.gloss: uncut, unedited (especially of films or broadcasts)

ノート.etymology: Loanword from English "note" (or notebook). This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: written record / book for writing
notebook, notes

ノート.notes: Used primarily for physical notebooks or the act of taking notes.
