notch cut into a tally stick; group of twenty

ハイスコア.etymology: Gairaigo compound borrowed from English high score, combining high (from Old English heah, Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, "tall, elevated") and score (from Middle English score, borrowed from Old Norse skor, "notch, incision, tally mark of twenty cut into a stick", from Proto-Germanic *skuro, related to *skeran "to shear, cut"). Entered everyday Japanese during the late-1970s and early-1980s video arcade boom (led by Space Invaders in 1978).

history.meaning: notch cut on a wooden tally stick to count twenty items
highest point total recorded in a game or contest
highest score achieved on an arcade machine or video game

morphemes.meaning: score, point tally (from Old Norse skor via English)

ハイスコア.notes: Popularized nationwide during the 1978–1980 Space Invaders craze in Japan's coffeehouses (kissaten), and later immortalized by the arcade magazine Gemest (famous for its typo "インド人を右に") and the manga High Score Girl.

ハガキ.etymology: Katakana spelling of 葉書・端書 (はがき 'postcard'), originally a compound of 端 (は 'margin, scrap, edge of paper') or 羽/葉 (は 'feather/leaf') + 書き (がき, stem of 書く 'to write'), denoting a brief note jotted on a single slip of paper before being adopted in 1873 as the official name for postal cards (郵便葉書).

history.meaning: memorandum jotted on a slip of paper
postcard

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 葉書

ハッタリ.etymology: Native Japanese noun (occasionally given the ateji 発破り) originating in Edo- and Meiji-period gambler (bakuto), street-merchant (tekiya), and underworld cant. It derives from an emphatic mimetic/verbal formation hattari (related to 張る haru, "to slap, stretch, put up a bold front", or the mimetic adverb hatto "striking suddenly with a sharp smack"), originally denoting an intimidating slap or theatrical gesture used to startle an opponent into backing down without real strength behind it.

history.meaning: sudden striking gesture or intimidating boast in gambler and street-vendor argot
bluff, empty bravado, showy exaggeration to impress or intimidate

ハッタリ.notes: Most idiomatic in the collocations ハッタリをかます ("to pull a bold bluff") and ハッタリを利かせる ("to use bluffing/showmanship to one's advantage").

rootFamily.gloss: to stretch, slap, put up a front
to put on airs, show off beyond one's means
to stubbornly stick to one's pride

sources.title: Wiktionary: ハッタリ / はったり

ハハッ.etymology: Native Japanese onomatopoeic vocalization (giseigo) directly imitating the acoustic burst of a short, breathy open-vowel laugh or chuckle (haha'), with the final small tsu (ッ, sokuon) marking an abrupt glottal stop or clipped exhalation. Like parallel imitative forms across languages, it arises from natural human respiratory vocalization, though in Japanese discourse it frequently signals a brief dry chuckle, sudden realization, or deferential acknowledgment.

history.meaning: imitative representation of open-mouthed laughter
short chuckle, wry laugh, or clipped laugh of realization

ハハッ.notes: The final glottal stop (ッ) gives ハハッ a clipped, often wry, self-conscious, or slightly sardonic nuance compared to prolonged open laughter (ハハハ or アハハ).

rootFamily.gloss: fufu, quiet suppressed chuckle or snicker

ハマる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) Godan intransitive verb written 填まる or 嵌まる (hamaru, often rendered in katakana as ハマる in colloquial registers), paired with transitive 填める / 嵌める (hameru). It descends from Old and Classical Japanese hamu ("to insert into an opening, submerge in water, cast into"). From the physical sense "to slot snugly into a groove or cavity", it evolved two major metaphorical branches: "to fall squarely into a trap/scheme" and "to become deeply hooked on or obsessed with a hobby or person".

history.meaning: to insert into an opening, plunge or submerge into
to fit tightly into a slot; to fall into a trap or mire
to fit snugly; to get hooked on or addicted to; to fall into a trap

morphemes.meaning: slot into a cavity, become immersed or entrapped

ハマる.notes: Writing ハマる in katakana is especially common for the colloquial senses "to be addicted to / obsessed with" (沼にハマる, "fall down the rabbit hole") or "to fit a role to perfection" (ハマり役, "a role one was born to play").

rootFamily.gloss: to fit/insert into place; to frame or entrap someone (transitive)
a role ideally suited to an actor, signature role
to inlay, set into a frame or socket

sources.title: Wiktionary: はまる / 嵌まる

ハミング.etymology: Borrowed from English *humming* ('crooning a melody with closed lips', verbal noun from the onomatopoeic verb *hum*).

history.meaning: singing with closed lips
humming a tune

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ハミング

cognates.meaning: informal greeting or call for attention

ハロー.etymology: Gairaigo loanword from English hello, attested from the early 19th century as a variant of hallo, hollo, hullo—an exclamation used to hail a ferryman or call attention from a distance (from Middle English halou, linked to Old High German halon "to fetch" or hala). After Thomas Edison championed hello in 1877 as the standard greeting when answering the telephone, it spread globally and entered Meiji/Taisho Japanese.

history.meaning: shout used to hail someone from afar or call hounds
telephone salutation and general greeting
informal English-style greeting; friendly prefix in public service names

ハロー.notes: While Japanese speakers use もしもし (moshimoshi) rather than ハロー when answering the phone in Japanese, ハロー is embedded in major public institutions like ハローワーク (Hello Work, the national employment office).

rootFamily.gloss: Hello Work (Japan's government-run Public Employment Security Office)

ハンコ.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato compound written 判子 (hanko, "personal or corporate seal stamp"). The first element 判 (han, from Middle Chinese phwanH, "to cleave in two, divide a tally, judge, official mark", composed of 半 "half" + 刀 "knife") referred in medieval Japan to a written cipher (kaō) or official seal; in the Edo period, the native Japanese diminutive/familiar object suffix -ko (written 子) was attached, parallel to 振り子 (furiko, "pendulum") and 張り子 (hariko, "papier-mache").

history.meaning: to divide a tally in half, judge, official verification mark
written signature cipher (kaō) or official stamped seal
carved personal or corporate name stamp used in place of a signature

morphemes.meaning: 判 (Middle Chinese phwanH): official seal, verification mark, judgment
子 (native wago -ko): diminutive or familiar suffix for everyday implements

ハンコ.notes: ハンコ is the everyday conversational word for the physical stamp used on contracts and deliveries, whereas 印鑑 (inkan) strictly refers to the registered ink impression itself (though often used interchangeably in speech).

rootFamily.gloss: to stamp one's seal (and thereby approve a document)
unconditional guarantee of quality (literally big drum-sized seal)

ハンドル.etymology: Borrowed from English *handle* ('part of an object grasped by the hand', from Old English *handlian* 'to touch with the hand'). In Japanese it denotes door handles, crank handles, bicycle handlebars, and automobile steering wheels.

history.meaning: handgrip or lever
door/crank handle; steering wheel; handlebars

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ハンドル

ハンマー.etymology: Borrowed from English *hammer* ('mallet or striking tool; piano action hammer that strikes the strings'), from Old English *hamor*.

history.meaning: striking tool; felt-covered piano hammer
hammer

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ハンマー

ハーブ.etymology: Borrowed from English *herb* ('aromatic plant used in cooking, tea, and medicine'), from Old French *erbe* and Latin *herba*.

history.meaning: culinary or medicinal aromatic plant
culinary/aromatic herb

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ハーブ

バイオリン.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English violin (alongside the older spelling ヴァイオリン Directly reflecting Italian violino), diminutive of viola, ultimately traced to Medieval Latin vitula ('stringed instrument'). Introduced into Japanese schools and salons during the late nineteenth-century Western music movement, it became one of the most familiar chamber instruments in Japan.

history.meaning: small viola, violin
four-stringed bowed instrument
violin

バイオリン.notes: Playing the violin takes the verb 弾く (バイオリンを弾く, 'to play the violin'), the same verb used for the piano and guitar.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — バイオリン

バイト.etymology: Clipped noun (ryakugo) shortened from アルバイト (arubaito, "part-time job, side work"), borrowed in the Meiji/Taisho era from German Arbeit ("work, labor"), from Middle High German arbeit, Old High German arabeit ("toil, hardship, affliction"), from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz. Initially adopted in pre-WWII Japanese higher-education slang for "student side work to fund tuition" (as well as "academic research paper"), it generalized after the war to any non-regular part-time job and shortened to バイト.

history.meaning: hardship, toil; later general work or labor
history.stage: Old High German to Modern German

history.meaning: student side job or academic research work
part-time job or part-time worker

バイト.notes: Denotes both the part-time job itself (バイトをする, "work a part-time job") and the part-time worker (バイトを雇う, "hire a part-timer"); not to be confused with its English-derived homophone バイト (byte).

rootFamily.gloss: wages earned from a part-time job

バインダー.etymology: Borrowed from English *binder* ('clip-board or ring-folder that holds loose sheets of paper together', agent noun from *bind*).

history.meaning: folder or clipboard holding loose pages
ring binder; clipboard

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — バインダー

バカ.etymology: Attested since the Muromachi period (e.g., the 14th-century Taiheiki and the 15th-century dictionary Setsuyōshū) and traditionally written with the phonetic ateji 馬鹿 ("horse-deer", secondarily linked to the Chinese Qin-dynasty anecdote 指鹿為馬, "pointing at a deer and calling it a horse", in the Shiji). Modern Japanese philology traces the spoken word to medieval Buddhist monastic slang borrowed from Sanskrit moha ("delusion, folly, spiritual ignorance", transcribed in Sino-Japanese sutras as 慕何 boka / baka) or Sanskrit mahallaka ("senile, ignorant", 摩訶羅 bakara).

history.meaning: delusion, spiritual ignorance, folly in Buddhist doctrine
fool, foolishness, absurd behavior
idiot, fool; foolish; single-minded enthusiast; absurdly (intensifier)

バカ.notes: In Kanto (Tokyo) speech バカ is a casual, all-purpose word ranging from playful teasing to sharp insult, whereas in Kansai (Osaka/Kyoto) アホ (aho) is the light everyday word and バカ sounds much harsher and more coldly dismissive.

rootFamily.gloss: to make a fool of, look down on, ridicule
doting parent blind to their child's faults

バケツ.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English bucket (with final -ツ reflecting either the English plural buckets or Meiji-era adaptation of word-final [-t] before epenthetic -u as -tsu; compare シャツ from shirt(s)). English bucket itself came from Anglo-Norman buquet ('tub, pail').

history.meaning: wooden or metal carrying pail
metal or plastic bucket, pail

sources.title: Shogakukan: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten / Kotobank — バケツ

バケツ.notes: Names tapered metal or plastic pails with a swinging wire handle, whereas traditional stave-built wooden tubs remain 桶 (おけ).

バス.etymology: Borrowed from English 'bus', short for 'omnibus' (from Latin omnibus, 'for all').

history.meaning: bus

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — バス

バター.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji period from English butter as Western dairy and baking spread across Japan.

history.meaning: churned dairy fat
butter

cognates.meaning: rear part of the body; offensive/defensive backline players

バックス.etymology: Gairaigo sports term borrowed from the English plural noun backs (from singular back, Middle English bak, Old English bæc, "back of the body, rear", from Proto-Germanic *baka). Introduced into Japanese with Western team sports—above all rugby union—to designate the fast, open-field backline players (scrum-half, fly-half, centers, wings, and fullback) positioned behind the scrum forwards (フォワード).

history.meaning: back of the human or animal body
players positioned behind the forwards in rugby and football
backline unit in rugby, American football, or baseball outfields

バックス.notes: In Japanese rugby commentary and team rosters, a squad is divided into FW (フォワード, forwards) and BK (バックス, backs); the plural -s is kept even when referring to a single player's unit affiliation (彼はバックスだ, "he plays in the backs").

バックレ.etymology: Nominalized stem (ren'yōkei) of the colloquial verb バックレる (bakkureru, "to feign ignorance, play dumb; to skip out on work or obligations without notice, go AWOL"). Despite its katakana spelling (influenced by folk-etymological association with English back), it is a native Kanto dialectal apheresis of しらばっくれる (shirabakkureru, "to play completely innocent, feign total ignorance"), which compounds 白 (shira-, "blank, feigned innocence", as in しらを切る) + an intensive suffixal verb -bakkureru ("to evade, slip away, conceal").

history.meaning: to feign complete ignorance, brazenly play innocent
to play dumb; to ditch work, school, or debts without notice
flaking out, going AWOL from a job or obligation, playing dumb

morphemes.meaning: evading, playing dumb, ditching duties (apheretic stem of shirabakkureru)

バックレ.notes: Frequently mistaken by native speakers for an English loanword from "back", which cemented its katakana spelling; in workplace slang, バックレ means abandoning a shift or quitting a job by simply disappearing without notice.

rootFamily.gloss: to flake out, ditch work without notice, play dumb
to feign complete ignorance, brazenly play innocent
to pretend not to know, play innocent

バッグ.etymology: Gairaigo loanword from English bag ("handbag, tote, carrying bag"), from Middle English bagge, borrowed from Old Norse baggi ("pack, bundle, pouch"), from Proto-Germanic *bagg-. In Japanese, バッグ underwent semantic division of labor alongside native 袋 (fukuro, "paper/plastic sack, pouch") and earlier Portuguese/Dutch-era 鞄 (kaban, "briefcase, rigid satchel"), specializing in fashion handbags, shoulder bags, and sports/travel bags.

history.meaning: bundle, pack, tied sack
flexible pouch, handbag, or traveling bag
handbag, shoulder bag, tote bag, carryall

バッグ.notes: Carefully distinguish voiced バッグ (baggu, "handbag/bag") from voiceless バック (bakku, "back/rear/background"), though in casual spoken Tokyo Japanese many speakers devoice or merge バッグ toward バック in compounds like エコバッグ.

バッチリ.etymology: Native Japanese mimetic/ideophonic adverb and na-adjective developed as the voiced, emphatic counterpart of パッチリ (patchiri, "wide open and clear [of eyes], distinctly defined"). Formed from the sound-symbolic root pati- / bati- ("clicking or snapping into place with a clean, decisive impact") with intensive medial consonant gemination (-tt-) and suffix -ri, conveying that preparations, timing, or execution hit the mark with 100% precision.

history.meaning: cleanly open, bright and distinct (especially of eyes)
spot-on, perfectly executed, completely ready without a flaw

バッチリ.notes: Used enthusiastically in spoken Japanese both as an adverb (バッチリ映っている, "caught clearly on camera") and as a standalone predicate (準備はバッチリ, "we're all set / ready to roll").

rootFamily.gloss: wide open and bright (especially of eyes)
fitting tightly and exactly, right on the mark
with a sharp snap or decisive precision

sources.title: Wiktionary: ばっちり / バッチリ

ババア.etymology: Vulgar, colloquial vowel-lengthened alteration of 婆 (baba, "grandmother, elderly woman"), a native Japanese reduplicated nursery/kinship word from Old and Classical Japanese baba (related to Old Japanese papa > Modern 母 haha, "mother", via voiced labial reduplication). In the Edo period, dragging out the final vowel to babā (婆あ / ババア) became a rough, disrespectful street form meaning "old hag, crone, old lady", symmetrical with ジジイ (jijī < jiji 爺, "old geezer").

history.meaning: grandmother, elderly woman, wet nurse
vulgar or familiar address/reference for an old woman
old hag, old bat (derogatory or rough colloquial)

ババア.notes: Coarse and insulting when directed at others (often intensified as クソババア, "old hag/bitch"), though occasionally used by women in rough self-deprecating humor about aging.

rootFamily.gloss: old geezer, old man (vulgar male counterpart)

sources.title: Wiktionary: ばばあ / ババア

バラ.etymology: Covers two distinct native Japanese lexical items commonly written in katakana: (1) "Rose" (薔薇, bara), which evolved phonologically from Old Japanese umara / ubara (茨・荊, "thorny shrub, bramble, wild rose", attested in the 8th-century Man'yōshū) -> Heian/Kamakura ibara -> bara through loss of the initial vowel. (2) "Loose, unbundled, scattered pieces" (bara), the unreduplicated mimetic base of バラバラ (barabara, "scattered, broken apart into separate units").

history.meaning: thorny bramble, briar, wild rose shrub
rose bush and its flower
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: rose flower; (homophone) loose, unbundled, or individual items

バラ.notes: "Rose" is regularly written in katakana as バラ because its Sino-Japanese kanji 薔薇 are complex (29 strokes combined); meanwhile, mimetic バラ ("loose/individual") appears in everyday commercial terms like バラ売り ("sold individually rather than in a pack") and バラ積み ("loading cargo in bulk").

rootFamily.gloss: thorny briar, bramble shrub (preserving the older vowel i-)
rose-colored; bright and optimistic (as in a rosy future)
selling items individually rather than as a boxed set

バラす.etymology: Native Japanese Godan transitive verb formed by attaching the transitive/causative verbal suffix -su (す) to the mimetic root bara- ("in separate pieces, scattered apart", the base of バラバラ barabara). From its core physical sense "to dismantle, take apart into pieces, butcher/fillet", it developed colorful extensions in Edo-modern underworld, merchant, and entertainment slang: "to blow open or expose a secret", "to dismember or kill", "to fence stolen goods piecemeal", and in film/TV production "to cancel/release a crew's booked schedule".

history.meaning: to break apart into pieces, dismantle, scatter
to take apart, butcher/fillet; to expose a secret; to cancel a production booking

morphemes.meaning: in separate pieces, apart, scattered (mimetic base of barabara)

バラす.notes: Highly polysemous across registers: 秘密をバラす ("spill a secret"), 魚をバラす ("fillet a fish"), 死体をバラす ("dismember a corpse"), and in Japanese TV/film industry jargon, 撮影をバラす ("call off a shoot and release the cast/crew").

rootFamily.gloss: dismantling a stage set; canceling a shoot; filleting fish (nominalized form)
to scatter around, hand out money or flyers lavishly

sources.title: Wiktionary: ばらす / バラす

バラエティ.etymology: Gairaigo loanword borrowed from English variety (and specifically used as a clipping of バラエティ番組 baraeti bangumi, modeled on English variety show). ヘアヌード.etymology: A Japanese-coined English compound (和製英語, wasei-eigo) combining ヘア (hea, from English hair, used euphemistically in Japanese media for 'pubic hair') + ヌード (nūdo, from English nude, borrowed from Latin nudus 'naked, bare, uncovered', from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós). Coined in the Japanese publishing industry around 1991—most famously catalyzed by photographer Kishin Shinoyama's bestselling photobook Water Fruit (水性) featuring actress Rie Miyazawa—to denote artistic or commercial nude photography in which pubic hair was left unretouched and uncensored.

history.meaning: English 'hair' + Latin/English 'naked, unclothed figure in art'
euphemistic 'pubic hair' + 'nude photography'

rootFamily.gloss: nude, nudity in art or photography
lifting the ban on pubic hair in media

ヘア解禁.etymology: A hybrid Sino-loanword compound (混種語, konshugo) combining gairaigo ヘア (hea, from English hair, in its specialized Japanese media sense of 'pubic hair') with the Sino-Japanese (漢語, kango) noun 解禁 (kaikin, 'lifting a ban, repealing a prohibition'). 解禁 is composed of 解 (Middle Chinese *kæiX, 'to untie, loosen, undo, release', originally depicting hands removing the horn of an ox) + 禁 (Middle Chinese *kimH, 'to prohibit, forbid, imperial restriction'). Refers to the watershed 1991 deregulation when Japanese police and customs authorities stopped prosecuting print publishers for showing pubic hair.

Formed by full reduplication of the sound-symbolic root *heto*, which evokes the expiratory sigh (*he-*) and collapsing limpness of a body drained of all physical stamina. It belongs to a closely related Early Modern and Modern Japanese phonesthemic cluster of exhaustion words starting with *he-*, alongside へたへた (hetaheta, 'sinking down weakly') and へばる (hebaru, 'to collapse from exhaustion').

The most widely accepted philological derivation analyses it as a compound or blend involving 間 (ma, 'interval, timing, luck, situational appropriateness', as seen in 間抜け manuke 'foolish, mistimed') preceded either by the pejorative prefixal root *he-* (as in へぼ hebo 'inept, bungling, clumsy' or 下手 heta 'unskillful') or as a contraction of 減り間 (herima, 'wasted time, unprofitable gap').

ペチャクチャ.etymology: A native Japanese (和語, wago) onomatopoeic reduplication with apophonic consonant-vowel alternation (擬音語, giongo), written in katakana as ペチャクチャ or hiragana as ぺちゃくちゃ (pechakucha). ペラペラ.etymology: A native Japanese (和語, wago) mimetic and onomatopoeic reduplication (擬音語・擬態語, giongo/gitaigo), written in katakana as ペラペラ or hiragana as ぺらぺら (perapera). From the image of thin pages turning effortlessly one after another, the meaning extended metaphorically to the smooth, rapid, uninterrupted flow of words when speaking a foreign language fluently (or talking glibly).

A widely cited Indo-European etymology (Kretschmer, Burkert) analyzes the name as a vocative compound of *pósis ('lord, husband', cf. Greek πόσις pósis, Sanskrit páti-) + *dā- ('earth', or 'waters'), originally meaning 'Lord of the Earth' or 'Lord of the Waters'. In Japanese nightlife and pop culture, mythological names like ポセイドン were frequently adopted for flamboyant cabarets, soaplands, and entertainment venues.

マヒ.etymology: Katakana rendering of the Sino-Japanese (kango) medical compound 麻痺 (mahi, 'paralysis, numbness, stupor'), borrowed from Middle Chinese *mæ-pjijH. The first element 麻 originally denoted hemp (Cannabis sativa), whose anesthetic properties led to the extended verbal and adjectival sense 'to go numb, tingling'; the second element 痺 carries the sickness radical (疒) and specifically denotes痹/痺 (rheumatic numbness or palsy of the limbs). Frequently written in katakana (マヒ) in modern Japanese media and prose because 痺 is outside the standard Jōyō kanji list, and used both literally for neurological paralysis and figuratively for institutional or moral stupor.

ヤクザ.etymology: Originated in Edo-period gamblers' cant (bakuto argot) from the three-card sequence 八・九・三 (ya-ku-za, 'eight-nine-three') in the traditional Hanafuda/Kabufuda card game Oicho-Kabu (おいちょかぶ). In Oicho-Kabu, points are counted modulo 10 (like Baccarat); a hand of 8 + 9 + 3 totals 20, yielding zero points—the worst possible, 'good-for-nothing' hand. Gamblers applied the term to a useless hand, then self-deprecatingly to themselves as social outcasts, and eventually to organized crime syndicates (暴力団 bōryokudan).

レンタルビデオ店.etymology: Three-part hybrid compound emblematic of 1980s Shōwa media culture, combining: (1) レンタル (rentaru, from English rental < Anglo-Norman rental < Old French rente 'income, payment' < Vulgar Latin *rendita 'something returned/yielded'), (2) ビデオ (bideo, from English video, substantivized from Latin videō 'I see'), and (3) the Sino-Japanese (kango) suffix 店 (ten, Middle Chinese *temH, 'shop, storehouse, inn'). Notice the Japanese word order レンタルビデオ ('rental video', versus English 'video rental') followed by 店 ('shop').

history.meaning: hired/leased + television tape ('I see') + merchant shopfront

history.form: レンタルビデオ店 (rentaru bideo-ten)
history.meaning: brick-and-mortar shop renting VHS and Betamax video cassettes (booming in early 1980s Japan)

morphemes.meaning: videocassette tape (< English video < Latin videō 'I see')

レンタルビデオ店.notes: The explosive proliferation of レンタルビデオ店 across Japan in 1983–1985 (as home VHS VCRs became affordable) transformed how movies and adult videos were distributed, normally partitioned with a famous noren curtain marking the 18+ corner.

rootFamily.gloss: video cassette rented from a shop (wasei-eigo word order)
rootFamily.word: レンタルビデオ (れんたるびでお)

rootFamily.gloss: specialty shop, retail store (販売 + 店)

レンチ.etymology: Borrowed from English *wrench* ('spanner tool for gripping and turning nuts and bolts', from Old English *wrenc* 'twisting').

history.meaning: tool for turning bolts and nuts
wrench; spanner

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — レンチ

レース.etymology: Borrowed from two English homophones: (1) English *lace* ('delicate openwork fabric of threads', from Old French *las* 'noose, cord' and Latin *laqueus*), as in レースのカーテン ('lace curtains'), and (2) English *race* ('speed competition').

history.meaning: delicate openwork fabric / competition of speed
lace fabric; race

ロケット.etymology: Gairaigo borrowed from English rocket, which entered 16th–17th century English (via French rochette) from Italian rocchetto ('small cylindrical bobbin or spool', and by visual analogy a cylindrical paper firework tube packed with gunpowder). Italian rocchetto is the diminutive of rocca ('distaff used for spinning wool or flax'), itself a borrowing from Lombardic/Germanic *rukko ('distaff', cognate with German Rocken). In Japanese, ロケット denotes both space/military rockets and, as a homophonous loan from English locket, a hinged pendant.

history.meaning: spinning distaff → small cylindrical bobbin; gunpowder firework tube
pyrotechnic projectile; jet-propelled space vehicle or missile
space rocket, missile; (homophone) hinged photo locket pendant

morphemes.meaning: rocket projectile (< English rocket < Italian rocchetto 'little bobbin')

ロケット.notes: Because Japanese merges English /r/ and /l/, ロケット (roketto) represents both English 'rocket' (space vehicle/projectile) and 'locket' (neck pendant for a photograph).

rootFamily.gloss: rocket firework, bottle rocket (ロケット + 花火)
rootFamily.word: ロケット花火 (ろけっとはなび)

rootFamily.gloss: explosive early start in a race or venture ('rocket start')
rootFamily.word: ロケットスタート (ろけっとすたーと)

ロッカー.etymology: Gairaigo borrowed from English locker ('a chest, compartment, or upright metal cabinet that can be secured with a lock'), derived from Middle English loker, formed from the noun/verb lock (< Old English loc 'fastening, bolt, enclosure', from Proto-Germanic *luką) + the suffix -er. (A homophonous Japanese borrowing ロッカー from English rocker also means a rock-and-roll musician.) Widely used in Japan for gym/workplace storage cabinets and station coin lockers.

history.meaning: bolt/fastening → small lockable chest on a ship → personal storage cabinet
lockable metal storage cabinet (in changing rooms or train stations)

ロッカー.notes: Ubiquitous across Japanese train stations in the compound コインロッカー (koin rokkā, 'coin-operated storage locker'), which became a recurring setting and plot device in Shōwa and Heisei Japanese fiction (such as Ryū Murakami's 1980 novel *Coin Locker Babies*).

rootFamily.gloss: coin-operated storage locker at a train station
rootFamily.word: コインロッカー (こいんろっかー)
ロッカールーム (ろっかーるーむ)

ロビー.etymology: Borrowed from English *lobby* ('spacious entrance hall or waiting foyer in a hotel, inn, or concert hall'), from Medieval Latin *lobia* ('covered walk, gallery').

history.meaning: foyer or reception hall of a building
hotel or theater lobby

cognates.meaning: work, labor (from the same Slavic root *orbota)

ロボット.etymology: Gairaigo borrowed via English robot from Czech robot, a neologism introduced to the world by Czech playwright Karel Čapek in his 1920 science-fiction drama *R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)* (and suggested to him by his brother, painter Josef Čapek). Derived from Czech robota ('feudal corvée labor, compulsory serf drudgery'), from Old Czech robota ('servitude'), from Proto-Slavic *orbota ('hard labor, servitude'), ultimately from PIE *h₃órbʰos ('orphan, servant, one bereft of free status', cognate with German Arbeit). Introduced to Japan in 1924 when *R.U.R.* was staged in Tokyo.

history.meaning: feudal serf/corvée drudgery → artificial humanoid laborer in Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.
mechanical automaton or programmable industrial machine
mechanical robot, anime mecha, or a figurehead puppet controlled by others behind the scenes

morphemes.meaning: robot, automaton (< Czech robot < robota 'forced labor')

ロボット.notes: Beyond Japan's famous industrial and anime mecha culture (ロボットアニメ), calling a company president or politician a ロボット in Japanese business dramas means they are a mere 'figurehead' or 'puppet' taking orders from shadowy backers.

rootFamily.gloss: giant-robot anime genre (such as Mazinger Z or Gundam)
rootFamily.word: ロボットアニメ (ろぼっとあにめ)
産業用ロボット (さんぎょうようろぼっと)

cognates.meaning: solitary, lonesome, sad from lack of company

ロンリー.etymology: Gairaigo borrowed from the English adjective lonely, formed in Early Modern English (first attested in Shakespeare's *Coriolanus*, c. 1607, as 'narrow and lonely') from lone + the adjectival suffix -ly. English lone is itself an aphetic (clipped initial vowel) shortening of alone, from Middle English al one, Old English eall āna ('all by oneself, wholly one'). In Japanese, ロンリー was popularized through postwar American pop songs and Shōwa kayōkyoku lyrics as a stylistic, sentimental alternative to native 寂しい (sabishii) or 孤独な (kodoku na).

history.meaning: all one → solitary, isolated → saddened by lack of companionship
lonely, lonesome (chiefly in pop music lyrics, titles, and playful colloquialism)

ロンリー.notes: In everyday Japanese conversation, people express loneliness with the native adjective 寂しい (sabishii); ロンリー is reserved for song titles, retro 1980s city-pop aesthetics, or lighthearted self-dramatization (e.g., ロンリーナイト 'lonely night').

rootFamily.gloss: native Yamato adjective: lonely, lonesome, desolate
solo, alone (from English solo; compare ロンリー)

ワイン.etymology: A modern gairaigo loanword borrowed from English wine, which descends from Old English win, an early West Germanic borrowing from Latin vinum ('wine, grapevine'), ultimately linked to a Mediterranean/Near Eastern wanderwort related to Proto-Semitic *wayn- and Classical Greek oinos. In Japanese, ワイン specifically designates Western-style fermented grape wine, contrasting with the older Sino-Japanese compound 葡萄酒 (ぶどうしゅ).

history.meaning: grape wine; vine
fermented grape juice
Western grape wine

ワイン.notes: In everyday modern Japanese, ワイン has largely superseded the formal kango term 葡萄酒 (ぶどうしゅ), though 葡萄酒 still appears on traditional domestic labels and in legal tax classifications. Pitch accent is initial-high [ワ]イン (1).

ワルツ.etymology: Borrowed from English *waltz* (and German *Walzer* 'ballroom dance and musical composition in triple 3/4 time', from German *walzen* 'to revolve, glide').

history.meaning: dance and music in 3/4 time
waltz

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ワルツ

ワンピース.etymology: Borrowed from English *one-piece (dress)*, referring in Japanese since the Taishō/Shōwa period to a woman's one-piece dress (whose bodice and skirt form a single garment).

history.meaning: dress made as a single garment
one-piece dress

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ワンピース

ワールド.etymology: A gairaigo borrowing from English world, which continues Old English weorold ('human existence, affairs of life, the earth'), a Proto-Germanic compound *weraldi- literally meaning 'age of man', formed from *weraz ('man', cognate with Latin vir) and *aldiz ('age, lifetime', related to old). In Japanese, ワールド is primarily used in commercial names, sports events, and figurative expressions denoting a distinct sphere or personal universe.

history.meaning: age or lifetime of man; human existence
human affairs; the earth and all life upon it
world; thematic sphere or realm (in compounds and media)

ワールド.notes: Unlike 世界 (せかい), which is the standard noun for the physical or geopolitical world, ワールド is stylistic and often suffixed to someone's name or genre to mean 'one's unique aesthetic/universe' (e.g., 村西ワールド).

一.etymology: Numeral 一 ('one'), read either with the Sino-Japanese borrowing いち / いつ (from Middle Chinese *'jit* 'one') or with the native Japanese root ひと (*pito* 'one').

history.meaning: the number one; first
one

一つ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *pitotu* (一つ 'one thing, one'), composed of the native numeral root ひと- (一 *pito* 'one') + the native general classifier suffix -つ (*-tu*).

history.meaning: one; a single thing
one (general counter); one thing

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一つ

一つ星.etymology: Native Japanese compound 一つ星 (ひとつぼし 'a single star; one-star rating'), combining 一つ (ひとつ 'one') + 星 (ほし > ぼし via rendaku, 'star', from Old Japanese *posi*). Originally denoting the evening star shining alone at dusk, and now also calquing culinary/hotel 'one-star' ratings.

history.meaning: solitary star in the evening sky
single star; one-star rating

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一つ星

一つ目.etymology: Ordinal numeral compound 一つ目 (ひとつめ 'the first one'), formed by attaching the ordinal/sequential suffix -目 (め, originally 'eye, notch on a measuring scale') to 一つ (ひとつ 'one').

history.meaning: the first item (also 'one-eyed' as a noun)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一つ目

一オクターブ.etymology: Hybrid musical measurement compound ('one octave'), combining Sino-Japanese numeral 一 (いち 'one') + loanword オクターブ (from French/English *octave*, ultimately from Latin *octāva* 'eighth degree of the diatonic scale').

history.form: 一 (いち) + オクターブ

一ダース.etymology: Hybrid numeral-classifier compound ('one dozen, twelve items'), combining Sino-Japanese numeral 一 (いち 'one') + Meiji-era English loanword ダース (from English *dozen*).

history.meaning: one dozen (12 units)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ダース

一ページ目.etymology: Trimorphemic compound combining the Sino-Japanese numeral 一 (ichi, 'one'), the English loanword counter ページ (pēji, from 'page'), and the native Japanese ordinal suffix 目 (-me, originally 'eye; notch on a measuring scale'). Attaching 目 to any number-plus-counter phrase converts a cardinal quantity (一ページ, 'one page') into an ordinal position (一ページ目, 'the first page').

history.meaning: borrowed from English 'page' as a noun and counter
the first page; page one

cognates.meaning: leaf of a book or score

一ページ目.notes: Pronounced イチページメ (or イッページメ in rapid speech).

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一ページ目

一ミリ.etymology: Hybrid metric measurement compound ('one millimeter; a tiny bit'), combining Sino-Japanese numeral 一 (いち 'one') + clipped loanword ミリ (from *millimètre / millimeter*).

history.meaning: one millimeter; the slightest bit

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ミリ

一万人.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) numerical compound read いちまんにん (ichimannin), composed of 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one'), 万/萬 (Middle Chinese *mjwɐnH, originally 'scorpion' used as a phonetic loan for the myriad unit '10,000'), and the counter 人 (Middle Chinese *nyin, 'person, human being'). Unlike 1 person (ひとり) and 2 people (ふたり), which retain native Yamato readings, numbers of people from 3 upwards regularly take the Sino-Japanese reading -にん (-nin).

history.meaning: one myriad of people; ten thousand people
ten thousand people

一万人.notes: East Asian myriad grouping counts in powers of 10,000 (万) rather than 1,000, so English 'ten thousand' requires explicitly stating 一万 (1 x 10,000) in Japanese.

rootFamily.gloss: tens of thousands of people; everyone

一万円.etymology: A Sino-Japanese monetary compound read いちまんえん (ichiman'en), combining 一 ('one'), 万 ('ten thousand'), and 円 (en, shinjitai simplification of 圓, Middle Chinese *hjwän, 'round, circular; round coin'). Following the New Currency Act of 1871 (Meiji 4), Japan adopted 圓 (えん) to designate its decimalized round silver and gold coinage modeled on Western dollars and Chinese silver rounds.

history.meaning: round; circular object or coin
basic unit of modern Japanese currency (adopted 1871)
ten thousand yen (highest standard banknote denomination)

一万円.notes: The 10,000-yen banknote (一万円札) is Japan's largest circulating bill; during the 1980s bubble era depicted in The Naked Director, it featured Meiji thinker Fukuzawa Yukichi and was colloquially nicknamed 諭吉 (Yukichi).

一人.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *pitori* (一人 'one person, alone, by oneself'), composed of the native numeral root ひと- (一 *pito* 'one') + the native human classifier suffix -り (*-ri*).

history.meaning: one person; alone
one person; alone

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一人

一人前.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound read いちにんまえ (ichininmae) with a hybrid Sino-Japanese numeral prefix: 一人 (originally read ひとり, here taking the kango reading いちにん in measuring compounds, 'one person') + 前 (まえ, native noun from Old Japanese ma-pe 'eye-side, in front', extended to mean 'an allotted share or portion placed before someone'). From the literal culinary sense of 'a single person's serving of food', it developed the figurative meaning of 'having the full competence, status, or earning power of an independent adult or artisan'.

history.meaning: portion of food or rations allotted set before one person
one serving; a full-fledged adult or professional

morphemes.meaning: portion; share; standing in front of

一人前.notes: Notice the reading distinction: 一人 alone is ひとり ('one person, alone'), whereas in 一人前 it must be read いちにんまえ, functioning both as a restaurant counter ('one serving') and as a predicate with に/の ('a full-fledged professional').

rootFamily.gloss: half a person's worth; wet behind the ears
two servings; working twice as hard as others
official principle; public stance (lit. 'standing in front')

一位.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read いちい (ichii), formed from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one, first') and 位 (Middle Chinese *hjwijH, 'court rank, throne, seat, position', a semantic compound of 人 'person' standing 立 at their assigned place at court). Under the ancient Ritsuryo code (Taiho Code of 701), 正一位 (Senior First Rank) and 従一位 (Junior First Rank) were the highest imperial court ranks; in modern usage, 一位 denotes 'first place' in a competition, chart, or ranking.

history.meaning: first court rank; highest official seat
first place; number one rank in a competition or survey

一位.notes: While 一番 (いちばん) is conversational and broad ('number one, best, most'), 一位 (いちい) belongs to formal rankings, sales charts, and athletic standings. Pitch accent is [い]ちい (1).

一体.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 一体 (いったい), from 一 ('one') + 体 ('body, form, substance'). Originally a Buddhist and philosophical noun meaning 'one body, a single whole', in Early Modern Japanese it also grammaticalized into an emphatic interrogative adverb ('what on earth?, in the world').

history.meaning: one body; one substance; overall
one body; (in questions) what/who on earth

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一体

一作目.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound read いっさくめ (issakume), consisting of 一 (いち, undergoing gemination to いっ before voiceless sibilant /s/, 'one'), 作 (さく, from Middle Chinese *tsak, 'to make, create; a literary or artistic work'), and the native ordinal suffix 目 (め, from Old Japanese me 'eye', metaphorically extended to the notches on a measuring scale or spaces on a go board, hence 'nth in sequence').

history.meaning: one creative work or agricultural harvest
the first work, film, or production in a series or career

一作目.notes: Common in film, publishing, and adult video industry jargon to refer to a director's or performer's debut release (デビュー作 / 一作目). Note the phonetic Assimilation (促音便): いち + さく -> いっさく.

一個.etymology: Sino-Japanese numeral-classifier compound 一個 (いっこ 'one piece, one small object'), combining 一 (いち > いっ 'one') + counter 個 (こ, originally a tally of bamboo stalks in Chinese, generalized to small discrete objects).

history.meaning: one piece; one individual item

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一個

一億.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) numerical compound read いちおく (ichioku), from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one') + 億 (Middle Chinese *ʔjik, originally 'to ponder, estimate, fill the mind', hence 'an unimaginably large number'). In ancient Chinese texts, 億 initially denoted 100,000 (ten myriad, 下数 system), before standardizing under the myriad-myriad (万万 = 10^8, 中数) system adopted in Japan during the Edo period via Yoshida Mitsuyoshi's 1627 mathematical treatise Jinkoki (塵劫記).

history.meaning: one hundred thousand (ancient); one hundred million (ten thousand myriads)
100,000,000 (10^8, one myriad myriads)

一億.notes: Unlike萬/万 (10,000), which requires 一 before it (一万, never bare 万 for 10,000), 億 (10^8) also mandates 一 (一億, never bare 億), whereas 100 (百) and 1,000 (千) normally stand without 一.

一億カラット.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and gairaigo compound read いちおくカラット (ichioku karatto), combining the Sino-Japanese numeral 一億 ('one hundred million', 10^8) with カラット ('carat'), borrowed from English carat, via French carat and Italian carato, from Arabic qirat ('carob seed; weight of four grains'), ultimately from Ancient Greek keration ('carob bean', diminutive of keras 'horn', referring to the curved pod of the carob tree whose uniform seeds served as ancient gemstone weights).

history.meaning: carob seed; small unit of mass for precious stones and gold
metric carat (200 mg) for gemstones; karat of gold purity

history.form: 一億カラット (いちおくカラット)
history.meaning: one hundred million carats (hyperbolic figure of dazzling brilliance)

一億カラット.notes: Used hyperbolically in Japanese pop culture, advertising, and showbiz (much like 'a million-dollar smile') to describe dazzling glamour or a star of astronomical value.

一億円.etymology: A Sino-Japanese monetary compound read いちおくえん (ichiokuen), composed of 一 ('one'), 億 ('one hundred million', Middle Chinese *ʔjik), and 円 ('yen; round coin', shinjitai of 圓, Middle Chinese *hjwän). In postwar and 1980s bubble-era Japan, 一億円 represented the archetypal threshold of astronomical wealth, heist jackpots (such as the famous 1968 Three Hundred Million Yen Robbery), and blockbuster business turnover.

history.meaning: one hundred million yen (pre-1946 orthography)
100 million yen

一億円.notes: At roughly $700,000–$1,000,000 USD depending on the exchange rate, 一億円 is the psychological equivalent of 'a million dollars' in English—hence a millionaire in Japanese is an 億万長者 ('hundred-millionaire').

一億四千万.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound numeral read いちおくよんせんまん (ichioku yonsenman), structured according to the East Asian myriad (10^4) place-value system: 一億 (1 x 10^8 = 100,000,000) + 四千万 (4,000 x 10^4 = 40,000,000). The components derive from Middle Chinese *ʔjit ('one'), *ʔjik ('10^8'), *sijH ('four', read here with the native Yamato numeral よん to avoid confusion with し 'death'), *tshen ('thousand'), and *mjwɐnH ('ten thousand').

history.meaning: one hundred million and four thousand myriads (140,000,000)

history.form: 一億四千万 (いちおくよんせんまん)

一億四千万.notes: To convert between English millions and Japanese 億/万 quickly, remember that 1 million is 100万 (百万), 10 million is 1,000万 (一千万), and 100 million crosses into the next myriad tier: 1億 (一億). Thus 140 million = 1億 + 4,000万.

一億弱.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound read いちおくじゃく (ichiokujaku), formed by suffixing 弱 (jaku, Middle Chinese *nyak, originally 'slender, pliable, weak, young', depicting two bows with decorative plumes) to the numeral 一億 ('one hundred million'). In Japanese quantitative usage, 弱 functions as a post-numeral approximation suffix meaning 'slightly less than, just under', contrasting directly with 強 (きょう, 'slightly more than, just over').

history.meaning: weak; pliant; deficient in strength or quantity

history.form: 一億弱 (いちおくじゃく)
history.meaning: slightly short of one hundred million; just under 100 million

一億弱.notes: A classic modern usage trap: 弱 after a number always means 'just under' that number (e.g., 一億弱 = ~95–99 million), though younger speakers sometimes mistakenly interpret '100 million + a little bit'—the exact opposite of its standard dictionary meaning! Its antonym is 強 (きょう, 'just over').

一円.etymology: Sino-Japanese monetary compound 一円 (いちえん 'one yen'), combining 一 (いち 'one') + 円 (えん 'circle, round coin; yen', adopted in 1871 as Japan's modern decimal currency unit after round silver coins).

history.meaning: one yen (also classic adverb 'throughout')

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一円

一分.etymology: Sino-Japanese numeral-classifier compound 一分 (いっぷん 'one minute', or いちぶ 'one-tenth, one part'), combining 一 ('one') + 分 ('minute of time; fraction/tenth', from 'dividing an hour into sixty parts').

history.form: 一分 (いっぷん / いちぶ)
history.meaning: one minute; one-tenth part

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一分
Wiktionary — 一分 (いっぷん / いちぶ) (Japanese)

一切れ.etymology: Native Japanese numeral-classifier compound 一切れ (ひときれ 'one slice, one piece, one cut'), combining ひと- (一 'one') + 切れ (きれ, nominalized stem of 切る *kiru* 'to cut, slice').

history.meaning: one slice (of bread, cake, fish)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 一切れ

一列.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read いちれつ (ichiretsu), combining 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one, single') and 列 (Middle Chinese *ljät, originally 'to divide, dismember, arrange in order', composed of 歹 'bone fragments' and 刀 'knife', from cutting up meat in orderly sequence, hence 'row, rank, file, line').

history.meaning: to divide in order; an orderly rank or row
a single row, line, or file

一列.notes: Used both as a noun (一列に並ぶ, 'to line up in single file') and with the ordinal suffix 目 (一列目, 'the front row' of a theater or classroom). Pitch accent is flat い[ちれつ] (0) or [いちれ]つ (3).

一割.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound read いちわり (ichiwari), combining the Sino-Japanese numeral 一 (いち, 'one') with 割 (わり, nominalized stem of the native Yamato verb 割る waru, 'to divide, split, cleave'). In Edo-period merchant arithmetic (ワリ算), 割 was established as the primary decimal fraction unit representing one-tenth (1/10 or 10%) of a whole, followed by 分 (ぶ, 1%), 厘 (りん, 0.1%), and 毛 (もう, 0.01%).

history.meaning: division; allotment; proportional rate of one-tenth
one-tenth; ten percent (10%)

morphemes.meaning: one-tenth; ten percent (from 割る 'to divide')

一割.notes: Crucial false friend within Japanese: 割 (わり) is 10%, so 一割 is 10%, and 五割 (ごわり) is 50%. However, when 分 (ぶ) follows 割 (as in 一割五分, 15% or .150 batting average), 分 means 1% (one-tenth of a 割), whereas alone (五分五分) 分 means 10%!

一千万.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) numerical compound read いっせんまん (issenman), formed from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one', geminating to いっ before /s/), 千 (Middle Chinese *tshen, 'thousand'), and 万/萬 (Middle Chinese *mjwɐnH, 'ten thousand'). Because East Asian numerals group by powers of 10^4 (myriads), 10,000,000 (10^7) is expressed as 'one thousand myriads' (1,000 x 10,000). In literary contexts, 千万 (せんまん / ちよろず) also meant 'countless, myriad'.

history.meaning: one thousand myriads; a countless multitude
ten million (10,000,000)

一千万.notes: Unlike 1,000 alone, which is usually just 千 (せん), 10,000,000 (1,000 x 10,000) mandates the leading 一: 一千万 (いっせんまん), never bare *千万 in modern numerical counting, to avoid ambiguity with the adverbial/archaic word 千万 ('exceedingly, myriad').

一口.etymology: Native Japanese compound 一口 (ひとくち 'one bite, one mouthful, a sip, a brief word'), combining ひと- (一 'one') + 口 (くち 'mouth, opening, share').

history.meaning: one mouthful; one utterance

一層.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) word read いっそう (issou), from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one', geminating to いっ before /s/) + 層 (Middle Chinese *dzong, 'story of a building, tier, stratum, layer', from 尸 'roof/building' + 曾 'to add on, pile up'). Originally a literal architectural noun meaning 'one story or tier of a pagoda/tower', it underwent metaphorical extension—recorded in Zen Buddhist koan literature (such as the Blue Cliff Record) as 'rising one story higher'—to function adverbially as 'one degree further, even more, all the more'.

一応.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) adverb read いちおう (ichiou), written 一応 (shinjitai of 一應), from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one, once') + 応/應 (Middle Chinese *ʔjing / *ʔjingH, 'to respond, correspond, deal with, ought'). In medieval and early modern Japanese, it replaced the older homophonous phrase 一往 (いちおう, 'one going, once, for a first pass') by kanji conflation, shifting semantically from 'responding once to a matter' to 'for the time being, tentatively, as a precaution, more or less'.

一文字.etymology: Compound combining the native numeral prefix ひと- (hito-, written 一, 'one, a single') with the Sino-Japanese word 文字 (moji, from Middle Chinese 文 'written pattern' + 字 'character, graph'). 一斉.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) noun and adverbial base read いっせい (issei), written 一斉 (shinjitai of 一齊), from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one', geminating to いっ before /s/) + 斉/齊 (Middle Chinese *dzej, originally a pictograph of three even heads of grain growing to the same height, hence 'even, uniform, equal, together'). Together, the compound literally means 'uniformly as one', yielding 'all at once, simultaneously, in unison'.

history.meaning: uniformly together; of equal height or order; all at once
simultaneity; all together at once; in unison

一斉.notes: Used adverbially with に (一斉に声を上げる, 'to raise voices all at once') or as a no-adjective/prefix before action nouns (一斉調査 'simultaneous nationwide survey', 一斉射撃 'volley fire'). Pitch accent is flat い[っせい] (0).

一斉摘発.etymology: A four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read いっせいてきはつ (issei tekihatsu), combining 一斉 ('all at once, simultaneous', from 一 'one' + 斉 'uniform, together') with 摘発 (てきはつ, 'exposure, uncovering, police raid/crackdown', composed of 摘 Middle Chinese *tæk 'to pluck, pick out, point out' and 発/發 Middle Chinese *pjwot 'to shoot forth, open up, disclose, uncover'). Literally, 'picking out and exposing lawbreakers simultaneously'.

history.meaning: to pick out and expose hidden faults or crimes

history.form: 一斉摘発 (いっせいてきはつ)
history.meaning: coordinated simultaneous police raid or crackdown on illegal operations

一斉摘発.notes: A staple of Japanese crime reporting and adult-entertainment/vice history (such as police crackdowns on unedited vinyl-shop pornography in 1980s Kabukicho), where authorities raid multiple branches at the exact same hour so targets cannot tip each other off.

rootFamily.gloss: pointing out; identification of a flaw

一斉検挙.etymology: A four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) legal/police compound read いっせいけんきょ (issei kenkyo), joining 一斉 ('simultaneous, all at once') with 検挙 (けんきょ, 'arrest, roundup, apprehension', shinjitai of 檢擧, composed of 検/檢 Middle Chinese *kjemX 'to inspect, examine, restrain' and 挙/擧 Middle Chinese *kjoX 'to lift up, raise, cite, apprehend'). Literally, 'simultaneously inspecting and hauling in suspects'.

history.meaning: official investigation and apprehension of offenders by authorities

history.form: 一斉検挙 (いっせいけんきょ)

一斉検挙.notes: Compare nuances: 一斉摘発 focuses on uncovering/raiding illicit operations or contraband, whereas 一斉検挙 emphasizes rounding up and arresting the suspects themselves.

一日.etymology: A dual-reading compound: as a Sino-Japanese (kango) word read いちにち (ichinichi), it combines 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one') + 日 (Middle Chinese *nyit, 'sun, day') to mean 'one day, all day long, per day'. As a native Yamato (wago) word written jukujikun with the same characters and read ついたち (tsuitachi), it is a phonetic contraction of Old Japanese つきたち (tukitati, 月立ち, literally 'moon-rising / appearance of the new moon'), denoting 'the first day of the month'.

history.form: 月立ち (つきたち) / 一日 (*ʔjit nyit)
history.meaning: rising of the new moon (1st of the month) / a single day's duration

history.form: 一日 (ついたち / いちにち)
history.meaning: first day of the month (tsuitachi); one day or all day (ichinichi)

一日.notes: Both readings and pitch patterns matter: いちにち means 'one day' (pitch いちにち [4] for duration 'one day', or [1] in some dialects/adverbial 'all day'), while ついたち means 'the 1st of the month'. In formal compounds like 一日署長 ('police chief for a day'), it is read いちにち.

rootFamily.gloss: all day long; throughout the day

一日一日.etymology: A reduplicated Sino-Japanese temporal expression read いちにちいちにち (ichinichi ichinichi), formed by repeating 一日 (いちにち, 'one day', from Middle Chinese *ʔjit 'one' + *nyit 'sun, day'). In Japanese morphology, full reduplication of temporal nouns (such as 一日一日, 一歩一歩 'step by step', 一年一年 'year by year') expresses distributive progression and steady, mindful accumulation across each individual unit of time.

history.meaning: one single day

history.meaning: day by day; each and every single day in succession

一日一日.notes: Unlike 毎日 (まいにち, neutrally 'every day'), 一日一日 highlights the preciousness or steady progression of each individual day (e.g., 一日一日を大切に生きる, 'to live cherishing each single day', or 一日一日と暖かくなる, 'to grow warmer day by day'). Often written 一日いちにち or １日１日.

rootFamily.gloss: day by day; daily (native wago reduplication)

一日中.etymology: Temporal compound 一日中 (いちにちじゅう 'all day long, throughout the whole day'), combining 一日 (いちにち 'one day') + Sino-Japanese suffix -中 (じゅう 'throughout the entire span of').

一杯.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read いっぱい (ippai), from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one') + 杯 (Middle Chinese *pwoj, 'wooden wine cup, bowl, goblet', composed of 木 'wood' and phonetic 不 *pjuw). one cupful; a drink of alcohol; filled to capacity / full

From the literal physical image of 'ascending by one stair-step or platform tier', it grammaticalized into an intensifying adverb meaning 'by a whole notch, even more, noticeably, especially'.

human life; one's course of life

一発.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read いっぱつ (ippatsu), from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one') + 発 (shinjitai of 發, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to shoot an arrow from a bow 弓, launch, discharge, emit'). Phonologically, いち + はつ (< *patu) underwent assimilation to いっぱつ, preserving the voiceless bilabial stop /p/. From the literal military/archery sense of 'one shot of a bow or firearm', it expanded in colloquial Japanese to mean 'one punch/blow, a single attempt, a big hit/home run, or a quick sexual encounter'.

one shot/bullet; a single blow; a big hit; one go/try; (slang) a quickie

morphemes.meaning: shot; blow; discharge; hit (read ぱつ)

Pitch is flat い[っぱつ] (0).

rootFamily.gloss: instant death; guaranteed kill with one blow

一発逆転.etymology: A modern four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) idiomatic compound read いっぱつぎゃくてん (ippatsu gyakuten), combining 一発 ('one shot, a single decisive blow or home run') with 逆転 (ぎゃくてん, 'reversal, turnaround, tables turned', composed of 逆 Middle Chinese *ngjæk 'contrary, reverse, upside down' and 転/轉 Middle Chinese *trjwenX 'to turn, revolve, shift'). Popularized through Japanese baseball broadcasting (where a walk-off home run turns a losing game around in one swing), it means 'turning the tables completely with a single bold stroke'.

history.meaning: revolving in the opposite direction; reversal of a situation or score

history.form: 一発逆転 (いっぱつぎゃくてん)
history.meaning: one-shot turnaround; dramatic comeback with a single decisive blow or gamble

morphemes.meaning: shot; blow; home run (read ぱつ)

一発逆転.notes: A quintessential Japanese idiom for high-stakes entrepreneurship, gambling, sports, and drama (e.g., 一発逆転を狙う, 'to aim for a one-shot comeback'). Compare 起死回生 (きしかいせい, a more literary classical Chinese yojijukugo meaning 'reviving from the brink of death').

rootFamily.gloss: one shot; big hit; single blow

一瞬.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read いっしゅん (isshun), formed from 一 (Middle Chinese *ʔjit, 'one', geminating to いっ before /ɕ/) + 瞬 (Middle Chinese *sywinH, 'to blink, wink, twinkle', composed of the semantic radical 目 'eye' and phonetic 舜 *sywinH). Literally 'one blink of an eye', it parallels the Latin-derived English 'moment' or German Augenblick ('eye-glance') to denote a fleeting split second or instant.

a split second; an instant; (adverbially) for a fleeting moment

morphemes.meaning: blink of an eye; wink; instant

The native Yamato verb reading of 瞬 is まばたく (mabataku, 'to blink'). Pitch accent is flat い[っしゅん] (0).

rootFamily.gloss: blinking of the eyes; twinkling of stars (native wago)
in the blink of an eye; in an instant

一秒.etymology: Sino-Japanese temporal compound 一秒 (いちびょう 'one second'), combining 一 (いち 'one') + 秒 (びょう, originally 'the fine beard/awn on a grain of rice', adopted in East Asian astronomy and clockwork for 'one-sixtieth of a minute').

Just as nodes divide a stalk of bamboo into distinct segments, 節 evolved semantically to denote a division of time, a musical measure or melody (fushi), and a discrete section or verse of a text or song.

Under the Meiji government's New Currency Act of 1871 (新貨条例), 圓 (en) was adopted as Japan's modern decimal currency unit—modeled on the round silver Mexican and Hong Kong dollars circulating in East Asia—replacing the oblong Edo-period gold koban and ryō.

三田村.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) habitational surname and toponym (三田村, Mitamura) composed of three native Yamato roots: 三 (mi-, from Old Japanese *mi, "three"), 田 (ta, from Old Japanese *ta, "irrigated rice field, paddy"), and 村 (mura, from Old Japanese *mura, "village, settlement; cluster of people"). Toponymically, 三田 (Mita) often referred either to three rice fields or served as an auspicious ateji spelling for 御田 (mita, "imperial, shrine, or lordly rice fields", with honorific prefix mi- < 御), to which 村 ("village") was suffixed to denote "village of the Mita estate".

Following the East Asian myriad (10^4) grouping system, three million (3,000,000) is structured as "three hundred ten-thousands" (300 × 10,000).

三百億.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) numerical compound (三百億, sanbyakuoku) composed of 三 (san, from Middle Chinese *sam, "three"), 百 (byaku, rendaku voiced form of hyaku, from Middle Chinese *pæk, "hundred"), and 億 (oku, from Middle Chinese *ʔik, "one hundred million, 10^8"). In the myriad-based (10^4) place-value system, thirty billion (30,000,000,000) is expressed as "three hundred hundred-millions" (300 × 100,000,000).

三秒.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) temporal compound (三秒, sanbyō) combining 三 (san, from Middle Chinese *sam, "three") and 秒 (byō, Kan-on from Middle Chinese *mjewX, composed of the grain radical 禾 and 少 "small", originally denoting the tiny beard or awn at the tip of an ear of grain, and hence any minute fraction). In late Imperial Chinese and Edo/Meiji Japanese astronomical and horological translation, 分 (fun, "minute, first division") and 秒 (byō, "second, second tiny division") were adopted to render Western minutes and seconds of arc and time.

上がり.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun (上がり, agari) derived from the continuative/infinitive stem (ren'yōkei) of the intransitive verb 上がる (agaru, "to rise, go up, ascend, be completed", from Old Japanese *agaru, an intransitive derivative built on the root of 上 *kami / *upe "upper part, top"). From the core physical sense of "rising or coming out (e.g., of a bath or rain)", it developed rich secondary senses: the completion of a process or craft, the final winning hand in games like mahjong or sugoroku, freshly brewed green tea at sushi restaurants (あがり), and financial proceeds, yield, or gross take from a business venture.

上出来.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound (上出来, jōdeki, a jūbako-yomi or "on-kun" compound) combining the Sino-Japanese prefix 上- (jō-, Go-on from Middle Chinese *dzyangH, "upper, superior, first-rate, high quality") with the native Japanese compound noun 出来 (deki, nominalized stem of 出来る dekiru < 出で来 idzuku, "to come out, emerge, be produced, be completed"). Literally meaning "superior turnout" or "first-rate production", it describes a result, performance, or piece of work that has turned out splendidly well.

上司.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (上司, jōshi) borrowed from Literary Chinese 上司, combining 上 (jō, Go-on from Middle Chinese *dzyangH, "upper, higher, above") and 司 (shi, from Middle Chinese *si, "to take charge of, administer; official bureau or officer"). In premodern Chinese and Japanese bureaucratic administration, 上司 referred to a higher-ranking government office or magistrate overseeing a lower jurisdiction; in modern Japanese corporate and institutional usage, it came to denote one's direct boss or organizational superior.

上品.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (上品, jōhin) combining 上 (jō, Go-on from Middle Chinese *dzyangH, "upper, highest") and 品 (hin, Kan-on from Middle Chinese *phimX, "class, rank, grade, article, character"). In Chinese and Japanese Pure Land Buddhism (浄土教), believers and rebirths in Amitābha's Pure Land were classified into nine grades (九品, kuhon), of which the highest tier was 上品 (jōbon, Go-on reading). Read with the Kan-on hin as jōhin in secular Edo and modern Japanese, it shifted from "top-grade goods/rebirth" to "refined, elegant, graceful, classy" in manners, taste, or appearance.

上手.etymology: A compound written with the kanji 上 (upper, superior) and 手 (hand, skill, performer), boasting two distinct phonological and semantic layers in Japanese. As the Sino-Japanese-styled reading 上手 (jōzu, combining Go-on jō < Middle Chinese *dzyangH "upper" + vocalized native/hybrid -zu < te/shu "hand, skill"), it evolved from "upper hand / master practitioner" to a na-adjective meaning "skilled, adept, good at", and also "flattering, smooth-talking" (お世辞が上手). Read with pure native kun'yomi as uwate (うわて) or kamite (かみて), it means "the upper grip in sumo / having the upper hand" or "stage left / upstream".

Politeness rules discourage calling oneself 上手 (jōzu); use 得意 (tokui) for your own strengths.
