不動産.etymology: Meiji-era Sino-Japanese legal and economic coinage 不動産 (ふどうさん 'real estate, immovable property', calquing French *biens immeubles* / English *immovable property*), combining 不動 ('unmoving, fixed') + 産 ('property, asset').

history.meaning: immovable property (land and buildings)
real estate; property

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 不動産

不動産管理室.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 不動産管理室 ('property management office'), combining 不動産 (ふどうさん 'real estate, property') + 管理 (かんり 'management, administration') + 室 (しつ 'office, room').

history.form: 不動産 + 管理 + 室
history.meaning: property management office

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 不動産

不可能.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) negative compound (不可能, fukanō) formed by prefixing the negator 不- (fu-, from Middle Chinese *pjuw, "not, un-, in-") to 可能 (kanō, "possible, capability", composed of 可 ka < Middle Chinese *khaX "permissible, able, can" + 能 nō < Middle Chinese *nong "ability, talent, capacity; originally a mythological bear-like beast of great strength"). Popularized during the Meiji period as the standard philosophical and scientific translation of English "impossible" and German "unmöglich".

history.meaning: not permissible and not within one's capability
impossible, unattainable; impossibility (Meiji philosophical/scientific term)
impossible, unfeasible (noun and na-adjective)

不可能.notes: Functions both as a na-adjective (不可能な計画 fukanō na keikaku, "an impossible plan") and as an abstract noun (不可能を可能にする fukanō o kanō ni suru, "to make the impossible possible"); more formal and absolute than 無理 (muri, "unreasonable / impossible to do").

不在.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (不在, fuzai) borrowed from Literary Chinese 不在, combining the negative prefix 不- (fu-, from Middle Chinese *pjuw, "not") and the verb/noun root 在 (zai, Go-on from Middle Chinese *dzojX, "to exist, be present, reside at a place", written with the earth radical 土 and phonetic 才). Literally meaning "not being at (one's place)", it denotes physical absence from home or the office, or more broadly the lack or absence of a leader or quality.

history.meaning: not present, not in place; passed away (euphemistic)
absence from one's residence, post, or seat

morphemes.meaning: to be present, exist, reside at (Go-on zai, MC *dzojX)

不在.notes: More formal than 留守 (rusu, "being away from home"); delivery couriers in Japan leave a 不在票 (fuzaihyō, "missed-delivery slip") when you are out, and business phone etiquette uses ただいま不在にしております ("He/she is currently away from the desk").

rootFamily.gloss: staying at home; working from home (za宅勤務)

不安.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (不安, fuan) borrowed from Literary Chinese 不安, combining the negative prefix 不- (fu-, from Middle Chinese *pjuw, "not, un-") and 安 (an, from Middle Chinese *ʔan, "peaceful, calm, settled, secure", pictographically depicting a woman 女 beneath a roof 宀). Originally denoting a lack of peace or physical/political instability, it developed psychologically to mean emotional unease, anxiety, apprehension, or nervousness about an uncertain outcome.

history.meaning: unsettled, lacking peace or security; ill at ease
uneasiness, instability, physical or mental discomfort
anxious, nervous, uneasy; anxiety, insecurity (noun and na-adjective)

不安.notes: Functions both as a noun (不安を感じる fuan o kanjiru, "to feel anxiety") and a na-adjective (将来が不安だ shōrai ga fuan da, "anxious about the future"); its direct emotional opposite is 安心 (anshin, "peace of mind, relief").

不幸.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (不幸, fukō) borrowed from Literary Chinese 不幸, combining the negative prefix 不- (fu-, from Middle Chinese *pjuw, "not, un-") and 幸 (kō, Kan-on from Middle Chinese *ghængX, "good fortune, luck, blessing, imperial favor, happiness"). Denoting the absence of good fortune, it covers objective calamity or bad luck ("misfortune, tragedy"), subjective emotional misery ("unhappiness"), and—especially with the polite prefix ご (ご不幸 go-fukō)—a bereavement or death in the family.

history.meaning: lack of good fortune, calamity, untimely death
misfortune, adversity, grief; bereavement
misfortune, unhappiness, tragedy (noun and na-adjective)

morphemes.meaning: good fortune, luck, happiness (Kan-on kō, MC *ghængX)

不幸.notes: Watch out for the homophone 不孝 (fukō, "filial impiety / being a bad child to one's parents", from 孝 "filial piety"), as well as the polite euphemism ご不幸がありました (go-fukō ga arimashita), which specifically means "there has been a death in the family". Its antonym is 幸福 (kōfuku) or 幸せ (shiawase).

rootFamily.gloss: happiness, good fortune, blessing (native Yamato reading)

不当.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of the negative prefix 不 (fu, Middle Chinese *pjuw, 'not, un-') and 当 (tō, traditional 當, Middle Chinese *tang, 'to match, be fitting, ought'). Borrowed from Literary Chinese 不當 ('not matching what is right; improper'), it is used in modern Japanese especially in legal, labor, and formal contexts for 'unjust' or 'unlawful'.

history.meaning: not matching what is proper; inappropriate
improper, unreasonable, unjust
unjust, unfair, unlawful

不当.notes: Functions as a na-adjective (不当な) and a noun prefix in legal compounds such as 不当解雇 (futō kaiko, 'unfair dismissal') and 不当利得 (futō ritoku, 'unjust enrichment').

不快.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 不快, combining the negative prefix 不 (fu, Middle Chinese *pjuw, 'not') with 快 (kai, Middle Chinese *khwaejH, 'pleasant, cheerful, brisk'). In pre-modern Japanese and Chinese it also meant 'slightly ill, indisposed', while in modern usage it primarily denotes emotional displeasure or sensory offensiveness.

history.meaning: unhappy, displeased; unwell in body
unwell, indisposed; unpleasant
unpleasant, offensive, displeased

不快.notes: Commonly paired with 感 to form 不快感 (fukaikan, 'feeling of displeasure/revulsion'); belongs to a more formal register than native イヤ (iya).

不思議.etymology: Sino-Japanese Buddhist compound 不思議 (ふしぎ), shortened from 不可思議 ('beyond thought or words, unfathomable', translating Sanskrit *acintya*, from 不 'not' + 思 'think, conceive' + 議 'discuss'). In everyday Japanese it softened to 'wonderful, mysterious, strange, curious'.

history.meaning: beyond human conception; miraculous
mysterious; strange; curious; marvelous

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 不思議

不景気.etymology: Japanese-coined Sino-Japanese (wasei-kango) formation prefixing 不 (fu, 'not, un-') to 景気 (keiki, originally 'scenery and atmosphere, vigor, lively spirit', from 景 'view, light' + 気 'spirit, vital breath'). As 景気 shifted in the Edo period from 'lively atmosphere' to 'business activity, economic conditions', 不景気 came to mean 'dull atmosphere' and then 'economic slump, recession', later borrowed into Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: atmosphere, appearance, liveliness
gloomy atmosphere; sluggish trade
economic recession, business slump; glumness

不景気.notes: Can also be used as a na-adjective (不景気な顔, 'a glum/downcast face') when describing someone's gloomy demeanor.

不満.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 不滿, formed from the negative prefix 不 (fu, Middle Chinese *pjuw, 'not') and 満 (man, traditional 滿, Middle Chinese *mwanX, 'full, filled, satisfied'). Literally 'not full', the concrete spatial sense of an unfilled vessel metaphorically yielded psychological discontent or dissatisfaction.

history.meaning: not full; unsatisfied
lack of fulfillment; discontent
dissatisfaction, discontent, complaint

不満.notes: Functions as both a noun (不満を抱く, 'harbor dissatisfaction') and a na-adjective (不満な点, 'a point of dissatisfaction'); its direct antonym is 満足 (manzoku).

不謹慎.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by adding the negative prefix 不 (fu, 'not, un-') to 謹慎 (kinshin, 'prudence, circumspection, self-restraint'), which combines 謹 (kin, Middle Chinese *kjinX, 'careful, respectful, solemn') and 慎 (shin, Middle Chinese *dzyinH, 'cautious, discreet'). It denotes a lack of solemn restraint or tact, especially in serious or somber situations.

history.meaning: respectful caution, circumspection, penitent confinement
indiscreet, imprudent, lacking due solemnity

不謹慎.notes: Frequently used in Japanese media and social commentary (e.g., 不謹慎発言, 'an insensitive/inappropriate remark') when someone jokes or acts lightly during a tragedy or scandal.

rootFamily.gloss: to restrain oneself, be discreet; to do respectfully

不釣り合い.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato (jūbako-yomi /湯桶読み style) formation combining the Sino-Japanese negative prefix 不 (fu, 'not, un-') with the native Yamato compound noun 釣り合い (tsuriai, 'balance, equilibrium, proportion'), nominalized from 釣り合う (tsuriau, 'to balance one another', from 釣る tsuru 'to suspend, hang' + 合う au 'to match, meet'). The metaphor derives from hanging weights on a balance scale so that both sides counterpoise.

history.meaning: mutual counterbalancing of suspended weights; equilibrium
out of proportion, unbalanced, mismatched
ill-matched, disproportionate, unbecoming

不釣り合い.notes: Often used for romantically or socially mismatched couples (不釣り合いなカップル) or clothing/status that seems out of place or 'out of one's league'.

rootFamily.gloss: to balance, be in proportion, suit each other

与える.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese あたふ (atafu, lower bigrade verb), the transitive/causative counterpart of the intransitive quadrigrade verb あたふ (atafu, 'to be fitting, be equivalent, be capable of', whence modern 能う atō). Derived from an Old Japanese root *ata- ('equivalent value, match, reach'), so that 'to make something reach or match someone' developed into 'to bestow, grant, give'.

history.meaning: to cause to reach; to bestow, grant, allot
to give, grant, confer (upon an inferior or generally)
to give, bestow, provide; to cause (an effect or impression)

morphemes.meaning: to bestow, grant, cause to reach

与える.notes: More formal and top-down than あげる (ageru); used for granting awards, assigning roles, or abstractly 'giving an impression/impact' (影響を与える, 印象を与える).

rootFamily.gloss: to be able to (literary, in negative 能わず)

rootFamily.word: 褒美を与える (hōbi o ataeru)

世の中.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) phrasal noun attested since Old Japanese (Man'yōshū) as よのなか (yo₂ no₂ naka), composed of 世 (yo, 'age, generation, lifetime, world of human affairs'), the genitive particle の (no), and 中 (naka, 'inside, midst'). Influenced by Buddhist conceptions of the temporal human realm (世間 seken), it literally means 'within the span of this life/world' and hence 'human society, the world at large'.

history.meaning: the span of human life; this transient world
human society, the state of the world, public life
society, the world, how the world works

世の中.notes: Refers to human society and lived reality ('the way the world works', e.g., 世の中お金だ, 'money makes the world go round') rather than the physical planet Earth (世界/地球).

rootFamily.gloss: worldly affairs, making one's way in the world

世界.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Buddhist Chinese 世界 (Middle Chinese *sjejH-keajH), coined in Chinese translations of Sanskrit Buddhist sutras (such as the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) to render Sanskrit लोकधातु (lokadhātu, 'world-realm, cosmos'). In Buddhist exegesis, 世 (se, 'generation, time') translates time (過去・現在・未来) and 界 (kai, 'boundary, space') translates spatial directions, together denoting the spacetime universe; in the Meiji period it was adapted to translate English 'world'.

history.meaning: cosmic realm, world-system in Buddhist cosmology
the spatiotemporal cosmos, realm of sentient beings
the world, the globe; a specific sphere or milieu

世界.notes: Besides the physical globe, 世界 often means a specific professional or subcultural 'milieu/sphere' (e.g., AVの世界, 'the world of adult video', 勝負の世界, 'the world of competition').

世界中.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound attaching the suffix 中 (-jū,voiced via rendaku from chū, Middle Chinese *trjuwng, 'middle, throughout, all within') to 世界 (sekai, 'the world'). In Japanese morphology, when 中 follows a spatial noun and means 'all over, throughout the entirety of', it is read -jū (as in 日本中 nihonjū, 家中 iejū).

history.meaning: world + within/throughout
throughout the whole world, all over the world

morphemes.meaning: throughout, all over, the entirety of

世界中.notes: Pronounced せかいじゅう (sekaijū) with a voiced -jū because it means 'throughout the entire world' (compare -chū for 'during an action', as in 会議中 kaigichū).

rootFamily.gloss: all year round, throughout the year

世界初.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 世界 (sekai, 'the world') with the suffixoid 初 (hatsu, Middle Chinese *tsrhjo, originally 'beginning of cutting cloth with a knife', hence 'first, initial'). Used in modern news, marketing, and broadcasting to mean 'a world first, the first time in the world'.

history.meaning: world + first/initial
world first, first in the world

morphemes.meaning: first, initial, for the first time in

世界初.notes: Beware of the homophone 世界発 (sekaihatsu, 'originating from the world'); 世界初 takes の to modify nouns (世界初の試み, 'a world-first attempt').

世界観.etymology: Meiji-period Sino-Japanese (wasei-kango) philosophical calque of German Weltanschauung ('world-perception, worldview', coined by Immanuel Kant in Kritik der Urteilskraft, 1790), combining 世界 (sekai, 'world', rendering Welt) with 観 (kan, traditional 觀, Middle Chinese *kwanH, 'view, contemplation, outlook', rendering Anschauung). In late 20th-century Japanese creative industries, it expanded from philosophical 'worldview' to mean the cohesive 'fictional universe, lore, or visual/artistic aesthetic' of a film, anime, or creator.

history.meaning: philosophical perception or conception of the world
philosophical worldview, conception of the universe and human life
worldview; cohesive aesthetic, setting, or lore of a creative work

世界観.notes: In media, film, and pop culture (like *The Naked Director*), 世界観 very often means 'creative vision, atmosphere, or fictional universe/aesthetic' rather than political or philosophical ideology.

rootFamily.gloss: view of life, philosophy of life (calque of Lebensanschauung)

世話.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 世話 (せわ), from 世 ('the world, everyday society') + 話 ('talk, speech'). Originally a Buddhist and medieval term for 'everyday vernacular talk or worldly affairs', in the Edo period it shifted to 'everyday assistance, looking after someone, care, trouble'.

history.meaning: common everyday speech; worldly matters
looking after; care; help; assistance

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 世話

cognates.meaning: the world, society (esp. in Buddhist or literary contexts)

世間.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Buddhist Chinese 世間 (Middle Chinese *sjejH-kean, read with go-on pronunciation seken rather than kan-on sekan), translating Sanskrit लोक (loka, 'the world of living beings, the mundane realm of transmigration'). In Japanese cultural usage, it evolved from the Buddhist 'secular world of mortals' into the watchful 'surrounding social community, public eye, and conventional society'.

history.meaning: the transient realm of sentient existence; the secular world
human society, secular life, the social world around oneself
the public, society, social appearances and norms

morphemes.meaning: space between, interval, realm among people

世間.notes: Carries a strong cultural nuance of 'what other people will think' or 'the public eye'—seen in 世間体 (sekentei, 'social appearances/reputation') and 世間知らず (sekenshirazu, 'naive about the world').

rootFamily.gloss: appearances before society, public reputation, decencies
small talk, chatting about everyday things

丘.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *woka* (丘・岡 'hill, gentle knoll, rising ground'), attested throughout the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: hill; rising ground
hill; knoll

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 丘

両手.etymology: The term '両手' (meaning 'both hands') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: both hands
both hands

両手.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 両手

両方.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 両方 (りょうほう 'both sides, both'), combining 両 (りょう 'both, pair') + 方 (ほう 'side, direction, party').

history.meaning: both sides; both

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 両方

両足.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato compound combining the Sino-Japanese prefix 両- (ryō-, from Middle Chinese *ljangX 'pair, both of two symmetrical things') with the native Yamato noun 足 (ashi, 'foot, leg', Old Japanese asi). Because human limbs come in natural pairs, 両- attaches productively to native body-part nouns (両足 ryōashi 'both feet/legs', 両手 ryōte 'both hands') without shifting the noun to its Sino-Japanese reading.

history.meaning: foot, leg

history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese
history.meaning: both feet, both legs
both feet, both legs

両足.notes: Used with で (両足で立つ) to emphasize standing balanced squarely on both feet.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 両足

並ぶ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *narabu* (並ぶ 'to stand side by side, line up in a row, rival/equal'), the intransitive four-grade counterpart of 並べる (*naraberu*), built on the root *nara-* (seen in ならす 'level out').

history.meaning: stand in a row; be side by side
line up; stand in a row; queue

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 並ぶ

並べる.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) transitive verb 並べる ('to line up, arrange side by side, set out in order, compare'), continuing Old Japanese *narabu* (lower bigrade), transitive counterpart of 並ぶ.

history.meaning: place side by side; arrange in a row
line up; arrange; display

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 並べる

中.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *naka* (中 'inside, interior, middle, among, relationship'), or read with its Sino-Japanese borrowing ちゅう / じゅう ('in the middle of, throughout').

history.meaning: middle; interior; inside
inside; middle; among; during

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中
Wiktionary — 中 (なか / ちゅう) (Japanese)

中古.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 中古. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中古

中庭.etymology: Native Japanese compound (jukujikun/kun-reading) of 中 ('inside, inner') and 庭 ('garden, courtyard'), naming an enclosed courtyard surrounded by wings or walls of a house or inn.

中庭じゅう.etymology: Compound noun formed by attaching the Sino-Japanese totality suffix -じゅう (-jū, written 中, voiced by rendaku from chū 'inside, throughout the whole span of') to the native Yamato compound 中庭 (nakaniwa, 'inner courtyard', from 中 naka 'middle, inside' + 庭 niwa 'garden, courtyard'). Notice that the character 中 appears twice in the etymology—first in its native reading naka ('inner') and then at the end in its voiced Sino-Japanese reading -jū ('all throughout').

history.meaning: inner garden enclosed by buildings
all throughout the courtyard

morphemes.meaning: all over, throughout the entire space of

中庭じゅう.notes: When attached to a place noun, -じゅう means 'all across that entire place' (中庭じゅう = 'across the whole courtyard').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中庭

中庭カフェ.etymology: Hybrid compound noun 中庭カフェ ('courtyard café'), combining native Japanese 中庭 (なかにわ 'inner courtyard garden surrounded by a building', from 中 'inside' + 庭 'garden/courtyard') + French/English loanword カフェ (*café*).

history.form: 中庭 (なかにわ) + カフェ
history.meaning: café set in an inner courtyard

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中庭

中庭側.etymology: Native Japanese spatial compound 中庭側 ('courtyard side'), combining 中庭 (なかにわ 'inner courtyard') + 側 (がわ 'side, facing side').

history.form: 中庭 (なかにわ) + 側 (がわ)
history.meaning: side facing the inner courtyard

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中庭

中庭建築.etymology: Hybrid compound noun 中庭建築 ('courtyard architecture, building built around an inner courtyard'), combining native 中庭 (なかにわ 'inner courtyard') + Sino-Japanese 建築 (けんちく 'architecture, building construction').

history.form: 中庭 (なかにわ) + 建築 (けんちく)
history.meaning: courtyard-style building architecture

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中庭

中心.etymology: The term '中心' (meaning 'centre') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: centre
centre

中心.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 中心

中止.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 中止 (Middle Chinese *trjuwng-tsyiX), combining 中 (chū, 'middle, midway, in the course of') and 止 (shi, 'to stop, halt, cease', originally a pictograph of a foot). Literally 'stopping midway', it denotes calling off a planned event or halting an ongoing operation before completion.

history.meaning: to stop halfway through an action
halting midway; suspension, cancellation of an event or project

中止.notes: Used both for calling off a scheduled event before it starts (雨天中止, 'canceled due to rain') and for aborting an ongoing project or shoot (撮影中止, 'halting filming').

中身.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound of 中 (naka, 'inside, interior') and 身 (mi, 'body, flesh, fruit, main substance', originally 'flesh/meat inside a shell or rind', hence the substantial core). Historically also written 中実 ('interior fruit/substance') or applied specifically to the steel blade inside a sword scabbard before generalizing to 'contents, interior substance' of any container or work.

history.meaning: the blade inside a scabbard; the flesh or meat inside a shell
physical contents of a container; inner substance or merit
contents, interior; substance,实质/character of a person or work

中身.notes: Refers both to physical contents (箱の中身, 'contents of a box') and to intellectual/moral substance (中身のない話, 'an empty talk with no substance';compare formal 内容 naiyō).

rootFamily.gloss: yolk vs. egg white; heartwood vs. sapwood (literally 'red/white flesh')
half the body; half a filleted fish

中途半端.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by combining two synonymous binomes for emphasis: 中途 (chūto, from Literary Chinese 中途 'midway on a road/journey', from 中 'middle' + 途 'road, way') and 半端 (hanpa, 'fragment, incomplete fraction, odd remainder', from 半 'half' + 端 'edge, odd piece, fraction'). Together they reinforce the sense of stopping partway and leaving something neither one thing nor the other.

history.meaning: midway on a road + incomplete fraction or odd piece
halfway, incomplete, half-baked, noncommittal

中途半端.notes: A favorite Japanese critique of lukewarm effort or indecisiveness (中途半端な態度, 'a wishy-washy/half-hearted attitude'; 中途半端にやるな, 'don't do things by halves!').

rootFamily.gloss: on the way, midway through (variant writing of 中途)
odd remainder, incomplete, half-baked; (slang) no joke/extreme (ハンパない)

丸.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *maro* (丸・麻呂 'round thing; oneself'), which shifted phonetically in Middle Japanese to まる (*maru* 'circle, sphere, whole, perfection mark').

history.meaning: round thing
circle; round; whole

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 丸

丸い.etymology: Adjective 丸い・円い ('round, circular, spherical, harmonious'), formed in Middle Japanese by attaching the native *-i* adjective inflection to the noun/root まる (丸 'circle, round').

history.form: まるし → まるい (丸い)
history.meaning: round; circular; spherical
round; spherical; amicable

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 丸い

丸ごと.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound of 丸 (maru, 'round, whole, complete, undivided', from Old Japanese まろ maro 'round, spherical, whole') and the suffix ごと (-goto, written 共 or 如, 'together with, including the container or whole of', related to 共 tomo/goto). Just as 皮ごと (kawagoto) means 'skin and all', 丸ごと means 'as a single undivided whole, in its entirety'.

history.meaning: round, spherical; whole, intact
the whole thing together, in its entirety, lock, stock, and barrel

morphemes.meaning: together with, including the whole of

丸ごと.notes: Functions adverbially (丸ごと食べる, 'eat it whole') or before a noun (丸ごと一個, 'one whole piece'); conveys swallowing, buying, or accepting something completely without cutting or omitting anything.

rootFamily.gloss: memorizing by rote (swallowing whole without digesting)

丸一日.etymology: Hybrid Yamato-Sino compound prefixing native Yamato 丸 (maru, 'whole, full, complete', from Old Japanese まろ maro 'round, whole') to the Sino-Japanese temporal counter 一日 (ichinichi, 'one day', from 一 'one' + 日 'sun, day'). Here 丸 acts as an emphatic prefix meaning 'a full, uninterrupted span of'.

仕組み.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) nominalization (ren'yōkei) of the compound verb 仕組む (shikumu, 'to devise, contrive, construct'), composed of 仕 (shi-, stem of する suru 'to do') + 組み (kumi, nominalized stem of 組む kumu, Old Japanese *kumu, 'to braid, join together, assemble'). In Edo theater (kabuki and jōruri), 仕組み denoted the 'plotting/dramatic structure' of a play before generalizing to any 'mechanism, contrivance, or system'.

history.meaning: dramatic plot, plan, or contrived arrangement (esp. in Edo theater)
mechanism, structure, system, or behind-the-scenes setup

morphemes.meaning: doing, devising (stem of suru, ateji 仕)
joining, assembling, framework (stem of verb kumu)

仕組み.notes: Can be neutral ('how a machine/economy works', 社会の仕組み) or slightly suspicious ('a rigged setup/scheme'), especially because its parent verb 仕組む (shikumu) strongly implies 'to plot, stage, or rig behind the scenes'.

rootFamily.gloss: to devise, to plot, to set up, to rig
to put together, to cross, to partner with

他.etymology: Orthographic convergence of two etymological layers written with the kanji 他 ('other, another'): (1) the native Yamato noun ほか (hoka, Old Japanese *poka, 'outside, exterior place, something else', likely related to *puka 'outer') and (2) the Sino-Japanese reading た (ta, Middle Chinese *tha, 'other, another'). In modern prose, standalone 他 is most commonly read hoka ('other, the rest, besides'), while ta appears in formal writing (他の ta no) and Sino-Japanese compounds.

history.meaning: outside, exterior place; another place or thing
other, another, the rest, besides

morphemes.meaning: other, outside, elsewhere (kun'yomi: hoka; on'yomi: ta)

他.notes: When followed by の (他の), it can be read either ほかの (hoka no, everyday spoken and written register) or たの (ta no, formal/written register). The kanji 外 is also read hoka when emphasizing 'outside/except'.

rootFamily.gloss: the others, the rest, and so forth
rootFamily.word: その他 (そのほか / そのた)

付き.etymology: Continuative nominal stem (連用形) of the native intransitive verb 付く (tsuku, Old Japanese tuku, 'to adhere, attach, accompany'). When compounded directly after a noun X (X付き), it forms an adnominal or predicative noun meaning 'having X attached, accompanied by X, complete with X'—ubiquitous in Japanese hospitality and everyday life (朝食付き 'with breakfast included', 庭付き 'with a garden', ハンコ付き 'bearing an official stamp').

history.meaning: to attach; to adhere to
nominal suffix 'with ... attached/included'

付き.notes: Often pronounced -tsuki (ハンコ付き hankotsuki) or with rendaku -zuki (色付き irozuki, 条件付き jōkenzuki) depending on the preceding noun.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 付き

付き人.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 付き (tsuki, the continuative stem of the intransitive verb 付く tsuku, Old Japanese *tuku, 'to attach, attend upon, accompany closely') + 人 (bito, voiced via rendaku from hito, Old Japanese *pito₁, 'person'). Literally 'an attached person' or 'one who stays by another's side', historically used for retainers or brides' attendants and in modern entertainment/sumo for a star's live-in personal assistant or apprentice.

history.meaning: retainer, escort, or personal attendant accompanying a noble or bride
personal assistant, dresser, or apprentice attendant to an actor, director, or sumo wrestler

morphemes.meaning: attaching, attending upon (stem of verb tsuku)
person, attendant (kun'yomi hito voiced to -bito by rendaku)

付き人.notes: In Japanese showbiz (芸能界), comedy, and sumo, a 付き人 is not merely a hired secretary but often a junior apprentice who learns the craft while handling a senior star's errands, wardrobe, and schedule.

rootFamily.gloss: to be attached, to attend upon, to follow

付く.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tuku* (付く・着く・附く 'to stick to, attach, be included with, turn on [of lights or power], arrive').

history.meaning: adhere; make contact; arrive
be attached; stick; turn on; accompany

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 付く

付ける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive verb 付ける (tsukeru), evolving from Old Japanese lower bigrade (shimo nidan) 付く (tuku, 'to bring into contact, attach, apply, affix'), the transitive counterpart of four-grade (yodan) intransitive 付く (tuku, 'to stick, adhere'). From the core spatial sense of 'bringing one surface into contact with another', it branched into wearing items, applying substances, recording entries, assigning prices/names, and switching on lights/devices.

history.meaning: to bring into contact, attach, apply, set fire to
to attach, put on, apply, turn on, record, or assign

morphemes.meaning: to attach, bring into contact, apply (transitive stem)

付ける.notes: In the show's context (e.g., ゴムを付ける, 'to put on a condom'), it means 'to put on / wear / apply'. Note that Japanese orthography splits tsukeru across multiple kanji by nuance: 付ける (attach/apply/put on), 着ける (wear on the body), 点ける (turn on a light), 漬ける (pickle/soak).

rootFamily.gloss: to be attached, to stick, to come with (intransitive)

rootFamily.word: 取り付ける (とりつける)

rootFamily.gloss: to be careful, to pay attention (lit. 'attach one's spirit')
rootFamily.word: 気を付ける (きをつける)

付け根.etymology: Native Japanese compound joining 付け (tsuke, continuative stem of 付ける tsukeru, 'to attach, join') and 根 (ne, 'root, base, foundation'). Literally 'the root of attachment', it denotes the anatomical or structural junction where a projecting part meets its body—such as the base/heel of the palm (手のひらの付け根), the base of the neck or thigh, or where a branch joins a trunk.

history.meaning: point of attachment; anatomical base or joint
base; root; joint

付け根.notes: In bread-making, 手のひらの付け根 ('the base of the palm') is the exact equivalent of English 'the heel of your hand'.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 付け根

代わり.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun derived from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 代わる (kawaru, Old Japanese *kaparu, 'to change, take the place of, alternate'), the intransitive partner of 代える / 変える (kaeru < Old Japanese *kapu, 'to exchange, replace'). Originally denoting the act of substituting one thing or person for another, it grammaticalized in construction with に (代わりに kawari ni) to mean 'in place of' or 'in return/compensation for'.

history.meaning: alteration, succession, or substitution of one thing for another
substitute, replacement, stand-in; compensation or 'in return'; second helping (お代わり)

morphemes.meaning: to take the place of, substitute (verb stem kawar-)

代わり.notes: Used both for a stand-in/substitute (彼の代わり, 'his replacement') and in the high-frequency idiom その代わり(に) (sono kawari ni, 'in exchange for that / on the other hand'). With the honorific prefix お, お代わり (okawari) means 'a second helping of food/drink'.

rootFamily.gloss: to take the place of, to be substituted (intransitive)

代わる.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *kaparu* (代わる・替わる・変わる 'to take the place of, be replaced, alternate, change'), originally a single verb family built on the root *kapa-* ('exchange, shift'). The spelling 代わる specifically denotes 'taking someone's place or turn'.

history.form: かはる (代はる・変はる)
history.meaning: change places; alternate; shift
take the place of; substitute for; be relieved

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 代わる

代表.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 代 (dai, Middle Chinese *dojH, 'to substitute, act in place of') and 表 (hyō, Middle Chinese *pjewX, 'outer surface, to manifest, to display publicly'). Coined/popularized in Meiji Japan to translate Western political and legal concepts of 'representation' (standing in for a group and displaying its will publicly), and subsequently borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese. In Japanese business, it also serves as short for 代表取締役 (representative director / CEO).

history.meaning: political or legal representation; delegate standing for a group
representative, head of a company/group, exemplar; main switchboard number

morphemes.meaning: to substitute for, act on behalf of (on'yomi: dai)
surface, to express, to stand out publicly (on'yomi: hyō)

代表.notes: In Japanese corporate contexts, addressing someone as 代表 (or 代表取締役 daihyō torishimariyaku) identifies them as the legally registered head/CEO of a firm; on business cards next to a phone number, (代) indicates the company's main switchboard number.

rootFamily.word: 代表的 (だいひょうてき)
代表取締役 (だいひょうとりしまりやく)

令状.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 令 (rei, Middle Chinese *ljengH, 'command, order, decree') and 状 (jō, Middle Chinese *dzjangH, 'written document, form, certificate'). Under the medieval ritsuryō legal system, 令状 referred to an official written order issued by a court noble or imperial prince; in Meiji judicial modernization, it was revived as the technical term for a court-issued 'warrant' or 'writ' (such as an arrest warrant or search warrant).

history.meaning: written command or edict issued by high nobility or imperial family
judicial warrant (arrest warrant 逮捕状 or search warrant 捜索令状)

令状.notes: In police dramas and legal contexts, 令状 alone usually refers to either a 捜索差押令状 (search and seizure warrant) or a 逮捕状 (arrest warrant). Do not confuse with the homophone 礼状 (reijō, 'thank-you letter').

rootFamily.word: 招待状 (しょうたいじょう)

以上.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 以上 (いじょう 'and above, more than, beyond this; that is all; now that'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 以上 (combining 以 'taking this as the boundary' + 上 'above, upward').

history.meaning: from this point upward; the foregoing
more than; at least; that is all; since/now that

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 以上

以内.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) relational noun from Classical Chinese 以内 (Middle Chinese *yiX-nwojH), composed of 以 (i, originally a verb 'to take/use', grammaticalized in Classical Chinese before locative bounds as a marker of boundary or reference point, 'starting from / taking X as the limit') and 内 (nai, 'inside, within'). Literally 'bounded on the inside of X', including the boundary value itself ('within, up to and including').

history.meaning: taking [the stated limit] and staying inside it; within
within, no more than, up to and including (of time, distance, or quantity)

morphemes.meaning: by means of, taking as a boundary point (on'yomi: i)

以内.notes: Legally and mathematically inclusive of the endpoint: 3日以内 ('within 3 days') includes the third day itself. Attaches directly to quantitative phrases (e.g., 10万円以内, 1時間以内). Antonym: 以外 (igai) or 以上 (ijō).

rootFamily.gloss: other than, except for, outside of
more than, at least, from ... upward
less than, at most, from ... downward

以前.etymology: The term '以前' (meaning 'before') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: before
before

以前.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 以前

以外.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) relational noun from Classical Chinese 以外 (Middle Chinese *yiX-ngwajH), composed of the boundary marker 以 (i, 'taking X as the reference limit') and 外 (gai, 'outside, beyond'). Originally spatial ('beyond the boundary of'), it generalized to an exclusionary logical marker meaning 'everything outside of X', i.e., 'other than, except for, besides'.

history.meaning: beyond the boundary of; outside of
other than, except for, apart from

morphemes.meaning: taking as a reference point or boundary (on'yomi: i)

以外.notes: Watch out for the exact homophone 意外 (igai, 'unexpected, surprising', literally 'outside one's thought 意'): 以外 means 'except for / other than' (これ以外, 'other than this'), whereas 意外 means 'surprising' (意外な結果, 'an unexpected result').

rootFamily.gloss: unexpected, surprising (homophone with different first kanji)

以来.etymology: Sino-Japanese temporal compound 以来 (いらい 'since then, ever since'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 以来 (combining 以 'starting from' + 来 'come down to the present').

history.meaning: from that time onward until now
since; ever since

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 以来

仮に.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) adverbial phrase formed from the noun 仮 (kari, Old Japanese *kari, 'something temporary, provisional, borrowed for the moment', etymologically linked to the verb 借りる / 借る karu 'to borrow temporarily') + the dative/locative/manner particle に (ni). From the concrete sense 'on a temporary or makeshift basis', it developed a modal conditional sense: 'positing provisionally for the sake of argument — supposing, even if'.

history.meaning: temporarily, transiently, for the time being (contrasted with makoto/permanent)
provisionally; supposing, for the sake of argument, even if

morphemes.meaning: adverbial/manner marker ('in the manner of, as')

仮に.notes: As a sentence adverb, 仮に sets up a hypothetical or counterfactual clause and almost always pairs with としても, たら, or なら at the end of the clause (e.g., 仮に失敗したとしても, 'Even supposing we were to fail...').

仮払い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun combining 仮 (kari, 'temporary, provisional') + 払い (barai, voiced via rendaku from harai, the continuative nominalization of 払う harau, Old Japanese *parapu, 'to sweep away, clear away', which acquired the commercial sense 'to clear a debt, to pay out money' in Late Middle Japanese). Literally 'a provisional payout', denoting an advance disbursement of funds before final expense amounts are settled.

history.meaning: to sweep away, clear away; (later) to clear an obligation by paying money
history.stage: Old Japanese to Late Middle Japanese

history.meaning: provisional payment, cash advance (accounting term for suspense payments)

morphemes.meaning: payment, disbursement (stem of harau voiced to -barai by rendaku)

仮払い.notes: Standard corporate accounting term (often paired with 仮払金 karibaraikin, 'suspense payment / cash advance account') used when advancing travel or production cash to staff before actual receipts are submitted and reconciled (精算 seisan).

仲.etymology: Etymologically the same native word as 中 (なか 'inside, between', from Old Japanese *naka*). Written specifically with the kanji 仲 ('standing between people') when referring to personal relationships, intimacy, or terms between people.

history.meaning: space between; interpersonal relation
relationship; terms; friendship

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 仲

仲直り.etymology: Native Japanese compound 仲直り (なかなおり 'reconciliation, making up after a quarrel'), combining 仲 (なか 'interpersonal relationship') + 直り (なおり, nominalized stem of 直る 'to be restored, return to normal').

history.meaning: restoring good terms; making up

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 仲直り
Wiktionary — なかなおり (仲直り) (Japanese)

仲良く.etymology: Adverbial (*ren'yōkei*) form of the compound adjective 仲良い (なかよい 'on good terms, friendly, harmonious'), combining 仲 (なか 'relationship') + 良く (よく, adverbial form of 良い 'good').

history.meaning: harmoniously; on friendly terms; getting along well

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 仲良く

仲間.etymology: Native Japanese compound 仲間 (なかま 'companion, colleague, fellow member of a group'), combining 仲/中 (なか 'shared circle, relationship') + 間 (ま 'space, interval, shared realm'). In the Edo period it also designated licensed merchant guilds.

history.meaning: circle of associates; guild; companion
friend; companion; colleague; fellow member

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 仲間

件.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and counter 件 (けん 'matter, case, item, subject', or native reading くだん 'the aforementioned matter'), borrowed from Middle Chinese *gjenX* (件 'divide, itemize, distinct matter').

history.meaning: itemized matter; case
matter; subject; counter for cases or bookings

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 件

任す.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive yodan/godan verb 任す (makasu), historical doublet of the lower bigrade/ichidan verb 任せる (makaseru, Old Japanese *makasu, 'to entrust, leave to another's will'). Ultimately derived from an old causative formation on the root *mak- ('to yield, submit, turn over to', seen in 罷る makaru and 負ける makeru), meaning 'to cause someone to have full charge over something'.

history.meaning: to entrust to, leave to another's discretion, yield to
to entrust a task or decision to someone; to leave it up to someone

morphemes.meaning: to entrust, leave in charge of (verb stem makas-)

任す.notes: 任す (godan: 任さない, 任して, 任せ) is a punchier, slightly more colloquial/dialectal (esp. Western Japan and rough masculine speech) counterpart to standard ichidan 任せる (makaseru: 任せない, 任せて, 任せろ). In restaurant culture, お任せ (omakase) comes from the same stem.

rootFamily.gloss: to entrust, to leave to someone (standard ichidan form)
leaving the selection to the chef/expert (honorific noun)

任せる.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) transitive verb 任せる (まかせる 'to entrust to someone, leave a task or decision in someone's hands'), continuing Old Japanese *makasu* (derived from *maku* 任く 'to appoint, commission, send out').

history.meaning: entrust; leave to the course of
entrust to; leave up to someone

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 任せる

休み.etymology: Verbal noun 休み (やすみ 'rest, break, holiday, day off, absence'), nominalized from the continuative stem of 休む (*yasumu* 'to rest').

history.meaning: resting; repose
rest; break; holiday; closed day

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 休み

休む.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *yasumu* (休む 'to rest, take a break, pause, go to bed, be absent'), verbalized from the adjective root *yasu-* (seen in 安し *yasusi* 'peaceful, at ease, calm').

history.meaning: rest; set at ease
rest; take a break; take a day off

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 休む

休日.etymology: The term '休日' (meaning 'holiday') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: holiday
holiday

休日.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 休日

会.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) single-character noun and suffix 会 (kai, Middle Chinese *hwajH, 'to come together, assemble, meet; a gathering'). The character (traditional 會) originally depicted a lid fitting onto a vessel to represent 'joining together'. Borrowed into Japanese both for Buddhist assemblies (where it was often read e, as in 法会 hōe) and with its Kan-on reading kai for secular 'gatherings, receptions, parties, and clubs/associations'.

history.meaning: to assemble, converge; an assembly or meeting
gathering, party, reception, society, or club (both standalone noun and suffix)

会.notes: Extremely versatile both as an independent noun (会を開く, 'to hold a gathering/reception') and as a suffix for any social event or group (飲み会 nomikai 'drinking party', ファン会 'fan club', 励ます会 'reception/party in support of someone').

会いたい.etymology: Verb 会う (au, to meet) + desiderative suffix たい (tai). This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: want to meet

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 会いたい

会う.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *apu* (会う・逢う・遭う 'to meet, come together, encounter'), sharing its historical root with 合う (*apu* 'to fit together, match').

history.meaning: meet face to face; come together
meet; see (someone)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 会う

会える.etymology: Potential form of the native Yamato (wago) godan verb 会う (au, Old Japanese *apu, 'to meet, come together, face one another'), formed by shifting the stem vowel -u to the potential mid-front vowel -e- plus the ichidan inflectional ending -ru (a-u > a-e-ru). This shorter godan potential formation (-eru) arose in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese via morphological clipping of the older potential auxiliary construction 会うことができる / 会われ(る).

history.meaning: to meet, come face to face, join together
to be able to meet; to have the chance to see someone in person

morphemes.meaning: to meet, see in person (verb root a-)
potential voice ichidan suffix (-eru, 'can / be able to')

会える.notes: Takes the particle に for the person one can meet (あなたに会えてよかった, 'I'm glad I was able to meet/see you'). Because Japanese often uses potential verbs where English uses 'get to see' or 'finally see', 会える carries warm emotional relief or anticipation.

rootFamily.gloss: to meet, to see in person
to encounter, to come across by chance or destiny

会場.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 会 (kai, Middle Chinese *hwajH, 'gathering, assembly, event') and 場 (jō, Middle Chinese *drjang, 'open ground, arena, place for an activity'). Literally 'the ground or hall where an assembly takes place', covering any designated event space from a banquet hall, convention center, or wedding hall to an exhibition site or studio venue.

history.meaning: place where an assembly or examination is held
history.stage: Late Imperial Chinese / Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: venue, event hall, function room, or site of an event

会場.notes: Note the exact homophone 開場 (kaijō, 'opening of the doors/venue to the public', written with 開 'open'): announcements frequently pair both, e.g., 会場は18時開場 (Kaijō wa jūhachiji kaijō, 'The venue opens its doors at 18:00').

rootFamily.gloss: filming location, studio floor, actual site on the ground

cognates.meaning: company, firm (borrowed from Japanese in some dialects/contexts; compare 社會)

会社.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 会 (kai, Middle Chinese *hwajH, 'assembling, coming together') and 社 (sha, Middle Chinese *dzyaeX, originally 'altar of the soil god', hence 'community association, guild, society'). In the late Bakumatsu and early Meiji periods, scholars such as Fukuzawa Yukichi used 会社 (and its reverse 社会 shakai) to translate Dutch maatschappij and English 'company' or 'society'; 会社 settled specifically on a commercial 'business corporation/firm', while 社会 became 'society at large'.

history.meaning: communal association or religious/literary fellowship
commercial company, joint-stock firm, or society (used interchangeably with 社会 in early Meiji)
business company, corporation, firm; one's workplace

会社.notes: Notice the reversible kanji pair 会社 (kaisha, 'business company') vs. 社会 (shakai, 'society as a whole'). In everyday speech, 会社 often means 'work / the office' (会社に行く, 'to go to work'). When combined as a suffix (e.g., 株式会社 kabushiki-gaisha, 'joint-stock corporation'), kai voices via rendaku to -gaisha.

会議.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 会 (kai, Middle Chinese *hwajH, 'to assemble, meet together') and 議 (gi, Middle Chinese *ngjeH, 'to deliberate, discuss, consult on what is right'). Attested in Chinese historical chronicles (such as the Records of the Grand Historian) and in Heian Japanese court records for 'assembling to deliberate on affairs of state', and modernized in the Meiji period for any formal 'business meeting, conference, or council'.

history.meaning: to assemble officials to deliberate on state policy
formal meeting, conference, board deliberation, or council

会議.notes: Refers to a structured meeting where participants deliberate or make decisions (unlike 打ち合わせ uchiawase, a practical 'pre-arrangement/briefing meeting', or 会合 kaigō, a general 'get-together'). Takes the verb する (会議する, 'to hold a meeting').

cognates.meaning: president of an association or club
chairman of a conglomerate (chaebol) or president of an association

会長.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 会 (kai, Middle Chinese *hwajH, 'association, society, council, company') and 長 (chō, Middle Chinese *trjangX, 'elder, chief, head, leader'). Literally 'head of an association', used in two distinct modern spheres: (1) the president of a club, trade association, or committee (e.g., 生徒会長 'student council president'), and (2) the chairman of the board in a corporation (取締役会長), outranking the 社長 (company president).

history.meaning: chief of an assembly, society, or council; chairman of the board

morphemes.meaning: association, society, council, company board (on'yomi: kai)

会長.notes: In Japanese corporate hierarchy, when a 社長 (shachō, 'company president') steps up from day-to-day operations while retaining senior authority, they typically become 会長 (kaichō, 'chairman of the board'). Used directly as an honorific title after a surname or by itself (会長!).

伝える.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) transitive verb 伝える (つたえる 'to convey, tell, report, hand down, transmit'), continuing Old Japanese *tutapu*, transitive counterpart of 伝わる (*tutawaru*) and 伝う (*tutau* 'to go along').

history.meaning: hand down; pass along; report
convey; tell; pass on

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 伝える

伝説.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 伝 (den, traditional 傳, Middle Chinese *drjwenH, 'transmission, chronicle, that which is handed down across generations') and 説 (setsu, Middle Chinese *sywet, 'narrative, account, explanation, talk'). Attested in Tang-Song Chinese literature for 'stories handed down by word of mouth', and standardized in modern Japanese both for traditional folklore ('legend') and metaphorically for an iconic person or achievement ('living legend').

history.meaning: orally transmitted story or historical hearsay handed down through generations
legend, folklore; (figuratively) a legendary figure or iconic feat in pop culture/history

morphemes.meaning: to transmit, hand down, chronicle (on'yomi: den)

伴う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb 伴う (tomonau), from Old Japanese *to₂mo₂napu, formed by attaching the verbalizing/iterative suffix *-napu (expressing continuous or reciprocal action, compare 行う okonau, 商う akinau) to the noun 伴 / 友 (tomo, Old Japanese *to₂mo₂, 'companion, attendant, retinue'). Originally meaning "to peer secretly through a gap, spy on, or watch for an opportunity" (written 窺う), it underwent semantic elevation in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese: seeking to read a social superior's mood or awaiting their instructions (*okimochi wo ukagau*) grammaticalized into a humble (*kenjōgo*) verb meaning "to ask, inquire of, hear, or visit".

First well-attested in Muromachi and early Edo period texts for two things harmonizing in appearance or nature, it specialized into describing clothing, colors, roles, or styles that suit and flatter a person.

住民票.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) administrative compound *jūminhyō*, composed of 住民 (*jūmin*, "resident, inhabitant", from Middle Chinese *drjuH-mjin*, combining 住 "dwell, reside" and 民 "people, populace") plus the suffixoid noun 票 (*hyō*, from Middle Chinese *pjiewH*, "slip of paper, tally, certificate, warrant"). Formally codified in modern Japanese municipal law under the Resident Registration Act (住民登録法) of 1951 and the Basic Resident Register Act (住民基本台帳法) of 1967 as the official municipal ledger recording a citizen's current legal address, household composition, and identity.

体位.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound *taii*, formed from 体 (traditional 體 *tai*, from Middle Chinese *thejX*, "body, physical form, soma") and 位 (*i*, from Middle Chinese *hwiH*, "place, position, posture, rank"). Originally coined in Meiji–Taishō medical and physical-education terminology as a clinical term for body orientation or posture (such as supine, prone, or lateral decubitus positions in nursing), it underwent strong colloquial narrowing in twentieth-century Japanese to refer specifically to sexual positions (性交体位).

history.meaning: physical body + spatial position or rank

sexual position (short for 性交体位)

体位.notes: While nurses and physicians still use 体位変換 (taii henkan) for "repositioning a bedridden patient," in everyday conversation 体位 alone almost always means "sexual position," whereas ordinary bodily posture is called 姿勢 (shisei) or 体勢 (taisei).

何.etymology: Interrogative pronoun 何 (なに / なん 'what'), inherited from Old Japanese *nani* ('what'). Before dental/alveolar and bilabial consonants (*t, d, n, r, p, b, m*) or counters, *nani* regularly apocopates to なん (*nan*).

何する.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) interrogative verbal phrase/compound *nanisuru* (also realized with particle omission from 何をする *nani wo suru*), combining the Old Japanese interrogative pronoun 何 (*nani*, "what", built on the interrogative root *na-* + element *-ni*) with the light verb する (*suru*, from Old Japanese *su*, "to do, act"). Beyond its literal interrogative meaning ("to do what?"), *nanisuru* also functions in colloquial Japanese as a euphemistic placeholder verb ("to do *you-know-what*, to act up") when a speaker hesitates to name an action explicitly.

The copula *da* itself evolved in Late Middle and Early Modern eastern Japanese via phonological contraction of *de aru* ("is at / exists as" > *dea* > *da*), replacing Classical Japanese *nani nari* or *nan zo*.

何で.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) interrogative adverb *nande*, composed of the pre-alveolar bound allomorph *nan-* of 何 (*nani*, "what") plus the case particle で (*de*, meaning "by means of, with, because of"). The particle *de* grammaticalized in Late Heian and Kamakura Japanese from the contraction of the locative particle *ni* and the conjunctive suffix *te* (*ni te* > *nde* > *de*). Literally "by what means" or "for what cause," *nande* developed into the primary colloquial Japanese interrogative for "why, how come."

why, how come; with what (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: what (allomorph of nani before alveolar d)
by means of, because of (< ni te)

(instrument: 何で来たの？ "How did you get here—by train or car?"), disambiguated by context; in casual speech, it is slightly more informal and emotional than どうして (dōshite) and much more conversational than なぜ (naze).

何でも.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) universal/indefinite pronoun and adverb *nandemo*, formed from the pre-alveolar stem *nan-* of 何 (*nani*, "what") + the particle で (*de*, functioning either as the continuative form of the copula *da* or as the instrumental case particle) + the inclusive focus particle も (*mo*, "also, even"). Following the pan-Japonic syntactic pattern where an interrogative stem (*wh-* word) combined with inclusive *mo* yields a universal quantifier ("what-even" > "anything at all, everything"), it became fully established in Early Modern Japanese.

Literally meaning "saying something or other" or "in some way or other," it grammaticalized both as a placeholder for a forgotten name ("Mr. What's-his-name") and as an adverb of resourceful effort ("somehow, one way or another, managing despite difficulty").

何人.etymology: Hybrid interrogative counter compound combining the native Japanese interrogative root 何 (nan-, reduced before dental/alveolar consonants from なに nani 'what') with the Sino-Japanese person counter -人 (-nin, from Middle Chinese *nyin 'person'). morphemes.meaning: counter for flat, thin objects or sheets (MC *mwoj)

the previous head of a household, merchant house, or feudal lineage
predecessor, previous boss/master/owner, previous generation model

先代.notes: Especially common in traditional family businesses (老舗), rakugo/kabuki lineages, and yakuza organizations to refer respectfully to the previous boss or master.

rootFamily.gloss: first generation, founder of a business or lineage
successive generations, emperors, or bosses through history

先導.etymology: Sino-Japanese word. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

先払い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun combining 先 (saki, Old Japanese *saki₁*, "tip, front, ahead, beforehand") and 払い (harai > -barai via rendaku sequential voicing, the nominalized ren'yōkei of 払う harau, Old Japanese *faraf-*, "to sweep clear, drive away ritual impurity, clear a debt, pay money"). 先生.etymology: Sino-Japanese honorific noun and title 先生 (せんせい 'teacher, master, doctor'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 先生 (literally 'one born earlier, elder of learning', from 先 'before, earlier' + 生 'born, scholar').

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 先端

先走る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound godan verb combining 先 (saki, Old Japanese *saki₁*, "ahead, in front, before others") and 走る (hashiru > -bashiru via rendaku sequential voicing, Old Japanese *fasir-*, "to run, rush, dart forward"). Originally literal ("to run out ahead of the pack"), it developed the figurative sense "to jump the gun, act prematurely or rashly before getting the full picture."

history.meaning: to run ahead of others in a procession or battle
to jump the gun, get ahead of oneself, act rashly or prematurely

morphemes.meaning: run, rush forward (from hashiru 走る, with rendaku h -> b)

先走る.notes: Often appears in the past/adjectival modifier form 先走った行動 (sakibashitta kōdō, "premature/rash action") or warning someone 先走るな (sakibashiru na, "don't jump the gun!").

cognates.meaning: elder generation, predecessor; senpai (re-influenced by Japanese pop culture)
senior, upperclassman, mentor in school or work

先輩.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Tang-dynasty Classical Chinese 先輩 (attested in Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan for senior scholars), combining 先 (sen, Middle Chinese *sen, "before, earlier, preceding") and 輩 (hai > pai via labial assimilation after /n/, Middle Chinese *pwojH, "line of hundred war-chariots, cohort, generation, class of peers"). In modern Japanese institutional culture (schools, sports clubs, corporations), it became the foundational term for someone who entered an organization earlier.

history.meaning: those of an earlier cohort; senior scholars or elders
one's elder in age, learning, or experience
senior member, upperclassman, mentor in a school, club, or workplace

morphemes.meaning: cohort, generation, class of peers (hai -> pai)

先輩.notes: Paired with 後輩 (kōhai, "junior") and 同輩/同期 (dōhai/dōki, "peer/same-year cohort"); functions both as a common noun and as a direct honorific title after a surname (e.g., 田中先輩, Tanaka-senpai).

rootFamily.gloss: junior, underclassman, newer member of a group
peer, colleague of equal standing or cohort

先週.etymology: Sino-Japanese temporal compound 先週 (せんしゅう 'last week, the previous week'), combining 先 (せん 'previous, earlier') + 週 (しゅう 'week').

history.meaning: last week

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 先週

先進国.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound joining 先進 (senshin, "going ahead, advanced", attested in Analects 11:1 for "those who advanced first in礼楽 [ritual and music]", from 先 Middle Chinese *sen "first, ahead" + 進 Middle Chinese *tsinH "advance, move forward") and 国 (koku, shinjitai of 國, Middle Chinese *kwək, "state, country, nation"). Coined in modern Japanese political economy to translate "advanced / developed nation."

history.meaning: those who advanced earlier in learning and ritual (Confucian Analects)
economically and technologically advanced nation, developed country

morphemes.meaning: advanced, pioneering, going ahead (先 ahead + 進 advance)

先進国.notes: Historically contrasted with 後進国 (kōshinkoku, "backward/less-developed country"), which was later replaced in polite diplomatic usage by 発展途上国 (hatten tojōkoku, "developing country").

rootFamily.gloss: developing country (country on the road to development)

光.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *pikari* (光 'light, radiance, gleam'), nominalized from the continuative stem of the verb 光る (*pikaru* 'to shine').

history.meaning: light; radiance
light; ray; gleam

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 光

光り輝く.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intensifying compound godan verb joining the ren'yōkei (continuative stem) hikari of 光る (hikaru, Old Japanese *fikar-*, "to shine, emit light", built on the root *fi₁* 日/火 "sun, fire, light") with 輝く (kagayaku, Old Japanese *kagayak-*, "to sparkle, gleam, radiate dazzle", built on the mimetic/root *kaga-* "flickering bright light, reflection" + verbal suffix *-yaku*). The pairing of two near-synonymous native verbs creates an emphatic sense: "to shine and sparkle brilliantly."

history.meaning: to emit light + to gleam or sparkle radiantly
to shine brightly, glitter, radiate splendor or glory

morphemes.meaning: shine, emit light (continuative stem of hikaru 光る)

光り輝く.notes: Used both for literal dazzling light and figuratively for a person, career, or era radiating peak glamour and success (光り輝く時代, "a golden, glittering era").

光る.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *pikaru* (光る 'to shine, gleam, flash, sparkle'), built on the ancient light-root *pika-* (also preserved in ぴかぴか and 稲光 'lightning').

history.meaning: shine; flash; sparkle
shine; gleam; glisten

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 光る

光栄.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical Chinese 光榮, combining 光 (kō, Middle Chinese *kwɑŋ, "light, radiance, luster") and 栄 (ei, shinjitai of 榮, Middle Chinese *ɣjwæŋ, "flowering, flourishing, glory, honor"). Literally "radiant glory," using luminous brilliance as a metaphor for public honor and social prestige.

history.meaning: radiant glory, illustrious honor bestowed on a person or family
splendor, high honor, prestige
honor, privilege; feeling honored/privileged (na-adjective and noun)

光栄.notes: A staple of polite formal speech: 光栄です (kōei desu) or 身に余る光栄です (mi ni amaru kōei desu, "it is an honor beyond my desert") is the standard way to say "I am honored."

rootFamily.gloss: glory, crowning honor (inverted characters 栄 + 光)

cognates.meaning: license, permit (borrowed from Japanese administrative terminology)

免許.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 免 (men, Middle Chinese *mjenX, "to exempt, release from restriction, excuse") and 許 (kyo, Middle Chinese *xjoX, "to permit, approve, grant"). Etymologically "lifting a prohibition and granting permission." In medieval and Edo-period Japan, 免許 denoted a master's scroll certifying a disciple's mastery of a martial or traditional art (as in 免許皆伝 menkyo kaiden, "full transmission license"). In the Meiji period, it was adapted for state-issued legal permits and professional licenses, and today most commonly stands as shorthand for 運転免許 (unten menkyo, "driver's license").

history.meaning: to exempt from restriction + to permit, grant
master's certificate granting permission to teach a traditional art or martial school
official state license or permit; specifically a driver's license (運転免許)

免許.notes: When used alone in everyday conversation (e.g., 免許を取る menkyo o toru, "get a license"), 免許 almost always refers specifically to a driver's license (運転免許証).

rootFamily.gloss: full initiation and mastery scroll in a traditional martial or artistic school

児童福祉法違反.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound formed from 児童福祉法 (jido fukushiho, the 1947 Child Welfare Act) and 違反 (ihan, violation or contravention). Each constituent pairs classical Chinese lexical roots: 児童 (Middle Chinese *dzye-duwng, young child), 福祉 (*pjuwk-tsrhiX, blessedness and divine favor, repurposed in Meiji-Taisho social policy for "welfare"), 法 (*pjop, statute), and 違反 (*hjwoj-pjonX, going against and turning back on a rule).

history.form: 兒童 / 福祉 / 法 / 違反
history.meaning: juvenile; blessings and happiness; law; to go against or contravene
Child Welfare Act (postwar Japanese statutory protection for minors)

history.form: 児童福祉法違反 (じどうふくしほういはん)
history.meaning: violation of the Child Welfare Act

児童福祉法違反.notes: In news broadcasts and police procedurals like The Naked Director, appending 違反 (ihan) to the name of a statute is the standard formula for naming a criminal charge (e.g., 児童福祉法違反容疑, suspicion of violating the Child Welfare Act, often invoked when minors are employed in the adult industry).

入り.etymology: Verbal noun and suffix 入り (いり 'entering, attendance, setting of the sun; containing, capacity'), nominalized from the continuative stem of 入る (*iru* 'to enter, go in').

history.meaning: going in; containing
containing (~入り); entering; beginning

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 入り

入り口.etymology: Native Japanese compound joining 入り (iri, continuative stem of 入る iru/hairu, 'to enter, go in') and 口 (kuchi,voiced to -guchi, originally 'mouth' and by extension 'opening, aperture, doorway'). Alongside its antonym 出口 (deguchi, 'exit'), 入り口 has served since Classical and Medieval Japanese as the primary everyday word for any doorway, gate opening, or beginning point.

history.form: いりくち / いりぐち (iriguchi)
history.meaning: opening for entering; doorway
entrance; doorway; threshold

入り口.notes: Spelled either 入り口 (showing the okurigana り) or 入口; both are pronounced イリグチ.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 入り口

入り用.etymology: Hybrid native Yamato and Sino-Japanese (yutomi/jukujikun-adjacent) compound combining 入り (iri, the continuative stem or ren'yokei of the native verb 入る iru, "to enter, to be needed/required", from Old Japanese iru) with the Sino-Japanese root 用 (yo, from Middle Chinese *yowngH, "use, expense, business"). Originally denoting something that enters into practical use or outlay, it developed in Edo-period merchant and townspeople speech into the sense of "necessity, demand, or required expense."

history.meaning: to enter / be needed + use, expenditure

history.form: 入用 / 入り用 (いりよう)
history.meaning: expense, outlay, something required for business or daily life
need, necessity, demand, required funds

morphemes.meaning: entering, being needed (stem of 入る / 要る iru)

入り用.notes: Often spelled without okurigana as 入用 (iriyo); it carries a slightly old-fashioned, polite, or commercial flavor compared to 必要 (hitsuyo), and frequently refers specifically to needing money or funds (e.g., お金が入り用だ, "I am in need of cash").

rootFamily.gloss: income and expenditure, revenue and expense

入る.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *papiru* (這入る > はひる > はいる, originally a compound of 這ふ *papu* 'to creep, move forward, stoop to enter a low doorway' + 入る *iru* 'to go in'). In Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese はいる largely replaced simple いり / いる as the everyday intransitive verb for 'to enter, go in, fit inside'.

history.form: いる (入る) / はひる (這入る)
history.meaning: enter; go inside
enter; go in; be contained

入れる.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) transitive verb 入れる (いれる 'to put in, let in, insert, brew tea or coffee, include'), continuing Old Japanese *iru* (lower bigrade), the transitive counterpart of four-grade 入る (*iru*).

history.meaning: put inside; admit; insert
put in; let in; brew (tea/coffee)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 入れる

入れ替わる.etymology: Compound intransitive verb 入れ替わる (いれかわる 'to change places with one another, be replaced, rotate'), combining 入れ (stem of 入れる 'to put in') + 替わる (かわる 'to change, take the place of').

入信者.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic derivative built from 入信 (nyushin, "entering a faith, religious conversion") plus the agentive suffix 者 (sha, "person who"). 入 (nyu, from Middle Chinese *nyip, "to enter") acts as a verbal element taking 信 (shin, MC *sinH, "trust, faith, religious belief") as its object, while 者 (MC *tsyaeX) nominalizes the compound into an agent noun denoting a convert or initiate.

history.meaning: to enter + faith/trust + person marker
embracing a religion, becoming a believer

history.form: 入信者 (にゅうしんしゃ)
history.meaning: religious convert, new believer or initiate in a religious sect

morphemes.meaning: person who does or is characterized by (MC *tsyaeX)

入信者.notes: In contemporary Japanese media, 入信者 often appears in discussions of new religious movements (新興宗教, shinko shukyo) or cults, contrasting with the broader term 信者 (shinja, believer/devotee).

入社.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) verb-object compound formed in the Meiji era from 入 (nyu, Middle Chinese *nyip, "to enter") and 社 (sha, MC *dzyaeX, originally "altar of the soil god" and hence the local community gathered around it, later extended in Meiji Japanese via 会社 kaisha to mean "commercial company, firm, or society"). Literally "entering the firm," it emerged alongside Japan's modern corporate employment system.

history.meaning: to enter + altar of the soil / local association
joining a society, guild, newspaper, or commercial company
joining a company, starting corporate employment

morphemes.meaning: company, firm, association (MC *dzyaeX, shrine of the earth deity > community > corporation)

入社.notes: A cornerstone of Japanese corporate culture (e.g., 入社式 nyushashiki, the April company entrance ceremony); note that in Japanese one says 会社に入社する or simply 入社する, while its antonym for leaving a company is 退社 (taisha) or 退職 (taishoku).

rootFamily.gloss: leaving a company (resigning or clocking out)

入金.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) financial compound combining 入 (nyu, Middle Chinese *nyip, "to enter, put in") and 金 (kin, MC *kim, "metal, gold, money"). Modeled on classical Chinese accounting compounds where 入 marks incoming receipts, it became standardized in modern Japanese banking and bookkeeping for money entering an account or cash register—covering deposits, wire transfers received, and partial payments.

history.meaning: to enter / bring in + gold, metal, money
receipt of money, cash intake in merchant ledgers
deposit, bank transfer payment, crediting an account

入金.notes: Used both from the payer's perspective ("making a deposit/payment into an account") and the payee's perspective (入金を確認する, "to confirm receipt of payment"); its direct opposite in banking is 出金 (shukkin, withdrawal/disbursement).

全.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) morpheme and prefix 全 (zen), borrowed from Middle Chinese *dzjwen ("intact, complete, whole, entire"), from Old Chinese *dzon. In the oracle bone and bronze scripts, the character depicts 入 ("entering/gathering") over 玉 ("jade"), originally signifying a piece of jade worked to perfection without flaw or chip, whence the generalized meanings "complete, intact, whole, all."

history.meaning: flawless jade; intact, whole, complete
completeness, wholeness; prefix meaning all or entire
all, whole, entire, total (used as prefix or standalone noun in set phrases)

全.notes: Most frequently operates as a productive Sino-Japanese prefix attached to nouns or numbers (e.g., 全日本 All-Japan, 全巻 all volumes), though it also functions as an independent noun in literary phrases like 全を尽くす (zen o tsukusu, to do one's utmost).

全く.etymology: Adverb 全く (まったく 'completely, entirely; [with negative] not at all; good grief'), the adverbial (*ren'yōkei*) form of the Old/Classical Japanese adjective 全し (*matasi / mattasi* 'whole, complete, intact').

history.form: またく / まったく (全く)
history.meaning: wholly; completely
completely; (not) at all; truly
