全て.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun and adverb derived from the lexicalized gerund (te-form) of the classical transitive verb 統ぶ / 総ぶ (subu, Modern Japanese 統べる suberu, "to gather together into one, to unite, to control or govern"), from Old Japanese subu. Originally meaning "gathering everything together into a single whole," the conjunctive form すべて (subete) grammaticalized into a universal quantifier meaning "all, the whole, in every respect." The spelling 全て applies the semantically matching kanji 全 ("whole, complete") via kun'yomi.

history.meaning: uniting, bringing together as one > in general, altogether
in all respects, entirely, everything
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: all, everything, the whole

morphemes.meaning: to unite, gather together into one (from 統ぶ subu)

全て.notes: While 全部 (zenbu) is conversational and みんな (minna) is casual/personal, 全て (subete) sounds slightly more literary, dramatic, or comprehensive—especially when used as a noun (全てを失う, "to lose everything"). Pitch accent is頭高 (atamadaka: す↓べて).

rootFamily.gloss: to unite, to rule over, to integrate
to control, to supervise (Sino-Japanese compound using the same kanji concept)
completely, wholly (native root 全し mattashi)

全ての.etymology: The term '全ての' (meaning 'all') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: all
all

全ての.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 全ての

全世界.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by prefixing 全 (zen, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "whole, entire") to 世界 (sekai, "world"). 世界 was originally a Chinese Buddhist translation of Sanskrit lokadhatu ("realm of existence"), combining 世 (MC *syejH, "generation, age, temporal flow of past, present, and future") and 界 (MC *keajH, "boundary, spatial directions of east, west, north, and south"). Thus 全世界 evolved from "the entirety of the spatiotemporal cosmos" to the modern secular sense of "the entire globe."

history.form: 世界 (MC *syejH-keajH, calque of Sanskrit lokadhatu)
history.meaning: spatiotemporal universe (time 世 + space 界) in Buddhist cosmology
the secular world, the earth and human society
the entire world, the whole globe

morphemes.meaning: generation, epoch, world of living beings (MC *syejH)

全世界.notes: Frequently used in grandiose advertising, cinema, and rhetoric (e.g., 全世界が泣いた, "the whole world wept"—a famous Japanese movie trailer cliche, or Toru Muranishi's ambition in The Naked Director to distribute media across the globe).

全体.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound formed from 全 (zen, 'whole, complete, entire', from Middle Chinese *dzwɛn) and 体 (tai, 'body, substance, structure', from Middle Chinese *tʰieiX). Literally 'the whole body/structure', it denotes an entity viewed as a complete, integrated whole rather than scattered parts, and attaches directly after nouns (キッチン全体 'the whole kitchen', 建物全体 'the entire building').

history.meaning: the whole body; the entirety
the whole; entirety

全体.notes: When placed directly after a noun X (X全体), it means 'the entirety of X' as a unified system or space.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 全体

全員.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 全 (zen, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "all, complete") and 員 (in, MC *hjwien, "round vessel > count, number, member of a group or staff"). Originally denoting a rounded ceremonial cauldron (鼎) with a circle (〇) at the top, 員 came in Classical Chinese to serve as a classifier for officials and personnel; 全員 thus literally means "the complete headcount of personnel."

history.meaning: complete/whole + number of officials or personnel
full complement of a crew, staff, or organization
all members, everyone (in a specified group)

全員.notes: Unlike みんな (minna), which can refer loosely to people in general, 全員 strictly implies "100% of the members of a defined group or team without exception" (e.g., 全員集合, "everyone assemble!").

rootFamily.gloss: member of a group, staff member
fixed capacity, maximum number of people

全国三千万.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) quantitative phrase combining 全国 (zenkoku, "the whole country, nationwide", from Middle Chinese *dzjwen-kwok) with the numeral compound 三千万 (sanzenman, "thirty million", literally three 三 *sam × thousand 千 *tshen × myriad/ten-thousand 万 *mjonH). Follows the East Asian myriad-based (万, 10^4) grouping system introduced from Chinese mathematics, where 30,000,000 is expressed as 3,000 (三千) myriads (万).

history.meaning: the entire state/realm + three thousand myriads (30,000,000)

history.form: 全国 (ぜんこく) + 三千万 (さんぜんまん)
history.meaning: throughout all provinces of Japan + thirty million

history.form: 全国三千万 (ぜんこくさんぜんまん)
history.meaning: thirty million nationwide (rhetorical address to a massive national demographic)

全国三千万.notes: In Showa-era sales pitches and broadcasting (such as Toru Muranishi's flamboyant pitches in The Naked Director), phrases like 全国三千万の〜 ("the 30 million [men/fans/households] across the nation") are used as hyperbolic rhetorical appeals to a vast national audience. Note the rendaku in 三千 (san + sen > sanzen).

全然.etymology: Sino-Japanese adverb 全然 (ぜんぜん 'wholly, completely; [with negative] not at all'), borrowed from Chinese 全然 (combining 全 'whole, complete' + adverbial suffix 然 'in that state'). Used in both negative ('not at all') and colloquial affirmative ('completely, totally fine') contexts.

history.meaning: completely; wholly
(not) at all; completely; totally

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 全然

全資産.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) economic compound formed from the prefix 全 (zen, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "all, entire") and 資産 (shisan, "assets, property, fortune"). 資産 combines 資 (shi, MC *tsij, "resources, capital, goods, provisions", containing the cowrie shell radical 貝 symbolizing currency) with 産 (san, MC *sreanX, "to give birth, produce, livelihood, estate"). Together they denote the entirety of a person's or firm's accumulated wealth and productive property.

history.meaning: stored resources/provisions + productive estate or livelihood
property, capital assets, financial estate (standardized in Meiji economics)
all of one's assets, total net worth or holdings

全資産.notes: Whereas 全財産 (zenzaisan) is used in everyday speech for "all of one's personal money/belongings," 全資産 (zenshisan) has a slightly more financial, corporate, or legal register referring to total liquid and fixed assets.

全速力.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic compound combining 全 (zen, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "all, full") with 速力 (sokuryoku, "speed, velocity"). 速力 pairs 速 (soku, MC *suwk, "rapid, swift", containing the movement radical 辶) and 力 (ryoku, MC *lik, "strength, force, power", originally a pictograph of a sinew or plow). Coined in the modern era to describe mechanical and locomotive power, 全速力 literally means "full speed-power."

history.meaning: whole/complete + swiftness + physical force or power

history.form: 速力 (そくりょく) > 全速力 (ぜんそくりょく)
history.meaning: locomotive speed (of ships, trains, or runners) > full speed, maximum velocity

history.form: 全速力 (ぜんそくりょく)
history.meaning: full speed, top speed, running or driving as fast as possible

全速力.notes: Almost always used adverbially with the particle で: 全速力で走る (zensokuryoku de hashiru, "to run at full speed / flat out"). Compare 全力 (zenryoku, full effort/might) and 全速 (zensoku, full speed, especially nautical/mechanical as in 全速前進 "full speed ahead").

全部.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and adverb 全部 (ぜんぶ 'all, the whole, every part'), from 全 ('whole, entire') + 部 ('part, section, set of volumes'). Originally denoting 'a complete set of volumes of a book', in Meiji–Modern Japanese it generalized to 'all, everything'.

history.meaning: complete set of book volumes
all; the whole; everything

全額.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 全 (zen, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "whole, entire") and 額 (gaku, MC *ngaek, originally "forehead", containing the head radical 頁). By semantic extension from "the prominent brow" to "an inscribed plaque hung over a gate," and then in Tang-Song administrative Chinese to "the fixed number or sum inscribed on a register," 額 came to mean "monetary sum or quota," yielding 全額 ("the entire monetary amount").

八割.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato (jubako-yomi) compound combining the Sino-Japanese numeral 八 (hachi, from Middle Chinese *peat, "eight") with the native Japanese counter 割 (wari, the continuative stem of the verb 割る waru, "to divide, split, proportion", from Old Japanese waru). In Edo-period merchant arithmetic, 割 was established as a proportional unit equal to one-tenth (10%) of a whole, making 八割 "eight tenths" or "eighty percent."

八方塞がり.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato (jubako-yomi) idiom combining 八方 (happo, from Middle Chinese *peat-pjang, "the eight compass directions: N, S, E, W, NE, NW, SE, SW", with *peat + *pjang assimilating to happo) and 塞がり (fusagari, nominalized continuative form of the native verb 塞がる fusagaru, "to be blocked, clogged, or closed off"). Originating in traditional Yin-Yang divination (陰陽道 Onmyodo), where directional taboos (方塞がり kata-fusagari) forbade travel or construction in unlucky directions, "blocking in all eight directions" meant a year or configuration in which every possible direction was astrologically cursed, whence the modern figurative sense of being completely cornered with no way out.

兵隊.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) military compound combining 兵 (hei, Kan-on reading from Middle Chinese *pjaeng, originally "weapon, arms"—a pictograph of two hands 廾 holding an axe 斤—later extended to the soldier wielding the weapon) and 隊 (tai, MC *dwojH, "squad, company, file of troops"). While originally denoting a military unit or detachment of troops, in colloquial Meiji-Showa Japanese 兵隊 shifted to refer to an individual enlisted soldier or rank-and-file operative.

In crime dramas and yakuza contexts like The Naked Director, 兵隊 specifically means "foot soldiers / muscle"—low-ranking syndicate members or sales grunts sent to the front lines.

具合.etymology: Originally a craftsman's joinery term written 工合 or 具合い (guai, combining 具/工 gu, 'tool, fitting, workmanship' + 合い ai, nominalized stem of 合う au, 'to fit together, match'). In Edo carpentry and metalwork, it referred to how snugly two fitted parts met and moved together; from there it broadened naturally to the working condition of a mechanism, the state of one's health or an injury (足首の具合, 'how one's ankle is doing'), and general convenience (具合がいい / 悪い).

history.meaning: fit of joined parts; working state; physical condition
health condition; working state; manner

内部.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) spatial and organizational compound formed from 内 (nai, Go-on reading from Middle Chinese *nwojH, "inside, within, interior", depicting 入 "entering" into an enclosure 冂) and 部 (bu, MC *buwX, "division, section, part, department"). Contrasting directly with 外部 (gaibu, "exterior, outside"), it denotes both the physical interior of a structure and the internal ranks or inner circle of an organization.

内部.notes: Very productive in corporate and investigative compounds such as 内部告発 (naibu kokuhatsu, whistleblowing), 内部事情 (naibu jijo, internal affairs/circumstances), and 内部犯行 (naibu hanko, an inside job). Its direct antonym is 外部 (gaibu).

円.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) noun 円 (en), the shinjitai simplification of 圓, borrowed from Middle Chinese *hjwen ("round, circular, spherical, complete"). In the late Ming and Qing dynasties, round Spanish-American and Mexican silver eight-real coins ("silver dollars") circulating in East Asian trade were called 銀圓 ("silver rounds"). When Meiji Japan modernized its mint under the New Currency Act of 1871 (新貨条例), it adopted 圓 (en) for its round silver and gold coins, creating the modern Japanese yen (spelled "yen" in English due to historical Hepburn romanization of palatalized /je/ before mid-vowels, and omdat "en" was already taken in Dutch/English).

history.meaning: round, circular, complete; round coin

history.form: 銀圓 > 圓 (ゑん / えん, 1871 New Currency Act)
history.meaning: round silver dollar coin > official decimal currency unit of Meiji Japan (replacing Edo ryo)
yen (Japanese currency); circle, roundness (also read まる maru in wago)

morphemes.meaning: circle, round; yen (currency unit, MC *hjwen, shinjitai of 圓)

円.notes: Why is えん (en) spelled "yen" with a "y" in English? In 16th-19th century historical kana orthography and early missionary dictionaries (like Hepburn's), initial /e/ had historically carried a palatal on-glide [je] (and was spelled ゑん wen by etymology from MC *hjwen); Hepburn romanized the currency as "yen" in the 1860s-70s, fixing the international spelling and symbol ¥ forever. In native kun'yomi, 円 is read まる (maru, circle) or まどか (madoka, serene/round).

rootFamily.gloss: smooth, harmonious, amicable (literally round and smooth)

In Tang-Song poetry (such as Bai Juyi's verses), 冷靜 described the physical chill and stillness of an autumn night or secluded courtyard; by the Early Modern and Meiji periods, it shifted metaphorically to psychological composure: having a "cool head and quiet mind" unclouded by passion or panic.

Also beware of Korean: the Korean cognate 냉정 (naengjeong, 冷情/冷靜) often leans closer to "cold/unfeeling" than Japanese 冷静.

Because the bevels were carved with unerring precision, in the Edo period 几帳面 came to describe a person who is scrupulously neat and exact.

処女.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Classical Chinese 處女 (Middle Chinese *tsrhjoX-nrjoX), attested as early as the Zhuangzi (莊子) and the Art of War (孫子: "At first, be like a maiden indoors [處女] so the enemy opens his door..."). 処 (shinjitai of 處, MC *tsrhjoX) means "to dwell, remain, stay inside (at home)," where the character combines 虍 (tiger) and 処/几 (a person sitting on a low stool). 処女 thus originally meant "a daughter who still dwells in her parents' home (i.e., an unmarried maiden)," which narrowed in modern Japanese to the physiological and figurative sense of "virgin."

In medieval Zen monasteries, becoming abbot of a major public temple was called 出世; during the Edo period, this prestige sense secularized to mean social advancement, promotion, and worldly career success—ironically the exact opposite of its original monastic sense of forsaking worldly ambition.

As a modern Sino-Japanese (kango) verbal noun read しゅってん (shutten, from Middle Chinese 出 *t͡ɕʰwɪt + 店 *tɛmH), it means 'opening a new store or commercial branch' in a shopping district or mall.

利益.notes: A textbook example of kan-on vs. go-on semantic splitting on the exact same kanji: 利益 read りえき (rieki, kan-on) means 'business profit / financial gain,' whereas (御)利益 read (ご)りやく ((go)riyaku, go-on) means 'divine blessing / good luck from a shrine or temple.'

rootFamily.gloss: divine blessing, spiritual benefit (go-on reading of same kanji)

cognates.meaning: to arrive, to reach a destination

到着.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 到着 (traditional 到着 / 到著, *tɑuH ɖjɑk), uniting 到 (*tɑuH, 'to reach, arrive at a destination,' composed of 至 'arrive at' + 刀 phonetic) and 着 (*ɖjɑk, 'to attach to, touch ground, settle in place'). Because both characters share the core meaning of reaching and making contact with a destination point, the coordinate compound reinforces the completion of a journey or shipment—'reaching and touching down at' a place.

history.meaning: to reach and make contact with a destination
arrival of a person, vehicle, letter, or shipment at its destination

到着.notes: Standard antonym of 出発 (shuppatsu, 'departure'). Note how 着 (chaku) also functions as a suffix in station/airport announcements: 東京着 (Toukyou-chaku, 'arriving at Tokyo') vs. 東京発 (Toukyou-hatsu, 'departing from Tokyo').

rootFamily.gloss: to arrive, to reach (native verb written with 着)
reaching an ultimate goal or level, attainment

制作本数.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) media-industry compound joining 制作 (seisaku, 'creative production of films, television programs, or artworks,' from 制 *t͡ɕiᴇH 'cut out, regulate, fashion' + 作 *t͡sɑk 'make, create') with 本数 (honsuu, 'number of long cylindrical items, reels, or feature works,' from the counter 本 *pwonX 'tree root/trunk -> scroll, film reel, videotape, feature work' + 数 *ʃjuH 'number, count'). Because films and videos were physically stored on cylindrical reels and cassette tapes counted with 本 (-hon/-bon/-pon), 制作本数 became the standard industry metric for total titles or episodes produced.

history.meaning: creative production + count of scrolls/reels/cylindrical units
history.stage: Modern Japanese (20th-century film and broadcast vocabulary)

history.meaning: number of films, videos, or programs produced

morphemes.meaning: counter for scrolls, film reels, videotapes, and movies (MC *pwonX)

制作本数.notes: Japanese publishing and media distinguish two homophones read せいさく (seisaku): 制作 is used for creative/artistic production (movies, TV shows, AV videos, art), whereas 製作 is used for industrial manufacturing (machinery, hardware) or overall studio executive financing. Also note why movies/videos are counted with 本 (hon): they were originally wound on cylindrical film reels (フィルム) and VHS tapes!

rootFamily.gloss: production of films, broadcasts, or art; creative work
number of cylindrical objects, movies, tapes, or trains
creative work, film, literary or artistic piece

制作費.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic compound uniting 制作 (seisaku, 'creative production, manufacture', from Middle Chinese 制 tsjejH 'cut to measure, regulate, fashion' + 作 tsak 'make, construct') with the productive financial suffix -費 (-hi, from Middle Chinese 費 phj+jH 'expend, outlay, cost'). In modern Japanese media terminology, 制作 specifically denotes the artistic, editorial, and creative side of producing films, broadcasts, or stage works, in contrast to 製作, which emphasizes physical manufacturing or executive financing.

history.meaning: to fashion/make + expenditure/outlay

history.form: 制作 (せいさく) + 費 (ひ)
history.meaning: expenditure required to craft or produce a work
production budget (for film, television, or creative works)

制作費.notes: In the Japanese film and TV industry, 制作費 refers to the practical line-production budget, whereas 製作費 (with 衣-radical 製) often refers to the total capital raised by the production committee.

rootFamily.word: 制作会社 (せいさくがいしゃ)

制約.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 制 (sei, from Middle Chinese tsjejH 'to cut cloth with a knife, regulate, restrain, govern') and 約 (yaku, from Middle Chinese 'jak 'to bind with cord, bundle, covenant, restrict'). Both characters originally referred to physical acts of shaping and binding materials—cutting fabric to a strict pattern and tying cords tight—which metaphorically converged in classical Sinitic and modern Japanese to denote legal, institutional, or situational constraints.

history.meaning: to cut/regulate + to bind with rope/restrict
binding condition, restriction, limitation on action

制約.notes: Often used in the phrase 制約を受ける (seiyaku o ukeru, 'to be subject to restrictions'), and is a homophone of 誓約 (seiyaku, 'sworn oath/pledge').

制裁.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound of 制 (sei, from Middle Chinese tsjejH 'to cut, regulate, hold in check') and 裁 (sai, from Middle Chinese dzoj 'to cut cloth into garments, trim, judge, decide'). Both characters share the primordial tailoring metaphor of cutting fabric to proper measure; in Meiji legal and diplomatic prose, the compound was standardized to render Western concepts of legal penalty, social chastisement, and international sanctions.

history.meaning: to cut to measure + to trim cloth / adjudicate
regulation and judgment; coercive penalty or sanction

制裁.notes: Collacates frequently with 加える in 制裁を加える (seisai o kuwaeru, 'to inflict punishment / impose sanctions'), ranging from economic boycotts to vigilante retaliation (私的制裁).

刷毛.etymology: Native Japanese word はけ (attested since the Heian period), etymologically linked to the verb 掃く (はく, 'to sweep, stroke across a surface'), and written with semantic jukujikun / ateji characters 刷毛 ('brushing' + 'bristle/hair') rather than read Sino-Japanesely.

history.meaning: flat bristle brush for paste, dye, or lacquer
wide flat brush (for painting, woodworking, or pastry glazing)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten / Kotobank — 刷毛（はけ）

刷毛.notes: Read irregularly as はけ as a whole two-kanji unit (jukujikun); names wide flat brushes for glazing tarts, lacquering wood, or painting walls, whereas pointed writing/art brushes are 筆 (ふで).

刺激.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 刺 (shi, from Middle Chinese tshjeH 'to stab, prick, pierce with a thorn or blade') and 激 (geki, from Middle Chinese kewk 'water surging violently against stones, arouse, excite, fierce'). Historically written 刺戟 in pre-war Japanese (where 戟 geki meant 'halberd, pointed lance', literally 'pricking with a halberd'), the second character was officially replaced by homophonous 激 ('surge, excite') following post-war kanji reforms.

history.meaning: to prick/stab + halberd / surging water
physiological or sensory stimulus (Meiji medical/psychological term)
stimulation, sensory thrill, provocation, incentive

刺激.notes: Used both clinically for sensory/neural stimuli and colloquially for sensational thrills, as in 刺激が強い (shigeki ga tsuyoi, 'too graphic, provocative, or intense').

刻む.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *kizamu* (刻む 'to notch, carve, mince or chop finely, tick away time, engrave in memory'), attested in eighth-century texts.

history.meaning: cut notches; carve; chop finely
chop finely; mince; carve; tick (time)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 刻む

剃る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb soru, attested from the late Heian period onward and etymologically linked by vowel ablaut to native suru (擦る・摩る, Old Japanese suru 'to rub, scrape, chafe closely against a surface'). Written with the kanji 剃 (Middle Chinese thejH 'to shave hair'), which entered Japan alongside Buddhist monastic tonsure practices (剃髪 teihatsu) and was assigned as the kun'yomi spelling for scraping hair from the skin with a razor.

history.meaning: to rub, scrape closely along a surface
to shave hair or beard with a blade

剃る.notes: Shares the exact phonetic reading soru with 反る ('to warp, bend backward'), differentiated by kanji and context; its conditional form 剃れば (soreba) means 'if one shaves'.

削りくず.etymology: The term '削りくず' (meaning 'shavings') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: shavings
shavings

削りくず.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 削りくず

前.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *mape* (前 > まへ > まえ 'front, before in space or time, presence'), a compound of 目 (ま *ma* 'eye, face') + 辺 (へ *pe* 'side, direction': 'the direction one's eyes face'). Also read ぜん in Sino-Japanese compounds.

history.meaning: in front of the eyes; before
front; before; ago; previous

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 前

前人未到.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) four-character idiom (yojijukugo) structured as a classical Sinitic clause: 前人 (zenjin, 'people of former times, predecessors', from Middle Chinese dzen 'before' + nyin 'person') + 未 (mi, Middle Chinese mj+jH 'not yet, never up to now') + 到 (tō, Middle Chinese tawH 'arrive at, reach'). Literally 'a place where no predecessor has yet arrived', also written with the synonymous variant 前人未踏 (using 踏 tō 'to tread, set foot').

history.form: 前人 (dzen nyin) + 未 (mj+jH) + 到 (tawH)
history.meaning: former people have not yet reached

history.meaning: unexplored territory; an unprecedented feat or achievement

前人未到.notes: Modifies nouns using の (前人未到の記録, 'an unprecedented record'); the orthographic variant 前人未踏 originally described mountaineering and exploration before merging in figurative usage.

rootFamily.word: 前代未聞 (ぜんだいみもん)

前半.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound formed from 前 (zen, 'before, front, earlier part', from Middle Chinese *dzek/dzen) and 半 (han, 'half', from Middle Chinese *pɑnH). Paired symmetrically with 後半 (kōhan, 'latter/second half'), it designates the first half of any temporal, musical, sporting, or textual span—such as the first half of a piece of sheet music, a week, or a match.

history.meaning: the former half
first half

前半.notes: Pronounced ゼンハン; always pairs naturally with 後半 (コウハン).

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 前半

前向き.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound joining 前 (mae 'front', from Old Japanese ma-pe, a compound of ma- 'eye' + pe 'side, direction', literally 'the direction facing the eyes') and 向き (muki, the continuative nominalized stem of the verb muku 'to face, turn toward'). Originally a purely spatial term meaning 'facing the front', it underwent metaphorical extension in twentieth-century Japanese to describe a proactive, constructive, and optimistic attitude toward future challenges.

history.meaning: eye-direction (front) + facing toward
physically facing forward or toward the front
positive, constructive, forward-looking (attitude)

前向き.notes: In bureaucratic and business Japanese, 前向きに検討する ('to consider positively/favorably') is a classic polite formula that often masks non-committal deferral.

rootFamily.gloss: to face, turn toward, be suited to

前払い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound combining 前 (mae 'before, in advance', from Old Japanese ma-pe 'direction of the eyes, front') with 払い (-barai, via rendaku voicing from harai, the nominalized stem of harau < Old Japanese parapu 'to sweep away, clear away, purge'). In medieval and Edo commercial usage, parapu > harau evolved from 'sweeping away ritual impurity or obstacles' to 'clearing a debt or settling an account', yielding maebarai for 'paying in advance'.

history.meaning: beforehand + sweeping/clearing away
settling a payment prior to delivery or service
advance payment, prepayment, cash up front

morphemes.meaning: payment, clearing an obligation (voiced from harai)

前払い.notes: Contrasts directly with 後払い (atobarai, 'deferred payment / paying after service'); note the mandatory rendaku voicing of h > b in -barai.

rootFamily.gloss: to pay, sweep away, clear out

前科.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound formed from 前 (zen, Middle Chinese dzen 'former, previous, prior') and 科 (ka, Middle Chinese khwa 'class, statutory category, legal penalty, offense'). Because classical Chinese administrative law graded crimes and punishments into measured tiers or statutes (科條), 科 came to mean 'offense, crime, penalty' in both Sinitic jurisprudence and traditional Japanese law (where it was also read natively as toga 'fault, crime'), giving 前科 the sense of 'prior statutory conviction'.

history.meaning: previous + statutory category / legal penalty
prior offense recorded under criminal law; criminal record

前科.notes: An ex-convict or person with priors is called a 前科者 (zenkamono), and multiple convictions are counted with the suffix -犯, as in 前科三犯 ('three prior convictions').

rootFamily.gloss: person with a criminal record, ex-con
to impose or inflict a punishment/fine

cognates.meaning: front line, military or meteorological front

前線.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 前 (zen, Middle Chinese dzen 'front, forward, ahead') and 線 (sen, Middle Chinese sjenH 'thread, cord, line'). Coined in modern Japan as a semantic calque of European military terminology (English front line, French ligne de front, German Frontlinie) to denote the foremost line of combat forces, and subsequently extended to meteorology (weather fronts, after Bjerknes's polar front theory) and figurative arenas of intense enterprise.

history.meaning: front/forward + thread/line
military front line; weather front; cutting edge of a field

前線.notes: Frequently reinforced with the superlative prefix 最- in 最前線 (saizensen, 'the very forefront / cutting edge') when describing business, media, or technology.

rootFamily.word: 梅雨前線 (ばいうぜんせん)

剥ぎ取る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound godan verb joining 剥ぎ (hagi, the continuative stem ren'yōkei of hagu < Old Japanese pagu 'to flay, peel, strip off bark, skin, or clothing') with 取る (toru < Old Japanese toru 'to take in hand, seize, remove'). The combination intensifies the forceful, complete removal of an outer layer, covering, or possession, evolving from literal skinning orbark-stripping to figurative divestment of disguises, titles, or pretenses.

history.meaning: to flay/peel off + to seize/take
to strip off clothes/skin; to rob or tear away completely

morphemes.meaning: peel, flay, strip off (continuative stem of hagu)

剥ぎ取る.notes: Carries a visceral, forceful nuance—used both for physically tearing off a label or garment and for stripping away someone's facade or privileges.

割.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun derived from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the verb 割る (waru < Old Japanese waru 'to split, cleave, divide into parts'). From the literal act of dividing a whole into shares, Edo-period merchants and mathematicians standardized wari (割) as the base unit of decimal proportion equal to one-tenth (10%), while also preserving its broader senses of 'allotment, comparative ratio, dilution ratio, and profitability'.

history.meaning: splitting, dividing into pieces
proportional share; one-tenth (10%) in mercantile arithmetic
ten percent; rate, ratio, comparative advantage, drink dilution

morphemes.meaning: division, proportion, one-tenth (nominalized stem of waru)

割.notes: In Japanese decimal percentages, 1割 (ichiwari) is 10%, 3割 (sanwari) is 30% (or a .300 batting average in baseball), and 割に合う (wari ni au) means 'to be worth the cost/effort'.

割る.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *waru* (割る 'to split, crack, break into pieces, divide, dilute a drink'), transitive counterpart of 割れる (*wareru*).

history.meaning: split apart; break; divide
crack (an egg); break; divide; dilute

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 割る

割れる.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) intransitive verb 割れる (われる 'to crack, break, split open, be divided'), continuing Old Japanese *waru* (lower bigrade), intransitive counterpart of four-grade 割る.

history.meaning: split; crack; break apart
break (glass, dish); crack; split

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 割れる

割引.etymology: Compound of 割り ('tenth-part proportion, rate', from 割る 'divide') and 引き ('pulling back, subtracting', from 引く), literally 'subtracting a proportion off the price'.

創造主.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic compound uniting 創造 (sōzō 'creation, origination', from Middle Chinese 創 tshjangH 'to initiate, carve out, found' + 造 dzawX 'to construct, fashion, make') with the agentive head noun 主 (-shu, Middle Chinese tsjuX 'lord, master, sovereign, principal'). Popularized in Meiji-era Protestant and philosophical translations to render English Creator and Latin Creator (the divine architect of the cosmos), and later applied figuratively to visionary artists or auteurs.

history.meaning: to initiate + to construct + lord/master
the Divine Creator (Meiji theological translation); supreme creator

創造主.notes: Read sōzōshu (with the Sino-Japanese on'yomi shu for 主, rather than native nushi), lending the word a solemn, cosmic, or theological register.

rootFamily.word: 救世主 (きゅうせいしゅ)

劇場.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 劇 (geki, from Middle Chinese gjak 'intense, severe, arduous', which evolved in Tang–Song Chinese into 'lively theatrical performance, stage drama') and 場 (jō, from Middle Chinese drjang 'leveled ground, ritual arena, public space'). Adopted during the Meiji modernization of performing arts to designate permanent playhouses and opera houses, replacing the humbler Edo-period native term 芝居小屋 (shibaigoya, 'play shack').

history.meaning: intense action / stage play + leveled arena/ground
theater, playhouse, movie palace; dramatic arena

劇場.notes: Covers both live stage playhouses and cinemas (as in 劇場版 gekijōban, 'theatrical film version' of a TV series), and is used figuratively in 劇場型 (gekijōgata, 'theatrical/melodramatic style').

rootFamily.word: 劇場版 (げきじょうばん)

力.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tikara* (力 'physical strength, power, energy, effort, capability, help'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

strength; power; effort; ability

力仕事.etymology: Native Japanese compound 力仕事 (ちからしごと 'heavy manual labor, work requiring physical strength'), combining 力 (ちから 'physical strength') + 仕事 (しごと 'work, task').

加わる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive godan verb descending from Old Japanese かははる / くははる (kupaparu, 'to be added to, to join in, to increase'). 加盟.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 加 (ka, from Middle Chinese kæ 'to add, augment, join') with 盟 (mei, from Middle Chinese mjwæng 'solemn covenant, blood oath'). In Zhou-dynasty Chinese antiquity, a meng (盟) was an interstate treaty ratified over a sacrificial vessel (皿) under the witness of the sun and moon (明); 加盟 thus literally signifies 'adding one's name to a sworn covenant', used in modern Japanese for joining treaties, unions, trade associations, or franchise networks.

accession to a treaty; affiliation with a federation or cartel

助かる.etymology: Inherited from Early Middle Japanese *tasukaru* (助かる 'to be saved, rescued, spared; to be a great help, have one's burden lightened'), the intransitive counterpart of 助ける (*tasukeru*).

助ける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) ichidan transitive verb descended from Old Japanese tasuku (shimo-nidan conjugation, 'to aid, rescue, support'). Morphologically analyzed by historical linguists as the prefix ta- (bound form of te 'hand', indicating manual intervention) prefixed to a verbal root related to sukufu (救う 'to scoop up, rescue from danger') or suku ('to prop up, support'), literally 'to lend a hand to lift someone out of distress'. 助監督.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic compound created in the twentieth-century Japanese studio system by prefixing 助- (jo-, from Middle Chinese dzrjoH 'to assist, deputy, auxiliary') to 監督 (kantoku 'director, supervisor', from Middle Chinese 監 kæm 'to look down upon, inspect, oversee' + 督 tuwk 'to command, superintend'). assistant director (in film and television production)

助言.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 助 (jo, from Middle Chinese dzrjoH 'to help, assist, lend strength') and 言 (gen, from Middle Chinese ngjon 'spoken words, discourse, counsel'). Attested in classical Chinese texts for 'speaking up in support of someone' and adopted in medieval Japanese initially with the Go-on reading jogon ('putting in a helpful word from the side'), before standardizing in modern Japanese to the Kan-on hybrid reading jogen ('constructive advice, counsel').

advice, counsel, constructive suggestion

効く.etymology: Native Yamato intransitive godan verb きく (kiku, Old Japanese kiku), etymologically identical to the root of 聞く ('to hear, perceive with the senses'). to function effectively, show results
to work, take effect, be effective

It derives from the classical Chinese image 千鈞一髪 (senkin ippatsu) in Han Yu's Tang-dynasty letter and the Book of Han, picturing a thousand-catty weight suspended by a single human hair—a metaphor for a moment where catastrophe is averted by a hair's breadth.

history.meaning: a massive weight hanging by a single hair
a perilous situation or narrow escape by a hair's breadth

cognates.meaning: hanging by a single hair; critical juncture

危険.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Literary Chinese 危險 (Middle Chinese ngjwe xjemX), composed of 危 (ki, Middle Chinese ngjwe, "high and precarious, unstable, perilous", originally depicting a person kneeling atop a steep cliff 厂) and 険 (ken, shinjitai of 險, Middle Chinese xjemX, "steep mountain defile, rugged terrain, hazardous pass", containing the mound/cliff radical 阜). In classical Chinese texts such as the Mencius and Xunzi, 危險 described treacherous physical terrain or political instability; in Meiji Japanese it became the standard abstract noun and na-adjective for danger and risk.

即金.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) commercial compound coined in Edo-period merchant usage (washei-kango), combining 即 (soku, Middle Chinese tsik, "at once, on the spot, immediately", originally depicting a person kneeling beside a vessel of food 皀 about to eat immediately) and 金 (kin, Middle Chinese kim, "metal, gold, money, cash"). Phonologically, the final vowel of soku elides and its velar stop assimilates to the following initial k- of kin, producing the geminate reading sokkin ("cash paid on the spot").

即金.notes: Whereas 現金 (genkin) simply means physical cash (as opposed to checks or credit cards), 即金 (sokkin) specifically emphasizes the immediacy of the payout — "cash on the barrelhead / paid on the spot" (即金で払う sokkin de harau).

instant decision, deciding on the spot

卵.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tamago* (卵・玉子), a transparent compound of 玉 (たま *tama* 'round jewel, sphere') + 子 (こ > ご via rendaku, 'child, young, small round thing'): literally 'jewel-child / round-offspring'. Gradually replaced older かひご (*kapigo* 'shell-young') from Late Middle Japanese onward.

原動力.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) three-character compound coined in Meiji-era Japan (washei-kango) to translate Western physics and mechanical engineering terms such as English motive power / prime mover and German Triebkraft. It combines 原 (gen, Middle Chinese ngjwon, "spring, source, origin", depicting water 泉 emerging from beneath a cliff 厂) + 動 (dō, Middle Chinese duwngX, "to move, set in motion") + 力 (ryoku, Middle Chinese lik, "force, power"). From steam and hydraulic engines, it quickly extended metaphorically to the psychological or economic driving force behind human ambition and social change, and was loaned into Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: fountainhead, origin + move, motion + strength, force

history.form: 原動力 (げんどうりょく)
history.meaning: mechanical motive power (prime mover in Meiji physics and engineering)

history.form: 原動力 (げんどうりょく)

原動力.notes: Structurally analyzed as [原動 ("primary motion")] + [力 ("force")] — compare 原動機 (gendōki, "prime mover / engine motor"); in everyday Japanese it describes what fuels someone's hustle (成功の原動力 seikō no gendōryoku, "the driving force of success").

原因.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese and Sino-Buddhist philosophical vocabulary, combining 原 (gen, Middle Chinese ngjwon, "fountainhead, source, origin", depicting a spring flowing from a cliff) and 因 (in, Middle Chinese 'jin, "cause, basis, to rely upon", graphically depicting a person 大 resting on a woven mat 口, and used in Chinese Buddhist logic to translate Sanskrit hetu, "primary cause"). In the Meiji period, scholars standardized 原因 as the philosophical and scientific counterpart of 結果 (kekka, "effect, result") to render Western causality.

history.meaning: original basis, underlying root cause (in classical history and Buddhist hetu-vidyā logic)
scientific or philosophical cause (paired with 結果 "effect" in Meiji thought)
cause, origin, source of an event or problem

原因.notes: Whereas 理由 (riyū) refers to a human motive, justification, or logical reason ("why someone chose to act"), 原因 (gen'in) refers to the objective causal factor that produced an outcome, often an accident, illness, or failure (失敗の原因 shippai no gen'in).

rootFamily.gloss: cause and effect, karma, fate (Buddhist hetu-phala)

cognates.meaning: raw stone, uncut gem; diamond in the rough

原石.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 原 (gen, Middle Chinese ngjwon, "original, raw, unworked source") and 石 (seki, kan-on reading from Middle Chinese dzyek, "stone, rock, mineral", depicting a rock beneath a cliff 厂). Originally a mineralogical and lapidary term denoting an uncut gemstone or raw mineral ore prior to faceting and polishing (echoing the classical Chinese image of 璞玉, an uncarved jade boulder), it developed a vivid metaphorical meaning in modern Japanese talent scouting for a "diamond in the rough."

history.meaning: source, original state + stone, mineral

厳しい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) shiku-adjective continuing Classical Japanese きびし (kibishi, Early Middle Japanese kipisi). Philologically linked to the Old Japanese root kipu / kifu ("to crowd closely, press tightly, pack together") and the noun きび (kibi, "tightness, acute subtlety"), it originally described something packed without gaps, tightly sealed, or acutely intense in Heian court literature (such as The Tale of Genji). Over the medieval and early modern periods, it was orthographically matched with the Chinese character 厳 ("stern, rigorous") and shifted toward strictness of discipline, harshness of standards, and grim difficulty.

history.meaning: tightly sealed, closely packed, intense, acute
stern in manner, uncompromising, intense in degree (cold, heat, guard)
strict, severe, harsh, grim, hard to pull off

morphemes.meaning: tight, intense, stern, severe (native wago stem kibishi-)

厳しい.notes: Beyond describing a strict boss or harsh winter (寒さが厳しい), modern business and colloquial Japanese constantly uses 厳しい as a polite, indirect refusal meaning "that's tough / unfeasible / unlikely to work" (ちょっと厳しいですね chotto kibishii desu ne).

rootFamily.gloss: solemn, majestic, grave (older wago variant derived from the same root)
strict, rigorous, severe (Sino-Japanese compound sharing the kanji 厳)

厳禁.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 厳禁 (げんきん 'strict prohibition, strictly forbidden'), combining 厳 (げん 'strict, severe, stern') + 禁 (きん 'forbid, prohibit').

strictly forbidden

厳選.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 厳 (gen, shinjitai of 嚴, Middle Chinese ngjæm, "stern, strict, rigorous, severe") and 選 (sen, Middle Chinese swjenX, "to choose, select, screen", containing the movement radical 辶 and 巽). Constructed on the model of modifier + verb (厳しく選ぶ, "to choose strictly"), it functions as both a noun and a transitive suru-verb denoting rigorous screening or handpicking of only top-grade talent, candidates, or materials, and has been re-borrowed into commercial Mandarin (嚴選) as a marketing term.

rootFamily.gloss: strict, rigorous, unsparing (of rules or punishments)

In Modern Japanese it functions as the standard humble/polite verb for 'to go, come' and 'to visit a shrine/grave'.

参加.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Literary Chinese 參加 (Middle Chinese tsrhim kæ), combining 参 (san, shinjitai of 參, Middle Chinese tsrhim, "three; to join in as a third party, enter a group, consult") and 加 (ka, Middle Chinese kæ, "to add to, augment, join", graphically combining 力 "strength/plow" and 口 "mouth"). Originally used in Chinese bureaucratic prose for adding one's presence or counsel to an official deliberation, it became the universal modern Japanese noun and suru-verb for participating in an event, project, or movement.

joining an enterprise, alliance, or assembly (pre-1946 orthography)
participation, joining, taking part

参謀.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical Chinese 參謀 (Middle Chinese tsrhim mjuw), first attested in the Book of Later Han (後漢書, 5th century CE), combining 参 (san, shinjitai of 參, Middle Chinese tsrhim, "to participate in, consult together") and 謀 (bō, kan-on reading from Middle Chinese mjuw, "to plan, devise strategy, take counsel"). Originally denoting participation in military or state planning, it was institutionalized in 1878 when the Imperial Japanese Army established the 参謀本部 (Sanbō Honbu, General Staff Office) modeled on the Prussian Generalstab, and subsequently entered business slang for the "brains" or right-hand strategist behind a leader.

history.meaning: to take part in strategic counsel; military adviser to a commander (Book of Later Han)
commissioned staff officer of the Imperial Japanese Army or Navy (Meiji military term)
military chief of staff; right-hand strategist or mastermind in business or politics

plan, strategize, devise counsel (kan-on bō, MC mjuw)

参謀.notes: In corporate dramas and startup culture, calling someone the 参謀 (or 参謀役 sanbōyaku) of a charismatic company president means they are the shrewd number-two strategist who turns the visionary's wild ideas into executable plans.

rootFamily.gloss: plot, conspiracy, secret scheme (using the go-on reading mu of 謀)
participation in government or corporate management

反省.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound rooted in Classical Confucian moral philosophy — echoing Zengzi's famous maxim in the Analects (論語, Xue Er 1.4), 吾日三省吾身 ("Each day I examine myself on three counts") — combining 反 (han, Middle Chinese pjonX, "to turn back, invert, return") and 省 (sei, kan-on reading from Middle Chinese srijengX, "to inspect closely, examine, reflect upon", distinct from Middle Chinese srængX > shō, "to omit / ministry"). Literally "turning one's gaze back inward to examine oneself," it evolved from neutral philosophical introspection to critical self-reflection and remorse over wrongdoings or failures.

history.meaning: turning inward to examine one's own moral conduct (Confucian self-cultivation)

In Japanese schools, workplaces, and courtrooms, 反省している ("showing remorse/self-reflection") is a key cultural expectation after any misstep.

収める.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb continuing Classical Japanese shimo-nidan をさむ (wosamu, Old Japanese wosamu), paired with the intransitive yodan/godan counterpart をさまる (wosamaru > osamaru, "to settle into place, be contained, subside"). All senses of native osameru radiate from a single core concept: "to bring something dispersed, disordered, or external into its proper place or container." Modern orthography splits this single native verb across four kanji by nuance: 治める ("to govern/quell"), 修める ("to master a study"), 納める ("to pay/deliver into a storehouse"), and 収める ("to gather in, capture within a frame or container, or achieve a result").

収賄容疑.etymology: A four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound formed from 収賄 (shūwai, 'accepting a bribe') and 容疑 (yōgi, 'suspicion of a criminal offense'). 収賄 combines 収 (shū, Middle Chinese syuw, 'gather, collect, receive') and 賄 (wai, Middle Chinese xwojH, 'wealth, property, bribe'), a classical Chinese legal term for official venality paired in contrast with 贈賄 (zōwai, 'giving a bribe'). 容疑 combines 容 (yō, Middle Chinese yowng, 'contain, harbor, admit') and 疑 (gi, Middle Chinese ngi, 'doubt, suspect'), standardized in modern Japanese criminal procedure and journalism for formal suspicion prior to indictment.

accepting bribes + harboring suspicion of an offense
formal police or prosecutorial suspicion of bribery

収賄容疑.notes: Standard newsroom and prosecutorial phrasing; adding 者 (sha) produces 収賄容疑者 ('bribery suspect'), and its active counterpart is 贈賄容疑 ('suspicion of offering a bribe').

叔母.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *woba* (叔母・伯母 'aunt'), a reduced compound of 小 (を *wo* 'lesser, secondary') + 母 (*ba* 'mother, female elder'). In kanji usage, 叔母 specifically denotes an aunt younger than one's parent, while 伯母 denotes an older aunt.

取っ払い.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) colloquial noun derived from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 取っ払う (topparau), an emphatic geminated form of the compound verb 取り払う (toriharau). It combines 取り (tori, from 取る toru, 'take, seize') with 払う (harau, Old Japanese parapu, originally 'sweep away, clear off, banish' and in medieval commercial usage 'disburse, pay out'). Via phonetic attrition (tori-harai > topparai), the noun developed two distinct senses: clearing away physical obstacles, and in Edo-to-Shōwa merchant and day-labor argot, immediate spot-cash settlement at the end of a job or delivery without running a tab.

取りかかる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 取り (tori, the continuative stem of 取る toru, 'take in hand', functioning here as an inchoative and intensive verbal prefix) and かかる (kakaru, written 掛かる or 懸かる, Old Japanese kakaru, 'hang upon, make contact with, direct one's effort toward'). Originally describing physically laying one's hands upon an object or engaging an opponent, it grammaticalized into a general inchoative verb meaning to set about or embark upon a task or project.

取り分.etymology: A hybrid Yamato–Sino (wago–kango) compound noun combining native Japanese 取り (tori, continuative nominal stem of 取る toru, 'take, claim, receive') with Sino-Japanese 分 (bun, Middle Chinese bjunH, 'allotted portion, share, status', as as contrasted with verbal reading fun/pun 'divide'). Literally 'the portion one takes', it emerged in commercial and household division contexts to denote an individual's rightful cut of profits, spoils, or inheritance.

取り合う.etymology: Compound verb 取り合う (とりあう 'to take each other's hands; scramble or compete for something; pay attention to'), combining 取り (stem of 取る 'to take') + reciprocal auxiliary 合う (あう 'to do mutually').

Originally describing the physical give-and-take of commodities and money across a merchant's counter—taking payment and drawing goods—it solidified during the Muromachi and Edo periods as the standard term for mercantile transactions, negotiation, and business dealings.

pulling, drawing, delivering (continuative stem of 引く)

取り引き.notes: The spelling 取り引き with okurigana highlights its native verbal roots and is slightly softer or more narrative than the compressed legal/financial form 取引, though both are pronounced identically (torihiki) without rendaku.

取り戻す.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) resultative compound verb combining 取り (tori, continuative stem of 取る toru, 'take, seize, reclaim') with 戻す (modosu, transitive verb meaning 'return, put back, restore', paired with intransitive 戻る modoru, historically linked to twisting or turning back). Literally 'to take and put back in one's possession', it applies both to physically recovering lost or stolen property and abstractly regaining lost trust, youth, territory, or composure.

to recover, regain, win back, or restore something lost

morphemes.meaning: take, seize (continuative stem of 取る)

取り戻す.notes: Contrast with 引き戻す (hikimodosu, 'pull back someone/something moving away'): 取り戻す focuses on reclaiming ownership, status, or a lost state into one's own hands.

rootFamily.gloss: to recapture, retake, win back (kango equivalent)

取り柄.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 取り (tori, continuative stem of 取る toru, 'take hold of, grasp, adopt') and 柄 (e, Old Japanese ye, 'handle, shaft, grip of a tool or weapon'). Literally meaning 'a handle by which something can be grasped and put to use', the concrete tool metaphor shifted by the medieval and Edo periods to denote a person's saving grace, redeeming quality, or one worthwhile capability. Often alternatively written 取柄 or phonetically associated with 取得 (torie, 'gain').

history.meaning: wooden shaft, handle, or grip of an axe or tool
a part one can grasp; a useful feature worth adopting
redeeming quality, strong point, merit, worth

morphemes.meaning: grasping, taking hold of (continuative of 取る)

取り柄.notes: Watch the reading of 柄: when meaning a physical handle or grip (and by extension 'redeeming point' in 取り柄), it is read e (とりえ), whereas when meaning 'pattern, build, or character' (e.g., 人柄 hitogara, 柄 gara), it is read gara.

rootFamily.gloss: handle, grip, shaft of a tool or umbrella

取り消す.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb composed of 取り (tori, continuative stem of 取る toru, 'take back', acting as a reversative and intensive verbal prefix) and 消す (kesu, Old Japanese ketu / kesu, transitive counterpart of 消ゆ kiyu, 'extinguish, erase, cause to vanish'). Combining the sense of 'taking back' with 'erasing', it developed from wiping away a written mark or spoken statement to the formal legal and administrative sense of revoking a license, retracting words, or canceling a reservation.

history.meaning: to take back and blot out a statement or record
to cancel, revoke, retract, annul, or rescind

morphemes.meaning: take back, intensive prefix (continuative of 取る)

取り消す.notes: Its nominalized form 取り消し (torikeshi) is the standard Japanese label for the 'Cancel' or 'Undo' action in software interfaces and legal revocations.

rootFamily.gloss: to negate, drown out, cancel out

取り締まり.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun from the continuative stem of 取り締まる (torishimaru, 'control, oversee, crack down on'), itself compounded from 取り (tori, intensive verbal prefix from 取る toru, 'take in hand') and 締まる (shimaru, 'tighten, bind firmly, be taut', related to 締む shimu). Note that despite 締まる being intransitive in isolation, the compound 取り締まる is transitive ('to tighten control over'). In the Edo bakufu and Meiji state, it denoted administrative supervision and policing, leading to its modern sense of a police or regulatory crackdown.

history.meaning: to bind tightly; to enforce strict order over a household or guild
administrative oversight, policing, regulatory crackdown

morphemes.meaning: take in hand, manage (continuative of 取る)
tightening, strict control (nominal stem of 締まる)

取り締まり.notes: This same word gives rise to the corporate title 取締役 (torishimariyaku, 'company director / board member', lit. 'officer in charge of oversight').

rootFamily.gloss: to crack down on, control, supervise, police
rootFamily.word: 取り締まる (とりしまる)

rootFamily.gloss: to tighten, tie up, strangle, conclude

取り違え.etymology: Compound verbal noun 取り違え (とりちがえ 'mistaking one thing for another, mix-up'), nominalized from the continuative stem of 取り違える ('to take the wrong one by mistake', from 取り 'take' + 違える 'make a mistake, alter').

取る.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *toru* (取る・採る・執る・撮る 'to take in the hand, hold, pick up, remove, reserve, obtain'), attested throughout eighth-century texts.

history.meaning: take in hand; grasp; gather

取れる.etymology: The term '取れる' (meaning 'taken') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: taken

取引.etymology: The standard okurigana-omitted kanji spelling of the native Yamato (wago) compound 取り引き (torihiki), composed of 取 (tori, continuative stem of 取る toru, 'take, receive') and 引 (hiki, continuative stem of 引く hiku, 'pull, withdraw, deliver'). While etymologically pure native Japanese referring to the reciprocal taking and pulling of goods and payments in a market, dropping the okurigana visually aligns the two-kanji compound with Sino-Japanese legal and commercial terminology in statutes, contracts, and financial exchanges.

history.meaning: reciprocal taking and pulling in physical exchange
commercial trade, guild dealings, brokerage exchange
business transaction, financial trading, deal

morphemes.meaning: take, receive (native kun-reading stem of 取る)

取引停止.etymology: A hybrid commercial and banking four-kanji compound joining native Yamato 取引 (torihiki, 'business transaction, commercial dealings', from 取る 'take' + 引く 'pull') with Sino-Japanese 停止 (teishi, 'suspension, halt'). 停止 combines 停 (tei, Middle Chinese deng, 'halt, lodge, pause') and 止 (shi, Middle Chinese tsyiX, 'foot, stop, cease'). In Japanese corporate finance, 取引停止 (specifically 銀行取引停止処分, 'suspension of bank clearinghouse transactions') is the de facto death sentence for a company after dishonoring two promissory notes (不渡り fuwatari) within six months.

取引停止.notes: In Japanese corporate dramas like *The Naked Director*, 取引停止 carries immense dramatic weight: when a clearinghouse imposes 銀行取引停止 ('suspension of bank transactions'), the firm is barred from credit and bills for two years, triggering immediate bankruptcy (事実上の倒産).

cognates.meaning: gather material; press reporting/interviewing (reborrowed from Japanese)

取材.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 取 (shu, Middle Chinese tshjuX, 'take, select, gather') and 材 (zai, Middle Chinese dzoj, 'timber, raw material, resource'). Attested in classical Chinese literary criticism (whereを取材 meant selecting raw themes or historical materials for poetry and prose), the compound was revitalized in Meiji–Taishō Japanese journalism and filmmaking to mean going into the field to gather facts, conduct interviews, and shoot coverage—a sense subsequently reborrowed into modern Mandarin (qǔcái) and Korean (chwijae).

gathering source material for an article, book, or film; journalistic reporting and interviewing

受ける.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) Shimo Ichidan verb descending from Old Japanese 受く (uku, Shimo Nidan conjugation, continuative stem uke-), from Proto-Japonic *uka- / *uke- ('to catch, hold up to receive'). Originally describing the physical act of holding out a vessel, palm, or shield to catch something falling or approaching (such as water, wind, or a sword blow), it expanded across Japanese history to cover receiving favors or orders, undergoing an examination or surgery, and—in modern colloquial usage—getting a laugh or favorable reaction from an audience (ウケる).

history.meaning: to catch in a vessel or hand; to receive something coming toward one

history.form: 受くる / 受ける (ukuru > ukeru)
history.meaning: to receive, accept, undergo, sustain; to be well-received by an audience

受ける.notes: In entertainment and colloquial speech (often written in katakana as ウケる), it functions intransitively to mean 'to land well with an audience, be hilarious', derived from theatrical jargon for 'receiving' applause or laughter (受けがいい).

rootFamily.gloss: to undertake, take charge of, guarantee
rootFamily.word: 引き受ける (ひきうける)

受け入れ続ける.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) three-morpheme agglutinative compound verb constructed from 受け入れる (ukeireru, 'accept, take in, adopt') plus the aspectual auxiliary verb 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'continue doing'). 受け入れる itself combines 受け (uke, continuative stem of 受ける ukeru, 'receive, catch') and 入れる (ireru, Old Japanese iru, 'put in, admit inside'), literally 'to receive and let inside'. Attaching 続ける (from Old Japanese tuduku, 'follow in unbroken succession') expresses sustained, ongoing acceptance of people, ideas, or demands over time.

history.meaning: to receive and admit inside + to keep in unbroken succession
to continue accepting, admitting, or accommodating over time

morphemes.meaning: receive, catch (continuative stem of 受ける)
let in, put inside (continuative stem of 入れる)

受け入れ続ける.notes: Illustrates Japanese V-V-V verbal compounding: any Ichidan or Godan verb's continuative stem (ren'yōkei) can productively attach 続ける to express uninterrupted continuation.

rootFamily.gloss: to accept, receive, take in, adopt
rootFamily.word: 受け入れる (うけいれる)

rootFamily.gloss: to continue, keep up, carry on (transitive)

受け取る.etymology: Compound transitive verb 受け取る (うけとる 'to receive, accept, take delivery of, interpret'), combining 受け (continuative stem of 受ける *ukeru* 'to receive, catch') + 取る (とる 'to take in hand').

history.meaning: receive into one's hands; accept

受け止める.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb uniting 受け (uke, continuative stem of 受ける ukeru, 'receive, catch') and 止める (tomeru, Old Japanese tomu, transitive counterpart of 止まる tomaru, 'stop, halt, arrest movement'). Literally meaning 'to catch and bring to a halt', it originated in martial arts and physical labor for stopping a sword strike, arrow, or falling load with one's body or weapon, and later developed a rich psychological sense: taking a harsh reality, criticism, or someone's feelings seriously and absorbing the impact without deflection.

history.form: 受け留む / 受け止む (uketomu)
history.meaning: to parry and halt a blow; to catch and arrest a moving object
to catch physically; to take to heart, face squarely, and come to terms with

morphemes.meaning: receive, catch (continuative stem of 受ける)
stop, halt, hold in place (transitive 止める)

受け止める.notes: Compare 受け入れる (ukeireru, 'let inside / comply with / adopt') and 受け止める (uketomeru, 'catch and absorb the weight of'): you can 受け止める someone's grief or criticism empathetically and seriously (真摯に受け止める) without necessarily agreeing to every demand.

rootFamily.gloss: to ward off, parry, dodge a question/blow

受け皿.etymology: Native compound of 受ける ('receive, catch, support') in stem form 受け and 皿 ('plate, dish', voiced to ざら by rendaku), literally 'a dish that catches a cup above it'.

受付.etymology: Compound verbal noun 受付 (うけつけ 'reception desk, information counter; accepting applications or guests'), nominalized from 受け付ける ('to receive and attach to the register', from 受け 'receive' + 付け 'enter/attach').

受信.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 受 (ju, Middle Chinese dzyuwX, 'receive, accept') and 信 (shin, Middle Chinese sinH, originally 'trustworthy speech, envoy', and by extension 'letter, tidings, message, signal'). Popularized in Meiji-era postal and telegraph administration alongside its antonym 送信 (sōshin, 'transmission, sending a message') and 通信 (tsūshin, 'telecommunications, correspondence'), it subsequently expanded to radio, satellite broadcasting (as in satellite TV dish reception in *The Naked Director*), and email/mobile data reception.

receiving radio, television, satellite, or digital signals and messages

受信.notes: Forms an exact antonym pair with 送信 (sōshin, 'sending/transmitting'); in Japan, public broadcaster NHK collects a mandatory statutory fee known as 受信料 (jushinryō, 'broadcast reception fee').

rootFamily.gloss: transmission, sending a signal or message

受容.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 受 (ju, Middle Chinese dzyuwX, 'receive, accept') and 容 (yō, Middle Chinese yowng, 'contain, hold within a vessel, tolerate, accommodate'). Attested in classical Chinese and Buddhist translations (where 受容 denoted receiving and holding the Dharma in mind), it was adopted in modern Japanese academic, psychological, and scientific prose to translate English 'reception' and 'acceptance' (e.g., literary reception 文学受容, psychological self-acceptance 自己受容, and biological sensory receptors 受容体 juyōtai).

history.meaning: to receive and contain within; to accommodate teachings
formal acceptance, cultural reception, or physiological receptor uptake

受容.notes: A high-register kango peer of native 受け入れ (ukeire); beware the homophone 需要 (juyō, 'economic demand'), which is paired with 供給 (kyōkyū, 'supply').

rootFamily.gloss: biological receptor (e.g., hormone or neurotransmitter receptor)

受領.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and verbal noun 受領 (じゅりょう 'receipt, formal acknowledgment of receiving goods or documents'), combining 受 (じゅ 'receive') + 領 (りょう 'take into possession, govern'; in Heian Japan ずりょう also designated a provincial governor).

history.form: 受領 (ずりょう / じゅりょう)

口.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *kuti* (口 'mouth, lips, spoken words, opening, entrance/exit, share'). In compounds its initial *k-* often voices via rendaku to -ぐち (e.g. 入り口, 非常口).

history.meaning: mouth; opening; speech

口コミ.etymology: Modern Japanese compound noun 口コミ (くちコミ 'word of mouth, customer reviews'), coined in the postwar Shōwa era by combining native 口 (くち 'mouth, spoken word') + コミ (clipped from マスコミ *mass communication*, from English *communication*).

口出し.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) somatic compound noun formed from 口 (kuchi, Old Japanese kuti < Proto-Japonic *kutuy, 'mouth, opening, speech') and 出し (dashi, continuative nominal stem of 出す dasu, 'put out, thrust forth', with rendaku voicing t > d precluded because dashi is already voiced). Literally 'thrusting out one's mouth', it belongs to a rich set of Japanese body-part idioms for uninvited interference, alongside 手出し (tedashi, 'sticking one's hand in / physical meddling or fighting') and 顔出し (kaodashi, 'showing one's face').

口紅.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 口 (kuchi, Old Japanese kuti, 'mouth, lips') and 紅 (beni, 'crimson safflower pigment'). The reading beni derives via phonetic reduction (benu < *ureni < kurenai) from Old Japanese 呉藍 (kure-no-awi, literally 'indigo/dye of Wu [China]'), referring to the safflower (*Carthamus tinctorius*) introduced from continental Asia. In the Edo period, refined safflower lip rouge (笹紅 sasabeni, which dried to an iridescent beetle-green sheen when layered) was applied with a brush from a porcelain cup (紅猪口 benichoko); in the Meiji–Shōwa eras, 口紅 came to designate modern stick lipstick.

history.meaning: safflower dye imported from the Wu region of China
safflower rouge applied to the lips with a brush
lipstick, lip rouge

口紅.notes: To 'put on lipstick' in Japanese can be expressed either with the verb 塗る (口紅を塗る, 'apply lipstick') or the traditional Edo verb 引く (紅を引く / 口紅を引く, 'draw/stroke on rouge').

口説く.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) Godan verb written with the semantic kanji compound (jukujikun) 口説 ('mouth' + 'explain/persuade'). Etymologically, it is linked to the adjective くどい (kudoi, 'repetitive, wordy, insistent, tedious') via the verbalizing suffix -ku (compare 続く tuduku, 靡く nabiku), or else influenced by a vernacular reanalysis of Buddhist/medieval Sino-Japanese 口説 (kuzetsu, 'oral exposition, verbal dispute'). In Heian and Kamakura literature (such as *The Tale of Genji*), kudoku meant to recount one's grief or complain at length; by the Edo period's pleasure quarters, it narrowed to persistently wooing a lover or talking someone into a deal.
