命令.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Classical Chinese 命令 (Middle Chinese *mjengH ljengH, 'sovereign decree, command, order'). Both characters share the Old Chinese root *m-rəŋ-s ('to command, decree'): 命 (mei, with mouth radical 口 plus 令) meant an authoritative decree from heaven or a ruler, while 令 (rei, originally depicting a kneeling person receiving orders under a roof/bell) meant an official order or law. Joining the two near-synonyms created an emphatic disyllabic compound.

history.meaning: imperial decree, authoritative command (attested in Mengzi and Han histories)
directive from a superior, official or military order, command

命令.notes: Refers to a top-down, authoritative order (命令を下す, 'to issue a command'; 命令に従う, 'to obey an order'); in grammar, 命令形 (meireikei) is the imperative verb form.

命綱.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) compound noun formed from 命 (inochi, 'life, breath of life', from Old Japanese inoti, likely analyzed as i 'breath' + no 'genitive' + ti 'vital force/spirit') and 綱 (tsuna, 'rope, hawser, cord', from Old Japanese tuna), with regular rendaku voicing (/ts/ > /z/, spelled づな / ずな) on the second element. Originally referring to a physical safety tether used by steeplejacks, sailors, or mountaineers, it is widely used metaphorically for anything indispensable to survival or financial solvency.

history.meaning: breath of life / vital spirit + rope, cord
safety rope protecting a worker's life; vital lifeline or last resort

命綱.notes: Notice the rendaku voicing: 綱 (tsuna) becomes -zuna (phonetically [dzuna]). Frequently used figuratively in business and drama for a company's sole remaining revenue stream or a desperate person's last lifeline.

命運.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound derived from Literary Chinese 命運 (Middle Chinese *mjengH hjunH), combining 命 ('heavenly mandate, allotted lifespan, decree') and 運 ('revolving movement, cycle of fortune, turn of fate'). While its reverse compound 運命 (unmei) is the everyday Japanese word for personal 'fate' or 'destiny', 命運 (meiun) retains a lofty, dramatic register, typically referring to the ultimate survival, doom, or historical destiny of a nation, enterprise, or ambitious venture.

history.meaning: heaven's mandate / allotted life + revolving cycle of fortune
allotted fortune; ultimate fate or survival of a house, state, or enterprise

命運.notes: Compare 運命 (unmei, everyday word for 'fate/destiny', including romantic destiny) with 命運 (meiun, a weightier, literary word often paired with 尽きる—命運が尽きる, 'one's luck/time runs out; to meet one's doom'—or 命運を握る, 'to hold the fate [of an organization] in one's hands').

和子.etymology: Traditional Japanese female given name 和子 (かずこ), combining 和 (かず 'harmony, peace, gentle calm') + naming suffix 子 (こ 'child').

history.meaning: female given name (lit. child of harmony)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 和

和室.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in Japan from 和 (wa, 'Japan, Japanese-style; harmony', from Old Chinese/Middle Chinese *hwa, historically applied via graphic substitution for 倭 Wa, the ancient name for Japan) and 室 (shitsu, 'room, chamber', from Middle Chinese *syit). The term arose during the Meiji and Taishō eras when Western architecture entered Japan, requiring a retronym to distinguish a traditional tatami-floored room (和室) from a Western-style room (洋室, yōshitsu).

history.meaning: harmony / Wa (Japan) + inner chamber, room
Japanese-style room floored with tatami mats (coined in contrast to 洋室 yōshitsu)

和室.notes: The prefix 和- (wa-, 'Japanese-style') systematically contrasts with 洋- (yō-, 'Western-style'): 和室 vs. 洋室 (room), 和食 vs. 洋食 (cuisine), 和服 vs. 洋服 (clothing), and 和風 vs. 洋風 (aesthetic style).

和音.etymology: Sino-Japanese musical compound 和音 (わおん), from 和 ('harmony, blending together') and 音 ('musical tone').
和音.notes: Standard term for a musical chord sounded simultaneously on piano or strings.

品格.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 品格 (ひんかく 'dignity, grace, refined quality, character'), combining 品 (ひん 'refinement, class, quality') + 格 (かく 'status, standard, character').

history.meaning: rank and character; dignified refinement
dignity; grace; nobility of character

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 品格

唱える.etymology: Lower bigrade (now ichidan) transitive verb 唱える (となえる 'to chant, recite aloud, intone a sutra or spell, advocate a theory'), continuing Old Japanese *tonapu* ('to call out aloud in unison or recitation').

history.meaning: recite aloud; chant
chant; recite; advocate

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 唱える

商品.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 商 (shō, 'commerce, trade, merchant', from Middle Chinese *syang; after the fall of the Shang 商 dynasty, its displaced people became renowned itinerant traders, giving the dynastic name the meaning 'merchant, trade') and 品 (hin, 'article, item, class of goods, quality', from Middle Chinese *phimX, originally three mouths/objects 品 representing numerousness or sorted grades of goods). Widely popularized in Meiji political economy to render English 'commodity' and 'merchandise'.

history.meaning: merchant, trade (from Shang dynasty traders) + sorted articles, goods, grade
commercial goods, articles of trade; economic commodity (Meiji economics)

商品.notes: Refers specifically to goods offered for commercial sale (merchandise/commodities), whereas 製品 (seihin) emphasizes a 'manufactured product' made in a factory, and 品物 (shinamono) is an everyday word for physical 'articles/goods'.

rootFamily.gloss: commercialization, turning into a salable product

cognates.meaning: trade, buying and selling (rare/literary compared to 買賣)

商売.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 商 (shō, 'trade, commerce, merchant', from Middle Chinese *syang) and 売 (bai, traditional 賣, 'to sell', from Middle Chinese *meaH, composed of 出 'to put out' over 買 'to buy/net cowries'). Becoming ubiquitous among Edo-period townspeople (chōnin), 商売 shifted from the literal act of 'trading and selling' to mean any commercial business, shopkeeping, livelihood, or occupation that deals with customers.

history.meaning: commerce, trade + to sell goods
mercantile trade, buying and selling, shopkeeping livelihood (Edo chōnin usage)
business, trade, commercial transaction, profession/racket

商売.notes: More earthy and street-level than ビジネス (bijinesu) or 商業 (shōgyō); appears in classic expressions like 商売繁盛 (shōbai hanjō, 'thriving business') and 人気商売 (ninki shōbai, 'an occupation dependent on public popularity', such as entertainment).

rootFamily.gloss: tools of one's trade, professional asset

商売敵.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Japanese (kango + wago) compound combining 商売 (shōbai, 'business, trade, commerce') with the native noun 敵 (kataki, 'rival, enemy, adversary, match', undergoing rendaku voicing to -gataki). Old Japanese kataki ('opponent, counterpart, rival') likely derives from kata ('side, counterpart, partner'); while the kanji 敵 is read teki in Sino-Japanese compounds (like 強敵 kyōteki), here it carries its native kun'yomi reading -gataki to denote a competitor in the same line of trade.

history.meaning: counterpart, match, opponent, enemy
fellow merchant or competitor in the same trade (Edo mercantile vocabulary)
business rival, trade competitor

morphemes.meaning: rival, adversary, opponent in the same sphere

商売敵.notes: Be careful with the reading: 敵 at the end of this word is read via its native Japanese reading -gataki (shōbaigataki), NOT the Sino-Japanese reading -teki! Compare 恋敵 (koigataki, 'rival in love').

rootFamily.gloss: formidable enemy, tough rival (kango reading teki)

商店.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 商店 (しょうてん 'shop, store, commercial establishment'), combining 商 (しょう 'trade, commerce, merchant') + 店 (てん 'shop, store').

history.meaning: retail shop; commercial store

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 商店

商才.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 商 (shō, 'commerce, trade, business', from Middle Chinese *syang) and 才 (sai, 'natural talent, ability, genius, flair', from Middle Chinese *dzoj, originally a pictograph of a sprouting plant shooting upward through the soil, representing innate potential). Together they signify an instinctive knack or talent for making money and seizing commercial opportunities.

history.meaning: trade, commerce + innate talent, sprouting ability
commercial flair, natural talent for trade and profit-making

商才.notes: Commonly used in phrases like 商才がある (shōsai ga aru, 'to have a head/flair for business') or 商才に長けている (shōsai ni takete iru, 'to be gifted in business acumen').

商業オフィス.etymology: Hybrid compound noun 商業オフィス (しょうぎょうオフィス 'commercial office'), combining Sino-Japanese 商業 (しょうぎょう 'commerce, business', from 商 'trade' + 業 'enterprise') + English loanword オフィス (*office*).

history.form: 商業 (しょうぎょう) + オフィス
history.meaning: commercial business office

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 商業

商談.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 商 (shō, 'commerce, trade, OR to deliberate/measure/consult', from Middle Chinese *syang) and 談 (dan, 'to talk, discuss, converse', from Middle Chinese *dam, composed of 言 'speech' and phonetic 炎). While in Chinese 商談 can mean general 'consultation/discussion', in modern Japanese 商談 specifically denotes a 'business negotiation' or sales meeting aimed at closing a commercial deal.

history.meaning: commerce / to deliberate + to discuss, converse
commercial negotiation, sales talks over terms and prices

商談.notes: Standard corporate Japanese vocabulary: 商談を進める ('to advance business talks') and 商談がまとまる / 成立する ('to successfully close a business deal'). Note the false friend with Korean 상담 (sangdam), which usually means 'counseling/consultation' (= Japanese 相談 sōdan).

rootFamily.gloss: consultation, discussing a problem for advice

問屋.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) mercantile term whose irregular reading toiya (or ton'ya) reflects its medieval institutional history. In the Kamakura and Muromachi periods, port warehousing, cargo consignment, and transport brokerage were handled by agents called 問い丸 (toimaru), where 問い (toi, noun stem of 問う tou, 'to inquire, check cargo, consign') meant 'cargo inquiry and brokerage'. Replacing the medieval guild suffix -丸 (-maru) with the shop suffix -屋 (-ya, 'house, merchant') yielded 問屋 (toiya); phonetic assimilation before the palatal glide later produced the colloquial variant ton'ya.

history.meaning: cargo inquiry and consignment agent at medieval ports and estates
history.stage: Early to Late Middle Japanese (Kamakura–Muromachi period)

history.meaning: wholesale merchant and distributor financing artisans and retailers (Edo guild system)
wholesaler, wholesale distributor, middleman

morphemes.meaning: inquiry, consignment brokerage (from 問う tou)

問屋.notes: Both readings とんや (ton'ya) and といや (toiya) are valid, though ton'ya is mandatory in the famous idiom そうは問屋が卸さない (sō wa ton'ya ga orosanai, literally 'the wholesaler won't sell it at that price' > 'things won't go that easily / don't count on it!').

rootFamily.gloss: to ask, inquire, question, charge with
wholesale (selling in bulk from wholesaler to retailer)

問題.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 問題 (もんだい 'question set for answer or examination; problem, issue, matter under discussion'), combining 問 (もん 'ask, inquire') + 題 (だい 'topic, heading, subject').

history.meaning: question posed for discussion or test
question; problem; issue

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 問題

cognates.meaning: good and evil, virtue and vice

善悪.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) dvandva (coordinative antonym) compound from Classical Chinese 善惡 (Middle Chinese *dzyenH 'ak), pairing 善 (zen, 'good, virtuous, auspicious', originally depicting sheep 羊 and speech 言, signifying propitious or commendable words/conduct) with 惡/悪 (aku, 'bad, ugly, foul, evil', composed of phonetic 亞 'crooked/hunchbacked' over 心 'heart'). Central to both Confucian moral philosophy and Buddhist karma doctrine (善悪の報い, retribution for good and evil deeds).

history.meaning: virtuous, good + foul, wicked, evil
good and evil deeds in Buddhist karmic ethics; moral right and wrong

善悪.notes: Normally read ぜんあく (zen'aku) for moral 'good and evil' (e.g., 善悪の判断, 'judging right from wrong'); when read via native kun'yomi as よしあし (yoshiashi), the same kanji pair means 'pros and cons; quality (whether good or bad)'.

rootFamily.gloss: malice, ill will, bad faith (antonym of 善意)

善良.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) synonymous compound (na-adjective and noun) from Classical Chinese 善良 (Middle Chinese *dzyenH ljang), combining two near-synonyms for moral goodness: 善 (zen, 'virtuous, morally good, kind') and 良 (ryō, 'good, fine, upright, conscientious'). In modern Japanese legal and civic discourse, it frequently modifies 市民 (shimin, 'citizen') to mean 'upstanding, law-abiding, innocent'.

history.meaning: virtuous, moral + fine, upright, honest
good-natured, virtuous, honest, law-abiding

善良.notes: Functions as a na-adjective (善良な, zenryō na) and is most famously heard in the collocation 善良な市民 (zenryō na shimin, 'law-abiding/innocent citizens')—often used either earnestly by police or ironically in crime dramas.

喜ばせごっこ.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) compound noun formed from 喜ばせ (yorokobase, the continuative stem 連用形 of 喜ばせる yorokobaseru, the causative of 喜ぶ yorokobu, 'to rejoice, be glad') plus the suffix ごっこ (-gokko, 'make-believe game, mutual play-acting'). The suffix -gokko derives from Early Modern Edo-dialect -goko / -koko, itself from 事 (koto, 'matter, act, game') or 子 (ko) with gemination and rendaku, used after nouns or verb stems to denote children's pretend play or a reciprocal game (literally 'a pretend game of delighting each other').

history.form: よろこぶ (yorokobu) + -さす (-sasu) > よろこばせる (yorokobaseru)
history.meaning: to cause to rejoice, to make happy or delight someone
a mutual game or act of trying to please/delight one another

morphemes.meaning: pretend game, mutual play-acting, doing back and forth

喜ばせごっこ.notes: The productive suffix -ごっこ (-gokko) turns any role or action into a game of pretend or reciprocal play (e.g., 鬼ごっこ onigokko 'tag', お医者さんごっこ oishasan-gokko 'playing doctor', 褒め合いごっこ homeai-gokko 'mutual flattery game'); 喜ばせごっこ can suggest either heartwarming mutual devotion or slightly superficial people-pleasing.

rootFamily.gloss: to make happy, to delight, to please
to rejoice, to be delighted or glad

喜ばせる.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) ichidan verb formed as the regular causative derivation of the godan verb 喜ぶ (yorokobu, 'to rejoice, to be glad, to take delight in', attested in Old Japanese as yoroko₂bu). Because 喜ぶ is fundamentally intransitive/experiential ('a person feels joy'), Japanese requires the causative suffix -せる (-seru, attached to the irrealis stem 未然形 yorokoba-) to express the transitive English concepts 'to please someone', 'to make someone happy', or 'to delight someone'.

history.form: よろこぶ (yoroko₂bu) + しむ (simu) / す (su)
history.meaning: to cause someone to rejoice (classical causative constructions)
history.stage: Old to Early Middle Japanese (8th–12th c.)

history.meaning: to make happy, to please, to delight, to gratify (modern ichidan causative)

morphemes.meaning: to make/let someone do or feel

喜ばせる.notes: English speakers often mistakenly try to use 喜ぶ (yorokobu) transitively for 'to please someone'; in Japanese, you must use the causative 喜ばせる (e.g., お客さんを喜ばせる, 'to delight/satisfy the customers').

rootFamily.gloss: to rejoice, be glad, be delighted

喜ぶ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *yorokobu* (喜ぶ・歓ぶ・慶ぶ 'to rejoice, be glad, feel delight, welcome gladly'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; built on the root *yoro-* (shared with 宜し *yorosi* 'good, auspicious').

history.meaning: rejoice; be delighted; celebrate
be glad; rejoice; be pleased

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 喜ぶ

喝上げ.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Japanese (kango + wago) underworld slang noun (often written in katakana as カツアゲ), nominalized from the compound verb 喝上げる (katsuageru). It combines 喝 (katsu, 'to shout menacingly, browbeat, intimidate', as in 恐喝 kyōkatsu 'extortion, blackmail' and Zen Buddhist 喝! 'shout!', from Middle Chinese *xat) with the native verb 上げる (ageru, 'to raise, lift up, take away / clean out'). Originating in thief and yakuza argot (隠語, ingo), it denotes intimidating a victim on the street into handing over money.

history.meaning: menacing shout / intimidation + to lift up, confiscate, take away
street-level shakedown, mugging by intimidation, extortion (underworld and youth slang)

morphemes.meaning: menacing shout, threat, intimidation (cf. 恐喝)
lifting up, taking away, cleaning out

喝上げ.notes: Frequently written in katakana as カツアゲ (katsuage); while 恐喝 (kyōkatsu) is the formal legal term for 'extortion/blackmail', 喝上げ refers specifically to a street-level shakedown (e.g., delinquents or thugs cornering someone in an alley and demanding their wallet).

喧嘩.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and verbal noun 喧嘩 (けんか 'quarrel, fight, argument'). In Classical Chinese and Heian Japanese, 喧嘩 (combining 喧 'noisy clamor' + 嘩 'uproar, shouting') meant 'noisy bustling clamor'; from Late Middle Japanese onward it specialized into 'a heated argument or fight'.

history.meaning: noisy clamor; uproar
quarrel; argument; fight

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 喧嘩

喫茶店.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 喫 (kitsu, 'to ingest, drink, smoke, partake of', from Middle Chinese *khet, with irregular gemination kitsu + cha > kissa), 茶 (sa, tō'on/kan'on reading of 'tea', from Middle Chinese *dræ), and 店 (ten, 'shop, establishment', from Middle Chinese *temH). 喫茶 (kissa, 'drinking tea') originated in Song-dynasty Chinese Chan (Zen) monastic phraseology (喫茶去, 'go drink tea!'), introduced to Japan by Eisai's 喫茶養生記 (1211); in early 20th-century Taishō and Shōwa Japan, 喫茶店 was coined for modern urban cafes serving coffee, tea, and light Western fare.

history.meaning: drinking tea (Song-dynasty Chan Buddhist monastic expression)

history.form: 喫茶 (kissa, as in Eisai's 喫茶養生記, 1211)
history.meaning: partaking of tea for health and Zen practice
coffeehouse, traditional Japanese-style cafe serving coffee, tea, and snacks

喫茶店.notes: In contemporary Japan, 喫茶店 (kissaten, often shortened in speech to 喫茶 or 純喫茶 junkissa) evokes a retro Shōwa-era sit-down coffeehouse with siphon coffee, thick toast, cream soda, and often smoking tables, in contrast to modern espresso chains called カフェ (kafe).

営業.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and verbal noun 営業 (えいぎょう 'running a business, being open for business, commercial sales'), combining 営 (えい 'plan, manage, conduct') + 業 (ぎょう 'business, trade, occupation').

history.meaning: conducting business; shop operations; sales

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 営業

営業マン.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and English loanword (kango + gairaigo) compound combining 営業 (eigyō, 'business operations, commercial sales', built from Middle Chinese 營 *yeng 'to plan, manage, build a camp' and 業 *ngjop 'work, enterprise, trade') with the English loan suffix マン (-man < English man, from Old English mann, Proto-Germanic *mann-). Modelled on English 'salesman' and post-war Japanese サラリーマン (sararīman), it denotes a corporate sales representative who visits clients to pitch and close deals.

history.meaning: commercial business operations + man / male worker in a profession
corporate salesman, client-facing sales representative (Shōwa economic boom)

morphemes.meaning: person engaged in an occupation, representative

営業マン.notes: In Japanese corporate culture, 営業 (eigyō) specifically refers to active client-facing sales (not just general business operations); while 営業マン was ubiquitous in the Shōwa era (as in Toru Muranishi's encyclopaedia-selling days), gender-neutral terms like 営業担当 (eigyō tantō) or 営業職 (eigyōshoku) are increasingly preferred in formal HR contexts today.

cognates.word: 營業成績 / 营业成绩 (yíngyè chéngjì)

営業成績.etymology: A four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) compound joining 営業 (eigyō, 'business operations, sales', from 營 'to manage/operate' + 業 'enterprise/trade') and 成績 (seiseki, 'results, achievement, record', from 成 *dzyeng 'to accomplish, complete' + 績 *tsek 'to spin hemp/silk thread into yarn > accumulated merit or achievement', containing the silk radical 糸). Literally 'the spun-up accomplishments of one's sales operations'.

history.meaning: commercial/sales operations + accomplished results/merit
sales performance, sales track record or quota rankings

morphemes.meaning: to spin thread > accumulated results, merit, record

営業成績.notes: A high-stakes term in Japanese sales companies, where monthly 営業成績 graphs are often posted publicly on office walls to rank salespeople from top earner (トップ営業マン) to bottom.

器.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *utupa* (器 > うつは > うつわ 'vessel, bowl, container, utensil; personal capacity or caliber'), attested in eighth-century texts.

history.meaning: vessel; container; capability
bowl; dish; vessel; caliber

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 器

cognates.meaning: implement, utensil, vessel (concrete noun; false friend!)

器用.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) na-adjective and noun derived from Classical Chinese 器用 (Middle Chinese *khijH yowngH), combining 器 (ki, 'vessel, receptacle, implement > a person's capacity or talent', depicting four mouths/vessels 口 around a dog 犬 guarding them) and 用 (yō, 'use, function, employment'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Analects 子曰、君子不器), 器 denoted specialized functional capacity, and 器用 meant 'useful vessels/implements' or 'employing according to capacity'. In medieval Japanese, the meaning shifted from 'having useful capacity/talent for an art' to 'manually dexterous, deft, adroit, resourceful'.

history.meaning: sacrificial or household vessels and implements; functional utility
possessing talent or aptitude for arts and governance (vs. 無器用 'untalented')
history.stage: Early to Late Middle Japanese (Heian–Muromachi period)

history.meaning: deft, handy, skillful with one's hands, versatile/resourceful in handling tasks

器用.notes: Commonly paired with 手先 (tesaki, 'fingertips'): 手先が器用 (tesaki ga kiyō, 'good with one's hands, dexterous'). Its antonym 不器用 (bukiyō) means both 'clumsy with one's hands' and 'socially awkward / bad at expressing feelings'. Also note 器用貧乏 (kiyōbinbō, 'jack of all trades, master of none').

rootFamily.gloss: jack of all trades and master of none (deft-poor)
vessel, container; caliber/capacity of a person (wago reading)

噴水.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 噴水 (ふんすい 'fountain, jet of water'), combining 噴 (ふん 'spout forth, gush out') + 水 (すい 'water').

history.meaning: water fountain; spouting water

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 噴水

四.etymology: Numeral 四 ('four'), read either with the native Japanese root よ / よん (*yo* 'four', from Old Japanese *yo*, with final nasal *yon* generalized to stay distinct from し 'death') or with the Sino-Japanese borrowing し (from Middle Chinese *sijH* 'four').

history.meaning: the number four
four

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 四
Wiktionary — 四 (よん / し / よ) (Japanese)

四つ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *yotu* (四つ 'four things, four', with expressive gemination よっつ in Middle and Modern Japanese), composed of the native numeral root よ- (四 *yo* 'four') + general counter suffix -つ (*-tu*).

history.meaning: four
four (general counter)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 四つ

四テーブル.etymology: Hybrid numeral-noun compound 四テーブル (よんテーブル 'four tables'), combining numeral 四 (よん 'four') + English loanword テーブル (*table*).

history.meaning: four tables

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — テーブル

四億.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) numerical compound formed from 四 (yo- / shi, 'four', here read with the native Japanese kun'yomi stem yo- > yon- via nasal insertion by analogy with 三 san, rather than Sino-Japanese shi which is avoided due to homophony with 死 shi 'death') and 億 (oku, 'one hundred million, 10^8', from Middle Chinese *'ik, originally 'fullness, peace of mind, a vast myriad-fold number'). In the East Asian myriad-based (万進法, manshinhō) grouping by powers of 10^4, 1 億 equals 10,000 万 (10^4 × 10^4 = 10^8), so 四億 is 4 × 100,000,000 = 400 million.

history.meaning: four + vast number (100,000 in ancient texts, standardized as 10^8 in myriad-scale arithmetic)
four hundred million (400,000,000) in standard Japanese myriad-group numeration (established in Jinkōki, 1627)

四億.notes: Always pronounced よんおく (yon'oku), never *shioku. When converting between Japanese 億 (10^8) and English 'million' (10^6), remember that 1 億 = 100 million, so 四億 = 400 million.

天気予報.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese compound 天気予報 (てんきよほう), pairing 天気 ('weather', literally 'sky energy') with 予報 ('advance report, forecast').
天気予報.notes: Coined in the Meiji meteorological service and used daily in broadcasts and conversation.

天職.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 天 (ten, from Middle Chinese *then, 'heaven, supreme cosmos') and 職 (shoku, from Middle Chinese *tsjik, 'office, duty, post'). In Classical Chinese (such as Mencius and Xunzi), it denoted the cosmic duty of heaven or the ruler's mandate; in modern Japanese it was repurposed to translate the Protestant and Western concept of a divine 'vocation' or lifelong calling.

history.meaning: the work of Heaven; ruler's sacred mandate
divinely ordained calling; ideal lifelong profession or vocation

天職.notes: Homophonous with 転職 (tenshoku, 'changing jobs'), creating a frequent and ironic pun in workplace conversations; both share heiban [0] pitch accent.

太い.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *puto₁si* (太し, 'thick, stout, grand, sacredly auspicious'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: thick; stout; grand
thick; fat; deep (of a voice); bold

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 太い

太っ腹.etymology: Colloquial compound formed from the geminated stem ふとっ- (from 太い 'thick, big') + はら (腹, 'belly, gut, spirit, disposition'), literally 'big-bellied' in the figurative sense of 'magnanimous, generous, big-hearted'.

history.meaning: bold-spirited; generous; magnanimous
generous; big-hearted; lavish

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 太っ腹

太陽.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 太陽 (taiyō), from Classical Chinese 太陽 ('supreme yang; the sun', in contrast to 太陰 'supreme yin; the moon').

history.meaning: supreme yang energy; the sun
the sun

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 太陽

失う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese usinapu, derived from the intransitive verb 失す (usu, modern useru, 'to vanish, disappear, pass away') plus the iterative or transitive verbal suffix *-napu (similar to 商う akinau or 養う yashinau). Orthographically represented via kun'yomi by the kanji 失 ('to lose, let slip').

history.meaning: to cause to vanish, be deprived of, lose
to lose, miss, be bereaved of
to lose, part with, be deprived of

失う.notes: More formal and literary than なくす (nakusu); while nakusu is preferred for misplacing everyday objects (like keys), ushinau is used for abstract, irreversible, or weighty losses (life, trust, consciousness, opportunity).

失くす.etymology: Transitive godan verb *nakusu* ('to lose, misplace, get rid of'), formed from the adverbial stem なく of ない (無い, 'nonexistent, gone') + transitive verbalizer -す (written with 失 by semantic association with 'losing').

history.meaning: cause to disappear; do away with; lose

history.form: 失くす / 無くす (なくす)
history.meaning: lose; misplace; part with

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 無くす

失敗.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound of 失 (shitsu, Middle Chinese *sjit, 'to lose, miss, err') and 敗 (hai, Middle Chinese *bwejH, 'to be defeated, ruined, spoiled'). Notice the sandhi gemination (sokuonbin) where shitsu + hai assimilates to shippai. Originally referred to military defeat and ruin before generalizing to any unsuccessful attempt or blunder.

history.meaning: military defeat, ruin, loss

history.form: しつぱい / しっぱい (shippai)
history.meaning: failure, mistake, falling short of a goal

失敗.notes: Functions as both a noun and a suru-verb (失敗する). Ranges from major career or business collapses down to everyday slips like overcooking a meal or misspeaking.

失望.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) verb-object compound formed from 失 (shitsu, Middle Chinese *sjit, 'to lose, forfeit') and 望 (bou, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese *mjangH, 'to gaze afar, hope, expect'). Literally 'to lose one's hope or expectation', attested since early Chinese dynastic histories and adopted into Japanese for profound letdown or despair.

history.meaning: loss of hope, dashed expectations
losing hope, deep disappointment
disappointment, despair, disillusionment

失望.notes: Stronger and heavier in register than がっかり (gakkari); 失望 conveys serious disillusionment or loss of faith in a person or outcome, whereas gakkari is used for everyday letdowns.

失礼.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 失礼 (shitsurei), from Classical Chinese 失禮 ('to fail in礼/etiquette, commit a breach of manners'); used in Japanese both for 'discourtesy, rudeness' and in polite apologies ('excuse me').

history.meaning: fail in propriety; breach etiquette
rudeness; breach of etiquette; excuse me

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 失礼

奇跡.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 奇 (ki, Middle Chinese *kje, 'strange, marvelous, extraordinary, rare') and 跡 (seki, Middle Chinese *tsjek, 'footprint, trace, vestige, deed'; historically also written 奇蹟). Literally 'marvelous trace' or 'extraordinary deed', used to translate both religious miracles and astonishing strokes of fortune.

history.meaning: extraordinary footprint, wondrous deed or vestige
miracle, wonder, marvel defying common sense

奇跡.notes: Prior to post-WWII script reforms, 奇蹟 was often preferred for supernatural or religious miracles while 奇跡 was used for remarkable human achievements; today 奇跡 is the standard spelling for both.

奇遇.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 奇 (ki, Middle Chinese *kje, 'strange, unexpected, rare') and 遇 (guu, Middle Chinese *ngjuH, 'to meet by chance, encounter'). Originally denoted an unexpected or fateful encounter in classical Chinese prose and poetry, evolving in Japanese into a noun and na-adjective celebrating a surprising coincidence when running into someone or discovering a shared connection.

history.meaning: unexpected encounter, rare fateful meeting
remarkable coincidence, chance meeting

奇遇.notes: Most famously used in the set conversational exclamation 奇遇ですね (Kiguu desu ne!, 'What a coincidence! / Fancy meeting you here!').

契約.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 契約 (keiyaku), from Classical Chinese 契約 ('binding agreement, covenant'), combining 契 ('notched tally, deed, contract') + 約 ('bind, promise').

history.meaning: deed; covenant; formal agreement
contract; agreement

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 契約

契約料.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 契約 (keiyaku, 'contract, agreement, subscription', itself from 契 kei 'notched tally, covenant' + 約 yaku 'bind, promise') and the suffixal noun 料 (ryou, Middle Chinese *ljewH, 'measured grain, material, fee, charge'). Coined in modern commercial and broadcasting Japanese to denote a contract fee, signing fee, or satellite/cable subscription charge.

history.meaning: binding covenant + measured fee/material
contract fee, signing fee, subscription fee

契約料.notes: In the context of satellite broadcasting and telecoms (central to *The Naked Director*), 契約 refers specifically to a customer subscription contract, making 契約料 the initial or recurring subscription fee.

契約見込み.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato (jukujikun/wago-kango) compound combining the kango noun 契約 (keiyaku, 'contract, subscription', from 契 'tally, pledge' + 約 'bind, promise') with the native deverbal noun 見込み (mikomi, nominalization of 見込む mikomu: 見る miru 'to look, see' + 込む komu 'inward, deeply', hence 'looking ahead into, estimating, prospect'). Literally 'projected or anticipated contract sign-ups'.

history.meaning: looking deeply into; expectation, prospect, forecast
projected subscriptions, prospective contract sign-ups

契約見込み.notes: A core sales and business-forecasting term; 見込み客 (mikomikyaku) is the standard term for a 'prospective client' or 'sales lead'.

rootFamily.word: 見込み客 (みこみきゃく)

契約課.etymology: Sino-Japanese administrative compound combining 契約 (keiyaku, 'contract') + 課 (ka, 'administrative section, division, department').

history.meaning: contracts section; contract division

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 契約

奔放.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 奔 (hon, Middle Chinese *pwon, 'to run fast, gallop, rush') and 放 (hou, phonetic assimilation to -pou after moraic nasal ん; Middle Chinese *pjangH, 'to release, let go, unbridled'). Originally evoked the image of surging waters or an unbridled steed galloping freely in classical Chinese literary criticism before describing uninhibited human behavior and artistic style.

history.meaning: galloping unchecked, surging without restraint (of water, horses, or prose)

history.form: ほんぱう -> ほんぽう (honpou)
history.meaning: uninhibited, wild, free-spirited, unconventional

奔放.notes: Frequently appears in the four-character idiom 自由奔放 (jiyuu-honpou, 'free and uninhibited') or 奔放な生き方 ('a free-spirited lifestyle'); Note the rendaku/sequential p-sound change (hon + hou -> honpou).

rootFamily.gloss: free and uninhibited, wild and free
rootFamily.word: 自由奔放 (じゆうほんぽう)

奥.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *o₂ku* ('interior, inner depths, far back'), attested in the Man'yōshū; contrasted with はし (端, 'edge') or おもて (表, 'front').

history.meaning: deep interior; innermost part
inner part; back; depths

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 奥

奥さん.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) spatial noun 奥 (oku, from Old Japanese *oku, 'innermost part, deep interior of a house or mountain') combined with the polite titular suffix さん (-san, shortened phonological reduction of 様 -sama, 'appearance, direction, honorable person'). Historically, aristocratic and samurai wives resided in the private inner quarters (奥 oku) of the estate, so referring to 'the person of the inner quarters' became the standard polite metonym for another household's wife.

history.meaning: deep interior, innermost private quarters of a residence
lady of the inner quarters; polite term for a married woman or another's wife

奥さん.notes: Used exclusively for someone else's wife or a married woman in the neighborhood; never use 奥さん to refer to your own wife (use 妻 tsuma or 家内 kanai instead).

rootFamily.gloss: madam, someone else's wife (more formal honorific)
inner palace quarters of Edo Castle

rootFamily.word: 奥義 (おうぎ / おくぎ)

奥手.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound of 奥 (oku, 'deep, late, behind', cognate with 遅い osoi / 後れる okureru 'to be late') and 手 (te, 'hand, kind, type, crop variety'). Originally an agricultural term written 晩稲 or 奥手 (okute) denoting late-ripening rice varieties (contrasted with 早稲 wase, early-ripening rice, and 中手 nakate, mid-season rice). By metaphorical extension in the Edo period, it came to describe a late bloomer or someone bashful and slow to mature in romance and sexuality.

history.meaning: late-ripening rice crop variety
late bloomer; person who is shy or uninitiated in romance and sex

morphemes.meaning: hand, type, variety, person characterized by (-te)

奥手.notes: Its direct antonym in both agriculture and romance is 早熟 (soujuku) or the native word 早稲 / 早手 (wase, 'precocious, early bloomer'). Functions as both a noun and a na-adjective (奥手な人).

奥様.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) honorific compound uniting 奥 (oku, Old Japanese *oku, 'deep interior, inner private quarters of a noble house') and 様 (sama, Old Japanese *sama, 'shape, manner, direction toward', used as a deferential euphemism to avoid naming a high-ranking person directly). Originally restricted in the Muromachi and Edo periods to wives of daimyo and high-ranking samurai before broadening in modern Japanese to a polite, upscale form of address for any married woman or female client.

history.meaning: noble lady residing in the inner quarters of a daimyo or high samurai household
madam; high-register honorific for another person's wife or a married female customer

奥様.notes: Higher in register and deference than 奥さん (okusan); standard in hospitality, luxury retail, and formal social settings when addressing or referring to a client's or superior's wife.

rootFamily.gloss: young lady, daughter of a good family

奪う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese ubapu ('to snatch away by force, plunder, strip'). Likely derived from a pre-Old Japanese root *uba- with the transitive/iterative verbal suffix *-pu (compare 失う ushinau < usinapu). Written via kun'yomi with the kanji 奪, whose original Chinese seal script depicted a bird escaping from a hand (隹 + 又/寸), signifying 'to let slip' before inverting in Chinese to mean 'to seize by force'.

history.meaning: to snatch away by force, plunder, strip
to rob, seize, captivate (the heart or eyes)
to snatch, seize, rob, deprive of, fascinate

奪う.notes: Unlike 盗む (nusumu, 'to steal stealthily'), 奪う implies overt, forceful seizure or taking away — and is frequently used figuratively for 'stealing' someone's heart (心を奪う) or attention (目を奪う).

女.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun evolving by phonological reduction from Old Japanese 乎美奈 (womina, 'woman'), itself a compound of the diminutive/endearing prefix 乎 (wo-, 'small, young') and 美奈 (mina, cognate with め me 'female', as preserved in 女神 megami and 乙女 otome). Across the Heian and Kamakura periods, womina underwent syncope and assimilation: womina -> wonna -> onna.

history.meaning: woman, adult female (contrasted with womuna 'old woman' and wotoko 'man')
woman, female lover
woman, female; (colloquial) female lover, mistress

女.notes: Used bare in modern speech, 女 (onna) can sound blunt, earthy, or sexually charged (often meaning 'mistress' or 'my woman' in hardboiled contexts); in polite conversation, 女性 (josei) or 女の人 (onna no hito) is strongly preferred.

女の子.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) phrasal compound consisting of 女 (onna < Old Japanese womina, 'woman, female'), the genitive/attributive particle の (no), and 子 (ko < Old Japanese ko, 'child, young person'). Literally 'female child', lexicalized as a single noun denoting a girl, baby daughter, or (in casual modern usage) an attractive young woman.

history.meaning: female child, young girl
girl, female child; (colloquial) young unmarried woman

女の子.notes: In entertainment and nightlife contexts (such as *The Naked Director*), 女の子 is routinely used by directors and club managers to refer to young adult women in their twenties, not just children.

女体育教師.etymology: Compound noun prefixing native Yamato 女 (onna, 'female, woman') to the Sino-Japanese (kango) occupational title 体育教師 (taiiku kyoushi, 'physical education teacher'). 体育 ('physical education', from 体 tai 'body' + 育 iku 'nurture, educate') was coined in the Meiji era to translate Western gymnastics/PE, and 教師 ('teacher, instructor', from 教 kyou 'teach' + 師 shi 'master, mentor') denotes a school instructor.

history.meaning: bodily cultivation + teaching master (Meiji educational coinage)
female physical education teacher, female gym teacher

女体育教師.notes: Prefixing native 女 (onna-) rather than 女性 (josei-) to a profession carries a pulp, dramatic, or sensationalist nuance (often seen in film titles and adult video tropes, e.g., 女教師 onna-kyoushi), whereas neutral administrative speech uses 女性体育教師.

rootFamily.word: 女教師 (おんなきょうし)

女優.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in the Meiji era from 女 (jo, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *nrjoX, 'woman, female') and 優 (yuu, Middle Chinese *'juw, originally meaning 'actor, entertainer, mime' as in 俳優 haiyuu, before developing the secondary sense ' abundant, superior, gentle'). Created as the female counterpart to 俳優 when women returned to the Japanese stage after the Edo-period ban on female kabuki performers.

history.meaning: court entertainer, comic actor, theatrical performer
female stage or screen actor, actress

morphemes.meaning: actor, theatrical performer (yuu, as in haiyuu)

女優.notes: While 優 most commonly means 'gentle' (優しい yasashii) or 'excellent' (優秀 yuushuu) to modern learners, its oldest etymological meaning in Chinese (a person 人 performing a ritual dance 憂) is literally 'actor'. In recent years, many Japanese media outlets increasingly use 俳優 (haiyuu) gender-neutrally for both men and women.

女同士.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the native Yamato (wago) noun 女 (onna < Old Japanese womina, 'woman') with the Sino-Japanese (kango) relational suffix 同士 (doushi, from 同 dou 'same' + 士 shi 'person, retainer, scholar', historically also written 同志 'comrades sharing the same intent'). Denotes a group consisting exclusively of women or interactions taking place strictly among women.

history.meaning: persons of the same mind, fellow members of the same group or status
women together, exclusively among women, fellow women

女同士.notes: 同士 attaches productively to any noun denoting a category of people to mean 'among themselves / fellow Xs' (e.g., 男同士 otokodoushi 'between men', 恋人同士 koibitodoushi 'between lovers', 親しい者同士 'among close friends').

rootFamily.word: 人間同士 (にんげんどうし)

女帝.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 女 (jo, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *nrjoX, 'female, woman') and 帝 (tei, Middle Chinese *tejH, 'supreme ruler, sovereign, emperor'). Historically designates a female sovereign who reigns in her own right (empress regnant, such as Empress Suiko or Catherine the Great), in strict contrast to 皇后 (kougou, 'empress consort', the wife of an emperor).

history.meaning: female reigning sovereign, empress regnant
empress regnant; (figurative) powerful woman dominating an industry or nightlife district

女帝.notes: In modern Japanese media and pop culture, 女帝 is widely used metaphorically for a formidable, reigning 'queen' of a specific domain (e.g., Ginza nightlife, politics, or entertainment), while 皇后 (kougou) is a reigning emperor's spouse.

女性.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 女性 (josei), from 女 ('woman, female') + 性 ('sex, nature, gender'), used since classical times for the female sex and in modern Japanese as the standard polite noun for 'woman'.

history.form: 女性 (にょしょう / じょせい)
history.meaning: female sex; woman
woman; female

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 女性

女性主導.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) compound uniting 女性 (josei, 'woman, female sex', from 女 jo 'female' + 性 sei 'inborn nature, sex, gender') and 主導 (shudou, 'leadership, taking the initiative', from 主 shu 'master, main, principal' + 導 dou 'guide, lead'). Coined in modern sociological and commercial discourse to describe relationships, projects, or industries where women hold the primary initiative.

history.meaning: female sex/womanhood + principal leadership/guidance

history.form: じょせいしゅどう (josei shudou)
history.meaning: woman-led, female-driven, female-initiated

女性主導.notes: Often modified with の (女性主導の...) to describe everything from progressive corporate governance and consumer trends to romantic or sexual dynamics where the woman takes the lead.

女性像.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 女性 (josei, 'woman, womanhood', from 女 jo 'female' + 性 sei 'nature, sex') and the suffixal noun 像 (zou, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese *zjangX, 'resemblance, carved figure, statue, mental image'). Literally 'statue or image of a woman', used both concretely in art history for female portraits/sculptures and abstractly in sociology for a society's 'ideal or conceptual image of womanhood'.

history.meaning: woman/female + carved figure or mental likeness
female figure (in art); societal image or ideal of womanhood

morphemes.meaning: statue, portrait, conceptual image or ideal (-zou)

女性像.notes: The suffix -像 (-zou) is highly productive in Japanese for abstract ideals or archetypes, such as 理想像 (risouzou, 'ideal image'), 人間像 (ningenzou, 'view/portrayal of humanity'), and リーダー像 ('ideal leader profile').

rootFamily.gloss: ideal image, model, conception of the ideal

女神.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound uniting the bound archaic prefix 女 (me-, from Old Japanese me 'female, woman', as opposed to wo- 'male') and 神 (kami -> -gami with rendaku sequential voicing, from Old Japanese kami2 'deity, spirit, sacred power'). Literally 'female deity'. An alternative formal Sino-Japanese reading じょしん (joshin) also exists in literary contexts, but めがみ (megami) is the universal everyday reading.

history.form: めかみ / めがみ (mekami / megami)
history.meaning: female Shinto deity, goddess
goddess (in mythology); muse, adored female benefactor or idol

女神.notes: Notice that 女 is read with its ancient bound kun'yomi め (me) rather than おんな (onna), and 神 undergoes rendaku voicing from kami to gami. Famous examples include 自由の女神 (Jiyuu no Megami, 'Statue of Liberty', lit. 'Goddess of Liberty').

rootFamily.gloss: male deity, god (archaic bound prefix wo- + kami)

好き.etymology: Nominal and na-adjectival form derived from the continuative stem of the Old Japanese verb すく (好く, 'to set one's heart on, be fond of, fancy').

history.meaning: fondness; devotion to poetry, love, or art
liked; fond of; favorite

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 好き

好き勝手.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) four-character compound pairing 好き (suki, nominalization of the verb 好く suku 'to like, be fond of') with 勝手 (katte, originally 台所 'kitchen' from 粮手 kate-te 'provisions-side', or 勝つ手 'the winning/favorable hand in archery', which evolved in the Edo period to mean 'one's own convenience, doing as one pleases'). Together, 好き勝手 intensifies the sense of acting purely out of personal whim and self-indulgence without regard for others.

history.meaning: kitchen side of a house; one's own convenience or familiarity
doing whatever one likes, acting selfishly at one's own whim

好き勝手.notes: Almost always carries a critical or exasperated tone when describing someone else's behavior (e.g., 好き勝手なことを言う 'to say whatever selfish thing one pleases', 好き勝手に生きる 'to live however one wants').

好み.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun formed from the ren'youkei (continuative stem) of the Old Japanese verb 好む (konomu, 'to prize, favor, take pleasure in, choose'), written with the kanji 好 ('fond of, pleasing'). While 好き (suki) expresses immediate emotional attraction or affection, 好み (konomi) denotes cultivated taste, aesthetic preference, or personal inclination.

history.meaning: finding pleasure in, aesthetic preference, favored choice
personal taste, preference, liking, type (of person or style)

好み.notes: Used both for aesthetic/culinary tastes (お好み焼き okonomiyaki, literally 'grilled as you like it') and romantic types (彼女は僕の好みだ 'She is my type').

rootFamily.gloss: to like, prefer, be fond of

rootFamily.word: お好み焼き (おこのみやき)

好待遇.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound prefixing 好 (kou, Middle Chinese *xawH, 'good, favorable, advantageous') to 待遇 (taiguu, 'treatment, reception, remuneration', from 待 tai 'wait upon, treat, entertain' + 遇 guu 'encounter, receive, treat'). Literally 'favorable treatment', widely used in modern Japanese labor and recruitment contexts to mean generous pay, perks, and working conditions.

history.meaning: manner of receiving and treating a guest or subordinate; rank and pay
generous treatment, attractive salary and benefits package

好待遇.notes: A staple buzzword in Japanese job recruitment ads (求人広告), where 高収入・好待遇 ('high income, generous benefits/treatment') is frequently used to attract applicants—including in the nightlife and adult entertainment recruitment depicted in *The Naked Director*.

cognates.meaning: in good form, doing well (borrowed from Japanese)

好調.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 好 (kou, Middle Chinese *xawH, 'good, favorable') and 調 (chou, Middle Chinese *dew, 'harmony, musical tone, rhythm, condition', clipped from 調子 choushi 'tune, tempo, physical or business condition'). Literally 'good rhythm/condition', describing a person, athlete, or business enterprise performing smoothly and at peak momentum.

history.meaning: favorable + musical tone / bodily or operational rhythm
in good form, going strong, brisk, thriving (of sales, health, or performance)

morphemes.meaning: tone, rhythm, condition (chou, clipped from choushi)

好調.notes: Its direct antonym is 不調 (fuchou, 'slump, bad form, out of order') or 低調 (teichou, 'sluggish, low-key'); often amplified as 絶好調 (zekkouchou, 'in absolute peak form').

rootFamily.gloss: in absolute peak form, firing on all cylinders
rootFamily.word: 絶好調 (ぜっこうちょう)

妙.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and na-adjective 妙 (myō), from Middle Chinese 妙 (*mjiewH*, 'wondrous, subtle, exquisite'). From Buddhist 'wondrous, beyond ordinary comprehension', it developed the colloquial sense 'strange, curious, peculiar'.

history.meaning: subtle; marvelous; profound
wondrous excellence; mystery
strange; odd; curious; exquisite skill

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 妙

cognates.meaning: to compromise, come to terms (borrowed from Japanese)

妥協.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 妥 (da, Middle Chinese *thwaX, 'secure, settled, peaceful, appropriate', composed of 爪 'hand' over 女 'woman') and 協 (kyou, Middle Chinese *xjep, 'harmonize, unite forces, agree', featuring 十/劦 'three strengths working together'). Coined or popularized in Meiji-era Japan to translate Western diplomatic and political 'compromise' (settling a dispute by mutual concession), and subsequently re-borrowed into modern Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: calm settlement + mutual agreement/harmony
compromise, meeting halfway, settling for less than the ideal

妥協.notes: In Japanese work and artistic culture, 妥協しない (dakyou shinai, 'refusing to compromise / uncompromising craftsmanship') is a high compliment, whereas 妥協点を探る (dakyouten o saguru, 'to look for a point of compromise') is standard in negotiations.

姉妹.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound (dvandva) pairing 姉 (shi, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *tsijX, 'older sister') and 妹 (mai, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *mwojH, 'younger sister'). Both characters combine the semantic radical 女 ('woman') with phonetic components (市 and 未 respectively). Together they denote female siblings collectively ('sisters').

history.meaning: older sister and younger sister; female siblings
sisters (collective Sino-Japanese reading); compare native kun'yomi あねいもうと (ane-imouto)

姉妹.notes: Used attributively for institutional or commercial pairings, such as 姉妹都市 (shimai toshi, 'sister cities'), 姉妹校 (shimaikou, 'sister schools'), and 姉妹品 (shimaihin, 'companion product'). Note the homophone 仕舞い (shimai, 'end, finish').

始まり.etymology: Deverbal noun from the continuative stem of はじまる (始まる, 'to begin, start').

history.meaning: beginning; origin; inception
beginning; start; origin

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 始まり

始まる.etymology: Intransitive godan verb *hajimaru* ('to begin, start'), attested from Old Japanese, derived from the root of はじめ/はじむ (始む, 'to begin') + intransitive suffix *-aru*.

history.meaning: begin; originate; commence
begin; start; open

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 始まる

始める.etymology: Transitive ichidan verb *hajimeru* ('to begin, start, initiate'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade はじむ (始む), cognate with はし (端, 'tip, first edge').

history.meaning: initiate; begin; do for the first time
start; begin; open

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 始める

委員会.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) institutional compound coined in Meiji Japan by suffixing 会 (kai, Middle Chinese *hwojH, 'meeting, assembly, association') to 委員 (iin, 'committee member, commissioner, delegate', from 委 i 'entrust, delegate' + 員 in 'member, official, personnel'). Created to translate Western parliamentary, regulatory, and corporate 'committees' or 'commissions', and later exported across the Sinosphere.

history.meaning: assembly of delegated commissioners or members
committee, commission, regulatory board

委員会.notes: Applies across all registers from student councils (生徒会委員会) to national regulatory bodies like the Fair Trade Commission (公正取引委員会) or industry ethics boards such as ビデ倫 (the video ethics commission central to *The Naked Director*).

姿.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *sugata* ('bodily form, figure, appearance'), attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: bodily figure; shape; appearance
figure; form; appearance; posture

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 姿

威勢.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Middle Chinese 威勢 (MC 'jwij syejH), combining 威 (i, 'majesty, awe-inspiring power, intimidation') and 勢 (sei, 'force, momentum, vigour'). Originally denoting imperial or martial authority in classical Chinese, in Japanese it broadened in vernacular usage to mean spirited vigour, bravado, or lively bluster.

history.meaning: awesome power, imperial or military authority
authority, influence, imposing power
high spirits, vigour, bluster, swagger

威勢.notes: Most frequently heard in the set phrase 威勢がいい (isei ga ii, 'lively, energetic, full of bravado'), often describing bustling market vendors or someone talking big.

威圧的.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) adjectival noun formed from the compound 威圧 (iatsu, 'coercion, intimidation') plus the suffix 的 (-teki, '-like, -ic'). 威圧 combines Middle Chinese-derived 威 (i, 'awe, majesty, threat') and 圧 (atsu, simplified from 壓, 'press down, crush, suppress'), literally 'crushing through awe-inspiring force'.

history.meaning: suppressing or overpowering others through authority or force
intimidating, coercive, overbearing in manner

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix (-ic, -like, having the quality of)

威圧的.notes: Functions as a na-adjective (威圧的な態度, 'an intimidating attitude'); describes an overbearing presence that pressures others without necessarily using physical violence.

嫁さん.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun 嫁 (yome, 'bride, daughter-in-law, wife') followed by the polite hypocoristic suffix さん (-san). Old Japanese yome1 is traditionally analyzed as a compound of 吉 (yo-, 'good, auspicious') and 女 (me1, 'woman'), originally referring to a newlywed woman entering a household; the kanji 嫁 (Middle Chinese kaeH, 'woman marrying into a family') was applied via semantic matching (jukujikun/kun'yomi).

history.meaning: bride, young woman entering a family by marriage
daughter-in-law, bride, wife
wife, bride (colloquial and familiar)

嫁さん.notes: In colloquial speech (especially in western Japan and working-class registers), husbands often refer to their own wife as うちの嫁さん (uchi no yomesan), though younger speakers sometimes find 嫁 patriarchal because of its literal 'woman entering the household' kanji.

rootFamily.gloss: marrying into a family, marriage of a bride

嫌.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) word いや (iya, 'reluctant, unpleasant, disagreeable; no'), derived from the stem of the Old Japanese verb いやぶ (iyabu) or related to the exclamation of refusal いな / いや (ina / iya). Originally spelled with phonetic or semantic kanji such as 否 or 厭, in modern orthography it is standardly written with 嫌 (originally a Sino-Japanese character meaning 'suspect, dislike, resent').

history.meaning: exclamation of refusal or reluctance; unwilling
disagreeable, detestable, tiresome
unpleasant, disliked, offensive; no!

嫌.notes: Read iya as a standalone na-adjective or interjection of refusal ('No way!'), whereas the same kanji 嫌 followed by okurigana 嫌い (kirai) means 'to dislike/hate'.

rootFamily.gloss: to feel disgusted by, to show reluctance

嫌がらせ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun formed as the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 嫌がらせる (iyagaraseru, 'to make someone feel disgusted or annoyed'), which in turn is the causative form of the verb 嫌がる (iyagaru, 'to show dislike, to feel repulsed'), derived from the adjective 嫌 (iya, 'unpleasant, unwelcome') + verbalizing suffix -garu ('to show signs of feeling') + causative -seru.

history.meaning: to outward-display reluctance or aversion
act done deliberately to annoy or spite someone
harassment, spiteful act, bullying tactic

morphemes.meaning: verbalizer indicating outward display of emotion (-garu)

嫌がらせ.notes: Covers everything from petty spiteful pranks (like silent phone calls) to systematic workplace or neighborhood harassment; literally 'making someone feel grossed out/annoyed'.

rootFamily.gloss: to dislike openly, to hate, to recoil from

嬉しい.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *uresi* (嬉し, 'joyful, delightful, pleasing'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; likely built on the emotional root *ura-* (裏・心, 'inner heart').

history.meaning: delightful; glad; happy
happy; glad; pleased

history.meaning: child; offspring; young person

history.meaning: children; one's offspring
child; children

字.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun 字 (ji), from Middle Chinese 字 (*dziH*, 'written character, graph, courtesy name'), originally derived from 'to bear a child under a roof' > 'breed,衍生/derive characters'.

history.meaning: written character; script; style name
character; letter; handwriting

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 字

存在.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 存在 (MC dzwon dzojX), composed of 存 (son, 'survive, remain, preserve, be present') and 在 (zai, 'be located at, dwell, exist'). Already attested in Classical Chinese prose to mean 'remaining alive or present', it was repurposed and popularized in Meiji-era philosophical translations to render German Dasein / Existenz and English 'existence'.

history.meaning: to remain alive, to be present or extant
subsisting, remaining in place
existence, philosophical being, felt presence

存在.notes: Beyond abstract philosophy, 存在 often refers to a person's social weight or role, as in 大きな存在 (ōki na sonzai, 'an important figure/someone who means a lot to me') or 存在感 (sonzaikan, 'charisma/presence').

孤立.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical and Middle Chinese 孤立 (MC ku lip), combining 孤 (ko, 'fatherless child, orphan; solitary, alone') and 立 (ritsu, 'stand upright, establish'). Literally 'standing alone like an orphan without support', used in Chinese historical texts for a ruler or official lacking allies, and in modern Japanese for social, political, or physical isolation.

history.meaning: standing alone without kinship or political allies
isolation, being cut off from support or society

孤立.notes: Used with する (koritsu suru, 'to become isolated'); carries the nuance of being stranded without allies or cut off from a group rather than peaceful solitude.

rootFamily.gloss: solitary island; being stranded without help (孤島 / 孤立無援)

学ぶ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb 学ぶ (manabu, 'to learn, to study'), derived from Old Japanese まねぶ (manebu, 'to imitate, to mimic, to study by copying a master'), which is built on the noun root まね (mane, 'imitation, mimicry') plus the verbalizing suffix -bu. The vowel shift from manebu to manabu occurred during the Middle Japanese period via vowel assimilation, reflecting the traditional East Asian view of learning as emulation of a model.

history.meaning: to imitate, to copy, to learn by emulating a model
to study, to learn deeply
to learn, to study (academic or life lessons)

学ぶ.notes: Doublet of 真似る (maneru, 'to imitate'); compared to 習う (narau, 'to take lessons/practice from a teacher'), 学ぶ sounds slightly more elevated and encompasses self-directed intellectual inquiry or learning from experience.

学園祭.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) three-morpheme compound coined in modern Japan from 学園 (gakuen, 'academy, school campus', from 学 'study, learning' + 園 'garden, park, grounds') and 祭 (sai, 'ritual festival, celebration'). Modeler on older seasonal and shrine festivals, the term denotes the annual student-organized open-house cultural festival held at Japanese universities and high schools.

history.meaning: garden of learning; school campus or educational institution
annual university or school campus cultural festival

学園祭.notes: Often abbreviated in casual student slang to 学祭 (gakusai); typically used for university festivals, whereas high school festivals are more commonly called 文化祭 (bunkasai).

学校.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 学校 (gakkō), from Classical Chinese 學校 ('school, place of learning'), combining 學 ('study, learn') + 校 ('school building, examine').

history.meaning: institution of learning; school
school

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 学校

学生.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 學生 (MC haewk sraeng), combining 學/学 (gaku, 'study, learning, school') and 生 (sei, 'be born, live; scholar, disciple, youth'). In medieval Japan it was also read gakushō to denote Buddhist novice monks studying at monastic complexes like Mount Hiei, before standardizing as gakusei in the Meiji era for secular school and university students.

history.meaning: disciple studying at an academy, scholar-in-training
monastic student or scholar-monk at a Buddhist temple
student (especially a university or college student)

学生.notes: Strictly speaking in official Japanese usage, 学生 (gakusei) refers specifically to university/college students, while middle and high schoolers are 生徒 (seito) and elementary pupils are 児童 (jidō), though in everyday speech 学生 covers students broadly.

孫.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *mago₁* (earlier *umago₁*, 'grandchild'), attested in the Wamyō Ruijushō; often analyzed as *uma-* + *ko₁* ('child').

history.meaning: grandchild
grandchild

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 孫

宇宙.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Classical Chinese 宇宙 (MC hjuX drjuwH). Famous from early Daoist and philosophical texts such as the Zhuangzi and Huainanzi, which explicitly define 宇 (u, originally 'eaves of a house') as all four directions plus above and below (three-dimensional space), and 宙 (chū, originally 'ridgepole/roof support') as past, present, and future (all of time) — hence the totality of spacetime, the cosmos, and in modern usage, outer space.

history.meaning: the entirety of spatial extent (宇) and temporal duration (宙); the cosmos
heaven and earth, the whole universe
the universe, the cosmos, outer space

morphemes.meaning: eternity, infinite time from past to future

宇宙.notes: Translates both philosophical/scientific 'the universe' and astronomical 'outer space' (as in 宇宙へ行く, 'to go into space').

宇宙時代.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 宇宙 (uchū, 'cosmos, outer space', from 宇 'all space' + 宙 'all time') and 時代 (jidai, 'era, epoch, age', from 時 'time, season' + 代 'generation, era'). Coined in the late 1950s as a loan translation (calque) of English 'Space Age' following the launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

history.meaning: combining classical 'cosmos' with 'historical epoch'
the Space Age (era of space exploration and satellite technology)

宇宙時代.notes: Evokes the optimistic futuristic ethos of late-Shōwa Japan, when satellite broadcasting and global media began transforming everyday life.

cognates.word: 宇宙空間 / 宇宙空间 (yǔzhòu kōngjiān)

宇宙空間.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound joining 宇宙 (uchū, 'universe, outer space', from 宇 'infinite space' + 宙 'infinite time') and 空間 (kūkan, 'space, room, expanse', from 空 'empty, sky, void' + 間 'interval, space between'). Used to specify physical 'outer space' (the vacuum beyond Earth's atmosphere) as distinct from the abstract philosophical totality of the universe.

history.meaning: three-dimensional physical space (Meiji philosophical/scientific coinage)
outer space, the physical expanse of the cosmos beyond Earth's atmosphere

宇宙空間.notes: While 宇宙 alone can mean 'the universe' (including Earth), 宇宙空間 specifically highlights the physical vacuum of outer space where satellites and astronauts float.

宇宙衛星.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 宇宙 (uchū, 'outer space, cosmos', from 宇 'all space' + 宙 'all time') and 衛星 (eisei, 'satellite', literally 'guarding/attendant star', from 衛 'guard, protect, escort' + 星 'star, celestial body'). 衛星 was coined in early modern East Asian astronomy to translate European 'satellite' (from Latin satelles, 'bodyguard, attendant').

history.meaning: planetary moon ('escort star' orbiting a primary planet)
space satellite (artificial satellite launched into orbit)

宇宙衛星.notes: In everyday media and broadcasting, man-made satellites are also called 人工衛星 (jinkō eisei, 'artificial satellite') or 放送衛星 (hōsō eisei, 'broadcasting satellite', BS).

宇宙開発.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 宇宙 (uchū, 'outer space, universe', from 宇 'space' + 宙 'time') and 開発 (kaihatsu, 'development, exploitation, pioneering', from 開 'open up' + 発 'issue forth, uncover, launch'). Originally 開発 (read kaihotsu in Buddhist texts) meant 'awakening spiritual insight', before shifting in modern Japanese to economic, technological, and aerospace development.

history.meaning: opening up innate Buddhist wisdom or clearing uncultivated land
industrial, technological, or resource development
space development and exploration programs

宇宙開発.notes: Standard institutional term in Japanese for what English often calls 'space exploration' or 'the space program' (e.g., JAXA is 宇宙航空研究開発機構).

守る.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *mamo₂ru* ('to watch closely, guard, protect'), attested in the Man'yōshū, derived from ま- (目, 'eye') + もる (守る, 'to guard, keep watch').

history.meaning: watch over with the eyes; guard; protect
protect; defend; obey (a rule); keep (a promise)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 守る

安い.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *yasusi* (安し・易し, 'peaceful, calm, easy, free from anxiety'). In the Edo period, 'worry-free, easy to obtain' specialized when written 安い to 'inexpensive, cheap'.

history.meaning: peaceful; at ease; easy
cheap; inexpensive; peaceful

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 安い

安すぎる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from the stem 安- (yasu-) of the adjective 安い (yasui, 'inexpensive, cheap; originally peaceful, easy, trouble-free', from Old Japanese yasusi) plus the auxiliary verb すぎる (sugiru, 'to pass beyond, to exceed, to be excessive', from Old Japanese sugu). Literally 'to exceed in cheapness, to be overly cheap'.

history.meaning: easy/tranquil + to pass through or exceed bounds
easy, peaceful; low in price, inexpensive (semantic shift in merchant towns)
to be too cheap, suspiciously or excessively inexpensive

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb meaning 'to exceed, to be too much'

安すぎる.notes: The auxiliary -sugiru attaches directly to any i-adjective stem (dropping the final -i) or verb stem to express excess; 安すぎる often implies that a price is 'too good to be true' or undervalues the product.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass, to exceed, to be too much

安全.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 安全 (anzen), from Classical Chinese 安全 ('safe and whole, free from danger'), combining 安 ('peaceful, secure') + 全 ('whole, intact').

history.meaning: secure and unharmed
safety; security; safe

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 安全

安全だ.etymology: The term '安全だ' (meaning 'safely') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: safely
safely

安全だ.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 安全だ

安全圏.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 安全 (anzen, 'safety, security', from 安 'peaceful, secure, stable' + 全 'whole, intact, complete') and the suffixoid noun 圏 (ken, 'sphere, circle, range, zone', originally Middle Chinese gjuenX 'enclosure for livestock, circle'). Literally 'sphere of intact peace', denoting a physical or metaphorical zone free from danger.

history.meaning: peaceful and completely unharmed; safety
history.stage: Middle Chinese and Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: safe zone, margin of safety (in sports, exams, or business risk)

安全圏.notes: Frequently used figuratively in exams, elections, or business for having a comfortable lead or staying inside one's 'comfort zone' out of harm's way.

安心.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 安 ('peaceful, settled, safe') and 心 ('heart, mind'), literally 'a settled heart'—feeling relieved and free from worry.

history.meaning: peace of mind; relief

安酒.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from the adjective stem 安- (yasu-, 'cheap, low-grade', from 安い yasui) and 酒 (zake, the rendaku voiced form of sake 'rice wine, alcoholic drink', from Old Japanese sake2). Literally 'cheap liquor', with sequential voicing (rendaku) turning sake into -zake to mark a tight compound.

history.meaning: fermented rice beverage, alcoholic drink
inexpensive, low-quality sake or liquor
cheap booze, rotgut liquor

morphemes.meaning: alcohol, sake (voiced from sake via rendaku)

安酒.notes: Note the mandatory rendaku voicing (yasu + sake -> yasuzake); often appears in gritty dramas in phrases like 安酒を煽る (yasuzake o aoru, 'to knock back cheap booze').

完了.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 完了 (kanryō), combining 完 ('complete, whole') + 了 ('finish, bring to a close').

history.meaning: complete; finish entirely
completion; conclusion; perfective aspect

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 完了

完全.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 完全 (kanzen), from Classical Chinese 完全 ('intact, whole, without defect'), combining 完 ('whole, complete') + 全 ('entire, intact').

history.meaning: keep intact; complete and undamaged
complete; perfect; intact

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 完全

完全だ.etymology: The term '完全だ' (meaning 'completely') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: completely
completely

完全だ.notes: A common term in daily use.

完成.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 完成 (kansei), from Chinese 完成 ('to bring to completion, accomplish'), combining 完 ('complete') + 成 ('accomplish, form').

completion; perfection; finishing

完璧.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 完璧 (kanpeki), from a Classical Chinese historical idiom in the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) in which Lin Xiangru returned the priceless He氏 jade disc (璧) intact (完) to the state of Zhao; hence 'flawless, utterly complete'.

history.meaning: return the jade disc whole and unblemished
perfect; flawless; complete

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 完璧

完璧な.etymology: The term '完璧な' (meaning 'perfect') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: perfect
perfect

完璧な.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 完璧な

宗教.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 宗教 (MC tsuwng kjaewH), combining 宗 (shū, 'ancestral temple, lineage, sect, ultimate principle') and 教 (kyō, 'teaching, doctrine'). Originally a Chinese Chan (Zen) Buddhist term denoting the core principle (宗) of the Buddha's verbal teachings (教), it was repurposed by Meiji-era scholars in the 1860s–1870s as a translation of English 'religion' and German 'Religion', and subsequently re-borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: ultimate lineage principle and doctrinal teachings of Buddhism
sectarian Buddhist doctrine or lineage teaching
religion (general category of faith systems)

morphemes.meaning: ancestral shrine, main lineage, sect, ultimate principle

宗教.notes: A classic example of wasei-kango (Japanese-repurposed Sino-vocabulary): before the Meiji era, Japanese had no single umbrella word equating Shinto, Buddhism, and Christianity under the Western category of 'religion'.

cognates.word: 宗教團體 / 宗教团体 (zōngjiào tuántǐ)

宗教団体.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 宗教 (shūkyō, 'religion', from 宗 'sect/ultimate principle' + 教 'teaching') and 団体 (dantai, 'organization, group, body, association', from 団 'round mass, group, corps' + 体 'body, substance'). Used in modern Japanese legal, journalistic, and sociological discourse for organized religious bodies or sects.

history.meaning: organized group or corporate body (Meiji coinage)
religious organization, organized religious group or sect

宗教団体.notes: In Japanese news and drama, 宗教団体 is a neutral-to-formal term (alongside legal 宗教法人, 'religious corporation'), often used by media to refer to new religious movements or cults without naming them directly.

定める.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive verb 定める (sadameru, 'to decide, to establish, to settle, to stipulate'), continuing Classical Japanese さだむ (sadamu, shimo-nidan conjugation), which shares its root sada- ('settled, fixed, certain; prime time') with the intransitive partner 定まる (sadamaru, 'to become settled') and the archaic adjectival noun 定か (sadaka, 'certain, clear'). Written with the semantic kanji 定 ('fix, settle, determine').

history.meaning: to settle disorder, to fix a rule or decision
to establish, to appoint, to determine (shift to ichidan conjugation)
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: to establish (a law or rule), to stipulate, to fix (a goal)

定める.notes: Belongs to a classic Japanese transitivity pair: 定める (sadameru, transitive: 'to establish/set') vs. 定まる (sadamaru, intransitive: 'to be settled/become stable'); also yields the noun 定め (sadame, 'fate, destiny, law').

rootFamily.gloss: to become settled, to be fixed (intransitive)
certain, sure, clear (usually in 定かではない)

定年.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 定 (tei, 'fix, settle, stipulate', Middle Chinese dengH) and 年 (nen, 'year, age, lifespan', Middle Chinese nen). Originally written 停年 (also read teinen, literally 'stopping-work age') in military and bureaucratic regulations of the Meiji era; following post-WWII script reforms placing 停 usage restrictions or preferring simpler characters, 定年 ('fixed/stipulated age') became the standard orthography for mandatory retirement age.

history.meaning: fixed age at which military officers or officials must step down from active duty
mandatory retirement age in corporate or civil employment

定年.notes: Central to the post-war Japanese lifetime employment (終身雇用) system, where salaried workers traditionally worked at one company until reaching 定年 (historically 55, later 60 or 65).

定年後.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 定年 (teinen, 'mandatory retirement age', from 定 'fixed, stipulated' + 年 'year, age') and the temporal suffix 後 (-go, 'after, behind, following', from Middle Chinese huwX). Denotes the period of life following mandatory retirement from a career.

history.meaning: fixed retirement age + temporal suffix 'after'
post-retirement period, life after mandatory retirement

定年後.notes: When 後 attaches as a Sino-Japanese suffix to a kango noun, it is consistently read -go (e.g., 定年後 teinengo, 戦後 sengo, 食後 shokugo), whereas standalone it is read ato or ushiro.

定規.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 定規 (じょうぎ), from 定 ('fix, establish') and 規 ('compass, standard rule').
定規.notes: Originally denoted carpenter's measuring standards before becoming the everyday word for a straightedge ruler.

In Old Japanese, mi2 ('fruit, seed, nut') was phonemically distinct from mi1 ('body, flesh, self', written 身), though the two merged phonetically into mi in Early Middle Japanese and remain closely associated in idioms relating to substance and fullness. Written with the kanji 実 (traditional 實, 'fruit, seed, full, real').

Originally coined in Meiji physics and optics to translate 'real image' (as opposed to 虚像 kyozō, 'virtual image'), it broadened metaphorically in journalism and biography to mean the 'true portrait' or 'unvarnished real self' behind a public persona.

実話.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 実 (jitsu, traditional 實, 'true, factual, real', Middle Chinese zyit) and 話 (wa, 'story, talk, narrative, account', Middle Chinese hwaejH). Literally 'factual narrative', contrasting with fictional tales (作り話 tsukuribanashi or 虚構 kyokō).

In modern Japanese media and publishing, the term shifted from state historiography to "true-life account", "documentary", or gritty "expose" genres in film and adult video.

実際.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango), read jissai, originally a Chinese Buddhist technical term 實際 (Middle Chinese zyit tsjejH) rendering Sanskrit bhutakoti ("the limit of reality" or "ultimate truth/nirvana"). During the Meiji period, the term underwent secular semantic extension to mean empirical "reality", "actual state of affairs", or adverbially "in fact / actually". Notice the gemination (sokuon) where jitsu + sai assimilates to jissai.

実際.notes: Functions widely both as a noun (実際を知る, "to know the reality") and directly as an adverb orwith に (実際に, "actually, in practice").

Originating in Edo-period Kabuki theater terminology, 小道具 referred to handheld or portable stage props carried by actors or placed in rooms, in explicit contrast to 大道具 (odogu, large scenic sets and backdrops). 屋.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) noun and productive suffix, read ya, inherited from Old Japanese ya ("house, roofed building, dwelling"). Written with the kanji 屋 (which in Chinese meant "roof, room, house"). From the late Heian and Kamakura periods onward, 屋 attached to commodities or trades to denote the shop or merchant selling them (e.g., 酒屋 sakaya "sake shop/brewer", 本屋 hon'ya "bookstore"). By the Edo period, it also became a suffix for professional trade names (屋号 yago, used by merchant houses and Kabuki actors) and figuratively a person with a characteristic trait (e.g., 恥ずかしがり屋, "shy person").
