Coined/standardized in Meiji-era Japan to translate English "factory", "plant", or "workshop" during rapid industrialization. It famously has two standard readings in modern Japanese: こうじょう (kojo, full Sino-Japanese kango reading) and こうば (koba, hybrid jubakoyomi reading combining on'yomi ko + kun'yomi ba).

巨峰.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango), read kyoho, literally "giant mountain peak" (from Middle Chinese 巨峰 gjoX phjowng: 巨 "huge, great" + 峰 "mountain peak, summit"). As a grape cultivar, it was bred in 1937 (and trademarked in 1942/1945) by Japanese viticulturist Yasushi Ohinoue at his research institute in Izu, Shizuoka Prefecture, by crossing Ishihara Wase and Centennial grapes; he named the large, dark-purple tetraploid grape 巨峰 in homage to the majestic view of Mount Fuji ("the Giant Peak") visible from his vineyard.

巫女.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) compound noun, read miko, inherited from Old Japanese miko ("child of a god, sacred medium"), formed from the honorific/sacred prefix み- (mi-, written 御/神, referring to deities or the sovereign) + 子 (ko, "child, young woman"). The spelling 巫女 is a mature orthographic borrowing (jukujikun) from Chinese 巫女 ("female shaman, spirit medium", where 巫 depicts shamans dancing to summon spirits). Historically, miko were ecstatic female shamans who entered trances to channel kami or spirits of the dead (口寄せ kuchiyose); since the Meiji restoration's separation of Shinto and shamanism, the term primarily denotes unmarried young women in white kosode and red hakama who assist at Shinto shrines and perform sacred kagura dances.

history.form: みこ (miko, written 御子 / 神子 / 巫女)

In pre-modern Chinese texts (such as the History of the Northern Dynasties), 市民 simply denoted urban market-dwellers in contrast to rural farmers, but during the Meiji period Japanese political theorists and translators repurposed it to render French citoyen, German Bürger, and English citizen as a member of civil society.

Originally a reverent title for supreme dynastic monarchs and sage-rulers in Chinese historiography, in modern Japanese it is widely applied metaphorically to an unrivalled mogul or 'kingpin' dominating a sphere of business or entertainment.

席.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) single-character noun from Middle Chinese 席 (*zjek 'woven straw or reed mat for sitting and sleeping'). The Chinese character depicts fabric/cloth (巾) beneath a shelter/spreading roof (庶 provincial variant). Because ancient East Asians sat on individual woven floor mats rather than raised chairs before the Tang–Song transition, the word naturally underwent metonymic extension from 'sitting mat' to 'one's assigned seat or place', and further to 'a banquet, assembly, or formal occasion'.

常に.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) adverbial phrase formed from the noun 常 (tsune, Old Japanese tune 'an unchanging state, constancy, perpetuity, ordinary custom', possibly related to 綱 tsuna 'continuous rope/line' or 連ぬ tsuranu 'to string together continuously') + the locative/adverbial case particle に (ni). Attested from the earliest 8th-century poetry in the Man'yōshū, where tune denotes permanence in contrast to worldly transience, evolving into the standard high-register adverb for 'always, constantly, at all times'.

常識.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) neologism (wasei-kango) coined in the Meiji era to translate English common sense and French sens commun (ultimately from Aristotle's koinē aisthēsis and Scottish Common Sense philosophy's sensus communis). It combines 常 (jō, Middle Chinese *dzyang 'constant, ordinary, shared, normal') + 識 (shiki, Middle Chinese *syik 'knowledge, cognition, discernment'). After stabilizing in late 19th-century Japanese philosophical and journalistic prose, the compound was borrowed into modern Chinese (chángshí) and Korean (sangsik).

history.meaning: constant/ordinary + knowledge/discernment (Classical Chinese roots)

常連.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound formed in the Edo period from 常 (jō, 'always, constant, usual', from Middle Chinese *dʑɨɐŋ) and 連 (ren, shortened from 連中 renjū, 'company, group of companions, habitués'). Borrowed in the Nara and Heian periods for court and monastic headgear, 帽子 broadened in the Meiji era to become the universal everyday word for all Western and Japanese hats and caps.

平和.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical Chinese 平和 (Middle Chinese *bjaeng hwa), combining 平 (hei, MC *bjaeng 'level, flat, even, pacified') + 和 (wa, MC *hwa 'harmony, mildness, tuning in accord'). In Classical Chinese (such as the莊子 Zhuangzi and 史記 Shiji), 平和 described a balanced, mild temperament, climate, or musical harmony. During the Meiji era, Japanese diplomats, Christian translators, and legal scholars standardized 平和 as the equivalent of Western peace (both civic tranquility and the absence of war between states).

平気.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical Chinese 平氣 (Middle Chinese *bjaeng khj+jH), composed of 平 (hei, MC *bjaeng 'level, even, calm, unruffled') + 気 (traditional 氣, ki, MC *khj+jH 'vital breath, pneuma, spirit, emotional disposition'). In traditional Chinese medical treatises such as the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon), 平氣 denoted the normal, balanced respiration of a healthy person free of fever or agitation. In Japanese it shifted from 'calmness of breath and spirit' to 'unbothered composure, nonchalance, feeling fine despite adversity'.

history.meaning: even, unhurried respiration; balanced vital energy and calm temperament
equanimity, unruffled composure of mind in the face of danger or surprise

rootFamily.gloss: calmness, composure, presence of mind (higher register synonym)
vital energy, vigor, good health, high spirits

In the Meiji Enlightenment, Fukuzawa Yukichi and legal scholars repurposed this Buddhist term to translate Western social and legal equality.

social, political, and legal equality; treating all people equally without discrimination

evenness, uniformity, equal distribution (read with kan-on kintō)
equality of the sexes, gender equality

year; age; time of life

The system of proclaiming auspicious regnal era names was inaugurated in 140 BCE by Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty (with 建元 Jiànyuán) and formally adopted by the Japanese imperial court in 645 CE with 大化 (Taika), continuing unbroken today under the legal synonym 元号 (gengō).

Formed in 20th-century Japanese business terminology as a concise compound for 年間の商業売上高 ('annual commercial turnover'), denoting the total gross sales revenue generated by a company or merchant over a single fiscal or calendar year.

年商.notes: A classic trap in Japanese media and dramas like *The Naked Director*: boasting of 年商100億円 ('annual revenue of 10 billion yen') sounds massive, but 年商 is gross top-line revenue (売上高 uriagedaka), not net profit (利益 rieki) or personal income (年収 nenshū)!

commerce, trade, business deal; commercial transaction

年配.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 年配 (nenpai, originally written 年輩), from 年 ('year, age') + 輩 ('generation, peer group, cohort'). From 'approximate age bracket', it specialized to 'advanced in years, elderly'.

弁償.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 辨償 (Middle Chinese *bjenX dzyang), combining 弁 (ben, functioning here as the postwar Japanese shinjitai graphic merger replacing traditional 辨, MC *bjenX 'to distinguish, manage, settle an obligation, prepare, defray', originally written with the knife radical 刀 between two 辛) + 償 (shō, MC *dzyang 'to repay a debt, make restitution, compensate for value lost'). Together they mean 'to settle and repay a loss', specifically reimbursing someone in money or kind for damaged or lost property.

弁償.notes: Note how postwar Japanese 弁 merged three distinct traditional characters (辨 'distinguish/settle' in 弁償, 辯 'argue/speech' in 弁護士 lawyer, and 瓣 'petal/valve' in 花弁); in everyday usage, 弁償する is for personal/practical replacement ('You broke it, you pay for it!'), whereas 賠償 (baishō) is for large-scale legal/court-ordered damages or war reparations.

弁当売り.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese + native Yamato compound combining 弁当 (bentō 'portable boxed meal') + 売り (uri, the nominalized ren'yōkei stem of the native verb 売る uru, Old Japanese uru 'to sell'). The word 弁当 itself derives from Southern Song and Yuan vernacular Chinese 便當 (biàndāng 'convenient, handy, expedient'), borrowed into medieval Japanese as 便当 (bentō) for 'something convenient' and later written with ateji 弁当 (using 弁 for 辨 'to prepare/arrange' + 当 'fitting/provision') as it narrowed during the Azuchi–Momoyama period (under Oda Nobunaga's castle distributions and portable lacquered tea-gathering boxes) to mean a single-portion boxed meal. Adding 売り yields an itinerant boxed-lunch vendor—an iconic fixture of Japanese railway stations (ekiben hawkers) and baseball stadiums.

history.meaning: convenient, handy, opportune, easily arranged

history.form: 便当 → 辨当 / 弁当 (bentō)

引き取る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb (hikitoru), formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 引く (hiku, Old Japanese piku, 'to pull, draw back, withdraw') and 取る (toru, Old Japanese toru, 'to take, receive, claim into one's custody'). 引っかかる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb (hikkakaru) showing geminate consonant assimilation (sokuonbin) of 引き掛かる (hikikakaru). From the literal physical sense of getting snagged on a hook, thorn, or obstacle, it developed figurative meanings of falling for a scam/trap, getting caught in an inspection, or nagging at one's mind.

影響.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) metaphorical compound (eikyō), borrowed from Classical Chinese 影響 (Middle Chinese *'jangX xjangX), combining 影 (ei, Middle Chinese *'jangX, 'shadow cast by light') and 響 (kyō, Middle Chinese *xjangX, 'echo, reverberating sound'). In pre-Qin texts such as the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents, 'Counsels of the Great Yu': 惠迪吉，從逆凶，惟影響, 'Follow the right path and it is auspicious; follow the perverse and it is ominous—just like shadow and echo') and *Xunzi*, the pair functioned as a vivid simile for an instantaneous, inevitable response: as a shadow follows a body and an echo answers a sound. 役.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun 役 (yaku / eki), from Middle Chinese 役 (*jwek*, 'corvée labor, military service, official duty'); in Japanese extended to 'assigned office, role, dramatic part, usefulness'.

役者.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (yakusha), formed in Japan from 役 (yaku, Middle Chinese *ywek, originally 'border-guard corvée, official duty, assigned service', later 'dramatic role or character part') and the agentive suffix 者 (sha, Middle Chinese *tsyaeX, 'person who performs or embodies'). In medieval Japanese (Kamakura–Muromachi periods), 役者 referred to officials assigned to liturgical or administrative duties at temples and ceremonies, then narrowed in Noh, Kyōgen, and Edo-period Kabuki theater to performers who played a specific dramatic role (役), becoming the standard word for 'actor'.

彼.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese distal demonstrative *kare* (彼, 'that thing or person over there', formed from distal root *ka-* + suffix *-re*). Under Western translation influence in the Meiji era, it specialized as the third-person masculine pronoun 'he' (and 'boyfriend').

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 彼ら

彼氏.etymology: Early-modern Japanese hybrid compound (kareshi), combining the native Yamato (wago) distal pronoun 彼 (kare, Old Japanese kare, 'that thing/person over there', used since the late Meiji era to translate English 'he/him' and by extension 'male lover') with the Sino-Japanese honorific/courtesy title 氏 (shi, Middle Chinese *dzyeX, 'clan name; Mister, gentleman'). Coined in Taishō- and early Shōwa-era urban youth and literary slang as a playfully respectful or teasing way to refer to a woman's male romantic partner ('Mr. Him'), it rapidly lexicalized into the everyday word for 'boyfriend'.

history.meaning: that one over there; third-person pronoun ('he')

industrial or commercial worker engaged in an enterprise's operations
employee, worker, staff member (both full-time and part-time)

従業員.notes: An umbrella labor term: unlike 社員 (shain, which usually implies a regular corporate member/full-time employee of a 会社), 従業員 (jūgyōin) covers everyone working at a business or shop, including part-timers and shop floor staff (e.g., 従業員専用 'Employees Only').

得る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb (eru or uru), descending from Old Japanese 得 (conclusive form *u*, attributive form *uru*, continuative form *e-*), a monomorphemic root meaning 'to acquire, take into possession, or succeed in doing'. In Classical Japanese it belonged to the lower bigrade (shimo nidan) conjugation (*e / e / u / uru / ure / eyo*); during the transition to Modern Japanese, the attributive *uru* was reshaped into the standard ichidan verb える (*eru*), though the classical conclusive/attributive うる (*uru*) survives in formal prose and in the potential auxiliary suffix -得る (*-eru* / *-uru*, 'can, be possible to').

to obtain, gain, win; auxiliary of possibility (-uru / -eru)

history.meaning: to gain, obtain, acquire; (as suffix -える/-うる) to be possible to

morphemes.meaning: gain, obtain, acquire; be able to

得る.notes: As an independent transitive verb ('to obtain, gain', e.g., 利益を得る 'gain profit'), it is almost always pronounced *eru*; when attached to a verb stem to mean 'possible to ~' (e.g., あり得る 'possible/conceivable'), the dictionary form may be read either *ariuru* (more literary) or *arieru* (more conversational), while conjugated forms like あり得ない (*arienai*, 'impossible / no way!') are always *-e-*.

得意.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound (tokui), borrowed from Classical Chinese 得意 (Middle Chinese *tok 'jijH), composed of 得 (toku, Middle Chinese *tok, 'to obtain, attain, get') and 意 (i, Middle Chinese *'jijH, 'mind, wish, intention, inner thought'). In classical Chinese texts (*Zhuangzi*, *Shiji*, and Tang poetry), 得意 meant 'attaining one's heart's desire' and hence feeling elated, triumphant, or self-satisfied. In Japanese, alongside the sense 'proud/elated' (得意になる), it developed two distinctive secondary meanings: (1) one's strong suit or specialty (where one feels confident and at ease), and (2) in Edo merchant usage, a regular patron or valued customer (お得意様, o-tokui-sama) whose goodwill the merchant has won.

history.meaning: having attained one's wish; satisfied, elated, in one's element
self-satisfaction, pride; a merchant's regular patron (お得意)
history.stage: Medieval to Early Modern Japanese (Edo period)

history.meaning: one's strong suit, skilled at; proud/triumphant; regular customer (with お-)

得意.notes: Beware the false friend with Mandarin Chinese 得意 (déyì, 'smug/proud') and notice its three distinct Japanese uses: (1) 料理が得意だ ('skilled at cooking', antonym 苦手 nigate), (2) 得意満面 ('beaming with pride/triumph'), and (3) お得意先 ('valued client / regular customer').

得策.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) strategic compound (tokusaku), borrowed from Literary Chinese 得策 (Middle Chinese *tok tshrek), formed from 得 (toku, Middle Chinese *tok, 'to obtain, hit upon the right thing; advantageous, profitable') and 策 (saku, Middle Chinese *tshrek, originally 'bamboo riding whip or divination slip', hence 'inscribed plan, stratagem, policy'). Literally 'an advantageous or well-chosen stratagem', contrasted with 失策 (shissaku, 'blunder, misguided policy').

history.meaning: hitting upon the right stratagem; an advantageous policy
sound statecraft or military counsel; wise course of action
wise policy, smart move, advisable course of action

得策.notes: Most commonly appears in negative or conditional evaluations of strategy: それは得策ではない (sore wa tokusaku de wa nai, 'that wouldn't be a smart move / that is ill-advised') or ここは待つのが得策だ ('waiting is the wisest course here').

御母.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) honorific kinship compound (on-haha or mi-haha), combining the exalted prefix 御 (read *on-* < *o-mi-*, or *mi-*, Old Japanese *mi-*, 'august, sacred, imperial, divine') with 母 (haha, Old Japanese papa, 'mother'). While historically used in courtly Japanese for a noble or imperial mother (alongside the phonological fusion おんも *onmo* or みおも *miomo*), in Christian liturgical and biblical Japanese 御母 (commonly read *on-haha* or *mi-haha*) translates Latin *Mater Dei* / English 'Holy Mother' (referring to the Virgin Mary, alongside 聖母 seibo) or serves as a solemn, archaic invocation of a revered mother.

revered mother of a high personage; Holy Mother (in Christian liturgy)
history.stage: Early Modern to Meiji liturgical and literary Japanese

history.meaning: Holy Mother (honorific); revered/sacred mother

御母.notes: Distinct from everyday polite お母さん (okāsan) or formal お母様 (okāsama): 御母 (on-haha / mi-haha) belongs to a lofty, liturgical, or theatrical register (such as prayers to the Virgin Mary, '神の御母マリア' Kami no On-haha Maria, 'Mary, Mother of God').

Sacred Heart, will of God or a sovereign

御社.etymology: Hybrid Japanese business honorific (onsha), composed of the honorific prefix 御- (read with the kun/wago-derived reading *on-*, evolved from classical 御 *o-mi-* via syllabic nasal reduction *on-*) attached to the Sino-Japanese (kango) noun 社 (sha, Middle Chinese *dzyaeX, 'shrine; association, commercial company', clipped from 会社 kaisha). Popularized in modern Japanese business etiquette to provide an unambiguous spoken counterpart to 貴社 (kisha, 'your esteemed company'), because *kisha* has numerous homophones in speech (記者 'reporter', 汽車 'steam train', 帰社 'returning to the office').

御社.notes: Crucial job-interview and business rule: use 御社 (onsha) in *spoken* conversation and interviews for 'your company', use 貴社 (kisha) in *written* emails/letters, and pair both with 弊社 (heisha, 'our company').

Formed from the Sino-Japanese honorific prefix 御- (go-, Middle Chinese *ngjoH, originally 'to drive a royal chariot; imperial, divine') and 託 (taku, Middle Chinese *thak, 'to entrust a message, convey words through another', from 託宣 takusen 'oracle').
