weighing on one's conscience; feeling bad or apologetic toward another

心苦しい.notes: Note the rendaku voicing (/kurushii/ -> /gurushii/); used in polite apologies when receiving an undeserved favor or burdening someone, expressing moral discomfort rather than criminal guilt.

rootFamily.word: 心苦しさ (こころぐるしさ)

心配.etymology: Japanese-coined or Early Modern Sino-Japanese compound 心配 (shinpai), combining 心 ('mind, heart') + 配 ('distribute, deploy, pay attention to' — compare native 気を配る 'to pay attention, be on guard').

history.meaning: putting one's mind to every detail; anxiety; care
worry; anxiety; concern; care

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 心配

必ず.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese adverb *kanarazu* (必ず, 'without fail, certainly, necessarily'), lexicalized from the negative form *kanarazu* of a defective verb *kanaru* ('to be tentative/partial' or related to 兼ねる 'to hold two possibilities').

history.meaning: without fail; inevitably; certainly
certainly; without fail; always

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 必ず

必要.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 必要 (hitsuyō), from Classical/Tang Chinese 必要 ('indispensable, must-have'), combining 必 ('certainly, inevitably') + 要 ('essential, need').

history.meaning: indispensable; essential
necessary; needed; necessity

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 必要

必要性.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) abstract noun formed by suffixing 性 (sei, from Middle Chinese *sjèng, 'nature, quality, -ness/-ity') to 必要 (hitsuyō, 'necessary, indispensable', from Middle Chinese 必 *pjit 'certainly, inevitably' + 要 *ʔjewH 'essential, demand, waist'). Standardized during the Meiji era to translate European philosophical and legal terms such as English 'necessity' and German 'Notwendigkeit', and later re-exported across the Sinosphere.

history.meaning: indispensable, essential requirement
the quality or state of being necessary; necessity

必要性.notes: Used frequently in formal arguments and business contexts with verbs like 感じる (feel the need) or 訴える (appeal to the necessity of), whereas 必要 alone acts as a na-adjective or simpler noun.

必須.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Literary Chinese 必須 (Middle Chinese *pjit-sju, 'must inevitably wait for / require'), composed of 必 (*pjit, 'certainly, without fail', originally an orthographic derivative of a ladle or weapon handle dividing two sides) + 須 (*sju, 'to await, require, must', originally depicting facial hair/beard and used as a phonetic loan for 'wait, need'). In Japanese, final *-t of 必 assimilates to the following /s/ to yield geminate /hissu/.

history.meaning: must certainly require; indispensable
mandatory, compulsory, essential prerequisite

必須.notes: Traditionally read hitsuju in older legal or Buddhist contexts, 必須 is now overwhelmingly read hissu and modifies nouns directly (e.g. 必須条件 'mandatory condition') or with の.

忍耐強い.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for patient. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: patient

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 忍耐強い

志願.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 志願 (Middle Chinese *tsyiH-ngjwonH), originally prominent in Buddhist texts where it denoted a bodhisattva's resolve (志, *tsyiH, 'aim, will, determination of the mind', from 士/之 phonetic over 心 'heart') and solemn vow (願, *ngjwonH, 'earnest wish, vow', from 原 phonetic + 頁 'head'). In the Meiji period it was adapted into military and academic administration to mean 'volunteering for service' or 'applying for admission'.

history.meaning: spiritual resolve and solemn vow; earnest aspiration
volunteering (for a task or military service); applying (for school or a position)

志願.notes: Unlike ボランティア (unpaid community service), 志願 implies stepping forward eagerly to take on a demanding role, mission, or competitive application (e.g. 志願兵 'volunteer soldier', 志願者 'applicant').

忘れる.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese lower bigrade verb *wasuru* (忘る, 'to let slip from the mind, forget'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, becoming modern ichidan *wasureru*.

history.meaning: forget; lose from memory
forget; leave behind

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 忘れる

忘れ物センター.etymology: Modern hybrid compound combining わすれもの (忘れ物, 'lost article, item left behind', from 忘れる + 物) + loanword センター (from English *center*).

history.form: 忘れ物センター (わすれものセンター)
history.meaning: lost-and-found center; lost property office

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 忘れ物

忙しい.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) shiku-adjective derived from the verb root isogu (急ぐ, 'to hurry, hasten, press forward'), which in Old Japanese is attested alongside the adjective form isogasi ('pressing, urgent, restless of mind'). Orthographically written with the kanji 忙 (borrowed from Chinese *mang, 'hurried, pressed for time', composed of 忄 'heart' + 亡 'perish/flee', suggesting a mind so pressed it loses itself).

history.meaning: restless, pressing, urgent in spirit
busy, occupied, hectic

morphemes.meaning: characterized by an emotional or experiential state (-shii)

忙しい.notes: folk-etymologized in Japan via the kanji 忙 as 心 (heart) + 亡 (lose), i.e., 'being so busy one loses one's heart/mind'—a memorable mnemonic that reflects the actual Chinese paleography.

忙しさ.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) deadjectival noun formed by attaching the nominalizing suffix -sa (さ, from Old Japanese -sa, indicating objective degree, extent, or measurable state) to the stem of the adjective 忙しい (isogashii, 'busy, hectic', itself from the verb root isogu 'to hurry, press on'). Literally denotes 'the degree or state of being busy'.

history.meaning: the state or degree of urgency and restlessness
busyness, hecticness, pressure of work or activity

忙しさ.notes: In Japanese morphology, -sa (忙しさ) emphasizes the objective degree or quantifiable pressure of busyness (e.g., 忙しさにかまけて 'wrapped up in the busyness'), whereas -mi doesn't apply to this word.

応える.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) ichidan verb kotaeru, from Classical Japanese kotafu (答ふ / 応ふ), derived from the noun koto (言 / 事, 'word, speech; matter, affair', Old Japanese koto) + the verbalizing iterative/reciprocal suffix -afu (合ふ, 'to meet, match, join together'). Originally meant 'to match words with words, to answer', then split orthographically and semantically into 答える ('to answer a question') and 応える ('to respond to expectations, appeals, or stimuli; to strike home').

history.meaning: to match words, answer, respond in kind
to respond to, live up to (expectations); to take a toll on (one's body/heart)

応える.notes: Distinguish by kanji: 答える answers a question or test (質問に答える), while 応える responds to expectations, cheers, or feelings (期待に応える), or means something 'hits hard' physically (寒さが身に応える).

忠誠.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 忠誠 (Middle Chinese *trjuwng-dzyeng), uniting two near-synonymous Confucian moral virtues: 忠 (*trjuwng, 'unswerving loyalty, devotion from the center of one's heart', composed of 中 'center/middle' + 心 'heart') + 誠 (*dzyeng, 'sincerity, truthfulness, integrity without deceit', composed of 言 'speech/words' + 成 'complete, accomplish'). Deeply entrenched in samurai ethics (bushidō) and organizational fealty.

history.meaning: wholehearted devotion and unfeigned sincerity toward one's sovereign
loyalty, allegiance, steadfast devotion (to a leader, state, or organization)

忠誠.notes: Commonly appears in the collocation 忠誠を誓う (chūsei o chikau, 'to swear allegiance/loyalty') or 忠誠心 (chūseishin, 'sense of loyalty'), carrying a weighty hierarchical nuance.

rootFamily.word: 忠誠心 (ちゅうせいしん)

快適.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 快適 (kaiteki), from Chinese 快適 ('pleasant and agreeable'), combining 快 ('pleasant, refreshing') + 適 ('fit, comfortable, agreeable').

history.meaning: cheerful and comfortable; agreeable
comfortable; pleasant; agreeable

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 快適

念.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) noun borrowed from Middle Chinese 念 (*nemH, 'to hold in mind, reflect, care, thought'), whose character combines 今 ('now, present') over 心 ('heart, mind')—literally 'holding something present in the heart'. In everyday Japanese it survives most famously in the set phrase 念のため(に) (nen no tame ni, 'for the sake of careful thought, just in case').

history.meaning: present thought, mindfulness, care
careful attention, precaution
precaution, care (esp. in 念のため 'just in case')

cognates.meaning: thought, to think of, read aloud

念.notes: 念のために ('just in case') and 念を押す ('to make doubly sure') are two of the most common everyday idioms built on 念.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 念

怒る.etymology: Read both as *okoru* (originally 興る・起こる 'to rise up, flare up' of temper, applied to 怒る in Early Modern Japanese) and *ikaru* (inherited from Old Japanese *ikaru* 'to bristle with rage, become furious').

history.meaning: be furious; rage
lose one's temper; get angry; scold

history.form: 怒る (おこる / いかる)
history.meaning: get angry; be offended; scold

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 怒る

怒鳴る.etymology: Early Modern Japanese compound verb *donaru* ('to shout, bellow, yell angrily'), formed from a reinforced prefix ど- (度 / 怒) + なる (鳴る, 'to sound, roar, ring out'), later spelled ateji-style with 怒 ('anger').

history.form: どなる (度鳴る・怒鳴る)
history.meaning: shout loudly; bellow in anger
yell; shout angrily; roar

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 怒鳴る

怖い.etymology: Shifted in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese from classical こはし (強し・剛し, 'hard, stiff, unyielding, intimidating') to 'frightening, scary, fearful'.

history.meaning: hard; stiff; tough; formidable
intimidating; frightening; scary
scary; frightening; afraid

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 怖い

思い.etymology: The nominalized continuative form (ren'yōkei) of the native Yamato (wago) verb 思う (omou, 'to think, feel, yearn, hold in mind'), from Old Japanese omofu (stem omop-). Etymologically analyzed by historical linguists as containing the root omo ('face, surface, heavy/deep') + verbal suffix -fu, reflecting how deep inner emotion and contemplation manifest on one's countenance or weigh upon the heart. In Classical Japanese, omoi often specifically denoted 'romantic longing' or 'brooding sorrow' (pointing to the 'fire' 火 hi in the final syllable).

history.meaning: deep feeling, yearning, brooding thought, romantic passion
thought, feeling, emotion, expectation, wish

morphemes.meaning: to think, feel, hold in mind

思い.notes: Also spelled 想い when emphasizing tender emotions, romantic feelings, or cherished memories; the idiom 思いをする means 'to have a (good/bad/painful) experience'.

思いも寄らない.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) idiomatic adjectival clause composed of 思い (omoi, 'thought, imagination, expectation', from Old Japanese omopi) + emphatic focus particle も (mo, 'even') + 寄らない (yoranai, negative of 寄る yoru, 'to approach, come near, lean toward', from Old Japanese yoru). Literally means 'not even a thought approaches (it)', i.e., something so far outside the realm of expectation that the mind never even came close to conceiving it.

history.form: 思ひも寄らず (omohi mo yorazu)
history.meaning: not even approaching one's thoughts; wholly unimagined

history.form: 思いも寄らない (omoi mo yoranai)
history.meaning: unimaginable, completely unexpected, unforeseen

思いも寄らない.notes: Often encountered in its literary/archaic negative form 思いもよらぬ (omoi mo yoranu) before nouns (e.g. 思いもよらぬ結果 'an unforeseen outcome') for heightened dramatic flair.

rootFamily.gloss: to approach, drop by, lean on

rootFamily.word: 思いがけない (おもいがけない)

思い出.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem おもひで of the classical verb おもひいづ / おもひづ (思ひ出づ, 'to come to mind, recall, recollect').

history.meaning: recollection; something memorable
memory; recollection; reminiscence

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 思い出

思い出す.etymology: Compound godan verb combining the continuative stem おもい (思い, 'think, feel') + だす (出す, 'bring out, call forth'), replacing earlier lower bigrade 思ひ出づ.

history.form: おもひいだす / おもひだす (思ひ出す)
history.meaning: call back to mind; remember
remember; recall; recollect

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 思い出す

思い込み.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound deverbal noun from the verb 思い込む (omoikomu, 'to be under a strong impression, to be convinced, to set one's heart on'), formed from the continuative stem 思い (omoi, 'thinking, feeling') + the aspectual auxiliary verb 込む (komu, 'to crowd into, go deeply into, become entrenched in'). Literally depicts a thought plunging deep inside the mind and lodging there rigidly as an unexamined assumption or fixation.

history.meaning: deeply setting one's mind on something; intense conviction
unfounded assumption, preconceived notion, mental fixation or bias

思い込み.notes: In contemporary usage, 思い込み almost always carries a slightly critical nuance: a subjective jump to conclusions or blind spot (激しい思い込み 'a strong delusion/preconception'), rather than a rational belief.

rootFamily.gloss: to plunge into, be absorbed in

思う.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *o₂mo₂pu* (思ふ, 'to think, feel in one's heart, love, yearn for'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; often connected with おも (面, 'face, expression').

history.meaning: feel; think; ponder; love
think; feel; believe; consider

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 思う

急ぐ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *iso₁gu* (急ぐ, 'to prepare busily, hasten, hurry'), attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: busy oneself with preparations; hasten
hurry; hasten; make haste

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 急ぐ

急に.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese adverb formed from the kango adjectival noun 急 (kyū, from Middle Chinese *kip < Old Chinese *kɯb, 'urgent, pressing, sudden, steep', originally an ideogrammic compound of 及 'to catch up with / overtake' + 心 'heart', depicting a heart being overtaken or pressed hard) + the native Japanese adverbial/dative particle に (ni, 'in a ... manner'). Historical kana spelling was きふに (kifu ni), which underwent regular labial lenition and monophthongization (*kipu > kifu > kyū).

history.meaning: urgently, hastily, precipitously
suddenly, abruptly, all of a sudden; steeply

急に.notes: Unlike 突然 (totsuzen, a dramatic, out-of-the-blue shock), 急に is everyday and conversational, describing a rapid change of state, mood, or weather (急に雨が降り出した 'it suddenly started raining').

rootFamily.word: 急成長 (きゅうせいちょう)

rootFamily.gloss: sudden change, turn for the worse

急便.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 急便 (kyūbin), combining 急 ('urgent, rapid, express') + 便 ('dispatch, mail/courier service').

history.meaning: express delivery; urgent courier

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 急便

急成長.etymology: A trimorphemic Sino-Japanese (kango) compound uniting the prefixoid modifier 急 (kyū, Middle Chinese *kip, 'rapid, sudden, steep') + 成長 (seichō, 'growth, maturation', from Middle Chinese 成 *dzyeng 'to accomplish, become whole, mature' + 長 *trjangX 'to grow tall, increase, develop'). Popularized in post-war Japanese economic and corporate discourse (echoing 高度経済成長 'high-speed economic growth') to describe explosive business expansion or personal development.

history.meaning: growing up to maturity; biological or personal growth
rapid growth, explosive expansion (especially of industries, companies, or skills)

急成長.notes: Takes the verb する (急成長する 'to grow rapidly') or 遂げる (急成長を遂げる 'to achieve rapid growth'), and is a staple of business dramas describing startup booms.

急須.etymology: Borrowed from early modern southern Chinese (Min / Wu pronunciation of 急須 or 急焼, a small vessel for quickly warming wine or steeping tea), adopted in Edo-period sencha culture for a small side-handled teapot.

history.meaning: small quick-heating pot for wine or tea
small Japanese teapot

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 急須

性.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) noun from Middle Chinese 性 (*sjèng, 'inborn nature, innate disposition, life-force'), phono-semantically formed from 忄 (心, 'heart, mind') + 生 (*sraeng, 'birth, life, to be born'). In Classical Chinese philosophy (Mencius: 性善説), it meant exclusively 'innate human nature'. During the Meiji era, Japanese scholars extended 性 to translate Western biological and psychological concepts of 'sex', 'gender', and 'sexuality'—a semantic innovation subsequently borrowed back into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: inborn nature, innate disposition, fundamental essence
sex, gender, sexuality; innate nature or quality (-ity)

morphemes.meaning: inborn nature, life disposition; sex, gender, sexuality

性.notes: Read sei when meaning 'sex/sexuality/gender' or as a suffix ('-ity'), shō (Kan'on/Go'on distinction) when meaning 'personal temperament' (性が合う 'to be compatible'), and saga in native Yamato reading ('one's inescapable nature/fate').

性欲.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in modern Japanese medical and psychological terminology from 性 (sei, Middle Chinese *sjèng, in its Meiji-era sense of 'sex, sexuality') + 欲 (yoku, Middle Chinese *jowk, 'desire, appetite, craving', originally 谷 'valley/hollow' phonetic + 欠 'yawning/gaping person', expanded in 慾 with 心 'heart'). Replaced older Buddhist and Edo-period terms like 色欲 (shikiyoku, 'carnal/sensual lust') with a clinical, scientific term equivalent to German 'Sexualtrieb' or Latin 'libido'.

history.meaning: carnal passion, worldly lust (Buddhist and pre-modern terms)
sexual desire, sex drive, libido

性欲.notes: Forms part of the famous Japanese triad 人間の三大欲求 ('the three great human drives'): 食欲 (appetite for food), 睡眠欲 (need for sleep), and 性欲 (sex drive).

性癖.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 性癖 (Middle Chinese *sjèng-phjek), originally composed of 性 (*sjèng, 'inborn nature, temperament') + 癖 (*phjek, 'chronic ailment, deep-seated habit, quirk, addiction', composed of 疒 'sickness radical' + 辟 phonetic). Traditionally meant simply 'an eccentric personal habit or psychological quirk'; however, in late-20th and 21st-century colloquial Japanese, users reinterpreted 性 as 'sex/sexuality' rather than 'temperament', shifting its dominant vernacular meaning to 'sexual proclivity, fetish, or kink'.

history.meaning: innate temperament, psychological quirk, habitual eccentricity
eccentric habit (formal); sexual proclivity, fetish, kink (colloquial dominant)

性癖.notes: A classic example of modern semantic shift: dictionaries still list 'mental quirk/disposition' first (e.g., 盗み聞きする性癖 'a habit of eavesdropping'), but in everyday speech and media like The Naked Director, it almost always means 'sexual fetish/kink'.

怪しい.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) shiku-adjective from Old Japanese ayasi (あやし, 'incomprehensible, wondrous, supernatural, eerie, strange'), derived from the exclamatory interjection aya (あや, 'ah! oh!', expressing astonishment, awe, or bewilderment at something beyond normal comprehension) + the adjectival suffix -si (> -shii). In Heian court literature, ayashi also meant 'humble, lowly, unsightly' (because commoners' lives seemed strange to aristocrats), before settling into its modern sense of 'suspicious, shady, dubious, or eerie'.

history.meaning: marvellous, supernatural, inexplicable; strange, humble, lowly
suspicious, shady, dubious, fishy; eerie, uncanny, bewitching

怪しい.notes: Written 怪しい for 'suspicious, shady, dubious' (怪しい人物 'a shady character', 雲行きが怪しい 'things look dicey') and sometimes 妖しい when meaning 'bewitchingly alluring, eerily seductive'.

恋.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) noun derived from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the Old Japanese upper-bigrade (kami nidan) verb kofu (恋ふ, stem kop- > koh- > ko-, modern 恋う kou, 'to yearn painfully for someone or something absent'), written in the Man'yōshū as 孤悲 (literally 'lonely grief'). Originally encompassed deep homesickness or longing for the dead as well as absent lovers, before narrowing to passionate romantic yearning. Orthographically represented by the Chinese character 恋 (traditional 戀, 'tangled/bound heart', depicting threads 糸 flanking speech 言 over heart 心).

history.meaning: ache of longing for an absent person, place, or season; passionate yearning
romantic love, passion, falling in love

morphemes.meaning: romantic longing, passionate love (from verb kofu 'to yearn for')

恋.notes: Japanese sharply contrasts 恋 (koi, passionate, self-interested romantic yearning—often compared through its kanji bottom 心 to 'a heart wanting something below') with 愛 (ai, selfless, nurturing devotion and affection).

恋人.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 恋 (koi, Old Japanese kopi, 'romantic longing, passionate love') + 人 (hito, voiced via rendaku to bito, Old Japanese pito, 'person'), attested since the Heian period (e.g., in Ise Monogatari and Genji Monogatari). Originally denoted 'the person for whom one yearns' (even unrequitedly), later shifting to a mutual romantic partner ('sweetheart, lover, boyfriend or girlfriend').

history.meaning: the person one longs for; object of one's romantic yearning
lover, sweetheart, boyfriend or girlfriend

恋人.notes: Gender-neutral and slightly poetic/romantic compared to 彼氏 (kareshi, 'boyfriend') or 彼女 (kanojo, 'girlfriend'), and lacks the illicit or purely sexual connotation that English 'lover' (愛人 aijin in Japanese) often carries.

恐れる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) ichidan verb from Old Japanese osoru (恐る / 畏る, originally conjugated both as a quadrigrade yodan and lower-bigrade shimo-nidan verb before shifting to modern ichidan osoreru). Likely related to the root oso- ('dreadful, terrifying, awe-inspiring', also seen in 恐ろしい osoroshii). In early Japanese, osoru encompassed both 'reverent awe before gods or sovereigns' (written 畏る) and 'fear of danger or harm' (written 恐る).

history.meaning: to feel reverent awe or dread; to be afraid of
to fear, dread, be afraid of, be apprehensive about

morphemes.meaning: to fear, dread, stand in awe of

恐れる.notes: Its nominalized form 恐れ (osore) is frequently used in formal announcements and news reports to mean 'risk or danger that something bad might happen' (台風による被害の恐れがある 'there is a risk of damage from the typhoon').

rootFamily.gloss: humbly, with due respect (lit. entering in awe)

恐喝.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) legal and criminal compound from Literary Chinese 恐喝 (Middle Chinese *khjowngX-xat), formed from 恐 (*khjowngX, 'to terrify, frighten, intimidate', composed of 巩 phonetic + 心 'heart') + 喝 (*xat, 'to shout angrily, bellow, threaten loudly', composed of 口 'mouth' + 曷 phonetic). Literally 'frightening by shouting threats', it was codified in the modern Japanese Penal Code (Article 249, 恐喝罪 kyōkatsuzai) to denote the crime of extorting money or property through intimidation or blackmail short of outright robbery.

history.meaning: frightening and intimidating someone by shouting threats
extortion, blackmail, shakedown (obtaining property via intimidation)

恐喝.notes: In Japanese law and crime dramas, 恐喝 (extortion/blackmail—forcing the victim to hand over money out of fear) is distinguished from 脅迫 (kyōhaku, pure intimidation/threats) and 強盗 (gōtō, violent robbery).

rootFamily.gloss: to shout down, browbeat, roar at

恐怖.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) synonym compound borrowed from Literary and Buddhist Chinese 恐怖 (Middle Chinese *khjowngX-phuH), famous from the Heart Sutra line 無有恐怖 ('having no fear or terror'). Composed of two synonymous roots meaning 'fear, dread': 恐 (*khjowngX, 'to fear, dread', 巩 phonetic + 心 'heart') + 怖 (*phuH, 'to be terrified, frightened, panicked', 忄 'heart' + 布 *puH phonetic). Both kanji share the heart radical, underscoring intense psychological terror.

history.meaning: trepidation, dread, existential terror (especially in Buddhist scripture)
fear, terror, horror, panic; phobia (in compounds)

恐怖.notes: Note that the second kanji 怖 is also used in native Japanese to write 怖い (kowai, 'scary, afraid'); as a suffix, 恐怖症 (kyōfushō) translates '-phobia' (e.g. 高所恐怖症 'acrophobia').

rootFamily.gloss: scary, frightening, afraid (native reading of 怖)
to fear, be afraid of (native reading of 恐)

rootFamily.word: 恐怖症 (きょうふしょう)

恥.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) noun derived from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the Old Japanese upper-bigrade verb hadu (恥づ, stem pad- > had-, modern 恥じる hajiru, 'to feel ashamed, to be embarrassed'). Written with the kanji 恥 (composed of 耳 'ear' + 心 'heart', reflecting the ancient Chinese observation that when the heart feels shame, one's ears burn and flush red). Central to Japanese cultural anthropology (as analyzed in Ruth Benedict's 'shame culture' vs. 'guilt culture' framework).

history.meaning: disgrace, humiliation, feeling of shame before others' eyes
shame, embarrassment, dishonor, loss of face

morphemes.meaning: shame, disgrace, embarrassment (from verb hadu 'to feel ashamed')

恥.notes: Key idioms include 恥をかく (haji o kaku, 'to embarrass oneself / suffer humiliation'), 恥を知る (haji o shiru, 'to have a sense of honor/decency'), and 恥さらし (hajisarashi, 'public disgrace').

rootFamily.word: 恥ずかしい (はずかしい)

恥じらい.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun from the verb 恥じらう (hajirau, 'to feel bashful, act shyly, show coy modesty'), formed in Early Middle Japanese by adding the iterative/continuative verbal suffix -rafu (らふ, indicating an ongoing, wavering, or outward-manifesting emotional state) to the verb stem haji- (恥じ, from Old Japanese padu 'to feel ashamed'). Thus, while 恥 (haji) is heavy disgrace, 恥じらい (hajirai) evolved to mean delicate, lingering bashfulness or graceful modesty.

history.meaning: ongoing state of bashfulness; coy hesitation or modesty
shyness, bashfulness, delicate modesty, coyness

恥じらい.notes: Unlike 恥 (disgrace) or 恥ずかしさ (embarrassment), 恥じらい has a distinctly positive, aesthetic, and often sensual or romantic nuance—describing charming modesty or a coy blush.

rootFamily.word: 恥ずかしい (はずかしい)

恥ずかしい.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *padukasi* (恥づかし, 'admirable to the point of making one feel inadequate; bashful; ashamed'), derived from the verb はづ (恥づ, modern 恥じる 'to feel shame').

history.meaning: so impressive as to humble the observer; bashful; shameful

history.form: 恥ずかしい (はずかしい)
history.meaning: embarrassing; shy; ashamed

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 恥ずかしい

恨む.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) godan verb from Old Japanese uramu (恨む / 怨む, 'to resent, bear a grudge, feel bitter regret toward'). Etymologically derived by Japanese philologists from ura (裏 / 心, 'the inner side, back, deep interior of the heart', as in uraganashi 'sad at heart') + the verbalizing suffix -mu ('to feel, view as, experience', or 'to see the underside of'). Written with 恨 (忄 'heart' + 艮 'stubborn, stopping, staring back', depicting a feeling that refuses to move on and remains stuck in the heart).

history.meaning: to feel inner bitterness, regret, or reproach toward someone or fate
to resent, hold a grudge against, bear ill will toward, curse (one's fate)

恨む.notes: In Japanese folklore and drama, 恨み (urami, deep-seated resentment) is a quiet, smoldering emotion held by a wronged party (leading to the stock phrase 恨むなら自分を恨め 'if you're going to blame someone, blame yourself').

cognates.meaning: benefactor, person who has shown great kindness

恩人.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 恩人 (Middle Chinese *ʔon-nyin), combining 恩 (*ʔon, 'grace, favor, benevolence, moral debt of gratitude', composed of 因 *ʔjin phonetic 'cause, rely on' + 心 'heart') + 人 (*nyin, 'person', read jin in Go'on). In Japanese ethical culture, 恩 (on) represents an enduring moral obligation incurred when someone bestows life-saving help, mentorship, or patronage upon you, making an 恩人 far more than a casual helper.

history.meaning: person who has bestowed benevolence or grace upon one
benefactor, patron, lifesaver (to whom one owes a lifelong debt of gratitude)

morphemes.meaning: grace, favor, benevolence, moral debt of gratitude

恩人.notes: Most famously used in 命の恩人 (inochi no onjin, 'savior of one's life / lifesaver'); repaying an 恩人 is called 恩返し (ongaeshi), while betraying them makes one 恩知らず (onshirazu, 'an ingrate').

rootFamily.gloss: repaying a favor or moral debt

息.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *oki₁* > *iki₁* ('breath, respiration, vital spirit'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; cognate with いく (生く, 'to live').

history.meaning: breath; respiration; life force
breath; breathing; tone/accord

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 息

息切れ.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun combining いき (息, 'breath') + ぎれ (切れ, rendaku form of きれ from 切れる 'to run out, be cut off').

history.meaning: shortness of breath; panting; running out of steam

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 息切れ

息子.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun musuko, from Old Japanese musuko (むすこ), formed from the verb stem musu (生す / 産す, 'to generate, sprout, come into being, give birth to', seen in Kimi ga Yo's koke no musu made 'until moss grows' and in Shinto deity names like Musubi) + ko (子, 'child, offspring'), parallel to 娘 (musume, 'daughter', from musu + me 'female/woman'). The kanji 息子 is a mature orthographic borrowing (jukujikun) from Literary Chinese 息子 ('offspring who grow/multiply', where 息 meant 'breath -> to grow/proliferate').

history.meaning: male child born/generated; boy, youth
son (and in colloquial slang, 'penis')

息子.notes: Because the kanji 息uko is jukujikun (meaning-based assignment of Chinese 息子 to native musuko), you cannot guess the reading from 息 (iki/soku) + 子 (ko/shi); used for one's own son, while 息子さん (musukosan) or ご子息 (goshisoku) refers respectfully to someone else's son. Also used humorously in adult contexts like The Naked Director as slang for a man's penis.

悩み.etymology: Deverbal noun from the continuative stem of なやむ (悩む, Old Japanese *nayamu* 'to suffer illness, ache, be troubled or distressed').

history.meaning: physical ailment; distress; torment
worry; trouble; distress;悩み

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 悩み

悪.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) noun and prefix from Middle Chinese 惡 (*ʔak, 'bad, ugly, foul, wicked, evil'), composed of 亞 (*ʔjaeH, phonetic, originally depicting a cross-shaped foundation or hunchbacked/deformed figure) + 心 ('heart'). In Buddhist and Confucian thought imported into Japan, 悪 (aku) stood in cosmic and moral opposition to 善 (zen, 'good, virtue'), while in medieval warrior culture 悪 also meant 'fierce, formidable, audaciously strong' (as in 悪源太 Akugenta, 'Fierce Genta').

history.meaning: ugly, foul, morally bad, karmic evil; fierce and formidable (medieval Japan)
evil, wickedness, vice, villainy; bad guy (colloquial waru)

悪.notes: Read aku in Sino-Japanese philosophical or dramatic contexts ('evil, vice', e.g., 必要悪 hitsuyōaku 'necessary evil'), and waru as a native-derived noun meaning 'a mischievous rogue, bad boy, or villain'.

悪い.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *warusi* (悪し, 'inferior, poor in quality, undesirable, bad'), attested in the Man'yōshū; gradually took over the semantic territory of classical あし (悪し).

history.meaning: inferior; poor; unseemly; bad
bad; wrong; faulty; sorry (colloquial)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 悪い

情報.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) neologism (wasei-kango) coined in Japan during the Meiji period—originally in 1876 by military translator酒井忠恕 (Sakai Tadayoshi) translating French 'renseignement' (military intelligence regarding enemy conditions)—from 情 (jō, Middle Chinese *dzjeng, 'actual circumstances, reality of a situation, feelings') + 報 (hō, Middle Chinese *pawH, 'report, dispatch, news'). In the 20th century, it broadened from military 'intelligence/tip-off' to general 'information, data, and news', and was borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: report on enemy conditions; military intelligence or tip-off
information, news, data, intelligence, tip

morphemes.meaning: actual circumstances, condition, state of affairs

情報.notes: A classic false friend with Mandarin Chinese: in Japanese (and Korean 정보), 情報 means everyday 'information, data, or a tip', whereas in Mandarin 情報 (qíngbào) retained the original Meiji military sense of 'secret intelligence / espionage'.

情感.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 情 (jō, from Middle Chinese dzjeng, 'feeling, disposition, inner reality') and 感 (kan, from Middle Chinese komX, 'to be moved, to feel, response of the heart'). While reverse-ordered 感情 (kanjō) denotes psychological emotion in general, 情感 (jōkan) specifically highlights aesthetic sensibility, atmospheric pathos, or an evocative emotional texture awakened by art, scenery, or human intimacy.

history.meaning: inner disposition and heartfelt stirring
deep emotional resonance, aesthetic sensibility

morphemes.meaning: feeling, emotion, inner nature (Middle Chinese dzjeng)
to feel, be moved in the heart (Middle Chinese komX)

情感.notes: Unlike 感情 (kanjō, everyday emotions like anger or joy), 情感 (jōkan) belongs to an elevated, artistic register (e.g., 情感あふれる演技, 'a performance brimming with pathos and sensibility').

情熱的.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) adjectival derivative formed from 情熱 (jōnetsu, 'passion, ardor' — a Meiji-era conceptual compound uniting 情 jō 'emotion, feeling' and 熱 netsu 'heat, fever') plus the adjectival suffix 的 (-teki, from Middle Chinese tek 'target, mark', adapted in Meiji Japanese to render European '-ic' / '-ical' adjectives). Literally 'having the character of emotional heat'.

history.meaning: feeling + heat + target/attributive marker
fervent emotion, passion (coined/popularized in the Meiji period)
passionate, ardent, enthusiastic

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix forming -ic/-like attributes (Middle Chinese tek)

情熱的.notes: Functions as a na-adjective (情熱的な人, 'a passionate person'); the suffix -的 (-teki) productively turns Sino-Japanese nouns into descriptive modifiers.

rootFamily.word: 感情的 (かんじょうてき)

惜しむ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb derived from the Old Japanese adjective stem *osi- (modern 惜しい oshii, 'precious, regrettable to lose, grudged') verbalized with the deadjectival suffix *-m- (which forms transitive verbs of subjective attitude, cf. 悲しむ kanashimu from 悲しい kanashii, 楽しむ tanoshimu from 楽しい tanoshii). Originally meant to prize something so dearly that one cannot bear to part with it, whence both 'to begrudge/spare' and 'to regret the loss of'. Orthographically mapped to Chinese 惜 (Middle Chinese sjek, 'to pity, begrudge, cherish').

history.form: をしい / をしむ (wosi- / wosimu)
history.meaning: to prize dearly, hold precious, begrudge parting with
to regret losing, spare, hold back
to begrudge, spare (effort/money), lament a loss

morphemes.meaning: precious, regrettable to part with (native root *wosi-)

惜しむ.notes: Most frequently encountered in negated idioms like 努力を惜しまない (doryoku o oshimanai, 'to spare no effort') or 惜しみなく (oshiminaku, 'unstintingly, generously').

rootFamily.word: 名残惜しい (なごりおしい)
ケチ / 出し惜しみ (だしおしみ)

cognates.word: 상상 이상 (想像以上, sangsang isang)

想像以上.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) compound joining 想像 (sōzō, 'imagination, mental image', from 想 sō 'to picture in the mind' + 像 zō 'likeness, image, figure') and 以上 (ijō, 'above and beyond, more than', from 以 i 'by means of, taking as boundary' + 上 jō 'above, exceeding'). Literally 'above what is pictured in the mind'.

history.meaning: mental image + from that point upward
exceeding one's imagination, better/greater than expected

morphemes.meaning: to think, picture mentally (Middle Chinese sjangX)
starting from, by means of (Middle Chinese jix)

想像以上.notes: While standalone 以上 (ijō) in legal or mathematical contexts means 'or more (inclusive)', attached to cognitive nouns like 想像以上 or 期待以上 it strictly means 'exceeding/beyond'.

rootFamily.word: 想像力 (そうぞうりょく)
期待以上 (きたいいじょう)

意味.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 意味 (imi), from Classical and Buddhist Chinese 意味 ('thought and flavor; underlying significance, purport, meaning').

history.meaning: import and flavor of words; meaning
meaning; significance; sense

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 意味

意地.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 意地 (iji), originally a Buddhist term translating Sanskrit *manobhūmi* ('the ground/plane of mind and thought'); in Early Modern Japanese it shifted to 'disposition, stubborn pride, willpower'.

history.meaning: state of mind; mental ground
stubbornness; pride; willpower; appetite (in 意地が汚い)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 意地

意外.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Literary Chinese 意外 (Middle Chinese 'ijH-ngwajH), composed of 意 (i, 'thought, expectation, mind') and 外 (gai, 'outside, beyond'). Already attested in Classical Chinese historiography (e.g., *Book of Han*) for events falling 'outside one's thought or anticipation', and borrowed into Japanese both as a noun ('something unforeseen') and as a na-adjective ('surprising, unexpected').

history.meaning: outside of what one thought or anticipated
unexpected, surprising, unforeseen

意外.notes: Beware the common native homophone confusion with 以外 (igai, 'other than, except for'): 意外 takes the particle に or な ('surprisingly'), whereas 以外 attaches directly to a noun ('aside from X').

cognates.meaning: meaning, idea, opinion, token of affection

意思.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 意思 (Middle Chinese 'ijH-si), pairing 意 (i, 'mind, intent, inner purpose', written with 音 'sound/voice' over 心 'heart') and 思 (shi, 'reflective thought, inclination', written with 田 'field/fontanel' over 心 'heart'). In Japanese legal and everyday usage, 意思 denotes what one intends or wishes to do ('intention, mind'), contrasting with its homophone 意志 (ishi, 'resolute willpower').

history.meaning: thoughts, state of mind, inner intention
intention, inclination, communicative intent

意思.notes: Distinguish the homophones 意思 (intention/what one wants to do, as in 意思表示 'declaration of intent') and 意志 (firm willpower/resolve to carry something through, as in 意志が強い 'strong-willed'). Also a false friend with Mandarin 意思 (yìsi, 'meaning' or 'interesting').

rootFamily.gloss: declaration of intention, signaling one's mind
rootFamily.word: 意思表示 (いしひょうじ)

意気込み.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato (jūbako-style) deverbal noun nominalized from the compound verb 意気込む (ikigomu, 'to be fired up, to muster one's spirit'). The first element 意気 (iki) is a Sino-Japanese compound of 意 (i, 'mind, intent') and 気 (ki, 'vital breath, spirit, qi'), which also converges folk-etymologically with native 息 (iki, 'breath'); the second element 込み (-gomi, with rendaku voicing k > g) is the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of native 込む (komu, 'to pack in, surge inward, concentrate'). Literally 'packing/charging one's vital spirit into an endeavor'.

history.meaning: spirit, disposition, vital energy
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Early Modern Japanese

history.form: 意気込む (ikigomu) > 意気込み (ikigomi)
history.meaning: charging oneself with spirit > enthusiasm, drive, determination

morphemes.meaning: vital breath, spirit, energy (Middle Chinese khj+jH)
concentrating inward, packing into (nominalized stem of 込む komu, voiced via rendaku)

意気込み.notes: A staple interview and business word (e.g., 今後の意気込みを語る, 'to speak about one's enthusiasm/determination going forward'); notice the mandatory rendaku voicing of komi to -gomi.

rootFamily.gloss: to be enthusiastic, gear up for
being in complete agreement, hitting it off in spirit
rootFamily.word: 意気投合 (いきとうごう)

意見.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Literary Chinese 意見 (Middle Chinese 'ijH-kenH), formed from 意 (i, 'mind, thought, inner judgment') and 見 (ken, 'seeing, view, standpoint'). Originally signified 'what is seen within the mind' in Buddhist and Tang-dynasty prose. In medieval and Edo-period Japanese, 意見する (iken suru) developed a secondary sense of 'to admonish, remonstrate with, give someone a piece of one's mind', alongside its primary modern sense of 'personal view or opinion'.

history.meaning: mental view, personal judgment
view, counsel; admonishment or remonstrance (Muromachi–Edo)
opinion, viewpoint, idea

morphemes.meaning: to see, view, perspective (Middle Chinese kenH)

意見.notes: In modern standard Japanese 意見 means a neutral 'opinion', whereas in Mandarin Chinese 有意見 (yǒu yìjiàn) often implies having a complaint or objection, and in older Edo Japanese 親に意見される meant 'to be lectured/scolded by one's parents'.

rootFamily.gloss: one's true intention or real opinion

意識.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) philosophical term originating in Chinese Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *mano-vijñāna* ('mind-consciousness', the sixth of the six consciousnesses in Yogācāra and Abhidharma Buddhism), combining 意 (i, Middle Chinese 'ijH, rendering Sanskrit *manas* 'mind, mental faculty') and 識 (shiki, Middle Chinese syik, rendering Sanskrit *vijñāna* 'discernment, cognitive awareness'). During the Meiji era, Japanese scholars (such as Nishi Amane) repurposed this Buddhist term to translate modern Western psychological and philosophical 'consciousness' (German *Bewusstsein*, English *consciousness*).

history.meaning: the sixth consciousness: cognitive discernment arising from the mind-organ
mental discernment (Buddhist); re-adopted in Meiji philosophy for Western 'consciousness' and 'awareness'

morphemes.meaning: mind, mental faculty (Middle Chinese 'ijH, translating Sanskrit manas)
discernment, cognition, awareness (Middle Chinese syik, translating Sanskrit vijñāna)

意識.notes: Used both as a noun (意識を失う, 'to lose consciousness') and a transitive suru-verb (カメラを意識する, 'to be self-conscious/aware of the camera'). Colloquial 意識高い系 ('hyper-ambitious/pretentiously self-improving type') is a major modern buzzword.

愚か.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) na-adjective descending from Old Japanese *oroka* ('sparse, incomplete, negligent, rough, lacking'). Built on the bound root *oro-* ('incomplete, sketchy, sparse', also seen in おろそか orosoka 'neglectful, remiss' and dialectal/archaic *oro* 'imperfectly') plus the adjectival/stative suffix *-ka* (cf. 静か shizuka, 愚か oroka, 遥か haruka). Semantic evolution moved from 'sketchy/neglectful/deficient in care' in Nara and Heian texts to 'mentally deficient, foolish, unwise', written with the Chinese character 愚 ('foolish, slow-witted').

history.meaning: sparse, insufficiently attentive, rough, remiss
negligent, inadequate; foolish, lacking wisdom
foolish, stupid, unwise (also surviving in the grammar pattern Xはおろか 'not to mention X')

愚か.notes: The older sense of 'barely worth mentioning / goes without saying' survives fossilized in the advanced grammar construction Nはおろか (N wa oroka, 'let alone N / not to mention N').

cognates.meaning: to make a fool of, dupe, mock
mockery, derision, making sport of someone

愚弄.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Literary Chinese 愚弄 (Middle Chinese ngju-luwngH), attested since the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*). Composed of 愚 (gu, 'foolish; to treat as a fool') and 弄 (rō, 'to play with, toy with, manipulate with both hands' — the graph depicts two hands 廾 holding jade 玉). Literally 'to toy with someone as if they were a fool', hence 'to mock, deride, or make sport of'.

history.meaning: to treat as a fool and toy with, deceive and mock
mockery, ridicule, derision (used as noun and suru-verb)

morphemes.meaning: foolish; to treat as a fool (Middle Chinese ngju)
to toy with, play with, manipulate (Middle Chinese luwngH)

愚弄.notes: A high-register, dramatic word (e.g., 人を愚弄するな！ 'Do not make a mockery of me!'), stronger and more literary than the everyday 馬鹿にする (baka ni suru).

rootFamily.gloss: to toy with, play with, trifle with
to trifle with someone's feelings, toss about

愚痴.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) Buddhist term 愚痴 (written historically as 愚癡, Middle Chinese ngju-trhi), coined in Chinese Buddhist scriptures to translate Sanskrit *moha* ('delusion, spiritual ignorance, folly'), one of the Three Poisons (*triviṣa* / 三毒 sandoku) alongside greed (貪 ton) and anger (瞋 jin). Composed of 愚 (gu, 'foolish, benighted') and 痴/癡 (chi, 'mentally sluggish, infatuated, unreasoning'). In medieval and Edo-period Japanese vernacular, 'speaking out of unreasoning delusion over things that cannot be helped' secularized into 'idle grumbling, futile complaining, venting'.

history.meaning: spiritual ignorance or delusion (one of the Three Poisons in Buddhism)
unenlightened bewilderment > futile lamenting over what cannot be changed
idle complaints, grumbling, venting frustrations

愚痴.notes: Commonly collocated as 愚痴をこぼす (guchi o kobosu, literally 'to spill grumbles') or verbalized as 愚痴る (guchiru, 'to vent/bitch over drinks'). Its solemn Buddhist origin as 'karmic delusion' explains why it specifically refers to complaining that changes nothing.

rootFamily.word: 痴情 (ちじょう) / 痴漢 (ちかん)

愛.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) single-character noun 愛 (ai, from Middle Chinese 'ojH, 'to love, cherish, hold dear, begrudge parting with'). The character 愛 originated in Old Chinese bronze and seal script as a phono-semantic compound depicting a person looking back with a full heart (心) and trailing feet (夊), expressing reluctant, lingering attachment. In pre-Meiji Japan, driven by Buddhist usage (where 愛 rendered Sanskrit *tṛṣṇā*, 'craving, worldly attachment', or parental tenderness toward inferiors), 愛 carried connotations of clinging desire or top-down fondness; in the Meiji era it was elevated via translations of Christian *agape* and Western *love* to signify noble romantic and universal love.

history.meaning: fondness, cherishing, reluctant attachment; Buddhist craving (tṛṣṇā)
parental fondness, passionate attachment; broadened in Meiji to translate Western romantic and spiritual 'love'

愛.notes: Whereas 恋 (koi, native wago) focuses on yearning, romantic passion, and desire for a specific partner, 愛 (ai, Sino-Japanese) encompasses selfless devotion, deep care, and universal or familial love.

愛す.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato verb formed by adapting the single-kanji Sino-Japanese noun 愛 (ai, from Middle Chinese 'ojH, 'love, affection') directly into the native Japanese five-grade (godan / yodan) -su verbal conjugation class (愛す aisu, negative 愛さない aisanai), evolving alongside the standard irregular suru-verb 愛する (aisuru). In Classical Japanese, single-character Sino-Japanese roots attached to -su (the ancestor of する suru) frequently reanalyzed as regular consonant-stem (-s-) verbs in literary, poetic, and dramatic registers.

history.meaning: to hold dear, cherish, feel affection for

history.form: 愛す (aisu, godan) / 愛する (aisuru, sa-hen)
history.meaning: to love deeply, cherish (with godan 愛す retaining a literary or lyrical cadence)

morphemes.meaning: verbalizing suffix derived from classical su ('to do')

愛す.notes: 愛す (aisu) is the shorter, slightly more literary/lyrical five-grade (godan) variant of 愛する (aisuru); both share forms like 愛している (aishiteiru, 'I love you') and passive 愛される (aisareru, 'to be loved').

愛情.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 愛 (ai, Middle Chinese 'ojH, 'love, cherishing care') and 情 (jō, Middle Chinese dzjeng, 'feeling, heart, inner disposition'). Literally 'the feeling of loving care'. While in modern Mandarin 愛情 (àiqíng) narrowed almost exclusively to romantic love between lovers, Japanese 愛情 retained a broader scope covering warm, nurturing affection toward family, children, pets, or craft as well as romantic partners.

history.meaning: cherishing attachment + heartfelt feeling
warm affection, loving care, devotion

愛情.notes: Watch the Mandarin-Japanese nuance difference: Japanese 愛情 (aijō) is warm, nurturing affection (often used for parental love, 親の愛情, or care put into cooking), whereas romantic passion is more specifically 恋愛 (ren'ai).

感じ.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem of the Sino-Japanese suru/zuru-verb 感ず / 感じる (from Middle Chinese 感 'to be moved, feel, sense').

history.meaning: emotional response; impression; sensation
feeling; impression; atmosphere; vibe

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 感じ

感じる.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato (kami-ichidan) verb evolved from Classical Japanese 感ず (kanzu), which attached the native verbalizer -su ('to do') to the Sino-Japanese root 感 (kan, Middle Chinese komX, 'to be moved, touched in the heart, respond emotionally'). The nasal coda -n of 感 triggered voicing (rendaku) of -su to -zu (kan-su > kanzu), and from Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese the irregular -zuru verb shifted regularly into the modern upper-monograde (kami-ichidan) conjugation 感じる (kanjiru, 'to feel, sense, perceive').

history.meaning: to be stirred in the heart, respond to stimulus
to be deeply moved, feel, sense (sa-hen voiced conjugation)
to feel, sense, experience a sensation or emotion (ichidan verb)

morphemes.meaning: to feel, be moved in the heart (Middle Chinese komX)
ichidan verbalizer evolved from classical -zu / -zuru (< -su 'to do')

感じる.notes: In addition to everyday 'to feel/sense' (寒さを感じる, 'to feel the cold'), in adult/intimate contexts (such as *The Naked Director*) intransitive 感じる specifically means 'to feel sexual pleasure / be aroused'.

感傷.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 感傷 (kanshō), from Classical Chinese 感傷 ('to be moved to sorrow, feel sentimental grief'), combining 感 ('be moved, feel') + 傷 ('wound, grieve').

history.meaning: be touched with sorrow; lament
sentimentality; pathos

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 感傷

感情.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 感 (kan, Middle Chinese komX, 'to be stirred, moved by external things') and 情 (jō, Middle Chinese dzjeng, 'inner feelings, nature of the heart'). In classical Chinese poetics and philosophy, 感 denoted the heart's reaction to external stimuli while 情 denoted the resulting inner emotional state. In the Meiji era, 感情 was standardized as the psychological translation for Western 'emotion' (contrasted with 理性 risei 'reason' and 知性 chisei 'intellect').

history.meaning: being stirred by things + inner emotional disposition
emotional stirring; standardized in Meiji psychology as 'emotion, passion, affect'

morphemes.meaning: to feel, respond to stimulus (Middle Chinese komX)
feeling, inner nature, emotion (Middle Chinese dzjeng)

感情.notes: Important false friend with Mandarin: in Japanese 感情 (kanjō) means psychological 'emotion' (joy, anger, grief), whereas in Mandarin 感情 (gǎnqíng) usually means 'interpersonal affection / bond between two people'.

rootFamily.gloss: emotional, easily carried away by feelings
rootFamily.word: 感情的 (かんじょうてき)

感覚.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound uniting 感 (kan, Middle Chinese komX, 'to feel, respond to a stimulus') and 覚 (kaku, Middle Chinese kaewk, 'to wake up, perceive, become aware'). Standardized in Meiji-period philosophy and physiology (notably by Nishi Amane) to translate European *sensation* / *Sinnesempfindung* — the immediate physical or intuitive registration of stimuli through the senses, distinct from 感情 (kanjō, 'emotion') and 知覚 (chikaku, 'cognitive perception').

history.meaning: to be touched/moved + to awaken/perceive
bodily sensation, sensory perception, intuitive flair (Meiji philosophical coinage/adaptation)

morphemes.meaning: to feel, respond to stimulus (Middle Chinese komX)
to perceive, awaken, realize (Middle Chinese kaewk)

感覚.notes: Covers both raw physical sensation (手の感覚がない, 'I have no feeling in my hand') and intuitive flair or knack (ファッション感覚, 'fashion sense'; 遊び感覚で, 'as if playing a game'). Beware the homophone 間隔 (kankaku, 'interval, spacing').

感謝.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Literary Chinese 感謝 (Middle Chinese komX-zjaeH), composed of 感 (kan, 'to feel deeply moved in the heart') and 謝 (sha, 'to express in words, acknowledge a debt or favor, decline/apologize'). Originally meant 'to be moved in the heart by someone's kindness and express acknowledgment in words', serving in modern Japanese as the standard formal noun and suru-verb for 'gratitude, appreciation, thanking'.

history.meaning: to be moved by kindness and express verbal acknowledgment
gratitude, thanksgiving, appreciation

morphemes.meaning: to feel moved in the heart (Middle Chinese komX)
to thank, acknowledge in words, apologize (Middle Chinese zjaeH)

感謝.notes: Notice that 謝 (sha) means both 'to thank' (感謝 kansha, 謝礼 sharei) and 'to apologize' (謝罪 shazai, 謝る ayamaru), because in classical Chinese etiquette both actions involved bowing and acknowledging a moral debt to another person.

rootFamily.gloss: to apologize, beg pardon (native verb written with 謝)

態度.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Literary Chinese 態度 (Middle Chinese thojH-duH, attested in *Zhuangzi* and Tang prose), composed of 態 (tai, 'bodily bearing, posture, outward manifestation of the heart' — written with 能 'ability/bear' over 心 'heart') and 度 (do, 'measure, standard, deportment'). Originally denoted a person's physical bearing or external demeanor, and in modern Japanese broadened to cover both outward manner (態度が悪い, 'having a bad/rude demeanor') and one's stance toward an issue (態度を明らかにする, 'to clarify one's stance').

history.meaning: outward bearing, physical deportment, manner
demeanor, manner, behavioral attitude or stance

morphemes.meaning: bearing, appearance, figure, state of heart (Middle Chinese thojH)

態度.notes: Idiomatic 態度がでかい (taido ga dekai, literally 'one's attitude is huge') means 'arrogant, bossy, acting like one owns the place'.

rootFamily.word: 節度 (せつど) / 程度 (ていど)

慌てる.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese lower bigrade verb *awatu* (慌つ, 'to be flustered, lose one's composure, panic'), attested in the Nihon Shoki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: be flustered; be thrown into confusion
hurry in confusion; panic; be flustered

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 慌てる

慕う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese *sitapu* (したふ, modern 慕う shitau), built on the directional/spatial root *sita* (下, 'below, beneath; deep inside the heart', cf. Old Japanese *sita-gokoro* 'secret/innermost heart') plus the iterative/intensive verbal suffix *-pu*. Originally meant 'to follow closely behind someone (as an inferior following a superior or a child trailing a parent), unable to bear separation', evolving naturally into 'to yearn after, adore, look up to with fond devotion'. Orthographically matched with Chinese 慕 (Middle Chinese muH, 'to long for, admire').

history.meaning: to follow closely after someone one cannot bear to part from; to yearn for
to long for, miss fondly, revere and follow a mentor or loved one
to adore, look up to fondly, yearn for (especially a respected leader, parent, or departed loved one)

morphemes.meaning: beneath, following behind; innermost heart (Old Japanese *sita)

慕う.notes: Often used in the passive 慕われる (shitawareru, 'to be beloved and looked up to by subordinates/followers', e.g., 部下に慕われる上司).

rootFamily.gloss: yearning, adoration, longing (Sino-Japanese reading of 慕)
rootFamily.word: 思慕 (しぼ) / 敬慕 (けいぼ)

rootFamily.gloss: to obey, follow along behind (sharing the *sita- root)

憎い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) i-adjective descending from Old Japanese stem *niku-* (adverbial *nikuku*, classical conclusive *nikusi*). Etymologically linked to the verbal root seen in 憎む (nikumu, 'to hate, detest', formed with deadjectival *-m-*) and the grammaticalized auxiliary adjective -にくい (-nikui, 'hard to do, awkward, resistant to doing'). Originally denoted something unpleasant, refractory, or provoking irritation because it resists one's wishes, whence 'odious, detestable, hateful' (and by playful inversion in Edo and modern speech, 'annoyingly good/impressive').

history.meaning: disagreeable, unpleasant, provoking irritation or resentment
history.stage: Old & Early Middle Japanese (e.g., Makura no Sōshi 'Nikuki mono')

history.meaning: hateful, detestable, resented; (ironically) admirably clever or cool

憎い.notes: Besides literal hatred, 憎い is frequently used in playful praise (憎い演出だね, 'What a delightfully clever touch!' — so good it makes you jealous), and as a verb suffix -にくい it simply means 'difficult to' (読みにくい, 'hard to read').

憧れる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb descending from Old and Early Middle Japanese あこがる (*akogaru*, lower-bigrade / shimo-nidan), transparently analyzed as *ako* ('place, where one is', related to そこ soko / ここ koko / あそこ asoko) + 離る (*karu*, 'to separate, depart, drift away from', voiced to *-garu* via rendaku). Originally meant literally 'to wander away from one's place'—and in Heian waka poetry (such as by Izumi Shikibu), 'for one's soul or heart to float away from one's body in restless longing'. By the modern era, this 'soul-wandering' narrowed positively into 'to yearn after, idolize, aspire to be like'. Orthographically assigned the character 憧 (Middle Chinese tsyhowng, 'unsettle, waver in mind').

history.form: あこがる (akogaru = ako 'place/here' + karu 'to part from')
history.meaning: to wander away from a place; for one's spirit/heart to drift away from the body in restless longing
to yearn for, admirefrom afar, aspire to an ideal person or lifestyle

morphemes.meaning: place, locus, where one belongs (archaic demonstrative root *ako)
to separate from, drift away from (archaic verb 離る karu > ichidan -gareru)

憧れる.notes: Takes the particle に for the target of admiration (都会の生活に憧れる, 'to yearn for city life'). Its poetic Heian origin—'one's soul floating out of one's body toward something distant'—captures why 憧れる implies admiring something slightly out of reach.

rootFamily.gloss: yearning, aspiration, object of admiration (noun stem)
yearning, longing (formal Sino-Japanese compound using 憧)
rootFamily.word: 憧憬 (しょうけい / どうけい)

rootFamily.gloss: to part from, separate (cognate second element *karu)
rootFamily.word: 離れる (はなれる / かれる)

懐かしい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) shiku-adjective derived from the native verb 懐く (natsuku, Old Japanese *natuku*, 'to become attached, grow fond and familiar, cling close to'), extended with the desiderative/emotional adjective formant *-asi-* (modern -ashii, cf. 羨ましい urayamashii from 羨む urayamu, 嘆かわしい nagekawashii from 嘆く nageku). In Old and Heian Japanese, *natukasi* meant 'drawing the heart close, endearing, charmingly familiar, hard to part from' (even of a present person or flower); from the medieval period onward, it shifted toward 'fondly remembered from the past, evoking warm nostalgia'. Orthographically written with 懐 ('bosom, pocket next to the heart; to hold in the bosom').

history.form: なつかし (natukasi, from verb natuku 'to cling/grow attached')
history.meaning: endearing, drawing one's heart close, charmingly familiar
fondly remembered, dear, nostalgic, missed from the past

morphemes.meaning: to grow attached, keep close to the bosom (native verb stem 懐く natsuk-)

懐かしい.notes: One of the most culturally loaded words in Japanese: exclaiming 懐かしい！ (Natsukashii!) upon seeing an old song, toy, or hometown expresses warm, happy fondness for shared memories, without the painful homesickness of English 'nostalgia'.

rootFamily.gloss: to become emotionally attached, warm up to (of children/pets)

rootFamily.word: 人懐っこい (ひとなつっこい)

rootFamily.gloss: bosom, breast pocket; one's wallet/inner space (noun behind 懐)

懐中電灯.etymology: Meiji/Taishō-era Sino-Japanese compound 懐中電灯 (kaichū dentō), combining 懐中 ('inside the breast pocket, pocket-sized') + 電灯 ('electric lamp/light').

history.form: 懐中電灯 (かいちゅうでんとう)
history.meaning: flashlight; electric torch

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 懐中電灯

cognates.meaning: penal servitude, imprisonment with labor (borrowed from Meiji Japanese law)
imprisonment, penal servitude (re-borrowed from Meiji legal terminology)

懲役.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound coined in early Meiji Japan (1870 *Shinritsu Kōryō* / New Penal Code Outline) to modernize traditional Tokugawa punishments (such as banishment and stockade labor) along Western penitentiary lines. Composed of 懲 (chō, Middle Chinese drjeng, 'to chastise, discipline, correct through punishment') and 役 (eki, Middle Chinese ywek, 'corvée labor, compulsory service'). Literally 'corrective labor', denoting imprisonment with mandatory prison work (contrasted in Japanese criminal law with 禁錮 kinko, imprisonment without forced labor).

history.meaning: to chastise/correct + compulsory labor service

history.form: 懲役 (chōeki, Meiji Penal Code of 1870)
history.meaning: penal servitude, prison sentence with mandatory corrective labor

morphemes.meaning: to chastise, discipline, warn by punishment (Middle Chinese drjeng)

懲役.notes: In courtroom and crime dramas, sentences are announced as 懲役X年 (chōeki X-nen, 'X years of imprisonment with labor'). Note that in 2022 Japan passed a penal reform merging 懲役 and 禁錮 into a unified sentence called 拘禁刑 (kōkinkei, effective 2025).

rootFamily.gloss: to learn one's lesson the hard way, be chastened (native verb)

rootFamily.word: 苦役 (くえき) / 使役 (しえき)

懸かる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive five-grade (godan) verb kakaru ('to hang, be suspended, depend on, be at stake'), forming a classic transitivity pair with transitive 懸ける / 掛ける (kakeru, 'to hang, suspend, stake'). Reconstructed from a pre-Old Japanese verbal root *kak-* ('to hook, latch onto, suspend') + the intransitive suffix *-ar-* (parallel to 上がる agaru vs. 上げる ageru, 止まる tomaru vs. 止める tomeru). While general 'to hang/take time' is written 掛かる, the kanji 懸 (Middle Chinese hwen, 'to suspend in midair, hang anxiously in the balance', with 心 'heart' beneath 県 'suspended head') specifically highlights high-stakes suspense: a prize, life, honor, or fate hanging on the line.

history.meaning: to be hung, catch on, depend upon, rest upon
to hang in the balance, be at stake (life, fortune, honor), be offered as a prize

懸かる.notes: When spelled with 懸 (rather than 掛), 懸かる signals high drama or risk: 命が懸かっている (inochi ga kakatte iru, 'lives are on the line') or 賞金が懸かる ('a cash prize is at stake').

rootFamily.gloss: devotion of one's whole life/effort, risking everything
rootFamily.word: 命懸け (いのちがけ) / 一生懸命 (いっしょうけんめい)

懸ける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive lower-monograde (shimo-ichidan) verb kakeru ('to hang up, suspend, wager, stake'), descending from Old Japanese *kaku* (lower-bigrade stem *kake-*), formed from the root *kak-* ('to hook, suspend') + the transitive/causative formant *-e-* (contrast intransitive 懸かる kakaru < *kak-ar-u*). Orthographically differentiated in modern Japanese: 掛ける covers everyday hanging, sitting, or multiplying, 賭ける means gambling on a game of chance, and 懸ける (using Chinese 懸, 'to suspend high with an anxious heart') specifically means to stake one's life, pride, fortune, or passion on a decisive endeavor.

history.meaning: to hang, suspend, attach, set one's heart upon
to stake (one's life, honor, future), offer a prize, hang in suspense

morphemes.meaning: transitive ichidan verbal ending (< Old Japanese *-e-ru)

懸ける.notes: Three kanji split the sense of 'bet/stake/hang' for kakeru: 掛ける (hang a coat, spend time), 賭ける (bet money on horse racing/gambling), and 懸ける (stake one's life, dreams, or career: 人生を懸ける, 'to stake one's whole life on it').

rootFamily.gloss: to be at stake, hang on the line (intransitive counterpart)
to gamble, wager (homophonous specialization of the same native verb)

成り上がる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb uniting 成り (nari, the continuative stem of 成る naru, Old Japanese *naru* 'to become, come into being, bear fruit, be promoted') and 上がる (agaru, Old Japanese *agaru* 'to rise, ascend, move up in rank'). Originally used in shogi (where a pawn or minor piece 'promotes' — 成る naru — upon entering the opponent's camp) and in medieval/Edo social mobility for someone of humble birth rising rapidly to wealth, high rank, or power.┴In *The Naked Director*, it encapsulates the quintessential rags-to-riches ambition of postwar Japan.

history.meaning: to rise in status or rank from a lowly position; to promote (in board games/ranks)
to rise from the bottom to wealth and fame, make it big from nothing

morphemes.meaning: to become, transform into, be promoted (continuative stem of 成る naru)
to rise, ascend, climb in status (native intransitive verb)

成り上がる.notes: While the noun 成り上がり (nariagari) or 成金 (narikin, literally a shogi pawn promoted to gold general) can sound snobbish ('parvenu, nouveau riche, upstart'), the verb 成り上がる is also used proudly in rock, sports, and entrepreneurship for clawing one's way from rock bottom to the top.

rootFamily.word: 成り上がり (なりあがり)

rootFamily.gloss: nouveau riche (from a shogi piece promoting to a Gold General)
to become, come to be; promote in shogi

成功.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from Classical Chinese 成功 (Middle Chinese dzyeng-kuwng, attested in the *Book of Documents* / *Shangshu* and *Analects*), originally a verb-object phrase meaning 'to bring a public work or meritorious task (功) to completion (成)'. In Meiji Japan—famously popularized by Nakamura Masanao's 1871 translation of Samuel Smiles's *Self-Help* (*Saikoku Risshi Hen*) and early 20th-century *seikō* ('success') magazines—成功 took on its modern capitalist and personal-ambition sense of 'achieving worldly success, wealth, or fame'.

history.meaning: to accomplish a meritorious deed or state project; completed achievement
completion of a Buddhist/court building project in exchange for court rank (Heian–Kamakura); worldly 'success' in Meiji–Modern Japanese

morphemes.meaning: to complete, accomplish, become (Middle Chinese dzyeng)
meritorious deed, work, achievement (Middle Chinese kuwng)

成功.notes: Fascinating historical trivia: in Heian-period court bureaucracy, the same kanji 成功 were read *jōgō* and referred to a wealthy provincial governor funding a temple or palace construction project in exchange for official reappointment!

cognates.meaning: achievement, positive result, fruit of labor

成果.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 成 (sei, Middle Chinese dzyeng, 'to complete, bring to maturity, accomplish') and 果 (ka, Middle Chinese kwaX, 'fruit on a tree; outcome, realization', originally a pictograph of fruit  田 atop a tree 木, and used in Buddhism for Sanskrit *phala* 'karmic fruit/result'). Literally 'the ripened fruit of what one has accomplished', denoting tangible positive results yielded by effort, training, or investment.

history.meaning: to mature/complete + tree fruit / karmic outcome
tangible results, fruits of one's labor or research

morphemes.meaning: to accomplish, bring to maturity (Middle Chinese dzyeng)
fruit, outcome, positive result (Middle Chinese kwaX)

成果.notes: Unlike 結果 (kekka), which is a neutral 'result/outcome' (good or bad), 成果 (seika) almost always implies positive 'fruits/payoff' earned through hard work (練習の成果が出る, 'the fruits of practice pay off'; 成果主義, 'performance-based pay system').

cognates.meaning: to be established, to be founded, to hold water

成立.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 成 (/d͡ʑiᴇŋ/, "to complete, accomplish, become") and 立 (/liɪp̚/, "to stand, establish, set up"). Originally referring to the successful erection of an institution or completion of a structure, it developed the legal and commercial sense of a contract, deal, or hypothesis coming into valid existence.

history.meaning: to accomplish and establish; to stand completed
coming into existence, materialization, conclusion of a deal or argument

成立.notes: Used with する (成立する) in business and law when a contract, bargain, or crime is formally satisfied ("the deal went through"). Pitch accent is flat (heiban, [0]).

我々.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) pronoun formed by full reduplication of Old Japanese 我 (ware, "I, oneself, we"), itself an extended form of the ancient first-person root *wa- with the pronominal suffix -re (compare kare, tare). spelled logographically with the Chinese character 我 ("I, self") and the iteration mark 々. Reduplication marks collective plurality ("we all").

history.meaning: I, oneself; first-person singular or unspecifed pronoun
we, people like us (collective plural)
history.stage: Early Middle Japanese to Modern Japanese

我々.notes: Carries a formal, public, or corporate tone ("we as an organization/group"); frequently used by executives, politicians, and in boardroom speeches.

我が社.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the classical Japanese adnominal possessive phrase 我が (wa ga, from Old Japanese first-person pronoun wa + possessive case particle ga, "my, our") with the Sino-Japanese noun 社 (sha, from Middle Chinese /d͡ʑiaX/, originally "altar of the soil deity, community", later "association, business firm").

history.meaning: my, our (first-person pronoun + genitive particle)
our company, our firm (formal corporate self-reference)

我が社.notes: Used internally among colleagues or by company presidents in speeches to rally employees ("our firm"). When speaking to outsiders/clients with humility, 弊社 (heisha) is required instead.

我ら.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) plural pronoun composed of Old Japanese 我 (ware, "I, self", from root *wa- + pronominal suffix -re) and the pluralizing collective suffix -ら (-ra, originally a locative/collective marker in Old Japanese). Preserves an older plural formation alongside reduplicated 我々 (wareware).

history.meaning: we, I and my companions (humble or collective plural)
we, us (literary, rhetorical, or dramatic solidarity)

我ら.notes: Has a literary, dramatic, or solidarity-invoking ring ("we comrades/fellows"), often followed by が (我らが, "our beloved/champion...").

戦.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun いくさ (ikusa, or read たたかい tatakai as a verbal noun), written logographically with the kanji 戦 ("war, battle"). In Old Japanese, ikusa originally meant an "armed troop, army" or "military expedition", likely derived from *i- (sacred/intensive prefix or arrow root *ya-) + *kusa ("group, troop, kind"), before shifting in Middle Japanese to mean "battle, warfare" itself.

history.meaning: soldiers, army, military host; shooting arrows in battle
battle, combat, war, campaign

戦.notes: When read いくさ (ikusa), it evokes samurai warfare or metaphorical high-stakes turf wars ("going into battle"). As a Sino-Japanese suffix -せん (-sen), it means "match, bout, campaign" (e.g., 宣伝戦).

戦う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb たたかう (tatakau < historical tatakafu), derived from the verb 叩く (tataku, "to strike, beat, hit", itself an onomatopoetic/iterative stem *tatak-) plus the continuous/reciprocal verbal suffix -ふ (-fu > -u, indicating mutual or repeated action). Literally "to strike at one another repeatedly", hence "to fight, wage battle, struggle".

history.meaning: to exchange blows, engage in combat, fight
to fight, battle, compete, struggle against obstacles or rivals

morphemes.part: たたか- (tataka-, from 叩く tataku)

戦う.notes: By convention, 戦う is used for organized battles, competitions, or ideological struggles, whereas homophonous 闘う emphasizes grappling against inner adversity, illness, or oppression.

戻す.etymology: Transitive godan verb *modosu* ('to put back, return, restore, vomit'), paired with intransitive もどる (戻る).

history.meaning: turn back; restore to an earlier state
put back; return; restore; reconstitute

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 戻す

戻る.etymology: Intransitive godan verb *modoru* ('to turn back, return'), attested in classical Japanese in the sense 'to twist back, go against, turn around', whence 'to return to a point of departure'.

history.meaning: go counter to; twist back; return
return; go back; turn back

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 戻る

所.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *to₂ko₂ro₂* (所・処, 'place, spot, locality'), formed from spatial root *to₂ko₂* (compare 床 'bed/platform') + suffix *-ro₂*.

history.meaning: place; locality; point
place; spot; aspect; just about to

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 所

所有権.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound forged during the Meiji-era translation of European civil law (specifically French droit de propriete and German Eigentumsrecht). Combines 所有 (shoyuu, "possession, owning", from Classical Chinese 所 "that which" + 有 "to have, possess") with the suffix 権 (-ken, from Middle Chinese /ɡiwan/, "steelyard weight, power, authority", repurposed in Meiji Japan to translate Western legal "right").

history.meaning: that which one possesses; holdings
legal right of ownership, title to property or copyright assets

所有権.notes: Crucial in media and real-estate business contexts (such as master tape ownership or property rights). Pronounced with pitch drop before 権 (しょゆ↓うけん).

扇風機.etymology: Meiji/Taishō Sino-Japanese coinage 扇風機 (せんぷうき), combining 扇 ('fan, stir breeze'), 風 ('wind'), and 機 ('machine').
扇風機.notes: Coined in Japan for early electric fans and adopted across East Asia (compare Korean 선풍기).

扉.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun とびら (tobira), derived from Old Japanese 戸 (to, "door, entrance, shutter") + ひら (pira > hira, "flat thin object, leaf, panel, petal", triggering rendaku voicing *p > b). Literally "door-leaf" or "hinged door panel", written with the single kanji 扉 (consisting of 戸 "door" + phonetic/semantic 非 "two wings spreading apart").

history.meaning: hinged wooden door leaf or double-door panel
swinging door, gate leaf; frontispiece or title page; metaphorical portal to a new era

morphemes.meaning: flat panel, leaf, sheet (< hira 平/枚)

扉.notes: Unlike ドア (ordinary Western door) or 戸 (sliding door), 扉 refers to substantial hinged doors, double doors, vault doors, or figuratively "the door to a new world/future" (新しい時代の扉を開く).

手.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *te* (compound combining form *ta-*, 'hand, arm, skill, handwriting, means'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: hand; arm; handle; skill
hand; arm; effort; means; move (in games)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 手

手がかり.etymology: Compound of 手 (te, 'hand') + 掛かり (kakari, 'hanging/catching/hold'). Literally 'something for the hand to catch hold of', extending metaphorically to 'clue' or 'lead'.

history.meaning: handhold/clue

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 手がかり

手のひら.etymology: Lexicalized native Japanese genitive compound consisting of 手 (te, 'hand'), the possessive particle の (no), and ひら (hira, written 平, 'flat surface, broad side'). Attested since Old and Classical Japanese (alongside the older compound たなごころ tanagokoro, 'heart of the hand'), 手のひら literally names 'the flat part of the hand', i.e., the palm.

history.meaning: the flat inner surface of the hand; palm
palm of the hand

手のひら.notes: Most often written 手のひら (or 手の平) in modern prose.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 手のひら

手仕事.etymology: Native Japanese compound combining て (手, 'hand') + しごと (仕事, 'work, craft'), meaning manual craftwork or handiwork.

history.meaning: handiwork; manual labor; handicraft

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 手仕事

手付.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 手 (te, "hand") + 付 (tsuke, nominalized stem of つける tsukeru, "to attach, apply, seal"). Originally denoted placing one's handprint or token on goods to mark a binding reservation; in commercial usage (often shortened from 手付金 tetsukekin), it came to mean earnest money or a down payment paid to seal a contract.

history.meaning: touching with the hand; a pledge token or earnest payment binding a sale
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese (Edo period)

history.meaning: earnest money, deposit, down payment, retainer fee

拒む.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb こばむ (kobamu), attested since Early Middle Japanese.
