history.meaning: to stand firm against, obstruct, resist, refuse entry or compliance
to refuse, reject, turn away, spurn, balk at

morphemes.meaning: resist, refuse, turn away (likely < *kopa- "stiff, unyielding" + verbalizer -mu)

拒む.notes: More literary and dramatic than 断る (kotowaru, "to decline politely/practically"); 拒む evokes actively blocking, spurning, or refusing to yield (e.g., 受け取りを拒む, "to refuse acceptance", or 行く手を拒む, "to bar someone's path").

rootFamily.gloss: flat refusal, total rejection, allergy/visceral aversion

rootFamily.word: 強い / 強ばる (こわい / こわばる)

拒否.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 拒 (/ɡiʌX/, "to ward off with the hand, resist, repel, refuse") and 否 (/pɨuX/, "not, no, to negate, disapprove"). Combines active resistance (拒) with categorical negation (否) to express formal or resolute refusal, rejection, or veto.

history.meaning: to ward off/repel + to say no/negate
categorical refusal, rejection, denial, veto (of a demand, testimony, or bill)

拒否.notes: Stronger and more official than 断り (kotowari). Used in legal and political contexts such as 証言拒否 ("refusal to testify"), 拒否権 ("veto power"), and 着信拒否 ("blocking incoming calls").

rootFamily.gloss: to refuse, reject, turn away (native verb)

招待.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 招 (/t͡ɕiɛu/, "to beckon with the hand, summon, invite") and 待 (/dʌiX/, "to wait for, await, treat or entertain a guest"). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., Sima Qian's Shiji) in the sense of summoning worthy guests and treating them hospitably; in Japanese it specifically means extending an invitation as host (often covering all expenses).

history.meaning: to summon/beckon and hospitably entertain guests
invitation to an event, banquet, or VIP preview as an honored guest

招待.notes: False friend with Mandarin: in Japanese, 招待 means "invitation (as a non-paying guest)", whereas in Mandarin 招待 (zhaodai) primarily means "to entertain/serve guests, hospitality". In Japanese, "hospitality/entertaining clients" is 接待 (settai).

rootFamily.word: 招待状 (しょうたいじょう)

rootFamily.gloss: corporate entertaining, wining and dining clients

拡大.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 拡 (simplified shinjitai of 擴, /kʰwɑk̚/, "to stretch out, widen, extend the boundaries of") and 大 (/dɑiH/, "big, great, large"). Literally "stretching out to make large", used for scaling up business operations, market share, territory, or optical magnification.

history.meaning: to stretch/widen + large/great
expansion, enlargement, scaling up, magnification

拡大.notes: Focuses on increasing the size, scale, or volume of a single entity or operation (e.g., 事業拡大, "business expansion / scaling up"; 拡大鏡, "magnifying glass"). Contrast with 拡散 (kakusan, dispersing outward in many directions).

rootFamily.gloss: expansion, extension (of facilities, power, or territory)

rootFamily.word: 拡大鏡 (かくだいきょう)

cognates.meaning: to diffuse, spread out, proliferate, metastasize

拡散.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 拡 (simplified shinjitai of 擴, /kʰwɑk̚/, "to stretch out, widen, extend") and 散 (/sɑnH/, "to scatter, disperse, break up, strew"). Originally a scientific term translating physical "diffusion" (of gases, light, or particles), it broadened to mean the rapid outward spread of rumors, media content, or disease.

history.meaning: to widen/extend + to scatter/disperse
physical diffusion; wide dispersal or viral spreading of information, goods, or contagion

拡散.notes: While 拡大 means growing larger in scale or size, 拡散 means scattering or spreading widely across many points (used for physical diffusion, word-of-mouth distribution, and modern social media "going viral / sharing widely").

rootFamily.word: 散る / 散らす (ちる / ちらす)

rootFamily.gloss: dissolution, breaking up (a group or parliament)

拭き跡.etymology: Native Japanese compound combining ふき (拭き, continuative stem of 拭く 'to wipe') + あと (跡, 'mark, trace, streak').

history.meaning: wipe mark; streak left after wiping

wipe; dry; mop

持ちこたえる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 持ち (mochi, the continuative stem of 持つ motsu, 'to hold, to maintain', from Old Japanese motu) + こたえる (kotaeru, written 堪える, 'to endure, to withstand', from Late Middle Japanese kotafuru / kotayuru). Literally 'to hold and withstand', describing holding one's ground or keeping something intact against pressure or adversity.

持ちつ持たれつ.etymology: An idiomatic Yamato (wago) phrase preserving the classical Japanese correlative suffix -つ (-tsu, originally the terminal form of the perfective auxiliary つ tsu, paired as ...つ...つ to express alternating or reciprocal actions) attached to the active stem 持ち (mochi, 'holding/supporting') and the passive stem 持たれ (motare, 'being held/supported'). Literally 'sometimes supporting, sometimes being supported'.

history.meaning: supporting and being supported in turn
mutual give-and-take, interdependence

morphemes.meaning: to hold, to support (ren'youkei of 持つ)
classical correlative marker indicating alternating action
to be held, to be supported (passive ren'youkei of 持つ)
classical correlative marker indicating alternating action

持ちつ持たれつ.notes: A fossilized classical grammatical pattern (...つ...つ, like 行きつ戻りつ 'going back and forth'); often used in business or relationships to stress mutual dependence.

持ち上げる.etymology: Compound verb combining the continuative stem もち (持ち, from 持つ 'to hold') + あげる (上げる, 'to raise, lift up'); also used figuratively for 'to flatter'.

history.meaning: lift up in one's hands; praise highly

history.form: 持ち上げる (もちあげる)
history.meaning: lift up; raise; flatter

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 持ち上げる

持ち主.etymology: Native Japanese compound combining もち (持ち, 'holding, possessing') + ぬし (主, 'master, owner').

owner; possessor

持ち帰る.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb combining 持ち (mochi, the continuative stem of 持つ motsu, 'to hold, to carry', from Old Japanese motu) + 帰る (kaeru, 'to return, to go home', from Old Japanese kaferu < *kapey-ru). Literally 'to carry and return home', evolving both a literal sense ('to take home') and a commercial sense ('to buy takeout food').

to return, to go back home

持ち帰る.notes: Its nominalized form お持ち帰り (omochikaeri) means 'takeout/to-go' at restaurants, but in nightlife slang it also means 'taking someone home for the night'.

持ち手.etymology: Native Japanese compound combining もち (持ち, 'holding, carrying') + て (手, 'hand; handle; person who does').

history.meaning: handle; grip; strap (of a bag); bearer/owner

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 持ち手

持ち歩く.etymology: Compound godan verb combining もち (持ち, 'hold, carry') + あるく (歩く, 'walk, go about').

history.meaning: carry around with one
carry around; carry on one's person

持ち逃げ.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) nominalized compound formed from the continuative stems of two verbs: 持ち (mochi, from 持つ motsu, 'to hold, to carry', Old Japanese motu) + 逃げ (nige, from 逃げる nigeru, 'to flee, to run away', Old Japanese nigu). Literally 'carrying and fleeing', referring to absconding with entrusted money or goods.

history.meaning: fleeing while carrying away another's property or funds
running off with money or goods, absconding

morphemes.meaning: to hold, to carry in hand (ren'youkei of 持つ)
fleeing, running away (ren'youkei of 逃げる)

持ち逃げ.notes: Functions as both a noun and a する (suru) verb (持ち逃げする); parallels compounds like 食い逃げ (kuinige, 'dine and dash') and 乗り逃げ (norinige, 'skipping out on a fare').

rootFamily.gloss: dine and dash, eating and running

持っていく.etymology: Native Yamato directional compound verb built from 持って (motte, the conjunctive te-form of 持つ motsu 'to hold, take in hand') plus the motion verb いく / 行く (iku, 'to go away from the current location'). Literally 'hold and go', it expresses taking or carrying an object from where the speaker is to another destination.

history.meaning: to take in hand and go
to take along, carry away (there)

morphemes.meaning: deictic motion verb 'to go (away from here)'

持っていく.notes: Forms a deictic pair with 持ってくる ('hold and come' = 'bring here'): 持っていく moves away toward a destination ('take there').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 持っていく

持ってくる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) syntactic verb construction combining 持って (motte, the conjunctive -te form with geminate assimilation /促音便 sokuonbin of 持ちて mochite, from 持つ motsu, 'to hold, to carry', Old Japanese motu) + くる (kuru, written 来る, directional subsidiary verb 'to come', Old Japanese ku). Because Japanese lacks a monomorphemic verb for 'bring', it serializes 'take/hold and come'.

history.meaning: to take in hand and come toward the speaker
to bring (something toward the speaker's deictic center)
to bring, to fetch and come back with

morphemes.meaning: holding, carrying (te-form of 持つ motsu < mochite)
to come (indicating motion toward the speaker)

持ってくる.notes: Strictly used for inanimate objects (or plants/small creatures); for bringing a person or higher animal, Japanese requires 連れてくる (tsurete kuru) instead.

rootFamily.gloss: to take away, to carry and go
to bring a person or animal along

持つ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *mo₂tu* (持つ, 'to take in the hand, hold, carry, possess'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: hold in the hand; carry; possess
hold; carry; have; possess; last/endure

finger; toe

指す.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *sasu* (指す・差す, 'to point toward, indicate, aim for, nominate'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

point to; indicate; name; play (shogi)

指切り.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun from 指 (yubi, 'finger', shifted in Early Middle Japanese from Old Japanese oyobi / yobi) + 切り (kiri, the nominalized stem of 切る kiru, 'to cut, to sever', Old Japanese kiru). Originally an Edo-period pleasure-quarter (遊廓 yuukaku) custom where a courtesan literally amputated the tip of her little finger to prove undying fidelity to a patron; later softened into a children's ritual of hooking pinkies to seal a vow.

history.meaning: literally severing a fingertip as a courtesan's pledge of love and fidelity
pinky promise, interlocking little fingers to seal an oath

morphemes.meaning: finger (especially the little finger in this compound)
cutting, severing (nominalized ren'youkei of 切る)

指切り.notes: Famous from the children's rhyme 指切りげんまん、嘘ついたら針千本飲ます ('Pinky promise, ten thousand fist-strikes; if you lie, I'll make you swallow a thousand needles').

rootFamily.gloss: pinky swear rhyme with fist-strike pledge

指切る.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 指 (yubi, 'finger', from Old Japanese oyobi) + 切る (kiru, 'to cut, to sever, to cross/interlock', from Old Japanese kiru), or as a back-formed verbalization of the noun 指切り (yubikiri, 'pinky promise'). While originally referring to the literal Edo-period practice of severing a pinky tip as an oath, in colloquial speech it means to interlock little fingers to seal a promise.

history.meaning: to cut off a finger as a pledge; to interlock fingers in an oath
to make a pinky promise, to hook pinkies on an oath

morphemes.meaning: to cut, to cross or seal decisively

指切る.notes: In standard prose, the nominal phrase 指切りをする (yubikiri o suru) is far more common, whereas verbal 指切る (often in past tense 指切った！ 'Promised!') is lively and colloquial.

指図.etymology: Sino-Japanese / hybrid medieval compound 指図 (sashizu), combining 指 ('point with the finger, indicate') + 図 ('plan, diagram'). Originally 'pointing out on a plan; architectural blueprint' in Kamakura/Muromachi usage, whence 'directions, orders, instructions'.

history.meaning: floor plan; pointing out instructions
instruction; direction; order; command

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 指図

指定.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound built from Middle Chinese roots: 指 (shi < Middle Chinese *tɕiɪX, 'finger; to point out, to indicate') + 定 (tei < kan'on reading of Middle Chinese *dengH, 'to fix, to settle, to establish'). Literally 'to point out and fix definitely', hence 'designation, specification, appointment'.

history.meaning: pointing out and fixing or determining officially
designation, specification, appointment

morphemes.meaning: to fix, to settle, to determine (MC *dengH)

指定.notes: Ubiquitous in daily life for reserved train/theater seating (指定席 shiteiseki) as well as legal designations like 指定暴力団 ('designated yakuza syndicate').

指揮権.etymology: Compound of 指揮 (shiki, command) and 権 (ken, right/authority).

history.meaning: right of command

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 指揮権

指示.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 指示, composed of 指 (shi < Middle Chinese *tɕiɪX, 'finger; to point with a finger') + 示 (ji < go-on reading of Middle Chinese *ʑiɪH, 'to show, to manifest, originally an altar sign from heaven'). Literally 'to point at and show', evolving into 'instructions, directions, operational orders'.

history.meaning: to point out and show clearly to someone
instructions, directions, orders; demonstration

morphemes.meaning: to show, to display, to indicate (MC *ʑiɪH, go-on reading ji)

指示.notes: Note the voiced go-on reading じ (ji) for 示 here (contrast kan'on し shi in 示唆 shisa 'suggestion'); takes する (shiji suru) or the phrase 指示を出す ('to issue instructions').

挑む.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) verb attested since Old Japanese as idomu ('to contend, to vie for, to court assertively'), written with the semantic kanji 挑 ('to provoke, to challenge'). In Heian literature it frequently described either martial defiance or ardent amorous wooing; in Modern Japanese it means to boldly challenge an opponent, record, or daunting endeavor.

history.meaning: to vie with, to contend against, to woo or court assertively
to challenge, to take on, to defy, to make a bid for

morphemes.meaning: to challenge, to contend with, to take on

挑む.notes: Takes the particle に (ni) to mark the target or challenge (e.g., 記録に挑む 'to challenge a record', 戦いに挑む 'to take on a fight'); shares the kanji 挑 with Sino-Japanese 挑戦 (chousen).

rootFamily.gloss: provocation, stirring up (kango sharing the kanji)

挑戦.etymology: Sino-Japanese word. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: to challenge to battle
challenge

挑戦.notes: Originally meant challenging to a battle.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 挑戦

get caught between; be wedged; be sandwiched

The nominalized stem 挟み (hasami < Old Japanese fasami) gave rise to the Japanese word for 'scissors, pincers, crab claws'—literally 'the pincher'.

挟む.notes: Used both physically (パンにハムを挟む 'to sandwich ham in bread') and figuratively (口を挟む 'to butt into a conversation', 疑問を挟む 'to harbor doubts').

to be caught or sandwiched between (intransitive)

挨拶.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 挨拶 (aisatsu), from Zen Buddhist Chinese 挨拶 ('pressing forward and pushing against one another' — testing a disciple's awakening through verbal exchange), which broadened in Early Modern Japanese to 'polite exchange, greeting, salutation'.

history.meaning: exchange of probing questions and answers between master and monk
verbal exchange; mediation; polite greeting
greeting; salutation; formal address/speech

振らせる.etymology: The regular causative derivation of the native Yamato (wago) verb 振る (furu < Old Japanese furu, 'to wave, to shake, to swing, to cast'), formed by attaching the productive causative auxiliary suffix -せる (-seru, from earlier -saseru / Classical -su) to the irrealis stem (mizenkei) 振ら- (fura-). to make (someone) shake/wave/nod; to make someone reject; to have assigned

振らせる.notes: Because 振る (furu) appears in idioms like 首を縦に振る ('to nod yes', lit. 'shake one's head vertically') and 男を振る ('to dump a man'), 振らせる takes on vivid context-dependent meanings.

to be shaken; to be dumped romantically (passive)

振り仮名.etymology: A hybrid Yamato compound noun formed from 振り (furi, the continuative stem of 振る furu, 'to shake, to sprinkle, to attach/assign Alongside', Old Japanese furu) + 仮名 (kana, 'syllabic script', phonological reduction via kanna < karina of 仮 kar-i 'borrowed/temporary' + 名 na 'name, character'). history.meaning: phonetic kana glosses printed or written beside kanji characters
pronunciation kana, ruby characters glossing kanji readings

morphemes.meaning: attaching, sprinkling alongside (ren'youkei of 振る)

振り仮名.notes: The verb for adding furigana is 振る (e.g., ルビを振る / 振り仮名を振る 'to attach reading glosses'); in printing and web typography, it is also called ルビ (rubi, from English 'ruby' 5.5-point type).

okurigana, inflectional kana following a kanji stem

振り向く.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb combining 振り (furi, the continuative stem of 振る furu, 'to swing, to turn one's head or body briskly', Old Japanese furu) + 向く (muku, 'to face, to turn toward', Old Japanese muku). morphemes.meaning: to swing, to turn briskly (ren'youkei of 振る)

振り向く.notes: In negative contexts like 見向きもしない / 振り向きもしない ('not even turning to look'), it figuratively means to completely ignore someone's romantic or professional overtures.

rootFamily.gloss: to look back, to reflect on the past
to turn around (one's whole body or head)

振り込む.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb from 振り (furi, the continuative stem of 振る furu, 'to shake, to sprinkle, to allocate/transfer across accounts', Old Japanese furu) + 込む (komu, 'to put into, to move inward', Late Middle Japanese komu). Originally meaning 'to sprinkle or pour into (e.g. salt or seasoning)', in modern banking and postal systems it became the standard term for wiring or transferring funds into a bank account.

history.meaning: to sprinkle or pour something into a vessel; to allocate into
to wire money, to make a bank transfer or deposit into an account

morphemes.meaning: to shake, to allocate, to transfer (ren'youkei of 振る)
to go into, to put inside, to deposit into

振り込む.notes: Its nominalized form 振り込み (furikomi, 'bank transfer') is central to Japanese commerce—and notoriously appears in 振り込め詐欺 (furikome sagi, 'wire-transfer phone scams targeting the elderly').

rootFamily.gloss: to pay into, to deposit, to cram into

振り返る.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb composed of 振り (furi, the continuative stem of 振る furu, 'to swing, to turn briskly', Old Japanese furu) + 返る (kaeru, 'to turn back, to reverse direction', Old Japanese kaferu). to turn back, to reverse, to return

rootFamily.gloss: to turn toward, to look around at
to turn over, to return, to reverse

振る.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *puru* (振る, 'to wave, shake, swing, brandish'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: shake; wave; swing

支店長.etymology: Three-kanji Sino-Japanese (kango) institutional compound formed by adding the title suffix 長 (chou, from Middle Chinese *trjangX, 'elder, chief, head') to 支店 (shiten, 'branch office/store', itself composed of 支 shi, MC *tsje, 'branch, offshoot, limb', and 店 ten, MC *temH, 'shop, commercial establishment'). Coined during Japan's modern banking and corporate expansion to designate the head manager of a regional branch office.

history.meaning: branch/limb + shop/inn + elder/chief
head of a commercial or banking branch office

history.form: 支店長 (してんちょう, shitenchou)
history.meaning: branch manager (of a bank, corporation, or retail chain)

支店長.notes: Like 社長 (shachou) and 部長 (buchou), 支店長 is used directly as a polite vocative title by subordinates and clients without attaching -san (Calling someone「支店長さん」sounds Either overly folksy or patronizing).

支払い.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem (連用形, ren'youkei) of the hybrid compound verb 支払う (shiharau, 'to pay out money'). It unites the Sino-Japanese element 支 (shi, from Middle Chinese *tsje, here used in its accounting sense of 'to disburse, pay out, allocate', as in 支出 shishutsu) with the native Yamato verb stem 払い (harai, from 払う harau, 'to sweep away, clear off, settle an account').

history.meaning: disbursing funds, clearing a debt or account
payment, disbursement, settlement of a bill

morphemes.meaning: sweep clear, pay off, settle (native stem of 払う)

支払い.notes: Frequently takes the honorific prefix お in customer service and business contexts (お支払い o-shiharai, 'your payment').

rootFamily.gloss: to pay, to sweep away, to clear

支払う.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Yamato (jübako-yomi) compound godan verb combining the Sino-Japanese on'yomi 支 (shi, from Middle Chinese *tsje, 'to branch out, disburse, defray expenses') with the native Yamato verb 払う (harau, from Old Japanese parafu, 'to sweep away, drive off, clear away impurities or debts'). Developing in Edo-period merchant accounting, the compound literally conceptualized paying a bill as 'disbursing and sweeping clear' an obligation.

history.form: ぱらふ → はらふ (parafu → harafu)
history.meaning: to sweep away, purge, clear off
to disburse funds and settle commercial accounts
to pay money, settle a bill or obligation

支払う.notes: More formal and institutional than the simple verb 払う (harau); 支払う is preferred in contracts, invoices, wages, and official transactions.

rootFamily.gloss: to pay; to sweep or brush away

支払期限.etymology: Compound commercial-legal term formed by juxtaposing 支払 (shiharai, 'payment, disbursement'—written with dropped okurigana い in four-kanji institutional compounds) and the Sino-Japanese noun 期限 (kigen, 'time limit, deadline', from 期 ki, MC *gij, 'appointed time, period', and 限 gen, MC *hɛnX, 'boundary, limit, threshold'). Literally 'payment time-boundary', denoting the final date by which a debt or invoice must be settled.

history.meaning: disbursement of payment + appointed time limit

history.form: 支払期限 (しはらいきげん, shiharai kigen)
history.meaning: payment deadline, due date for an invoice or loan

morphemes.meaning: pay off, clear an account (native stem harai)

支払期限.notes: Notice the standard orthographic rule where okurigana (い) is omitted inside multi-kanji financial/legal nouns (支払期限 rather than 支払い期限, though both are read shiharai kigen).

rootFamily.gloss: expiration date (of a ticket, license, or contract)

支援者.etymology: Three-kanji Sino-Japanese (kango) agentive noun built from 支援 (shien, 'support, backing, aid'—comprising 支 shi, MC *tsje, 'to prop up, sustain', and 援 en, MC *hjwon, 'to pull up by the hand, rescue, assist') plus the agentive suffix 者 (sha, MC *tsjæX, 'person who does'). It designates an active backer, financial patron, political campaign supporter, or humanitarian aid provider.

history.meaning: sustain/branch + pull to safety/assist + person
person providing material, political, or financial backing

morphemes.meaning: aid, rescue, pull by the hand (MC *hjwon)

支援者.notes: Whereas 支持者 (shijisha) emphasizes someone who endorses or votes for a leader's views ('adherent/endorser'), 支援者 (shiensha) emphasizes someone who actively provides tangible help, funds, or campaign labor ('backer/benefactor').

cognates.meaning: to control, dominate, allocate (influenced by Japanese sense)

支配.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 支 (shi, from Middle Chinese *tsje, 'to divide, branch out, disburse') and 配 (hai, from Middle Chinese *phwojH, 'to distribute, apportion, match'). In medieval and Edo-period Japan, 支配 originally meant 'apportioning duties' and hence 'administering a fief or managing staff'. In the Meiji era, it was repurposed to translate Western concepts of political 'domination', 'rule', and 'control' (e.g., German Herrschaft), while retaining its older managerial sense in 支配人 (shihainin, 'hotel/theater manager').

history.meaning: to divide up and distribute, apportion
supervision and administration of feudal lands or merchant affairs
domination, political rule, control over others

支配.notes: Beware the striking semantic split between 支配 ('domination/rule') and 支配人 (shihainin), which preserves the Edo-Meiji administrative sense and simply means 'general manager' of a hotel, bank, or theater!

rootFamily.gloss: general manager (of a hotel, theater, or bank)

改めて.etymology: Lexicalized adverb formed from the conjunctive (-te) form of the transitive verb あらためる (改める, 'to renew, change, do over'), from the root of あらた (新た, 'new, fresh').

history.meaning: renewing; doing over again
anew; once again; formally

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 改めて

cognates.meaning: to change the imperial era name

改元.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) institutional compound borrowed from classical Chinese imperial historiography, consisting of 改 (kai, from Middle Chinese *kojX, 'to change, alter, reform, renew') and 元 (gen, from Middle Chinese *ngjwon, 'head, origin, first year of a reign, imperial era name [元号 gengou]'). Following the system instituted by Emperor Wu of Han in 140 BCE and adopted in Japan with the Taika (大化) era in 645 CE, it denotes the proclamation of a new imperial era name, such as the transition from Showa to Heisei in January 1989.

history.meaning: changing the imperial reign-era title in Chinese court ritual
proclaiming a new Japanese era name upon enthronement or auspicious/calamitous omen
official change of the imperial era upon the accession of a new Emperor

morphemes.meaning: origin, primary, imperial era name [元号] (MC *ngjwon)

改元.notes: Since the Meiji Era (and codified in the 1979 Era Name Act), Japan practices 一世一元 (issei ichigen, 'one reign, one era name'), so 改元 occurs only upon imperial succession (e.g., Showa → Heisei in 1989, Heisei → Reiwa in 2019).

rootFamily.gloss: imperial era name (e.g., Showa, Heisei, Reiwa)
first year of a new imperial era

改築費.etymology: Three-kanji Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 改築 (kaichiku, 'structural rebuilding or renovation of a building'—combining 改 kai, MC *kojX, 'to alter, renew', and 築 chiku, MC *trjuwk, 'to ram earth, build, construct') plus the suffixal noun 費 (hi, MC *phjɨjH, 'expense, cost, expenditure'). It designates the capital expenditure required to remodel, rebuild, or structurally renovate a building.

history.meaning: alter/renew + construct/ram earth + expenditure
costs incurred in rebuilding or structurally renovating a property

改築費.notes: In Japanese real estate and architecture, 改築 (kaichiku) strictly implies altering or rebuilding part of the structure/floor area, whereas 改装 (kaisou) refers to interior/exterior redecorating and リフォーム (rifoumu) is general remodeling.

改装.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 改装 (kaisō), combining 改 ('change, renew, alter') + 装 ('dress, outfit, interior/exterior fitting').

history.meaning: remodeling; renovation; redecoration

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 改装

攻める.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) ichidan verb evolving from Old Japanese semu (lower nidan conjugation: seme- / semu / semuru), which is derived from the same Proto-Japonic root *sema- as the adjective 狭い (semai, 'narrow, cramped, constricted') and 迫る (semaru, 'to press close, draw near'). Originally meaning 'to constrict, crowd, or press someone into a tight corner', it broadened semantically to mean 'to assault militarily, press an attack, push aggressively, or torment'.

history.meaning: to press closely, constrict, harass, urge
to assault a stronghold, press an enemy, torture or blame
to attack, go on the offensive, push boundaries aggressively

morphemes.meaning: press close, attack, go on the offensive
ichidan transitive verb ending (from classical lower nidan -mu)

攻める.notes: Orthographically split from its twin 責める (semeru, 'to blame, condemn, torture'), which is the exact same native word written with a different kanji; in modern colloquial Japanese, 攻める also means 'to be bold, edgy, or boundary-pushing' (e.g., 攻めた企画 'a daring/edgy project').

rootFamily.gloss: to blame, reproach, torture (same native root, different kanji)
to press close, draw near,迫る (intransitive counterpart from root *sema-)

攻勢.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound uniting 攻 (kou, from Middle Chinese *kuwng, 'to attack, assault, work upon') and 勢 (sei, from Middle Chinese *sjejH, 'power, momentum, force of circumstances, strategic posture'). Originally a military term for an active attacking posture or strategic momentum (as opposed to 守勢 shusei, 'defensive posture'), it is widely used in business, sports, and politics for an aggressive campaign or push.

history.meaning: to attack + strategic force, momentum, posture
military offensive posture or forward momentum
military, commercial, or political offensive; aggressive push

攻勢.notes: Commonly used in the idiom 攻勢に出る (kousei ni deru, 'to go on the offensive / make a bold push') or 攻勢をかける (kousei o kakeru, 'to launch an offensive'). Antonym: 守勢 (shusei, 'the defensive').

rootFamily.gloss: defensive posture, being on the back foot
momentum, vigor, force (native reading of 勢)

攻撃.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound attested in classical Chinese military and historical texts (such as the Records of the Grand Historian), composed of two near-synonymous verbal roots: 攻 (kou, from Middle Chinese *kuwng, 'to attack, besiege, assail') and 撃 (geki, shinjitai of 擊, from Middle Chinese *kek, 'to strike, beat, smash'). It denotes a direct physical, military, verbal, or sporting attack.

history.meaning: to assault and strike an enemy force
military assault or siege strike
military, physical, verbal, or sporting attack/offense

攻撃.notes: Functions both as a noun and a する verb (攻撃する), and encompasses everything from military strikes and team-sport offense to harsh personal criticism (個人攻撃 kojin kougeki).

放っておく.etymology: Syntactic verbal compound combining the germinated te-form of the native verb 放る (houru, 'to toss, fling away, abandon', historically a phonetic sound change from 葬る houmuru 'to bury, cast away' or 放る hofuru) with the subsidiary aspectual verb おく (oku, 'to put, leave in a state for future reference'). Literally 'to toss aside and leave as is', it grammaticalized into the standard idiomatic expression for leaving someone or something alone, neglecting, or ignoring a situation.

history.meaning: to cast aside, fling away + to place/leave
to toss aside and leave untouched; to leave be

history.form: 放っておく (ほうっておく, houtte oku)
history.meaning: to leave alone, leave untouched, ignore or neglect

morphemes.meaning: toss away, abandon, cast aside (stem of 放る houru)
leave in a state, set aside (auxiliary verb 置く)

放っておく.notes: In casual spoken Japanese, 放っておく (houtte oku) frequently contracts to ほっとく (hottoku), and its imperative/request form「ほっといてくれ！」(Hottoite kure! 'Leave me alone!') is ubiquitous in drama dialogue.

rootFamily.gloss: to throw out, abandon midway, give up on
leaving things as they are, neglect (kango sharing 放)

cognates.meaning: broadcast (historically used, now largely replaced by 廣播)

放送.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 放 (hou, from Middle Chinese *pjangH, 'to release, let go, emit') and 送 (sou, from Middle Chinese *suwngH, 'to send, transmit, escort'). While classical Chinese used 放送 in the literal sense of 'releasing and sending away (prisoners or exiles)', Japanese wireless pioneers in the 1920s (when regular radio transmissions began in 1925) repurposed the compound to translate English 'broadcasting'—literally 'emitting and transmitting' radio (and later television) waves to the public.

history.meaning: to release from custody and send away; to expel or banish
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Pre-modern Japanese legal usage

history.meaning: wireless radio transmission to the general public (coined ca. 1924–1925)
radio, television, or satellite broadcasting

放送.notes: A major modern media term coined in Japan and exported to Korean 방송 (bangsong); note also how 放映 (houei, replacing 送 with 映 'project image') is sometimes used specifically for televising a film.

放送権.etymology: Three-kanji Sino-Japanese (kango) media-law compound formed by attaching the legal suffix 権 (ken, shinjitai of 權, from Middle Chinese *gjwon, originally 'scale weight, balance of power, authority', repurposed in Meiji Japan to translate Western legal 'right' / German Recht) to 放送 (housou, 'broadcasting', from 放 hou 'emit' + 送 sou 'transmit'). It denotes the exclusive commercial license to broadcast an event (such as professional sports or films) over television, radio, or satellite.

history.meaning: release/emit + send/transmit + steelyard weight / authority

history.form: 放送権 (ほうそうけん, housouken)
history.meaning: legal and commercial right to broadcast programming or live events

放送権.notes: In sports and television business contexts, 放映権 (houeiken, 'televising rights') is frequently used interchangeably with 放送権 when specifically referring to video/TV broadcasts.

政治.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound attested in classical Chinese statecraft texts (including the Book of Documents and Zhouli), composed of 政 (sei, from Middle Chinese *tsjengH, 'government, rectifying state affairs', related to 正 'correct/upright') and 治 (ji, go-on reading from Middle Chinese *drjɨH, 'to regulate, order, govern, pacify', originally 'controlling floodwaters'). In the Meiji era, this classical compound for benevolent governance was adopted as the standard translation for Western 'politics'.

history.meaning: rectifying and ordering the affairs of state; governance
imperial or shogunal administration and public governance
politics, political science, statecraft, party and electoral affairs

morphemes.meaning: order, regulate, govern (MC *drjɨH, go-on reading ji)

政治.notes: Notice that 治 uses its older Go-on reading ji in 政治 (seiji) and 治安 (chian uses kan-on chi), so learners must take care not to misread 政治 as *seichi.

故郷.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 故郷. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 故郷

救い.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem (連用形, ren'youkei) of the native Yamato godan verb 救う (sukuu, 'to rescue, save, relieve'), which derives from Old Japanese sukufu ('to scoop up, lift out of danger or water'). It shares its ultimate Proto-Japonic root *sukupa- with 掬う (sukuu, 'to scoop up water or fish with the hands or a net')—conceptualizing rescue and spiritual salvation as 'scooping' a person out of peril or suffering.

history.meaning: act of scooping up or rescuing from distress or karmic suffering
deliverance, religious salvation (Buddhist and Kirishitan usage), relief
salvation, rescue, redemption, saving grace or emotional relief

morphemes.meaning: scoop out of danger, rescue, save (stem of 救う)

救い.notes: Used both for lofty religious salvation (魂の救い tamashii no sukui) and everyday emotional relief, as in 救いようがない (sukuiyou ga nai, 'hopeless, beyond redemption') or それがせめてもの救いだ ('that is the one saving grace').

rootFamily.gloss: to rescue, to save, to relieve
to scoop up (liquid, fish, etc.)—cognate native verb from the same root

救い出す.etymology: Compound godan verb combining the continuative stem すくい (救い, from 救う 'to save, rescue') + だす (出す, 'to take out, bring out').

history.meaning: rescue; save and bring out

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 救い出す

救う.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *sukupu* (救ふ・掬ふ, 'to scoop up out of water or danger, rescue, save, relieve'), attested in the Nihon Shoki and Man'yōshū; etymologically the same verb as 掬う ('to scoop up').

history.meaning: scoop up; rescue from distress
save; rescue; relieve

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 救う

救世主.etymology: Sino-Japanese religious compound 救世主 (kyūseishu), combining 救世 ('saving the world', originally a Buddhist epithet of bodhisattvas such as Guanyin/Kannon) + 主 ('lord, master'), adopted in Christian translation for 'Savior, Messiah'.

history.form: 救世主 (きゅうせいしゅ)
history.meaning: Savior of the world; Messiah; lifesaver

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 救世主

教える.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese lower bigrade verb *osipu* (教ふ, 'to point out, instruct, teach, tell'), becoming modern ichidan *oshieru*.

history.meaning: instruct; teach; show
teach; instruct; tell; inform

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 教える

教わる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb derived from the transitive verb 教える (oshieru, 'to teach, instruct, show'—from Old Japanese osifu, 'to point out, direct, love/cherish') by replacing the transitive suffix -eru (classical -fu) with the detransitivizing/receptive suffix -waru. Rather than a syntactic passive, 教わる lexicalizes the recipient's active experience of being taught or learning skills directly from a mentor or instructor.

history.meaning: to instruct, direct, guide

history.form: をしはる → おそわる (osiharu → osowaru)
history.meaning: to receive instruction, be taught by a master or teacher
history.stage: Early Modern Japanese (with vowel assimilation o-i-a → o-o-a)

history.meaning: to be taught, learn (a skill, lesson, or fact) from someone

morphemes.meaning: teach, instruct (bound allomorph oso- of oshi-)

教わる.notes: Unlike 学ぶ (manabu, 'to study/learn academically') or 習う (narau, 'to take lessons/practice repeatedly'), 教わる emphasizes receiving direct personal guidance or a tip from someone (marked with に or から).

rootFamily.gloss: to teach, to instruct, to tell

教会.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 教 (kyou, from Middle Chinese *kæwH, 'teaching, doctrine, religion') and 会 (kai, shinjitai of 會, from Middle Chinese *hwajH, 'gathering, assembly, society'). Propagated across East Asia by 19th-century Protestant and Catholic missionaries in China and Meiji Japan to translate Greek ekklēsia ('assembly') and English 'church'—originally denoting the religious congregation ('assembly of the teaching') and by extension the physical church building or chapel.

history.meaning: teaching, doctrine + assembly, gathering
Christian congregation or religious society; church building
Christian church, chapel (including wedding chapels)

教会.notes: Be careful of homophones with identical pitch accent or spelling: 協会 (kyoukai, 'association/society', using 協 'cooperate') and 境界 (kyoukai, 'boundary/border', using 境 'border').

教室.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 教 (kyou, from Middle Chinese *kæwH, 'to teach, instruct') and 室 (shitsu, from Middle Chinese *srjit, 'room, inner chamber, hall'). While attested rarely in classical Chinese for a dynastic ancestral or instructional chamber, it was popularized in Meiji Japan upon the establishment of the modern school system (1872) to translate 'classroom', and subsequently extended to private hobby schools or lessons (e.g., 料理教室 ryouri kyoushitsu, 'cooking class').

history.meaning: to instruct/teach + inner chamber, room
schoolroom in the modern Meiji public education system
school classroom; university department; private lesson studio or workshop

教室.notes: Beyond physical schoolrooms, 教室 is widely used in Japan for commercial lesson studios or workshops for adults and children (e.g., ピアノ教室 'piano lessons/school', 英会話教室 'English conversation school').

rootFamily.gloss: teacher, instructor (specifically as an occupation or institutional role)

教師.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Literary Chinese 教師 (Middle Chinese *kæwH srij), combining 教 (kyō, "to teach, instruct, doctrine") and 師 (shi, "master, expert, model"). Originally referring in Tang-era Chinese to military drill instructors or religious preceptors, it became the standard institutional term in Meiji-era Japan for a formal schoolteacher or academic instructor.

history.meaning: military or religious instructor, preceptor
master of a discipline; schoolteacher (Meiji onward)

教師.notes: 教師 (kyōshi, pitch accent [1]) refers objectively to the profession or role of teaching (used when speaking of oneself or the occupation in general), whereas 先生 (sensei) is an honorific title used to address or show respect to a teacher.

教授.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for professor. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: professor

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 教授

教材.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 教 (kyō, Middle Chinese *kæwH, "to teach, instruction") and 材 (zai, Middle Chinese *dzoj, "timber, raw material, resource, talent"). Coined and popularized in modern Japanese educational terminology and subsequently re-borrowed as an orthographic loan into modern Chinese and Korean to denote instructional materials.

history.meaning: instruction + timber/raw material/resource
teaching materials, instructional resources

教材.notes: Pronounced with heiban (flat, [0]) pitch accent; beyond school textbooks, 教材 is also used idiomatically (e.g., いい教材になる) to mean a "good object lesson" or case study to learn from.

cognates.meaning: founder of a religion or sect

教祖.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Buddhist and Literary Chinese 教祖 (Middle Chinese *kæwH tsuX), combining 教 (kyō, "religious teaching, doctrine, sect") and 祖 (so, "ancestor, patriarch, founder"). Originally an honorific title in Chinese Buddhism for Śākyamuni Buddha as the primordial founder of the dharma, it broadened in Japanese to denote the founder of any religious sect or charismatic cult movement.

history.meaning: patriarch of the teaching (originally an epithet of the Buddha)
founder of a religious sect; charismatic guru or cult leader

教祖.notes: In contemporary colloquial Japanese, 教祖 (often with honorific 教祖様, kyōso-sama) is frequently used figuratively for a charismatic trendsetter, pop icon, or industry pioneer with a devoted cult-like following.

教科書.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound coined in the Meiji educational reforms by joining 教科 (kyōka, 'subject of instruction, curriculum', from 教 'teach' + 科 'branch/course') and 書 (sho, 'book, written volume'). Afterward, 教科書 was also borrowed into Chinese and Korean as the standard modern term for a school textbook.

history.meaning: printed textbook for school instruction
textbook; manual; model example

教科書.notes: In colloquial similes (教科書みたいに話す, 'to talk like a textbook'), it means speaking stiffly or overly formally.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 教科書

教育学部.etymology: Modern Sino-Japanese (wasei-kango) institutional compound combining 教育 (kyōiku, "education, upbringing", from Classical Chinese 孟子 Mengzi: 得天下英才而教育之 "to obtain the finest talents under heaven and educate them") and 学部 (gakubu, "university faculty or department", composed of 学 gaku "learning, study" + 部 bu "division, section").

history.meaning: to instruct and nurture/rear
university faculty or school of education

教育学部.notes: In the Japanese university system, 学部 (gakubu) denotes an undergraduate faculty (e.g., Faculty of Education) as opposed to 大学院 (daigakuin, graduate school) or 学科 (gakka, a specific sub-department within a faculty).

敬礼.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 敬禮 (simplified in shinjitai to 敬礼; Middle Chinese *kjængH lejX), combining 敬 (kei, "reverence, respect, honor") and 礼 (rei, "ritual, propriety, bow, courtesy"). Originally denoting deferential ritual etiquette in Confucian and court contexts, it was adopted by the Meiji military and police forces to translate the Western military hand salute and command "Salute!".

history.meaning: reverent courtesy, ritual bow of respect
formal bow of respect; military/police salute and command "Salute!"

敬礼.notes: As a sharp vocal command ("Keirei!"), it is used across military, police, railway staff, and school ceremonies, and also appears colloquially in humorous contexts when mock-saluting a superior or boss.

数.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun kazu ("number, quantity, count"), attested in Old Japanese (Man'yōshū) as かず (kazu), spelled semantically with the logograph 数 (Middle Chinese *srjuH, "number, count"). Internally related within Japonic to the verb かぞふ (kazofu > modern 数える kazoeru, "to count"), probably derived from a Proto-Japonic root *kansu meaning a tally mark or notched count.

history.meaning: number, tally, quantity
number, quantity, amount, figures

数.notes: The single kanji 数 is read kazu (native Yamato word, pitch [1]) when used as a standalone everyday noun for "quantity/number of things", but sū (Sino-Japanese on'yomi) in mathematical contexts, compounds (e.g., 数字 sūji), or as a prefix meaning "several" (e.g., 数日 sūjitsu, "several days").

数える.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) ichidan verb kazoeru ("to count, calculate"), evolving regularly via labial lenition and vowel coalescence from Classical and Old Japanese quadrigrade/shimo-nidan verb かぞふ (kazofu < *kazopu). Derived denominal verb from the noun かず (kazu, "number, tally") via ancient vowel alternation (*u ~ *o) plus the verbalizing suffix *-pu denoting iterative or continuous action ("to make tallies one after another").

history.meaning: to tally, reckon, enumerate, calculate

history.form: かぞふる (kazofuru) > かぞへる (kazoferu)
history.meaning: to count, reckon (attributive-to-finite shift and /f/ > /w/ > Ø)
to count, enumerate

数える.notes: Compare traditional East Asian age reckoning 数え年 (kazoedoshi), where a baby is counted as one year old at birth and gains a year every New Year's Day, versus 満年齢 (mannenrei, full chronological age).

数分.etymology: Sino-Japanese numerical expression 数分 (sūfun), combining prefixal 数 ('several, a few') + counter 分 ('minute').

history.meaning: several minutes; a few minutes

未亡人.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) three-character compound borrowed from Classical Chinese, first attested in the Zuo Zhuan (左傳, 4th century BCE). Composed of 未 (mi, Middle Chinese *mj+jH, 'not yet'), 亡 (bō, Middle Chinese *mjang, 'to perish, die, flee'), and 人 (jin, Middle Chinese *nyin, 'person'). In ancient China, a noblewoman whose husband had died used 未亡人 as a self-deprecating first-person pronoun meaning 'the person who has not yet died [along with her husband]'. In modern Japanese, it shifted from humble first-person usage to a third-person noun meaning 'widow'.

history.meaning: I, the one who has not yet perished with my late husband (humble self-reference by a widow)

未亡人.notes: Because of its literal meaning ('one who has not yet died'), never use 未亡人 to address a widow directly or refer to one's own relatives; in adult media and melodrama (*The Naked Director*), it is also a well-known trope genre title.

未完成.etymology: Sino-Japanese prefix 未- (み-, 'not yet') attached to 完成 (かんせい, 'completion': 完 'whole' + 成 'accomplish').

未成年.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal and administrative compound formed from the negative aspectual prefix 未 (mi, Middle Chinese *mj+jH, 'not yet') prefixed to 成年 (seinen, 'coming of age, legal majority', from 成 *dzyeng 'to complete, reach full growth' + 年 *nen 'year, age of life'). Coined in Meiji-era civil law codification to designate individuals who have not yet attained the statutory age of majority.

history.meaning: reaching full maturity of years, adulthood

未成年.notes: Refers to the legal status of being under the age of majority (historically 20 in Japan during the 1980s era of *The Naked Director*, lowered to 18 in 2022); adding 者 (sha) forms 未成年者 ('a minor').

未払い.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound (jūbako-yomi, 'nested-box reading'). It combines the Sino-Japanese aspectual prefix 未 (mi-, from Middle Chinese *mj+jH, 'not yet') with 払い (-barai, voiced via rendaku from harai, the continuative nominalized stem of the native Yamato verb 払う harau < Old Japanese parapu, 'to sweep away, clear off, disburse money'). Literally 'not-yet-cleared-off [payment]', used for outstanding bills or wages.

未払い金.etymology: Tripartite hybrid Japanese compound combining the Sino-Japanese prefix 未 (mi-, 'not yet'), the native Yamato deverbal noun 払い (-barai < harai, 'payment, clearing of accounts', from 払う harau 'to sweep clear, pay'), and the Sino-Japanese noun suffix 金 (-kin, Middle Chinese *kim, 'metal, gold, money, funds'). Formed in modern commercial and labor accounting to denote accrued but undisbursed wages, bills, or debts.

未払い金.notes: A sandwich compound (Sino-Japanese + native Yamato + Sino-Japanese); in accounting and labor disputes, 未払い金 specifically highlights the concrete sum of money owed (such as unpaid salaries or vendor invoices).

Literally 'that which has not yet come', it gained widespread currency in East Asia through Chinese Buddhist translations of Sanskrit anāgata ('not come, future'), forming one of the Three Worlds (三世 sanze): 過去 (past), 現在 (present), and 未来 (future).

未発表.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound formed by attaching the negative aspectual prefix 未- (mi-, from Middle Chinese *mjwɨiH, 'not yet', contrasting with 不- 'not' and 非- 'non-') to 発表 (happyō, 'public presentation, publication, release'). Together, 未発表 describes a musical composition, manuscript, or design that has been created but never yet presented to the public.

末.etymology: Represents both the native Yamato noun suwe > sue ('tip, upper end, conclusion, future outcome, descendant') and the Sino-Japanese morpheme matsu (Middle Chinese *mwat, 'treetop twigs, extremity, end of a period'). The kanji 末 is an ancient Chinese ideograph adding a long horizontal stroke to the top of a tree (木), pointing to the uppermost twigs—the direct visual inverse of 本 (root, base, with the stroke at the bottom). In temporal expressions like 交渉の末 ('at the end of / after negotiations') or 月末 (getsumatsu, 'end of the month'), it marks the final culmination of a span.

本格.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 本 (hon, Middle Chinese *pwonX, 'root, original, fundamental, true') and 格 (kaku, Middle Chinese *kaek, 'tree branch frame, lattice, rule, standard, proper style'). Originally an aesthetic and poetic term in medieval and Edo Japan denoting the 'orthodox rule or proper standard' of verse and art (as opposed to 変格 henkaku, 'irregular/variant form'), it broadened in modern Japanese to mean 'authentic, orthodox, full-scale'.

本格的.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) adjectival derivative formed in modern Japanese by suffixing 的 (-teki, Middle Chinese *tek, originally 'white bullseye target', adapted in Meiji Japan to translate European adjectival suffixes like -ic and -al) to 本格 (honkaku, 'fundamental standard, orthodoxy', from 本 'root/true' + 格 'standard/frame'). It describes either something authentic and true to form or an activity getting underway in full earnest.

本棚.etymology: Hybrid compound combining Sino-Japanese ほん (本, 'book') + native Japanese だな (棚, rendaku form of たな 'shelf, rack').

本気.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in Japan from 本 (hon, Middle Chinese *pwonX, 'root, original, true, real') and 気 (ki, Middle Chinese *khj+jH, 'breath, vapor, vital energy, spirit, mind'). Originally attested in the Edo period in contrast to 狂気 (kyōki, 'madness') or 冗談 (jōdan, 'jest') to mean 'one's normal, sane mind' or 'true intention', it evolved to mean 'dead seriousness, earnestness, putting one's full spirit into something'.

history.meaning: one's normal, sober, sane state of mind (as opposed to madness or drunkenness)
seriousness, earnestness, meaning what one says or acting with full effort

本気.notes: Used constantly in spoken Japanese with で: 本気で言ってるの？ ('Are you saying that seriously / Do you really mean it?') and 本気を出す ('to get serious / show one's true strength').

本物.etymology: Hybrid compound combining Sino-Japanese ほん (本, 'true, genuine, original') + native Japanese もの (物, 'thing, article').

history.meaning: genuine article; real thing

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 本物

本番.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in Japan from 本 (hon, Middle Chinese *pwonX, 'main, real, actual') and 番 (ban, Middle Chinese *phjon, originally 'animal footprint, turn in rotation, guard watch, bout'). Initially denoting one's regular duty shift (as opposed to an auxiliary shift), in 20th-century theatre, broadcasting, and film it came to mean the 'live take' or 'actual performance' after rehearsals. In Japan's adult entertainment and AV industry (central to *The Naked Director*), it further specialized as slang for real, unsimulated penetrative sex on camera or in a brothel.

history.meaning: regular watch duty or scheduled turn in an official rotation
the actual stage performance, live broadcast, or camera take (versus rehearsal)
actual performance / live take; by extension in sex work and AV production, real penetrative sex

本番.notes: In everyday life, TV, exams, and sports, 本番 is completely clean ('the real thing / game time / live take', e.g. 本番に強い 'good under pressure when it counts'), but in nightlife and *The Naked Director*'s AV context it specifically means actual penetrative sex.

rootFamily.gloss: one's turn to go on stage or act

本腰.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound (jūbako-yomi) combining Sino-Japanese 本 (hon-, 'true, real, earnest') with native Yamato 腰 (-goshi, voiced via rendaku from koshi < Old Japanese kosi, 'waist, lower back, hips'). Derived from traditional sumo wrestling and martial arts, where planting one's hips firmly down (as opposed to 及び腰 oyobigoshi, a tentative bent-over posture) is the physical foundation of real power. By metaphor, it denotes committing oneself seriously to a task.

history.meaning: waist, loins, lower back
a firmly planted hip stance in wrestling or physical labor; serious commitment
serious effort, earnest commitment (almost always in 本腰を入れる)

morphemes.meaning: waist, lower back, hips (seat of physical stability)

本腰.notes: Almost always used in the idiom 本腰を入れる (hongoshi o ireru, literally 'to put one's real hips into it', meaning 'to buckle down / get serious about a project'); part of a rich set of Japanese waist-posture idioms like 腰が重い ('slow to act / reluctant').

rootFamily.gloss: to sit down; to settle down to work (腰を据える)
arrogant, haughty attitude (cf. 低姿勢 / 腰が低い 'humble')
rootFamily.word: 高飛車 / 腰が低い (こしがひくい)

本題.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 本 (hon, Middle Chinese *pwonX, 'root, trunk, main, original') and 題 (dai, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese *dej, originally 'forehead', extended in Classical Chinese to 'heading, inscription, title, thesis, subject of an essay or poem'). Literally 'the main heading or root subject', it contrasts with introductory small talk (前置き maeoki) or digressions (余談 yodan).

history.meaning: forehead; heading, title, or assigned theme of a composition
the original or principal theme of a poem, sermon, or discourse

history.meaning: main topic, real business at hand (e.g., 本題に入る 'to get down to business')

本題.notes: Most commonly heard in meetings and negotiations in the set phrase 本題に入る (hondai ni hairu, 'to get to the main point / get down to brass tacks') or 本題に戻る ('to return to the main topic').

札.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *puda* (札, 'wooden writing tablet, tag, placard, talisman'), undergoing medial *-p- > -f-* to *fuda*; also read Sino-Japanese *satsu* ('banknote, bill').

history.meaning: inscribed wooden tablet or slip

材料.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 材料 (*dzoj ljewH), combining 材 (zai, 'cut timber, wood suitable for construction, raw material, natural talent') and 料 (ryō, originally a ladle 斗 measuring grain 米, hence 'measured grain, provisions, material, to reckon'). From concrete building timber and cooking ingredients, its meaning expanded in Japanese to include abstract 'source material, data, evidence, or grounds for a judgment or stock price movement'.

history.meaning: timber and measured provisions; raw physical materials for crafting
raw materials, cooking ingredients; data, evidence, or factors for a decision

rootFamily.gloss: raw material, unprocessed matter; subject matter

村西.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) toponymic surname composed of 村 (mura < Old Japanese mura, 'cluster, settlement, village', related to 群れ mure 'flock, crowd, group') and 西 (nishi < Old Japanese nisi, 'west', likely derived from inisi 'direction where the sun has gone'). Originally designating a homestead or family located in the western part of a village ('village-west'), it is famously borne by Toru Muranishi (村西とおる, born 1948 in Fukushima Prefecture), the pioneering adult video director portrayed in *The Naked Director* (全裸監督).

history.meaning: village settlement + west
habitational surname denoting a family from the western side of a village

村西.notes: Follows the classic Japanese habitational surname pattern [landform/settlement + cardinal direction], parallel to 村東 (Murahigashi), 村北 (Murakita), and 村南 (Muraminami); in *The Naked Director*, 村西 refers to protagonist Toru Muranishi.

cognates.meaning: to bind, tie up, fetter, restrict

束縛.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) tautological compound from Classical and Middle Chinese 束縛 (*syowk bjak), combining 束 (soku, 'to tie wood into a bundle', an ideograph of a tree 木 tied around the middle with a cord 口) and 縛 (baku, 'to tie fast with rope, truss up a prisoner', from 糸 'silk/rope' + 尃 phonetic). From the literal act of binding a captive with cords, it developed the figurative sense of social, legal, or romantic restraint and control.

history.meaning: to tie up in bundles, bind a prisoner with cords
physical binding; restriction of freedom, emotional or contractual control

morphemes.meaning: to tie fast with rope, truss, arrest

束縛.notes: Frequently used in modern Japanese not only for institutional rules or time (拘束時間) but especially for possessive, controlling behavior in romantic relationships (束縛が激しい彼氏, 'a controlling/possessive boyfriend').

rootFamily.gloss: promise, appointment, pact (lit. 'bundling with a rope')
catching and tying up a criminal; arrest (捕縛)

条件.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 条 (jō, traditional 條, Middle Chinese *dew, 'slender tree branch, strip, itemized clause or article of law') and 件 (ken, Middle Chinese *gjenX, 'to divide, item, distinct matter or case', composed of 人 'person' + 牛 'ox'). Originally denoting 'itemized articles or clauses of a document' in pre-modern Chinese and Japanese, it was repurposed in Meiji-era legal and philosophical translation to render European terms like English condition, German Bedingung, and French condition.

history.meaning: itemized legal clause / distinct matter or case
itemized articles of an agreement; prerequisite, stipulation, or contractual terms

条件.notes: Used for contractual terms (契約の条件), prerequisites (必要条件), and conditioning (条件反射, 'conditioned reflex'); unconditionally is 無条件で (mujōken de).

条例.etymology: Sino-Japanese legal compound 条例 (jōrei), from Chinese 條例 ('itemized regulations, statutes, precedents'), combining 条 ('clause, article') + 例 ('rule, precedent'); in modern Japan, a municipal or prefectural ordinance.

history.meaning: itemized rules and statutes
local ordinance; regulation; bylaw

架空.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 架空 (*kaeH khuwng), combining 架 (ka, 'to prop up, build a frame, span across') and 空 (kū, 'empty sky, void, midair'). Originally a literal architectural and poetic expression meaning 'spanning across empty sky' (like a high mountain bridge or aerial pavilion), it developed the metaphorical sense of 'suspended in midair with no foundation on the ground', hence 'baseless, imaginary, fictitious, fabricated'.

history.meaning: spanning or built high across the empty sky (of bridges or lofty towers)
unfounded, imaginary, fictitious (e.g., a fictional character or fake billing account)

morphemes.meaning: to span across, prop up, build a frame

架空.notes: Takes の to modify nouns: used both neutrally for fiction (架空の人物, 'a fictional character') and negatively for fraud (架空請求, 'fake/fraudulent billing', or 架空口座, 'fictitious bank account').

rootFamily.gloss: stretching a bridge; suspension bridge (架橋)

柄.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun gara (voiced via rendaku from Old Japanese kara, 'bloodline, clan, inherent nature, stem/stalk'). Originally written 族 or 韓/幹 in Old Japanese compounds like うから (ukara, 'clan') and はらから (harakara, 'siblings from the same womb'), it came to be written with the kanji 柄 (originally e, 'handle, shaft, grip of a tool', and by extension 'authority, structural build'). From 'inherent lineage or build', gara evolved to mean 'one's innate character, social standing, physique, or textile pattern'.

history.meaning: clan, blood relation, inherent nature or constitution
social standing, inherent character, bodily build, or fabric design
one's nature/character (柄じゃない), textile pattern, or demeanor (柄が悪い)

柄.notes: In the idiom 柄にもなく (gara ni mo naku, 'uncharacteristically / out of character') or 俺の柄じゃない ('It's not like me / not my style'), it means 'one's nature'; in 柄が悪い (gara ga warui), it means 'rough-mannered, sketchy, ill-bred'. When read e (柄), the same kanji means 'handle/grip'.

rootFamily.gloss: family lineage, social standing of a house
nature of a matter, situation; appropriately (事柄 / 時節柄)

柔らかい.etymology: Derived in Late Middle Japanese as an i-adjective from the classical naru-adjective やはらかなり (柔らかなり・軟らかなり, 'soft, pliant, gentle'), built on the root *yapa-* + suffixes *-ra-ka*.

history.form: やはらかなり (柔らかなり)

soft; tender; pliant; flexible; gentle

栄養.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound originally written 営養 (eiyō) in Chinese medical classics and Meiji-era physiology, formed from 営 (ei, Middle Chinese *ywing, 'to build, manage, circulate vital blood/qi') and 養 (yō, Middle Chinese *yangX, 'to feed, nourish, rear'). After World War II, under the Tōyō Kanji script reforms and character substitution (同音の漢字による書きかえ), 営 was officially replaced by the homophonous 栄 (ei, Middle Chinese *hjweng, 'to flourish, blossom, thrive'), yielding modern 栄養 ('nourishment that makes the body thrive').

history.meaning: sustaining and nourishing the body through vital circulation and food
nutrition, nourishment, dietary sustenance (and figuratively 'fuel' for growth)

morphemes.meaning: to flourish, thrive (replacing 営 'to sustain, manage')

栄養.notes: A textbook example of 20th-century Japanese kanji replacement (書きかえ): 営養 ('sustaining and nourishing') was rewritten as 栄養 ('thriving and nourishing') because 栄 felt more intuitively positive for health.

rootFamily.word: 栄養失調 (えいようしっちょう)

根性.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read in the ancient Go-on pronunciation (konjō rather than Kan-on konseī), reflecting its origin in Chinese Buddhist scriptures. Composed of 根 (kon, Middle Chinese *kwon, 'root', translating Sanskrit indriya 'spiritual faculty, capacity for enlightenment') and 性 (jō, Middle Chinese *sjengH, 'inborn nature, disposition'). In medieval Buddhism it meant a person's innate spiritual capacity for salvation; in the Edo period it secularized to 'one's underlying disposition or temper' (as in 根性が曲がっている 'twisted nature'), and in modern sports and business it came to mean 'grit, guts, indomitable willpower'.

history.meaning: innate spiritual faculties and predisposition toward enlightenment (translating Sanskrit indriya-prakṛti)
history.stage: Buddhist Hybrid Chinese / Early Middle Japanese

history.meaning: one's fundamental temperament, underlying character (often negative, e.g. 根性悪)
guts, grit, sheer willpower, fighting spirit to endure hardship

根性.notes: Notice the Buddhist Go-on reading jō for 性 (also seen in 相性 aishō and 本性 honjō); in postwar Japan, 根性論 (konjōron, 'the gospel of sheer grit') became a famous cultural buzzword for overcoming any obstacle through pure willpower.

rootFamily.gloss: true nature, real character (also uses Go-on reading jō)

格好.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) word derived via phonetic gemination (*kaku-kō > kakkō) from 恰好 or 格好. Originally borrowed from Vernacular Chinese 恰好 (Middle Chinese *khaep xawX, 'just right, fittingly, opportunely'), in Edo-period Japanese it was increasingly written with 格 (kaku, 'form, standard, frame') + 好 (kō, 'good, pleasing, suitable') to mean 'a pleasing or well-proportioned shape, reasonable price, or suitable manner'. From 'well-proportioned form', it generalized into the everyday word for 'outward appearance, outfit, posture, or shape'.

history.meaning: just right, exactly fitting, opportunely

In medieval Japanese, 案ずる meant 'to ponder over a desk, investigate, or compose a plan', before narrowing emotionally in Early Modern and Modern Japanese to 'to brood over, worry, be anxious about'.

guidance; showing around; information; notification

history.meaning: police checkpoint, security inspection, stop-and-question

検問.notes: Most frequently encountered in compounds like 検問所 (kenmonjo, 'checkpoint station') and 飲酒検問 (inshu kenmon, 'sobriety checkpoint').

検査.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 検査 (kensa), from Chinese 檢査 ('to examine, inspect, verify'), combining 検 ('examine, check') + 査 ('investigate').

history.meaning: inspect and verify
inspection; examination; medical test

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 検査

検討.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 檢討 (jiǎntǎo), composed of 検 (ken, Middle Chinese kjemX, 'to inspect, verify, check against a standard') and 討 (tō, Middle Chinese thawX, 'to seek out, investigate, discuss, chastise'). In Song- and Ming-dynasty China, 檢討 was also an official title in the Hanlin Academy responsible for examining historical records; in modern Japanese it denotes carefully examining, reviewing, or considering a plan, proposal, or issue.

history.meaning: to investigate texts thoroughly; Hanlin Academy historiographical editor
careful scholarly or administrative investigation and debate
consideration, review, examination of a plan or option

morphemes.meaning: to seek out, investigate, debate, probe

検討.notes: Watch out for two famous false friends/traps: in Japanese business speech, 前向きに検討します ('We will consider it positively') is often a polite refusal, and in modern Mandarin 检讨 (jiǎntǎo) means 'self-criticism/apology' rather than neutral 'review'.

cognates.meaning: business sector, industry circle (loan from Japanese)

業界.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in modern Japan from 業 (gyō, Middle Chinese ngjaep, 'occupation, trade, business, enterprise; Buddhist karma') and 界 (kai, Middle Chinese kaejH, 'boundary, realm, world, sphere'). Built on the productive Meiji–Taishō pattern of attaching -界 ('world/community of...') to a domain noun, it denotes all enterprises and professionals within a specific line of business, and colloquially (when spoken without a modifier) refers specifically to the showbusiness, television, or adult video industry.

history.meaning: occupation/deed + boundary/realm (originally Buddhist sphere of karma)
commercial sector, trade community, business circle
industry, business sector; (colloquial) the entertainment or AV industry

業界.notes: Pitch accent distinguishes nuance in casual speech: standard ぎょ↓うかい (atamadaka) means any business sector, whereas flat ぎょうかい (heiban) or inverted slang かいぎょう refers to showbiz/media insiders (as in 業界人, 'industry insider')!

rootFamily.word: 業界用語 (ぎょうかいようご)

業者.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 業 (gyō, Middle Chinese ngjaep, 'trade, business, occupation, enterprise') and the nominalizing agent suffix 者 (sha, Middle Chinese tsyaeX, 'person who performs or belongs to'). Literally 'a person engaged in a trade or commercial enterprise,' it functions both as a suffix in specific trade compounds (such as 不動産業者, 'real estate agent') and as an independent noun meaning contractor, vendor, merchant, or—in colloquial and underworld contexts—an illicit or gray-market dealer.

history.meaning: trade/occupation + agentive nominalizer ('one who practices a trade')
merchant, commercial operator, practitioner of a specified trade
vendor, contractor, operator; (slang) shady dealer or bot account operator

業者.notes: When used standalone without specifying the trade (e.g., 業者を呼ぶ, 'call a contractor', or あいつは業者だ, 'that guy is a commercial/illicit dealer'), it can carry either a utilitarian service-provider nuance or a slightly shady, transactional ring.

rootFamily.gloss: practitioner of the same trade, competitor
rootFamily.word: 同業者 (どうぎょうしゃ)
商人 / 商業 (しょうぎょう)

極道.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read in go-on: 極 (goku, Middle Chinese gik, 'ridgepole, extreme limit, utmost point') + 道 (dō, Middle Chinese dawX, 'way, path, moral principle'). Originally a Buddhist term translating Sanskrit paramārtha ('having attained the highest spiritual truth or ultimate path'), it underwent ironic semantic inversion in Edo-period Kamigata (Kyoto–Osaka) vernacular to mean 'one who goes to the utmost extreme in dissipation—a profligate, libertine, or rogue,' before becoming the romanticized self-designation of chivalrous gangsters (yakuza).

history.meaning: the supreme Buddhist path; attaining ultimate spiritual truth (paramārtha)
one who carries dissipation to the extreme; profligate, ne'er-do-well, rake
yakuza, underworld gangster following the code of the streets

極道.notes: Whereas ヤクザ (yakuza, from the losing 8-9-3 hand in Oicho-Kabu card gambling) originated as a self-deprecating gambler's term, 極道 is favored by gangsters themselves to project an image of living by an uncompromising code—though in traditional Kansai dialect 極道者 (gokudōmono) still simply means a lazy, good-for-nothing prodigal!

rootFamily.gloss: chivalrous spirit, yakuza code of honor
rootFamily.word: 任侠道 (にんきょうどう)

楽しい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) i-adjective descending from Old Japanese たのし (tanosi, attested in the Man'yōshū and Nihon Shoki). Traditionally analyzed as a derivation from 手伸し (ta-nosi, 'stretching out the hands in joyful dance or ease') or cognate with the verbal root of 頼む (tanomu, 'to rely on, feel secure in abundance') and 満ち足る ('to be full and satisfied'). In Old and Early Middle Japanese, たのし primarily meant 'materially abundant, prosperous, wealthy, comfortable,' before shifting in Late Middle and Modern Japanese to emotional enjoyment, merriment, and fun. The kanji 楽 (Middle Chinese lak, 'music, joy') was applied via semantic matching (ateji/kun'yomi).

history.meaning: abundant, prosperous, materially well-off, satisfying
history.stage: Old to Early Middle Japanese (8th–12th c.)

history.form: たのし / たのしい (tanosi / tanoshii)
history.meaning: wealthy; pleasant, joyful, heart-warming (shifting from ku- to shiku-inflection)
fun, enjoyable, pleasant, delightful

楽しい.notes: While 嬉しい (ureshii) describes sudden personal happiness or gratitude at a specific event ('glad/thrilled'), 楽しい (tanoshii) describes the ongoing enjoyable quality of an activity, atmosphere, or shared experience ('fun/pleasant').

rootFamily.gloss: to enjoy, to take pleasure in; to look forward to
enjoyment, pleasure; something to look forward to
comfort, ease; pleasure, music (Sino-Japanese reading of same kanji)

楽しみ.etymology: Deverbal noun from the continuative stem of たのしむ (楽しむ, 'to enjoy, take pleasure in, look forward to').

history.meaning: pleasure; enjoyment; delight
enjoyment; pleasure; something looked forward to

楽しむ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *tanosimu* / *tanosibu* (楽しむ・楽しぶ, 'to feel joy, take delight in'), derived from the adjective たのし (楽し, 'delightful, abundant, joyful') + verbalizer *-mu*.

history.form: たのしぶ / たのしむ (楽しむ)

enjoy; have fun; take pleasure in

楽譜.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 楽 ('music') and 譜 ('chronicle, systematic chart, notation'), denoting written musical notation or a score.

構う.etymology: Inherited from Classical Japanese lower bigrade verb *kamafu* (構ふ, 'to build, set up, prepare'), which shifted to a four-grade/godan verb in Late Middle Japanese with the senses 'to mind, care about, look after, tease, banish'.

構える.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) ichidan verb descending from classical shimo-nidan 構ふ (kamafu, Old Japanese kamapu). Etymologically derived from an older root meaning 'to fit or interlock structural pieces together' (compare 噛む kamu, 'to bite, mesh, engage gears'). Originally denoting the physical construction of a timber framework, wall, or dwelling, its meaning extended to setting up a household or business, assuming a ready martial or camera posture, and mentally bracing oneself in anticipation.

history.meaning: to fit timbers together, construct a framework, build; to devise or fabricate
to build a residence; to prepare in advance; to assume a fighting stance
to set up (a shop/house); to adopt a posture or ready a weapon/camera; to brace oneself

morphemes.meaning: to frame, assemble, set up, assume a posture

構える.notes: Essential on film sets (カメラを構える, 'to ready/aim the camera'), in martial arts (構え, 'stance/guard'), and in psychology (構えてしまう, 'to stiffen up / become overly guarded'). Notice that 構う (kamau, 'to mind, care about, tease') is a historical doublet from the same Old Japanese verb kamapu!

rootFamily.gloss: to mind, care about, interfere with (godan doublet)

構想.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 構想 (gòuxiǎng), formed from 構 (kō, Middle Chinese kuwH, 'to interlock timbers, build a framework, compose') and 想 (sō, Middle Chinese sjangX, 'to think, visualize, form a mental image'). Literally 'constructing a mental framework,' the term originated in classical Chinese literary criticism for organizing the structural vision of a poem or painting before execution, and now denotes a grand concept, strategic vision, or narrative plot outline.

history.meaning: to mentally frame and organize the composition of a literary or artistic work
artistic or philosophical conception, structural plan of a work
concept, grand design, plot outline, blueprint for a project or policy

morphemes.meaning: to construct, frame, fit together, compose

構想.notes: Frequently collocates with 練る in 構想を練る (kōsō o neru, 'to knead/refine a concept or plot outline over time').

様.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun descending from Old Japanese さま (sama, 'visible shape, appearance, state, manner, direction'). In Early and Late Middle Japanese, out of courtly deference, speakers avoided naming a high-ranking person directly and instead referred obliquely to their general direction or noble bearing (sama, parallel to 方 kata 'direction/person' and 殿 dono 'palace/lord'). From this spatial-deferential metonymy, sama grammaticalized into the polite honorific suffix -sama ('honored Mr./Ms.') while also retaining its independent noun senses ('manner, state, plight'). The kanji 様 (Middle Chinese yangH, 'wooden pattern, mold, model, appearance') was matched semantically.

history.meaning: visible shape, outward appearance, manner, direction
history.stage: Old to Early Middle Japanese (8th–12th c.)

history.meaning: respectful indirect reference to a person's direction; polite epistolary and spoken honorific suffix
honored Mr./Ms.; hospitality suffix for 'party of...'; (as zama) unsightly state or plight

morphemes.meaning: appearance, manner, direction; honored person or party (honorific suffix)

様.notes: Demonstrates remarkable register polarization: as -sama (お客様, 3名様 'party of three'), it is high-respect keigo, whereas with rendaku or raw noun phrasing—ざまを見ろ (zama o miro, 'look at the pathetic state of you / serves you right!') or いいざまだ—the very same word becomes a biting insult!

rootFamily.gloss: various, varied, all kinds of (from 'in each manner')
manner, state, aspect; outward appearance (on'yomi compound)

様子.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 様子 (yōsu), from Tang/Song vernacular Chinese 樣子 ('model, shape, appearance, air, state of affairs').

history.meaning: pattern; shape; outward appearance
state of affairs; appearance; look; sign
