標本.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 標 (hyō, Middle Chinese pjew, 'treetop, topmost branch, surface mark, indicator') and 本 (hon, Middle Chinese pwenX, 'tree root, trunk, fundamental basis'). In classical Chinese philosophy and medicine (such as the Huangdi Neijing), 標本 (biāoběn) contrasted the 'treetop/secondary symptoms' (hyō) with the 'root/underlying cause' (hon). During the Meiji era, Japanese natural scientists repurposed the compound—interpreting 標 as 'indicative sign' and 本 as 'original exemplar/model' (compare 見本 mihon)—to translate Western scientific 'specimen' and statistical 'sample', a sense subsequently re-borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: the topmost branches and the root; secondary symptoms versus fundamental cause in medicine and statecraft
preserved biological, mineral, or anatomical specimen for scientific study; representative sample
scientific specimen; statistical sample; quintessential archetype of a trait

morphemes.meaning: treetop, mark, sign, surface indicator, standard

標本.notes: Used both literally for preserved museum/laboratory specimens (昆虫の標本, 'insect specimen') and figuratively for someone who is a 'walking textbook example' of a trait (e.g., 悪徳業者の標本のような男, 'a man who is a walking specimen of a crooked dealer').

cognates.meaning: legal or moral right, entitlement (semantic loan via Martin & Meiji Japan)

権利.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 権 (ken, Middle Chinese gjwen, originally 'metal sliding weight of a steelyard balance,' hence 'weighing circumstances, leverage, political power') and 利 (ri, Middle Chinese lijH, 'sharp reaping blade,' hence 'benefit, advantage, profit'). In classical Chinese texts such as Xunzi (荀子) and Shiji (史記), 權利 meant 'political power and material profit.' In 1864, American missionary W. A. P. Martin used 權利 in his Chinese translation of Wheaton's Elements of International Law (萬國公法) to render English 'right', and Meiji legal scholars such as Nishi Amane and Tsuda Mamichi adopted and popularized 権利 in Japanese jurisprudence, whence it spread across modern East Asia.

history.meaning: political power/leverage and material profit/gain
legal or natural right (used to translate Western 'right' / Dutch 'regt' in 萬國公法)
right, legal entitlement, privilege, copyright or distribution claim

morphemes.meaning: steelyard weight; power, authority, leverage, claim

権利.notes: Do not confuse with its homophone 権力 (kenryoku, 'political/coercive power'): 権利 (kenri) is a legal or moral entitlement/claim (including media distribution rights or copyrights, 著作権・放映権).

cognates.meaning: scope of authority, jurisdiction (loan from Japanese)

権限.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in Meiji-era legal and bureaucratic Japanese from 権 (ken, Middle Chinese gjwen, 'steelyard weight; official power, authority') and 限 (gen, Middle Chinese haenX, 'threshold, boundary, limit, prescribed scope'). Literally 'the bounded scope of official power,' it was created to translate European legal and administrative concepts such as German Kompetenz / Befugnis and English jurisdiction or authorized scope of authority vested in a public organ, corporate officer, or agent.

history.meaning: weighing power/authority + boundary/limit
legally defined scope of competence or jurisdiction of a state organ or official
authority, jurisdiction, authorized decision-making power (or digital access permissions)

権限.notes: Unlike 権力 (raw political or coercive might) or 権威 (prestige/moral authority), 権限 specifically refers to *bounded, delegated institutional or legal authority* (e.g., 決定権限がない, 'I do not have the authority to make that decision', or 管理者権限, 'administrator permissions').

横.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *yo₂ko₂* (横, 'horizontal direction, side, width, crosswise'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: crosswise; horizontal; side
side; beside; horizontal; width

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 横

横やり.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 横 (yoko, 'side, flank, horizontal') and やり (yari, written 槍 in kanji, 'spear, lance,' etymologically nominalized from the verb 遣る yaru, 'to thrust forward, send, drive'). The term originated in Sengoku-period battlefield tactics, where a warrior or unit drove a spear thrust into the flank (yokoyari) of an enemy engaged in front-line combat. From this literal flanking spear-thrust, it evolved into a metaphor for uninvited third-party interference or meddling in someone else's negotiations or affairs.

history.meaning: a flanking spear attack thrust from the side into an ongoing battle or duel
interrupting or criticizing someone else's conversation or transaction from the sidelines
meddling interference, butting in, uncalled-for objection from a third party

横やり.notes: Almost always used in the set idiom 横やりを入れる (yokoyari o ireru, literally 'to thrust in a side-spear' → 'to butt in, meddle, or throw a wrench into someone else's deal'). Because 槍 is not on the Jōyō kanji list, mixedorthography 横やり is very common in modern media subtitles and print.

rootFamily.gloss: spear, lance; first-spear battlefield honor (一番槍)
interference, snatching away from the side
cutting into a line; interrupting from the side

樫.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *kasi* (橿・樫, 'evergreen oak, *Quercus* subgenus *Cyclobalanopsis*'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, prized for its hard, dense timber (written with the kokuji 樫 from 木 'tree' + 堅 'hard').

history.meaning: evergreen oak
evergreen oak

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 樫

橋.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *pasi* (橋, 'bridge, stepping structure across a gap'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; cognate with 階 (*pasi*, 'stairs, ladder') and 間 (*pasi*, 'interval between two points').

history.meaning: bridge
bridge

機.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) single-morpheme noun from Middle Chinese 機 (kj+j, Old Chinese *kləj). The character combines 木 ('wood') and 幾 ('minute, subtle, near'), originally denoting the wooden treadle-and-shuttle mechanism of a weaving loom or the finely balanced release trigger of a crossbow. Because a microscopic movement of a crossbow trigger or loom mechanism unleashes decisive action, classical Chinese philosophy and military strategy extended 機 to mean the 'subtle spring of action, pivotal juncture, or ripe opportunity.'

history.meaning: weaving loom mechanism; crossbow trigger; subtle pivot of change
pivotal juncture, spiritual readiness or karmic capacity in Buddhism; secret spring of statecraft
ripe opportunity, occasion, critical moment; aircraft counter (-ki)

morphemes.meaning: loom, trigger mechanism; pivotal juncture, ripe opportunity

機.notes: As a standalone noun meaning 'opportunity/moment', 機 belongs to crisp, elevated expressions such as 機を見るに敏 (ki o miru ni bin, 'quick to seize an opportunity'), 機が熟す (ki ga jukusu, 'the time is ripe'), and 機を逸する (ki o issuru, 'to miss the chance').

rootFamily.gloss: crisis, critical moment of danger and поворот

機会.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 機會 (jīhuì), composed of 機 (ki, Middle Chinese kj+j, 'crossbow trigger, loom mechanism, pivotal moment') and 会 (traditional 會, kai, Middle Chinese hwajH, 'to meet, converge, assemble, juncture'). Literally 'the convergence of the trigger-moment,' it originally described the critical alignment of timing and circumstances in classical Chinese military and political texts, and became the standard modern Japanese word for 'opportunity, chance, or occasion.'

history.meaning: favorable convergence of timing and circumstances; pivotal juncture
favorable juncture, timely occasion, opportunity for action
opportunity, chance, occasion

機会.notes: A classic homophone pair in Japanese is 機会 (kikai, 'opportunity', pitch accent きかい↓ [2] or [0]) versus 機械 (kikai, 'machine', pitch accent きか↓い [2]); kanji choice reflects whether 会 ('meeting/occasion') or 械 ('wooden fetter/instrument') is involved.

rootFamily.word: 機会均等 (きかいきんとう)

rootFamily.gloss: waiting for a ripe opportunity, opportunism

cognates.word: 機密情報 / 机密情报 (jīmì qíngbào)

機密情報.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) four-character compound uniting two distinct historical strata: 機密 (kimitsu, from Literary Chinese 機密, combining 機 ki 'pivotal mechanism or affair of state' + 密 mitsu, Middle Chinese mit, 'dense, covert, secret,' hence 'vital state or corporate secret') and 情報 (jōhō, a Meiji-era military coinage of the 1870s–1880s attributed to Mori Ōgai and early Imperial Army strategists translating French renseignement and German Nachricht from 情 jō 'actual conditions of the enemy' + 報 hō 'report, dispatch'). Together, 機密情報 means 'classified intelligence' or 'strictly confidential information.'

history.meaning: crucial, covert affairs of the imperial court or military command
military intelligence report on enemy conditions (Meiji translation of French renseignement)
classified intelligence, top-secret governmental or corporate information

morphemes.meaning: pivotal affair, critical mechanism of state or enterprise

機密情報.notes: While 秘密 (himitsu) covers any personal or everyday secret, 機密 (kimitsu) specifically denotes high-stakes institutional, governmental, military, or corporate secrets whose leak threatens operations or security.

rootFamily.gloss: top secret, confidential matter; Discretionary State Secret funds (機密費)

cognates.meaning: equipment and materials (especially filming, audio, or technical gear)

機材.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) portmanteau compound formed in modern Japanese by combining 機 (ki, Middle Chinese kj+j, abbreviating 機械 kikai 'machinery, apparatus' or 機器 kiki 'devices') and 材 (zai, Middle Chinese dzoj, 'timber, raw material, supplies,' abbreviating 資材 shizai or 材料 zairyō). Originally an industrial and aviation logistics term for 'machinery and materials' (and aircraft fleet units), it became the standard production term in film, television, photography, music, and stagecraft for technical gear and filming equipment.

history.meaning: mechanical apparatus/loom + timber/raw material
machinery and industrial materials (blend of 機械 + 資材)
filming, audio, photographic, or broadcasting equipment; airline aircraft unit

morphemes.meaning: machine, apparatus, camera/technical device (from 機械)

機材.notes: In film and video production (such as in *The Naked Director*), 撮影機材 (satsuei kizai) is the indispensable term for cameras, lighting rigs, tripods, and boom mics; in commercial aviation, 機材卻 refers to the specific physical airplane assigned to a flight (e.g., 機材繰り, 'aircraft rotation').

rootFamily.gloss: subject matter, raw material for filming or reporting
instrument, apparatus, equipment (homophone written with 器)

機転.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 機転 (kiten), combining 機 ('pivotal moment, mental trigger, opportunity') + 転 ('turn, shift quickly'), denoting quick-wittedness or presence of mind.

history.meaning: quick mental adaptability to the moment
quick wit; tact; resourcefulness

locomotive; engine

next; following; subsequent

次に.etymology: The term '次に' (meaning 'next time') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: next time
next time

次に.notes: A common term in daily use.

欲しい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) i-adjective descending from Old Japanese ほし (posi, a shiku-inflected adjective 欲し), derived from the same Proto-Japonic verbal root *por- seen in the Old Japanese verb 欲る (poru → horu, 'to desire, wish for, covet') and 惚れる (horeru, 'to fall in love with, be infatuated'). The Sino-Japanese character 欲 (Middle Chinese yowk, 'to desire, covet') was mapped onto the native word as kun'yomi. Grammatically, it marks the desired object as the grammatical subject with が (originally 'X is desirable to me'), while shifting in modern Japanese toward a transitive-like expression of personal want.

history.meaning: desirable, enviable, wished-for (modifying or predicated of the desired object)
wanted, desired; (after -te) wishing for someone to perform an action
wanted, desired, wished for; (-te hoshii) wanting someone else to do something

to desire, wish for (archaic/literary verb preserving the verbal root)
to fall in love with, be charmed by (cognate root)

欲しさ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deadjectival abstract noun formed by suffixing the Old Japanese nominalizer -さ (-sa, indicating objective degree, extent, or state of a quality) to the stem 欲し- (hoshi-, Old Japanese posi-, 'desired, wanted'). While grammatically parallel to degree nouns like 高さ (takasa, 'height'), 欲しさ (hoshisa) idiomatically specialized to express the motivating intensity of craving or wanting something, especially when followed by the causal/purpose particle に (-hoshisa ni, 'out of desire for...').

history.meaning: the degree or state of being desirable or wanted

history.meaning: desire for, wanting, craving (that drives an action)

欲しさ.notes: Almost always used directly after a noun without a particle and followed by に to explain an ulterior or desperate motive: 金欲しさに嘘をつく (kane-hoshisa ni uso o tsuku, 'to tell a lie out of greed for money') or 褒め言葉欲しさに ('out of a craving for praise').

死.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) single-morpheme noun from Middle Chinese 死 (sijX, Old Chinese *sijʔ, 'to die, death', cognate with Proto-Sino-Tibetan *səj). Borrowed into Japanese, the on'yomi し (shi) serves both as a productive Sino-Japanese root and as an independent, elevated noun for 'death, decease, or mortality' (contrasting with the everyday native verbal nominalization 死に shini).

死ぬ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese 死ぬ (sinu, Proto-Japonic *sinu-). In classical Japanese grammar, 死ぬ (alongside 往ぬ / 去ぬ inu, 'to depart, pass away, vanish') belonged to the unique na-gyō henkaku (irregular n-stem) conjugation, leading historical linguists to analyze it as an ancient compound of a root *si- (variously linked to 'breath/wind expiring,' compare 息 iki and 風 shi in 嵐 arashi, or 'withering/stiffening,' compare 萎ゆ nayu / しなびる shinabiru) + the inchoative/perfective auxiliary -ぬ (-nu, itself derived from 往ぬ inu, 'to go away completely'). Alternatively, because Old Japanese sin- and Old Chinese 死 (*sijʔ) share a striking phonetic and semantic match, some philologists propose a prehistoric continental loan into Proto-Japonic prior to historical Sino-Japanese borrowing.

Captures both physical sinking (of a ship, body, or the setting sun) and emotional or financial depression (気が沈む 'spirits sink').

history.meaning: to sink to the bottom of water; to fall into ruin or obscurity
to sink, set (of the sun); to feel downcast
to sink, submerge; to set; to feel depressed

沈む.notes: Paired with the transitive verb 沈める (shizumeru, 'to sink something, submerge; to quell/calm').

沸く.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb descending from Old Japanese わく (waku, 'to well up, bubble forth, seethe with heat'). Etymologically identical to 湧く (waku, 'for spring water to bubble up from the ground'), it is written 沸く when thermal bubbling brings water in a kettle or bath to temperature. Its transitive partner is 沸かす (wakasu, 'to boil water').

history.meaning: to bubble up; to seethe and boil
to come to a boil (intransitive)

沸く.notes: In Japanese culinary usage, 沸く is for water becoming hot/boiling (お湯が沸く), whereas 煮える (nieru) is for food simmering/cooking through.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 沸く

沸騰.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound combining 沸 (futsu -> fut-, 'to bubble up, boil', from Middle Chinese *pjwɨt) and 騰 (tō, 'to leap up, rise, surge upward', from Middle Chinese *dəŋ). Literally 'bubbling and surging upward', 沸騰 denotes a liquid reaching its boiling point (100°C for water) where vigorous bubbles break the surface—crucial in cooking instructions such as 沸騰させないで ('never let it boil!').

history.meaning: bubbling up and surging
ebullition; rolling boil

沸騰.notes: Used with する (沸騰する, 'to boil') or causative させる (沸騰させる, 'to bring to a boil / let boil').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 沸騰

油.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *abura* (油・脂, 'oil, fat, grease, tallow'), attested in the Nihon Shoki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: vegetable oil or animal fat
oil

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 油

油断.etymology: Sino-Japanese / Buddhist compound 油断 (yudan), literally 'cutting off the flow of oil'. Derived from a parable in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (涅槃経) in which a man ordered to carry a bowl brimful of oil without spilling a single drop on pain of death must never relax his attention; hence 'momentary lapse of attention, carelessness, negligence'.

history.meaning: letting one's guard or attention lapse
negligence; carelessness; inattention; being off one's guard

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 油断

治る.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb なほる > なおる (naoru, from Old Japanese naporu, 'to return to its proper/straight state', related to 直 naho, 'straight, right, normal'). Japanese orthography splits this single native verb into two kanji by subject: 直る for broken objects, habits, or mood returning to normal, and 治る (using the medical character 治 'to heal, cure') for the body, illnesses, or injuries recovering.

history.meaning: to return to a right/whole state
to heal; to recover from illness or injury

治る.notes: Takes the subject particle が: 足首が治る ('the ankle heals') or 風邪が治る ('a cold gets better').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 治る

cognates.word: 治安維持 / 治安维持 (zhì'ān wéichí)

cognates.meaning: maintenance of public peace and order

治安維持.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) political-legal phrase combining 治安 (chian, 'public peace and order', attested since Han-dynasty statesman Jia Yi's memorials, from 治 'govern well' + 安 'peaceful, secure') and 維持 (iji, 'maintenance, preservation', from 維 'tie, hold together' + 持 'uphold, sustain'). In modern Japanese history, strongly echoes the notorious prewar Peace Preservation Law (治安維持法, Chian Ijihō of 1925) as well as contemporary policing.

history.meaning: stable governance and public tranquility
preservation of public order and state security
maintaining public order, law enforcement peace-keeping

治安維持.notes: Evokes both everyday police security (治安維持にあたる 'to work on maintaining public order') and historical censorship/policing under the 1925 治安維持法.

沿い.etymology: The term '沿い' (meaning 'along') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: along
along

沿い.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 沿い

沿う.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese intransitive verb *so₂pu* (添ふ・沿ふ, 'to accompany closely, run alongside, conform to'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; spelled 沿う specifically when following a line, river, road, or policy.

history.meaning: accompany closely; follow alongside
run along; follow (a river, road, or plan); meet (expectations)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 沿う

泊まる.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese intransitive verb *to₂maru* (泊まる・止まる・留まる, 'to stop, come to rest, anchor in a harbor, stay overnight'), specialized in orthography as 泊まる for anchoring a boat or lodging for the night.

history.meaning: moor a boat for the night; lodge overnight
stay overnight; lodge; be berthed

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 泊まる

泊める.etymology: Native Yamato ichidan transitive verb tomeru ('to lodge someone, let someone stay overnight; to anchor a boat'), derived from the Old Japanese transitive verb とむ (tomu, 'to stop, detain, bring to rest'). Etymologically identical to 止める / 留める (tomeru, 'to stop, halt, detain'), specialized orthographically with 泊 ('anchor, spend the night') for giving someone lodging or keeping a ship at anchor.

history.meaning: to bring to a halt; to moor a boat or lodge a traveler for the night
to put up a guest overnight; to berth a vessel
to let someone stay overnight, give lodging

morphemes.meaning: to cause to stay or stop overnight

泊める.notes: Transitive counterpart of 泊まる (tomaru, 'to stay overnight'); e.g., 友達を家に泊める ('to let a friend crash/stay overnight at one's house').

法律.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 法律 (hōritsu), from Classical Chinese 法律 ('laws and statutes'), combining 法 ('law, norm, model') + 律 ('penal statute, code'); adopted in the Meiji era as the standard term for statutory law.

history.meaning: laws and criminal statutes
law; statute; act of parliament

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 法律

泡.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *awa* (泡・沫, 'foam, bubble, froth on water'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: foam; bubble; froth
bubble; foam; froth; lather

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 泡

泡立てる.etymology: Compound ichidan verb combining あわ (泡, 'foam, bubbles') + たてる (立てる, 'to raise, whip up').

history.form: あわだつ / あわだてる (泡立てる)
history.meaning: work into a foam; whip up lather
whip; beat into foam; lather

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 泡立てる

泣きだす.etymology: Native Yamato compound verb formed from 泣き (naki, the ren'yōkei stem of 泣く naku, 'to cry, weep', from Old Japanese naku) + the inchoative auxiliary verb 出す (dasu, 'to burst out doing, begin suddenly'). Literally 'to burst into tears, start crying suddenly.'

history.meaning: to weep, cry aloud

history.form: 泣き出す / 泣きだす (nakidasu)
history.meaning: to burst into tears, start crying

morphemes.meaning: crying, weeping (stem of 泣く naku)
inchoative auxiliary verb ('to start suddenly, burst out')

泣きだす.notes: Unlike 泣き始める (which simply marks the beginning of crying), 泣きだす highlights a sudden, involuntary emotional outburst.

泣く.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *naku* (泣く・鳴く, 'to cry out, weep, sing/call of birds and animals'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; written 泣く for human weeping and 鳴く for animal/bird cries.

history.meaning: weep aloud; cry; call
cry; weep; shed tears

注ぎ口.etymology: Native Japanese compound combining そそぎ (注ぎ, continuative stem of 注ぐ 'to pour') + ぐち (口, rendaku form of くち 'mouth, opening, spout').

history.meaning: spout; pouring lip; nozzle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 注ぎ口

注ぐ.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *so₂so₂ku* > *sosogu* (注ぐ・灌ぐ, 'to pour liquid into, flow into, sprinkle, devote oneself to') and *tsugu* (注ぐ・継ぐ, 'to pour into a cup or vessel').

history.form: そそく / そそぐ (注ぐ)
history.meaning: pour water; flow into; rinse
pour; flow into; devote (attention/love)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 注ぐ

cognates.meaning: to pay attention to, take note of; caution

注意.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) verb-object compound from 注 (chū, from Middle Chinese tsyuwH, 'to pour water into a vessel, direct a stream toward, fix upon') and 意 (i, from Middle Chinese 'ijH, 'mind, thought, attention'). Literally 'to pour or direct one's mind toward a single point,' attested in Classical Chinese histories (such as the Records of the Grand Historian), and used in Japanese both for paying heed/care and for reprimanding or warning someone.

history.meaning: to direct one's thoughts or focus toward something
attention, caution, care; admonition or warning

注意.notes: Has two everyday verbal uses with する: 車に注意する ('watch out for cars', with に) and 部下を注意する ('warn/scold a subordinate', with を or に).

注文.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 注 ('pour, fix attention, annotate') and 文 ('writing, document'), which shifted in medieval/early-modern Japanese commerce from 'an itemized written list' to 'placing an order for goods'.

洋服.etymology: Sino-Japanese (wasei-kango) compound coined in the late Edo and Meiji Westernization period from 洋 (yō, from Middle Chinese yang, 'ocean', shortened from 西洋 seiyō 'the West, Western nations across the ocean') and 服 (fuku, from Middle Chinese bjuwk, 'garment, clothing'). Created to contrast Western-style tailored garments with traditional Japanese kimono (和服 wafuku), and now frequently used in everyday speech simply for 'clothes, outfit.'

history.meaning: Western-style attire (suits, dresses) as opposed to kimono (和服)
Western clothes; clothes or everyday wardrobe in general

morphemes.meaning: Western, Occidental (short for 西洋 seiyō)

洋服.notes: Since Western clothing became the daily norm in postwar Japan, 洋服を買う ('to buy clothes') is commonly used as a general synonym for 服を買う.

cognates.meaning: Western music (as opposed to traditional Korean gugak)

洋楽.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 洋 (yō, 'Western, Occidental', from 西洋 seiyō) and 楽 (gaku, from Middle Chinese ngæwk, 'music'). Originally coined in the Meiji era to distinguish European classical and military music from traditional Japanese music (邦楽 hōgaku); in postwar record-industry and radio usage, 洋楽 shifted to mean Western (especially English-language American and British) pop, rock, and R&B music.

history.meaning: Western music (classical, choral, brass) as opposed to traditional 邦楽
foreign (especially Western/English-language) popular music

morphemes.meaning: Western, overseas (short for 西洋 seiyō)

洋楽.notes: In modern Japanese music stores and streaming charts, 洋楽 (Western pop/rock) is paired directly with 邦楽 (hōgaku, now meaning domestic J-pop/Japanese music).

洋画.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 洋 (yō, 'Western, overseas', short for 西洋 seiyō) and 画 (ga, from Middle Chinese hweH, 'picture, painting; moving picture'). First coined in the Meiji art world for Western-style oil painting (contrasted with 日本画 nihonga), and extended in the Taishō/Shōwa cinema boom (as an abbreviation of 西洋映画 seiyō eiga) to denote foreign—especially Hollywood and European—movies, in contrast to domestic Japanese films (邦画 hōga).

history.meaning: Western-style painting (oil painting, watercolor)
Western/foreign film (contrasted with 邦画 domestic Japanese film); Western painting

morphemes.meaning: picture, painting; motion picture (from 映画 eiga)

洋画.notes: In everyday conversation and video-rental/streaming categories (as in 1980s video shops in *The Naked Director*), 洋画 almost always means 'Hollywood / foreign movies.'

洋風.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 洋風 (yōfū), combining 洋 ('Western, overseas', short for 西洋 *seiyō*) + 風 ('style, manner'), contrasted with 和風 (wafū, 'Japanese style').

history.meaning: Western style; European/American style

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 洋風

洗う.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *arapu* (洗ふ, 'to wash with water, cleanse, rinse, investigate'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: wash; cleanse in water
wash; cleanse; inquire into

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 洗う

洗濯.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound of 洗 (sen, from Middle Chinese senX, 'to wash, rinse, bathe') and 濯 (taku, from Middle Chinese dræwk, 'to rinse, wash clothes in running water'). Attested in Classical Chinese (including Mencius) for washing garments or purifying oneself, and established in Japanese since the medieval period as the standard word for doing laundry.

history.meaning: to wash and rinse garments or feet in clean water
washing clothes; figuratively refreshing one's spirit
laundry, washing clothes

morphemes.meaning: to rinse, scrub clothes in water

洗濯.notes: Also famous in the idiom 命の洗濯 (inochi no sentaku, 'refreshing one's soul / taking a rejuvenating break from daily cares').

洗脳.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 洗 (sen, Middle Chinese *sengX, "to wash, cleanse") and 脳 (nō, shinjitai of 腦, Middle Chinese *nawX, "brain, marrow"). Originally a Chinese Daoist and Buddhist meditative expression (xǐnǎo, "cleansing the mind of worldly impurities"), it was repurposed in mid-20th-century Maoist China for coercive ideological "thought reform" (which journalist Edward Hunter calqued into English as "brainwashing" in 1950) and borrowed into modern Japanese.

history.meaning: to cleanse the mind or brain of worldly thoughts in meditation
coercive ideological re-education or thought reform
brainwashing; psychological indoctrination

洗脳.notes: Functions as a noun and a suru-verb (洗脳する, "to brainwash"); frequently used in discussions of cults, propaganda, and high-pressure corporate or media manipulation.

sources.title: Kotobank: 洗脳 (精選版 日本国語大辞典)

洗面所.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 洗面所 (senmenjo), combining 洗面 ('washing the face', from 洗 'wash' + 面 'face') + 所 ('place, room').

history.meaning: washroom; lavatory; bathroom sink area

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 洗面所

派手.etymology: Native Japanese (wago) word written with ateji characters 派 ("faction, splash") and 手 ("hand, style, manner"). Originating in late Muromachi and early Edo-period musical terminology as 破手 or 派手 (hade, with rendaku voicing of 手 te to -de), it designated a lively, ornate shamisen playing style that contrasted with traditional, understated 本手 (honde, "orthodox style"). A secondary folk-etymological reinforcement connects it to 映え手 (haete, "striking or showy manner").

history.meaning: ornate, innovative shamisen accompaniment style (contrasted with honde 本手)
flashy, showy, extravagant in dress, color, or behavior

morphemes.meaning: striking, ornate, branching out (from 破/映え)
hand, style, technique, manner (te > -de via rendaku)

派手.notes: Takes the na-adjective particle (派手な) and stands in direct antonymy with 地味 (jimi, "plain, subdued, understated").

流される.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) passive and spontaneous form of the transitive verb 流す (nagasu, "to let flow, set adrift, wash away, exile"), constructed from the stem nagas- plus the passive/spontaneous auxiliary -areru (Classical Japanese -aruru). Ultimately derives from the Proto-Japonic root *nanka- ("to flow, stretch out continuously", likely related to 長い nagai, "long"). Semantically evolved from being physically carried away by water or banished into exile to being swept along by temptation, mood, or social pressure.

history.meaning: to be washed away by a current; to be banished into exile
to be swept along physically or swayed by atmosphere, temptation, or others

流される.notes: Often used in psychological or moral contexts (e.g., 雰囲気に流される, "to get swept up in the mood" or 周りに流される, "to bow to peer pressure").

rootFamily.gloss: to let flow, drain, wash away

流す.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese transitive verb *nagasu* (流す, 'to let flow, set adrift, wash away, exile'), paired with intransitive ながる/ながれる (流れる).

history.meaning: set afloat on a current; wash away; banish
let flow; drain; flush; broadcast/play (music); shed (tears/sweat)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 流す

流れる.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese lower bigrade verb *nagaru* (流る, 'to flow, stream, drift along, pass by'), becoming modern ichidan *nagareru*.

history.meaning: flow (of water); drift; pass (of time)
flow; stream; drift; be washed away; be called off

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 流れる

流通.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 流 (ryū, Middle Chinese *ljuw, "to flow, circulate") and 通 (tsū, Middle Chinese *thuwng, "to pass through unobstructed, communicate"). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and Buddhist texts to describe the unimpeded flow of water, vital energy (qi), or teachings through the realm, it was adopted in Meiji-era Japanese political economy to denote the circulation of currency and the commercial distribution of goods from producers to consumers.

history.meaning: unobstructed flow of water, air, or Buddhist teachings
monetary circulation and commercial distribution of commodities

流通.notes: In business and media contexts (including video retail in The Naked Director), 流通 refers specifically to the wholesale and retail distribution network or pipeline.

sources.title: Kotobank: 流通 (日本国語大辞典)

cognates.meaning: to float, rise to the surface

浮かぶ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive godan verb from Old Japanese ukabu (浮ぶ), formed by extending the core root uk- (seen in 浮く uku, "to float, become buoyant", from Proto-Japonic *uka-) with the verbal suffix -abu, which expresses a continuous state or outward manifestation. Alongside literal buoyancy on water or in the sky, it developed the figurative sense of thoughts, ideas, memories, or emotions surfacing into consciousness or onto one's face.

history.meaning: to float upon water; to drift or hover in the air
to float to the surface; to come to mind or appear on one's expression

浮かぶ.notes: Whereas 浮く (uku) focuses on the physical state of being buoyant or detached from the bottom, 浮かぶ (ukabu) is strongly preferred for ideas popping into mind (アイディアが浮かぶ) or expressions surfacing on a face (笑みが浮かぶ).

rootFamily.gloss: to set afloat; to express (a smile or tear)
to get carried away, be in high spirits

sources.title: Kotobank: 浮かぶ (日本国語大辞典)

浮かべる.etymology: Native Japanese transitive ichidan verb descending from Classical Japanese うかぶ (ukabu, shimo-nidan transitive, 'to cause to rise to the surface, set afloat'), the transitive counterpart of intransitive 浮かぶ (ukabu, godan, 'to float, rise to mind'). Beyond floating physical objects on water, Japanese uses 浮かべる idiomatically for emotions rising visibly to the surface of the face or eyes: 目に涙を浮かべる ('to well up with tears in one's eyes') and 笑みを浮かべる ('to let a smile play across one's face').

history.meaning: to set afloat; to let rise to the surface
to float; to show a smile or tears on the surface

rootFamily.gloss: to float; to come to mind

浮かべる.notes: The collocation 目に涙を浮かべる ('to float tears in one's eyes') is the classic Japanese expression for eyes brimming with tears without crying aloud.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 浮かべる

浮かれる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive ichidan verb descending from Classical Japanese ukaru (浮かる, Lower Bigrade stem ukare-), derived from the verbal root uk- (浮く, "to float, come unmoored") plus the spontaneous/passive suffix -aru (-areru in modern Japanese). Literally meaning "to become unmoored and float away involuntarily", it shifted in Heian poetry from emotional restlessness and wandering to the modern sense of getting carried away, feeling giddy, or losing composure in excitement.

history.meaning: to drift unmoored; for one's soul or heart to feel restless and unsettled
to be buoyed up with excitement, make merry, or get carried away

morphemes.meaning: spontaneous state suffix ("to come to float on its own")

浮かれる.notes: Often carries a mildly critical nuance that someone has let success, romance, or festivity go to their head and lost their vigilance (e.g., 浮かれている場合じゃない, "this is no time to be getting carried away").

sources.title: Kotobank: 浮かれる (日本国語大辞典)

cognates.meaning: to float, rise to the surface

浮く.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive godan verb from Old Japanese uku (浮く), inherited from Proto-Japonic *uka- / *uk- ("to float, rise to the surface, lift off"). Beyond physical buoyancy in water or air, it developed rich metaphorical extensions: teeth feeling loose, money or time being spared ("floating free" from budget), feeling restless or frivolous, or sticking out awkwardly from a group.

history.meaning: to float, rise to the surface
to float on water; to become buoyant or unsettled
to float; to be saved (of money/time); to stand out awkwardly in a group

morphemes.meaning: to float, be buoyant, rise up

浮く.notes: In colloquial Japanese, 場から浮く ("to float from the scene") means to stick out like a sore thumb or fail to fit in with the surrounding atmosphere or dress code.

rootFamily.gloss: to get carried away, be festive

sources.title: Kotobank: 浮く (日本国語大辞典)

cognates.meaning: to bathe, pour water over oneself

浴びる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb from Old Japanese abu (浴ぶ, Upper Bigrade stem abi-), descending from Proto-Japonic *ampu- ("to pour water over oneself, bathe"). Originally denoted pouring water over the body for washing or Shinto ritual purification, and subsequently shifted from Upper Bigrade (abu) to modern Ichidan (abiru). By metaphor, one can "bathe" in sunlight, stage lights, public attention, criticism, or alcohol.

history.meaning: to pour water over the body, bathe
to pour water over oneself; to bathe in a river or hot spring
to take a shower; to be bathed in light, attention, or criticism

morphemes.meaning: to pour over the body, douse oneself, bathe

浴びる.notes: Unlike お風呂に入る ("to get into a bath tub"), シャワーを浴びる is used for taking a shower; the hyperbole 浴びるほど飲む ("to drink as if bathing in it") means to drink alcohol like a fish.

rootFamily.gloss: to pour upon, shower someone with (questions/blows)
bathing in Water (Shinto purification or cold-water austerity)

sources.title: Kotobank: 浴びる (日本国語大辞典)

海.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun from Old Japanese umi₁ (海 / 宇美), descending from Proto-Japonic *umi ("expanse of water, sea"). In Old Japanese, umi₁ referred to any vast body of water, distinguishing the saltwater ocean (潮海 sipo-umi) from large freshwater lakes (淡海 apa-umi > Ōmi, modern Lake Biwa). Internally often analyzed as a compound of *u- / *o- ("great, vast", cf. 大 ō-) + *mi₁ ("water", cf. 水 mizu < Old Japanese mi₁du).

history.meaning: vast expanse of water, sea or great lake
the sea, ocean, or any great body of water
sea, ocean, beach

海.notes: In everyday speech, 海へ行く ("to go to the sea") frequently means "to go to the beach"; in compounds, 海 uses the Sino-Japanese reading kai (e.g., 海外 kaigai, 海岸 kaigan) or poetic wago bound form wata / una- (e.g., 海原 unabara).

rootFamily.gloss: expanse of the ocean, the deep sea

sources.title: Kotobank: 海 (日本国語大辞典)

海塩.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 海塩 (かいえん), from 海 ('sea, ocean') and 塩 ('salt').
海塩.notes: Distinguishes evaporated sea salt from rock salt (岩塩 がんえん).

海外.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 海 (kai, Middle Chinese *xojX, "sea, ocean") and 外 (gai, Middle Chinese *ngwajH, "outside, beyond"). First attested in early Chinese geographical-mythological texts such as the Shanhaijing (山海經, "Classic of Mountains and Seas", which includes chapters titled 海外經 "Classic of Regions Beyond the Seas") to denote distant lands beyond the Four Seas surrounding China; in insular Japan, it naturally became the primary word for "overseas, abroad".

history.meaning: remote lands beyond the Four Seas surrounding the Central Plains

潰しがい.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from the continuative stem tsubushi (潰し) of the transitive verb 潰す (tsubusu, "to crush, smash, ruin, shut down") plus the bound suffix -gai (甲斐, voiced via rendaku from kai, Old Japanese kapi₁, "effect, worth, reward for effort"). 潰す.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive godan verb from Classical Japanese tubusu (潰す), paired with intransitive 潰れる (tsubureru). Built on the root *tubu- (cognate with 粒 tsubu, "grain, drop, round lump, blister") plus the transitive verbalizer -su, originally evoking bursting a blister or squashing a round lump flat. Semantically expanded to crushing objects, melting down metal, slaughtering animals for meat, driving a rival or business into bankruptcy, and "killing" time.

潰す.notes: Extremely versatile in colloquial Japanese: 時間を潰す ("to kill time"), 顔・面目を潰す ("to make someone lose face"), 会社を潰す ("to drive a company under"), and 相手を潰す ("to crush an opponent").

rootFamily.gloss: to be crushed, collapse, go bankrupt (intransitive)

Originally describing a blister bursting or a round object collapsing under pressure, it broadened to structural collapse, organ failure (voice or eyes giving out), getting dead drunk, and a business going bankrupt.

潰れる.notes: In business contexts, 会社が潰れる is the standard everyday way to say "a company goes belly-up / bankrupt" (equivalent to formal 倒産する tōsan suru); 酔い潰れる means to drink oneself unconscious.

Attested in Japan from the Kamakura and Muromachi periods onward as "a fire incident / emergency", specifically distinguishing an uncontrolled, destructive conflagration (burning buildings or neighborhoods) from the physical element or cooking flame 火 (hi). Historically also written with the ateji 夥事 ("tremendous incident").

accidental or destructive fire, blaze, conflagration (especially of buildings)

火事.notes: Japanese strictly separates 火 (hi, the physical flame or fire element) from 火事 (kaji, an uncontrolled destructive fire emergency); a famous Edo proverb goes 火事と喧嘩は江戸の華 ("Fires and brawls are the flowers of Edo").

Tuesday

灰色.etymology: Compound combining native Japanese はい (灰, from Old Japanese *papi* 'ash') + いろ (色, 'color'), literally 'ash color'.

無修正.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by prefixing the privative morpheme 無 (mu, Middle Chinese *mju, "without, non-, un-") to 修正 (shūsei, "revision, correction, retouching", from 修 shū, Middle Chinese *sjuw, "to repair, embellish" + 正 sei, Middle Chinese *tsjengH, "to make right, rectify"). Originally used in publishing and photography for unretouched negatives or unamended drafts, in post-war Japanese print and video regulation (central to The Naked Director) it specialized to mean "uncensored" adult media lacking mandatory mosaic or black-bar masking of genitalia (as prohibited under Article 175 of the Penal Code).

history.meaning: unamended text or unretouched photographic negative
uncensored (lacking optical blurring, black bars, or mosaic pixelation)

rootFamily.gloss: unconditional, without conditions (sharing prefix 無 mu-)

無垢だ.etymology: The term '無垢だ' (meaning 'solid') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

solid

history.meaning: unsalted; without added salt

無塩バター.etymology: Modern culinary compound combining Sino-Japanese 無塩 (muen, 'unsalted, salt-free', from 無 'without' + 塩 'salt') + loanword バター (from English *butter*).

history.form: 無塩バター (むえんバター)
history.meaning: unsalted butter

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — バター

Originally a Buddhist term 愛相 ("attachment to pleasing appearances"), aisō came to denote amiable sociability and hospitality; prefixed with bu-, it describes a blunt, curt, unsmiling, or unsociable demeanor.

unreasonable

無計画.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) formation combining the privative prefix 無 (mu-, 'without, non-') with the noun 計画 (keikaku, 'plan, project, scheme'), itself a compound of 計 (kei, 'calculate, reckon, devise') and 画 (kaku, 'draw lines, delineate, lay out'). history.meaning: lacking calculation and delineation of a scheme
unplanned, lacking a plan, reckless

無許可.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by prefixing the negative/privative morpheme 無 (mu-, 'without, lacking') to 許可 (kyoka, 'permission, approval, license'), which unites 許 (kyo, 'grant, allow, accede to') and 可 (ka, 'approve, deem permissible'). Denotes an act or operation conducted without official sanction or regulatory licensing.

history.meaning: to accede to and approve officially
without permission, unlicensed, unauthorized

無許可.notes: Often linked with で (無許可で, 'without permission/unlicensed') in legal and policing contexts, such as unauthorized filming or street vending.

無謀.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound attested in classical Chinese historiography, combining the privative 無 (mu, Middle Chinese *mju, 'without, lacking') and 謀 (bō, Middle Chinese *mjuw, 'counsel, stratagem, deliberation'). Originally describing a commander or actor operating without strategic forethought, it evolved into a general adjectival noun for rash, foolhardy, or reckless behavior that ignores foreseeable danger.

history.meaning: lacking counsel, devoid of strategic deliberation
reckless, rash, ill-advised, thoughtless

infinity, boundlessness, unlimitedness

history.meaning: roasted or broiled meat; Western-style roast meat dish
Japanese-Korean style tabletop grilled meat barbecue

morphemes.meaning: grill, broil, roast, burn (continuative stem of 焼く)

焼き肉.notes: Frequently written without okurigana as 焼肉 on restaurant signage and menus; combines a native kun'yomi verb stem with an on'yomi noun.

焼き鳥.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 焼き (yaki), the nominalized continuative form (ren'yōkei) of 焼く (yaku, 'to grill, broil, roast, char'), and 鳥 (tori, 'bird, fowl, poultry', from Old Japanese *töri). skewered and charcoal-grilled chicken pieces

morphemes.meaning: grill, broil, roast (continuative stem of 焼く)

焼き鳥.notes: In parts of Japan (such as Muroran or Higashimatsuyama), 焼き鳥 (often written in hiragana as やきとり) can also refer to skewered pork offal or pork belly.

焼く.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese transitive verb *yaku* (焼く, 'to burn, set on fire, roast, bake, fire clay, char'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: burn; roast; fire
bake; grill; roast; toast; burn; tan

morphemes.meaning: heat, fever, high temperature (assimilated to nek-)

熱気.notes: Commonly used in expressions like 熱気に包まれる (nekki ni tsutsumareru, 'to be enveloped in feverish excitement') or 熱気あふれる ('brimming with electric energy').

燃える.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive ichidan verb derived from Old Japanese and Classical Japanese 燃ゆ (moyu, shimo-nidan conjugation, 'to burn, blaze, catch fire'), which is etymologically related to 萌ゆ (moyu, 'to sprout, bud, burst forth', sharing a root meaning of 'to flare or spring up irrepressibly'). Beyond physical combustion, it developed the vibrant figurative sense of burning with ambition, passion, or competitive spirit.

history.meaning: to burn, blaze, flare up (intransitive lower bigrade verb)
to burn, blaze; to be fired up, burn with passion or determination

燃える.notes: Intransitive counterpart to transitive 燃やす (moyasu, 'to burn something / stoke'); in colloquial speech, 燃えてきた ('Now I'm getting fired up!') expresses rising motivation.

爆発的.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) adjectival derivative formed by attaching the adjectival suffix 的 (-teki, 'having the character of, -ive, -ic') to the noun 爆発 (bakuhatsu, 'explosion, detonation, eruption'), which unites 爆 (baku, 'crackle in fire, burst violently, explode') and 発 (hatsu, 'shoot forth, discharge, erupt'). Used both literally for physical detonations and figuratively for sudden, meteoric surges in popularity or sales.

history.meaning: violent bursting forth, detonation, eruption
explosive, meteoric, sudden and overwhelming in scale

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix (-ive, -ic, having the nature of)

爆発的.notes: Frequently collocates with 爆発的な人気 ('explosive popularity') or 爆発的ヒット ('blockbuster/explosive hit').

父.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) kinship noun ちち (chichi), attested in the 8th-century *Man'yōshū* and *Kojiki* as Old Japanese *titi* (written phonographically as 知々). Originating in reduplicated nursery or Lallwort syllables (*ti-ti*), it paralleled Old Japanese *papa* (母, 'mother') and underwent regular Japanese affrication of *ti* > *chi* during the late Middle Japanese period. Written with the logogram 父 ('father, elder male holding an axe/rod of authority').

history.meaning: father, male parent
father (especially one's own father in humble/neutral reference)

父.notes: In modern polite conversation, ちち (父) is uchi-go (in-group humble language) used when speaking about one's own father to outsiders, contrasting with お父さん (otōsan).

父ちゃん.etymology: Colloquial and affectionate kinship noun combining תō (父, a long-voweled familiar stem abstracted from お父さん otōsan, itself likely deriving from honorific *tōto- / *tatto- 'revered, esteemed' or nursery *tō) with the hypocoristic suffix ちゃん (-chan, palatalized diminutive alteration of the polite title さん -san). Conveys warmth, working-class down-to-earth familiarity, or childlike intimacy.

history.form: てて / とと (tete / toto -> tō)
history.meaning: papa, daddy (vernacular kinship stem)
Dad, Daddy, Pop (colloquial/affectionate address or reference)

父ちゃん.notes: Pairs naturally with 母ちゃん (kāchan, 'Mom/Ma'); evokes an unpretentious, nostalgic, or Shōwa-era working-class family atmosphere.

片付く.etymology: The term '片付く' (meaning 'tidy') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: tidy
tidy

片付く.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 片付く

片付ける.etymology: Compound ichidan verb *katazukeru* (片付ける, 'to put in order, tidy up, clear away, finish off, marry off'), transitive partner of かたづく (片付く, literally 'to settle to one side [片]').

history.meaning: put away neatly to one side; settle; dispose of
tidy up; put in order; clear away; finish

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 片付ける

片思い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound attested since the *Man'yōshū* (8th century, written 片思ひ *kata-ömöpi*), formed from the prefixal stem 片- (kata-, 'one-sided, single of a pair, incomplete') and 思い (omoi, nominalized continuative form of 思ふ / 思う omou, 'to think, yearn, love, long for'). Literally 'one-sided longing', where romantic affection flows in only one direction without reciprocation.

history.meaning: yearning or longing from only one side
unrequited romantic love, one-sided yearning (poetic waka theme)
unrequited love, one-sided crush

morphemes.meaning: one-sided, single of a pair, partial
thought, feeling, romantic longing (stem of 思う)

片思い.notes: Its exact antonym is 両思い (ryōomoi, 'mutual love / reciprocated feelings'); 片- productively forms words for half-pairs like 片道 (katamichi, 'one-way trip') and 片手 (katate, 'one hand').

片方.etymology: The term '片方' (meaning 'one side') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: one side
one side

片方.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 片方

牛乳.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 牛 ('cow, cattle') and 乳 ('milk'), literally 'cow's milk'.

history.meaning: cow's milk

cognates.meaning: to hold the bull's ear; to hold sway or leadership in an alliance

牛耳る.etymology: Hybrid denominal godan verb created by attaching the native Japanese verbalizing suffix -る (-ru) to the Sino-Japanese noun 牛耳 (gyūji, 'ox's ear'). Alludes to the ancient Chinese Spring and Autumn period covenant ritual (*zhí niú'ěr* 執牛耳, recorded in the *Zuo Zhuan*), in which the hegemon or presiding leader of a feudal alliance cut the ear of a sacrificial ox and smeared its blood to seal an oath; hence 'to hold supreme control, dominate a faction, or call the shots'.

history.meaning: to hold the sacrificial bull's ear as presiding leader of a blood covenant
to take the lead or command over a group or faction
to control, dominate, boss around, call the shots in an industry or group

牛耳る.notes: Despite ending in -iru, 牛耳る conjugates as a consonant-stem (godan) verb (牛耳らない gyūjiranai, 牛耳って gyūjitte), just like サボる or 皮肉る.

物.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *mo₂no₂* (物, 'thing, tangible object, being, spirit, matter'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; also read Sino-Japanese *butsu / motsu* (from Middle Chinese 物 *mjut*).

history.meaning: thing; object; substance; spirit/being
thing; object; article; goods; quality

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 物

物件売却.etymology: Sino-Japanese real-estate and legal compound combining 物件 (bukken, 'property, real-estate object, article') + 売却 (baikyaku, 'sale, disposal by sale').

history.form: 物件売却 (ぶっけんばいきゃく)
history.meaning: property sale; sale of real estate

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 売却

物理.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 物理 (butsuri, from 物 'things, matter' + 理 'inner principle, natural order'). Originally a classical Chinese philosophical term in Du Fu and Neo-Confucianism for 'the inherent principles of all things', it was adopted in Meiji Japan (shortened from 物理学 butsurigaku) to translate Western 'physics', and subsequently re-entered modern Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: the natural principles governing things
the science of physics
physics; physical laws

物理.notes: Used both for the academic subject and casually for everyday physical principles (基本の物理, 'basic physics!').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 物理

物語.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 物語. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 物語

特に.etymology: Adverbial construction formed from the Sino-Japanese bound morpheme 特 (toku, Middle Chinese *dok, originally 'a sacrificial bullock standing apart from the herd', hence 'single, exceptional, special, distinctive') combined with the native Japanese dative/adverbial case particle に (ni). Functions as a high-frequency adverb singling out an item or circumstance as above the ordinary.

history.meaning: singled-out bullock; exceptional, distinctive, alone
especially, particularly, above all

特に.notes: Often paired with negative predicates (特にない, 'nothing in particular') to give a polite, understated refusal or non-committal reply.

特上.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 特 (toku, 'special, exceptional, extraordinary') and 上 (jō, 'upper, superior, first-class, top grade'). Developed in commercial and culinary grading systems—where standard tiers ascend from 並 (nami, 'regular') to 上 (jō, 'superior') to 特上 (tokujō, 'special deluxe top grade')—to designate the finest cut or highest tier of goods.

history.meaning: exceptionally superior, above the upper grade
deluxe top grade, finest quality (especially sushi, unagi, yakiniku)

特上.notes: In traditional Japanese restaurant menus (sushi, eel, beef), ordering 特上 signals indulgence or treating guests lavishly above 並 (regular) and 上 (choice).

特別.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 特別 (tokubetsu), combining 特 ('special, singled out, exceptional') + 別 ('separate, distinct, different').

history.stage: Late Imperial Chinese / Early Modern Japanese
history.meaning: specially distinguished from the ordinary
special; particular; extraordinary

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 特別

特権.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal and political neologism coined or popularized in Meiji-era Japan to translate European concepts of 'privilege' and 'prerogative' (ultimately from Latin *privilegium*), formed from 特 (toku -> tok- via gemination before k, 'special, exclusive') and 権 (ken, 'steelyard balance weight; power, authority, legal right'). Re-borrowed into modern Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: special right or exclusive authority (Meiji legal translation of 'privilege')
privilege, special right, exclusive prerogative

特権.notes: Used both in serious sociopolitical critique (特権階級 tokken kaikyū, 'privileged class') and everyday speech (若さの特権, 'the privilege of youth').

犯人.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound from Literary Chinese 犯人, uniting 犯 (han, Middle Chinese *bjonX, 'transgress, encroach upon, violate a law or taboo') and 人 (nin, 'person, individual'). Literally 'a person who transgresses the law', serving as the standard investigative and everyday term for the perpetrator or culprit of a crime or misdeed.

history.meaning: one who violates the law, offender, prisoner
culprit, perpetrator, criminal offender

犯人.notes: In media and police procedure, 犯人 means 'the perpetrator/culprit' of an act, whereas a formal legal suspect before conviction is called 容疑者 (yōgisha).

rootFamily.gloss: to commit (a crime or sin), violate

cognates.meaning: to commit a crime; crime, offense

犯罪.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from classical Chinese legal vocabulary, originally a verb-object construction 犯罪 ('to transgress into guilt / commit an offense') composed of 犯 (han, 'transgress, violate, infringe') and 罪 (zai, 'guilt, sin, punishable offense, statutory crime'). In Japanese, it lexicalized primarily as a noun (and suru-verb) meaning 'crime' or 'criminal offense'.

history.meaning: to commit a punishable transgression against the law (verb-object phrase)
crime, criminal offense, unlawful act

犯罪.notes: Attaches रेगुलरली to 者 to form 犯罪者 (hanzaisha, 'criminal') and 軽犯罪 (keihanzai, 'minor offense / misdemeanor').

状.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 状. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 状

状況.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound combining 状 (jō, 'form, appearance, state, condition') and 況 (kyō, 'how much more so; aspect, prevailing circumstances, state of affairs'). Denotes the dynamic, evolving state of affairs or operational circumstances surrounding an event, contrasting slightly with 状態 (jōtai, 'static condition or state').

history.meaning: appearance and prevailing aspect of things
situation, circumstances, evolving state of affairs

状況.notes: Historically also written 情況 when emphasizing subjective or emotional circumstances, though 状況 is now the standard unified spelling for shifting external conditions.

狂い.etymology: Deverbal noun from the continuative stem of くるう (狂う, Old Japanese *kurupu* 'to go mad, get out of order, warp, go awry').

history.meaning: madness; frenzy; deviation from true alignment
warping (of wood); going out of order; discrepancy; madness

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 狂い

狂う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb derived from Old and Classical Japanese 狂ふ (kurupu > kurufu > kuruu). Etymologically linked to the mimetic and spatial root *kuru- ('to spin around, whirl, turn awry', seen in くるくる kurukuru, 'spinning round and round', and 車 kuruma, 'wheel/cart'). From the physical sense of whirling erratically out of alignment, it developed the meanings 'to go mad, lose one's sanity' and 'to get out of order or go awry (of plans or machinery)'.

history.meaning: to spin wildly out of alignment; to become deranged or possessed
to go mad, lose one's mind; to get out of order, go awry (of schedules, plans, or mechanisms)

狂う.notes: Used not only for madness (気が狂う, 'to lose one's mind') but very frequently for disrupted plans (計画が狂う, 'the plan went awry') or broken watches/senses.

rootFamily.gloss: to throw out of order, derange, disrupt (transitive)

狙う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive godan verb descending from Classical Japanese 狙ふ (nerafu < *nerapu). Most philologists derive *nerapu from an iterative/continuative formation (-fu / -pu) built on a verbal root cognate with 練る / 煉る (neru, 'to knead, temper, train, work over carefully and patiently') or 寝る (neru, 'to lie low in ambush'). Written with the kanji 狙 (originally 'a monkey watching stealthily for an opening'), it means to watch closely for a chance and take deliberate aim at a target or prize.

history.meaning: to watch stealthily from ambush, wait for an opening to strike
to aim at, target deliberately, set one's sights on, stalk

morphemes.meaning: stalk, watch for an opening, aim at

狙う.notes: The nominalized stem 狙い (nerai) means 'aim, objective, or target' (狙い通り, 'just as aimed/planned').

rootFamily.gloss: to be targeted, be aimed at (passive)

狙われる.etymology: Passive voice conjugation of the native Yamato (wago) transitive verb 狙う (nerau, 'to aim at, target, stalk'), formed by taking the imperfective/irrealis stem (mizenkei) 狙わ- (nerawa-, preserving the historical labial glide *w* from Old Japanese *-pa-) and attaching the passive auxiliary suffix -れる (-reru). Expresses being the object of someone's deliberate targeting, ambush, or predation.

history.meaning: to be watched stealthily or targeted by an adversary
to be targeted, be aimed at, have a target on one's back

morphemes.meaning: aim at, target, stalk (imperfective stem of 狙う)

狙われる.notes: Common in crime and thriller contexts: 命を狙われる (inochi o nerawareru, 'to have one's life targeted') or 警察に狙われる ('to be targeted by the police').

rootFamily.gloss: to aim at, target, set one's sights on
looking for a specific target or opening

独占.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Literary Chinese 獨佔 / 独占, combining 独 (doku, Middle Chinese *duwk, 'alone, single, solitary, sole') and 占 (sen, Middle Chinese *tsjemH, 'to occupy, take possession of, hold'). Literally 'to occupy or hold all by oneself', serving as both the standard economic term for market monopoly and the general word for hogging or exclusive control.

history.meaning: to occupy or possess exclusively by oneself
monopoly, exclusive possession, monopolization

独占.notes: Appears in media as 独占インタビュー ('exclusive interview') and in economics as 独占禁止法 ('Antimonopoly Act / antitrust law'); native Yamato synonym for 'hogging' is 独り占め (hitorijime).

cognates.word: 獨佔販賣 / 獨家銷售

独占販売.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) commercial compound uniting 独占 (dokusen, 'monopoly, exclusive possession', from 独 'sole' + 占 'occupy') with 販売 (hanbai, 'sale, marketing, distribution', from 販 'trade, peddle, deal in merchandise' + 賣/売 'sell'). Designates commercial distribution in which a single enterprise holds exclusive rights to sell a product or media title.

history.meaning: exclusive possession combined with commercial selling
exclusive sale, sole distribution rights, monopolized retail

独占販売.notes: Often extended with 権 as 独占販売権 (dokusen hanbaiken, 'exclusive distribution/sales rights'), a key concept in publishing, video distribution, and import businesses.

狭い.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *se₂basi* / *se₂masi* (狭し, 'narrow, cramped, small in area'), built on the spatial root *se-* (狭, 'narrow place, rapids', as in 瀬戸 *seto*). Medial *-b-* and *-m-* alternated in Middle Japanese, yielding standard *semai*.

history.meaning: narrow; confined; cramped
narrow; cramped; small (in area); limited

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 狭い

猶予.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 猶予 (yūyo), from Classical Chinese 猶豫 ('hesitation, indecision, delay' — traditionally explained via two cautious animals, 猶 and 豫, or as an alliterative binome *juw-jo* for wavering); in Japanese extended to 'postponement, grace period, reprieve'.

history.meaning: hesitate; waver undecidedly; delay
postponement; grace period; extension of time; hesitation

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 猶予

獲物.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 獲 (e, the stem of the transitive verb 獲る / 得る eru, Classical Japanese 得 u, 'to get, acquire, catch, capture') and 物 (mono, 'thing, creature, object'). Literally 'a captured thing or creature', originating in hunting and fishing vocabulary for game, quarry, or catch, and extending metaphorically to a prized target, victim, or spoils.

history.meaning: that which is gained or captured; game taken in hunting or fishing
history.stage: Late Middle to Edo Period Japanese

history.meaning: prey, quarry, game, catch; target of a predator or schemer, spoils

morphemes.meaning: catch, capture, obtain (stem of 獲る / 得る)

獲物.notes: Do not confuse with its homophone 得物 (emono), which uses 得 and refers to one's weapon of choice or specialty tool.

玄関.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 玄 ('deep, profound') and 関 ('gate, barrier'). Originally a Zen Buddhist term for the gateway to profound teachings and the formal entry hall of a temple, it generalized to the entranceway of Japanese homes and inns where shoes are removed.

history.meaning: temple entrance hall
front foyer / entranceway

玉ねぎ.etymology: Descriptive Japanese compound coined in the Meiji era by prefixing 玉 (tama, 'round ball, sphere, bulb') to ねぎ (negi, 'green onion, Welsh onion, scallion', Old Japanese ki). Because traditional Japanese kitchens used long green stalk-onions (長ねぎ naganegi), newly introduced Western round bulb onions (Allium cepa) were naturally named 玉ねぎ ('ball-scallions').

history.meaning: round Western bulb onion, named in contrast to long green onions
onion

玉ねぎ.notes: Almost always written in mixed kanji-hiragana as 玉ねぎ in recipes and supermarkets.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 玉ねぎ

現在.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound originating in Chinese Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *pratyutpanna* ('arisen in the present moment'), uniting 現 (gen, 'appear, become manifest, visible now') and 在 (zai, 'exist, be present, reside'). In Buddhist cosmology it formed the triad of 過去 (kako, 'past'), 現在 (genzai, 'present'), and 未来 (mirai, 'future'), before becoming the standard temporal noun and adverb for 'now, at present, as of [time]'.

history.meaning: manifestly existing in the present world/kalpa (translation of Sanskrit pratyutpanna)
the present time, currently, as of [a given time or count]

現在.notes: Placed directly after a time or date (午後五時現在, 'as of 5:00 PM'), it functions as an official timestamp marker meaning 'as of'.

rootFamily.gloss: to appear, come into view, materialize

現実.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 現 (gen, 'manifest, visible right now, actual') and 実 (jitsu, 'fruit, seed, substance, truth, actuality'). Used in pre-modern texts for 'tangible manifestation or actual fact', it was repurposed and popularized during the Meiji period by philosophers (such as Nishi Amane) to translate Western philosophical and literary concepts of 'reality' (*Realität* / *reality*) in contrast to 理想 (risō, 'ideal') or 虚構 (kyokō, 'fiction').

history.meaning: manifest substance, actual fact before one's eyes
reality, actuality, the real world (contrasted with ideals or illusion)

現実.notes: Frequently appears in idioms like 現実を見る ('to face reality'), 現実味 (genjitsumi, 'a sense of realism/plausibility'), and 現実逃避 (genjitsu tōhi, 'escapism').

現実的.etymology: A Meiji-era Sino-Japanese (kango) neologism formed by affixing the adjectival suffix 的 (-teki, from Middle Chinese *tek "target, mark", adapted in modern Japanese to translate European suffixes like English -ic and -ical) to the compound 現実 (genjitsu, "reality, actuality"). 現実 originated in Chinese Buddhist texts (such as the Avatamsaka Sutra) where 現 (gen, Middle Chinese *ɣwenH, "to appear, manifest, present") and 実 (實 jitsu, Middle Chinese *ʑiɪt, "fruit, substance, truth") meant "manifest truth before one's eyes," before philosophers Nishi Amane and Inoue Tetsujiro repurposed it to translate German Wirklichkeit and English reality.

history.meaning: manifest fact, tangible truth (Buddhist Chinese)
actual reality as opposed to ideal or illusion
realistic, pragmatic, practical

現実的.notes: As a na-adjective (keiyōdōshi), it always takes な (現実的な) before nouns and に (現実的に) as an adverb; it contrasts with 理想的 (risōteki, "idealistic").

現職.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 現 (gen, from Middle Chinese *ɣwenH, "to manifest, appear; current, present") and 職 (shoku, from Middle Chinese *tɕɨk, "official duty, post, employment"). Originally used in bureaucratic Chinese and Japanese administrative records to denote the office a person currently holds, it came to designate both the current post itself and an incumbent officeholder (such as a sitting politician, police officer, or executive).

history.meaning: current official post or appointment
present occupation; incumbent officeholder

現職.notes: Often modifies another noun via の (e.g., 現職の警官 "an active-duty police officer" or 現職の大統領 "the sitting president") and contrasts with 前職 (zenshoku, "previous job/predecessor") and 元職 (motoshoku, "former officeholder").

現金.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 現 ('present, on the spot, actual') and 金 ('money, gold'), literally 'money right in front of you' as opposed to credit or ledger accounts.

理不尽.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) three-character compound formed and popularized in Japan during the Muromachi and Edo periods from 理 (ri, Middle Chinese *lɨX, "veins in jade; cosmic principle, reason, justice"), 不 (fu, Middle Chinese *pɨu, negative prefix "not"), and 尽 (盡 jin, Middle Chinese *dzinX, "to exhaust, fulfill completely, carry through to the end"). Literally meaning "not exhausting/fulfilling reason," it originally described actions that failed to follow moral or legal reason through to completion, evolving into a strong adjective for high-handed, arbitrary, and unfair treatment.

history.meaning: failing to exhaust reason; acting contrary to just principle
high-handed, arbitrary, unreasonable, absurd

morphemes.meaning: exhaust, fulfill, carry to the end

理不尽.notes: In Japanese workplace and drama contexts, 理不尽 specifically describes unfair, abusive demands from superiors or fate where logic does not apply (unlike 単なる不合理 "mere illogicality").

理想.etymology: Meiji-era philosophical Sino-Japanese coinage 理想 (risō), introduced by Nishi Amane to translate Western *ideal*, combining 理 ('reason, principle, idea') + 想 ('conception, thought').

history.meaning: philosophical ideal
ideal; highest standard envisioned

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 理想

理由.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 理由 (riyū), from Classical Chinese 理由 ('underlying principle and cause/origin'), combining 理 ('principle, logic') + 由 ('cause, whence something comes').

history.meaning: cause and principle; grounds
reason; ground; motive; excuse

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 理由

瓶.etymology: Read both as Sino-Japanese *bin* (from Middle Chinese 瓶 *beng*, 'jug, pitcher, vase, bottle') and native Japanese *kame* (inherited from Old Japanese *kame₂* 'wide-mouthed earthenware jar or crock').

history.meaning: pitcher; vase; bottle
earthenware jar
bottle; jar; decanter

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 瓶

甘い.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *amasi* (甘し, 'sweet-tasting, delicious, mildly salted, indulgent'), attested in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; cognate with うまし (旨し・美し, 'savory, delicious').

history.meaning: sweet; savory; pleasant to taste
sweet; lightly salted; lenient/indulgent; naive/optimistic; loose

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 甘い

甘やかす.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) transitive godan verb built on the root of the adjective 甘い (amai, Old Japanese amasi, from Proto-Japonic *ama-, meaning "sweet, pleasant, lenient, indulgent"). The adjectival stem ama- was extended with the descriptive nominal/adjectival suffix -yaka (forming the stem amayaka, "indulgent, doting, soft") and then verbalized with the transitive/causative suffix -su (Old Japanese -su), yielding the literal sense "to treat someone in a sweet, indulgent manner; to pamper or spoil."

history.meaning: sweet to the taste; mild, indulgent
to dote upon, pamper, coddle, spoil

生.etymology: A polysemous character representing both the native Japanese (wago) word nama ("raw, uncooked, unprocessed, live, cash") and the Sino-Japanese (kango) morpheme sei/shō ("life, birth, living"). The native word nama descends from Old Japanese nama ("fresh, raw, unripe, green"), from Proto-Japonic *nama. Mapped onto the Chinese character 生 (Middle Chinese *ʃˠæŋ, originally a pictograph of a plant sprouting from the earth, meaning both "to live/grow" and "raw/unripe"), it developed modern senses ranging from draft beer and live broadcasts to unedited footage.

生きていく.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) syntactic compound verb phrase formed from 生きて (ikite, the conjunctive -te form of the verb 生きる ikiru, "to live, stay alive", from Old Japanese iku "to breathe, live") followed by the auxiliary verb いく (行く iku, "to go", from Old Japanese yuku). In Japanese aspectual grammar, attaching -te iku to a verb projects the action continuously forward from the present point into the future, yielding the sense "to go on living, continue surviving through life."

生きる.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) kami-ichidan (upper monograde) verb descending from Old Japanese iku ("to live, come to life, breathe"), from Proto-Japonic *iku. Originally a quadrigrade (yodan) verb in Old Japanese, it also developed a kami-nidan (upper bigrade) conjugation in Heian-period Classical Japanese, which regularly merged into the modern kami-ichidan form 生きる (ikiru). The verbal root *ik- is etymologically identical to the noun 息 (iki, Old Japanese iki, "breath, respiration"), reflecting the archaic identification of breath with the life force.

In Japanese morphology, full reduplication of a verbal stem expresses continuous, abundant, or vivid manifestation of that state; thus iki-iki literally means "living-living," describing someone or something brimming with life force, freshness, and animation.

While nurui alone means "lukewarm," prefixing nama- ("imperfectly, unpleasantly half-way") intensifies the неприятный (unpleasant) sensation of water or air that is neither refreshingly cool nor properly hot, and metaphorically condemns half-hearted, overly lenient, or spineless measures.

In Edo urban culture, iki denoted refined, worldly sophistication and proud spirit; prefixing nama- mocked someone who affected an air of dewasa sophistication or pride while still green and immature, yielding the modern sense of "cheeky, impertinent, cocky, audacious."

Composed of 生 (sei, "to live, be born, grow") and 活 (katsu, "to live, survive, be active"), it originally meant "staying alive, survival" in pre-modern texts before Meiji-era scholars expanded its scope to translate modern sociological and economic concepts of "daily life, standard of living, and livelihood."

In modern orthography, 産む focuses on biological parturition, egg-laying, or generating wealth, while 生む focuses on bringing things or ideas into existence.
