番組.etymology: A hybrid Japanese compound (yutō-yomi: on'yomi + kun'yomi) combining the Sino-Japanese (kango) morpheme 番 (ban, from Middle Chinese *pʰʉɐn, "turn, watch, numbered order, match") with the native Japanese (wago) noun 組 (kumi, nominalized stem of the verb 組む kumu "to plait, pair together, assemble", voiced to -gumi via rendaku). Coined in Edo-period sumo, kabuki theater, and yose vaudeville to mean "the assembled pairing of bouts or acts arranged in numbered order on a program bill," it was adopted by NHK in 1925 for radio broadcasts and in 1953 for television programs.

history.meaning: pairing of wrestlers or sequence of acts on a sumo/theater bill; guard roster
radio or television broadcast program, show

番組.notes: Refers strictly to broadcast shows (TV, radio, streaming programs) or event lineups; for a computer program or printed concert booklet, Japanese uses the loanword プログラム (puroguramu).

rootFamily.gloss: to assemble, put together, pair up, cross (arms)

異常.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Classical Chinese 異常 (Middle Chinese *jɨH *dʑɨɐŋ, attested in the Book of的后漢書 Later Han), composed of 異 (i, "different, strange, divergent, other") and 常 (jō, "constant, normal, regular standard"). Literally meaning "diverging from the constant norm," it functions in Japanese both as a noun denoting an anomaly, malfunction, or medical abnormality, and as a na-adjective describing extreme, pathological, or extraordinary states.

history.meaning: departing from the ordinary; unusual, extraordinary

history.form: いじゃう → いじょう (異常)
history.meaning: abnormality, anomaly, disorder; abnormal, extreme

異常.notes: A homophone of 以上 (ijō, "more than; that is all"); in safety checks and police/military reports, 異常なし (ijō nashi) is the standard formula for "All clear / Nothing abnormal to report."

疑い.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) deverbative noun derived from the ren'yōkei (continuative stem) of the godan verb 疑う (utagau, Old Japanese utagapu, "to doubt, suspect, distrust"). In Old Japanese, utagapu was formed by attaching the iterative/continuative verbal suffix -pu to an archaic stem *utaga- ("uncertain, dubious", possibly related to *uta- seen in utate "strange, worsening"). Phonological change of intervocalic /-p-/ > /-w-/ > Ø turned Old Japanese utagapi into modern utagai.

history.meaning: feeling of uncertainty, doubt, hesitation
doubt, suspicion, criminal charge/allegation

疑い.notes: In legal and news reporting, ～の疑いで逮捕された (~ no utagai de taiho sareta) is the standard phrasing for "was arrested on suspicion of ~."

疑問.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical and Buddhist Chinese 疑問 (Middle Chinese *ŋɨ *mɨunH), composed of 疑 (gi, "to doubt, hesitate, be uncertain") and 問 (mon, "to ask, inquire"). Originally used as a verbal compound in Tang and Song Chinese meaning "to ask questions in order to resolve a doubt," it was borrowed into Japanese both in scholarly/Buddhist contexts and in modern usage to denote an intellectual question, unresolved doubt, or grammatical interrogative.

history.meaning: to inquire into something doubtful; a query arising from uncertainty
question, doubt, misgiving; grammatical interrogative

疑問.notes: Unlike 質問 (shitsumon), which is a question you actually ask someone aloud for an answer, 疑問 (gimon) is an internal question or doubt you hold in your mind (e.g., 疑問を持つ "to have doubts/questions about something").

疲れ.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) deverbative noun formed from the ren'yōkei (continuative stem) of the shimo-ichidan verb 疲れる (tsukareru, "to get tired, become exhausted"), which descends from the Old Japanese shimo-nidan verb tukaru ("to lose strength, become emaciated or worn out"). Historical linguists connect Old Japanese tukaru to the root of 尽きる (tsukiru, Old Japanese tuku, "to be exhausted, used up, run out"), as weariness was conceptualized as the depletion of bodily vitality.

history.meaning: depletion of physical strength, emaciation, weariness
fatigue, tiredness, physical or mental exhaustion; wear and tear

morphemes.meaning: grow weary, become depleted of strength

疲れ.notes: Forms the basis of Japan's most ubiquitous workplace greeting, お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu, literally "You are in an honorable state of fatigue"), used to acknowledge colleagues' hard work.

rootFamily.gloss: thank you for your hard work (lit. honorable fatigue)
to run out, be exhausted, come to an end

病気.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 病 (byō, kan'on reading of Middle Chinese *bɨɐŋH, "illness, disease, ailment", containing the sickness radical 疒) and 気 (氣 ki, Middle Chinese *kʰɨjH, "vital breath, pneuma, energy, state"). In Classical Chinese medical treatises and Heian-period Japanese diaries (where it was also read in go'on as byōke or wago-hybrid yamai-ke), 病気 originally meant "disordered vital energy (qi) causing sickness" or "symptoms/touch of an illness." By the Edo and Meiji periods, it displaced native 病 (yamai) as the standard everyday noun for any physical or mental illness.

history.meaning: morbid vital energy (qi), pathogenic humor
onset of sickness; physical ailment or disease
illness, sickness, disease; (colloquial) crazy obsession or bad habit

病気.notes: Contrasts with 元気 (genki, "healthy/energetic — original vital ki"): in traditional Sino-Japanese thought, health is when your 気 (ki) is in its original state (元), and sickness is when your 気 is afflicted (病). In slang, 病気だ means "that's sick / an unhealthy obsession."

痛い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('painful, sore, aching'), continuing Old Japanese *itasi* (stem *ita-*), attested in the Man'yōshū; closely related to the intensive root *ita* / *ito* ('exceedingly, sorely, intensely').

history.meaning: painful; sore; extreme
painful; sore; aching

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 痛い

痛み.etymology: Native Yamato deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the verb 痛む (itamu, 'to hurt, ache, feel pain', Old Japanese itamu, cognate with the i-adjective 痛い itai 'painful, sore'). It denotes physical pain, a twinge in a joint or muscle, or emotional heartache.

history.meaning: pain, ache, grief
pain, soreness, ache

morphemes.meaning: nominalized stem of 痛む ('to hurt, ache')

痛み.notes: Whereas 痛い is the adjective ('it hurts!'), 痛み is the noun ('the pain', as in 痛みもゼロ 'zero pain').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 痛み

痴話ゲンカ.etymology: An Early Modern (Edo-period) Sino-Japanese compound combining 痴話 (chiwa, "foolish lover's talk, sweet nothings, amorous banter", from 痴 Middle Chinese *ʈʰɨ "foolish, infatuated, lovesick" + 話 Middle Chinese *ɣwæiH "speech, talk") and 喧嘩 (kenka, voiced via rendaku to -genka, "noisy quarrel, brawl", from 喧 Middle Chinese *xʉɐn "noisy, clamorous" + 嘩 Middle Chinese *ɣwæ "uproar, hubbub"). Popularized in Edo-period kabuki, rakugo, and pleasure-quarter literature, it describes a petty, passionate spat between lovers driven by jealousy or affection. Writing ゲンカ in katakana is a modern stylistic choice to give the word a punchy, colloquial feel.

history.form: 痴話 (ちわ) + 喧嘩 (けんか) → 痴話喧嘩 (ちわげんか)
history.meaning: amorous lovers' banter turning into a jealous spat

history.form: 痴話ゲンカ / 痴話喧嘩 (ちわげんか)
history.meaning: lovers' quarrel, romantic tiff

morphemes.meaning: quarrel, noisy fight (from kenka 喧嘩)

痴話ゲンカ.notes: Summed up in the famous Japanese proverb 犬も食わない (inu mo kuwanai — "even a dog wouldn't eat [a lovers' quarrel]"), warning third parties not to meddle in a couple's spat because they will soon make up.

rootFamily.gloss: molester, groper (from 痴 foolish/lewd + 漢 man)

癒やし.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) deverbative noun formed from the ren'yōkei (continuative stem) of the transitive godan verb 癒やす (iyasu, Old Japanese iyasu, "to heal, cure, soothe"), which is the lexical causative of the intransitive verb 癒える (ieru, Old Japanese iyu, "to be healed, recover from illness or pain"). Historically restricted to medical recovery, relieving physical pain, or quenching thirst/hunger, 癒やし underwent a major semantic expansion in 1999 during Japan's "healing boom" (癒やし系 iyashikei) to denote emotional solace, psychological comfort, and stress relief in a high-pressure society.

history.form: いゆ (癒ゆ) → いやす (癒やす)
history.meaning: to recover from sickness (intransitive) → to cure illness, pain, or thirst (transitive)
curing of disease or physical suffering

history.form: いやし (癒やし / 癒し)
history.meaning: emotional healing, solace, soothing comfort, stress relief

癒やし.notes: Often written 癒し without the या (ya) okurigana in everyday media; central to the term 癒やし系 (iyashikei, "soothing/healing type"), used for gentle, comforting people, music, or pets that calm an exhausted person's soul.

rootFamily.gloss: to be healed, recover (of a wound or heartache)

cognates.meaning: to put on sale, to sell

発売.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 発 (hatsu, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to send forth, issue, launch') and 売 (bai, shinjitai of 賣, Middle Chinese *meaH, 'to sell'). Literally 'issuing for sale', originally used in classical Chinese commercial and administrative contexts for releasing goods onto the market, and specialized in modern Japanese publishing and media for the commercial release of books, magazines, videos, and products.

history.meaning: to put goods out for sale; to distribute commercially
putting commodities on sale in the market
commercial release or sale of a publication or product

発売.notes: Used with する as a transitive verb or in passive/intransitive phrases like 発売中 ('now on sale'); distinguishes commercial release from 公開 (theatrical/public release).

rootFamily.gloss: publication, issue (of a book or magazine)

発想.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 発 (hatsu -> hass- by gemination before s-, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to bring forth, generate, initiate') and 想 (sō, Middle Chinese *sjangX, 'thought, conception, mental image'). Originally used in aesthetics, rhetoric, and musical theory to denote the expressive realization or generation of a theme, it broadened in twentieth-century Japanese to mean a creative conception, angle of thought, or way of framing an idea.

history.meaning: to bring forth + mental image or thought
artistic or musical expression; generation of a mental concept
conception, creative idea, mindset or way of thinking

発想.notes: Often appears in phrases like 発想の転換 ('a paradigm shift / change in way of thinking') or 自由な発想 ('free-spirited creative thinking').

cognates.meaning: to excavate, to unearth, to tap talent

発掘.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 発 (hatsu -> hakk- via gemination before k-, Middle Chinese *pjwot, here carrying its ancient sense 'to open up, uncover, expose') and 掘 (kutsu, Middle Chinese *gjwot, 'to dig, excavate'). Literally 'uncovering by digging', used first for archaeological excavation of tombs and ruins, and extended metaphorically to scouting and unearthing hidden talent or obscure works.

history.meaning: to dig open, to unearth (especially graves or buried objects)
archaeological excavation; unearthing buried artifacts
excavation; scouting and discovering unknown talent or resources

発掘.notes: In the entertainment and publishing industries, 新人を発掘する ('to scout/discover new talent') is the standard idiom for finding a diamond in the rough.

発明.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 発 (hatsu, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to open up, reveal, bring forth') and 明 (mei, Middle Chinese *mjaeng, 'bright, clear'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Sima Qian's *Shiji* and Song Neo-Confucian texts), 發明 meant 'to illuminate, clarify, or open up the meaning of a text or principle'. In Meiji Japan it was repurposed to translate English 'invention' (creating a novel device or method), a sense subsequently borrowed back into modern Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: to illuminate, expound, or make clear a hidden meaning
cleverness, mental acuity; clarification of a principle
technical or creative invention of something unprecedented

morphemes.meaning: open up, reveal, bring forth (Middle Chinese *pjwot)

発明.notes: In older Edo-period usage and dialects, 発明な (hatsumei na) functioned as a na-adjective meaning 'clever, bright, quick-witted'.

cognates.meaning: placing an order (for goods or contracting)

発注.etymology: Modern Sino-Japanese (wasei-kango) commercial compound formed from 発 (hatsu -> hatch- via gemination before ch-, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to send out, issue') and 注 (chū, Middle Chinese *trjuH, originally 'to pour, direct toward', and by abbreviation of 注文 chūmon, 'commercial order'). Coined in modern Japanese business administration as the sender-side counterpart of 受注 (juchū, 'receiving an order').

history.meaning: to dispatch + to pour/record an order (abbr. of 注文)
issuing a purchase or production order to a supplier or contractor

morphemes.meaning: order, note down (from 注文 chūmon; Middle Chinese *trjuH)

発注.notes: Used specifically for B2B procurement, publishing print runs, or subcontracting; its antonym is 受注 (juchū, 'receiving an order'), whereas everyday consumer ordering is 注文 (chūmon).

cognates.meaning: to publish, to issue a statement, to present
to make a statement, to express

発表.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 発 (hatsu -> happy- via gemination and labial Assimilation before h-/hy-, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to send forth, reveal') and 表 (hyō, Middle Chinese *pjewX, 'outer surface, to make manifest, display publicly'). Literally 'bringing out to the surface', it evolved from classical Chinese usage meaning 'to manifest outwardly' (or in traditional Chinese medicine, 'to induce sweating to expel surface pathogens') into the standard modern East Asian word for a public announcement, presentation, or press release.

history.meaning: to manifest outwardly; to bring to the surface
public disclosure, official announcement or publication of findings
announcement, presentation, press release, or debut of a work

発表.notes: Notice the phonetic shift: 発 (hatsu) + 表 (hyō) undergoes gemination and semi-voicing to become happyō; covers everything from school presentations to corporate press announcements.

cognates.meaning: (archaic) to set out on foot; (modern) to inaugurate

発足.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 発 (hatsu -> hoss- or hass-, Middle Chinese *pjwot, 'to start forth, set out') and 足 (soku, Middle Chinese *tsjowk, 'foot, step'). In Classical Chinese, 發足 meant 'to lift one's feet and set out on a journey'. In modern Japanese, this concrete travel sense was extended metaphorically to the inauguration, launch, or starting up of a new company, committee, or organization.

history.meaning: to lift one's feet and set out on a journey; to depart
setting out on a trip; beginning an activity
inauguration, establishment, or launch of an organization or project

morphemes.meaning: set forth, start, depart (Middle Chinese *pjwot; go-on *hochi -> hoss-)

発足.notes: Traditionally and prescriptively read hossoku (using the older Go-on reading hotsu + soku), though hassoku (Kan-on hatsu + soku) is now widely accepted in contemporary broadcasts.

発車.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 発 (hatsu, 'departure/emit') + 車 (sha, 'vehicle/car').

history.meaning: departing vehicle

発車.notes: Specifically refers to a vehicle leaving its stop or station.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 発車

登る.etymology: Native Japanese word (wago). From Old Japanese noboru 'to ascend'.

history.meaning: to climb/ascend

登る.notes: Written as 登る for mountains/stairs, 上る for general going up or reaching a total.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 登る

白.etymology: Native Yamato word (wago) shiro ('white; innocence'), written with the logographic kanji 白 (originally depicting a brightness, flame, or acorn/thumb in Shang oracle bone script). Attested in Old Japanese as sirwo (with kō-rui vowel wo), bound root sira- in ancient compounds (e.g. 白雪 sirayuki 'white snow', 白髪 siraga 'white hair'). Derived from the same root as the adjective 白い (shiroi) and likely related to 著し / 顕し (ichijirushi / shirushi, 'clear, conspicuous, manifest'). In criminal and colloquial jargon, 白 also means 'innocent, clean' in contrast to 黒 (kuro, 'guilty, culpable').

history.meaning: bright, clear, white, unstained
the color white; blankness; purity
white; blank space; innocence (opposite of 黒 'guilty')

morphemes.meaning: white, bright, clear, innocent (native Yamato root < OJ sirwo / sira-)

白.notes: In police and drama slang, シロ (shiro) means 'innocent / clean' and クロ (kuro, 'black') means 'guilty / dirty'; in compounds, note the ancient combining form shira- (e.g., 素人 shirōto 'amateur', 白昼 hakuchū in Sino-Japanese).

rootFamily.gloss: white hair, gray hair (< sira + ka 'hair')
to become white, to grow light at dawn, to turn awkward/sober

白い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('white, fair, blank'), continuing Old Japanese *sirosi* (stem *siro-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū for bright, clear white; cognate with 著し (*ichijirushi* 'conspicuous, clear') and 知る (*shiru* 'to perceive, know').

history.meaning: white; bright; clear
white

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 白い

cognates.meaning: written statement or confession; plain condition

白状.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 白 (haku, Go-on byaku, Middle Chinese *baek, 'white, clear; to state plainly, declare, confess') and 状 (jō, shinjitai of 狀, Middle Chinese *dzjangH, 'condition, circumstances, written statement'). Literally 'stating the facts plainly without concealment', used in medieval and Edo-period judicial interrogations for a suspect's formal confession of guilt, and today used broadly for coming clean or admitting a secret.

history.meaning: to state the circumstances plainly; a written confession
formal confession by a suspect under magistrate interrogation
confessing, coming clean, owning up to wrongdoing or a secret

morphemes.meaning: plain, clear, declare openly, confess (Middle Chinese *baek)

白状.notes: More colloquial and personal than 自白 (jihaku, formal legal/police confession); often used when pressing someone to spill the beans (早く白状しろ 'Come clean already!').

白紙.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 白 ('white, unmarked') and 紙 ('paper'), denoting an unwritten sheet of paper and figuratively a clean slate.

白黒.etymology: Native Japanese dvandva (coordinative) compound noun ('black and white, monochrome; right and wrong, guilt and innocence'), formed from 白 (しろ 'white') + 黒 (くろ 'black').

history.meaning: white and black; monochrome; right and wrong

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 白黒

百.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) numeral 百 (hyaku, Middle Chinese *paek < Old Chinese *pˤrak, 'one hundred; numerous, myriad'), alongside the older native Yamato reading momo (attested in Old Japanese as mwomwo 'hundred; a great number'). In modern Japanese counting and arithmetic, the Sino-Japanese reading hyaku is standard, while native momo survives in fossilized words, surnames (e.g., 百瀬 Momose), and poetic expressions like 八百万 (yaoyorozu, 'eight million / myriad').

history.meaning: one hundred; all, numerous
one hundred (native mwomwo alongside borrowed Sino-Japanese hyaku)
one hundred; numerous (in compounds)

morphemes.meaning: hundred; numerous, all kinds of (Middle Chinese *paek)

百.notes: Undergoes regular morphophonemic changes with preceding numerals: 三百 (sanbyaku, rendaku), 六百 (roppyaku), and 八百 (happyaku).

rootFamily.gloss: farmer, peasant (historically 'all the hundred surnames / common folk')

百万冊.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) numeral-classifier compound composed of 百 (hyaku, Middle Chinese *paek, 'hundred'), 万 (man, shinjitai of 萬, Middle Chinese *mjonH, 'ten thousand, myriad'), and the bound counter 冊 (satsu, Middle Chinese *tsrheak, 'bound volume, bamboo slip book'). Because East Asian numeral systems group by powers of ten thousand (万 man = 10^4) rather than thousands, one million (10^6) is expressed structurally as 百万 (hyakuman, 'one hundred ten-thousands'), followed by 冊 for bound books or magazines.

history.meaning: one hundred myriads (one million) + bamboo-slip book/register
one million copies of bound books or magazines (a benchmark for a million-seller)

morphemes.meaning: counter for bound volumes, books, and magazines (Middle Chinese *tsrheak)

百万冊.notes: Always remember that Japanese large numbers increment by 10,000 (万 man): 100 × 10,000 = 1,000,000 (百万 hyakuman), and 冊 (satsu) depicts ancient bamboo slips tied together with cord.

百億.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) numerical compound of 百 (hyaku, Middle Chinese *paek, 'one hundred') and 億 (oku, Middle Chinese *'jok, 'one hundred million' in the modern myriad-based scale). Since East Asian numbers scale in myriad powers (万 man = 10^4, 億 oku = 10^8), 百億 (hyakuoku) equals 100 × 100,000,000, or ten billion (10^10).

history.meaning: one hundred + a hundred thousand or a hundred million (large myriad unit)
ten billion (100 × 10^8) in the standardized myriad-scale system

百億.notes: Translating 億 (oku = 100 million) into English requires shifting decimal groupings by two places: 1億 = 100 million, 10億 = 1 billion, 100億 (百億) = 10 billion.

rootFamily.gloss: tens of billions, hundreds of millions of yen in revenue

百円.etymology: Sino-Japanese numeral-classifier compound ('one hundred yen'), formed from 百 (ひゃく 'one hundred', Middle Chinese *pæk*) + 円 (えん 'yen; round coin', adopted in 1871 as Japan's modern decimal currency unit).

history.meaning: one hundred yen

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 百

百回.etymology: Sino-Japanese numeral-counter compound ('one hundred times'), formed from 百 (ひゃく → ひゃっ with consonant assimilation before *k-*, 'one hundred') + 回 (かい 'time, turn, occurrence').

history.meaning: one hundred times

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 回

百科事典.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 百科 (hyakka, 'all branches of knowledge', from 百 'hundred, all' + 科 'branch, category, discipline') and 事典 (jiten, 'reference book of matters/subjects', from 事 'matter, affair, phenomenon' + 典 'canon, standard reference book'). Modeled in modern Japan as a translation of European 'encyclopedia' (first popularized via Nishi Amane's 1870 *Hyakugaku Renkan* and later Meiji *Hyakka Zensho*), with 事典 (subject encyclopedia) orthographically distinguished from 辞典 (word dictionary) despite identical pronunciation (jiten).

history.meaning: all the hundred branches of learning or official categories

history.form: 百科全書 / 百科事典 (hyakka zensho / hyakka jiten)
history.meaning: comprehensive reference compendium covering all fields of knowledge (calquing 'encyclopedia')

morphemes.meaning: branch of study, category, department (Middle Chinese *khwa)

百科事典.notes: Japanese distinguishes 事典 (jiten, encyclopedia of *things/matters*, 事) from 辞典 (jiten, dictionary of *words*, 辞) and 字典 (jiten, dictionary of *kanji characters*, 字)—all pronounced jiten!

的.etymology: Native Japanese noun (read まと, 'target, mark, bullseye'), continuing Old Japanese *mato*, attested in the Nihon Shoki and Wamyō Ruijūshō; traditionally analyzed as *ma-* (bound form of 目 'eye' or 間 'space') + *to* (処 'place, spot'), i.e. the spot aimed at with the eyes, written logographically with kanji 的 ('target, white mark').

history.meaning: archery target; mark
target; mark; object of focus

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 的

皆さま.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) honorific address compound formed from 皆 (mina, Old Japanese mina, 'all, everyone') and the honorific suffix さま (sama, originally a noun meaning 'appearance, manner, direction', used from Late Middle Japanese as a deferential indirect form of address 'toward the direction of'). Written with mixed kanji and hiragana (皆さま) in contemporary public announcements, journalism, and customer-facing copy to soften the visual formality of all-kanji 皆様.

history.meaning: all, everyone + direction, manner, respectful title
everyone (honorific collective address to an audience or clientele)

morphemes.meaning: all, everyone, everything (native Yamato root < OJ mina)
honorific suffix of respect (< 'direction, manner, appearance')

皆さま.notes: Spelling さま in hiragana (皆さま) is favored in modern advertising, customer service, and broadcasting as slightly warmer and more approachable visually than the all-kanji 皆様, though pronunciation and polite register are identical.

皆さん.etymology: Polite plural pronoun and form of address ('everyone, all of you'), formed from native Japanese 皆 (みな 'all, everyone', Old Japanese *mina*) + polite honorific suffix -さん (reduced from 様 *-sama*).

history.meaning: everyone; all of you (polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 皆さん

皆様.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) honorific pronoun/noun formed from 皆 (mina, Old Japanese mina, 'all, everyone, the entirety') and the respectful suffix 様 (sama, originally 'form, manner, direction', grammaticalized in Muromachi–Edo Japanese into an honorific title of address). Avoiding direct reference by naming a person's 'direction/appearance' (sama) is a hallmark of Japanese honorifics (keigo), making 皆様 more deferential than 皆さん (minasan, where -san itself evolved as a phonetic contraction of -sama).

history.meaning: all, everyone, in entirety
respectful address to a group of lords or honored guests ('all your esteemed directions')
everyone, ladies and gentlemen (honorific collective address or pronoun)

morphemes.meaning: all, everyone (native Yamato root < OJ mina)
honorific suffix (< native noun sama 'appearance, direction')

皆様.notes: More formal and deferential than 皆さん (minasan); essential when addressing customers, viewers, shareholders, or guests at ceremonies.

rootFamily.gloss: everyone (neutral-polite; -san is a worn-down form of -sama)
how someone is doing, state, appearance

皮.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('skin, hide, pelt, bark, peel, rind'), continuing Old Japanese *kapa*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū for the outer covering of bodies, trees, and fruits (orthographically distinguished from 革 'tanned leather' in modern usage, though sharing the same etymon).

history.meaning: skin; hide; bark; outer covering
skin; peel; rind; bark

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 皮

皿.etymology: Native Yamato word (wago) sara ('plate, dish, saucer, shallow bowl-like vessel'), attested in Old Japanese (8th century *Man'yōshū* and *Nihon Shoki*) as sara, and written logographically with the kanji 皿 (originally an oracle-bone and bronze-script pictograph of a shallow footed ritual vessel or platter). Used both as an independent noun for a plate/dish and as a counter for servings of plated food, as well as in anatomical metaphors for plate-like structures such as the kneecap (膝の皿 hiza no sara) or the crown of a kappa's head.

history.meaning: shallow vessel, dish, or bowl for food and offerings
plate, dish, saucer; counter for servings on a plate

morphemes.meaning: plate, shallow dish, platter (native Yamato root < OJ sara)

皿.notes: Voices to -zara via rendaku in many compounds (e.g., 小皿 kozara 'small side plate', 灰皿 haizara 'ashtray'), and also serves as the counter for servings of curry or pasta (一皿 hitosara).

盗み見.etymology: The term '盗み見' (meaning 'peeking') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: peeking
peeking

盗み見.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 盗み見

盗む.etymology: Native Yamato verb (wago) nusumu ('to steal, pilfer, do furtively'), attested in Old Japanese (8th century) as nusumu. A widely cited internal philological hypothesis connects the root nusu- to ぬす / のそ (noso, 'quietly, stealthily, slowly') or to 寝 (nu, 'to sleep, lie still') + verbalizer -sumu, evoking the act of creeping stealthily while others sleep. Beyond physical theft, it developed idiomatic senses such as 'stealing a glance or spare moment' (目を盗む / 暇を盗む) and 'learning a craft by observing a master without formal instruction' (技を盗む).

history.meaning: to act stealthily; to steal or take another's property in secret
to steal; to do behind someone's back; to absorb a skill by watching

morphemes.meaning: steal, act furtively (native Yamato verb stem < OJ nusum-)

盗む.notes: In Japanese apprenticeship and entertainment culture, 技を盗む (waza wo nusumu, 'to steal a technique') has a positive nuance: mastering a senior's craft through sharp observation rather than waiting to be spoon-fed.

盛り上げる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 盛る (moru, Old Japanese moru, 'to heap up, pile high, Mound earth or food onto a vessel') and 上げる (ageru, 'to raise, lift up'). Originally literal—'to heap soil or food up into a high mound'—it developed a vivid metaphorical sense of building up energy, excitement, or enthusiasm at a party, show, or business venture.

history.meaning: to pile up, heap high + to raise upward
to heap up earth or food into a mound; to build up a climax or lively atmosphere

morphemes.meaning: heap up, pile high, serve generously (< moru)

盛り上げる.notes: Transitive pair to the intransitive 盛り上がる (moriagaru, 'to get lively, reach a climax, swell up'): a host or director 場を盛り上げる ('livens up the room'), so the crowd 盛り上がる ('gets pumped up').

rootFamily.gloss: to swell up; to get excited, to liven up (intransitive)

監督.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('supervision, direction; director, manager, coach'), from Classical Chinese 監督 (attested in the Book of Later Han), composed of 監 (かん 'oversee, inspect from above') + 督 (とく 'supervise, command'). Adopted in modern Japanese for administrative supervisors, film directors, and team coaches.

history.meaning: inspect and command; oversee
supervision; director; coach; manager

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 監督

cognates.meaning: to monitor, to keep under surveillance

監視.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 監 (kan, Middle Chinese *kaem, originally 'to look down into a basin of water as a mirror', hence 'to inspect, oversee, supervise') and 視 (shi, Middle Chinese *dzyijX/H, 'to look at, observe, inspect'). Literally 'overseeing and watching closely', used in institutional, police, and regulatory contexts for keeping suspects, prisoners, or systems under close watch.

history.meaning: to look down upon and inspect; to oversee officials or subjects
police, institutional, or technical surveillance and monitoring

morphemes.meaning: oversee, inspect, look down from above (Middle Chinese *kaem)
look at, observe, watch closely (Middle Chinese *dzyijX)

監視.notes: Carries a strong nuance of watchful control or suspicion (e.g., 監視カメラ 'security/survaillance camera', 警察の監視下 'under police surveillance'), unlike neutral 観察 (kansatsu, scientific observation).

rootFamily.gloss: director (of a film or team), supervision

目.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('eye; sight; mesh, grain; experience; ordinal suffix'), continuing Old Japanese *me₂* (alternating with bound prefix *ma-* in compounds like まぶた 'eyelid'), from Proto-Japonic *\*mai* ('eye').

history.meaning: eye
eye; mesh; view
eye; sight; texture; ordinal marker

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 目

目の敵.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) idiomatic noun phrase formed from 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye, gaze, sight'), the genitive particle の (no), and 敵 (kataki, Old Japanese kataki, originally 'fellow, match, counterpart, rival' and later narrowed to 'enemy, adversary, object of vengeance'). Literally 'an enemy of one's eyes'—someone whose very sight provokes hostility or whom one glares at constantly as a sworn target of animosity or persecution.

history.form: me (目) + no (の) + kataki (敵 / 仇)
history.meaning: eye + of + rival/enemy (someone hateful even to look upon)
sworn target of hostility; someone singled out for constant antagonism or attack

morphemes.meaning: eye, sight, gaze (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
enemy, rival, adversary (native Yamato root < OJ kataki)

目の敵.notes: Almost always used in the construction Aを目の敵にする ('to treat A as a sworn enemy / single A out as a target to attack').

rootFamily.gloss: eyesore, obstacle in one's sight ('lump above the eye')
rootFamily.word: 目の上のたんこぶ (me no ue no tankobu)

目の高さ.etymology: Native Japanese word. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 目の高さ

目安.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound of 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye, visual perception') and 安 (yasu, stem of the adjective 安い yasui, Old Japanese yasusi, 'easy, calm, peaceful, effortless'). Originally in medieval and Edo-period Japanese, 目安 meant 'something easy on the eyes to read or grasp'—specifically an itemized petition, legal bill of complaint, or readable summary written in accessible script—before evolving into its modern sense of a rough visual guide, yardstick, benchmark, or standard to aim for.

history.meaning: pleasing or easy to look at; clearly itemized written petition or summary
written legal complaint (as in Edo-period 目安箱 meyasubako 'petition box'); visual guidepost
benchmark, rough standard, yardstick, or guideline

morphemes.meaning: eye, sight, visual look (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
easy, calm, comfortable (stem of 安い yasui < OJ yasu-)

目安.notes: Unlike a strict 基準 (kijun, formal criterion/standard), 目安 denotes a rough, practical rule-of-thumb or guideline (e.g., あくまで目安です 'This is just a rough guide/estimate').

rootFamily.gloss: aim, rough target, outlook (< me + to 'place/door')

目当て.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound of 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye, gaze') and 当て (ate, nominalized stem of the transitive verb 当てる ateru, 'to hit, apply, direct toward a target'). Literally 'that upon which one fixes one's eyes', shifting from a physical visual target or guidepost to the specific prize, profit, or attraction that someone is secretly or eagerly after.

history.meaning: visual mark or target at which one directs one's gaze; guidepost
aim, object of desire, ulterior motive, or main attraction one is after

morphemes.meaning: eye, gaze, sight (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
applying, hitting, directing at a target (nominalized stem of 当てる ateru)

目当て.notes: Often used as a suffixal noun after another noun (e.g., カネ目当て 'after the money / gold-digging', お目当ての品 'the coveted item one came looking for').

rootFamily.gloss: to hit, to apply, to guess, to direct toward
expected target, prospect, aim (< me + ate)

目指す.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye, gaze') and 指す (sasu, Old Japanese sasu, 'to point at, direct toward, aim for', voiced to -zasu via rendaku). Originally meaning 'to point one's eyes at a specific spot or destination', it broadened into the standard transitive verb for heading toward a destination or aspiring toward an ambitious goal.

history.meaning: to fix one's eyes upon; to point one's sight toward a target or place
to head toward a destination; to aim for or aspire to a goal

morphemes.meaning: eye, sight, gaze (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
point at, direct toward, aim for (< 指す sasu with rendaku voicing)

目指す.notes: Takes the direct object particle を (e.g., 世界一を目指す 'to aim to be number one in the world', 頂上を目指す 'to head for the summit').

rootFamily.gloss: to point at, to indicate, to head toward

目標.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 目 (moku, Middle Chinese *mjuwk, 'eye, sight, item') and 標 (hyō, Middle Chinese *pjew, originally 'topmost branch of a tree', hence 'high wooden marker, signpost, beacon, target'). Originally denoting a visible physical landmark or military target for the eyes to fix upon, it was popularized in Meiji Japan (and subsequently borrowed across modern East Asia) for an abstract goal or objective.

history.meaning: eye/vision + treetop marker or wooden signpost
visual landmark; military firing target or range marker
concrete target, benchmark, or goal to achieve

目標.notes: Distinguish 目標 (mokuhyō, a concrete milestone or target along the way) from 目的 (mokuteki, the ultimate underlying purpose or reason why).

目立つ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye, sight, visual attention') and 立つ (tatsu, Old Japanese tatu, 'to stand up, rise, become prominent', voiced to -datsu via rendaku). Literally 'to stand up in the eyes (of observers)', follows a productive Japanese compounding pattern where -datsu means 'to become prominent in X' (compare 際立つ kiwadatsu 'to stand out sharply', 役立つ yakudatsu 'to be useful').

history.meaning: to rise up before the eyes; to catch visual notice
to stand out, be conspicuous, attract attention (for better or worse)

morphemes.meaning: eye, sight, visual notice (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
stand up, rise, become prominent (< 立つ tatsu with rendaku voicing)

目立つ.notes: In Japanese social contexts, 目立つ can be positive ('eye-catching, impressive') or cautionary (出る杭は打たれる—standing out too much invites pushback); its attributive past form 目立った (medatta) is frequently used adjectivally ('noticeable, remarkable').

rootFamily.gloss: to stand out sharply, to be prominent (< kiwa 'edge/border' + tatsu)
to be useful, to serve a purpose (< yaku 'role' + tatsu)
eager to get attention, show-off ('wanting to stand out')

目覚まし.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('alarm clock; waking up; eye-opener'), nominalized from the連用形 of 目覚ます (*mezamasu* 'to wake up, open one's eyes from sleep', from 目 'eye' + 覚ます 'to awaken'); in modern everyday use, frequently elliptical for 目覚まし時計 ('alarm clock').

history.meaning: waking from sleep; something striking that opens the eyes
waking up; alarm clock

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 目覚まし

目覚める.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb from 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye') and 覚める / 醒める (sameru, Old Japanese samu, 'to awaken from sleep, sober up from intoxication, come to one's senses', voiced to -zameru via rendaku). Originally contracted from the clause 目が覚める (me ga sameru, 'one's eyes awaken'), it denotes both literal waking from sleep and figurative awakening to truth, passion, or self-awareness.

history.meaning: for one's eyes to open from sleep; to awaken (nidan verb)
to wake up from sleep; to awaken to a new realization, talent, or calling (ichidan verb)

morphemes.meaning: eye, sight (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
wake up, sober up, come to one's senses (< 覚める sameru with rendaku)

目覚める.notes: Often used figuratively with に (Xに目覚める, 'to awaken to X / discover a passion for X', e.g., 才能に目覚める 'to awaken to one's talent'); its transitive counterpart is 目覚ます / 目を覚ます ('to wake someone up').

rootFamily.gloss: to wake up, to sober up, to cool down (of enthusiasm)

目障り.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound of 目 (me, Old Japanese me2, 'eye, line of sight') and 障り (sawari, nominalized stem of 障る sawaru, Old Japanese saparu, 'to hinder, obstruct, interfere with, offend', voiced to -zawari via rendaku). Literally 'an obstruction or irritation to the eye', parallel to 耳障り (mimizawari, 'grating on the ears') and 気障り (kizawari, 'disagreeable to one's feelings').

history.meaning: eye + hindrance, obstruction, or irritation
an eyesore; something or someone irritatingly in one's line of sight

morphemes.meaning: eye, sight, view (native Yamato root < OJ me2)
hindrance, obstruction, irritation (nominalized stem of 障る sawaru with rendaku)

目障り.notes: Notice the kanji distinction: 目障り uses 障 ('hinder/irritate', sawaru), NOT 触 ('touch/feel', sawaru as in 肌触り hadazawari 'texture against the skin'). Can describe both ugly objects and annoying people one wants out of sight.

rootFamily.gloss: to hinder, to interfere with, to affect negatively
grating on the ear, unpleasant to hear
obstacle, impediment, harm (as in 差し支え / 支障)

cognates.meaning: blindness; blind devotion or uncritical action

盲目.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 盲 (mō, Middle Chinese *maeng, 'blind, sightless, unperceiving', composed of 亡 'lost, gone' + 目 'eye') and 目 (moku, Middle Chinese *mjuwk, 'eye'). Literally 'blind eyes', attested in classical Chinese medical and philosophical texts for physical blindness, and widely used in modern Japanese (often with the suffix -的, 盲目的 mōmokuteki) to mean 'blindly devoted, uncritical, lacking rational discernment'.

history.meaning: sightless eyes; physical blindness
blindness; uncritical, irrational, or blindly devoted state of mind

morphemes.meaning: blind, sightless (Middle Chinese *maeng; 亡 'lost' + 目 'eye')

盲目.notes: In contemporary Japanese, 盲目 is most commonly used figuratively in expressions like 恋は盲目 ('love is blind') or 盲目的な愛 ('blind devotion'), while clinical visual impairment is referred to as 視覚障害 (shikaku shōgai).

rootFamily.gloss: guide dog for the blind ('leading-blind dog')

直し.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the transitive verb 直す (naosu, Old Japanese naposu, 'to make straight, restore to the proper state, correct, repair, cure'), itself the transitive counterpart of 直る (naoru < OJ naporu) from the root nao- ('straight, direct, right', as in 直ぐ sugu / なお nao). In publishing, film, and crafts, 直し specifically denotes a round of revisions, retakes, alterations, or touch-ups.

history.meaning: act of straightening, restoring to normal, or correcting
repair, mending, correction, or alteration
repair, clothing alteration, makeup touch-up (お直し), or editorial/creative revision and redoing

morphemes.meaning: straight, right, restore, repair (transitive verb stem < OJ napos-)

直し.notes: With the polite prefix お, お直し (onaoshi) means 'clothing alterations', 'makeup touch-up', or (in restaurants/editing) 'correcting/redoing an order or draft'; as a verbal suffix -直す (-naosu), it means 'to re-do from scratch' (やり直し yarinaoshi).

rootFamily.gloss: to repair, to correct, to cure, to alter (transitive verb)
redoing, doing over again, fresh start

直す.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to fix, repair, correct, restore, cure, alter'), continuing Old Japanese *naposu*, the transitive counterpart of *naporu* (直る 'to be restored, get better'), built on the root *napo-* ('straight, right, normal', seen in classical adjective 直し *naposi*).

history.meaning: make straight; restore to normal; correct
fix; repair; correct; restore

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 直す

直せる.etymology: Potential verb ('to be able to fix, can repair, can correct'), formed as the regular *e*-grade potential derivative (*naos-e-ru*) of the consonant-stem (godan) transitive verb 直す (*naosu* 'to fix, repair, correct').

history.meaning: can fix; be able to repair or correct

morphemes.meaning: potential stem of 直す (fix, repair)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 直す

直る.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to be fixed, be repaired, be corrected, return to normal'), continuing Old Japanese *naporu*, derived from the root *napo-* ('straight, upright, normal', as in classical adjective 直し *naposi*).

history.meaning: become straight; return to normal
be fixed; be repaired; be corrected

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 直る

直接.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and adverbial ('direct, immediate, firsthand'), formed from 直 (ちょく 'straight, unmediated, direct') + 接 (せつ 'touch, connect, come into contact'). Standardized in the Meiji period to render Western concepts of 'direct' (in contrast to 間接 'indirect').

history.meaning: direct; immediate; firsthand

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 直接

相変わらず.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) idiomatic adverbial phrase composed of the reciprocal/emphatic prefix 相 (ai-, Old Japanese api-, nominal stem of 逢ふ / 合ふ apu 'to meet, come together, match'), the negative stem of the intransitive verb 変わる (kawaru, Old Japanese kaparu, 'to change, alter'), and the classical negative adverbial/conjunctive suffix -ず (-zu, Old Japanese -zu < *-n-su). Literally 'mutually/continuously without changing (from before)', lexicalized in Early Modern Japanese as a fixed adverb meaning 'as ever, as usual, still the same'.

history.meaning: mutually / together + without changing from the prior state
unchanged as before; in the same old way (often in letter greetings and conversation)
as ever, as usual, still the same (both fondly and with wry exasperation)

morphemes.meaning: mutually, together, emphatically (< stem of 合ふ au, OJ api-)
change, alter (irrealis/mizenkei stem of 変わる kawaru < OJ kapar-)

相変わらず.notes: Can function both as an adverb (相変わらず忙しい 'busy as usual') and as a predicate with だ/ですね (相変わらずだね 'You haven't changed a bit / Same old you!', often said with affectionate teasing or mild exasperation).

rootFamily.gloss: to change, to be altered, to be unusual (intransitive)
instead of, replacement, substitute, second helping
partner, companion, the other party (< ai 'mutual' + te 'hand/person')

cognates.meaning: compatibility of natures in Five Elements divination

相性.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese compound originating in traditional Chinese Five Elements (Wu Xing / Gogyō 五行) astrology and divination, where it denoted the mutual harmony or generation (相生) between two individuals' natal elements and inborn natures. Orthographically composed of 相 (mutual, reciprocal; read with the native Yamato kun'yomi ai-) and 性 (inborn nature, character; read with the Go-on Sino-Japanese reading shō, from Middle Chinese sjejH), forming a classic jūbako-yomi (kun + on) compound that broadened from astrological compatibility to interpersonal chemistry.

history.meaning: astrological compatibility of two people's natal Five Elements natures
interpersonal compatibility, natural chemistry, or affinity between people or things

morphemes.meaning: inborn nature, character, disposition (Go-on reading shō)

相性.notes: Read with a hybrid jūbako-yomi (kun'yomi 相 ai + on'yomi 性 shō); most commonly used in the pattern 相性がいい / 悪い (to have good / bad chemistry).

相手.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('partner, companion, other party, opponent'), attested from the Heian period onward, formed from 相 (あい, from 合う 'to meet, face each other, match') + 手 (て 'hand; person filling a role or performing an action').

history.meaning: counterpart; partner; opponent
partner; companion; other party; opponent

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 相手

相棒.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Japanese compound noun ('partner, buddy, sidekick, colleague'), originating in Edo-period palanquin-bearer (*kago*) jargon for the fellow bearer who shared the same carrying pole: formed from native 相 (あい 'mutual, fellow') + Sino-Japanese 棒 (ぼう 'carrying pole, staff'). Later generalized to any close partner or collaborator.

history.meaning: fellow bearer sharing a palanquin carrying pole
partner; buddy; sidekick

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 相棒

相談.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('consultation, discussion, talking things over'), formed from 相 (そう 'mutually, together') + 談 (だん 'talk, converse, discuss'). Attested in Japanese from the Muromachi period onward.

history.meaning: talking together; mutual consultation
consultation; discussion; seeking advice

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 相談

眉.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('eyebrow'), continuing Old Japanese *mayu*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; generally analyzed as containing the bound eye root *ma-* (目 'eye').

history.meaning: eyebrow
eyebrow

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 眉

眉毛.etymology: The term '眉毛' (meaning 'eyebrows') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: eyebrows
eyebrows

眉毛.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 眉毛

看板.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 看 ('look at, watch') and 板 ('wooden board'), originally a painted wooden shop board hung outside to catch passers-by's eyes.

看護婦.etymology: A Meiji-era Sino-Japanese occupational compound formed by appending the gender-specific suffix 婦 (fu, from Middle Chinese bjuwX, meaning married woman or female professional) to the verbal noun 看護 (kango, nursing or tending a patient, composed of 看 kan 'to watch over, attend to with hand over eye' and 護 go 'to guard, protect'). It served as the standard statutory and everyday term for a female nurse throughout the twentieth century until legal reforms in 2002 replaced gender-marked titles with the gender-neutral 看護師 (kangoshi).

history.meaning: female medical attendant or nurse tending the sick and injured
female nurse (standard twentieth-century term, officially superseded by 看護師 in 2002)

看護婦.notes: While prevalent in 1980s period settings like The Naked Director, modern contemporary Japanese uses the gender-neutral 看護師 (kangoshi) in hospitals and official contexts since the 2002 legal revision.

真.etymology: A foundational logograph uniting two distinct etymological strata in Japanese: the Sino-Japanese noun and formal modifier shin (borrowed from Middle Chinese tsyin 真, originally a Daoist term denoting an realized, untransformed immortal or ultimate reality) and the native Yamato root and prefix ma (from Old Japanese ma, denoting purity, completeness, and unalloyed genuineness). As an independent noun read shin, it expresses philosophical or emotional truth and genuineness, in contrast to falsehood (偽 gi / uso).

history.form: 真 (Middle Chinese tsyin) / Old Japanese ma
history.meaning: unfeigned reality, Daoist perfection (Chinese); pure, exact, genuine (Old Japanese)
truth, reality, genuineness; prefix for pure or exact qualities

morphemes.meaning: truth, reality, genuine, unalloyed (on'yomi shin / kun'yomi ma)

真.notes: Read shin when used as an independent formal noun or with no (真の友 'a true friend'), and ma (often with gemination, e.g., 真っ黒 makkuro) when prefixed to native Yamato words.

真っ平ら.etymology: Intensive native Japanese na-adjective formed by attaching the emphatic prefix 真っ- (ma- + gemination, from 真 'true, pure, utter', as in 真っ白 masshiro 'pure white' and 真っ暗 makkura 'pitch dark') to the na-adjective 平ら (taira, 'flat, level, even'). The geminate triggers fortition of *t- (or preserves emphasis), yielding マッタイラ (mattaira, 'completely flat without a single wrinkle').

history.meaning: flat; level; even
completely flat; perfectly level

真っ平ら.notes: Takes な before nouns (真っ平らなクロス) and に as an adverbial modifier (真っ平らにアイロンをかける, 'to iron completely flat').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真っ平ら

真っ白.etymology: Emphatic native Japanese adjectival noun ('pure white, snow-white, completely blank'), formed from intensive prefix 真- (ま- 'true, pure, complete', with expressive consonant gemination まっ-) + 白 (しろ 'white').

history.meaning: pure white; snow-white; blank

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真っ白

真っ直ぐ.etymology: Emphatic native Japanese adjectival noun and adverb ('straight, direct, upright, honest'), formed from intensive prefix 真- (ま- with expressive gemination まっ-) + 直ぐ (すぐ 'straight, direct, upright', stem of classical adjective 直ぐし).

history.meaning: completely straight; direct; upright
straight ahead; upright; frank

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真っ直ぐ

真っ直ぐだ.etymology: Compound of prefix 真っ (ma-, intensifying prefix with geminate consonant) + 直ぐ (sugu, 'straight/immediate') + copula だ (da).

history.meaning: perfectly straight

真っ直ぐだ.notes: Also functions as an adverb without the copula.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真っ直ぐだ

真ん中.etymology: Emphatic native Japanese compound noun ('exact center, dead center, right in the middle'), formed from intensive prefix 真- (ま- 'true, exact', with nasal insertion まん- before *n-*) + 中 (なか 'inside, middle, center').

history.form: まなか → まんなか (真ん中)
history.meaning: exact middle; dead center
right in the middle; center

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真ん中

真上.etymology: The term '真上' (meaning 'right above') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: right above
right above

真上.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真上

真下.etymology: Native Yamato spatial compound combining the intensive prefix 真- (ma-, Old Japanese ma- 'true, pure, exact, dead-centre') with the noun 下 (shita, 'under, below, beneath'). Parallel to 真上 (maue, 'directly overhead') and 真ん中 (mannaka, 'dead centre'), 真下 pinpoints the spot vertically straight beneath something.

history.meaning: exact + below
directly underneath, right below

真下.notes: Notice that unlike 真ん中 (mannaka) and 真っ白 (masshiro), 真下 (mashita) does not insert a nasal or geminate consonant after 真-.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真下

cognates.meaning: real sword; earnestness, seriousness (borrowed from Japanese)

真剣.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound of 真 (shin, from Middle Chinese tsyin, meaning real or genuine) and 剣 (ken, from Middle Chinese kjaemH, meaning double-edged blade or sword). Literally denoting a live, forged steel sword in contrast to a wooden practice sword (木刀 bokutō) or bamboo foil (竹刀 shinai) used in martial arts kata and sparring, the term underwent metaphorical extension during the Edo and Meiji periods: because facing an opponent with live blades carried mortal stakes, 真剣 came to describe dead-serious, all-out earnestness.

history.meaning: a real forged steel blade, as opposed to a wooden or bamboo training sword
deadly serious, in earnest, with total commitment (na-adjective and noun)

真剣.notes: Still retains its literal martial meaning in the set phrase 真剣勝負 (shinken shōbu, a duel with real swords; figuratively a high-stakes, no-holds-barred showdown).

rootFamily.gloss: high-stakes contest, duel with real blades

真夜中.etymology: Native Japanese prefix 真- (ま-, 'true, exact, dead centre') + 夜中 (よなか, 'middle of the night': 夜 よ + 中 なか).
真夜中.notes: Parallel to 真ん中 ('right in the middle') and 真夏 ('midsummer').

真実.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound borrowed from Middle Chinese 真實 (tsyin zyit), combining 真 (shin, genuine, unfeigned, true) with 実 (jitsu, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese zyit, originally meaning fruit full of seed, and by extension substance, fullness, and actuality). Widely propagated through Chinese and Japanese Buddhist texts as a translation of Sanskrit tattva and satya (ultimate reality devoid of illusion), it entered general literary and legal prose to denote objective or moral truth.

history.meaning: substantial reality, Buddhist ultimate truth (tattva/satya) free of falsehood
the truth, factual reality, sincerity

真実.notes: Unlike 事実 (jijitsu), which refers strictly to objective, verifiable facts, 真実 (shinjitsu) carries a deeper philosophical or emotional weight—'the hidden or ultimate truth.'

真鍮.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 真 ('true, pure') and 鍮 ('brass, copper-zinc alloy'), attested from the Muromachi and Edo periods for golden-yellow brass hardware.

真鍮バルブ.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and Western loanword compound ('brass valve'), combining 真鍮 (しんちゅう 'brass', borrowed from early modern Chinese 真鍮 for copper-zinc alloy) + バルブ (borrowed from English *valve*).

history.form: 真鍮バルブ (しんちゅうバルブ)
history.meaning: brass valve

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真鍮

真鍮プレート.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and Western loanword compound ('brass plate, brass plaque'), combining 真鍮 (しんちゅう 'brass') + プレート (borrowed from English *plate*).

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真鍮

真鍮ランプ.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and Western loanword compound ('brass lamp'), combining 真鍮 (しんちゅう 'brass') + ランプ (borrowed from Dutch *lamp* / English *lamp*).

history.form: 真鍮ランプ (しんちゅうランプ)
history.meaning: brass lamp

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 真鍮

真面目.etymology: An ateji and semantic compound combining the native Yamato prefix 真 (ma-, genuine, straight, unfeigned) with jime, traditionally analyzed either as a phonetic shift of 面目 (menboku, facial appearance, countenance, honor) or as a compound with the native verb stem 締め (shime, tightening, composing oneself, voiced to -jime via rendaku), reinforced orthographically by writing 面目 ('face and eyes'). Attested from the Edo period as a description of a composed, unsmiling, earnest countenance, it broadened to denote a diligent, rule-abiding, and serious character.

history.meaning: a solemn, composed facial expression free of jesting or pretense
earnest, serious, diligent, honest, and upright in attitude or conduct

morphemes.meaning: face, countenance (orthographic component of 面目)
eye, look, appearance (orthographic component of 面目)

真面目.notes: Source of the ubiquitous modern slang abbreviation マジ (maji, 'seriously, for real'), which was already used by Edo-period stage performers and courtesans before surging back in late twentieth-century youth speech.

眠い.etymology: A native Yamato (-i) adjective descending from Classical Japanese nemusi, built on the Old Japanese verbal root ne- (寝, 'to lie down, to sleep') extended with the stative/experiential formant -mu- (also seen in the verb 眠る nemuru < Old Japanese neburu 'to sleep, close the eyes, doze') plus the adjectival inflection -i (from Classical conclusive -si). It expresses the subjective physiological sensation of drowsiness felt by the speaker.

history.form: ねぶし / ねむし (nebusi / nemusi)
history.meaning: heavy-lidded, drowsy, inclined to sleep
history.stage: Late Old to Early Middle Japanese

history.meaning: sleepy, drowsy; (slang) dull or soporific

morphemes.meaning: sleep, doze, feel drowsy (stem nemu- < root ne- 'lie down, sleep')

眠い.notes: Alternates in everyday speech with the augmented variant 眠たい (nemutai), which incorporates the desiderative-like suffix -tai without changing the core meaning of 'sleepy, drowsy.'

眠る.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to sleep, fall asleep'), continuing Old Japanese *neburu* > Middle Japanese *nemuru*, derived from the sleep root *ne-* (seen in 寝 *ne* / 寝る *neru* 'to sleep, lie down') + verbal derivative element *-buru* / *-muru*.

history.meaning: doze; sleep; close the eyes
sleep; fall asleep

眠れる.etymology: Potential verb ('to be able to sleep, can fall asleep'), formed as the regular *e*-grade potential derivative (*nemur-e-ru*) of the consonant-stem (godan) verb 眠る (*nemuru* 'to sleep').

history.meaning: can sleep; be able to fall asleep

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 眠る

眺め.etymology: Native Japanese verbal noun ('view, prospect, scenery, gazing'), nominalized from the連用形 of 眺める (*nagameru*, Old Japanese *nagamu* 'to gaze fixedly into the distance while lost in thought, look out over', related to 長し *nagasi* 'long' + 目 *me* 'eye' / 見 *mi* 'look').

history.meaning: pensive gazing into the distance; long rain
view; scenery; prospect

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 眺め

眼鏡.etymology: Jukujikun spelling pairing 眼 ('eye') + 鏡 ('mirror, lens') with native reading めがね (from 目 'eye' + 金 'metal frame').

着く.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to arrive, reach, touch, take a seat'), continuing Old Japanese *tuku* (four-grade *tuk-* 'to come into contact with, attach, reach a point'). Written with 着 for arriving at a destination or sitting down at a place (etymologically identical to 付く).

history.meaning: touch; adhere; reach a place
arrive at; reach; sit at

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 着く

着る.etymology: Native Japanese transitive upper monograde (kami-ichidan) verb ('to wear, put on [clothing on the upper or whole body]'), continuing Old Japanese *kiru* (stem *ki₁-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*ki-ru*.

history.meaning: put on; wear
put on; wear on the body
wear; put on (clothes)

着地.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun and suru-verb ('landing, touching down on the ground'), formed from 着 (ちゃく 'arrive, reach, touch') + 地 (ち 'ground, earth').

history.meaning: landing on the ground; touchdown

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 着地

着実.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound of 着 (chaku, from Middle Chinese drjak, originally 'to adhere, make contact, touch the ground, settle in place') and 実 (jitsu, from Middle Chinese zyit, 'fruit, substance, solidity'). Combining the image of planting one's feet firmly on the ground (着) with substantial, unvarnished reality (実), it describes conduct or progress that is steady, methodical, and free of reckless speculation.

history.form: 著實 / 着實 (Middle Chinese drjak zyit)
history.meaning: substantial, grounded, earnestly applied
history.stage: Late Imperial Chinese & Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: steady, methodical, step-by-step and reliable

morphemes.meaning: attach, reach, settle firmly on the ground

着実.notes: Frequently used adverbially as 着実に (chakujitsu ni, 'steadily, step by step') with verbs of progress like 進む (advance) or 歩む (walk forward).
