着替える.etymology: Native Japanese compound verb ('to change clothes'), formed from the連用形 *ki* of 着る ('to wear, put on clothes') + 替える (かえる → がえる with rendaku, 'to exchange, replace, switch').

history.meaning: change one's garments
change clothes

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 着替える

cognates.meaning: instant, moment, twinkling of an eye

瞬間.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound formed from 瞬 (shun, from Middle Chinese sywinH, composed of the eye radical 目 plus 舜, meaning 'to blink or wink the eye') and 間 (kan, from Middle Chinese kean, 'interval of space or time'). Rooted in classical Chinese and Buddhist temporal terminology—where a single blink of the eye (一瞬 isshun) measured an infinitesimal unit of time alongside Sanskrit kṣaṇa (刹那 setsuna)—it denotes the briefest perceptible interval of time.

history.meaning: the brief interval of a single blink of the eye
moment, split second, exact instant

morphemes.meaning: blink, wink of an eye, twinkle

瞬間.notes: When following a plain-form verb (e.g., 見た瞬間 mita shunkan), it functions as an immediate temporal conjunction meaning 'the very instant that...'

rootFamily.gloss: a brief instant, a blink of an eye
blinking of the eyes, twinkling of stars

矢印.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('arrow symbol, directional arrow mark'), formed from 矢 (や 'arrow', Old Japanese *ya*) + 印 (しるし → じるし with rendaku, 'mark, sign, emblem'). Originally denoting an ownership mark on an arrow shaft, it came in modern usage to mean an arrow-shaped pointer indicating direction.

history.meaning: identifying mark on an arrow shaft
arrow symbol; directional pointer

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 矢印

知らせ.etymology: Native Japanese verbal noun ('notice, notification, news, report, omen'), nominalized from the連用形 of 知らせる (*shiraseru* 'to let know, inform, notify', causative of 知る *shiru* 'to know').

history.meaning: informing; notice; sign
news; notice; notification; word

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 知らせ

知り合い.etymology: A native Yamato compound noun derived via zero-nominalization of the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the reciprocal compound verb 知り合う (shiriau, 'to know one another, become mutually acquainted'). That verb combines the continuative stem 知り (shiri) of 知る (shiru, from Old Japanese siru, 'to come to know, perceive, command') with the reciprocal auxiliary verb 合う (au, from Old Japanese apu, 'to meet, come together, do mutually').

history.meaning: mutual acquaintance or knowing one another
history.stage: Early Middle to Late Middle Japanese

history.meaning: acquaintance, personal contact, someone one knows socially or professionally

morphemes.meaning: know, become acquainted with (continuative stem of 知る shiru)
do mutually, meet together (nominalized stem of 合う au)

知り合い.notes: Occupies an important social register in Japanese interpersonal hierarchy: closer than a stranger (他人 tanin), but less intimate than a true friend (友達 tomodachi / 友人 yūjin); its Sino-Japanese formal counterpart is 知人 (chijin).

rootFamily.gloss: to get to know each other, become acquainted

知る.etymology: Native Japanese consonant-stem (godan) verb ('to know, come to know, learn, be aware of'), continuing Old Japanese *siru* (attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū with the dual senses 'to discern, know' and 'to rule, govern'); cognate with 白し (*sirosi* 'bright, clear') and 著し (*ichijirushi* 'conspicuous, manifest').

history.meaning: perceive; know; govern
know; find out; become acquainted with

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 知る

知恵.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound borrowed from Middle Chinese 智慧 (trjeH hwejH), originally propagated in East Asia through Chinese Buddhist scriptures as the standard translation for Sanskrit prajñā ('transcendental insight, liberating wisdom that discerns the true nature of phenomena'). Following postwar Japanese script reforms (kakikae), the non-Jōyō character 智 ('wisdom, intellect') was replaced by 知 (chi, 'to know'), paired with 恵 (e, the Go-on reading of Middle Chinese hwejH, 'favor, grace, mental discernment').

history.form: 智慧 (chie, Middle Chinese trjeH hwejH)
history.meaning: Buddhist prajna: transcendental wisdom discerning ultimate reality
practical wisdom, sagacity, resourcefulness, know-how

morphemes.meaning: know, perceive, wisdom (replacing historical 智 chi)
discernment, insight, grace (Go-on reading e, replacing historical 慧)

知恵.notes: Whereas 知識 (chishiki) refers to accumulated factual knowledge, 知恵 (chie) denotes practical wisdom, cleverness, and real-world resourcefulness—as in 生活の知恵 ('everyday life hacks/wisdom') or 知恵を絞る ('to rack one's brains').

rootFamily.gloss: wisdom tooth (erupting after one gains wisdom)

知識.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound from Middle Chinese 知識 (trje syik), uniting 知 (chi, from Middle Chinese trje, 'to know, apprehend') and 識 (shiki, from Middle Chinese syik, 'to recognize, distinguish, consciousness'). In classical Chinese and pre-modern Japanese Buddhist texts, it rendered both Sanskrit vijñāna ('discriminative consciousness') and mitra ('a learned spiritual friend or acquaintance', as in 善知識 zenchishiki); during the Meiji modernization, it was repurposed to translate Western epistemological 'knowledge.'

history.form: 知識 (chishiki, Middle Chinese trje syik)
history.meaning: discriminative cognition (vijnana); a learned spiritual guide or acquaintance in Buddhism
acquired knowledge, learning, systematic information on a subject

知識.notes: Pairs with verbs like 身につける (acquire) or 蓄える (accumulate), and forms 知識人 (chishikijin, 'intellectual, member of the intelligentsia').

短い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('short, brief'), continuing Old Japanese *mizikasi* (stem *mizika-*), attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: short in length or duration
short; brief

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 短い

石.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('stone, rock, pebble'), continuing Old Japanese *isi* (alongside variant *iso* 'rock, rocky shore'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*isi*.

history.meaning: stone; rock
stone; rock
stone; rock; pebble

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 石

石壁.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 石 (いし, 'stone') and 壁 (かべ, 'wall').
石壁.notes: Refers to dressed stone courtyard or garden walls.

石段.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Japanese compound noun ('stone steps, stone stairway'), combining native 石 (いし 'stone') + Sino-Japanese 段 (だん 'step, stair, tier').

history.meaning: stone steps; stone staircase

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 石段

石畳.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('stone paving, cobblestone pavement, flagstone walk'), formed from 石 (いし 'stone') + 畳 (たたみ → だたみ with rendaku, nominalized from 畳む 'to fold, layer, lay flat side by side').

history.meaning: layered stone paving; checkered pattern
stone pavement; cobblestone street

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 石畳

石鹸.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun ('soap'), read せっけん from the on'yomi of 石 ('stone, solid cake') + 鹸 ('alkali, lye, soda'). While soap introduced by the Portuguese in the 16th century was originally called シャボン (from Portuguese *sabão*), the Chinese-derived character compound 石鹸 read *sekken* became the standard term from the Meiji period onward.

history.meaning: soap (from Portuguese sabão)
soap

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 石鹸

石鹸水.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('soapy water, soapsuds'), formed from 石鹸 (せっけん 'soap') + 水 (すい 'water, liquid').

history.meaning: soapy water; soap solution

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 石鹸水

砂浜.etymology: A native Yamato determinative noun compound combining 砂 (suna, from Old Japanese su 'sandbar, fine grit' + land/earth formative -na, meaning 'sand') and 浜 (hama, from Old Japanese pama, meaning 'flat seashore, beach, waterside'). The compound transparently designates a coastal beach covered in fine sand as opposed to a rocky shore (磯 iso) or shingle beach (玉砂利浜).

history.meaning: sandy seashore or stretch of coastal sand
sandy beach

砂浜.notes: Notice the absence of rendaku (sequential voicing): it is pronounced sunahama, never *sunabama, whereas 浜 voices to -bama in place names like 横浜 (Yokohama) vs. 小浜 (Obama).

砂糖.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun ('sugar'), borrowed in the Muromachi period from Chinese 砂糖 / 沙糖 (Middle Chinese *sra-thang*, literally 'sand-like granular sugar'), composed of 砂 ('sand, grit') + 糖 ('sugar, sweet malt').

history.meaning: granulated sugar ('sand sugar')
sugar

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 砂糖

破く.etymology: A native Yamato transitive godan verb (yabuk-) formed as a consonantal stem variant of 破る (yaburu, from Old Japanese yaburu, 'to tear, rend, break through'). By replacing the liquid transitive suffix -r- with the velar action formative -k- on the shared root yabu-, late medieval and early modern spoken Japanese specialized 破く for the concrete, physical action of ripping or tearing thin sheet-like materials such as paper, cloth, or skin.

history.form: やぶく (yabuku, collateral variant of yaburu)
history.meaning: to physically rip or tear paper, cloth, or membrane into pieces
to tear, rip up (physical materials only)

morphemes.meaning: tear, rend, rip (native root yabu- + velar transitive formative -k-)

破く.notes: Crucial usage distinction: 破く (yabuku) can ONLY be used for physically tearing objects like paper, letters, or clothing (紙を破く), never for breaking rules, promises, or opponents—which require 破る (yaburu).

rootFamily.gloss: to tear; to break (a rule/promise); to defeat
to be torn, be worn out, be defeated (intransitive)

破る.etymology: A native Yamato transitive godan verb descending directly from Old Japanese yaburu (attested phonographically in the Man'yōshū and Nihon Shoki), built on a root yabu- ('to rend, breach, shatter') plus the transitive verbal suffix -ru. Orthographically represented by the kanji 破 ('to split stone, break, destroy'), its semantic range expanded from physically tearing barriers or garments to abstractly breaching rules, violating promises, breaking silence, and defeating rivals.

history.meaning: to tear apart, smash through a barrier, rout an enemy
to tear physically; to break a rule, promise, or record; to defeat an opponent

morphemes.meaning: tear, breach, break through, defeat (native stem yabur-)

破る.notes: Highly versatile transitive verb covering physical tearing (封を破る 'break a seal'), rule-breaking (規則・約束を破る 'break a rule/promise'), and sports/competition (記録・相手を破る 'break a record / defeat an opponent').

rootFamily.gloss: to be torn; to be broken; to be defeated (intransitive)

破れる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to tear, rip, be torn, be broken, be defeated'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *yaburu* (stem *yabure-*), the intransitive/mediopassive counterpart of four-grade transitive 破る (*yaburu* 'to tear, break').

history.meaning: be torn; be broken; be defeated
tear; rip; be broken; be defeated

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 破れる

cognates.meaning: catastrophe, collapse, breakup of a relationship

破局.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound combining 破 (ha, from Middle Chinese phaH, 'to break, shatter, ruin') and 局 (kyoku, from Middle Chinese gjowk, 'game board of Go or Shogi, match, state of affairs, concluding phase'). Originally referring to a ruined board-game position or the catastrophic denouement of a play (used in Meiji-Taishō literary criticism to translate Greek/English catastrophe), it specialized in postwar media and everyday speech to denote the final collapse of a romance, marriage, or alliance.

history.meaning: ruined conclusion of a game or affairs; theatrical catastrophe or tragic finale
catastrophic collapse; final breakup of a romantic relationship or engagement

morphemes.meaning: board-game situation, phase of affairs, conclusion

破局.notes: A staple of Japanese entertainment journalism and tabloid headlines (破局を迎える 'to reach a breakup/collapse'), sounding more dramatic and final than the casual 別れる (wakareru, 'to part ways').

rootFamily.gloss: situation, phase, state of a game or affair
after all, in the end, final outcome

cognates.meaning: split seam; flaw, weak point, giveaway in an argument or alibi

破綻.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound borrowed from Literary Chinese 破綻 (pòzhàn), composed of 破 (ha, from Middle Chinese phaH, 'to tear, break open') and 綻 (tan, from Middle Chinese dreanH, containing the silk/thread radical 糸 plus 定, meaning 'a split seam or unpicked stitching in a garment'). Originally a concrete sartorial metaphor for a garment coming apart at the seams, it evolved to signify a fatal breach in logic, financial insolvency, or the total breakdown of a plan or marriage.

history.meaning: a ripped seam or split stitching in clothing; a visible flaw or gap in workmanship
complete collapse, financial bankruptcy, irreparable breakdown of a plan or relationship

morphemes.meaning: come unsewn, split at the seam (native reading hokorobiru)

破綻.notes: Notice the false friend with modern Mandarin: in Chinese 破綻 (pòzhàn) means 'a subtle flaw or giveaway in a lie/plot,' whereas in Japanese 破綻 (hatan) means 'full-scale collapse or bankruptcy' (e.g., 経営破綻 'corporate bankruptcy').

rootFamily.gloss: to come unsewn at the seams; to begin to bloom or smile

cognates.word: かたくん (katakun) / かたさん (katasan)

硬い.etymology: A native Yamato (-i) adjective descending from Old Japanese katasi ('hard, solid, unyielding, tight'), sharing a prehistoric root kata- with 固まる (katamaru, 'to harden, congeal') and 型 / 形 (kata, 'fixed mold, form'). While representing a single etymological word in spoken Japanese, modern orthography assigns 硬い (using 硬, containing the stone radical 石) specifically to stone-like physical rigidity, unyielding texture, or stiff, tense bodily posture and facial expression.

history.meaning: physically hard, solid, tightly bound, firm
hard, rigid; stiff, tense, or wooden in expression, muscles, or manner

morphemes.meaning: hard, rigid, stiff, tense (native stem kata-)

硬い.notes: Japanese distinguishes three kanji for katai by nuance: 硬い (rigid, stiff, tense—as in 表情が硬い 'one's expression is stiff/tense'), 固い (tightly shut, resolute, formal—頭が固い 'stubborn'), and 堅い (reliable, sound, safe—手堅い 'steady').

rootFamily.gloss: to harden, stiffen, freeze up with tension
hard, firm, solid, safe, stubborn (orthographic variants)

確か.etymology: Native Japanese adjectival noun and adverb ('certain, sure, reliable, accurate; if I remember rightly'), continuing Old and Heian Japanese *tasika* ('firm, secure, trustworthy, definite'), built on the root *tasi-* ('thorough, full, reliable') + adjectival suffix *-ka*.

history.meaning: secure; reliable; clear; definite
certain; sure; reliable; if I recall

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 確か

確かに.etymology: A native Yamato deadjectival adverb formed from the na-adjective stem 確か (tashika, attested in Heian-period Middle Japanese as tasika, 'reliable, trustworthy, definite, clear') plus the adverbial particle に (ni, continuative form of the copula なり nari). Philologists derive tasika from the Old Japanese root tasi- ('complete, sufficient, thorough', cognate with 足す tasu 'to add, make full' and 確かむ tasikamu) combined with the adjectival state suffix -ka (as in 静か shizuka, 愚か oroka).

history.meaning: reliably, securely, without fail or negligence
certainly, indeed, sure enough, admittedly

morphemes.meaning: certain, reliable, definite (native stem tashika, written with 確)

確かに.notes: Watch the contrast between 確かに (tashika ni, 'certainly, indeed, it is true that...') and bare 確か (tashika, 'if I remember correctly, I'm pretty sure...'), which actually expresses mild uncertainty about a memory!

確かめる.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to ascertain, confirm, verify, make sure'), continuing classical lower bigrade *tasikamu* (確かむ), derived from the adjectival stem 確か (*tashika* 'certain, sure') + verbalizing suffix *-mu* > *-meru*.

history.meaning: make firm; verify; ascertain
confirm; verify; make sure

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 確かめる

確信.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound combining 確 (kaku, from Middle Chinese khaewk, originally meaning 'hard, solid stone' and by extension 'firm, unshakeable, definite') and 信 (shin, from Middle Chinese sinH, composed of person 人 plus word 言, meaning 'trustworthiness, faith, belief'). Standardized in the Meiji era to express an unshakeable subjective conviction or certainty of belief.

history.meaning: unwavering belief, firm conviction
firm conviction, confidence; to be thoroughly convinced (with する)

確信.notes: Gives rise to the famous modern Japanese idiom 確信犯 (kakushinhan): originally a legal term translating German Überzeugungstäter ('conscience/ideological offender acting out of moral or political conviction'), but now widely used colloquially to mean 'doing something bad deliberately while knowing full well it is wrong.'

確実.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound uniting 確 (kaku, from Middle Chinese khaewk, 'hard rock, firm, solid, definite') with 実 (jitsu, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese zyit, 'fruit full of seed, substance, reality'). Combining rock-like firmness with tangible substance, the compound denotes that which is objectively reliable, verified, and guaranteed to occur without doubt.

history.meaning: solid and substantial, authentic, true to fact
certain, reliable, sound, guaranteed (na-adjective and noun)

確実.notes: Whereas 確信 (kakushin) is internal, subjective conviction ('I am convinced'), 確実 (kakujitsu) describes external, objective certainty ('it is a sure thing / guaranteed').

確認.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('confirmation, verification, affirmation'), formed from 確 (かく 'firm, certain, definite') + 認 (にん 'recognize, acknowledge, verify').

history.meaning: confirmation; verification; checking

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 確認

磨く.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to polish, burnish, scrub, brush [teeth], cultivate [a skill]'), continuing Old Japanese *migaku*, attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: polish; burnish; make shine
polish; brush; refine

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 磨く

示す.etymology: A native Yamato transitive godan verb descending from Old Japanese simesu ('to point out, reveal, signify, make known'). Morphologically analyzed as a transitive/causative formation in -su derived from the Old Japanese root sime- ('a boundary mark, sign, token of possession', preserved in the noun 標 / 注連 shime 'sacred marker rope, sign' and the verb 占める shimeru 'to mark out, occupy'). It is written with the kanji 示, an ancient pictograph of a ritual altar table revealing auspicious or inauspicious signs from heaven.

history.meaning: to mark out with a sign, reveal, instruct, point out
to show, demonstrate, indicate, prove, express (an attitude or figure)

morphemes.meaning: show, point out, signify (native stem shimes- < root shime 'sign, mark')

示す.notes: More formal and abstract than 見せる (miseru, 'to let someone physically look at something'); 示す is preferred for proving resolve, displaying data, or indicating direction (誠意・態度・数字を示す).

rootFamily.gloss: implied meaning, hint, suggestion (Sino-Japanese reading shisa)
to occupy, take up, account for (cognate native root shime-)

cognates.meaning: society, the public (borrowed from Meiji Japanese)

社会.etymology: A classic Meiji-era wasei-kango (Japanese-coined Sino-compound) repurposed in the mid-1870s—notably by journalist Fukuchi Gen'ichirō in the Tōkyō Nichinichi Shinbun—to translate English society and Dutch maatschappij. In pre-modern Tang–Song Chinese, 社 (sha, Middle Chinese dzyaeX, 'altar to the tutelary deity of the soil, local village shrine guild') and 会 (kai, Middle Chinese hwojH, 'gathering, assembly') denoted a seasonal communal festival gathering around the village earth-god altar; Meiji intellectuals transformed this classical compound into the modern sociological concept of 'society' and exported it across East Asia.

history.meaning: a village gathering or religious association centered on the local earth-deity altar (社)
human society at large, the public sphere, the real world (translating English 'society')

morphemes.meaning: altar of the soil deity; community, association, company

社会.notes: Notice how 社会 (shakai, 'society') and 会社 (kaisha, 'commercial company') use the exact same two kanji in reverse order—both forged during Japan's Meiji modernization to build modern institutional vocabulary.

rootFamily.gloss: working adult, full-fledged member of society

cognates.meaning: working adult, person who has entered society outside school (borrowed from Japanese)
working adult, member of society (borrowed from Japanese)

社会人.etymology: A Japanese-coined Sino-compound (wasei-kango) formed in the Taishō and early Shōwa periods by adding the human agent suffix 人 (jin, from Middle Chinese nyin, 'person, member') to the Meiji neologism 社会 (shakai, 'society'). Rather than simply meaning any human living in society, Japanese institutional culture specialized 社会人 as the antonym of 学生 (gakusei, 'student'): a self-supporting adult who has graduated, entered the workforce, and assumed full social and tax responsibilities.

history.meaning: an adult citizen participating actively in public and economic life outside school
working adult, full-fledged member of the workforce (contrasted with 学生 'student')

morphemes.meaning: society, the public world outside school (社 + 会)
person, member of a group (Kan'on reading jin)

社会人.notes: Deeply embedded in Japanese life-stage milestones: graduating seniors speak of 社会人になる ('becoming a working adult'), and corporate recruits are called 新社会人 (shin-shakaijin, 'new working adults').

rootFamily.gloss: new graduate entering the workforce for the first time

社会勉強.etymology: A four-character Sino-Japanese compound combining 社会 (shakai, 'society, the real world outside home and school') with 勉強 (benkyō, 'study, learning'—itself derived from Classical Chinese 勉強 miǎnqiǎng, originally meaning 'to exert oneself to the utmost, force oneself to make an effort', which shifted in Edo-period Osaka merchant speech to 'bargaining hard/discounting' and in Meiji Japan to 'diligent study'). Together, 社会勉強 denotes learning how the real world operates through hands-on experience.

history.meaning: studying the workings of society and human affairs outside classroom textbooks
real-world education, learning life lessons, street smarts, or business realities firsthand

morphemes.meaning: society, the real world (社 + 会)
exert oneself, study, learn (勉 'endeavor' + 強 'force/strive')

社会勉強.notes: Often used with wry humor or pragmatism (いい社会勉強になった 'That was a good lesson in how the real world works') after paying a steep price, working a tough part-time job, or getting burned in a deal.

cognates.meaning: member of a commune, club, or news agency
company employee, staff member (borrowed from Japanese)

社員.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound coined in the Meiji era by combining 社 (sha, functioning as an abbreviation of 会社 kaisha 'commercial company, corporation' or 結社 kessha 'association', from Middle Chinese dzyaeX) with the suffix 員 (in, from Middle Chinese hjwien, originally a ding cauldron under a circle signifying a counted tally of officials or personnel). It designates an official member or employee on the roster of a company.

history.meaning: member of an association, society, or joint-stock company; corporate shareholder or partner in legal code
company employee, regular corporate staff member

morphemes.meaning: company, firm, association (short for 会社 kaisha)

社員.notes: In everyday business Japanese, 社員 (shain) often implies a 正社員 (seishain, permanent full-time employee with job security and benefits), as opposed to temporary (派遣 haken) or part-time (バイト baito) workers.

cognates.meaning: director of a news agency, publishing house, or club; company president (in Japanese contexts)

社長.etymology: A Sino-Japanese institutional title combining 社 (sha, from Middle Chinese dzyaeX, originally 'altar to the earth god' and in Meiji Japan abbreviating 会社 kaisha 'commercial company') with 長 (chō, from Middle Chinese trjangX, originally a pictograph of a long-haired elder with a staff, meaning 'chief, head, leader'). In pre-modern China 社長 denoted the headman of a village shrine-guild; Meiji corporate law and business practice repurposed it for the president of a business firm.

history.meaning: headman of a local village community guild (社) in imperial China
company president, chief executive of a corporation (short for 会社の長)

morphemes.meaning: company, corporation (short for 会社 kaisha)

社長.notes: Used directly as a title of address inside a company (社長！ 'President / Boss!'), or with the honorific -san (社長さん) by external vendors, cab drivers, and nightlife hosts in the 1980s bubble economy.

祈る.etymology: Native Japanese verb ('to pray, invoke, wish earnestly'), continuing Old Japanese *inoru*, attested in the Man'yōshū; traditionally analyzed as sacred/ritual prefix *i-* (斎 'consecrated, taboo', as in 忌む *imu*) + 宣る (*noru* 'to proclaim or recite solemn ritual words').

history.meaning: declare ritual words to a deity; pray
pray; wish earnestly

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 祈る

祖母.etymology: Sino-Japanese kinship noun ('grandmother'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 祖母 (Middle Chinese *tsuX-muwX*), composed of 祖 (そ 'ancestor, grandparent') + 母 (ぼ 'mother').

history.meaning: paternal grandmother; grandmother
grandmother

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 祖母

祖父.etymology: Sino-Japanese kinship noun ('grandfather'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 祖父 (Middle Chinese *tsuX-bjuX*), composed of 祖 (そ 'ancestor, grandparent') + 父 (ふ 'father').

history.meaning: grandfather
grandfather

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 祖父

祝い.etymology: A native Yamato deverbative noun formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the verb 祝う (iwau < historical iwafu < Old Japanese ipapu). In Old Japanese, ipapu (written 斎ふ or 祝ふ) meant 'to purify oneself through ritual abstinence, observe sacred taboos, and pray to the kami for auspicious protection.' As Shinto ritual prayers for good fortune evolved into communal festivities for births, weddings, and milestones, the noun 祝い shifted from 'sacred purification rite' to 'celebration, congratulations, and celebratory gift.'

history.meaning: ritual abstinence, purification, and prayers to the deities for auspicious blessings
history.stage: Old to Early Middle Japanese (8th–11th c.)

history.meaning: celebration, congratulatory event, or celebratory gift/money

morphemes.meaning: celebrate, bless, pray for good fortune (stem iwa- < Old Japanese ipap-)

祝い.notes: Frequently takes the honorific prefix お- as お祝い (oiwai), which means both 'congratulations/celebration' and 'a celebratory gift or cash envelope' given for a wedding, birth, or promotion.

rootFamily.gloss: public holiday, national festival day (Sino-Japanese reading shukujitsu)
to observe religious purification and abstinence (archaic etymological doublet of 祝う)

cognates.meaning: nerve, nervous system (reborrowed from Edo Japanese)

神経.etymology: A landmark Edo-period wasei-kango (Japanese-coined Sino-compound) created in 1774 by Rangaku (Dutch-learning) physicians Sugita Genpaku and Maeno Ryōtaku in their anatomical treatise Kaitai Shinsho (解体新書) to translate Dutch zenuw and Latin nervus ('nerve'). They synthesized Sino-medicalの神気 (shinki, 'vital mental spirit') and 経脈 (keimyaku, 'meridian pathways'), uniting 神 (shin, 'spirit, mind') with 経 (kei, 'warp threads, longitudinal channels'). From anatomical nerves, it expanded to denote psychological sensitivity, nerve, and composure, and was borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.form: 神経 (shinkei, coined 1774 in Kaitai Shinsho)
history.meaning: anatomical nerve fiber conducting sensation and motion (translating Dutch zenuw)
anatomical nerves; psychological sensitivity, sensibility, delicateness, or audacity

morphemes.meaning: spirit, mind, vital consciousness (from 神気 shinki)
warp thread, meridian channel, pathway (from 経脈 keimyaku)

神経.notes: Rich in everyday psychological idioms: 神経を使う ('to be on edge / pay exhausting attention to detail'), 神経が図太い ('thick-skinned, having nerves of steel'), and 無神経 (mushinkei, 'insensitive, tactless').

rootFamily.gloss: high-strung, nervous, overly sensitive to detail

禁止.etymology: The term '禁止' (meaning 'forbidden') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: forbidden
forbidden

禁止.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 禁止

cognates.meaning: taboo, something strictly to be avoided

禁物.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound combining 禁 (kin, from Middle Chinese kimH, 'prohibition, taboo, imperial ban') with 物 (motsu, the Go-on reading of Middle Chinese mjut, 'thing, substance, creature'). In medieval and Edo-period kampō medicine and religious practice, 禁物 specifically designated foods or substances strictly forbidden to a convalescent patient (comparable to dietary taboos or 忌み物 imimono); over time it generalized into a colloquial predicate noun meaning 'something strictly off-limits or to be avoided at all costs.'

history.meaning: foods, drinks, or activities medically or ritually forbidden to a patient or practitioner
something strictly to be avoided, a taboo, a recipe for disaster in a given situation

禁物.notes: Notice the Go-on reading motsu for 物 (rather than Kan'on butsu); most famously used in the proverbial warning 油断は禁物だ (Yudan wa kinmotsu da, 'Carelessness / letting your guard down is strictly to be avoided').

rootFamily.gloss: food and drink; cargo/luggage (sharing Go-on reading -motsu)

私.etymology: First-person pronoun ('I, me'), reduced in Early Modern Japanese from わたくし (私, originally a noun meaning 'private, personal, non-official matter' as opposed to 公 *ōyake* 'public, imperial court'). From meaning 'concerning oneself personally', わたくし grammaticalized in Late Middle Japanese into a humble first-person pronoun and contracted in general speech to わたし.

history.meaning: private affair; personal interest (vs. 公 public)
I; me (humble/polite first-person pronoun)
I; me

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 私

私たち.etymology: First-person plural pronoun ('we, us'), formed from 私 (わたし 'I, me') + pluralizing personal suffix -たち (Old Japanese *-tati*, originally an honorific collective marker for deities and nobles).

history.meaning: we; us

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 私たち

秋.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('autumn, fall'), continuing Old Japanese *aki₁*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; traditionally linked either to 飽き (*aki* 'fullness, abundance of ripened grain harvest') or 明き / 赤 (*aki* / *aka* 'clear, bright sky or crimson foliage').

history.meaning: autumn; harvest season
autumn; fall

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 秋

秘密.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and adjectival noun ('secret, secrecy, mystery'), borrowed from Chinese 秘密 (prominent in Buddhist scriptures translating Sanskrit *guhya* 'hidden, esoteric'), composed of 秘 (ひ 'conceal, keep secret') + 密 (みつ 'dense, covert, confidential').

history.meaning: esoteric; hidden; secret
secret; secrecy; confidentiality

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 秘密

秩序.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 秩 (chitsu, from Middle Chinese drit, originally meaning an official's grain stipend or regular sequence, as indicated by the grain radical 禾) and 序 (jo, from Middle Chinese dzjoX, originally the east-west side walls of a courtyard or school, extended to proper arrangement and sequence). Borrowed from Literary Chinese 秩序 (zhìxù), denoting hierarchical and social order.

history.meaning: regular sequence, hierarchical arrangement in rituals and administration
regular order, sequence, social or institutional discipline

morphemes.meaning: order, regular sequence, official rank (Middle Chinese drit)

秩序.notes: Refers to macro-level social, legal, or organizational order (e.g., 社会秩序, public order) rather than tidiness in a room or lining up in a queue (which use 整頓 or 順番). Pitch accent is [1] (chi'tsujo).

移動.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 移動 (いどう), combining 移 ('shift, transfer') and 動 ('move').
移動.notes: Covers shifting furniture across a room as well as travelling between places.

cognates.meaning: in the process of moving / in transit

移動中.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic compound consisting of the verbal noun 移動 (idō, movement, transfer, composed of 移 'shift, transplant grain' + 動 'move, act') and the productive suffix -中 (-chū, from Middle Chinese trjuwng, 'middle, inside, in the midst of'). Literally 'in the middle of moving', used adverbially and adnominally for being in transit.

history.meaning: shifting/moving + middle/interior
currently in transit, while moving between locations

morphemes.meaning: move, set in motion (Middle Chinese duwngX)
in the middle of, currently undergoing (Middle Chinese trjuwng)

移動中.notes: When -中 attaches to an action noun to mean 'in the middle of doing X', it is always read -chū (as in 移動中 idōchū, 営業中 eigyōchū), whereas when it means 'throughout an entire period/place' it is read -jū (e.g., 一日中 ichinichijū).

rootFamily.gloss: currently under construction or in progress
rootFamily.word: 作業中 (さぎょうちゅう)

程.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun ほど (hodo), attested in Old Japanese as ପൊଦൊ (podo, 'interval of time or space, degree, extent'). Orthographically represented by the kanji 程 (originally a Chinese measure of grain or a journey stage). Semantically evolved from a concrete span of space or time into a measure of degree, proper limit, moderation, and a grammatical particle indicating proportional extent ('the more... the more').

history.meaning: temporal or spatial interval, approximate span
social status, proper bounds, degree, moderation
limit, bounds, degree, extent; proportional particle

morphemes.meaning: interval, degree, proper limit or bounds (native Yamato root)

程.notes: As an independent noun meaning 'proper limit or moderation', it frequently appears in set phrases like 程がある (hodo ga aru, 'there is a limit [to what is acceptable]') or 程を知る (hodo o shiru, 'to know one's place/limits'). Usually written in hiragana when functioning as a particle of degree.

税金.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 税 (zei, from Middle Chinese sywejH, originally agricultural tithes paid in harvested grain, composed of 禾 'grain' + 兌 'exchange/strip off') and 金 (kin, from Middle Chinese kim, 'metal, gold, money'). Formed in Japanese as fiscal systems shifted from rice-based tribute (年貢 nengu) to monetary taxation during the Meiji modernization.

history.meaning: grain tithe/levy + metal/money
monetary tax levied by the state or local government

morphemes.meaning: tax, duty, agricultural tithe (Middle Chinese sywejH)
gold, metal, money, cash (Middle Chinese kim)

税金.notes: 税金 is the everyday word for taxes paid in money, whereas 税 (zei) alone is used as a suffix for specific tax categories (e.g., 消費税 shōhizei 'consumption tax', 所得税 shotokuzei 'income tax'). Pitch accent is [0] (heiban).

税金対策.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) four-character compound combining 税金 (zeikin, 'monetary taxes', from 税 'tithe/tax' + 金 'money') and 対策 (taisaku, 'countermeasure, strategic policy', originally referring to answering imperial examination questions written on bamboo slips 策 in ancient China, from 対 'face, respond to' + 策 'bamboo slip, plan, stratagem').

history.meaning: written policy response to an imperial inquiry on bamboo slips

history.form: 税金対策 (ぜいきんたいさく)
history.meaning: tax-saving measure, tax planning or shelter strategy

morphemes.meaning: face, counter, respond to (Middle Chinese twojH)
plan, scheme, bamboo slip (Middle Chinese tsrheak)

税金対策.notes: In Japanese business and entertainment contexts (like in The Naked Director), 税金対策 often carries a pragmatic or slightly cynical nuance of spending company profits on cars, real estate, or lavish expenses specifically to write them off and reduce taxable income, bordering between legal 節税 (tax saving) and 脱税 (tax evasion).

種類.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 種 (shu, from Middle Chinese tsyuwngX, 'seed, grain breed, botanical species', composed of 禾 'grain' + 重 'heavy/layered') and 類 (rui, from Middle Chinese lwijH, 'category, similar group, kind'). Borrowed from Literary Chinese 種類, where agricultural seed classification broadened to mean any general category or variety.

history.meaning: seed varieties, lineage, class of things sharing traits
kind, type, variety, taxonomic species or assortment

morphemes.meaning: seed, breed, species, sort (Middle Chinese tsyuwngX)

種類.notes: Used both as an abstract noun ('type, variety') and as a counter for distinct varieties (e.g., 三種類のワイン san-shurui no wain, 'three kinds of wine'). Pitch accent is [1] (shu'rui).

稲妻.etymology: Poetic native compound 稲妻 (いなずま), combining 稲 (いな-, bound form of いね 'rice plant') and 妻 (つま, 'spouse, partner', voiced to -ずま by rendaku).
稲妻.notes: Coined in ancient Japan because late-summer lightning storms coincided with the ripening of rice ears, inspiring the belief that lightning wedded and fertilized the rice crop.

稼ぐ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb かせぐ (kasegu). Originally denoted working tirelessly at agricultural labor or spinning thread (related to 桛 kase, an H-shaped reel for winding yarn, and regional senses of bustling about). Written with the kokuji-like usage of kanji 稼 (originally Chinese jià, 'to sow grain', composed of 禾 'grain' + 家 'household'). Semantically shifted from diligent farm labor to making a living and earning money.

history.meaning: to toil diligently at farming or spinning, to labor hard
to work for a living, to earn money, to score points or buy time

morphemes.meaning: work for a living, earn money, labor (native Yamato verb stem)

稼ぐ.notes: Carries a earthy, hustle-oriented nuance compared to the formal Sino-Japanese 収入を得る (to obtain income). Also used idiomatically with non-monetary objects: 時間を稼ぐ (jikan o kasegu, 'to buy/stall for time') and 点数を稼ぐ (tensū o kasegu, 'to rack up points').

rootFamily.gloss: leaving home to work temporarily in another region or country

稼げる.etymology: Potential verb (可能動詞 kanō dōshi) derived regularly from the native Yamato godan verb 稼ぐ (kasegu, 'to toil for a living, to earn money') by replacing the stem-final -u with the ichidan potential suffix -eru (-e-ru). Literally 'to be able to earn', which also developed an intransitive stative nuance of 'to be lucrative, to pay well'.

history.meaning: to be capable of earning money; to be profitable or lucrative

morphemes.meaning: toil, earn money, make a living
potential ichidan verbal suffix (capable of / lucrative)

稼げる.notes: Frequently used adnominally before a noun (e.g., 稼げる仕事 kasegeru shigoto, 'a lucrative job / a job that pays big money') where English would use an adjective like 'profitable' or 'high-paying'.

rootFamily.gloss: to earn money, to work for a living

積む.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan transitive verb つむ (tsumu), attested in Old Japanese as tumu ('to pile up, stack, load onto a vehicle or boat'). Orthographically matched with the kanji 積 (originally 'to hoard harvested grain', from 禾 'grain' + 責 'accumulate/demand'). Extended metaphorically to accumulating experience (経験を積む) and stacking cash on the table in negotiations or bribes (金を積む).

history.meaning: to heap up, stack physical objects, load cargo onto a vessel
to pile up, load, accumulate experience, put up large sums of money

morphemes.meaning: pile up, stack, load, accumulate (native Yamato transitive stem)

積む.notes: Pairs with the intransitive verb 積もる (tsumoru, 'to pile up by itself', as with snow or dust). In business and crime dramas, 金を積む (kane o tsumu) vividly evokes physically stacking bundles of yen notes to buy someone off or secure a deal.

rootFamily.gloss: to pile up, accumulate (intransitive, e.g., snow)

穏やか.etymology: Native Japanese adjectival noun ('calm, gentle, peaceful, quiet, moderate'), attested from the Heian period as *odayaka* (alongside *odahi* 'tranquil'), formed from the root *oda-* ('calm, settled') + descriptive suffix *-yaka*.

history.meaning: calm; tranquil; peaceful
calm; gentle; mild; peaceful

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 穏やか

空.etymology: Native Japanese noun (read そら, 'sky, heavens, air; weather; from memory'), continuing Old Japanese *sora*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*sora* ('sky, open space above'). Written with kanji 空 ('empty space, sky', which also represents *kara* 'empty' and Sino-Japanese *kū*).

history.meaning: sky; space above
sky; air; heavens; state of mind
sky; air; weather; by heart

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 空

空く.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb written with 空 for both *aku* (Old Japanese *aku* 'to open, become vacant or unoccupied') and *suku* (Old Japanese *suku* 'to become sparse, thin out, become empty or hungry').

history.meaning: become open/vacant; become sparse/empty
become vacant or free; become less crowded or hungry

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 空く

空っぽ.etymology: Colloquial native Japanese noun and adjectival noun ('completely empty, hollow'), formed in Early Modern Japanese from 空 (から 'empty, hollow, shell') + emphatic colloquial suffix -っぽ.

history.meaning: completely empty; hollow inside
empty; hollow; vacant

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 空っぽ

空気.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('air, atmosphere; mood of a situation'), formed from 空 (くう 'sky, open space, void') + 気 (き 'breath, vapor, gas, vital energy'). Standardized in late Edo Dutch studies (Rangaku) to translate Dutch *lucht* ('air, atmosphere').

history.meaning: atmospheric air (translating Dutch lucht)
air; atmosphere; social mood

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 空気

空洞.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound noun combining 空 (kū, from Middle Chinese *khung 'empty, hollow, void') and 洞 (dō, from Middle Chinese *duwngH 'cave, cavern, hollow passage'). Attested in classical Chinese prose and poetry for subterranean caverns and hollow spaces inside trees or stones, it denotes any hollow cavity beneath a surface.

history.meaning: empty cavern, hollow space
hollow cavity, void

空洞.notes: When a paving stone or wall sounds hollow when tapped, Japanese describes it as 空洞みたいな音 ('a sound like a hollow cavity').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 空洞

空間.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('space, room, expanse'), formed from 空 (くう 'empty, open, void') + 間 (かん 'interval, space between'). Used in classical Chinese for an open gap and standardized in Meiji philosophy and physics to translate English *space* and German *Raum*.

history.meaning: empty interval; open space
space; room; three-dimensional expanse

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 空間

突きつける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound ichidan verb formed from 突き (tsuki, continuative stem of 突く tsuku, 'to thrust, stab, poke') + つける (tsukeru, 'to attach, press against, bring into forceful contact'). Literally 'to thrust something right up against someone', evolving from pointing a weapon at someone's throat to confronting someone with undeniable evidence, demands, or harsh reality.

history.meaning: to thrust a blade or object directly in front of someone's eyes or chest
to thrust in someone's face, confront with demands, evidence, or reality

morphemes.meaning: thrust, jab, poke, pierce (continuative stem of 突く)

突きつける.notes: Used both physically (e.g., ナイフを突きつける 'to point a knife at someone') and figuratively for ultimata or unpleasant truths (e.g., 辞表を突きつける 'to slam down a resignation letter', 現実を突きつけられる 'to have harsh reality thrust in one's face').

rootFamily.gloss: to get to the bottom of, ascertain thoroughly
rootFamily.word: 突き止める (つきとめる)

突っ立つ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) expressive compound godan verb formed from 突き (tsuki, stem of 突く 'to thrust, jab', reduced to the emphatic prefixal geminate つっ- tsut-) + 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand'). The consonantal assimilation (tsuki-tatsu > tsuttatsu) intensifies the verb, depicting someone standing bolt upright like a driven stake, or standing around stiffly and idly without helping.

history.meaning: to stand upright, rise sharply, be stuck upright
to stand stiffly, stand around idly or dumbfounded in the way

morphemes.meaning: emphatic/intensive verbal prefix (phonologically reduced from 突き tsuki-)

突っ立つ.notes: Colloquial and often impatient or scolding in tone, especially in the progressive 突っ立っていないで手伝え (tsuttatte inaide tetsudae, 'don't just stand there like a post, help out!'). The prefix 突っ- (tsuk-/tsut-) creates many rough, energetic verbs like 突っ込む (tsukkomu) and 突っ走る (tsuppashiru).

rootFamily.gloss: to plunge into, cram in, retort/quip

cognates.meaning: rushing in, charging into, entering a new phase

突入.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 突 (totsu, from Middle Chinese dwot, originally depicting a dog 犬 rushing suddenly out of a cave or hole 穴, hence 'sudden, charge, thrust') and 入 (nyū, from Middle Chinese nyip, 'enter, go inside'). Originally a military term for charging into enemy lines, now also widely used for plunging into a new phase, era, or crisis.

history.meaning: to rush suddenly into a space or breach enemy formations
charging in (police/military); plunging into a new stage or season

morphemes.meaning: rush out suddenly, charge, thrust (Middle Chinese dwot, 犬 dog + 穴 cave)
enter, go in, penetrate (Middle Chinese nyip)

突入.notes: Takes the particle に (Xに突入する) and brings dramatic, high-energy momentum—used equally for SWAT teams storming a building (現場に突入する) and for a story or economy hurtling into a new phase (後半戦に突入する, バブル時代に突入する).

rootFamily.gloss: breaking through, surpassing a limit or barrier

cognates.meaning: to break through, make a breakthrough, surpass

突破.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 突 (totsu > top- by regressive assimilation before /p/, from Middle Chinese dwot, 'rush out, charge, ram') and 破 (pa, from Middle Chinese phaH, 'break, shatter, cleave stone', composed of 石 'stone' + 皮 'skin/split'). Originally denoted smashing through a defensive fortification; extended to overcoming difficulties or surpassing numerical milestones.

history.meaning: to charge and smash through a physical barrier or enemy line
breaking through an obstacle, passing a round/exam, surpassing a numerical figure

morphemes.meaning: charge, thrust, ram (Middle Chinese dwot, assimilated to top-)

突破.notes: Note the phonological gemination (sokuonbin): totsu + ha/pa becomes toppa (突破), just like totsu +発 becomes toppatsu (突発). Very common in media and sales announcements when sales or viewership pass a major threshold (e.g., 売上10億円突破! 'Sales surpass 1 billion yen!').

rootFamily.gloss: opening a way through a crisis, breakthrough

窃盗.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound of 窃 (setsu > set-, from Middle Chinese tshjet, 'to steal furtively, secret', traditionally 竊 depicting insects 卝/虫 boring into stored grain 米 inside a granary hole 穴) and 盗 (tō, from Middle Chinese dawH, 'robber, steal', depicting salivating 次/涎 with covetous desire over a vessel 皿). Both characters mean 'steal', forming a synonym compound for non-violent larceny.

history.meaning: furtive stealing, thief, larceny
theft, burglary, larceny (statutory crime under Japanese Penal Code Art. 235)

morphemes.meaning: steal secretly, furtive (Middle Chinese tshjet, assimilated to set-)

窃盗.notes: Formal legal and police register for theft without violence or threats (e.g., 窃盗罪 settōzai, 'crime of larceny'), contrasted in Japanese criminal law with 強盗 (gōtō, 'robbery using force or intimidation'). In everyday conversation, people say 泥棒 (dorobō) or 盗み (nusumi).

rootFamily.gloss: theft, being stolen, victimization by theft
armed robbery, mugging, burglary by force

窓.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('window'), continuing Old Japanese *mado*, attested in the Man'yōshū and Wamyō Ruijūshō; a compound of 間 (*ma* 'space, interval') or 目 (*ma-* 'eye, opening') + 戸 (*to* → *do* with rendaku, 'door, shutter, opening').

history.meaning: window opening
window

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 窓

窓ガラス.etymology: Hybrid native Japanese and Western loanword compound ('windowpane, window glass'), combining native 窓 (まど 'window') + ガラス ('glass', borrowed in the Edo period from Dutch *glas*).

history.meaning: window glass; windowpane

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 窓ガラス

窓辺.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 窓辺. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 窓辺

窓際.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('by the window, windowside, edge of a window'), formed from 窓 (まど 'window') + 際 (きわ → ぎわ with rendaku, 'edge, brink, side').

history.meaning: area right beside a window; windowside

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 窓際

立たせる.etymology: Productive causative verb (使役動詞) formed from the a-stem (未然形) 立た- (tata-) of the godan verb 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand up') plus the causative auxiliary suffix -せる (-seru). Depending on context, 立たせる expresses either compelling someone to stand or allowing/letting them stand on their feet.

history.meaning: to cause or allow to stand
to make/let stand (causative of 立つ)

立たせる.notes: Conjugates as a regular ichidan verb (立たせる, 立たせます, 立たせない, 立たせた).

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 立たせる

立ち止まる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound godan intransitive verb combining 立ち (tachi, continuative stem of 立つ tatsu, 'to stand, be on one's feet') and 止まる (tomaru, 'to stop, come to a halt', with rendaku voicing of /t/ to /d/). Literally 'to stop while standing / come to a standing halt', describing someone walking or running who pauses in their tracks, either physically or metaphorically to reflect.

history.meaning: to halt in one's footsteps, stop walking and stand still
to stop walking, pause in one's tracks, pause to reflect on one's life or actions

morphemes.meaning: stand, be on foot (continuative stem of 立つ)
stop, halt, come to rest (with rendaku voicing t -> d)

立ち止まる.notes: Applies specifically to people (or animals) halting on foot, or figuratively pausing in life's journey to reconsider (一度立ち止まって考える 'to pause and think for a moment'). Vehicles use 止まる (tomaru) or 停車する (teisha suru), not 立ち止まる.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop carefully in one's tracks, linger, loiter
rootFamily.word: 立ち止まる / 立ちすくむ (たちすくむ - freeze on the spot)

立ち返る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound godan verb formed from 立ち (tachi-, continuative stem of 立つ tatsu, functioning here as an aspectual/emphatic verbal prefix indicating a fresh or decisive movement) and 返る (kaeru, from Old Japanese kaperu, 'to turn back, return to an original state'). Literally 'to turn right back to', used predominantly for returning to one's original principles, starting point, or sanity.

history.meaning: to turn back on one's path, return to an earlier place or season (waves, mist, people)
history.stage: Old to Early Middle Japanese (Man'yōshū / Heian)

history.meaning: to return to a starting point, regain one's senses, revisit fundamental principles

morphemes.meaning: emphatic/inchoative verbal prefix (from 立つ 'stand, initiate motion')
return, turn back, revert to an original state

立ち返る.notes: Unlike plain 帰る (go home) or 戻る (go back physically), 立ち返る is used almost exclusively in abstract, reflective expressions with に: 原点に立ち返る (genten ni tachikaeru, 'to go back to basics / return to one's starting point') or 我に立ち返る (ware ni tachikaeru, 'to come back to one's senses').

rootFamily.gloss: to look back, reflect on the past
to rise again, recover, get back on one's feet

立つ.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to stand, rise, be erected, depart'), continuing Old Japanese *tatu* (four-grade *tat-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, paired with transitive *tatu* (lower bigrade > 立てる *tateru*).

history.meaning: stand up; rise; depart
stand; rise; be built; leave

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 立つ

立てかける.etymology: Native Japanese compound transitive verb ('to lean [something] against, prop up against'), formed from 立て (stem of 立てる 'to stand up, set upright') + かける (掛ける 'to hang, rest, or suspend against another surface').

history.form: 立てかける (たてかける)
history.meaning: lean or prop something upright against a surface

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 立て掛ける

立てる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) ichidan transitive verb たてる (tateru), evolved from Old Japanese and Early Middle Japanese nidan (lower bigrade) verb たつ (tatu, continuative tate-), the transitive counterpart of 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand, rise'). Derived via the archaic transitive/causative formant *-e- attached to the root *tat-. Means 'to make stand, erect', with rich metaphorical extensions: formulating plans, spreading rumors, saving someone's face, or playing a key role.

history.meaning: to set upright, erect a pillar, send forth (a messenger or smoke)
to stand something up, formulate (a plan), make a noise, show respect to someone's status

morphemes.meaning: stand, rise, become upright (native Yamato root *tat-)
transitive ichidan verbal formant (from Old Japanese *-e-ru)

立てる.notes: Extremely polysemous in idiomatic collocations: 計画を立てる (formulate a plan), 腹を立てる (get angry), 顔を立てる / 相手を立てる (save someone's face / defer to someone so they look good), 音を立てる (make a noise), and 役立てる (put to good use). When building houses or architecture, it is written 建てる.

rootFamily.gloss: leading role, protagonist; putting someone up as a leader (担ぎ立てる/立て役者)

立派.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) na-adjective formed in Japan from 立 (ritsu > rip- by gemination before /p/, from Middle Chinese lip, 'stand upright, establish') and 派 (pa, from Middle Chinese phaeH, 'branching stream, school, sect, style, bearing'). Originally used in medieval Zen and martial/artistic lineages for establishing an independent school or orthodoxy, then shifted in the Edo period to mean 'imposing, splendid, admirable, respectable'.

history.meaning: establishing a legitimate sect/lineage; stately and regular in form
splendid, fine, admirable, praiseworthy, full-fledged

morphemes.meaning: stand, establish, erect (Middle Chinese lip, assimilated to rip-)
branch, school, style, bearing (Middle Chinese phaeH)

立派.notes: Although built from Chinese characters, the adjectival sense 'splendid, admirable, respectable' is a distinctly Japanese semantic development (in Chinese, 立派 literally means 'to establish a faction/school'). Can also mean 'full-fledged, undeniable' even for negative things (e.g., 立派な犯罪だ 'that is a full-blown crime'). Pitch accent is [0] (heiban).

rootFamily.gloss: faction, clique, school of thought or art
becoming independent, standing on one's own feet

端.etymology: Native Japanese noun (read はし, は, or はた, 'edge, end, tip, border, margin'), continuing Old Japanese *pasi* ('extremity, tip, edge') and *pata* ('edge, rim, side').

history.meaning: edge; extremity; tip; border

history.form: 端 (はし / は / はた)
history.meaning: edge; end; tip; corner; side

端っこ.etymology: Colloquial native Japanese noun ('very edge, tip, corner, far end'), formed from 端 (はし 'edge, end, tip') + familiar/diminutive nominal suffix -っこ.

history.meaning: very edge; far end; corner

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 端っこ

競争.etymology: Meiji-era Sino-Japanese compound noun and suru-verb ('competition, contest, rivalry'), coined by Fukuzawa Yukichi in the 1860s to translate English *competition* by combining 競 (きょう 'vie, race, compete') + 争 (そう 'contend, strive').

history.meaning: competition (coined by Fukuzawa Yukichi for English competition)
competition; contest; rivalry

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 競争

笑う.etymology: Native Japanese verb ('to laugh, smile'), continuing Old Japanese *warapu*, attested in the Man'yōshū; built on the root *wara-* ('split open, burst open', shared with 割る *waru* 'to split'), originally describing the mouth or face opening wide in laughter.

history.meaning: laugh aloud; open the mouth in laughter
laugh; smile

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 笑う

笑わせる.etymology: Causative verb (使役動詞 shieki dōshi) derived from the native Yamato godan verb 笑う (warau, from Old Japanese warapu, 'to laugh, smile', originally an iterative derivative in *-ap- meaning 'to split/open the mouth repeatedly', related to 割る waru 'to split') + the productive causative auxiliary -せる (-seru, attached to the irrealis stem warawa-). Literally 'to cause someone to laugh'.

history.meaning: to cause to laugh or smile, to amuse
to make someone laugh, entertain; (ironically) to say something ridiculous/laughable

morphemes.meaning: laugh, smile (irrealis stem warawa- of 笑う)

笑わせる.notes: Beyond the positive sense 'to entertain / make people laugh', it is frequently used sarcastically in tough or confrontational dialogue: 笑わせるな! (warawaseru na!, 'Don't make me laugh! / You've got to be kidding me!') or 笑わせるぜ ('What a joke!').

笑顔.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('smiling face, smile'), formed from the stem *e-* of classical 笑む (*emu*, Old Japanese *wemu* 'to smile, bloom') + 顔 (かお → がお with rendaku, 'face, countenance').

history.meaning: smiling countenance
smiling face; smile

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 笑顔

笛.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun ふえ (fue), attested in Old Japanese as puye (布曳 / 笛). Etymologically analyzed as a compound or derivative of the native verb root *pu- / *puk- (吹く fuku, 'to blow with the breath') + a nominalizing or reed/sound element *-ye (compare 枝 e < ye 'branch/tube' or 音 ne 'sound'). Written with the kanji 笛 (bamboo 竹 + phonetic 由, 'bamboo flute').

history.meaning: bamboo flute, wind pipeblown with the mouth
flute, pipe, whistle (musical or signaling)

morphemes.meaning: flute, pipe, whistle (native Yamato noun related to 吹く fuku 'to blow')

笛.notes: Covers both traditional musical flutes (like 篠笛 shinobue) and small signaling whistles (口笛 kuchibue 'whistling with the lips', 警笛 keiteki / ホイッスル 'police/referee whistle'). Famous in the proverb 笛吹けど踊らず (fue fukedo odorazu, 'though the flute plays, nobody dances' — leaders piping up while no one follows). Pitch accent is [0] (heiban).

rootFamily.gloss: to blow (wind, breath, or a flute)
bagpipes or reed pipe; steam whistle (汽笛)

笠.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('conical woven hat of bamboo or sedge; lamp shade; mushroom cap'), continuing Old Japanese *kasa*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū (etymologically identical to 傘 'umbrella, parasol', both denoting an overhead protective cover against rain or sun).

history.meaning: rain/sun hat; overhead cover
conical sedge/bamboo hat; lamp shade; cap

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 笠

第一位.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic numeral-rank expression consisting of the ordinal prefix 第- (dai-, from Middle Chinese dejH, originally 'order of bamboo strips tied in a bundle', hence 'sequence, ordinal rank'), the numeral 一 (ichi, 'one'), and the counter/noun 位 (i, from Middle Chinese hwijH, depicts a person 人 standing 立 at their assigned court station, hence 'rank, position, place').

history.meaning: ordinal sequence + one + court rank/position
first place, number-one rank in a competition, chart, or priority list

morphemes.meaning: rank, place, position, throne (Middle Chinese hwijH)

第一位.notes: Adding 第- (dai-) before 一位 (ichi-i) makes the ranking sound more formal, emphatic, and broadcast-like (e.g., 売上ランキング第一位! 'Number one in the sales rankings!'). In casual speech, 一位 (ichii) or 一番 (ichiban) is often used without 第-.

rootFamily.gloss: ranking, order, standing in a competition
first line, forefront, front line of a field

第一作目.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound: ordinal prefix 第- (dai-, 'ordinal rank') + 一 (ichi > is- before /s/, 'one') + 作 (saku, from Middle Chinese tsak, 'make, work, artistic production or film') + native Yamato ordinal suffix -目 (-me, originally 'eye' or 'notch carved on a measuring stick/scale', marking a specific point in a sequence). Double-marked ordinal ('the very first work/production').

history.form: 第一作 (だいいっさく) + 目 (-め)
history.meaning: first creative work + ordinal sequence marker

morphemes.meaning: work, film, literary or artistic production (Middle Chinese tsak)
ordinal suffix (native Yamato, from 'notch on a scale / eye')

第一作目.notes: Strictly speaking, combining the Sino-Japanese ordinal prefix 第- (dai-) with the native ordinal suffix -目 (-me) is pleonastic (double ordinal marking, like 第一回目), which traditional style guides sometimes critique in favor of either 第一作 or 一作目; however, in spoken Japanese and entertainment marketing, 第一作目 is extremely common for emphasis ('the very first film/installment').

rootFamily.gloss: debut work, a creator's maiden work or film

rootFamily.word: 代表作 (だいひょうさく)

cognates.meaning: second installment / second wave (borrowed back or parallel usage)
cognates.word: 第二彈 / 第二弾 (dì-èr dàn)

第二弾.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) trimorphemic expression composed of the ordinal prefix 第- (dai-, 'ordinal number marker'), 二 (ni, 'two'), and 弾 (dan, from Middle Chinese danH, originally 'pellet shot from a crossbow弓', later 'bullet, artillery shell, projectile'). Metaphorically frames a series of commercial releases, campaigns, or films as successive artillery shots ('second round / second salvo / second installment').

history.meaning: crossbow pellet, projectile shot in a volley
second shot/salvo; second installment of a film series, campaign, or project

morphemes.meaning: bullet, shell, salvo, project installment (Middle Chinese danH)

第二弾.notes: A staple of Japanese advertising, publishing, and film promotion (following 第一弾 dai-ichidan 'first installment' and followed by 第三弾 dai-sandan 'third installment'). Gives a punchy, high-impact feel, as if launching the next wave of a campaign onto the market.

rootFamily.gloss: first installment, opening salvo of a project

第十四条.etymology: Sino-Japanese legal and statutory compound ('Article 14'), formed from ordinal prefix 第- (だい-) + 十四 (じゅうよん / じゅうし 'fourteen') + 条 (じょう 'article, clause, provision in a law or contract').

history.form: 第十四条 (だいじゅうよんじょう)
history.meaning: Article 14 (of a law, regulation, or contract)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 条

筆跡.etymology: The term '筆跡' (meaning 'handwriting') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: handwriting
handwriting

筆跡.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 筆跡

答え.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun こたえ (kotae), derived from the continuative stem (連用形 ren'yōkei) of the verb 答える (kotaeru, Old Japanese kotapu / kotape-, 'to reply, answer, respond'). Etymologically, Old Japanese *kotap- is widely analyzed as a compound of 言 (koto, 'word, speech') + 合ふ (apu > au, 'to meet, match, correspond') — literally 'matching words with another speaker'. Written with the kanji 答 ('bamboo tally/reply').

history.meaning: verbal reply, response matching an interlocutor's words
answer to a question, reply, solution to a problem or dilemma

答え.notes: Covers both a reply to a person and the solution to a test question or life problem (e.g., 答えを出す kotae o dasu, 'to arrive at an answer / make a final decision'). Contrast with 返事 (henji), which means a conversational reply or RSVP rather than the solution to a problem. Pitch accent is [2] (kota'e).

rootFamily.gloss: written answer or solution (to an exam or inquiry)
rootFamily.word: 回答 / 解答 (かいとう)

算段.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined or semantically specialized in Japan from 算 (san, from Middle Chinese swanH, 'counting rods made of bamboo 竹, calculate, reckon') and 段 (dan, from Middle Chinese dwanH, 'step, stage, measure, contrivance'). history.meaning: calculating steps, devising a plan or contrivance, scraping funds together
arranging means or money, contriving a way out of financial difficulty

morphemes.meaning: calculate, reckon with bamboo counting rods (Middle Chinese swanH)
step, stage, measure, arrangement (Middle Chinese dwanH)

算段.notes: Unlike neutral words like 計画 (plan) or 準備 (preparation), 算段 almost always implies hustling, juggling resources, or figuring out how to raise scarce money (e.g., 金の算段をつける kane no sandan o tsukeru, 'to figure out a way to scrape the money together'). Pitch accent is [1] (sa'ndan) or [0].

rootFamily.gloss: budget, estimate; (in 金算段) raising funds
stage, phase, step; preliminary arrangements (段取り)

箱.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('box, case, chest, container'), continuing Old Japanese *pako₁*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: box; chest; storage case
box; case; container

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 箱

範囲.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 範 (han, from Middle Chinese bjomX, originally a bamboo mold or frame used in casting bronze or a ritual ceremony before a chariot journey, hence 'model, rule, boundary') and 囲 (i, from Middle Chinese hjuwij, simplified from 圍, 'to surround, enclose, perimeter', depicting guards pacing around a walled enclosure 囗). Derived from Literary Chinese 範圍 (I Ching, Xici: 範圍天地之化 'molding and encompassing the transformations of heaven and earth').

history.meaning: to cast in a mold and enclose within bounds (Classical Chinese philosophical verb/noun)
bounded area, scope, extent, range of coverage or authority

morphemes.meaning: mold, frame, rule, boundary (Middle Chinese bjomX)

範囲.notes: Pronounced han'i (with a syllabic nasal followed by a vowel, three moras: は・ん・い), not ha-ni. Very common in expressions like 常識の範囲内 (jōshiki no han'inai, 'within the bounds of common sense'), 試験範囲 (shiken han'i, 'material covered on the exam'), and 守備範囲 (shubihan'i, 'one's area of expertise or romantic type'). Pitch accent is [1] (ha'n'i).

築八十年.etymology: Sino-Japanese architectural and real-estate compound ('built eighty years ago, eighty years old [of a building]'), formed from 築 (ちく 'construction, years elapsed since construction') + 八十年 (はちじゅうねん 'eighty years').

Evolved in Japan to mean both vegetarian Buddhist purification (精進料理) and secular wholehearted devotion to one's craft.

組.etymology: Deverbal noun derived from the ren'yōkei (continuative stem) of the native Yamato verb 組む (kumu, 'to braid cords, interlace, join together'), written with the kanji 組 ('braided silk cord, ribbon, group').
