morphemes.meaning: warp thread; order, govern, regulate [short for 経世] (MC *keng)
ford a river; relieve, rescue, aid [short for 済民] (MC *tsjejH)

経済.notes: One of the most famous Meiji-era *wasei-kango* semantic adaptations: a 4th-century Chinese statecraft term repurposed in Japan to translate Western 'economy' and later adopted back into modern Chinese (`jīngjì`).

rootFamily.gloss: governing the world and relieving the people (full source idiom)

cognates.meaning: to pass through and follow along

経由.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 経 (kei < MC *keng, originally 'warp threads running lengthwise through a loom', hence 'to pass through, traverse') and 由 (yu < MC *yuw, 'to follow a path from, proceed via, originate from'). Together they denote routing through an intermediate point, person, or channel on the way to a destination.

history.meaning: to pass through and proceed by way of a path or precedent
going via an intermediate stop, routing through a third party or network node

経由.notes: Used both spatially for travel routes (東京経由, 'via Tokyo') and figuratively in business or underground deals for routing money or introductions through an intermediary (知人経由で, 'through an acquaintance').

結ぶ.etymology: Native Japanese godan verb descending from Old Japanese むすぶ (musubu). In archaic Japanese mythology and poetry, むすぶ originally meant 'to scoop water in one's joined hands' and 'to bring together into a unified form' (linked to the creative spirit root 産霊 musubi), from which it developed its primary senses of tying threads into a knot, binding a bundle, forming fruit (実を結ぶ), and concluding an agreement (契約を結ぶ).

history.meaning: to join together; to tie a cord; to form
to tie; to knot; to bind; to conclude (a contract)

rootFamily.gloss: rice ball (shaped by pressing hands together)

結ぶ.notes: Its te-form is 結んで (musunde) and past form is 結んだ (musunda).

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 結ぶ

結婚.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 結 (ketsu < MC *ket, 'to tie a knot in silk cord, bind together, contract') and 婚 (kon < MC *xwon, 'marriage, taking a bride', composed of 女 'woman' + 昏 'dusk', because ancient Chinese wedding processions took place at twilight). The final entering-tone *-t of 結 assimilates before *k- of 婚 to yield the geminate reading kekkon ('tying the matrimonial bond').

history.meaning: to contract a marriage alliance between families
legal and social institution of marriage (popularized in Meiji Japan to replace older terms like 婚姻 and 縁組)

morphemes.meaning: tie a knot, bind together, unite (MC *ket)

結婚.notes: In everyday speech 結婚 (kekkon) is the standard word for marriage, while 婚姻 (kon'in) is reserved for formal legal/bureaucratic contexts (e.g., 婚姻届, 'marriage registration form').

cognates.meaning: concluding a board game or affair
after all, eventually, in the end

結局.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 結 (ketsu < MC *ket, 'to tie off a knot, conclude, wrap up') and 局 (kyoku < MC *gjowk, 'board game position in Go/chess; bounded situation or affair'). Originally a term from Go (囲碁) meaning 'finishing a game on the board and counting the territories', it generalized into a noun meaning 'final outcome' and an adverb meaning 'in the end, after all'.

history.meaning: bringing a game of Go to its conclusion; the closing phase of an affair
final outcome; adverbially, 'in the end, after all is said and done'

morphemes.meaning: tie off, conclude, bring to an end (MC *ket)
Go board match, situation, phase of affairs (MC *gjowk)

結局.notes: Like 駄目 (dame, 'neutral points on a Go board > no good') and 布石 (fuseki, 'opening stone placement > groundwork'), 結局 originates in Go terminology before becoming an everyday conversational adverb.

rootFamily.gloss: stage of a game, current situation/phase

結果.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 結 (ketsu < MC *ket, 'to tie, form, set [of blossoms setting into fruit]') and 果 (ka < MC *kwaX, 'tree fruit; Buddhist karmic fruit/effect'). Originally botanical ('to set and bear fruit') and Buddhist ('the ripening of karmic fruit from a prior cause, 因'), it broadened into the general word for any result, outcome, or consequence.

history.meaning: of a plant, to set blossoms and bear fruit; in Buddhism, karmic fruition (果報)
effect, result, or outcome following from a cause or action

morphemes.meaning: fruit on a tree; outcome, karmic effect (MC *kwaX)

結果.notes: Often paired with 原因 (gen'in, 'cause') in 原因と結果 ('cause and effect'), or compressed into the Buddhist-derived compound 因果 (inga, 'cause and fruit / karma').

rootFamily.gloss: fruits of one's labor, achievement,good result

cognates.meaning: to bind timbers and construct a framework

結構.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical Chinese 結構 (MC *ket-kuwH), combining 結 (ketsu < MC *ket, 'to tie, join together') and 構 (kō < MC *kuwH, 'to fit crossbeams together, construct a timber frame'). From 'architectural structure or well-built design', Japanese uniquely evolved the sense 'splendidly built > fine, good enough > no thank you (I am already well-supplied)' as well as the adverbial sense 'quite, fairly'.

history.meaning: joining timbers to erect a building; architectural or literary structure
splendid, well-crafted, admirable, satisfactory
fine, good enough; polite refusal ('no, thank you'); adverbially 'quite, surprisingly'

結構.notes: A classic pragmatic trap AND false friend: in Chinese `jiégòu` still means 'structure', whereas in Japanese 結構です (kekkō desu) can mean either 'That's fine / Yes, please' OR 'No, thank you (I have enough)' depending on context and intonation!

結構な.etymology: The term '結構な' (meaning 'quite a') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: quite a
quite a

結構な.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 結構な

絡み.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the ren'yōkei (continuative stem) of the native Yamato verb 絡む (karamu, 'to twine around, entangle, become involved with'), written with 絡 ('spun hemp/silk thread; to wind around, connect'). In theater, film, and the adult video industry depicted in *The Naked Director*, 絡み specialized from 'physical interaction/swordplay choreography between actors' to 'an intimate sex scene between performers'.

history.meaning: coiling, entwinement, or linkage between threads or vines
interaction between main actor and supporting players in kabuki/swordfight scenes (殺陣の絡み)
connection/involvement (as suffix -garami); industry jargon for an on-camera intimate or sex scene

morphemes.meaning: entwinement, involvement, intimate scene (nominalized stem of karamu)

絡み.notes: In film/AV production jargon, 絡み (karami) specifically denotes achoreographed physical or sexual scene between actors; as a suffix with rendaku (-がらみ, e.g., 金がらみ kane-garami), it means 'involving or tangled up with (money, politics, etc.)'.

rootFamily.gloss: to entwine, coil around, pick a quarrel with, get involved

絡む.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) quadrigrade (godan) intransitive verb karamu ('to twine around, coil, get tangled'), related to the older native root karu / karamaru ('to wind cord around, bind up') and written with the kanji 絡 ('unreeled silk/hemp fiber; to wrap around, net, connect'). Extended from physical threads or vines coiling around an object to human beings becoming emotionally, financially, or aggressively entangled with one another.

history.meaning: of threads, creepers, or snakes, to coil or twine around something
to be intertwined; to be involved in a scheme; to pester or pick a drunken quarrel with someone

morphemes.meaning: twine around, become entangled, interact/pester (native root karam-)

絡む.notes: Depending on context, 人に絡む (hito ni karamu) often means 'to drunkenly pester, badger, or pick a fight with someone', whereas 利権が絡む (riken ga karamu) means 'vested interests are tangled up in it'.

rootFamily.gloss: to get tangled up, become complicated

給料.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 給 (kyū < MC *kip, originally 'to supply silk thread continuously; to provide, grant, bestow from above') and 料 (ryō < MC *ljewH, written with 米 'grain' + 斗 'measuring scoop', originally 'measured grain rations, allowance, material fee'). Together they denote regular monetary compensation or wages paid by an employer.

history.meaning: to supply or grant + measured grain ration or material allowance
stipend, allowance, or wages paid to retainers and employees
salary, wages, paycheck

給料.notes: 給料 (kyūryō) is the everyday conversational word for salary/paycheck (e.g., 給料日 kyūryōbi, 'payday'), whereas 給与 (kyūyo) is more formal/administrative and includes bonuses and benefits.

絵.etymology: Early Sino-Japanese borrowing from Middle Chinese 絵 / 繪 (*hwojH* > Old/Heian Japanese *we* > modern *e*, originally 'multicolored embroidery or painting'), fully naturalized in Japanese for any picture, drawing, painting, or illustration.

history.meaning: multicolored embroidery; painting
painting; drawing; picture
picture; drawing; painting; illustration

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 絵

絵コンテ.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and gairaigo compound formed in the Japanese film and animation industry, combining 絵 (e < Middle Chinese *hwejH, 'painting, picture, drawing', written with the silk radical 糸 because silk cloth was a primary surface for painting and embroidery) with コンテ (konte), a Japanese clipping of English 'continuity' (a shot-by-shot script breakdown, ultimately from Latin continuus 'uninterrupted, holding together'). Denotes an illustrated continuity script, i.e., a storyboard.

history.meaning: multi-colored embroidery/painting on silk + English film term 'continuity sheet'
written continuity script listing camera angles, cuts, and durations in Japanese filmmaking
visual storyboard illustrating each shot, framing, and action sequence for film, TV, or anime

morphemes.meaning: shot-by-shot script breakdown (clipping of English continuity)

絵コンテ.notes: In Japanese film and anime production, plain コンテ (konte) can refer to a text-only shot list (字コンテ ji-konte), whereas 絵コンテ (e-konte) specifically means a drawn storyboard.

絵本.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 絵 (e < Late Old Japanese we < Middle Chinese *hwejH [go-on reading], 'variegated silk embroidery, painting, illustration') and 本 (hon < MC *pwonX, originally 'tree root, base, source text', hence 'bound book'). First flourished in the Edo period for woodblock-printed illustrated books (such as ukiyo-e *ehon*) before becoming the standard modern word for children's picture books.

history.meaning: colored silk painting + foundational text or volume
woodblock-printed illustrated book, artist's model book, or adult ukiyo-e album (including shunga)
picture book, illustrated book (especially for children)

morphemes.meaning: picture, painting, illustration (go-on reading e < we < MC *hwejH)

絵本.notes: Notice that 絵 uses the ancient *go-on* reading `e` (< `we`) in everyday words like 絵本 (ehon) and 絵コンテ (e-konte), but the *kan-on* reading `kai` in formal compounds like 絵画 (kaiga, 'painting').

rootFamily.gloss: script, screenplay, playbook (in theater/TV industry jargon)

絵葉書.etymology: Compound noun ('picture postcard'), formed in the Meiji period from 絵 (え 'picture, illustration') + 葉書 (はがき 'postcard', from native 葉 'leaf, slip' + 書き 'writing').

history.meaning: picture postcard

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 絵葉書

絶好調.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) three-character compound built by prefixing 絶- (zetsu- < MC *dzjwet, literally 'to sever a silk thread with a blade', hence 'beyond compare, utterly, superlative') to 好調 (kōchō, 'favorable condition, good rhythm/tone', from 好 MC *xawX 'good, favorable' + 調 MC *dew 'musical pitch, harmony, physical condition'). The final *-t of 絶 assimilates to the initial *k- of 好, producing the emphatic geminate reading zekkōchō ('in absolute peak form, booming').

history.meaning: surpassing all others (literally cutting off comparison) + harmonious tone or favorable state
in absolute peak condition, firing on all cylinders, booming (of sales, health, or athletic form)

絶好調.notes: The intensive prefix 絶- (zetsu- > zek-) means 'so extreme that nothing can follow it (the thread is cut)', also seen in 絶好 (zekkō, 'golden/perfect [opportunity]') and 絶景 (zekkei, 'breathtaking view'). Opposite: 絶不調 (zeffuchō, 'in a terrible slump').

rootFamily.gloss: in good form, going well, booming
in a slump, in poor condition
golden, ideal, best possible (e.g., 絶好の機会)

絶対.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun, adjectival noun, and adverb ('absolute, unconditional; absolutely, without fail'), originating in Buddhist Chinese 絶対 ('severing all opposition or comparison; beyond relativity', from 絶 'cut off, sever' + 対 'pair, opposite, comparison') and adopted in Meiji philosophy to translate Western *absolute* (contrasted with 相対 'relative').

history.meaning: transcending all comparison or duality
absolute; unconditional; definitely

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 絶対

絶対に.etymology: Adverbial phrase formed from the Sino-Japanese noun/na-adjective 絶対 (zettai, originally a Buddhist philosophical term meaning 'severing all relative oppositions, hence unconditional/absolute', from 絶 'cut off' + 対 'comparison/opposition') plus the adverbial particle に (ni). In everyday spoken Japanese, 絶対に acts as a strong emphatic adverb meaning 'definitely, without fail' in affirmative sentences and 'never, under no circumstances' in negative sentences.

history.meaning: transcending relative duality; unconditional
absolutely; unconditionally; never (with negative)

絶対に.notes: In casual speech the final に is sometimes dropped (絶対), while 絶対に is standard and clear across registers.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 絶対に

絶望.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 絶 (zetsu < MC *dzjwet, 'to cut off a silk thread, sever completely, come to an end') and 望 (bō < MC *mjangH, 'to gaze into the distance toward the full moon, look forward to, hope'). Literally 'the severing of all hope', it denotes utter despair or hopelessness.

history.meaning: to have one's expectations or hopes completely cut off
despair, hopelessness, giving up all expectation of rescue or success

morphemes.meaning: sever a thread, cut off completely, end (MC *dzjwet)

絶望.notes: The silk metaphor in 絶 ('snapping a thread') contrasts vividly with 続 ('joining threads to continue'); 絶望的 (zetsubōteki) is widely used to mean 'hopeless, bleak, beyond salvaging'.

継ぎ目.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('seam, joint, splice, juncture'), formed from 継ぎ (つぎ, nominalized stem of 継ぐ 'to join, patch, splice together') + 目 (め 'point, line, or crease where things meet').

history.meaning: seam; joint; juncture where two pieces meet

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 継ぎ目

続き.etymology: Native Yamato deverbal noun formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the intransitive godan verb 続く (tsuzuku, 'to continue, follow in succession', Old Japanese tuduku). As a noun, 続き means 'the continuation, the rest of a letter or story, or the next installment'.

history.meaning: succession, continuation, connection
continuation, sequel, the rest

morphemes.meaning: nominalized stem of 続く ('to continue')

続き.notes: 続きを読んで ('read the rest') and まだ続きがあります ('there is still more') are natural everyday ways to talk about the next part of a letter or story.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 続き

続く.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) quadrigrade (godan) intransitive verb descending from Old Japanese tuduku ('to follow in an unbroken line, adjoin, continue without interruption'), likely built on a reduplicated or compounded root related to tugu ('to succeed, join next') and orthographically assigned the kanji 続 ('to splice silk threads end-to-end, carry on continuously').

history.meaning: to be connected in sequence, adjoin spatially, or follow one after another
to continue, last, go on without break, or have a sequel ('to be continued')

morphemes.meaning: continue, follow in sequence, last (native root tuduk- > tsuzuk-)

続く.notes: Intransitive 続く (tsuzuku, 'something continues') pairs with transitive 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue doing something'). At the end of TV episodes or manga chapters, standalone つづく / 続く corresponds to 'To be continued...'.

続ける.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to continue, keep up, carry on, place in succession'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *tuduku* (続くる), the transitive counterpart of four-grade intransitive 続く (*tsuzuku* 'to continue, follow in a row').

history.meaning: join in succession; keep doing
continue; keep on; carry on

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 続ける

維持費.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) three-character compound combining 維持 (iji, 'maintenance, upkeep, preservation'—from 維 MC *ywij 'heavy mooring rope or stay-cord that holds a carriage canopy or net in place' + 持 MC *drjɨ 'to hold in the hand, support, sustain') with the suffix -費 (-hi < MC *phjɨjH, 'expenditure, cost, outlay', written with the cowrie-shell money radical 貝).

history.meaning: tethering with a main cord and holding firm + monetary expenditure
maintenance costs, ongoing overhead or upkeep expenses (for vehicles, buildings, or operations)

維持費.notes: Frequently used when discussing the ongoing financial drain of luxury goods, offices, or equipment (e.g., 車の維持費が高い, 'the upkeep costs on the car are high').

網.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('net, netting, mesh, web'), continuing Old Japanese *ami₁*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; closely related to the verb 編む (*amu* 'to plait, braid, knit, weave a net').

history.meaning: fishing or hunting net; mesh
net; mesh; screen; web

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 網

綺麗だ.etymology: The term '綺麗だ' (meaning 'clean') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: clean
clean

綺麗だ.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 綺麗だ

綿.etymology: The term '綿' (meaning 'cotton') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: cotton
cotton

綿.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 綿

緊張.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('tension, strain, nervousness, tautness'), formed from 緊 (きん 'bind tightly, taut, pressing') + 張 (ちょう 'stretch, draw a bowstring taut').

history.meaning: tension; tautness; nervousness

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 緊張

緊急.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and adjectival noun ('urgent, pressing, emergency'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 緊急 (attested in the History of the Southern Dynasties), composed of 緊 (きん 'tight, pressing, taut') + 急 (きゅう 'urgent, sudden, rapid').

history.meaning: pressing and urgent
urgent; emergency; pressing

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 緊急

cognates.meaning: total volume regulation / cap on aggregate lending or emissions

総量規制.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) policy compound joining 総量 (sōryō, 'total aggregate volume'—from 総 MC *tsuwngX 'to gather silk threads into a single bundle, total, overall' + 量 MC *ljang 'measured volume, quantity') and 規制 (kisei, 'regulation, restriction'—from 規 MC *kjwie 'carpenter's compass, rule, standard' + 制 MC *tsjejH 'to cut cloth to pattern, control, restrict').

history.meaning: aggregate bundled quantity + regulating by compass and cutting to limit

government cap on total volume—famed in Japan for the March 1990 Ministry of Finance curb on bank lending to real estate that pricked the Bubble Economy, and later caps on consumer loans or pollutant emissions

morphemes.meaning: bind threads together; total, aggregate, overall (MC *tsuwngX)
cut to measure; control, limit, system (MC *tsjejH)

総量規制.notes: In modern Japanese history and dramas set around 1990 (like *The Naked Director*), 不動産融資の総量規制 refers specifically to the Ministry of Finance's sudden directive capping real-estate lending, which triggered the collapse of the 1980s Bubble Economy.

rootFamily.gloss: total amount of money, sum total

緑.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('green, greenery, verdure'), continuing Old Japanese *midori*, attested in the Man'yōshū; originally denoting fresh, supple new shoots and buds sprouting in spring (cognate with 瑞 *mizu* 'fresh, moist, youthful'), and shifting in the Heian period to name the color green.

history.meaning: fresh new shoots;tender sprouting growth
green; greenery; foliage

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 緑

緑色.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('green color, green'), formed from 緑 (みどり 'green, fresh verdure') + 色 (いろ 'color').

history.meaning: green color; green

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 緑色

線.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 線. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 線

締めつける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 締める (shimeru < Old Japanese simu, 'to bind tightly, constrict, tie fast', written with 締 'to tie an unyielding knot') and the auxiliary-like transitive verb つける (tsukeru < OJ tuku, 'to attach, press hard against, apply force'). Literally 'to bind and press down hard upon', it means to constrict physically or clamp down on through strict regulation or coercion.

history.form: 締め付く (sime-tuku) > 締め付ける (shime-tsukeru)
history.meaning: to bind tightly around and press fast against (a sash, rope, or band)
to constrict tightly (e.g., one's chest with emotion); figuratively, for authorities or bosses to clamp down on or tighten control over subordinates or an industry

morphemes.meaning: tie tightly, constrict, tighten (stem of shimeru)
press against, apply forcefully (transitive verb tsukeru)

締めつける.notes: Used both for emotional/physical constriction (胸が締めつけられる思い, 'a heart-wrenching feeling that squeezes one's chest') and for police or regulatory crackdowns (警察が業界を締めつける).

rootFamily.gloss: to tie, tighten, buckle down, close

締める.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to tie, fasten, tighten, constrict, shut, sum up'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *simu* (締む), the transitive counterpart of 締まる (*shimaru* 'to tighten, become taut or fastened').

history.meaning: bind tightly; constrict; fasten
tie; tighten; fasten; buckle; total up

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 締める

締め出し.etymology: Nominalized native Yamato (wago) compound derived from the continuative stem of the compound verb 締め出す (shimedasu, 'to shut out, lock out, exclude'), itself composed of 締める / 閉める (shimeru, 'to close tightly, bar, fasten shut') and 出す (dasu, 'to put outside, drive out'). Denotes locking someone out of a building or freezing a competitor/rebel out of an industry cartel.

history.form: 締め出す (shime-dasu) > 締め出し (shime-dashi)
history.meaning: barring the door to keep someone outside; locking out
lockout (in labor disputes) or an organized industry freeze-out / boycott against an outsider or rule-breaker

morphemes.meaning: shut tightly, bar, close off (stem of shimeru)
forcing out, exclusion (nominalized stem of dasu, to put out)

締め出し.notes: Commonly used in the idiom 締め出しを食う / 締め出しを食らう (shimedashi o kuu / kurau, 'to get locked out / suffer an industry freeze-out'). In *kanji* usage, 締める ('tighten/bar') is standard here even though the sense overlaps with 閉める ('close a door').

rootFamily.gloss: to lock out, shut out, exclude from a group
to tighten, tie fast, clamp down

締め出す.etymology: Native Japanese compound transitive verb ('to lock out, shut out, exclude'), formed from 締め (しめ, stem of 締める / 閉める 'to shut, lock, fasten') + 出す (だす 'to put out, drive out').

history.meaning: lock out; shut out; exclude

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 締め出す

cognates.meaning: to bind bamboo slips with cord and gather materials together

編集.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) word 編集 (henshū), originally written 編輯 (MC *pen-dzjip), combining 編 (hen < MC *pen, 'to lace bamboo writing slips together in order with silk or leather cord; to weave, compile') and 輯 (shū < MC *dzjip, 'to fit chariot parts together, gather and harmonize written materials'). After post-WWII script reforms, the rarer character 輯 was officially replaced via *dōon-no-kanji* substitution by its homophone 集 (shū < MC *dzjip, 'to gather, collect'). Denotes editing texts, publications, or film/video footage.

history.meaning: lacing inscribed bamboo slips in sequence with cord and assembling writings into a book
compiling and editing newspapers, magazines, or books (respelt 編集 in 20th-century Japanese script reform)
editing (of print publications, film reels, video tape, or digital media)

morphemes.meaning: bind bamboo slips with cord; weave, compile, arrange in order (MC *pen)

編集.notes: The silk radical in 編 preserves the material history of pre-paper Chinese books: narrow bamboo strips (簡冊) had to be physically tied together in sequence with silk threads (編) so the text wouldn't scatter—a remarkably apt metaphor for cutting and splicing film or video tape in an editing room!

緩む.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to loosen, slacken, come untied, relax, abate'), continuing Heian Japanese *yurumu*, derived from the root *yuru-* ('loose, slack, gentle', seen in 緩い *yurui*) + intransitive verbal suffix *-mu*.

history.meaning: become loose or slack; relax
loosen; slacken; relax; ease up

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 緩む

練習.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('practice, training, drill, exercise'), formed from 練 (れん 'refine silk by boiling; polish, train, drill') + 習 (しゅう 'flap wings repeatedly; practice, learn by repetition').

history.meaning: train thoroughly; experienced practice
practice; training; drill; rehearsal

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 練習

縁.etymology: Native Japanese word (wago), reading 'fuchi'. Originally meant a border or edge of something deep (like a river pool, which is also 'fuchi' 淵).

history.meaning: edge/brink
edge

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 縁

縁石.etymology: Compound noun ('curbstone, edging stone, border stone'), read either Sino-Japanese えんせき or native へりいし, composed of 縁 ('edge, rim, border') + 石 ('stone').

history.form: 縁石 (えんせき / へりいし)
history.meaning: border stone; curbstone along a road or walkway

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 縁石

cognates.meaning: dependent origination, arising from conditions (translating Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda)

縁起悪い.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Yamato compound phrase combining 縁起 (engi, "omen, luck", originally a Buddhist kango term translating Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda "dependent origination", later shifting in medieval Japan to "origin legend of a shrine/temple" and then "auspiciousness, omen") with the native Yamato adjective 悪い (warui, "bad, unlucky", from Old Japanese warosi). Often used with or without the nominative particle が (縁起が悪い).

history.meaning: Buddhist dependent origination; inferior, unpleasant (Old Japanese)
inauspicious, portending bad luck, ill-omened

縁起悪い.notes: In casual speech, the particle が in 縁起が悪い (engi ga warui) is frequently dropped to form the compound-like 縁起悪い; its antonym is 縁起がいい (engi ga ii, "auspicious, lucky").

縄張り.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun derived from 縄 (nawa, "rope, cord", from Old Japanese napa) + 張り (hari, the連用形/continuative nominalization of 張る haru, "to stretch, spread, cordon off", with rendaku voicing /h/ > /b/). Originally referred to the literal stretching of ropes around a plot of land to demarcate boundaries for construction or property, before evolving in the Edo period among gamblers, merchants, and yakuza to mean exclusive "turf" or "jurisdiction".

history.meaning: stretching ropes to mark off land boundaries for building or surveying
exclusive territory, sphere of influence, yakuza or merchant turf

morphemes.meaning: stretching, stringing up (from haru, voiced via rendaku to -bari)

縄張り.notes: Exhibits regular rendaku (sequential voicing) where 張り (hari) becomes 張り (bari); used equally for animal territories in biology, police jurisdictions, and yakuza/business turf.

縛り続ける.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) syntactic V-V compound verb formed by joining the continuative stem (連用形, ren'yōkei) of 縛る (shibaru, "to tie up, bind, restrict") with the aspectual auxiliary verb 続ける (tsuzukeru, "to continue doing, keep on doing", transitive counterpart of 続く tsuzuku). Expresses continuous or prolonged physical or psychological restriction over time.

history.meaning: to bind tightly; to continue in succession
to keep tying down, to continue restricting or binding someone

morphemes.meaning: bind, tie up, restrict (continuative stem of shibaru)
continue, keep on (transitive ichidan stem tsuzuke-)

縛り続ける.notes: Productive aspectual compound pattern (V-masu stem + 続ける); often used figuratively in drama for rules, contracts, or guilt that keep someone bound.

縛る.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) godan verb inherited from Old Japanese 시바루 (sibaru, "to tie tightly, bind with cord or rope"). Likely related internal-etymologically to the root *siba ("dense, frequent, tightly packed", seen in 柴 shiba "brushwood bundled together" and 屡々 shibashiba "repeatedly, closely"), reflecting the action of cinching or bundling things tightly together. Written with the kanji 縛 (Middle Chinese *bjak, "to tie, bind").

history.meaning: to tie tightly, bind fast with rope or vine
to bind physically; to restrict by rules, contracts, or moral obligations

morphemes.meaning: tie up, bind, restrict (native Yamato shibar-)

縛る.notes: Its nominalized form 縛り (shibari) means both a "condition/restriction" in everyday speech (e.g., 契約の縛り, contract restriction) and rope bondage in adult media contexts.

rootFamily.gloss: binding hand and foot; complete immobilization

縦.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) noun 縦 (tate, "lengthwise, vertical direction"), derived from the continuative noun form (連用形) of the transitive verb 立てる (tateru, "to stand something up, erect", Old Japanese tatu / tate-). That which is stood upright defines the vertical axis, in contrast to 横 (yoko, "horizontal, sideways"). Written with the kanji 縦 (originally denoting the warp threads running lengthwise on a loom).

history.meaning: that which stands upright; the warp threads of a loom; lengthwise direction
vertical axis, height, length, front-to-back orientation

morphemes.meaning: vertical, lengthwise (from verb stem tate- "stand up")

縦.notes: Crucial in the common idiom 首を縦に振る (kubi o tate ni furu, literally "to shake one's neck/head vertically"), which means "to nod in agreement, to say yes" (contrasted with 首を横に振る, to shake one's head no).

rootFamily.gloss: vertical and horizontal, length and width; freely in all directions

繁栄.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound borrowed from Middle Chinese 繁榮 (*bjon-hjwaeng, "abundant and flourishing"), composed of 繁 (han, "luxuriant, numerous, thriving", originally referring to thick vegetation or horse-mane ornaments) + 栄 (ei, traditional 榮, "luxuriant blossoms, glory, flourishing"). Used in classical Chinese and Japanese for the flourishing of plants, dynasties, cities, and enterprises.

history.meaning: luxuriant growth of plants and blossoms; flourishing state
prosperity, thriving growth of a business, nation, or lineage

繁栄.notes: More formal and macro-level than 繁盛 (hanjō); 繁栄 applies to nations, civilizations, industries, or families, whereas 繁盛 typically describes a bustling shop or commercial trade.

rootFamily.gloss: to prosper, flourish (native verb using 栄)

繁盛.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound from Middle Chinese 繁盛 (*bjon-dzyengH, "abundant and flourishing/vigorous"), formed from 繁 (han, "abundant, bustling, numerous") + 盛 (jō, go-on reading of MC *dzyengH, originally "grain heaped high in a ritual vessel", hence "full, vigorous, thriving"). In Japanese, it specialized particularly in the Edo merchant class to denote bustling commercial success.

history.meaning: luxuriant, abundant, full of vitality
thriving trade, bustling commerce, booming business

morphemes.meaning: heaped full, vigorous, thriving (MC *dzyengH, go-on reading jō)

繁盛.notes: Historically also written 繁昌 (same reading hanjō); most famously heard in the merchant slogan 商売繁盛 (shōbai hanjō, "booming business!"). Note the go-on reading jō for 盛 (as opposed to kan-on sei in 全盛).

織物.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('woven fabric, textile, cloth'), attested since the Heian period, formed from 織り (おり, nominalized stem of 織る *oru* 'to weave', Old Japanese *woru*) + 物 (もの 'thing, article, goods').

history.meaning: patterned woven silk or cloth
woven fabric; textile; cloth

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 織物

繰り返す.etymology: Native Japanese compound transitive verb ('to repeat, do over again, reiterate'), formed from 繰り (くり, stem of 繰る *kuru* 'to reel in, draw a thread or cord hand over hand') + 返す (かえす 'to turn back, return, do over').

history.meaning: reel a cord back and forth; repeat over and over
repeat; do over again; reiterate

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 繰り返す

缶.etymology: Early modern loanword (read かん, 'can, tin'), borrowed in the late Edo / early Meiji period from Dutch *kan* ('jug, pot, tin canister'; cf. English *can*) and written with the kanji 缶 (originally an ancient Chinese earthenware jar, Sino-Japanese *fu*).

history.meaning: jug; pot; tin can
metal can; tin; canister

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 缶

罠.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('trap, snare, pitfall'), continuing Old Japanese *wana*, attested in the Man'yōshū for a looped cord or noose set to catch game or birds; traditionally linked to 輪 (*wa* 'ring, loop') + 縄 (*nawa* 'rope, cord').

history.meaning: looped snare; hunting trap
trap; snare; pitfall; ruse

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 罠

罪人.etymology: A compound written 罪人 with two established readings: the Sino-Japanese (kango, go-on) reading ざいにん (zainin, from Middle Chinese 罪人 *dzwojX-nyin, "person guilty of an offense or sin") and the native Yamato (jukujikun/wago) reading つみびと (tsumibito, from Old Japanese tumi "taboo violation, offense, sin" + pito "person", with rendaku voicing). Both readings denote a criminal offender in legal contexts and a "sinner" in Buddhist and Christian discourse.

history.meaning: transgressor against law or ritual taboo; offender
criminal, offender; moral or religious sinner

morphemes.meaning: offense, crime, sin, guilt (MC *dzwojX > zai; Yamato tsumi)
person, human being (MC *nyin > nin; Yamato hito > -bito)

罪人.notes: ざいにん (zainin) is the standard modern reading in legal, Buddhist, and everyday contexts, while つみびと (tsumibito) has a more literary, poetic, or biblical flavor.

rootFamily.gloss: criminal charge, nature of an offense

cognates.meaning: facts of a crime, criminal charge, guilt
circumstances of a crime, criminal charges

罪状.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 罪狀 (*dzwojX-dzrjangH, "the particulars or conditions of an offense"), composed of 罪 (zai, "crime, offense, guilt") + 状 (jō, go-on reading of MC *dzrjangH, "form, condition, state of affairs; written document/indictment"). Originally denoted either the concrete circumstances of a crime or the written bill of indictment detailing those offenses.

history.meaning: the circumstances of a crime; written statement of charges
criminal charge, counts of an indictment, nature of an offense

罪状.notes: Frequently collocated with 認否 (ninpi) in courtroom news: 罪状認否 (zaijō ninpi, "entering a plea / arraignment on criminal charges").

置かれる.etymology: The term '置かれる' (meaning 'placed') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: placed
placed

置かれる.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 置かれる

置く.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to put, place, set down, leave behind, establish'), continuing Old Japanese *oku* (four-grade *ok-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: set down; place; leave behind; settle (of dew/frost)
put; place; leave; establish

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 置く

置ける.etymology: The potential form (可能動詞, kanō dōshi) of the native Yamato godan verb 置く (oku, "to put, place, set down; to keep in stock", from Old Japanese oku). Formed via the regular Late Middle to Modern Japanese derivation replacing the godan conclusive ending -u with the ichidan potential suffix -eru (ok-u > ok-eru), meaning "can place, is able to stock or display (merchandise)". Distinct from the homophonous literary locative particle 於ける (okeru, "in, at").

history.meaning: to set down, place, leave behind
to be able to place, stock, or keep on hand (potential verb)

morphemes.meaning: put, place, stock, keep (native Yamato ok-)
potential ichidan verb ending ("to be able to...")

置ける.notes: In commercial dialogue (such as distributing videos to rental shops in *The Naked Director*), 置ける specifically means "able to stock/carry on store shelves"; also appears in the idiom 気を置ける / 一目置ける. Do not confuse with に於ける (ni okeru, formal "in/at").

rootFamily.gloss: leaving things as they are, neglecting

署名.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('signature, signing one's name, autograph'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 署名, composed of 署 (しょ 'write down, inscribe officially') + 名 (めい 'name').

history.meaning: inscribe one's name on a document
signature; signing one's name

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 署名

羊毛.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 羊毛 (ようもう), combining 羊 ('sheep') and 毛 ('hair, fleece, wool').
羊毛.notes: Dense compressed sheep's wool (羊毛フェルト) gives piano hammers their warm, rounded strike.

美.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) single-character noun and bound morpheme 美 (bi, kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *mijX, "beautiful, fine, good, admirable"). In Oracle Bone and Bronze script, the character 美 combines 羊 ("sheep/ram") above 大 ("big, great person"), traditionally explained either as a "fat, fine sheep" (prized for ritual sacrifice and taste) or a person wearing a ram-horn/feathered headdress in ritual dance, signifying visual splendor and excellence.

history.meaning: fine, savory, aesthetically pleasing, noble
beauty, aesthetic perfection, elegance (as an independent noun and prefix/suffix)

morphemes.meaning: beauty, fine, aesthetic ideal (MC *mijX > kan-on bi)

美.notes: Used independently as an elevated abstract noun (e.g., 日本の美, "Japanese beauty", 機能美, "functional beauty") in contrast to the everyday native adjective 美しい (utsukushii) or 綺麗 (kirei).

美しい.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('beautiful, lovely, fine'), continuing Old Japanese *utukusi*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, where it originally meant tender, doting affection felt toward a spouse, child, or small delicate creature ('dear, adorable, precious', cognate with 慈しむ *itsukushimu* 'to love tenderly'), before broadening from the Heian period onward to general aesthetic beauty.

history.form: うつくし (美し / 愛し)
history.meaning: dear; adorable; lovable (of family or small things)
beautiful; lovely; aesthetically fine

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 美しい

美央.etymology: Japanese female given name (read みお), formed from 美 (み 'beauty, beautiful', from the native stem seen in 美しい / 御) + 央 (お 'center, heart, middle').

history.meaning: female given name ('beautiful center/heart')

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 美

美学.etymology: A Meiji-era Sino-Japanese neologism (和製漢語, wasei-kango) coined in 1883 by the journalist and philosopher Nakae Chōmin (中江兆民) when translating Eugène Véron's French treatise *L'Esthétique* (as 維氏美学, *Ishi Bigaku*), superseding Nishi Amane's earlier trial translations. Constructed from Sino-Japanese roots 美 (bi, "beauty, aesthetic") + 学 (gaku, "study, science, philosophy"), calquing German *Ästhetik* / French *esthétique* and subsequently borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: academic discipline of aesthetics (translating French esthétique / German Ästhetik)
academic aesthetics; a person's personal code of honor, style, or aesthetic philosophy

美学.notes: Beyond academic philosophy, 美学 is widely used in everyday Japanese to mean someone's personal code or pride in how they live or work (e.g., 男の美学, "a man's personal code/style").

美容部員.etymology: A modern Sino-Japanese four-character institutional compound formed from 美容 (biyō, "beauty treatment, cosmetology, personal grooming", from 美 "beautiful" + 容 "appearance, countenance, face") + 部員 (buin, "department member, staff member", from 部 "department, division, section" + 員 "member, personnel"). Coined in the twentieth-century Japanese cosmetics and department-store industry to designate trained beauty advisors stationed at cosmetics counters.

history.meaning: cosmetic grooming + department staff member
cosmetics counter consultant, beauty advisor at a department store

美容部員.notes: In the Japanese retail industry, 美容部員 is often abbreviated to BA (from English "Beauty Advisor") or BC ("Beauty Consultant"), whereas a 美容師 (biyōshi) is a licensed hairstylist/beautician.

rootFamily.gloss: club member or department staff member

cognates.word: 美術學科 / 美术学科 (měishù xuékē)

美術学科.etymology: A Sino-Japanese compound combining 美術 (bijutsu, "fine arts", a Meiji-era wasei-kango coined in 1872 for the Vienna World's Fair entry rules to translate German *schöne Künste* / *Kunst*, from 美 "beauty" + 術 "art, technique, skill") and 学科 (gakka, "academic department, course of study", from 学 "learning, study" + 科 "branch, division, academic subject"). Denotes a university or high school department specializing in fine arts.

history.meaning: fine arts (1872 Meiji coinage) + academic branch/department
department of fine arts at a university or art school

美術学科.notes: In Japanese university structure, 学部 (gakubu, e.g., 芸術学部 "Faculty of Arts") is the larger faculty/school, while 学科 (gakka, e.g., 美術学科) is the specific major department within it.

cognates.meaning: group, crowd, flock (proposed Altaic/ areal comparison with Old Japanese mura/mure)

群れる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) ichidan intransitive verb 群れる (mureru, "to crowd together, flock, school, form a pack"), derived from Late Old Japanese むる (muru, lower bigrade verb), itself verbalized from the noun root *mura- / *mure ("cluster, flock, group", also the source of 村 mura "village, settlement of clustered houses" and 群れ mure "flock, herd, pack"). Written with the kanji 群 (originally "a flock of sheep", from 君 phonetic + 羊 semantic).

history.form: むる (muru, lower bigrade / 下二段)
history.meaning: to gather in a flock, crowd together in a mass
to school (of fish), flock (of birds), herd, or hang around in a pack/crowd (of people)

morphemes.meaning: flock, cluster, gather in a pack (native Yamato mure-)

群れる.notes: Used neutrally in biology for schooling fish or flocking birds, but when applied to people (e.g., 群れるのが嫌い, "I hate running in packs/crowds") it often carries a slightly critical nuance of conformist herd behavior.

rootFamily.gloss: flock, herd, pack, school of fish, crowd
crowd of people, multitude (Sino-Japanese reading gun)

羨ましい.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) shiku-inflecting adjective (originally うらやまし urayamasi in Old Japanese), derived from the verb 羨む (urayamu, "to envy, covet"), which is an ancient compound of 心 / 裏 (ura, "heart, inner mind, interior") + 病む (yamu, "to ache, suffer, feel pain"). Literally "one's inner heart aches (with longing at another's good fortune)". Written with the kanji 羨 (showing 羊 "sheep" above 次/涎 "saliva, drooling with desire").

history.form: うらやまし (urayamasi, from ura "heart" + yamu "to ache")
history.meaning: causing one's heart to ache with longing or envy
enviable, making one jealous (in a positive or wistful way)

morphemes.meaning: envy, ache in the heart (from ura "heart" + yam- "ache")

羨ましい.notes: In Japanese syntax, the person or thing envied is marked with が (e.g., 君が羨ましい, "I envy you / You are enviable"). Unlike 嫉妬 (shitto, dark jealousy), 羨ましい is openly said as a compliment ("Lucky you! I'm jealous!").

rootFamily.gloss: heartache; Mod.Jp:恨み (urami, resentment, sharing the ura "heart" root)

cognates.meaning: duty, obligation (modern legal sense borrowed from Japanese)

義務.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 義 (gi, Middle Chinese *ngjeH, "righteousness, moral duty, justice") + 務 (mu, Middle Chinese *mjuH, "task, service, to devote effort to"). Although attested sparingly in classical Chinese for "righteous affairs", its modern legal and philosophical sense as the correlative counterpart of 権利 (kenri, "right") — translating Dutch *plicht*, English *duty / obligation*, and German *Pflicht* — was established by Meiji legal scholars such as Nishi Amane and Tsuda Mamichi, and re-exported across East Asia.

history.meaning: matters of moral righteousness and service
legal, moral, or social duty and obligation (correlative to 権利 "rights")

義務.notes: Contrasts with 義理 (giri, interpersonal social reciprocity/debt of gratitude); 義務 (gimu) denotes an objective legal, institutional, or universal moral duty (e.g., 義務教育, compulsory education; 納税の義務, duty to pay taxes).

rootFamily.gloss: social obligation, duty of reciprocity, honor

羽.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) noun 羽 (hane, "feather, wing, plume"; also 羽 ha), inherited from Old Japanese はね (pane) and the bound root は (pa, "feather, wing"). Probably related internally to the verbal root はぬ / はねる (panu > haneru, "to spring up, leap, flip upward"), evoking the flapping propulsion of bird wings. Written with the kanji 羽, an ancient pictograph of two bird feathers or wings side by side.

history.meaning: bird feather, plumage, wing; fletching of an arrow
wing of a bird or insect, feather, shuttlecock, fan blade

羽.notes: Famous in the idiom 羽を伸ばす (hane o nobasu, literally "to stretch one's wings"), meaning "to let one's hair down, relax and enjoy freedom away from strict oversight". Note that 翼 (tsubasa) specifically means the whole anatomical or poetic "wing", whereas 羽 (hane) covers both feathers and wings.

rootFamily.gloss: the two wings of a bird; both wings of a building/organization

羽根板.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 羽根 (はね, 'feather, wing-like blade') and 板 (いた, 'wooden board').
羽根板.notes: Describes angled overlapping wooden slats on louvred shutters.

習う.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) godan verb 習う (narau, "to learn from a teacher, practice, take lessons"), from Old Japanese ならふ (narapu < *narap-u). Derived by adding the iterative/continuative verbal suffix *-ap- (indicating repeated or habitual action) to the intransitive root なる (naru / nareru, "to become accustomed to, get used to, be tamed"). Thus, etymologically "to repeatedly accustom oneself to a skill by imitation and practice". Written with 習 (pictograph of young birds flapping wings 羽 repeatedly in the sun 白 to learn to fly).

history.form: ならふ (narapu, iterative of naru "grow accustomed")
history.meaning: to grow accustomed through repetition; to imitate and practice
to learn (a skill) from an instructor, take lessons in

morphemes.meaning: practice, learn by imitation (native Yamato nara(w)-, from nar- "accustom" + iterative -ap-)

習う.notes: Unlike 学ぶ (manabu, studying bookish or academic subjects independently or formally), 習う implies hands-on practice or taking lessons from a master or teacher (preserved in the proverb 習うより慣れろ, narau yori narero, "better to get used to it by doing than to be taught" — pairing two verbs from the same root!).

rootFamily.gloss: to get used to, become accustomed to (intransitive cognate)

老眼鏡.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 老眼鏡 (ろうがんきょう), joining 老眼 ('farsightedness of age') with 鏡 ('mirror, optical lens').
老眼鏡.notes: Shares 眼鏡 ('glasses, spectacles') with everyday めがね.

考える.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) ichidan verb 考える (kangaeru, "to think, consider, ponder, reflect"), evolving via historical sound change (onbin: *kamugapu > *kaugafu > kangau > kangaeru) from Old Japanese かむがふ (kamugapu, "to examine by comparing, investigate, check against records"). Most philologists analyze *kamugapu as 向かふ (mukapu, "to face, confront, place side by side") with a prefix *ka-, originally meaning "to place two things (such as tally sticks or texts) face-to-face to compare and verify them".

history.meaning: to compare side-by-side, verify records, examine, deliberate

history.form: 考へる > 考える (kangafuru > kangaeru)
history.meaning: to think over, consider, ponder, devise a plan

morphemes.meaning: think, examine, consider (from Old Japanese kamugap-)

考える.notes: Whereas 思う (omou) refers to spontaneous feeling, intuition, or personal opinion ("I feel/believe"), 考える (kangaeru) refers to active, analytical, deliberate thought processing ("to think through, figure out").

者.etymology: Written with the kanji 者, which carries two distinct etymological layers in Japanese: (1) the native Yamato (wago) noun もの (mono, from Old Japanese mono₂, "person, individual, fellow", distinct in specific contexts from 物 mono₂ "thing/object" though sharing the same prehistoric root for an entity/being), and (2) the Sino-Japanese (kango) agentive suffix しゃ (sha, from Middle Chinese 者 *tsyaeX, a grammatical particle nominalizing verbs/adjectives into "one who does/is...").

history.meaning: person, individual (often of lower status or in compounds); agentive nominalizer "-er"
person, figure (mono, often in wago compounds like 若者); specialist or agent (-sha, in kango like 役者, 経営者)

morphemes.meaning: person, agent, figure (Yamato mono; Sino-Japanese -sha < MC *tsyaeX)

者.notes: As an independent noun read もの (mono), it is used in humble self-reference (こういう者ですが, "I am such-and-such a person...") or in native compounds like 若者 (wakamono, youth) and 人気者 (ninkimono, popular figure); as a Sino-Japanese suffix it is read -しゃ (-sha, e.g., 医者, 視聴者).

rootFamily.gloss: actor, performer; man of ability (Sino-Japanese reading sha)

耕す.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) godan transitive verb 耕す (tagayasu, "to plow, till, cultivate soil"), which evolved in Late Middle Japanese via metathesis or phonetic assimilation from the Classical and Old Japanese compound verb たかへす (takapesu > takahesu, literally 田返す "to turn over the rice field"), composed of 田 (ta, "rice paddy, cultivated field") + 返す (kaesu < kapesu, "to turn over, flip upside down"). Written with the kanji 耕 (plowing tool 耒 + phonetic 井).

history.form: たかへす (takapesu, from ta "field" + kapesu "turn over")
history.meaning: to turn over the soil of a field with a spade or plow
to plow, till, cultivate land (or figuratively cultivate the mind/market)

morphemes.meaning: field, rice paddy (native Yamato ta, fused inside tagayas-)

耕す.notes: A remarkable example of a lexicalized compound where a single kanji (耕) masks the original two-part native etymology 田返す (ta-kaesu > tagayasu, "to turn the field over").

rootFamily.gloss: to turn over, return, flip back

耳.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('ear; hearing; selvedge or crust edge'), continuing Old Japanese *mimi₁*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*mimi* ('ear').

history.meaning: ear
ear; hearing
ear; hearing; edge/crust

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 耳

聞かせる.etymology: The causative form (使役形, shiekikei) of the native Yamato godan verb 聞く (kiku, "to hear, listen, ask", from Old Japanese kiku). Constructed by attaching the productive ichidan causative auxiliary suffix -seru (from Classical Japanese -su / -sasu) to the mizenkei (irrealis/imperfective stem) kika-, yielding 聞かせる (kikaseru, "to let someone hear, make someone listen; to tell, inform; to move someone with a performance or story").

history.meaning: to cause or allow someone to hear; to tell; (in medieval usage) to show honorific action
to let someone hear, tell a story/news, impress an audience with singing or speech

morphemes.meaning: hear, listen (irrealis stem kika- of kiku)

聞かせる.notes: Often used with benefactive verbs like 聞かせてくれる / 聞かせていただく ("kindly let me hear / tell me"), or idioms like 泣かせる・聞かせる ("to really move an audience with a song or line") and 言い聞かせる ("to admonish/persuade").

rootFamily.gloss: to persuade, admonish, talk sense into someone
audible, able to be heard, sounding like (intransitive/potential)

聞き逃す.etymology: Compound of 聞き (kiki, stem of kiku 'to hear/listen') + 逃す (nogasu, 'to let loose/let escape').

history.meaning: to fail to hear

聞き逃す.notes: Commonly used when someone accidentally doesn't hear something important.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 聞き逃す

聞き飽きる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) V-V compound verb formed from the continuative stem (連用形, ren'yōkei) of 聞く (kiku, "to hear, listen to") + the ichidan verb 飽きる (akiru, "to grow tired of, have enough of, be fed up with", from Old Japanese godan aku, "to become satisfied, full, sated to excess"). Literally "to hear until one is completely sated and sick of it".

history.meaning: to listen to one's fill, grow weary of hearing
to be sick and tired of hearing the same thing repeatedly

morphemes.meaning: hear, listen to (continuative stem of kiku)
grow tired of, be sated/fed up with (ichidan stem aki-)

聞き飽きる.notes: Usually appears in the past/perfective form 聞き飽きた (kikiakita, "I've heard that a million times / I'm sick of hearing it!").ー飽きる (-akiru) attaches productively to many verbs (見飽きる, 食べ飽きる).

rootFamily.gloss: to get tired of, lose interest in, be fed up with
to get tired of seeing/looking at

聞く.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to hear, listen to; ask, inquire; grant'), continuing Old Japanese *kiku* (four-grade *kik-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: hear; listen to; ask; heed
hear; listen; ask; inquire

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 聞く

聞こえる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to be heard, be audible, sound; be renowned'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *kikoyu* (聞こゆ), derived from the verb root *kik-* (聞く 'to hear') + archaic mediopassive/spontaneous suffix *-oyu* > *-oeru*.

history.meaning: be audible; sound; become known; say humbly
be heard; be audible; sound

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 聞こえる

聴く.etymology: Orthographic specification of native Japanese *kiku* (Old Japanese *kiku* 'to hear, listen'), written with the kanji 聴 ('listen attentively, heed') when emphasizing active, deliberate, or appreciative listening (such as listening to music or a speech).

history.meaning: hear; listen closely
listen attentively (to music, radio, or a speaker)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 聞く

職業.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Middle Chinese 職業 (*tsyik-ngjaep, "official post and duties"), composed of 職 (shoku, "official post, duty, employment", originally signifying listening 耳 and recording/managing duties) + 業 (gyō, "work, enterprise, trade, karma/calling", originally a jagged wooden rack for hanging ritual bells, hence a grand undertaking). In Meiji Japan, it became the standard sociological term for one's livelihood or profession.

history.meaning: allocated official duties and regular work
occupation, profession, trade, vocation by which one earns a living

職業.notes: More formal and categorical than 仕事 (shigoto, everyday "work/job"); 職業 is what appears on official forms ("Occupation:") or in sociological phrases like 職業病 (shokugyōbyō, occupational hazard/habit).

肝.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) noun 肝 (kimo, from Old Japanese kimo, "liver; internal organs/viscera; seat of courage and spirit"). In pre-modern Japanese and East Asian physiological thought, the liver/gallbladder (肝/胆) rather than the brain was viewed as the seat of vital spirit, resolve, and emotional fortitude, giving rise to the metaphorical meanings "nerve, guts, pluck" and "the vital core/crux of a matter". Written with 肝 (flesh radical 月/肉 + phonetic 干).

history.meaning: the liver or internal organs generally; the seat of courage and emotion
liver (especially as food or in idioms); nerve, guts, courage; the crucial point (kimo) of something

morphemes.meaning: liver; guts, courage; vital essence (native Yamato kimo)

肝.notes: Used in vivid somatic idioms: 肝が据わっている (kimo ga suwatte iru, "to have nerves of steel / great pluck"), 肝を冷やす (kimo o hiyasu, "to be scared stiff / have one's blood run cold"), and ここが肝だ (koko ga kimo da, "this is the crucial point"). For the medical organ, 肝臓 (kanzō) is standard.

rootFamily.gloss: crucial, vital, most important (literally "liver and kidneys")
test of courage (walking through a spooky place at night)

肩.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('shoulder'), continuing Old Japanese *kata*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*kata* ('shoulder').

history.meaning: shoulder
shoulder
shoulder

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 肩

肩代わり.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun かたがわり (katagawari), formed from 肩 (kata, "shoulder") + 代わり (kawari, nominalized continuative form of 代わる kawaru, "to take the place of, substitute for", voiced to -gawari via rendaku). Originated in Edo-period palanquin (駕籠, kago) bearing and manual portage, where a bearer would switch shoulders or a relief bearer would step in to take the carrying pole onto their own shoulder, before shifting metaphorically to assuming another person's financial debt or burden.

history.meaning: switching shoulders or relieving a fellow bearer carrying a palanquin or heavy load
taking over another's debt, financial liability, or heavy responsibility

morphemes.meaning: substitution, taking the place of (from kawaru, with rendaku voicing to -gawari)

肩代わり.notes: Almost always used in financial and legal contexts today (e.g., 借金を肩代わりする, "to take over/pay off someone else's debt"), preserving the physical metaphor of lifting a crushing load off someone's shoulders. Also note the related relief-pitcher metaphor 肩を持つ ("to take someone's side").

rootFamily.gloss: to take the place of, substitute for

cognates.meaning: affirmation, positive, to affirm (modern sense borrowed from Japanese)

肯定.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 肯 (kō, kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *khongX, originally "meat adhering to bone", evolving to "to hit the mark, consent, be willing") + 定 (tei, kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *dengH, "to fix, settle, determine"). In Meiji logic and philosophy (notably in Nishi Amane's *Hyakuichi Shinron*), 肯定 was standardized as the formal translation of English/Latin *affirmation* (opposite of 否定 hitei, *negation*), later broadening to psychological acceptance and validation.

history.form: 肯定 (Meiji philosophical coinage from MC roots *khongX + *dengH)
history.meaning: logical affirmation (as opposed to negation 否定)
affirmation, positive endorsement, psychological validation or self-acceptance

肯定.notes: Direct antonym of 否定 (hitei, negation/denial). Very prominent in modern Japanese psychology and drama in compounds like 自己肯定感 (jiko kōteikan, "sense of self-worth / self-acceptance").

育つ.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to grow up, be raised, be brought up'), attested from Late Old / Heian Japanese as *sodatu* (paired with transitive 育てる *sodateru*); traditionally connected with 巣立つ (*sudatsu* 'for young birds to fledge and leave the nest', from 巣 'nest' + 立つ 'stand/rise').

history.meaning: grow up; be reared
grow up; be raised; develop

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 育つ

育てる.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to raise, rear, bring up, nurture, cultivate'), continuing classical lower bigrade *sodatu* (育つ, stem *sodate-*), the transitive counterpart of four-grade intransitive 育つ (*sodatsu* 'to grow up').

history.meaning: rear; bring up; nourish
raise; bring up; nurture; train

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 育てる

背.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('back, spine; stature, height; mountain ridge'), continuing Old Japanese *se* (alternating with bound form *so-* in compounds like *somuku* 'turn one's back'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: back of the body; rear; ridge
back; spine; height/stature

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 背

背く.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) godan intransitive verb 背く (somuku, "to turn one's back on; to defy, disobey, rebel against, go against"), inherited from Old Japanese そむく (somuku < *so₁-muk-u). Morphologically transparent as a prehistoric compound of the bound noun root そ (so₁, "the back, rear", preserved in 背向そがい sogai and written 背) + the verb 向く (muku, "to face, turn toward"), literally meaning "to turn one's back toward someone or something".

history.meaning: to physically turn one's back on; to estranged oneself from or disobey
to defy, disobey, rebel against (authority, rules, or expectations)

morphemes.meaning: turn the back on, defy (from Old Japanese so "back" + muk- "turn")

背く.notes: Takes the dative particle に for the person, law, or expectation defied (e.g., 親の期待に背く, "to go against one's parents' expectations", 法律に背く, "to violate/defy the law"). Its transitive counterpart ("to turn away") is 背ける (somukeru, as in 目を背ける, "to avert one's eyes").

rootFamily.gloss: to avert (one's eyes or face), turn away (transitive counterpart)
face, turn toward (the verbal element inside somuku)

cognates.meaning: behind, at the back, in the rear

背後.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) spatial and figurative compound from Middle Chinese 背後 (*pwojH-huwX, "behind the back, the rear"), composed of 背 (hai, "the back, spine, rear", originally depicting northern/opposing figures 北 above flesh 月/肉) + 後 (go, go-on reading of MC *huwX, "behind, after, rear"). Used both for physical space directly behind someone's back and figuratively for covert forces operating "behind the scenes".

history.meaning: the space behind a person's back; the rear side
physically behind someone; the hidden background or mastermind behind an incident

背後.notes: More formal and dramatic than the everyday native word 後ろ (ushiro, "behind"); 背後 suggests either vulnerability to a sneak attack (背後に気をつけろ, "watch your back!") or shadowy figures pulling strings behind a crime (事件の背後関係, "the hidden connections behind the case").

背徳.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Classical Chinese 背德 (Middle Chinese *pwojH tok), composed of 背 (hai, 'the back; to turn one's back on, betray, violate') and 徳 (toku, shinjitai of 德, 'virtue, moral integrity'). Literally 'turning one's back on virtue', attested in Chinese historiography such as the Book of Han and the Wen Xuan for forsaking moral duty.

history.meaning: turning one's back on moral virtue; forsaking duty
immorality, depravity, transgression against ethical norms

morphemes.meaning: back; to turn one's back on, betray, violate (MC *pwojH)

背徳.notes: A high-register literary word frequently used in drama, fiction, and adult media (especially in the adjectival derivative 背徳的 haitokuteki and the phrase 背徳感 haitokukan, 'a thrilling sense of guilt or forbidden pleasure').

rootFamily.gloss: sense of guilt or forbidden immorality

背負う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 背 (se, 'the back', from Old Japanese so₂ < Proto-Japonic *so) and the transitive verb 負う (ou, 'to bear, carry on the back, owe', from Old Japanese opu < Proto-Japonic *opu-). Originally transparent as 'to bear upon the back', it broadened metaphorically to carrying heavy responsibilities, debts, or fate.

history.meaning: to carry physically upon one's back
to carry on the back; to take on a burden or duty

history.form: 背負う (せおう / しょう)
history.meaning: to carry on one's back; to shoulder responsibility or burden

morphemes.meaning: to bear, carry, take on (OJ opu)

背負う.notes: In everyday spoken Japanese, せおう (seou) very frequently contracts to しょう (shou), especially in conjugated forms like しょっている (shotte iru, 'carrying / acting conceited').

rootFamily.gloss: to throw someone over one's back; to be conceited
rootFamily.word: 背負い投げる (せおいなげる)

胴体.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 胴 (dō, 'trunk of the body, cylinder, torso'; originally referring in Classical Chinese to the large intestine or tubular body cavity, Middle Chinese *duwng) and 体 (tai, shinjitai of 體, 'body, frame, substance', Middle Chinese *thejX). In Japanese, 胴 specialized early for the central trunk of armor (dōmaru) and the human torso, and 胴体 denotes the main trunk of a body or aircraft fuselage.

history.meaning: tubular cavity/trunk + physical body frame
human or animal trunk excluding head and limbs
torso, trunk of the body; fuselage of an aircraft

morphemes.meaning: body, form, frame (MC *thejX, shinjitai of 體)

胴体.notes: Used both anatomically for the human/animal torso (in contrast to 頭 'head' and 手足 'limbs') and mechanically for the fuselage of an airplane (as in 胴体着陸 dōtai chakuriku, 'belly landing').

rootFamily.gloss: tossing someone into the air in celebration

胸.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('chest, breast, bosom; heart, mind, feelings'), continuing Old Japanese *mune* (alternating with bound form *muna-* in compounds like 胸元 *munamoto*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: chest; breast; seat of emotions
chest; breast; heart; mind

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 胸

脅し.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun derived from the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the transitive verb 脅す (odosu, 'to frighten, threaten, intimidate'). 脅す is formed from the Old Japanese bound root odö- ('startle, tremble with fear', also seen in the intransitive verb 驚く odoroku 'to be startled' and the mimetic adverb おどおど odoodo 'timidly') plus the transitive suffix -su.

history.meaning: to startle, frighten away (birds or beasts), terrify
act of frightening; scarecrow; intimidation; armor lacing
threat, intimidation, bluff, blackmail

morphemes.meaning: to threaten, intimidate, frighten (from OJ root odö- + transitive -su)

脅し.notes: While written 脅し for verbal or physical threats and blackmail (e.g., 脅し文句 odoshimonku, 'threatening words'), the same etymological word written 威し refers to scarecrows (ししおどし shishiodoshi) or decorative samurai armor lacing.

rootFamily.gloss: to cower, be frightened, have nightmares

脚.etymology: Native Japanese noun (read あし, 'leg [of a person, animal, or piece of furniture]; gait'), continuing Old Japanese *asi* ('foot, leg, step'), written specifically with the kanji 脚 when distinguishing the lower limb or supporting leg from the foot proper (足).

history.meaning: leg; foot; limb
leg (of a body, table, or chair)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 足

脚本.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) loan from vernacular Chinese 脚本 (jiǎoběn), composed of 脚 (kyaku, literally 'foot, leg, base', used in Chinese theater as an abbreviation of 脚色 jiaose / kyakushoku 'actor's role,dramatis personae', Middle Chinese *kjak) and 本 (hon, 'root, book, written text', Middle Chinese *pwonX). Originated in Song and Yuan dynasty Chinese theater for the written promptbook setting out roles and dialogue.

history.meaning: storyteller's promptbook or theatrical role-book
kabuki playscript; theatrical text
screenplay, dramatic script for film, television, or stage

morphemes.meaning: foot, base; theatrical role or dramatization (MC *kjak)

脚本.notes: In the Japanese film and TV industry (as seen in The Naked Director), 脚本 refers specifically to the dramatic screenplay or teleplay, whereas 台本 (daihon) refers to the physical shooting/rehearsal script booklet handed to cast and crew.

脚立.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 脚 ('leg, support') and 立 ('stand'), originally a standing wooden trestle or footstool and now the standard word for a folding A-frame stepladder.

脱がせる.etymology: Causative transitive verb ('to undress [someone], take off [someone's clothes], make/let someone take off'), formed from the *a*-stem of 脱ぐ (*nugu* 'to take off clothes, undress') + causative suffix *-seru*.

history.meaning: undress someone; make/let someone take off clothes

morphemes.meaning: irrealis stem of 脱ぐ (take off clothes)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 脱ぐ

脱ぐ.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to take off [clothes, shoes, or headgear], undress, strip off'), continuing Old Japanese *nuku* / *nugu*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; cognate with 抜く (*nuku* 'to pull out, extract, slip out of').

history.meaning: strip off; slip out of garments or footwear
take off (clothes, shoes); undress

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 脱ぐ

脳.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) noun from Middle Chinese 腦 (*nawX, 'brain, marrow of the skull', from Old Chinese *nˤuʔ). The traditional character 腦 combines the flesh radical (月/肉) with 巛 ('hair') and 囟 ('fontanelle, skull'), graphically depicting the soft organ beneath the hairy cranium; Japanese shinjitai simplified the right component to 脳. It largely displaced the native Old Japanese word なづき (naduki) in standard usage.

history.meaning: brain, cranial marrow
anatomical brain; seat of intellect and memory
brain, mind, intellect

脳.notes: While 脳 (nō) is the anatomical and scientific word for the brain (and appears in compounds like 洗脳 sennō 'brainwashing' or 脳裏 nōri 'back of one's mind'), colloquial Japanese often uses 頭 (atama, 'head') for everyday intelligence and mental state.

腐る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan intransitive verb attested in Old Japanese as kusaru ('to rot, decay, spoil'). Derived from the bound adjectival root kusa- ('foul-smelling, stinking, putrid', seen in the adjective 臭い kusai 'stinking' < Old Japanese kusasi) plus the detransitivizing/spontaneous verbal suffix -ru (< Proto-Japonic *-ra-). Semantically broadened from organic putrefaction to metal corrosion and figuratively to moral corruption or a soured, dejected mood.

history.meaning: to putrefy, decay, become foul-smelling
to rot, spoil (of food), corrode; to become dejected or morally depraved

腐る.notes: Beyond literal food spoilage, 腐る is heavily used in colloquial Japanese for feeling discouraged or sulking (気が腐る ki ga kusaru, 'to feel down/fed up') and in the idiom 腐っても鯛 (kusatte mo tai, 'even if rotten, a sea bream is still a sea bream' — true quality endures even in decline).

rootFamily.gloss: to let rot, spoil; to belittle or disparage
inseparable bad company, bond one cannot sever

腕.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('arm; skill, ability, competence'), continuing Old Japanese *ude*, attested in the Man'yōshū and Nihon Shoki; traditionally analyzed as *u-te* ('upper part of the hand/arm', from *u-* 'upper' + 手 *te* 'hand/arm' with sequential voicing).

history.meaning: forearm; arm
arm; skill; ability

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 腕

腕時計.etymology: Compound noun ('wristwatch'), formed from native 腕 (うで 'arm, wrist') + 時計 (とけい → どけい with rendaku, Sino-Japanese 'clock, watch').

history.meaning: wristwatch

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 腕時計

腕次第.etymology: Hybrid Japanese compound combining native Yamato 腕 (ude, 'arm; skill, competence, craftsmanship', from Old Japanese ude, likely a compound of u- 'upper' + te 'hand') and Sino-Japanese 次第 (shidai, originally a Buddhist and Classical Chinese noun meaning 'order, sequence, step by step' from Middle Chinese *tshijH dejX, which grammaticalized in Japanese as a suffixal noun meaning 'depending on, in accordance with').

history.meaning: arm/manual skill + sequential order / dependence on circumstances
depending entirely on one's skill or ability

morphemes.meaning: arm; technical skill, ability (native wago ude)

腕次第.notes: 腕 (ude) is the standard Japanese metonym for practical skill or professional competence (as in 腕がいい ude ga ii, 'highly skilled'); attaching -次第 (-shidai) creates a brisk predicate meaning 'it's all up to how skilled you are'.

rootFamily.gloss: depending on one's mindset or attitude

腫れ.etymology: Deverbal noun from the continuative stem (連用形) of the native intransitive verb 腫れる (hareru, Classical Japanese はる haru, 'to swell up, puff out', etymologically sharing the root *par- 'to stretch taut, expand' with 張る haru 'to stretch' and 春 haru 'spring, when buds swell'). In Japanese medical and everyday usage, 腫れ denotes localized bodily swelling from a sprain, bump, or inflammation.

history.meaning: to swell; bodily swelling
swelling; puffiness

腫れ.notes: Note the idiomatic collocation 腫れが引く ('the swelling recedes/goes down', using the same verb as an ebbing tide).

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 腫れ

腫れる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to swell, become inflamed, puff up'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *paru* (腫る, stem *pare-*), related to four-grade 張る (*haru* 'to stretch, swell, become taut').

history.meaning: swell up; become inflamed
swell; become swollen or inflamed

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 腫れる

腹.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun from Old Japanese para ('belly, abdomen, stomach; womb; inner mind'), reconstructed to Proto-Japonic *para. Often compared areally to Middle Korean poy (modern Korean 배 bae, 'belly') and internally within Japonic to the root of 張る (haru < OJ paru, 'to stretch taut, swell') or 原 (hara < OJ para, 'wide flat plain'). In Japanese cultural semantics, the belly (hara) serves as the locus of true emotions, courage, and unspoken intentions.

history.meaning: abdomen, belly, womb; inner heart or intention
stomach, belly, gut; courage, true intentions, temper

morphemes.meaning: belly, stomach, gut; seat of emotion and intent (OJ para)

腹.notes: Central to dozens of Japanese psychological idioms: 腹が立つ (hara ga tatsu, 'to get angry', lit. 'belly stands up'), 腹を決める (hara o kimeru, 'to resolve oneself'), 腹を割る (hara o waru, 'to speak frankly', lit. 'split open the belly'), and 腹黒い (haraguroi, 'scheming, two-faced', lit. 'black-bellied').

rootFamily.word: 腹蔵なく (ふくぞうなく)

腹ごしらえ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 腹 (hara, 'belly, stomach', < Old Japanese para) and こしらえ (koshirae, the nominalized continuative form of the verb 拵える koshiraeru, 'to prepare, make ready, equip, fabricate', < Old Japanese kösirapu), linked with rendaku voicing of k to g (koshirae > goshirae). Literally 'preparing the stomach', i.e., fortifying oneself with food before undertaking work or travel.

history.meaning: belly + to equip, prepare, coax into readiness
eating a meal to fortify oneself before setting out

history.form: 腹ごしらえ (はらごしらえ)
