history.meaning: master of traditional artistic/martial accomplishments + person
professional entertainer, TV celebrity, show-business personality

morphemes.meaning: art, craft, performance skill (MC *ngjejH, shinjitai of 藝)

芸能人.notes: Covers actors, singers, idols, comedians (芸人 geinin), and TV personalities (タレント tarento); contrast with 芸術家 (geijutsuka, 'fine artist') and 文化人 (bunkajin, 'cultural/intellectual figure'). Note that 芸 (shinjitai of 藝 'art') merged graphically with a separate rare character 芸 (un, 'rue herb', as in Japan's first public library 芸亭 Untei).

rootFamily.gloss: performer, entertainer; specifically a comedian in modern usage

芸能界.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 芸能 (geinō, 'performing arts, public entertainment', composed of 芸 [shinjitai of 藝, Middle Chinese *ngjejH] 'art, craft, skill' and 能 [Middle Chinese *nong] 'talent, ability, performance') plus the suffixal head noun 界 (kai, 'boundary, realm, world, sphere', Middle Chinese *keajH, originally translating Sanskrit dhātu 'realm' in Buddhism and adopted in modern Japanese for professional or academic circles).

history.form: 藝能 (げいのう) + 界 (かい)
history.meaning: performing arts + professional sphere/realm
show business, the entertainment world, celebrity industry

morphemes.meaning: art, performance skill, accomplishment (MC *ngjejH, shinjitai of 藝)

芸能界.notes: In Japanese media discourse, 芸能界 refers to the tightly organized mainstream ecosystem of talent agencies (芸能事務所 geinō jimusho), television networks, music labels, and theatrical promoters—often contrasted in The Naked Director with the underground adult video industry (アダルトビデオ業界).

rootFamily.word: 芸能事務所 (げいのうじむしょ)

rootFamily.gloss: industry, business world, the trade (often read ぎょうかい or jargon ぎょーかい)

若い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('young, youthful; immature; low [of a number]'), continuing Old Japanese *wakasi* (stem *waka-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū for fresh, tender youthfulness.

history.meaning: young; youthful; fresh and tender
young; youthful; immature

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 若い

若手俳優.etymology: A hybrid wago-kango compound combining native Yamato 若手 (wakate, 'young person in a field; rising talent', from 若- waka 'young' + 手 te 'hand, person, skill') with Sino-Japanese 俳優 (haiyū, 'actor, player', from Middle Chinese 俳 bæj 'entertainer, jester, physical comedy' + 優 ʔjuw 'actor, performer; abundant').

history.form: わかて (若手) + はいゆう (俳優)
history.meaning: rising young practitioner + theatrical performer

history.form: 若手俳優 (わかてはいゆう)
history.meaning: young actor, up-and-coming actor

若手俳優.notes: The morpheme 手 (te) in 若手 functions as an agentive classifier ('hand/practitioner', as in 歌手 or 運転手), designating someone active in a craft who is still in the early stages of their career.

rootFamily.gloss: young person in a field, rising talent

苦しめる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) ichidan transitive verb derived from the stem of the adjective 苦しい (kurushii, 'painful, agonizing, distressing') plus the verbalizing transitive/causative suffix -める (-meru, from Classical Japanese nidan -む -mu, which forms transitive verbs meaning 'to make [adjective]'). Ultimately built on the root 苦 (kuru-), linked to 繰る (kuru, 'to wind, churn, spin') describing an inward twisting or churning sensation in the chest.

history.form: くるしむ (苦しむ, Yodan) / くるしむ (Nidan transitive)
history.meaning: to suffer pain (Yodan); to inflict pain or distress upon (Shimo Nidan)
to torment, to hurt, to cause suffering to

苦しめる.notes: Pairs with the intransitive 苦しむ (kurushimu, 'to suffer, groan in pain'); in Classical Japanese both shared the citation form くるしむ, distinguished only by conjugation class (yodan vs. shimo nidan).

rootFamily.gloss: to suffer, to struggle with pain

苦労.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound borrowed from Middle Chinese 苦勞 (khuX law, 'painful toil, hardship'), composed of 苦 (ku < MC khuX, 'bitter, painful, suffering') and 労 (rō < MC law, 'toil, labor, exertion, fatigue'). In Japanese it functions both as a noun for hardship and with する (suru) as a verb meaning to go through trouble or labor painstakingly.

history.meaning: bitter toil, exhausting physical labor

history.form: くらう (苦勞) > くろう (苦労)
history.meaning: suffering, hardship, painstaking effort

苦労.notes: The workplace phrase ご苦労様 (gokurōsama) is used by superiors to subordinates to acknowledge their hard work; using it toward a superior is considered a breach of etiquette (use お疲れ様でした instead).

rootFamily.gloss: person who has endured many hardships in life

苦手.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun and adjectival noun ('weak point, something one is poor at or dislikes dealing with'), formed from the stem *niga-* of 苦い (*nigai* 'bitter, unpleasant') + 手 (*te* 'hand; person, type, opponent'). Originally denoting a folk belief in a 'bitter hand' able to calm snakes, then a person hard to deal with, and finally any subject or task one is bad at or dislikes.

history.meaning: hand that subdues snakes; awkward opponent hard to handle
weak point; poor at; not fond of

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 苦手

英会話.etymology: A modern Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by prefixing 英 (ei, abbreviation of 英語 eigo 'English language', ultimately from the phonetic transcription 英吉利 Igirisu 'England') to 会話 (kaiwa, 'conversation, dialogue', from 会 kai < MC γwɑiH 'to meet, assemble' + 話 wa < MC γwæH 'speech, talk'). Coined in Meiji-to-Shōwa Japan to denote practical spoken English as a distinct subject of study from grammar-translation (英文解釈).

history.meaning: spoken dialogue in the English language
English conversation; commercial English-speaking instruction

morphemes.meaning: English (short for 英語 / 英吉利)

英会話.notes: In Japan, 英会話 specifically evokes the commercial industry of conversational English schools (英会話教室) and self-study programs rather than just any casual chat in English.

rootFamily.word: 英会話教室 (えいかいわきょうしつ)

英会話教材.etymology: A multi-morpheme Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 英会話 (eikaiwa, 'English conversation', from 英 ei 'English' + 会 kai 'meet' + 話 wa 'talk') with 教材 (kyōzai, 'teaching materials, instructional media', from 教 kyō < MC kæwH 'teach, instruct' + 材 zai < MC dzʌi 'timber, material, resource'). Popularized in postwar and Shōwa-era Japan with the boom in door-to-door sales of cassette-tape and textbook sets for learning spoken English.

history.form: 英会話 (English conversation) + 教材 (instructional materials)
history.meaning: study materials for spoken English

history.form: 英会話教材 (えいかいわきょうざい)
history.meaning: English conversation learning sets or courses

英会話教材.notes: During the 1970s and 1980s economic boom depicted in The Naked Director, high-priced boxed 英会話教材 sets of cassette tapes and encyclopedias were prime products for aggressive door-to-door salesmen.

英語.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed in the late Edo/early Meiji period from 英 (ei < MC ʔjæng, the first character of the ateji phonetic transcription 英吉利 Igirisu 'England/English', itself from Portuguese Inglês, and also of 諳厄利亜 Angeria) + 語 (go < MC ŋjoX, 'language, speech, words'). Subsequently borrowed from Japanese back into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese as the standard East Asian term for the English language.

history.meaning: England, the English nation
the English language

morphemes.meaning: England, Britain (short for 英吉利; MC ʔjæng 'flower, outstanding')

英語.notes: Because 英 originally meant 'flower petal' or 'outstanding/heroic' (as in 英雄 eiyū), its selection to transcribe Inglês / England gave compounds like 英語 and 英国 a flattering graphic connotation.

苺ジャム.etymology: Hybrid native Japanese and Western loanword compound ('strawberry jam'), combining native 苺 (いちご 'strawberry, berry', Old Japanese *itigo*) + ジャム (borrowed from English *jam*).

history.form: 苺ジャム (いちごジャム)
history.meaning: strawberry jam

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 苺

茶色い.etymology: Derived color adjective ('brown, brownish, tea-colored'), formed in Modern Japanese by adding the adjectival inflection -い to the compound noun 茶色 (*chairo* 'tea color, brown', from Sino-Japanese 茶 *cha* 'tea' + native 色 *iro* 'color').

history.meaning: tea color; brown (noun)
brown; brownish (adjective)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 茶色い

荒れる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) intransitive verb descending from Old Japanese 荒る (aru, shimo nidan conjugation), built on the root *ara- ('rough, wild, uncultivated, sparse', seen in 荒い arai and 粗い arai). By shift from Classical shimo nidan (-ru) to Modern shimo ichidan (-reru), 荒れる came to describe seas, weather, skin, moods, or social order growing turbulent, dilapidated, or chaotic.

history.meaning: to become desolate, wild, ruined, or turbulent

history.form: 荒れる (あれる, Shimo Ichidan)
history.meaning: to get rough, storm, fall into ruin, or turn chaotic and unruly

荒れる.notes: Used across physical and psychological domains: weather/seas (海が荒れる), neglected buildings (庭が荒れる), chapped skin (肌が荒れる), and rowdy or unruly behavior (酒に酔って荒れる).

rootFamily.gloss: to lay waste, to devastate, to troll/vandalize

荒波.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from the bound adjectival stem 荒- (ara-, 'rough, wild, violent, raging', related to 荒い arai and 荒れる areru) + 波 (nami, 'wave, billow', Old Japanese なみ nami). Attested since Old Japanese poetry (Man'yōshū) both literally for stormy ocean swells and figuratively for the harsh, turbulent vicissitudes of human society (世間の荒波).

history.form: あらなみ (荒波 / 荒浪)
history.meaning: fierce, raging ocean waves
rough waves, stormy seas; harsh trials of the world

荒波.notes: Frequently appears in the set metaphor 世間の荒波を乗り越える (seken no aranami o norikoeru, 'to ride out the stormy seas of the world'), referring to surviving fierce business or life competition.

荷台.etymology: A hybrid wago-kango (yutō-yomi) compound combining the native Yamato noun 荷 (ni, 'load, pack, cargo, burden', Old Japanese に ni) with the Sino-Japanese noun 台 (dai < Middle Chinese dʌi, 'platform, stand, raised terrace, pedestal'). Originally denoted a wooden rack or pack-saddle frame for carrying loads on horses or carts, and later extended to the cargo bed of a truck or luggage rack of a bicycle.

history.form: に (荷, load) + だい (臺/台, platform/rack)
history.meaning: pack-rack or platform for carrying goods on a cart or packhorse
truck cargo bed, flatbed, bicycle luggage carrier

荷台.notes: Exemplifies 重箱読み (jūbako-yomi) or 湯桶読み (yutō-yomi)—specifically yutō-yomi (native kun'yomi first, Sino-Japanese on'yomi second: ni + dai). Riding in a truck's 荷台 on public roads is strictly regulated in Japan.

荷物.etymology: A hybrid wago-kango (yutō-yomi) compound combining native Yamato 荷 (ni, 'load, burden, pack carried on the shoulder or back', Old Japanese に ni) with Sino-Japanese 物 (motsu, the go-on reading of Middle Chinese mjwət 'thing, object, article, goods', as in 食物 shokumotsu or 貨物 kamotsu). Literally 'load-things' or 'pack-goods', it also developed the figurative sense of an emotional burden or nuisance (お荷物 onimotsu).

history.form: に (荷, pack/load) + もつ (物, goods/articles)
history.meaning: goods packed for transport, traveler's baggage
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: luggage, baggage, parcel; burdensome person or obligation

morphemes.meaning: thing, object, goods (go-on reading of MC mjwət)

荷物.notes: Folks often mistake もつ (motsu) here for the native verb 持つ (motsu, 'to hold/carry'), which reinforces the meaning mnemonically, though philologically 物 (motsu) is the Sino-Japanese go-on reading for 'goods/things'.

rootFamily.gloss: freight, cargo (pure kango reading of 荷)

荷物室.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Japanese compound noun ('luggage room, baggage compartment, cargo hold'), combining 荷物 (にもつ 'luggage, baggage', from native 荷 'load' + Sino-Japanese 物 'thing') + Sino-Japanese 室 (しつ 'room, compartment').

history.meaning: luggage room; baggage compartment

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 荷物

荷造り.etymology: Native Yamato compound noun combining 荷 (ni, 'load, luggage, baggage, cargo', Old Japanese ni) with 造り / 作り (-zukuri, voiced by rendaku from tsukuri, the nominalized stem of 作る tsukuru 'to make, build, prepare'). Literally meaning 'making up loads', 荷造り denotes packing belongings neatly into boxes, trunks, or bundles for a move or journey.

history.meaning: bundling cargo or baggage for transport
packing luggage or boxes

荷造り.notes: Spelled with づ (ni-zu-ku-ri) in modern kana orthography because it is a compound where 造り (tsukuri) undergoes rendaku voicing.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 荷造り

cognates.meaning: none is greater than; enormous, vast

莫大.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) adjectival noun borrowed from Classical Chinese 莫大 (Middle Chinese mak dɑiH), originally a syntactic phrase meaning 'there is nothing (莫 mak, negative distributive pronoun) greater (大 dɑiH) than [this]' (as in Classical Chinese 莫大於此). Reanalyzed in Chinese and Japanese as an intensifying compound adjective meaning 'immeasurably great, enormous, vast, colossal'.

history.meaning: nothing is greater than; supreme in size or degree
enormous, vast, immense (especially of sums of money, costs, or damage)

莫大.notes: Almost always collocates with abstract quantities of scale—especially money, fortune, debt, profit, or damage (莫大な費用 bakudai na hiyō 'enormous expense', 莫大な利益 'vast profits')—rather than concrete physical objects.

rootFamily.gloss: huge, gigantic, colossal (of physical or structural scale)
vast, extensive, swelling (of numbers, data, or budgets)

菩提樹.etymology: Compound of 菩提 (ぼだい, phonetic transcription of Sanskrit bodhi, 'awakening') and 樹 (じゅ, 'tree').
菩提樹.notes: Applied in Japanese botany and German lied translations (Schubert's Der Lindenbaum -> 菩提樹) to the heart-leaved linden tree.

落ちる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive upper monograde (kami-ichidan) verb ('to fall, drop, come down, fail, fade'), continuing Old Japanese upper bigrade *otu* (落つ, stem *oti-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, paired with transitive 落とす (*otosu*).

history.meaning: fall; drop down; decline
fall; drop; come off; fail

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 落ちる

落ち着く.etymology: Native Japanese compound intransitive verb ('to calm down, settle down, compose oneself, harmonize'), formed from 落ち (おち, stem of 落ちる 'to fall, drop down into place') + 着く (つく 'to arrive, come to rest, settle').

history.meaning: come to rest in a place; settle down; regain composure
calm down; settle down; feel at home

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 落ち着く

落ち込む.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 落ち- (ochi-, the continuative/ren'yōkei stem of 落ちる ochiru 'to fall, drop, sink', Old Japanese おつ otsu) + 込む (komu, 'to go into, plunge inward', functioning as an aspectual/directional auxiliary verb indicating inward movement or deep progression into a state). Literally 'to fall into or cave in', it extended metaphorically to a slump in business/grades or sinking into dejection and depression.

history.meaning: to fall into a hole or water; to cave in, sink inward
to fall in; to slump (sales/economy); to feel depressed or downhearted

morphemes.meaning: to fall, drop, sink (stem of 落ちる)
to enter deeply, plunge in, move inward

落ち込む.notes: Has three distinct everyday senses: literal falling in (穴に落ち込む), quantitative slumping (売上が落ち込む), and emotional dejection (失恋して落ち込む).

rootFamily.gloss: to fall, to drop, to fail
to drop, to let fall, to remove/clean off
to calm down, to settle in (lit. 'fall and attach')

落とし前.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 落とし (otoshi, nominalized stem of 落とす otosu 'to drop, bring to a conclusion, settle a matter, knock down an auction bid') + 前 (mae, 'portion, share, due, proper state', as in 一人前 ichininmae or 手前 temae). Originating in Edo-period merchant and underworld argot for bringing a dispute or transaction to its proper final settlement, it came to mean paying one's dues or settling scores, especially in yakuza and outlaw parlance.

history.meaning: final settlement of a transaction or dispute; one's due share upon resolution
settling a score, taking responsibility, making amends (often by punishment or restitution)

morphemes.meaning: settling, concluding, dropping (nominalization of 落とす)

落とし前.notes: Almost exclusively used in the tough, confrontational idiom 落とし前をつける (otoshimae o tsukeru, 'to settle accounts / pay one's dues / make things right'), a staple of yakuza dramas and hardboiled speech.

rootFamily.gloss: to drop, to settle, to finish off
punchline of a story (rakugo); final outcome or resolution
full-fledged adult share or status (lit. 'one person's portion')

落とす.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) transitive godan verb descending from Old Japanese おとす (otosu), derived from the pre-Old Japanese verbal root *oti- / *oto- (seen in intransitive Old Japanese おつ otsu > Modern 落ちる ochiru 'to fall, drop, come off') + the productive transitive suffix -す (-su). Alongside its primary spatial meaning 'to let fall, drop', it developed broad causative senses corresponding to every sense of 落ちる: 'to make (dirt, stains, or makeup) come off', 'to lower (speed/volume)', 'to omit', and 'to capture/win over'.

history.meaning: to cause to fall, drop down, strip away, or conquer (a fortress)
to drop; to wash out or remove (stains/dirt/makeup); to lower; to miss (a credit)

morphemes.meaning: fall, drop, come off (alternant stem of 落つ/落ちる)

落とす.notes: Because 落ちる means both 'to fall' and 'to come off (of stains, grease, or makeup)' (汚れが落ちる), its transitive partner 落とす naturally means 'to wash/clean out (a stain)' or 'to remove (makeup)' (汚れを落とす, メイクを落とす).

rootFamily.gloss: to fall, to drop; to come off (of dirt or stains)

rootFamily.word: メイク落とし (めいくおとし)

葉.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('leaf, foliage, blade [of grass], needle [of pine]'), continuing Old Japanese *pa*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*pa* ('leaf').

history.meaning: leaf
leaf; foliage
leaf; blade; needle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 葉

葉っぱ.etymology: Colloquial native Japanese noun ('leaf, foliage'), formed in Early Modern Japanese from 葉 (は 'leaf', Old Japanese *pa*) + emphatic/familiar nominal suffix -っぱ (preserving the older bilabial stop after gemination).

history.meaning: leaf; foliage (colloquial)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 葉っぱ

著しい.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) i-adjective descending from Old Japanese いちしろし (itisirosi) and Classical Japanese いちしるし (itisirusi), composed of the intensifying prefix いち- (iti-, 'strikingly, unmistakably, completely', related to 逸/一 or native emphatic root *iti-) + しろし/しるし (sirosi/sirusi, 'distinct, clear, conspicuous, manifest', cognate with 白し shiroshi 'white, bright' and 知る shiru 'to know' / 印 shirushi 'sign, mark'). Sequential voicing (rendaku) produced いちじるし (ichijirushi), which modernized into the shiku-inflected adjective 著しい (ichijirushii).

history.form: いちしろし (著し) > いちしるし (著し)
history.meaning: unmistakably clear, conspicuous, plainly manifest to the eye
history.stage: Old to Early Middle Japanese (8th–11th c.)

history.form: いちじるし (著し) > 著しい (いちじるしい)
history.meaning: remarkable, striking, marked, pronounced (of changes, growth, or damage)

morphemes.meaning: clear, conspicuous, marked (from しるし shirushi + rendaku)

著しい.notes: Belongs to a formal written and journalistic register; its adverbial form 著しく (ichijirushiku, 'markedly, drastically, severely') frequently modifies verbs of change, decline, or violation (著しく損なう, 著しく低下する).

rootFamily.gloss: prominent, notable, conspicuous (kango reading of 著)

蓋.etymology: The term '蓋' (meaning 'lid') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: lid
lid

蓋.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 蓋

薄い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('thin, pale, light, weak, dilute'), continuing Old Japanese *ususi* (stem *usu-*), attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: thin; pale; faint; shallow
thin; pale; light; weak; sparse

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 薄い

薄まる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) intransitive godan verb formed from the stem 薄- (usu-, from the adjective 薄い usui 'thin, pale, weak, dilute, faint', Old Japanese うすし ususi) + the productive deadjectival intransitive suffix -まる (-maru, which means 'to become [adjective]', as in 高まる takamaru or 深まる fukamaru). Denotes a liquid becoming diluted, colors or fog growing paler, or feelings, memories, and suspicions fading away.

history.form: うすし (薄し, 'thin, pale, faint') + -まる (intransitive verbalizer)
history.meaning: to become thin, dilute, or pale
to become diluted; to fade, weaken, or grow fainter (of colors, impressions, or interest)

morphemes.meaning: thin, pale, weak, dilute, faint (stem of 薄い)

薄まる.notes: Forms a regular transitivity pair with 薄める (usumeru, transitive 'to dilute, thin out'): 氷が溶けて味が薄まる ('the ice melts and the flavor gets watered down') vs. 水で薄める ('to dilute with water').

rootFamily.gloss: to dilute, to thin out, to water down (transitive)
to grow dim, to fade, to thin out (intransitive)

薄める.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb formed from the adjectival stem 薄- (usu-, from 薄い usui 'thin, weak, dilute, pale', Old Japanese うすし ususi) + the productive deadjectival transitive suffix -める (-meru < Classical shimo nidan -む -mu, meaning 'to make [adjective]', parallel to 強める tsuyomeru and 深める fukameru). Literally 'to make thin or weak', it is used primarily for diluting liquids, lightening colors or makeup, and watering down intensity.

history.form: うすむ (薄む, Shimo Nidan transitive)
history.meaning: to make thin, pale, or less concentrated

history.form: 薄める (うすめる, Shimo Ichidan)
history.meaning: to dilute (a liquid), to thin out, to lighten (a color or shade)

morphemes.meaning: thin, pale, weak, dilute (stem of 薄い)

薄める.notes: In bartender and hospitality contexts (such as host clubs and snack bars in Shōwa Japan), お酒を薄める (osake o usumeru) refers to watering down alcoholic drinks.

rootFamily.gloss: to become diluted, to fade, to weaken (intransitive)

薦める.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb descending from Old Japanese すすむ (susumu, shimo nidan transitive conjugation), sharing its root with intransitive 進む (susumu, yodan/godan 'to advance, move forward', from a reduplicated root *susu- 'to press forward eagerly'). From the core sense 'to cause to move forward, urge onward', the verb branched orthographically in Japanese writing into 進める ('to advance a plan/clock'), 勧める ('to advise/encourage an action'), and 薦める ('to recommend a person, book, or item as worthy').

history.form: すすむ (進む / 勧む / 薦む, Shimo Nidan)
history.meaning: to move forward, urge on, present, or commend someone/something

history.form: 薦める (すすめる, Shimo Ichidan)
history.meaning: to recommend, endorse, or put forward (a candidate, work, or product)

morphemes.meaning: advance, put forward, commend (shared root with 進む)

薦める.notes: Japanese writers distinguish three heterographs for susumeru: 進める (advance a project), 勧める (encourage someone to do something or offer a drink), and 薦める (recommend a specific person, book, or product for its merits).

衛星.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) astronomical compound composed of 衛 (ei < Middle Chinese ɦjwejH, 'to guard, escort, patrol around a perimeter') + 星 (sei < Middle Chinese seŋ, 'star, celestial body'). history.meaning: to institute and fix firmly (laws, boundaries, or rights)
configuration, system settings; fictional premise or character persona setup in media

設定.notes: In the entertainment and adult video/film industry depicted in *The Naked Director*, 設定 specifically refers to the 'fictional scenario, role-play premise, or character backstory' devised for a shoot (e.g., 'the premise that she is a newlywed wife'). Note the gemination: setsu + tei -> settei.

cognates.meaning: to found, establish (an institution or company)

設立.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) combining 設 (Middle Chinese *ɕjet, 'to set up, arrange, institute') and 立 (Middle Chinese *lip, 'to stand upright, erect, found'). Literally 'to set up and make stand,' used in corporate and legal registers for the formal founding or incorporation of a company, organization, or institution.

history.meaning: to institute and erect (an office, altar, or policy)
formal founding, incorporation, or establishment of an organization or company

設立.notes: 設立 is used specifically for founding abstract institutional or legal entities (companies, schools, foundations), whereas 建設 (kensetsu) is used for physically constructing buildings or infrastructure, and 創立 (sōritsu) emphasizes the historical pioneering creation of an institution.

rootFamily.gloss: to set up, establish (native Yamato verb)

cognates.meaning: establishment preparation office / task force office

設立準備室.etymology: Multi-morphemic Sino-Japanese corporate compound (kango) built from 設立 (setsuritsu, 'corporate founding/establishment', from 設 'set up' + 立 'erect'), 準備 (junbi, 'preparation, readiness', from 準 'level/standard/prepare' + 備 'equip/make ready'), and the suffix 室 (shitsu, Middle Chinese *ɕit, 'room, chamber, organizational office/division'). Denotes a dedicated task-force office created inside a company to launch a new subsidiary or venture.

history.form: 設立 + 準備 + 室 (setsuritsu + junbi + shitsu)
history.meaning: establishment + preparation + organizational chamber/office

設立準備室.notes: In Japanese corporate culture, a ～準備室 (-junbishitsu) is an official pre-launch task force or incubator division formed before a new company, broadcast station, or department is legally incorporated—often a high-stakes, scrappy startup unit inside a larger enterprise.

rootFamily.word: 社長室 (しゃちょうしつ)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 準備室 (準備 + 室)

設計.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('design, plan, layout, engineering specification'), formed from 設 (せつ → せっ- with consonant assimilation before *k-*, 'set up, establish, prepare') + 計 (けい 'calculate, plan').

history.meaning: devise a stratagem or plan
architectural or engineering design; planning

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 設計

設計図.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('blueprint, architectural or engineering plan, design drawing'), formed from 設計 (せっけい 'design, layout plan') + 図 (ず 'drawing, diagram, chart').

history.meaning: blueprint; design drawing; architectural plan

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 設計図

許す.etymology: Native Yamato verb (wago) yurusu, attested in Old Japanese as yuru-su, formed by attaching the transitive-causative suffix -su to the bound adjective/verb root *yuru- ('loose, slack, relaxed', seen in 緩い yurui 'loose/lenient' and 緩む yurumu 'to slacken'). Literally 'to slacken tension or loosen restraint upon someone' -> 'to release, permit, pardon, or forgive.' Written with kanji 許 ('to permit, approve').

history.meaning: to make loose, slacken bonds, release from tension
to release, grant permission, pardon an offense, forgive

morphemes.meaning: loose, slack, unrestrained (cf. yurui 緩い)
transitive verbalizer suffix ('to make loose / release')

許す.notes: Because its core Yamato image is 'loosening tension/bonds,' 許す spans both 'to forgive/pardon' and 'to permit/allow,' and even appears in idioms like 気を許す (ki o yurusu, 'to let one's guard down / relax one's vigilance around someone').

訳あり.etymology: Native Yamato compound expression (wago) combining 訳 (wake, 'reason, meaning, underlying circumstance'—nominalized from the verb 分く waku 'to divide, distinguish, discern') and 有り (ari, classical conclusive/continuative form of ある aru 'to exist, to have'). Literally 'having an underlying reason or hidden circumstance,' meaning someone with a complicated past, a secret affair, or merchandise sold at a discount due to minor flaws.

history.meaning: having a distinction, reason, or special circumstance behind it
having a complicated past, secret circumstances, or hidden defect

morphemes.meaning: reason, meaning, special circumstance (from waku 'to discern')
existing, having (stem of aru 有る)

訳あり.notes: Often written in katakana for dramatic flair (ワケあり), it has two main uses: describing people or relationships with a 'complicated/checkered past or illicit secret,' and describing 'blemished/factory-second goods' (訳あり商品) sold cheaply online.

rootFamily.gloss: inexplicable, making no sense ('no reason exists')
rootFamily.word: 訳が分からない (わけがわからない)

訴える.etymology: Native Yamato verb (wago) uttaeru, resulting from consonant gemination (onbin) of Classical Japanese うったふ (uttafu) and Heian-period うれたふ (uretafu). Derived from the Old Japanese adjective stem うれたし (uretashi, 'grievous, distressing, infuriating, lamentable'—related to うら ura 'heart/inner mind' + いたし itashi 'painful') plus verbal suffix -fu. Literally 'to voice inner pain and grievance,' evolving into 'to appeal to authorities, bring a lawsuit, or appeal to emotions.'

history.meaning: to lament a grievance, voice distress or indignation
to petition a magistrate, bring a legal complaint or accusation
to sue in court, complain of pain, or appeal to emotions/public opinion

morphemes.meaning: to voice a grievance, petition, sue (from Classical uttafu < uretapu)

訴える.notes: Covers three distinct English verbs depending on the particle and context: legally 'to sue someone' (人を訴える), medically 'to complain of symptoms/pain' (痛みを訴える), and rhetorically 'to appeal to emotions or the public' (感情に訴える).

rootFamily.gloss: lawsuit, legal action, complaint, appeal (noun form)

証拠.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) combining 証 (shinjitai simplified form of 證, Middle Chinese *tɕɨŋH, 'to testify, verify, prove with words') and 拠 (shinjitai of 據, Middle Chinese *kjoH, 'to lean on, rely upon, have as a firm basis'). Literally 'verbal testimony and factual basis one can rely on,' denoting legal, scientific, or factual proof and evidence.

history.meaning: testimony and firm basis for verification
factual or legal evidence, proof, corroboration

morphemes.meaning: to testify, verify, prove (MC *tɕɨŋH, traditional 證)
to rely on, base upon, hold fast (MC *kjoH, traditional 據)

証拠.notes: In police and legal dramas, 証拠隠滅 (shōko inmetsu, 'destruction of evidence') and 決定的な証拠 (ketteiteki na shōko, 'smoking-gun / conclusive evidence') are staple collocations; in everyday speech, 何よりの証拠 means 'the best proof of all.'

詐欺.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) formed from two near-synonymous roots: 詐 (Middle Chinese *dzraH, 'to deceive with words, feign, counterfeit') and 欺 (Middle Chinese *khi, 'to cheat, delude, take advantage of'). Originally a classical Chinese legal and moral term for verbal deceit, codified in modern Japanese criminal law (Penal Code Article 246) as the crime of 'fraud' or 'swindling.'

history.meaning: to deceive with false words and cheat someone
criminal fraud, swindle, confidence trick, scam

morphemes.meaning: to lie, feign, deceive with words (MC *dzraH)

詐欺.notes: Pronounced sági (high-low pitch), contrasting with the homophone 鷺 (sagi, 'heron'). Interestingly, in underworld slang, a professional con artist is called a 詐欺師 (sagishi), or metaphorically クロサギ ('black heron') versus シロサギ ('white heron').

rootFamily.gloss: to deceive, cheat, delude (native reading of 欺)

評価.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) combining 評 (Middle Chinese *bjøng, 'to weigh words, judge fairly, comment on'—from 言 'words' + 平 'level, balanced') and 価 (shinjitai of 價, Middle Chinese *kæH, 'price, value, worth'). Literally 'weighing and judging the fair worth of something,' evolving from commercial price appraisal to general critical evaluation and reputation.

history.meaning: to adjudge and set the fair price or worth of goods
valuation, critical appraisal, performance rating, reputation

評価.notes: Often used in the positive sense of 'appreciating/recognizing someone's merit' when unmodified: 高く評価する means 'to think highly of / praise,' and 評価される alone frequently translates as 'to be praised or recognized for one's worth.'

試す.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to try, test, attempt, put to the test'), continuing Heian Japanese *tamesu*, related to 例 (*tameshi* 'precedent, example, trial') and 矯める (*tameru* 'to straighten, aim true, test').

history.meaning: put to the test; verify by trial
try; test; attempt

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 試す

試用期間.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('probationary period, trial period'), combining 試用 (しよう 'trial use, probation', from 試 'test, try' + 用 'use, employ') + 期間 (きかん 'period, term, interval of time').

history.form: 試用期間 (しようきかん)
history.meaning: probationary period; trial period

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 試用

試行錯誤.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese idiom (yojijukugo) coined in modern Japan to translate the English psychological and scientific term 'trial and error' (originally popularized by Edward Thorndike and Alexander Bain). Constructed from 試行 (shikō, 'trial execution'—試 'to test/try' + 行 'to carry out') and 錯誤 (sakugo, 'mistake, error'—錯 'mixed up, awry' + 誤 'to err, mistake').

history.meaning: trial performance + error/mistake (calque of English 'trial and error')
process of finding a solution through repeated trial and error

試行錯誤.notes: Unlike many yojijukugo that come from ancient Chinese classics, 試行錯誤 is a modern Japanese scientific translation of English 'trial and error'; it typically functions with the verb 重ねる (試行錯誤を繰り返す / 重ねる 'to repeat trial and error').

詰まる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to be clogged, be packed full, become blocked, shrink, be at a loss for words'), continuing Heian–Middle Japanese *tumaru*, the intransitive counterpart of 詰める (*tsumeru* 'to pack tightly, press to the end', derived from 積む *tsumu* 'to pile up').

history.meaning: be packed full; be blocked; reach the end
be clogged; be stuffed; be stuck for words

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 詰まる

話.etymology: Native Japanese verbal noun ('talk, speech, story, conversation, account'), nominalized from the連用形 of 話す (*hanasu* 'to speak, tell, converse').

history.meaning: spoken story; chat; conversation
talk; story; conversation; matter

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 話

話す.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to speak, talk, tell, converse'), emerging in Late Middle Japanese as a semantic specialization of 放す / 離す (*hanasu* 'to release, let loose, set free', Old Japanese *panasu*), from the metaphor of 'releasing words or thoughts from the mind'.

history.meaning: let go; release; utter
speak; talk; tell; converse

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 話す

cognates.meaning: topic of conversation, talking point (via Japanese)
topic of conversation, talk of the town

話題.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) combining 話 (Middle Chinese *ɦwæjH, 'speech, talk, conversation, story') and 題 (Middle Chinese *dej, 'forehead; heading, title, subject, theme'). Literally 'the heading or subject of conversation,' denoting both an ordinary conversation topic and a 'hot topic' or sensation that everyone is talking about.

history.meaning: spoken talk + heading/subject
history.stage: Middle Chinese roots / Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: subject of conversation; buzzworthy sensation, talk of the town

話題.notes: When used in expressions like 話題になる ('to become the talk of the town') or 話題の映画 ('the much-talked-about / buzzworthy movie'), 話題 means more than just 'a topic'—it implies viral fame, buzz, or public sensation.

詳しい.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('detailed, thorough, well-informed, well-versed'), continuing Old Japanese *kupasi* (stem *kupa-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, where it originally meant 'delicately beautiful, finely crafted, exquisite' before shifting to 'minutely detailed, thoroughly knowledgeable'.

history.form: くはし (細し / 詳し / 麗し)
history.meaning: finely wrought; delicate; exquisite; detailed
detailed; thorough; well-informed

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 詳しい

誇らしい.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('proud, triumphant'), attested from the Heian period as *hokorasi*, derived from the verb 誇る (*hokoru* 'to boast, take pride in, flourish') + adjectival suffix *-rashi* / *-ashii*.

history.meaning: triumphant; proud; exultant
proud; worthy of pride

morphemes.meaning: take pride in; boast (from 誇る)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 誇らしい

誇らしげ.etymology: Derived na-adjective formed by replacing the final -い of the i-adjective 誇らしい (hokorashii, 'proud', from the verb 誇る hokoru, 'to take pride in, boast') with the productive evidential suffix -げ (-ge, written 気, meaning 'having the air or outward look of'). In Japanese grammar, speakers attach -げ when describing someone else's visible emotional expression from the outside: 誇らしげに見ていた ('she was watching with a proud look on her face').

history.meaning: having a triumphant or proud demeanor
proud-looking; with an air of pride

誇らしげ.notes: Used with な before nouns (誇らしげな顔, 'a proud expression') and に before verbs (誇らしげに見る, 'to watch proudly').

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 誇らしげ

cognates.word: 誇大妄想 / 夸大妄想 (kuādà wàngxiǎng)

誇大妄想.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese psychiatric compound (kango) combining 誇大 (kodai, 'exaggerated, grandiose, boastful'—from 誇 'to boast, exaggerate' + 大 'great, big') and 妄想 (mōsō, 'wild delusion'—originally a Buddhist term from 妄 'false, absurd,reckless' + 想 'thought, mental image'). Coined in Meiji-era psychiatry to translate German Größenwahn ('delusions of grandeur / megalomania').

history.meaning: deluded, unwholesome mental conceptions (translating Sanskrit vikalpa)
delusions of grandeur, megalomania (translating German Größenwahn)

誇大妄想.notes: Adding 狂 (kyō, 'mania/enthusiast') yields 誇大妄想狂 (kodai mōsōkyō, 'megalomaniac'), often used in drama and everyday banter to mock someone with wildly unrealistic, grandiose business schemes or ego.

rootFamily.word: 誇大広告 (こだいこうこく)
被害妄想 (ひがいもうそう)

誇張.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) combining 誇 (Middle Chinese *khwa, 'to boast, talk big, magnify with words') and 張 (Middle Chinese *trjang, 'to stretch a bowstring, spread wide, expand, inflate'). Literally 'boasting and stretching something out beyond its true size,' used since classical Chinese rhetoric for hyperbole, overstatement, and theatrical exaggeration.

history.meaning: to talk big and stretch or magnify claims
exaggeration, overstatement, rhetorical hyperbole

morphemes.meaning: to stretch, draw a bow, expand, swell (MC *trjang)

誇張.notes: 誇張 is somewhat formal or analytical ('exaggeration / hyperbole'); in casual conversation, Japanese speakers also say 大げさ (ōgesa, 'overdramatic / exaggerated') or slang 盛る (moru, 'to pile on / embellish a story or photo').

rootFamily.gloss: pride, boast; to be proud of (native Yamato reading of 誇)
rootFamily.word: 誇り (ほこり) / 誇る (ほこる)

rootFamily.gloss: assertion, claim, insistence ('stretching one's main point')

認める.etymology: Native Yamato verb (wago) mitomeru, transparently derived in Old Japanese as 見留む (mi1-to2mu), a compound of the stem of 見る (mi1ru, 'to see, look at') and the transitive verb 留む / 止む (to2mu, modern tomeru, 'to stop, fix in place, hold fast'). Literally 'to fix one's gaze upon and register in mind,' evolving from 'catching sight of' to 'recognizing, acknowledging, approving, or admitting.' Written with the Sino-Japanese character 認 ('to recognize, acknowledge').

history.meaning: to fix one's eyes upon, catch sight of, take note of
to recognize, acknowledge as valid, admit (a fault), approve

morphemes.meaning: to see, look at (stem of miru 見る)
to stop, fix in place, hold fast (tomeru 留める)

認める.notes: Because the same kanji 認める also represents the literary verb したためる (shitatameru, 'to write down a letter or eat a meal'), context determines the reading, though みとめる (mitomeru, 'to recognize/admit/approve') is overwhelmingly more common.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop, fasten, fix in place (etymological second element)

cognates.meaning: to know, to recognize, to be familiar with

認識.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read ninshiki, combining 認 (nin, from Middle Chinese *nyinH, 'to recognize, acknowledge, admit') and 識 (shiki, from Middle Chinese *syik, 'to know, discern, distinguish'). Originating in Chinese Buddhist philosophical translations of Sanskrit jñāna ('cognition, consciousness'), it was repurposed in Meiji-era Japanese to translate German Erkenntnis ('epistemological cognition') before broadening into everyday usage for 'awareness' or 'recognition'.

history.meaning: mental discernment and conscious awareness in Buddhist epistemology
epistemological cognition (translating German Erkenntnis); general recognition or understanding

認識.notes: Often used in business and public apologies in the phrase 認識が甘い (ninshiki ga amai, 'one's understanding/awareness was naive or insufficient'). Takes する to form a transitive verb.

cognates.meaning: to be born, to come into being

誕生.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read tanjō, composed of 誕 (tan, from Middle Chinese *danX, 'great, grand; to give birth, be born') and 生 (shō, voiced by rendaku to jō, from Middle Chinese *sraeng, 'to be born, live, produce'). In Classical Chinese, 誕 served as an honorific particle or verb celebrating the birth of emperors, sages, and deities, a solemn nuance that broadened in Japanese to denote both human birth and the dramatic emergence of a new work, star, or institution.

history.meaning: auspicious birth of a ruler, sage, or deity
birth of a person; dramatic creation or emergence of something new

morphemes.meaning: life, birth, come into existence (jō < shō)

誕生.notes: Carries a celebratory or dramatic ring compared to 出生 (shussei, official/statistical birth). Ubiquitous in 誕生日 (tanjōbi, 'birthday') and media headlines announcing a new star or venture (新スター誕生).

語らせる.etymology: Causative ichidan verb formed from the a-stem (未然形) 語ら- (katara-) of the godan verb 語る (kataru, Old Japanese kataru, 'to recount, narrate, speak from the heart') plus the causative auxiliary -せる (-seru). In rhetorical and everyday expressions like 作品に語らせる or ピアノに語らせる ('to let the work/piano speak for itself'), it conveys letting genuine quality tell its own story without boastful speeches.

history.meaning: to recount; to tell a story
to let/make speak or recount (causative of 語る)

語らせる.notes: Its conditional form 語らせれば ('if we let them speak') is formed regularly by replacing final -る with -れば.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 語らせる

語る.etymology: Native Yamato word (wago), attested in Old Japanese as kataru ('to recount, narrate at length, tell a story'). Etymologically related to the bound stem kata- ('shape, form, pattern, model', seen in 形 kata) or the verb katu ('to join, mix, bring together'), reflecting the act of weaving events into a coherent narrative structure or sharing words back and forth. Written with the kanji 語 ('word, language, tell').

history.meaning: to recount myths, legends, or events coherently; to converse intimately
to narrate, recite (especially epic tales with musical accompaniment), speak passionately about

語る.notes: Unlike 話す (hanasu, everyday speaking or chatting), 語る implies narrating a substantive story, speaking passionately about ideals or dreams (夢を語る), or revealing deep personal truths.

誠に.etymology: Native Yamato adverbial phrase (wago) formed from the noun まこと (makoto, 'truth, reality, sincerity', attested in Old Japanese as maköto) plus the dative-locative-manner particle に (ni, '-ly, in'). The noun makoto is itself a compound of the intensifying prefix ま- (ma-, 'true, pure, genuine') and こと (koto, 'word, speech; affair, fact'), reflecting the archaic Japanese cultural ideal in which 'true words' and 'true reality' are one and the same. Written with the kanji 誠 ('sincerity').

history.meaning: true words, genuine fact, fidelity
truly, genuinely, indeed, sincerely

誠に.notes: Belongs to a formal, elevated register. Frequently heard in ceremonial apologies (誠に申し訳ございません, 'I am truly sorry') and formal expressions of gratitude (誠にありがとうございます).

誠実.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read seijitsu, combining 誠 (sei, from Middle Chinese *dzyeng, 'sincere, true, authentic', composed of 言 'speech' and 成 'accomplish, complete' — words fulfilled in deed) and 実 (jitsu, shinjitai of 實, from Middle Chinese *zyit, 'fruit, seed; full, solid, real, true'). Together they express a character whose speech and inner substance are wholly genuine and unfeigned.

history.meaning: true and substantial; unfeigned in speech and conduct
sincere, honest, faithful, conscientious (na-adjective and noun)

morphemes.meaning: sincere, true, words fulfilled in deed (sei)

誠実.notes: Functions as both a noun and a na-adjective (誠実な人, 'an honest/conscientious person'; 誠実に対応する, 'to respond in good faith'). Describes steady moral integrity rather than mere factual truthfulness (正直).

誠意.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read seii, uniting 誠 (sei, from Middle Chinese *dzyeng, 'sincerity, truthfulness, authenticity') and 意 (i, from Middle Chinese *'ijH, 'thought, intention, mind, heart', graphically 音 'sound/voice' over 心 'heart'). Rooted in the core Neo-Confucian doctrine of 誠意 ('making one's intentions sincere') from the Great Learning (大学, Dàxué), where moral self-cultivation begins with purifying the mind's motives.

history.meaning: making one's inner intentions pure and unfeigned (Confucian moral cultivation)
sincerity, good faith, earnest goodwill shown through action

誠意.notes: In Japanese social and underworld contexts, 誠意を見せる ('to show one's sincerity') often euphemistically implies offering tangible compensation, restitution, or apology money rather than mere words.

誤る.etymology: Native Japanese verb ('to make a mistake, err, be misled'), continuing Old Japanese *ayamaru*, attested in the Nihon Shoki (etymologically the same verb as 謝る 'to apologize', which developed from 'admit one's error and beg pardon').

history.form: あやまる (誤る / 過る)
history.meaning: err; make a mistake; do wrong
make a mistake; err; misjudge

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 誤る

説明.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('explanation, exposition, description'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 説明, composed of 説 (せつ 'expound, explain, discourse') + 明 (めい 'make clear, illuminate').

history.meaning: expound and make clear
explanation; description; account

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 説明

読ませる.etymology: The term '読ませる' (meaning 'let me read') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: let me read
let me read

読ませる.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 読ませる

読みやすい.etymology: Native Japanese compound adjective ('easy to read, legible, readable'), formed from 読み (よみ, stem of 読む 'to read') + やすい (易い 'easy to do').

history.form: 読みやすい (よみやすい)
history.meaning: easy to read; legible; readable

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 読む

読み終わる.etymology: Native Japanese word. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 読み終わる

読む.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to read, recite, chant; count; predict'), continuing Old Japanese *yomu* (four-grade *yom-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, where its primary sense was 'to count aloud one by one, enumerate' and hence 'to pronounce written characters in sequence or chant a text'.

history.meaning: count aloud; enumerate; recite a text
read; recite; decipher; read (a situation)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 読む

読書.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('reading books'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 読書 (Middle Chinese *duwk-syo*), composed of 読 (どく 'read aloud, study') + 書 (しょ 'book, writing').

history.meaning: read and study books
reading books

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 読書

読書ランプ.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and Western loanword compound ('reading lamp'), combining Sino-Japanese 読書 (どくしょ 'reading books') + ランプ (borrowed from Dutch/English *lamp*).

history.form: 読書ランプ (どくしょランプ)
history.meaning: reading lamp

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 読書

誰.etymology: Interrogative personal pronoun ('who'), reshaped in Late Middle / Early Modern Japanese from classical たれ (誰, Old Japanese *tare*, formed from interrogative root *ta* 'who' + pronominal suffix *-re*, parallel to *kore* / *sore* / *are*), with initial voicing *t-* > *d-* by analogy with the *do-* series (どれ, どこ, どの).

history.meaning: who
who

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 誰

誰か.etymology: Indefinite personal pronoun ('someone, somebody, anyone'), formed from interrogative pronoun 誰 (だれ 'who') + indefinite/interrogative particle か.

history.meaning: someone; somebody

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 誰か

誰も.etymology: Inclusive and negative-polarity personal pronoun ('everyone, anyone; [with negative] no one, nobody'), formed from interrogative pronoun 誰 (だれ 'who') + inclusive particle も ('also, even').

history.meaning: everyone; no one (with negative)
everyone; no one / nobody (with negative)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 誰も

cognates.meaning: section chief, head of an administrative division
section chief, manager of a department division

課長.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read kachō, composed of 課 (ka, from Middle Chinese *khwaH, 'to test, examine, assess, assign a quota or duty; administrative section') and 長 (chō, from Middle Chinese *trjangX, 'long; elder, senior, chief, head'). Coined in Meiji-era bureaucratic and corporate organization to designate the head of a 課 (ka, 'section'), the foundational operational unit inside a ministry or company.

history.meaning: assigned quota/division + elder/leader
chief of an administrative or corporate section (middle-management rank)

課長.notes: In the standard Japanese corporate hierarchy, 課長 (section chief) sits above 係長 (kakarichō, subsection chief) and below 部長 (buchō, department director). Used directly as a title of address (e.g., 田中課長 or simply 課長).

rootFamily.gloss: department director, general manager (one rank above kachō)

調.etymology: As Sino-Japanese ちょう ('musical key, tonality, tune, tone, style'), borrowed from Middle Chinese 調 (*dew* / *dewH* 'harmonize, musical mode, melody'); as native しらべ ('melody, tune; investigation'), nominalized from 調べる (*shiraberu* 'to tune strings, examine').

history.meaning: harmonize; musical mode or key; melody
musical key; tone; style / melody; inquiry

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 調

調べる.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to examine, investigate, check, look up; tune or play a musical instrument'), continuing Heian lower bigrade *sirabu* (調ぶ, stem *sirabe-* 'to harmonize musical tones, match and verify'), related to 知る (*shiru* 'to know, discern').

history.meaning: tune and play an instrument; verify; investigate
examine; investigate; check; look up

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 調べる

調べ物.etymology: Native Yamato compound noun (wago) read shirabemono, formed from 調べ (shirabe, the continuative/ren'yōkei nominalization of the verb 調べる shiraberu, 'to investigate, check, examine; originally to tune an instrument or align') and 物 (mono, 'thing, matter, task'). The verb shiraberu derives from Classical Japanese しらぶ (shirabu), itself linked to 知る (shiru, 'to know, perceive'), evolving from 'making sounds/facts known and harmonious' to 'investigating or looking something up'.

history.meaning: to tune strings, harmonize; to inquire into and verify facts
matter to be checked or looked up; reference research task

morphemes.meaning: investigating, checking, looking up (nominalized stem of shiraberu)

調べ物.notes: Used for practical, everyday information-gathering or library/archival lookup (図書館で調べ物をする, 'to look things up at the library'), whereas 研究 (kenkyū) or 調査 (chōsa) sound formal or academic.

rootFamily.gloss: to investigate, check, look up, examine

cognates.meaning: musical tone, pitch; manner, air (often borderline/eccentric in modern slang)

調子.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read chōshi, combining 調 (chō, from Middle Chinese *deuH, 'musical mode, pitch, tune, harmony; to regulate') and the nominal suffix 子 (shi, from Middle Chinese *tsiX, originally 'child', used across Tang-era Chinese as a noun formative). Borrowed into Japanese through gagaku (court music) theory to denote the specific pitch, key, and rhythmic tempo of a piece before metaphorically expanding to mean a person's or machine's working condition, momentum, and conversational manner.

history.meaning: musical pitch, modal tuning, and rhythmic meter in court music (gagaku)
tone of voice; physical or mechanical condition; momentum, form, stride

調子.notes: Extremely versatile in idioms reflecting the musical metaphor: 調子に乗る (chōshi ni noru, 'to get carried away / let success go to one's head', literally 'ride the rhythm'), 調子がいい ('to be in great form' or 'glib/opportunistic').

rootFamily.gloss: good condition, smooth progress, favorable form
slump, bad condition, out of form

調律.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 調律 (ちょうりつ), uniting 調 ('harmonize, adjust') and 律 ('standard pitch pipe, musical law').
調律.notes: Refers specifically to bringing musical strings or pipes into exact pitch harmony.

調査.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun and suru-verb ('investigation, survey, inquiry, inspection'), composed of 調 (ちょう 'examine, harmonize, check') + 査 (さ 'inspect, look into, verify').

history.meaning: investigation; survey; inquiry

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 調査

調査員.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('investigator, inspector, surveyor, examiner'), formed from 調査 (ちょうさ 'investigation, survey') + suffix -員 (-いん 'member, staff, official').

history.meaning: investigator; surveyor; inspector

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 調査員

諦める.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to give up, abandon, resign oneself to'), continuing Old and Heian Japanese lower bigrade *akiramu* (諦む / 明らむ 'to make clear, shed light on the truth, discern why things are so'), derived from the root *akira-* (seen in 明らか *akiraka* 'bright, clear, evident'). Under Buddhist influence ('clearly perceiving karmic truth and letting go of attachment'), its meaning shifted in Early Modern Japanese to 'resign oneself, give up'.

history.form: あきらむ (明らむ / 諦む)
history.meaning: make clear; discern the truth; calm one's mind
resign oneself to; give up; abandon

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 諦める

諸事情.etymology: Sino-Japanese trimorphemic compound (kango) read shojijō, formed by prefixing 諸 (sho, from Middle Chinese *tsyo, 'various, several, many, all') to the compound 事情 (jijō, 'circumstances, situation, reasons'), which itself combines 事 (ji, from Middle Chinese *dzriH, 'affair, matter, event') and 情 (jō, from Middle Chinese *dzjeng, 'feeling; actual state of affairs, reality, condition'). Literally 'the various realities of affairs'.

history.meaning: actual conditions and underlying realities of a matter
various (often unspecified) circumstances or reasons

諸事情.notes: Frequently used in polite formulaic phrase 諸事情により (shojijō ni yori, 'due to various circumstances') to diplomatically avoid stating embarrassing, confidential, or complicated reasons for a cancellation or resignation.

諸経費.etymology: Sino-Japanese accounting and business compound (kango) read shokeihi, built by attaching the plural/collective prefix 諸 (sho, from Middle Chinese *tsyo, 'various, sundry, miscellaneous') to 経費 (keihi, 'operating expenses, overhead'). 経費 combines 経 (kei, shinjitai of 經, from Middle Chinese *keng, 'warp threads; to pass through, manage, administer, regular') and 費 (hi, from Middle Chinese *phjijH, 'to expend, consume, outlay, cost'). Literally 'sundry administrative outlays'.

history.meaning: regular expenditure required to run an administration or enterprise
miscellaneous overhead expenses, incidental fees and costs

諸経費.notes: Standard accounting and real-estate term covering all incidental costs (registration taxes, brokerage fees, administrative charges, utilities) beyond the base price of an item or property.

謎.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('riddle, enigma, mystery, puzzle'), shortened from Heian–Middle Japanese *nazo-nazo* (謎々), which arose from the formulaic riddle-posing question 何ぞ (*nanzo* < *nani zo* 'What is it?').

history.form: なぞ / なぞなぞ (何ぞ → 謎)
history.meaning: 'What is it?' → verbal riddle
riddle; mystery; enigma; puzzle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 謎

謝る.etymology: Native Yamato verb (wago) read ayamaru, attested in Old Japanese with the core sense 'to err, make a mistake, deviate from the proper way' (derived from the bound root aya-, 'strange, awry, extraordinary', or related to ayabu, 'to be in danger/falter'). During the Edo period, acknowledging that one had 'erred' (あやまる) became the standard verbal formula for begging pardon, splitting orthographically into 誤る ('to make an error') and 謝る ('to apologize').

history.meaning: to go astray, make a mistake, commit an error or fault
to admit one's fault and beg pardon; to apologize; to be baffled/defeated by

謝る.notes: Etymologically the exact same native word as 誤る (ayamaru, 'to make a mistake')—apologizing in Japanese originally meant stating 'I have erred'. Contrast with the formal Sino-Japanese noun 謝罪する (shazai suru).

rootFamily.gloss: to make a mistake, err (etymological doublet)
going all-out to apologize, begging pardon earnestly

cognates.meaning: to apologize, admit an offense and beg pardon
apology, atonement for a fault or offense
to apologize for an offense, ask forgiveness for a crime

謝罪.etymology: Sino-Japanese verb-object compound (kango) read shazai, combining 謝 (sha, from Middle Chinese *zjaeH, 'to decline, take leave; to confess a fault, apologize; to thank', composed of 言 'speech' and 射 'shoot/release' — releasing words of acknowledgment) and 罪 (zai, from Middle Chinese *dzwojX, 'transgression, offense, crime, guilt'). Literally 'to acknowledge and beg pardon for one's offense'.

history.meaning: to confess a transgression and beg clemency from a superior or sovereign
formal apology, public admission of wrongdoing and contrition

謝罪.notes: Much weightier and more formal than お詫び (owabi) or 謝る (ayamaru); standard in press conferences (謝罪会見, shazai kaiken) and legal/corporate scandals where serious culpability is admitted.

譜面台.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('music stand'), formed from 譜面 (ふめん 'sheet music, musical score', from 譜 'musical notation' + 面 'surface, page') + 台 (だい 'stand, rack, support').

history.meaning: music stand

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 譜面台

cognates.meaning: to stand guard, take precautions, security guard duty

警備.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read keibi, composed of 警 (kei, from Middle Chinese *kjengX, 'to warn, admonish, be vigilant, guard against', combining 敬 'respectful attentiveness' and 言 'words') and 備 (bi, from Middle Chinese *bjijH, 'to prepare, make ready, equip against danger'). Attested in Chinese dynastic histories for military garrison readiness and adopted in modern Japanese for security guarding and policing operations.

history.meaning: vigilant military readiness against enemy attack or insurrection
security patrol, guarding of premises or events, security guard services

警備.notes: Used both as a verbal noun (警備する, 'to guard / provide security') and in compounds like 警備員 (keibiin, 'security guard'). Distinct from 警察 (police), as 警備 includes private security firms.

警官.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read keikan, serves as a syllabic contraction of 警察官 (keisatsukan, 'police officer'), combining 警 (kei, from Middle Chinese *kjengX, 'to keep watch, warn, police') and 官 (kan, from Middle Chinese *kwan, 'government official, public servant, magistrate'). Coined in Meiji Japan during the establishment of a modern Western-style uniformed police force and subsequently borrowed into Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: commissioned state police official in the Meiji administrative system
police officer, policeman/policewoman (everyday shortened form)

morphemes.meaning: police, keep watch, guard (kei, from 警察 keisatsu)

警官.notes: 警官 is the standard everyday word in news reports and conversation for 'police officer', whereas 警察官 (keisatsukan) is the full official statutory title and お巡りさん (omawarisan) is the friendly colloquial term.

警察.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read keisatsu, combining 警 (kei, from Middle Chinese *kjengX, 'to warn, guard against, keep watch') and 察 (satsu, from Middle Chinese *tshret, 'to examine closely, inspect, investigate, discern'). Although attested in Tang-dynasty Chinese texts in the verbal sense 'to stay vigilant and inspect closely', it was repurposed in early Meiji Japan (1871–1874, notably by Kawaji Toshiyoshi) to translate French police and English police, and was later exported as a modern institutional loanword across East Asia.

history.meaning: to keep vigilant watch and closely inspect administrative matters
modern state police system, police force, or police station (translating French/English police)

morphemes.meaning: warn, keep watch, guard against crime (kei)

警察.notes: Can refer to the police institution as a whole, a local police station (警察に行く), or colloquially a police officer on the scene (警察が来た). A classic Meiji wasei-kango (Japanese-repurposed Sino-compound) adopted throughout East Asia.

cognates.meaning: member of a legislative assembly, parliamentarian (borrowed from Japanese)
member of the National Assembly or local council

議員.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read giin, composed of 議 (gi, from Middle Chinese *ngjeH, 'to deliberate, discuss, debate policy', formed from 言 'words' and 義 'what is right/proper') and 員 (in, from Middle Chinese *hjwien, 'round vessel; number, personnel, member of an organization'). Coined in Meiji Japan during the creation of constitutional assemblies and the Imperial Diet (1890) to designate an elected member of a deliberative legislature.

history.meaning: to deliberate state affairs + official personnel/member
member of a legislative assembly, parliamentarian, Diet or council member

議員.notes: Exact homophone of 医院 (iin, 'medical clinic') and 委員 (iin, 'committee member'), though pitch accent and context distinguish them. Often specified as 国会議員 (Member of the National Diet).

譲る.etymology: Native Yamato godan verb (wago) read yuzuru, attested in Old Japanese as yuduru ('to hand over, yield, bequeath, defer to another'). Possibly derived from an archaic verbal root related to ゆつ (yutsu / utsuru, 'to shift, transfer from one place or holder to another'). Mapped onto the Chinese character 譲 (shinjitai of 讓, meaning 'to yield politely, cede, defer in accordance with ritual propriety').

history.meaning: to hand down a throne, office, or estate; to defer politely to another
to hand over, transfer ownership, give up (a seat/right), refuse to compromise (with negative)

譲る.notes: Spans polite everyday deference (席を譲る, 'to give up one's seat'), commercial transfer (権利を譲る, 'to hand over rights'), and stubbornness when negated: 一歩も譲らない ('will not yield a single inch').

rootFamily.gloss: transfer, assignment, conveyance of rights or property

豚.etymology: Native Japanese word (wago) read buta ('domestic pig, pork'), first attested from the late Muromachi and early Edo periods alongside increased contact with Ryukyuan, Chinese, and European trade in Kyushu. Previously, Japanese used 猪 (i / inoshishi) or 豕 (i) for both wild boar and swine. The word buta likely arose as a sound-symbolic root *bu- ('grunting or snorting noise; plump, bloated', seen in ぶうぶう būbū 'oink' and ぶと- / 太い futoi 'fat, thick') plus a nominal suffix -ta. Written with the kanji 豚 (originally 'suckling pig' in Chinese, composed of 肉/月 'flesh' + 豕 'swine').

history.meaning: wild boar or swine generally (pre-modern Japanese)
domesticated pig, hog; pork; (derogatory) fat or greedy person
history.stage: Late Muromachi / Edo to Modern Japanese

morphemes.meaning: pig, hog, pork (native reading of 豚)

豚.notes: Read buta as a standalone noun and in native compounds (豚肉 butaniku, 'pork'; 豚汁 tonjiru or butajiru), and read ton in Sino-Japanese compounds (豚カツ tonkatsu, 養豚 yōton 'pig farming'). Also used as a harsh insult ('pig!').

rootFamily.word: 豚の貯金箱 (ぶたのちょきんばこ)

cognates.meaning: pig's trotters (usually 豬蹄 / 豬腳 in Mandarin; 豚足 in Classical/dialectal usage)
pig's trotters (ordinarily called 족발 jokbal in everyday Korean)

豚足.etymology: Sino-Japanese culinary compound (kango) read tonsoku, combining 豚 (ton, from Middle Chinese *dwon, 'suckling pig, domesticated swine', formed from 月/肉 'flesh' and 豕 'pig') and 足 (soku, from Middle Chinese *tsjowk, 'foot, leg, trotter'). Popularized in Japan through Okinawan cuisine (where braised pig's feet are natively called てびち tebichi), Chinese cooking, and postwar Korean-Japanese yakiniku/horumon street stalls.

history.meaning: swine + foot/leg
pig's trotters (braised or grilled as a collagen-rich delicacy and bar snack)

豚足.notes: Uses the Sino-Japanese on'yomi reading of both characters (ton-soku), unlike 豚肉 (buta-niku, which mixes kun'yomi and on'yomi). A staple dish in izakaya, yakiniku restaurants, and Okinawan cuisine.

rootFamily.word: 両足 (りょうあし / りょうそく)

象徴.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read shōchō, combining 象 (shō, from Middle Chinese *zjangX, originally 'elephant', extended via the carving of ivory figurines to mean 'image, likeness, figure, phenomenon') and 徴 (chō, shinjitai of 徵, from Middle Chinese *trjeng, 'to summon, verify; sign, token, symptom, manifestation'). Coined by Meiji philosopher Nakae Chōmin in his 1883 translation of Eugène Véron's L'Esthétique (維氏美学) to render French symbole, and subsequently adopted throughout East Asia.

history.meaning: visible figure/image + outward sign or token
symbol, emblem (coined in 1883 by Nakae Chōmin to translate French symbole)

象徴.notes: Famously enshrined in Article 1 of the 1947 Constitution of Japan, which defines the Emperor as the 'symbol of the State and of the unity of the People' (日本国の象徴). Also used verbally with する.

豪華.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read gōka, composed of 豪 (gō, from Middle Chinese *haw, 'porcupine quill; heroic, bold, powerful, grand, unrestrained in scale or wealth') and 華 (ka, from Middle Chinese *xwae, 'blossom, flower; splendid, ornate, resplendent, flourishing'). In Classical Chinese it described powerful, ostentatious clans before coming to denote lavish material splendor and dazzling luxury.

history.meaning: powerful, wealthy, and ostentatious in lifestyle (of aristocratic clans)
lavish, luxurious, sumptuous, extravagant (na-adjective and noun)

morphemes.meaning: grand, bold, powerful, on a vast scale (gō)

豪華.notes: A na-adjective (豪華な食事, 'a lavish meal'; 豪華キャスト, 'an all-star cast') iconic of Japan's 1980s Bubble Era aesthetic of ostentatious wealth and spectacle.

rootFamily.gloss: magnificent, grand, lavish and dazzling (four-character idiom)
rootFamily.word: 豪華絢爛 (ごうかけんらん)

負ける.etymology: Native Yamato ichidan verb (wago) read makeru, from Old Japanese maku (shimo-nidan conjugation, 'to be defeated, yield, succumb'). Etymologically derived from an older transitive-intransitive root *mak- meaning 'to turn away, bow down, retreat, give way before superior force'. Written with the kanji 負, which in Chinese originally depicted a person (人) bearing a cowrie shell/burden (貝) on their back — turning one's back in battle and bearing the burden of defeat.

history.meaning: to yield, be vanquished in battle or contest, succumb to
to lose (a game, fight, or struggle); to give a discount (yield on price); to break out in a rash from

負ける.notes: In addition to 'losing' a contest or refusing to give in (負けないぞ, 'I won't lose!'), 負ける colloquially means 'to knock down the price / give a bargain' in shopping (少し負けてよ, 'give me a discount!').

rootFamily.gloss: sore loser, hating to lose, competitive spirit
rootFamily.word: 負けず嫌い (まけずぎらい)

cognates.meaning: to be in debt; financial liabilities, debt

負債.etymology: Sino-Japanese financial compound (kango) read fusai, originally a Classical Chinese verb-object construction meaning 'to carry a debt on one's back'. Combines 負 (fu, from Middle Chinese *bjuwX, 'to carry on the back, bear a burden, owe', from 人 'person' + 貝 'cowrie money') and 債 (sai, from Middle Chinese *tsreh, 'financial debt, obligation to repay', from 人 'person' + 責 'demand payment/duty'). In modern accounting, it serves as the technical term for 'liabilities'.

history.meaning: to bear a monetary debt; money owed to a creditor
financial debt, corporate liabilities, accumulated losses owed to creditors

morphemes.meaning: bear on one's back, owe, carry a burden (fu)

負債.notes: More formal and technical than 借金 (shakkin, everyday personal 'borrowed money / debt'). Standard in corporate bankruptcies (負債総額, 'total liabilities') and accounting balance sheets opposite 資産 (shisan, 'assets').

rootFamily.gloss: burden, share of expenses or responsibility

財布.etymology: Sino-Japanese word. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: wealth/money + cloth/pouch
wallet

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 財布

cognates.meaning: contribution, service to a cause or society

貢献.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read kōken, joining two near-synonymous Classical Chinese verbs of tribute: 貢 (kō, from Middle Chinese *kuwngH, 'to present local goods as tribute to a sovereign', composed of 工 'work/skill' phonetic and 貝 'cowrie/valuables') and 献 (ken, shinjitai of 獻, from Middle Chinese *xjonH, 'to offer up a sacrificial vessel or precious gift to a ruler or ancestral spirit'). From literal feudal tribute, the word generalized in modern Japanese to mean 'contributing positively to a cause, organization, or society'.

history.meaning: presenting regional tribute and ritual offerings to the imperial court
contribution, valuable service rendered to society, science, or an enterprise

morphemes.meaning: offer tribute, present valuables to a ruler (kō)

貢献.notes: Takes the particle に to mark the beneficiary (社会に貢献する, 'to contribute to society'; 売上に貢献する, 'to contribute to sales'). Always carries a positive nuance, unlike 寄与 (kiyo), which can be neutral/analytical.

rootFamily.gloss: tribute goods presented to a court or overlord

cognates.meaning: to traffic in, peddle, sell (often illicit goods in modern Mandarin, e.g. 販毒)

販売.etymology: Sino-Japanese commercial compound (kango) read hanbai, uniting 販 (han, from Middle Chinese *pjwonH, 'to buy and sell as a merchant, trade, traffic in goods', formed from 貝 'cowrie money' and 反 'turn over/exchange') and 売 (bai, shinjitai of 賣, from Middle Chinese *meaH, 'to sell, dispose of goods for money'). While in Classical Chinese it referred broadly to mercantile peddling, in modern Japanese it is the standard formal term for commercial sales, marketing, and retail distribution.

history.meaning: mercantile buying and selling of commodities in the marketplace
commercial sales, retail marketing, and distribution of products

販売.notes: False friend alert with Mandarin Chinese: in Japanese (and Korean 판매), 販売 is completely neutral and formal ('retail sales', as in 自動販売機 jidō-hanbaiki, 'vending machine'), whereas Mandarin 販賣 (fànmài) often implies illicit trafficking.

rootFamily.word: 自動販売機 (じどうはんばいき)

rootFamily.gloss: mail order, online shopping (contraction of 通信販売)
sale, putting on the market, release

販売中止.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read hanbai chūshi, joining 販売 (hanbai, 'commercial sales, distribution', from 販 'trade' + 売 'sell') and 中止 (chūshi, 'stopping midway, suspension, cancellation', from 中, Middle Chinese *trjuwng, 'middle, halfway', and 止, Middle Chinese *tsyiX, 'foot; to stop, halt, cease'). Literally 'halting commercial sales in the middle of distribution'.

history.meaning: commercial selling + halting midway / suspension
discontinuation of sales, pulling a product from shelves or circulation

販売中止.notes: Common in media, publishing, and consumer commerce when a product, book, or video is pulled from distribution due to regulatory crackdowns, defects, or scandals (販売中止になる, 'to be pulled from sale').

rootFamily.gloss: ban on publication or sale (contraction of 発売禁止)

販売本数.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read hanbai honsū, combining 販売 (hanbai, 'commercial sales', from 販 'trade' + 売 'sell') with 本数 (honsū, 'number of cylindrical/bound/reeled items'). 本 (hon, from Middle Chinese *pwonX, originally 'tree root/trunk', used in Japanese as the classifier for long cylindrical objects, scrolls, film reels, VHS cassettes, and software titles) joins 数 (sū, shinjitai of 數, from Middle Chinese *srjuH, 'number, count').

history.meaning: count of long cylindrical items, scrolls, or film reels
total number of copies/units sold (specifically for video tapes, films, or software)

morphemes.meaning: counter for reels, tapes, films, software, or long items (hon)

販売本数.notes: Because films, VHS videotapes, and video games are counted with the classifier 本 (-hon/-pon/-bon, originally for rolled scrolls and film reels), 販売本数 is the exact industry metric for video tape or game copies sold (whereas books use 販売部数).

rootFamily.gloss: number of cylindrical items, tapes, films, or bottles
number of copies sold/printed (for books, magazines, newspapers)

cognates.meaning: responsibility, duty, liability (reinforced via Meiji Japanese)

責任.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound (kango) read sekinin, composed of 責 (seki, from Middle Chinese *tsrek, 'to demand payment of a debt, hold to account, reprove; duty') and 任 (nin, from Middle Chinese *nyimH, 'to carry on a shoulder pole, bear a charge, entrust with an office'). Attested in Classical Chinese legal-administrative prose and standardized in Meiji Japan to translate English responsibility and German Verantwortung in modern law and ethics.

history.meaning: to hold an official accountable for an entrusted charge or duty
legal, moral, or institutional responsibility and liability (translating English responsibility)

morphemes.meaning: entrust, bear an office or burden (nin)

責任.notes: Central to Japanese organizational culture in phrases like 責任を取る (sekinin wo toru, 'to take responsibility', which often implies resigning from one's post to atone for a failure) and 責任者 (sekininsha, 'person in charge').

rootFamily.gloss: person in charge, supervisor, responsible party

買い上げる.etymology: Native Yamato compound verb (wago) read kaiageru, formed by joining 買い (kai, the continuative stem of 買う kau < Classical かふ kafu, 'to buy, purchase', originally 'to exchange, barter', cognate with 換える kaeru) and the auxiliary/completive verb 上げる (ageru, 'to raise up; to complete thoroughly; to procure for a higher authority'). The directional component 上げる conveys both buying up a stock completely and purchasing goods on behalf of an institution or government.

history.meaning: for a lord or government authority to purchase goods from commoners; to buy up stock
to buy up (entire stock or assets); to purchase (polite/honorific or institutional procurement)

morphemes.meaning: raise up, complete thoroughly, buy up (ageru)

買い上げる.notes: Has two distinct uses: (1) commercially buying up supplies or assets in bulk (在庫を買い上げる), and (2) as the humble/polite retail noun お買い上げ (okaiage) heard in every Japanese shop: お買い上げありがとうございます ('Thank you for your purchase').

rootFamily.word: お買い上げ (おかいあげ)

rootFamily.gloss: buying out, outright purchase (without return rights or royalties)

買い取る.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) compound verb (複合動詞, fukugō dōshi) formed from 買い (kai, the continuative stem or 連用形 of 買う kau, from Classical Japanese かふ kafu, Old Japanese kapu 'to exchange, trade, buy') and 取る (toru, from Old Japanese toru 'to take in hand, seize, acquire'). Combining commercial purchase with physical taking yields the sense of buying something outright or buying out all available stock.

history.meaning: to exchange/buy + to take hold of
to purchase and take into one's possession
to buy up, to buy out, to purchase outright

morphemes.meaning: to take, to acquire, to claim

買い取る.notes: A transitive godan verb (買い取る, kaitoru); its nominalized form 買取 (kaitori) is ubiquitous on storefronts for secondhand buyback shops in Japan.

買い手.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('buyer, purchaser'), formed from 買い (かい, nominalized stem of 買う 'to buy') + 手 (て 'hand; person performing an action or role').

history.meaning: buyer; purchaser

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 買い手

買い物.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 買い (stem of 買う 'to buy') and 物 (もの, 'things, goods'), attested from early-modern townspeople speech for everyday shopping.

買い物袋.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('shopping bag'), formed from 買い物 (かいもの 'shopping, purchased goods', from 買い 'buying' + 物 'thing') + 袋 (ふくろ → ぶくろ with rendaku, 'bag, sack').

history.form: 買い物袋 (かいものぶくろ)
history.meaning: shopping bag

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 買い物

買う.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to buy, purchase; value, appreciate; incur'), continuing Old Japanese *kapu* (four-grade *kap-*), attested in the Man'yōshū; etymologically identical to 換ふ / 替ふ (*kapu* 'to exchange, barter, trade one thing for another').

history.meaning: exchange; barter; buy
buy; purchase; value

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 買う

買える.etymology: The regular potential form (可能動詞, kanō dōshi) of the native Japanese (wago) godan verb 買う (kau, 'to buy', earlier かふ kafu < Old Japanese kapu 'to barter, exchange').
