Formed by shifting the final stem vowel from -a/-u to -e and attaching the ichidan suffix -ru, a productive morphological pattern for consonant-stem potential verbs that consolidated during the late Muromachi and Edo periods.

history.meaning: to exchange, to barter, to buy
to purchase, to trade for value
can buy, to be able to afford or purchase

morphemes.meaning: can, to be able to (ichidan potential marker)

買える.notes: Conjugates as a regular ichidan verb (買えない kaenai, 買えます kaemasu) and normally marks the purchasable item with が (ga) rather than を (o).

貸し.etymology: Deverbal noun converted from the continuative stem (連用形, ren'yōkei) of the native Japanese (wago) verb 貸す (kasu, 'to lend, to rent out'), attested in Old Japanese as kasu. Beyond literal financial lending or extending credit, it developed a strong interpersonal sense in Japanese reciprocity culture: a favor owed by someone else, contrasted with 借り (kari, a debt or obligation one owes).

history.meaning: to lend; the act of lending
lending, a loan, credit extended
loan, credit, favor owed by another person

morphemes.meaning: lending, loaning (nominalized stem of 貸す kasu)

貸し.notes: Frequently used in the idiom 貸しを作る (kashi o tsukuru, 'to put someone in one's debt / do someone a favor they will have to repay').

rootFamily.gloss: to lend, to loan, to rent out
lending and borrowing; give and take

貸し出し.etymology: Native Japanese word. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 貸し出し

貸し切り.etymology: Native Japanese compound verbal noun ('chartering, reserving exclusively, private hire'), nominalized from 貸し切る (*kashikiru*, from 貸し, stem of 貸す 'to lend, rent out' + 切る 'to cut off, do completely or exclusively').

history.meaning: exclusive rental; private charter or reservation

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 貸し切り

貸す.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to lend, loan, rent out, hire out'), continuing Old Japanese *kasu* (four-grade *kas-*), attested in the Man'yōshū, paired with 借りる / 借る (*karu* 'to borrow').

history.meaning: lend; loan
lend; loan; rent out

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 貸す

費用.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 費 (hi, from Middle Chinese *phj+jH 'to expend, squander; expense', containing the cowrie-shell wealth radical 貝) and 用 (yō, from Middle Chinese *jowngH 'to use, employ; outlay'). Already attested in Classical Chinese administrative prose for funds expended for a specific purpose, it entered Japanese as standard financial and bureaucratic terminology.

history.meaning: to expend and use; expenditure, outlay
expenditure, financial outlay, cost
expenses, cost, expenditure

費用.notes: Refers specifically to money spent to accomplish an activity or project (e.g., 制作費用 seisaku hiyō, 'production costs'), whereas 値段 (nedan) refers to retail price tags.

貼る.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to stick, paste, affix, attach a flat sheet'), continuing Old Japanese *paru* (four-grade *par-* 'to stretch taut, spread out over a surface'); written with 貼 when specifying pasting or sticking paper, labels, or patches onto a surface.

history.meaning: stretch or spread across a surface
stick; paste; affix (a label, poster, or patch)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 貼る

賃貸契約.etymology: Sino-Japanese legal and commercial compound noun ('lease agreement, rental contract'), combining 賃貸 (ちんたい 'leasing out, renting out for a fee', from 賃 'hire, rent' + 貸 'lend') + 契約 (けいやく 'contract, agreement').

history.form: 賃貸契約 (ちんたいけいやく)
history.meaning: lease agreement; rental contract

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 賃貸

資本力.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) derivative formed by adding the suffix -力 (-ryoku, from Middle Chinese *lik 'physical strength, power, capability') to the noun 資本 (shihon, 'capital', composed of 資 shi 'resources, wealth' + 本 hon 'root, foundation, principal fund', used since the Meiji period to translate English 'capital'). It denotes the sheer scale and leverage of an enterprise's backing capital.

history.meaning: principal fund; economic capital (Meiji translational coinage)
financial capital power, corporate financial clout

資本力.notes: Often used in business contexts (e.g., 圧倒的な資本力 attōteki na shihonryoku, 'overwhelming capital power') when large corporations outspend smaller rivals.

資金.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 資 (shi, from Middle Chinese *tsij 'provisions, property, resources, material backing', containing the cowrie radical 貝) and 金 (kin, from Middle Chinese *kim 'metal, gold, money'). It denotes liquid money or financial resources earmarked to fund business operations, investments, or enterprises.

history.meaning: resources/wealth + metal/money
working funds, liquid capital, financing

資金.notes: Whereas 資本 (shihon) refers to structural equity or economic capital in the abstract, 資金 (shikin) refers to usable cash and liquid funds needed to run a project.

資金力.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound built from 資金 (shikin, 'liquid funds, working capital', from 資 shi 'resources' + 金 kin 'money') and the productive capacity suffix 力 (ryoku, from Middle Chinese *lik 'strength, power, capability'). It denotes an individual's or organization's practical ability to mobilize cash and sustain heavy spending.

history.meaning: funds, working capital
financial power, cash reserves capacity, deep pockets

資金力.notes: Collocates frequently with 豊富な (hōfu na, 'abundant') or 潤沢な (juntaku na, 'ample') to mean having 'deep pockets'.

資金調達.etymology: A four-character Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 資金 (shikin, 'funds, capital', from 資 shi 'resources' + 金 kin 'money') and 調達 (chōtatsu, 'procurement, supply, fulfillment', from 調 chō < Middle Chinese *duw 'to arrange, prepare, levy' + 達 tatsu < Middle Chinese *dat 'to reach, accomplish, deliver'). Originally used for procuring military or administrative supplies, 調達 came to mean raising capital when paired with 資金.

history.meaning: arranging and delivering required supplies or taxes
fundraising, raising capital, corporate financing

資金調達.notes: The standard formal business and venture-capital term for raising capital (via bank loans, equity rounds, or bond issuance), more formal than 資金集め (shikin atsume).

資金集め.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Japanese and native Japanese (kango + wago) compound combining the Sino-Japanese noun 資金 (shikin, 'funds, working capital', from 資 shi 'resources' + 金 kin 'money') with 集め (atsume, the continuative nominalized stem of the native verb 集める atsumeru 'to gather, collect', from Old Japanese atumu). Literally 'the gathering of funds'.

history.meaning: to bring together, to gather into one place
gathering funds, fundraising, drumming up money

資金集め.notes: More conversational and concrete than 資金調達 (shikin chōtatsu); often evokes hustling to round up investors or donations in person (e.g., 資金集めに奔走する, 'to run around trying to raise money').

資金面.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed from 資金 (shikin, 'funds, capital', from 資 shi 'resources' + 金 kin 'money') and the relational suffix 面 (men, from Middle Chinese *mjienH 'face, surface, aspect, dimension'). Literally 'the funds surface/facet', it singles out the financial dimension of a project as opposed to technical, creative, or personnel aspects.

history.meaning: face, front surface, side
the financial aspect, funding side, monetary dimension

資金面.notes: Almost always followed by the particle で (de) or での (de no), as in 資金面で苦労する (shikinmen de kurō suru, 'to struggle on the financial front').

賛成.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 賛成. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 賛成

賜る.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) honorific/humble verb descending from Old Japanese tamaparu ('to receive respectfully from a social superior'), itself derived via the passive/stative suffix -aru from Old Japanese tamapu (給ふ / 賜ふ, 'for a noble or deity to bestow'), which is further related to the root たب (tabu / たぶ). Because the same kanji 賜 covers both bestowing from above and receiving from below, 賜る functions in modern formal Japanese both as a humble verb ('to humbly receive') and in set polite formulas requesting a favor ('to be granted').

history.meaning: to be bestowed upon by a superior; to humbly receive
to receive from a noble/sovereign; to deign to give
to humbly receive (from a superior); to be honored with (support, patronage)

賜る.notes: Belongs to very high, ceremonial register (ご愛顧を賜る go-aiko o tamawaru, 'to be favored with your patronage'); using it in casual speech sounds either archaic or deliberately theatrical.

rootFamily.gloss: to bestow, to deign to give (classical honorific)
something bestowed; a result or fruit of effort (e.g. 努力の賜物)

賞金.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 賞 (shō, from Middle Chinese *syangX 'to reward merit, bestow a prize; praise', containing the cowrie wealth radical 貝) and 金 (kin, from Middle Chinese *kim 'metal, gold, money'). Historically used for monetary rewards granted by a ruler for military or civic merit, it now covers prize purses in competitions as well as bounties on fugitives.

history.meaning: gold or money bestowed as a reward for merit
monetary reward, prize money, cash bounty

賞金.notes: Covers both legitimate competition prize money (賞金稼ぎ shōkin kasegi can mean either a pro tournament player or a 'bounty hunter').

賠償金.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound formed from 賠償 (baishō, 'indemnification, restitution, reparation', composed of 賠 bai < Middle Chinese *bwoj 'to make good a loss, compensate' + 償 shō < Middle Chinese *dzyang 'to repay, restore value') and 金 (kin, 'money, cash'). Standardized in Meiji civil and international law to translate legal 'damages' and war 'reparations'.

history.meaning: to compensate and repay a loss
monetary damages, financial compensation, indemnity payment

賠償金.notes: In civil lawsuits, 損害賠償金 (songai baishōkin) is compensation for actual losses, whereas 慰謝料 (isharyō) specifically means 'emotional distress / consolation money' (e.g., in divorce or defamation).

rootFamily.gloss: to compensate, to make up for, to atone

賢い.etymology: The term '賢い' (meaning 'clever') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: clever
clever

賢い.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 賢い

賢明.etymology: Sino-Japanese adjectival noun ('wise, sensible, prudent, sagacious'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 賢明, composed of 賢 (けん 'wise, worthy, virtuous') + 明 (めい 'clear-sighted, discerning, bright').

history.meaning: wise and discerning
wise; sensible; prudent

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 賢明

質問.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 質 (shitsu, from Middle Chinese *tsyit 'substance, truth; to verify, confront, pledge') and 問 (mon, from Middle Chinese *mjunH 'to ask, inquire'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Book of Han), 質問 meant 'to verify a point by asking an authority'. In modern Japanese it became the neutral everyday word for 'question'.

history.meaning: to verify the truth or substance of a matter by inquiring
questioning a teacher or authority to resolve doubts
question, inquiry (general and neutral)

質問.notes: Watch out for a Chinese-Japanese false friend: Japanese 質問 (shitsumon) is a polite, neutral 'question', whereas Mandarin 質詢/質問 (zhìwèn) means 'to interrogate or call someone to account' (which in Japanese is 詰問 kitsumon).

購入.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 購 (kō, from Middle Chinese *kuwH 'to seek and buy, purchase with cowries/money', combining the cowrie radical 貝 with phonetic 冓) and 入 (nyū, from Middle Chinese *nyip 'to enter, bring in, acquire'). Literally 'to buy and bring into one's possession', providing a formal Sino-Japanese counterpart to native 買い入れる (kaiireru) and 買う (kau).

history.meaning: to purchase with money + to bring in
purchase, acquisition by buying (formal/commercial)

購入.notes: Used as a formal noun or suru-verb (購入する kōnyū suru) in commerce, contracts, e-commerce buttons, and news reports where 買う (kau) would sound too casual.

rootFamily.gloss: paid subscription (to a newspaper or magazine)

贅沢.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound crafted in Edo-period Japan from 贅 (zei, from Middle Chinese *tsjwejH 'superfluous, excessive, unneeded appendage, wart', containing the wealth radical 貝) and 沢 (taku, traditional 澤, from Middle Chinese *drak 'marsh; moisture, lustre, abundant grace/enrichment'). Combining 'excessive wealth' with 'abundant lustre', it denotes lavishness beyond practical necessity, indulgence, or being spoiled.

history.meaning: superfluous excess + abundant lustre/moisture
extravagance, living or spending beyond one's station
luxurious, extravagant, lavish; spoiled or picky

贅沢.notes: Functions both as a noun (贅沢をする zeitaku o suru, 'to indulge in luxury') and a na-adjective (贅沢な暮し zeitaku na kurashi); saying 贅沢を言うな (zeitaku o iu na) means 'don't be picky / beggars can't be choosers!'.

贈る.etymology: An orthographic specialization of the native Japanese (wago) verb 送る (okuru, from Old Japanese okuru 'to send off, escort, dispatch, transmit'). By applying the Chinese character 贈 (whose meaning in Chinese is 'to bestow a gift, present a keepsake'), Japanese orthography split a single native verb okuru into 送る ('to send physically, see someone off') and 贈る ('to present a gift, confer an award or heartfelt message').

history.meaning: to send, dispatch, convey from one person to another
to send; to present a gift or poem to someone
to present as a gift, to bestow, to confer (an award or tribute)

贈る.notes: Shares the exact same pronunciation and etymology as 送る (okuru, 'to send/mail'); use 贈る specifically when gifting presents, flowers, awards, or words of encouragement (贈る言葉 okuru kotoba).

rootFamily.gloss: to send, to mail, to escort
presentation of a gift or award, donation

赤.etymology: A core native Japanese (wago) color and light term, attested in Old Japanese as aka ('bright light, dawn glow, red'), sharing the same root as 明かし / 明るい (akashi / akarui 'bright, illuminated') and 明く (aku 'for dawn to break'). In prehistoric Japanese color categorization, aka originally denoted the warm, bright pole of the spectrum (dawn sky, firelight) in opposition to kuro ('dark, night-black'), later narrowing to the color red.

history.meaning: brightness, dawn light; bright warm color, red
red, crimson, scarlet; clear/complete (in prefixes)
the color red; financial deficit (from red ink); communist (slang)

赤.notes: Because it derives from 'bright/clear/exposed', 赤 also means 'complete/stark' in idioms like 赤の他人 (aka no tanin, 'a complete stranger') and 赤恥 (akahaji, 'barefaced shame'), while in business it refers to 赤字 (akaji, 'being in the red').

rootFamily.gloss: financial deficit, being in the red

赤い.etymology: Native Japanese color adjective ('red, crimson, scarlet'), continuing Old Japanese *akasi* (stem *aka-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū; derived from the root *aka-* / *ak-* ('bright, radiant, light', shared with 明ける *akeru* 'to grow light, dawn' and 明るい *akarui* 'bright'), originally naming the bright glow of dawn and fire before specializing to red.

history.meaning: bright; radiant; red
red; crimson

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 赤い

走り回る.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) compound verb formed from 走り (hashiri, the continuative stem or 連用形 of 走る hashiru, from Old Japanese pasiru 'to run, rush, dart') and 回る (mawaru, from Classical まはる mafaru 'to turn round, revolve, go around from place to place'). As an auxiliary second verb in compounds, -回る (-mawaru) adds the aspectual meaning 'all around, hither and thither, from place to place'.

history.meaning: to run + to go around in circles
to run all around, to bustle about from place to place

morphemes.meaning: to go around, about, all over the place

走り回る.notes: Used both literally (children or dogs running around a yard) and figuratively for bustling around town on errands or desperately trying to raise money/support.

rootFamily.gloss: to walk all around, to wander about

走る.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to run, rush, dash, travel rapidly'), continuing Old Japanese *pasiru*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū (related to 馳す *pasu* 'to gallop, speed').

history.meaning: run; dart; flow swiftly
run; rush; travel (of vehicles)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 走る

起きる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive upper monograde (kami-ichidan) verb ('to get up, wake up, rise; happen, occur'), continuing Old Japanese upper bigrade *oku* (起く, stem *oki₂-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, paired with transitive 起こす (*okosu*).

history.meaning: rise upright; wake from sleep; occur
get up; wake up; happen; occur

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 起きる

起こす.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to wake [someone] up, raise up, set upright; cause, bring about'), continuing Old Japanese *okosu*, the transitive counterpart of 起きる (*okiru* < *oku*).

history.meaning: raise upright; rouse; initiate
wake up; raise up; cause; start

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 起こす

起訴.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) legal compound formed from 起 (ki, from Middle Chinese *khj+X 'to rise, raise, initiate, launch') and 訴 (so, from Middle Chinese *suH 'to accuse, bring a grievance, sue, appeal to a magistrate'). Literally 'to initiate a formal accusation in court', it was codified in Meiji-era criminal procedure law to denote formal indictment by a public prosecutor, and was subsequently borrowed into modern Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese legal codes.

history.meaning: to initiate/raise + to accuse/appeal to a court
initiation of a lawsuit; formal criminal indictment (Meiji legal codification)

起訴.notes: In Japanese criminal law, prosecutors (検察官) hold a monopoly on 起訴 (indictment), and Japan is famous for an over 99% conviction rate once a suspect is formally indicted (起訴される).

超えていく.etymology: A syntactic-aspectual verbal construction combining 超えて (koete, the te-form of the native wago verb 超える koeru 'to cross over, surpass, transcend', from Old Japanese koyu) with the subsidiary directional/aspectual verb いく (iku, grammaticalized from 行く iku/yuku 'to go', from Old Japanese yuku). Attached to a te-form, -いく expresses continuous progression forward from the present into the future ('to go on surpassing, to keep transcending from here on').

history.meaning: crossing over and going onward
passing beyond and continuing forward
to go on surpassing, to continue transcending into the future

morphemes.meaning: surpassing, crossing beyond (from 超える koeru)
to continue onward into the future (from 行く iku)

超えていく.notes: As a subsidiary verb after -て (-te), いく is normally written in hiragana rather than kanji (超えていく) to signal its grammaticalized aspectual function ('keep surpassing / move beyond') rather than physical locomotion.

rootFamily.gloss: to surpass, to exceed, to cross over
to get through, to overcome (a hardship or crisis)
to go; auxiliary marking future progression

超える.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) ichidan verb descending from Classical Japanese こゆ (koyu, lower bigrade / 下二段 conjugation) and Old Japanese koyu ('to pass over a mountain ridge, cross a boundary'). In modern orthography, the single native verb koeru is split between two kanji: 越える for physically crossing over a spatial barrier or time threshold (a mountain pass, a border, New Year's), and 超える for surpassing a numerical limit, standard, benchmark, or rival.

history.meaning: to cross over a mountain pass or physical boundary
to pass over, cross beyond, exceed (shift from shimo-nidan to ichidan)
to surpass, to exceed, to top a benchmark or limit

超える.notes: Remember the kanji distinction: use 超える for exceeding numbers, records, expectations, or rivals (予算を超える, 常識を超える), and 越える for crossing physical places or time periods (山を越える, 冬を越える).

rootFamily.gloss: to cross over (a mountain, border, or season) — orthographic doublet
to overcome, to climb over, to surmount

超大作.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound formed by prefixing 超- (chō-, from Middle Chinese *trhjew 'to leap over, surpass, super-, ultra-') to 大作 (taisaku, 'monumental work, magnum opus, major production', composed of 大 tai 'great, large-scale' + 作 saku 'work, creation, production'). Popularized in 20th-century cinema and publishing advertising to market high-budget Hollywood and domestic 'blockbuster epics'.

history.meaning: a large-scale literary or artistic work, magnum opus
super-epic, blockbuster film or monumental production

超大作.notes: A staple of movie trailers and entertainment marketing (ハリウッド超大作 Hariuddo chōtaisaku, 'a Hollywood blockbuster epic').

rootFamily.gloss: major work, epic production, monumental work
famous work, classic film or book

越し.etymology: Native Japanese verbal noun and suffix (read こし or ごし with rendaku, 'crossing over; across, over, through; spanning a period'), nominalized from the連用形 of 越す (*kosu* 'to cross over, pass beyond', Old Japanese *kosu*).

history.meaning: crossing over; passing beyond
over; across; through (a barrier or span of time)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 越し

趣向.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 趣 (shu, from Middle Chinese *tshjuH 'to hasten toward; inclination, purport, aesthetic flair') and 向 (kō, from Middle Chinese *xjwangH 'to face toward, direction, orientation'). Originally meaning 'the direction in which one's mind inclines' in Tang-Song Chinese poetry and criticism, in medieval and Edo-period Japanese arts (renga, kabuki, tea ceremony) it evolved to mean 'an ingenious artistic conceit, plan, or creative contrivance designed to entertain'.

history.meaning: direction of inclination, mental bent, poetic purport
artistic conceit, novel plot device, aesthetic design in poetry or theater
artistic plan, creative idea, novel angle or contrivance for entertainment

趣向.notes: Most commonly appears in the set phrases 趣向を凝らす (shukō o korasu, 'to devise an elaborate/clever plan or artistic touch') and 趣向を変える (shukō o kaeru, 'to try a different angle/approach').

趣味.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound of 趣 (shu, from Middle Chinese *tshjuH 'inclination, aesthetic appeal, charm') and 味 (mi, from Middle Chinese *mj+jH 'taste, flavor, subtle appreciation'). In Classical Chinese and pre-Meiji Japanese, 趣味 meant 'poetic flavor, evocative charm, aesthetic sensibility'. During the Meiji period, it was first used to translate English aesthetic 'taste' (as in 趣味がいい 'good taste'), and then broadened in the early 20th century to mean an avocation or 'hobby'.

history.meaning: evocative flavor, poetic appeal, subtle charm
aesthetic taste, appreciation of beauty (translating English 'taste')
hobby, pastime; personal taste or preference

趣味.notes: Retains both its older Meiji sense of 'taste' (趣味が悪い shumi ga warui, 'in bad taste / tacky') and its modern sense of 'hobby' (趣味は映画鑑賞です, 'my hobby is watching movies'). Also a Chinese false friend: Mandarin 趣味 (qùwèi) means 'interest/appeal', whereas 'hobby' in Mandarin is 愛好 (àihào).

足.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('foot, leg; step, pace; means of transport'), continuing Old Japanese *asi* (alternating with archaic bound stem *a-* in words like 歩む *ayumu* 'walk'), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*asi*.

history.meaning: foot; leg
foot; leg; step
foot; leg; pace; transportation

足す.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to add, supplement, top up, make up a lack'), continuing Old Japanese *tasu* (four-grade *tas-*), the transitive counterpart of 足る / 足りる (*taru* / *tariru* 'to suffice, be enough').

history.meaning: make sufficient; supplement; add
add; top up; supplement

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 足す

足りる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive upper monograde (kami-ichidan) verb ('to be enough, suffice, be sufficient, be worthy of'), reshaped in Early Modern and Modern Japanese from the older four-grade verb 足る (*taru*, Old Japanese *taru* 'to be full, be complete, suffice').

history.meaning: be full; be complete; suffice
be enough; suffice; be sufficient

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 足りる

足る.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) godan verb attested in Old Japanese as taru ('to become full, be complete, be sufficient, merit'), cognate with the transitive verb 足す (tasu, 'to add to, make full, supplement'). The kanji 足 ('foot/leg') is applied via semantic borrowing (訓読み kun'yomi) because in Classical Chinese 足 (Middle Chinese *tsjowk) itself meant both 'foot' and 'to suffice, be worthy of'. In modern Japanese, upper-monograde 足りる (tariru) has largely replaced 足る in everyday speech, leaving 足る for literary, elevated, or idiomatic expressions.

history.meaning: to become full (like the waxing moon), to suffice, to be complete
to be enough, to suffice; to be worthy of (with に)
to suffice, to be worthy of, to merit (literary/elevated register)

足る.notes: While 足りる (tariru) is standard for everyday 'be enough' (お金が足りない), classic godan 足る survives in elevated phrases like 信頼に足る人物 (shinrai ni taru jinbutsu, 'a person worthy of trust'), 取るに足らない (toru ni taranai, 'beneath notice / trivial'), and the proverb 足るを知る (taru o shiru, 'to know contentment').

rootFamily.gloss: to be enough, to suffice (modern ichidan doublet)

足跡.etymology: A compound of 足 ('foot, leg') and 跡 ('track, footprint, vestige, mark left behind'), which operates in Japanese with two distinct readings and etymological layers: as a native wago compound read あしあと (ashiato, from Old Japanese asi 'foot' + ato 'footprint, track, wake'), meaning literal physical footprints or an evidentiary trail; and as an elevated Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read そくせき (sokuseki, from Middle Chinese *tsjowk-tsjek), meaning the historical record or career achievements left behind by a person.

history.meaning: foot + track/mark left behind

history.form: あしあと (ashiato) / そくせき (sokuseki)

足跡.notes: Read あしあと (ashiato) for physical footprints, detective trails, paper trails, or digital browsing logs (足跡を残す ashiato o nokosu, 'to leave a trail/trace'); read そくせき (sokuseki) when honoring someone's life work or historical legacy (偉大な足跡をたどる idai na sokuseki o tadoru).

足音.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('sound of footsteps, footfall'), formed from 足 (あし 'foot') + 音 (おと 'sound').

In Japanese performance history, 踊り (odori, from leaping and rhythmic stamping movements) was traditionally contrasted with 舞 (mai, slow, stately, circling aristocratic movement where the feet glide rather than leap).

history.meaning: leaping up, springing, rhythmic jumping

踊り場.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('stair landing; dancing place'), formed from 踊り (おどり, nominalized stem of 踊る 'to dance, step about') + 場 (ば 'place, spot'), transferred to a flat platform partway up a staircase where one pivots and changes direction.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 踊り場

踊り子.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) compound of 踊り (odori, 'dance, dancing', the nominalized stem of 踊る odoru < Old Japanese wodoru 'to leap, dance') and 子 (ko, from Old Japanese ko 'child, young person, girl', used as an agentive suffix for a person, especially a young woman, practicing an art or trade). Originally designating young female ritual or folk dancers, it was immortalized in modern literature by Yasunari Kawabata's 1926 novella 『伊豆の踊子』 (*The Dancing Girl of Izu*) and later applied to revue showgirls and cabaret/strip-theater dancers.

rootFamily.gloss: apprentice geisha / traditional dancer in Kyoto

踏みにじる.etymology: A native Japanese (wago) compound verb formed from 踏み (fumi, the continuative stem or 連用形 of 踏む fumu, from Old Japanese pumu 'to step on, tread upon') and にじる (nijiru, 'to grind, crush by twisting, rub with pressure', related to 捻る nejiru 'to twist, wrench'). Literally 'to step on and grind into the dirt with a twisting motion of the foot', it developed a powerful figurative sense of ruthlessly trampling upon someone's dignity, goodwill, or human rights.

history.meaning: to step on + to crush by grinding/twisting
to trample underfoot, crush beneath one's heel; to violate or ride roughshod over (feelings, rights, pride)

morphemes.meaning: stepping on, treading upon (from 踏む fumu)
to grind, crush with a twisting motion, mash

踏みにじる.notes: Used far more often figuratively than literally in modern Japanese, especially with objects like 人の好意 (hito no kōi, 'someone's goodwill'), プライド ('pride'), or 人権 (jinken, 'human rights').

rootFamily.gloss: to step on, to tread upon
to stamp on, to trample flat
to step into, to raid, to take a bold step into

踏み出す.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) syntactic verb compound formed from 踏み (fumi), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 踏む (fumu, "to step on, tread", from Old Japanese fumu), combined with the auxiliary directional verb 出す (dasu, "to put out, to initiate an outward or forward action", transitive counterpart of 出る deru). Literally "to step out," it evolved both the physical sense of taking a step forward and the figurative sense of venturing into a new stage or enterprise.

history.meaning: to tread upon + to put forth outward
to step out of a space, to take a stride forward
to step forward; to embark upon a new endeavor

morphemes.meaning: to step, tread (ren'yōkei of 踏む)
to put out, move outward or initiate

踏み出す.notes: Often used figuratively in collocations like 新たな一歩を踏み出す (aratana ippo o fumidasu, "to take a new step forward").

rootFamily.gloss: railway crossing; stepping across a boundary line

踏み台.etymology: Hybrid compound of native 踏み (ふみ, masu-stem of 踏む 'to step on') and Sino-Japanese 台 (だい, 'platform, stand').
踏み台.notes: Denotes a low wooden stepstool kept in kitchens and shops for reaching high shelves.

踏み外す.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb uniting 踏み (fumi), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 踏む (fumu, "to step, tread"), with 外す (hazusu, "to unfasten, miss, slip off", transitive counterpart of 外れる hazureru, from Old Japanese fadusu). Originally denoting a physical misstep where the foot misses its intended purchase (as on a stair or ledge), it developed the metaphorical meaning of straying from the proper moral or social path.

history.meaning: to tread + to unfasten or miss a target
to miss one's footing, slip off a step
to lose one's footing; to stray from the right path

morphemes.meaning: to step, tread (ren'yōkei of 踏む)

踏み外す.notes: Frequently appears in the moral idiom 道を踏み外す (michi o fumihazusu, "to stray from the right path / go astray into delinquency or crime").

rootFamily.gloss: to unfasten, to miss, to remove
to make a bold decision, to take the plunge

踏む.etymology: The term '踏む' (meaning 'stepped on') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

stepped on

踏む.notes: A common term in daily use.

身.etymology: A core native Yamato (wago) noun descending from Old Japanese mi₂ (written phonographically in the Man'yōshū as 微 or 身, from Proto-Japonic *mǝi, "body, flesh, meat, fruit"). Spelled with the logographic kanji 身 (originally a pictograph of a pregnant or full-bellied human torso), it expanded from the physical flesh and living body to denote one's personal self, social station, and lived circumstances, as well as the main part of a container or blade.

history.meaning: physical body, flesh, fruit/seed, living person
body, self, social rank or personal circumstances
one's body, oneself, one's position, meat/flesh of fish or fruit

身.notes: The Old Japanese vocalic distinction between mi₁ (見 "seeing", 箕 "winnow") and mi₂ (身 "body", 実 "fruit/nut"—originally the same etymon meaning "fleshy substance/core") explains why 身 and 実 share so many idiomatic overlaps.

rootFamily.gloss: fruit, nut, substance (doublet from the same Proto-Japonic root)
tall stature, height of the body

身元引受人.etymology: A hybrid Japanese legal and administrative compound combining the native Yamato (wago) components 身元 (mimoto, "one's personal background, origin, identity", from 身 mi "body/self" + 元 moto "origin, base") and 引受 (hikiuke, "undertaking, assuming responsibility", nominalized stem of 引き受ける hikiukeru, "to pull toward oneself and receive/guarantee") with the Sino-Japanese (kango) agentive suffix 人 (nin, from Middle Chinese *nyin, "person"). It designates a guarantor who legally vouches for a person's identity, conduct, or release into custody.

history.meaning: personal origin/background + taking charge of someone
personal surety, custodial guarantor for employment, residency, or parole

身元引受人.notes: In Japanese law, hospitals, employment, and prison release procedures, a 身元引受人 carries serious practical obligation to take physical and financial responsibility if the person causes trouble or cannot care for themselves.

rootFamily.gloss: one's background, identity, history and whereabouts
to undertake, to take responsibility for, to guarantee

身内.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from 身 (mi, "body, self", Old Japanese mi₂) and 内 (uchi, "inside, interior, home circle", Old Japanese uti). Originally referring to the inside of one's own physical body, by the late Heian and Kamakura periods it shifted sociologically to denote people treated as extensions of oneself—first vassals and retainers of a feudal lord, and later blood relatives, family members, and trusted insiders of a tightly knit group or organization.

history.meaning: throughout the inside of one's physical body
retainers, vassals, and kin belonging to a house or lord
relatives, family, one's inner circle or in-group

身内.notes: Reflecting the Japanese sociolinguistic divide between ウチ (uchi, "in-group") and ソト (soto, "out-group"), 身内 extends beyond blood kin to include company colleagues or gang/crew members when speaking to outsiders.

身分.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 身 (mi / shin, here read with the irregular or assimilated kun-based reading mi-, or analyzed as a hybrid/phonetically reduced reading alongside classical shibun, representing Middle Chinese *syin, "body, person, self") and 分 (bun, Go-on reading of Middle Chinese *bjunH, "allotted portion, share, duty, station in life", from 分 *pjun "to divide"). It originally meant the lot or station apportioned to a person by society, later extending to personal identity credentials.

history.meaning: one's personal lot, social standing, or rank
hereditary social caste or rank within the feudal order
social status, standing; personal identity (as on an ID card)

morphemes.meaning: person, self, body (read with kun-reading mi)
allotted share, social station, status (Middle Chinese *bjunH)

身分.notes: Note the jukujikun-like hybrid reading (湯桶読み yutōyomi): 身 is read with its native kun-reading mi, while 分 takes its Sino-Japanese on-reading bun; used both for social rank (身分が高い "high status") and legal ID (身分証明書 mibun shōmeisho).

rootFamily.gloss: one's proper station or duty, knowing one's place

車.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('wheel; cart, carriage, vehicle, car'), continuing Old Japanese *kuruma*, attested in the Nihon Shoki and Man'yōshū; derived from the verb root *kuru* (繰る / 転る 'to turn round and round, revolve') + nominal suffix *-ma*.

history.meaning: wheel; wheeled cart or carriage
car; automobile; wheeled vehicle; wheel

wheel of a vehicle

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 車輪

転がり込む.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb composed of 転がり (korogari), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 転がる (korogaru, "to roll, tumble", formed from the older root *korob-/korog- seen in Old Japanese korobu "to roll over, fall down" plus the intransitive verbalizer -garu/-aru), and the directional auxiliary 込む (komu, "to move inward, enter deeply into"). From the literal sense of an object rolling into an enclosed space, it developed the colloquial senses of crashing/moving into someone's home uninvited or a windfall unexpectedly dropping into one's lap.

to roll or tumble inside; to come crashing into a place

morphemes.meaning: to roll, tumble (ren'yōkei of 転がる)
to enter into, go deep inside

転がり込む.notes: Colloquially used in two vivid ways: either moving into a friend's or lover's apartment unceremoniously (友人の家に転がり込む, "to crash at a friend's place"), or an unexpected windfall arriving (大金が転がり込む, "a fortune falls into one's lap").

rootFamily.gloss: to roll, to tumble, to lie around
to fall down, to tumble over
to jump in, to dive in, to burst into

軽い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('light [in weight], not heavy; slight, minor, nimble'), continuing Old Japanese *karusi* (stem *karu-* / *karo-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: light in weight; nimble; slight
light; slight; mild; easy

輝き.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) deverbal noun (ren'yōkei nominalization) of the verb 輝く (kagayaku, "to shine, glitter, sparkle"). 輝く derives from Old Japanese kagayaku, itself built on the bound root *kaga- ("bright, flickering light, reflection", related to 影 kage "light/reflection/shadow" and 篝火 kagaribi "watchfire, brazier") plus the inchoative/expressive suffix -yaku (seen in ささやく sasayaku "to whisper"). brilliance, sparkle, luster; youthful or charismatic vitality and glory

rootFamily.gloss: to shine, to glitter, to sparkle
light, reflection, shadow, silhouette (from the same *kaga- root)

輝く.etymology: The term '輝く' (meaning 'shining') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: shining
shining

輝く.notes: A common term in daily use.

輸出.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound popularized in Meiji-era political economy from 輸 (yu, customary kan'yō-on reading replacing historical shu, from Middle Chinese *syu, "to transport by wheeled vehicle, convey, send tribute", containing the radical 車 "cart") and 出 (shutsu, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *tsyhwit, "to go out, send out"). Patterned as the antonym of 輸入 (yunyū, "import"), it literally means "transporting outward" across national borders and was subsequently re-adopted into modern Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: to transport by cart + to send forth/outward
exportation of goods in international trade (Meiji economic neologism)
export, exporting (of commodities, culture, or technology)

morphemes.meaning: to transport, convey by vehicle (Middle Chinese *syu)
to go out, send out (Middle Chinese *tsyhwit)

辞める.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb (originally lower bigrade 下二段 yamu/yamuru in Old and Classical Japanese), paired with the intransitive quadrigrade verb 止む・已む (yamu, "to cease, come to a halt, stop"). While the underlying verb yameru is a single native word meaning "to bring to a halt, discontinue", modern Japanese orthography splits its spelling by sense: 止める for stopping an activity, and 辞める (using the kanji 辞, Middle Chinese *zi, "speech, to take leave, decline an office") specifically for resigning from a post, job, or school.

history.meaning: to cause to cease, to bring to an end, to quiet down
to stop doing, to give up, to step down from a role

history.meaning: to quit, resign from a job, office, or institution (orthographically differentiated with 辞)

辞める.notes: Do not confuse the kanji spellings of yameru: 辞める is strictly for quitting a job, role, or school (会社を辞める), whereas 止める is for stopping a habit or planned action (タバコを止める, 旅行を止める).

rootFamily.gloss: to cease, to stop (intransitive, e.g. of rain or wind)
resignation from office (Sino-Japanese compound with 辞)

cognates.meaning: peasant household; ancient school of agriculturalists

農家.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 農 (nō, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *nowng, "tilling the soil, agriculture, farming", historically composed of 林/艸 "vegetation" and 辰 "clam-shell sickle used to clear weeds") and 家 (ka, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *kæ, "house, household, family, specialist"). In classical Chinese it denoted both the Warring States philosophical School of Tillers and a peasant family; in Japanese it refers to a farming household, farmhouse, or professional farmer.

farming household, farmer, agricultural producer

辺.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) morpheme 辺 (simplified shinjitai of traditional 邊, read hen via Kan-on from Middle Chinese *pen, "side, edge, margin, borderland, vicinity"). The character 邊 combines the movement/road radical 辶 with 臱 ("to walk along a cliff edge / out of sight"). While the kanji 辺 is also used to write the native Yamato words atari ("vicinity") and -be ("shore/side"), the Sino-Japanese reading hen functions as a noun and spatial suffix meaning "area, neighborhood, around here."

近い.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) i-adjective descending from Old Japanese tikasi (stem tika-, Proto-Japonic *tika-). Written with the kanji 近 (meaning "near in space or time"), the stem tika- originally denoted physical proximity and closeness of kinship or intimacy, and early on extended metaphorically to temporal nearness ("soon, before long") as well as similarity or approximation ("close to a certain amount or state").

history.meaning: spatially near, closely related, intimate
near in space or time, closely resembling (attributive -ki > -i merger)
near, close, short (of distance), soon, akin to

morphemes.meaning: modern non-past adjectival ending (< Old Japanese -ki)

近い.notes: With a dative particle に (〜に近い), it expresses approximation ("almost, close to", e.g., 100万円に近い金額 "an amount close to one million yen"); also note the idiomatic 気が近い / 目が近い and 耳が遠い (antonym pair with 遠い "far").

rootFamily.gloss: to approach, to draw near, to get close to

近く.etymology: Native Japanese noun and adverb ('nearness, neighborhood, vicinity; nearly, shortly'), substantivized from the連用形 (adverbial form) *chikaku* of the adjective 近い (*chikai*, Old Japanese *tikasi* 'near, close').

history.meaning: closely; near (adverbial form of ちかし)
vicinity; neighborhood; nearby; nearly

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 近く

近づける.etymology: Native Japanese compound transitive verb ('to bring close, allow near, let approach'), continuing classical lower bigrade *tikaduku* (近づく), the transitive counterpart of four-grade intransitive 近づく (*chikazuku* 'to approach, draw near', from 近い stem *chika-* + 付く / 着く *tsuku*).

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 近づける

近所.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('neighborhood, vicinity, neighbors'), formed from 近 (きん 'near, close') + 所 (じょ, go-on reading of 所 'place, locality').

neighborhood; vicinity; neighbors

返す.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to return, give back, put back; turn over'), continuing Old Japanese *kapesu*, the transitive counterpart of 返る / 帰る (*kaeru* < *kaperu* 'to turn back, return').

history.meaning: turn over; send back; return
return; give back; turn over

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 返す

返済.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) financial and legal compound composed of 返 (hen, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *pjonX, "to return, give back, turn back") and 済 (sai, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *tsjejH, originally "to cross a river", which evolved in Classical and Middle Chinese to mean "to bring across to completion, settle, clear a debt, relieve"). Together, 返済 literally means "returning and settling in full," specifically denoting the repayment of borrowed money or loans.

history.meaning: to give back + to cross over / settle an account to completion
clearing and returning a monetary debt or obligation
repayment, reimbursement of a loan or debt

morphemes.meaning: to finish, settle an account, clear (Middle Chinese *tsjejH)

返済.notes: Used specifically for paying back loans or debts (借金を返済する shakkin o hensai suru); for returning borrowed physical objects, use 返却 (henkyaku), and for refunds, use 返金 (henkin).

rootFamily.gloss: return of a physical object or leased property
full payment, paying off a loan completely
to finish, to be settled (native verb written with 済)

返答.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound uniting 返 (hen, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *pjonX, "to return, send back") and 答 (tō, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *top, "to answer, reply, reciprocate"). Documented in Japanese since the Heian and Kamakura periods (originally alongside the voiced rendaku variant hendō in court and epistolary prose), it signifies sending back a verbal or written answer in response to an inquiry, demand, or proposal.

history.form: へんたう / へんだう (fentau / fendau)
history.meaning: a formal spoken or written reply to a question or missive
reply, answer, response (slightly more formal than 返事 henji)

返答.notes: Compared to everyday 返事 (henji, which covers any casual "okay" or reply), 返答 (hentō) carries a weightier register implying a substantive answer to a specific question, negotiation, or demand (返答に窮する, "to be at a loss for an answer").

rootFamily.gloss: answer, response, solution to an inquiry

返金.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun and suru-verb ('refund, repayment, returning money'), formed from 返 (へん 'return, give back') + 金 (きん 'money, gold').

history.meaning: refund; repayment of money

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 返金

cognates.meaning: compelling force, intensity, impact (borrowed from Japanese wasei-kango)

迫力.etymology: A modern Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in Japan (wasei-kango) from 迫 (haku, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *pæk, "to press closely upon, crowd, bear down on, urge", cf. native verb 迫る semaru) and 力 (ryoku, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *lik, "strength, power, force"). Literally "the power to press directly upon the observer," it denotes visceral intensity, dynamic impact, or overwhelming presence in a performance, image, or personality.

history.meaning: to press closely upon + physical or spiritual power
compelling force or lifelike intensity in art, drama, or action that presses upon the viewer

morphemes.meaning: to press upon, draw near, compel (Middle Chinese *pæk)

迫力.notes: Very commonly used in filmmaking and performance critique in the pattern 迫力がある (hakuryoku ga aru, "to be intense, gripping, full of impact") or 迫力満点 (hakuryoku manten, "packed with visceral impact").

rootFamily.gloss: to press upon, to draw near, to be imminent (native verb of 迫)

迷い込む.etymology: Native Japanese compound intransitive verb ('to stray into, wander into, lose one's way and enter'), formed from 迷い (まよい, stem of 迷う 'to lose one's way, wander') + 込む (こむ 'to go into, enter deeply').

history.meaning: stray into; wander inside by mistake

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 迷い込む

迷う.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) intransitive godan verb descending from Old Japanese mayofu ("to become tangled, frayed, confused, or disoriented; to wander"). It is etymologically related to Old Japanese mayu ("cocoon" / "eyebrow") and 繭 (mayu), rooted in the image of threads crossing, tangling, or blurring one's path. From the physical sense of losing one's way on a road, it developed the psychological senses of wavering between choices, hesitating, and being spiritually deluded.

history.meaning: (of cloth threads) to fray or tangle; to wander lost; to be thrown into mental confusion
to lose one's way; to waver in judgment; (in Buddhism) to remain unawakened or deluded in samsara
to get lost; to hesitate, waver, be torn between options; to be infatuated

迷う.notes: Notice the particle distinction: 道に迷う (michi ni mayou) means "to get lost on the way", while 判断に迷う (handan ni mayou) or 迷っている (mayotte iru) means "to hesitate / be undecided between options."

cognates.meaning: to perplex, confuse, infatuate (FALSE FRIEND to Japanese 'annoyance/trouble')

迷惑.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from 迷 (mei, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *mej, "to go astray, be confused, be deluded") and 惑 (waku, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *hwok, "to doubt, be bewildered, be misled"). Borrowed via Chinese Buddhist and classical texts where 迷惑 meant "mental delusion, moral bewilderment, or perplexity," it underwent a crucial semantic shift in Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese: from "feeling bewildered oneself" to "suffering trouble or annoyance caused by someone else's actions."

history.meaning: to go astray in delusion, to be perplexed or bewitched (especially in Buddhist doctrine)
history.stage: Middle Chinese and Early Middle Japanese

history.meaning: being troubled, distressed, or put in an awkward predicament
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: trouble, bother, annoyance, nuisance, inconvenience caused to others

morphemes.meaning: to stray, be lost, be confused (Middle Chinese *mej)
to be bewildered, doubt, mislead (Middle Chinese *hwok)

迷惑.notes: A classic Sino-Japanese false friend with Mandarin Chinese: in Chinese 迷惑 (míhuò) still means "to confuse, puzzle, or bewitch," whereas in Japanese 迷惑 (meiwaku) means "nuisance, bother, inconvenience" (as in ご迷惑をおかけします, "I apologize for the inconvenience").

rootFamily.gloss: bewilderment, perplexity, being at a loss

追いかける.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 追い (oi), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 追う (ou, "to chase, pursue", from Old Japanese ofu), and かける (kakeru, "to hang, cast upon, set in motion toward a target", from Old Japanese kaku). Combining the action of pursuing with the directed momentum of kakeru ("directing action at a target"), it means to run after or actively chase someone or something moving ahead.

history.form: おふ (ofu) + かく (kaku, lower bigrade)
history.meaning: to pursue + to direct/launch an action upon a target
to run after, pursue closely on someone's heels
to chase after, run after, pursue (physically or figuratively, as a dream)

morphemes.meaning: to chase, pursue (ren'yōkei of 追う)
to direct an action toward, begin vigorously (かける)

追いかける.notes: In colloquial speech, the first vowel cluster oi- often assimilates to a geminate consonant ok-, yielding 追っかける (okkakeru); the noun 追っかけ (okkake) specifically means an obsessive groupie or fan who follows a celebrity everywhere.

rootFamily.gloss: to chase, to pursue, to follow
obsessive fan, groupie (from colloquial 追っかける)
to corner, to drive into a tight spot

追いつく.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb combining 追い (oi), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 追う (ou, "to chase, pursue", Old Japanese ofu), with つく (tsuku, written 着く or 付く, "to arrive at, make contact with, reach", from Old Japanese tuku). Literally "to pursue and make contact," it denotes closing the distance with someone or something ahead—whether physically overtaking a runner or catching up with a schedule, rival, or standard.

history.meaning: to pursue from behind and reach/make contact with the quarry
to catch up with, come abreast of, keep pace with (takes particle に)

morphemes.meaning: to chase, follow after (ren'yōkei of 追う)
to arrive at, attach, reach (着く / 付く)

追いつく.notes: Always takes the dative/target particle に (先頭に追いつく, "to catch up to the leader"); contrast with 追い越す (oikosu) and 追い抜く (oinuku), which mean "to overtake and pass."

rootFamily.gloss: to overtake, to pass a person or vehicle ahead
to outstrip, to pass and leave behind

追い出す.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) compound verb formed from 追い (oi), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 追う (ou, "to drive, chase", Old Japanese ofu), and 出す (dasu, "to put out, force outward", reduced from Old Japanese idasu). Exploiting the sense of 追う meaning "to drive cattle or people away from behind," 追い出す literally means "to drive out into the open" and denotes evicting, expelling, or throwing someone out of a room, house, or organization.

history.meaning: to drive or force out of an enclosure
to expel, evict, or chase out of a household or territory
to throw out, chase out, evict, oust

morphemes.meaning: to drive away, chase (ren'yōkei of 追う)
to put out, force outside (出す)

追い出す.notes: Commonly used for being kicked out of an apartment for unpaid rent (アパートを追い出される) or ousted from a company/home; compare the more literary Sino-Japanese 追放する (tsuihō suru, "to banish/exile").

rootFamily.gloss: to drive away, to scatter, to shoo away
to drive into an enclosure, to herd in, to corner

追い返す.etymology: Native Japanese compound transitive verb ('to drive back, turn away, send packing, repulse'), formed from 追い (おい, stem of 追う 'to chase, drive away') + 返す (かえす 'to send back, turn back').

history.meaning: drive back; turn away; repulse

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 追い返す

追う.etymology: A fundamental native Yamato (wago) transitive godan verb descending from Old Japanese ofu (Proto-Japonic *ǝp-u), written with the logographic kanji 追 ("to pursue, follow behind"). Following the historical Japanese phonological shift of intervocalic *-p- > -f- > -w- > Ø before non-a vowels (ofu > owu > ou, though retaining the bilabial stop in geminated forms like 追って otte < ofite), it encompasses three core senses: pursuing a moving target, driving livestock/people away, and following a sequence or chronological order.

history.meaning: to pursue, run after; to drive away; to follow in succession
to chase, pursue; to follow a precedent or trend (with labial lenition of -f- > -w-/Ø)
to chase, pursue, follow; to drive out; to be pressed by (time/work)

追う.notes: In the passive voice (〜に追われる, owareru), it idiomatically expresses being hounded or pressed by deadlines, debt, or busyness: 仕事に追われる (shigoto ni owareru, "to be swamped/chased by work").

rootFamily.gloss: to chase after, to run after
to corner, to drive to the wall

追っかけっこ.etymology: A colloquial native Yamato (wago) noun built from 追っかけ (okkake), the consonant-geminated spoken variant of 追いかけ (oikake, continuative stem of 追いかける oikakeru, "to chase after", where oi-k- contracts to ok-k-), plus the reciprocal/ludic nominal suffix -っこ (-kko, derived from Early Modern Edo-dialect -kura / -kko indicating a mutual contest or game between two or more participants). It refers to a playful game of tag or a cat-and-mouse chase.

history.form: おひかけくら (ofikakekura) / おひかけっこ (ofikakekko)
history.meaning: a mutual race or game of chasing one another

history.form: 追っかけっこ (okkakekko) / 追いかけっこ (oikakekko)
history.meaning: game of tag, playful chasing; figurative game of cat and mouse

morphemes.meaning: to chase (contracted colloquial stem of 追いかけ-)
reciprocal game or mutual activity suffix ("doing X with each other")

追っかけっこ.notes: The suffix -っこ (-kko) is productive in lively conversational Japanese for mutual games or contests, as in にらめっこ (niramekko, "staring contest") and かくれんぼ / 隠れっこ ("hide-and-seek"). In adult contexts, 追っかけっこ often describes a cat-and-mouse chase with police or creditors.

rootFamily.gloss: standard uncontracted form: game of tag, chasing each other
to chase after, to run after (colloquial variant of 追いかける)
staring contest (sharing the reciprocal game suffix -kko)

追って.etymology: A lexicalized native Yamato (wago) adverb originating as the conjunctive participle (te-form) of the verb 追う (ou, "to follow behind, pursue", Old Japanese ofu → ofite → otte via regular sokuonbin consonant gemination). Literally meaning "following after [this]," it grammaticalized in epistolary and administrative Japanese to mean "subsequently, later on, in due course," and also as a formal conjunction introducing a postscript ("furthermore, P.S.").

history.meaning: following after, pursuing in sequence (te-form of ofu)
subsequently, at a later time; furthermore (in letters)
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: later on, shortly, in due course (especially regarding follow-up notice)

morphemes.meaning: to follow, pursue (geminated stem ot- < Old Japanese ofi-)

追って.notes: A staple of formal business Japanese, most famously in phrases like 詳細は追って連絡します (shōsai wa otte renraku shimasu, "I will contact you later with the details").

rootFamily.gloss: to chase, to follow, to pursue
pursuer; second report/follow-up; favorable tailwind ("following wind")

追伸.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for postscript; P.S..

history.meaning: postscript; P.S.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 追伸

cognates.meaning: to add to, make an addition to (borrowed/shared Sino-Japanese)

追加.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 追 (tsui, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *trwij, "to follow after, pursue, do retroactively or subsequently") and 加 (ka, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *kæ, "to add, increase, augment", combining 力 "strength/plow" and 口 "mouth"). Here 追 carries its temporal/sequential sense ("subsequently, after the initial action"), so 追加 literally means "adding afterward"—supplementing an existing order, budget, or list.

history.meaning: to follow after in time + to add or augment
adding a supplementary item or clause after an initial arrangement
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese

history.meaning: addition, supplement, extra (order, charge, or feature)

追加.notes: Extremely common in everyday dining and commerce: 追加注文 (tsuika chūmon, "an additional order at a restaurant/bar") or 追加料金 (tsuika ryōkin, "extra charge / surcharge").

rootFamily.gloss: supplementary collection, addendum, retroactive collection of taxes/penalties

追放.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound combining 追 (tsui, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *trwij, "to chase, drive away, pursue") and 放 (hō, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *pjangH, "to release, let go, banish, drive out into the wilds"). Historically a formal penal category under feudal (especially Edo-period Tokugawa) law whereby a criminal or disgraced samurai was stripped of status and banished from a domain or major cities, it now denotes exile, deportation, or purging someone from an industry or organization.

history.meaning: to drive away + to cast out or banish
feudal judicial punishment of banishing an offender from a domain or city limits
history.stage: Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese (Edo period)

history.meaning: banishment, exile, expulsion, purge (e.g., from politics or entertainment)

morphemes.meaning: to drive out, chase away (Middle Chinese *trwij)
to cast out, banish, release (Middle Chinese *pjangH)

追放.notes: Used both for literal exile/deportation (国外追放 kokugai tsuihō) and for being blacklisted or permanently expelled from an industry (芸能界から追放される, "to be banished/blacklisted from showbiz").

rootFamily.gloss: expulsion, ousting, driving out (synonymous Sino-Japanese compound)
exile, fleeing abroad for political reasons

cognates.meaning: degeneration, atrophy, regression (borrowed from Japanese wasei-kango)

退化.etymology: A Meiji-era Sino-Japanese (kango) scientific coinage (wasei-kango) formed from 退 (tai, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *thwojH, "to step back, retreat, recede, decline") and 化 (ka, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *xwaeH, "to transform, change into, become"). Created as the direct structural antonym of 進化 (shinka, "evolution / progressive transformation") to translate Western biological terms for evolutionary degeneration and vestigial atrophy, it was subsequently borrowed into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: to retreat/recede + to transform or change state
biological degeneration or reduction of organs across evolutionary time (antonym of 進化)
degeneration, atrophy, regression (biological, cultural, or personal skill loss)

morphemes.meaning: to retreat, recede, move backward (Middle Chinese *thwojH)

退化.notes: Paired directly with 進化 (shinka, "evolution/progress"); in casual modern speech, people also use 退化する humorously when their own skills, fitness, or technology seem to regress rather than improve.

cognates.meaning: to drop out or withdraw from school (from Japanese wasei-kango)

退学.etymology: A Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in the modern educational system from 退 (tai, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *thwojH, "to withdraw, step back, leave") and 学 (gaku, Kan-on reading of Middle Chinese *hæwk, "learning, study, school", simplified from traditional 學). Built on the V+O pattern "to withdraw from school" as the opposite of 入学 (nyūgaku, "entering school") and 進学 (shingaku, "advancing to higher education"), it covers both voluntary dropping out and disciplinary expulsion.

history.meaning: to withdraw from + place of learning/study
leaving an educational institution before graduation (Meiji educational terminology)
withdrawing or dropping out from school; disciplinary expulsion from school

morphemes.meaning: to withdraw, leave, step back (Middle Chinese *thwojH)

退学.notes: 退学 covers both voluntary withdrawal (自主退学 jishu taigaku or 中退 chūtai, "dropping out mid-course") and forced expulsion as punishment (退学処分 taigaku shobun, "expulsion from school").

rootFamily.gloss: temporary suspension from school or taking a leave of absence

退屈.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun, adjectival noun, and suru-verb ('boredom, tedium; bored, tedious'), originally a Buddhist term meaning 'shrinking back and losing heart in the face of rigorous ascetic practice or difficulty' (from 退 'retreat, shrink back' + 屈 'bend, yield, be exhausted'), which shifted in the Edo period to mean 'growing weary from having nothing to do, boredom'.

history.meaning: lose heart and retreat from austere practice; grow weary
boredom; tedium; feeling bored

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 退屈

送る.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to send, dispatch; see off, escort; spend [time]'), continuing Old Japanese *okuru*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: escort someone departing; send; pass time
send; see off; escort; spend (time)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 送る

逃がす.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) transitive godan verb formed from the root *nig- ("to flee, slip away", seen in Old Japanese nigu [lower bigrade] > Modern 逃げる nigeru, "to escape, run away") plus the causative/transitive verbal suffix -asu (Proto-Japonic *-as-u). Literally "to cause or allow to flee," it denotes either intentionally releasing a captive creature/person or inadvertently letting a quarry, fish, or golden opportunity slip through one's fingers.

history.form: にぐ (nigu, intransitive) → にがす (nigasu, transitive)
history.meaning: to allow to flee, to let a captive or quarry get away
to let escape, set free; to fail to catch, miss (a fish, suspect, or chance)

逃がす.notes: Compare with its close doublet 逃す (nogasu): 逃がす (nigasu) emphasizes letting a living thing or captured quarry physically get away (犯人を逃がす, 魚を逃がす), whereas 逃す (nogasu) is preferred for missing abstract opportunities (チャンスを逃す, 見逃す).

rootFamily.gloss: to flee, to run away, to escape (intransitive counterpart)
to miss a chance, to let slip by (vocalic doublet of nigasu)
to overlook, to let someone off the hook, to miss seeing

逃げきる.etymology: A native Yamato (wago) aspectual compound verb combining 逃げ (nige), the continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of 逃げる (nigeru, "to flee, run away", from Old Japanese nigu), with the completive auxiliary verb きる (kiru, originally 切る "to cut", which grammaticalized in Late Middle Japanese as an auxiliary meaning "to do completely, carry through to the very end"). It means to succeed in escaping all the way to the end without being caught—or in sports/races, to hold onto a lead until the finish line.

to escape completely to the end; to hold off pursuers until the finish

morphemes.meaning: to flee, run away, escape (ren'yōkei of 逃げる)
to do completely, carry through to the finish (切る)

逃げきる.notes: While the dictionary form 逃げきる (nigekiru) affirmatively means "to get away completely / hold the lead to the end," in crime dramas like *The Naked Director* it frequently appears in the negative potential 逃げきれない (nigekirenai, "cannot get away completely").

rootFamily.gloss: to flee, to run away, to escape
running away after a hit/win; running off with the money

逃げる.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to flee, run away, escape'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *nigu* (逃ぐ, stem *nige₂-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, paired with transitive 逃がす (*nigasu*).

history.meaning: flee; run away; escape
run away; flee; escape

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 逃げる

逃げ出す.etymology: Native Japanese compound intransitive verb ('to run away, bolt, break into flight, flee from a place'), formed from 逃げ (にげ, stem of 逃げる 'to flee, run away') + 出す (だす 'to go out, burst forth, begin suddenly').

history.meaning: flee out of a place; bolt; start running away

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 逃げ出す

逆.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) noun and prefix using the Kan-on reading gyaku, borrowed from Middle Chinese ngjaek (逆, 'to go against, oppose, meet head-on, invert'). history.meaning: upside-down figure; to go against or receive oncoming movement
to oppose, rebel against, contrary, inverted
opposite, reverse, converse

逆.notes: The conversational connector 逆に (gyaku ni, 'on the contrary, conversely, actually') is ubiquitous in modern spoken Japanese, often used even when only mildly shifting perspective.

rootFamily.gloss: to go against, oppose (native wago reading)

透ける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) intransitive ichidan verb (from Classical Japanese shimo-nidan sukuru), derived from the verb suku (透く / 空く, 'to become sparse, have gaps, let light or air pass through'), from Old Japanese suk- ('gap, opening, interval'). to be visible through an opening or thin material
to show through, be see-through or transparent
