適任.notes: Often paired with the suffix 者 in 適任者 (tekininsha, 'the right candidate / suitable person for the role') or echoed in the four-character idiom 適材適所 (tekizai-tekisho, 'the right person in the right place').

rootFamily.gloss: the right person for the post/job

適切.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) adjectival noun (keiyoudoushi) from Classical Chinese tek-tshet (適切), combining 適 (teki, 'to fit, suit, hit the mark') and 切 (setsu, 'to cut close to the bone, touch closely, exact, urgent'). Originally used in Chinese literary criticism for phrasing that hits the exact mark without superfluity; in modern Japanese it is the standard formal word for 'appropriate, proper, pertinent'.

history.meaning: hitting the exact point; closely fitting the facts or rhetoric
appropriate, proper, suitable, well-advised

morphemes.meaning: fit, suit, match, hit the mark
cut close, exact, keen, directly touching

適切.notes: Its negative form 不適切 (futekisetsu, 'inappropriate, improper') is a staple of Japanese media compliance, broadcasting ethics boards, and public apologies (不適切な発言 'inappropriate remarks').

rootFamily.gloss: proper, reasonable, appropriate (especially of prices or procedures)

遭う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) godan verb from Old Japanese ap- ('to come together, meet face to face, converge'), etymologically the exact same native word as 会う, 逢う, and 合う (au). In modern Japanese orthography, the kanji 遭 (Middle Chinese tsaw, 'to encounter by chance, run into misfortune') is specifically assigned when the subject meets with an unwelcome, accidental, or harmful event such as a crime, disaster, or accident.

history.meaning: to come together, meet, encounter (neutral or adverse)
to meet with a sudden or unfortunate event
to encounter (misfortune), fall victim to, run into (bad weather/trouble)

遭う.notes: Always takes the particle に (ni) and collocates with negative outcomes: 事故に遭う ('get into an accident'), 被害に遭う ('fall victim to a crime/damage'), ひどい目に遭う ('have a terrible time / get burned').

rootFamily.gloss: to meet (a person, neutral) — same wago root
to meet with a disaster or distress (Sino-Japanese reading of 遭)

選ぶ.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to choose, select, elect, sort out'), continuing Old Japanese *erabu* (derived from the simpler verb *eru* 選ぶ / 択る 'to pick out, select'), attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: select; pick out; sort
choose; select; elect

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 選ぶ

選挙.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound from Classical Chinese sjwenX-kjoX (選舉, attested in the Huainanzi and Book of Han), combining 選 (sen, 'to choose, select, sift out') and 挙 (kyo, 'to raise up with both hands, recommend, promote'). In imperial China from the Han through the Tang and Song dynasties, xuanju referred to the state bureaucracy's system of selecting and recommending candidates for civil office; Meiji political reformers repurposed the term to translate Western democratic 'election'.

history.meaning: imperial selection and recommendation of worthy candidates for civil office
popular democratic election by voting for political representatives

選挙.notes: Both kanji also have common native wago verb readings worth linking in memory: 選ぶ (erabu, 'to choose') and 挙げる (ageru, 'to raise / nominate').

rootFamily.gloss: to choose, select, elect (native wago verb)

rootFamily.word: 選挙運動 (せんきょうんどう)

避ける.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive ichidan verb (from Classical Japanese shimo-nidan sakuru), derived from the Old Japanese root sak- ('to split apart, separate, put distance between'), which also produced 裂く / 割く (saku, 'to tear, divide') and 離る (sakaru, 'to move away from'). Orthographically matched with the kanji 避 ('step aside from, shun, evade').

history.meaning: to step aside from, put distance between oneself and a taboo or danger
to avoid, evade, shun, stay clear of

morphemes.meaning: keep away from, evade, separate from

避ける.notes: Note the two native readings of 避ける: sakeru means to avoid a situation, topic, or person altogether (トラブルを避ける), whereas yokeru means to physically dodge or step out of the way of an oncoming object (車を避ける/よける).

rootFamily.gloss: to dodge, step aside physically (doublet reading)
evacuation, taking refuge (Sino-Japanese reading of 避)

cognates.meaning: death, the Tempter/Demon who obstructs enlightenment (phonetic source of 魔)

邪魔.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) Buddhist compound using Go-on readings jama, from Middle Chinese zjae-ma (邪魔). It combines 邪 (ja, 'wicked, crooked, heterodox') and 魔 (ma, clipped from 魔羅 mara, a Chinese phonetic transcription of Sanskrit Mara, the Buddhist personification of temptation, delusion, and spiritual obstruction, from the Indo-European root *mer- 'to die'). Originally meaning 'evil demons who obstruct Buddhist practice', it secularized during the Muromachi and Edo periods into 'hindrance, obstacle, nuisance, getting in the way'.

history.meaning: heterodox demons who obstruct a practitioner's path to awakening
demonic hindrance; any secular obstacle, nuisance, or intrusion

邪魔.notes: Remarkably, this ancient Buddhist term for 'evil demon' is embedded in the polite everyday greeting お邪魔します (O-jama shimasu, literally 'I am going to intrude/be a hindrance', said when entering someone's home or office).

rootFamily.gloss: person in the way, third wheel, nuisance

cognates.meaning: part, section, ministry, classifier for books/films/machines

部.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) noun, suffix, and counter using the Go-on reading bu, from Middle Chinese buwX (部, 'division, section, tribe, government board'). In Han and Tang China, bu denoted an administrative or military division and later one of the four bibliographical divisions of classic literature (四部); hence its extension as a classifier for bound sets of books, printed periodicals, organizational departments, and school clubs.

history.meaning: regional/military division, government board, bibliographic category of books
department, division, club; counter for copies of newspapers, magazines, or documents

morphemes.meaning: division, section, department, counter for printed copies

部.notes: In publishing and media (like magazine distribution in The Naked Director), 部数 (busuu) measures circulation/print run (e.g., 10万部 '100,000 copies').

rootFamily.gloss: number of copies, print run, circulation
department head, director of a division

部分.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) coordinate compound combining 部 (bu, 'division, section, group', from Middle Chinese buwX) and 分 (bun, 'part, share, segment, allot', from Middle Chinese pjun / bjunH, depicting a knife 刀 cleaving something in two 八). By pairing two near-synonymous morphemes of division, the compound designates a constituent part or portion in contrast to 全体 (zentai, 'the whole').

history.meaning: section/division + allotted share or segment
constituent part, section, portion of a whole

部分.notes: Adding the suffix 的 creates 部分的 (bubunteki, 'partial, localized'), the standard antonym of 全体的 (zentaiteki, 'overall, across the board').

部屋.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 部 (*he*, 'partition, divided section') with rendaku voicing + 屋 (*ya*, 'roof, chamber, house'), literally 'a partitioned-off chamber'.

history.meaning: partitioned chamber; wing
room

部屋番号.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Japanese compound noun ('room number'), combining native 部屋 (へや 'room, chamber') + Sino-Japanese 番号 (ばんごう 'assigned number').

history.form: 部屋番号 (へやばんごう)
history.meaning: room number

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 番号

郵便.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound coined in 1871 by Maejima Hisoka, founder of Japan's modern postal system, combining 郵 (yū, from Middle Chinese *hjuw 'posthouse, relay station for dispatches') and 便 (bin, from Middle Chinese *bjenH 'convenient dispatch, courier opportunity, message'). Chosen to replace the Edo-period courier term 飛脚 (hikyaku), 郵便 was later borrowed from Meiji Japanese into both Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: modern national postal service and mail
mail, postal service

郵便.notes: In everyday conversation, 郵便 refers both to the postal system and to the physical letters and postcards delivered in the mail.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 郵便

郵便屋さん.etymology: Colloquial polite compound noun ('mail carrier, postman; post office'), formed from Meiji Sino-Japanese 郵便 (ゆうびん 'postal service, mail', from 郵 'post-stage relay' + 便 'dispatch, message') + occupational suffix -屋 (-や) + polite suffix -さん.

history.form: 郵便屋さん (ゆうびんやさん)
history.meaning: mail carrier; postman (friendly/polite)

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 郵便屋

郵便物.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for mail; postal items.

history.meaning: mail; postal items

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 郵便物

郵送.etymology: Native Japanese or Sino-Japanese compound for mailing. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: mailing

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 郵送

都会.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound combining 都 (to, 'capital, metropolis', from Middle Chinese *tuo) and 会 (kai, 'coming together, assembly, junction', from Middle Chinese *ɣuɑiH). Attested in Classical Chinese (Records of the Grand Historian) for a major commercial hub where people and goods converge, 都会 in modern Japanese contrasts the noisy, fast-paced big city with quiet neighborhoods or the countryside (田舎 inaka).

history.meaning: great convergence of people; major city
big city; urban center

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 都会

都内.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) locative compound combining 都 (to, Kan-on reading from Middle Chinese tu, 'capital city, metropolis') and 内 (nai, Go-on reading from Middle Chinese nwojH, 'inside, within'). While classically capable of meaning 'inside any capital city', since the July 1943 administrative merger of Tokyo Prefecture (東京府) and Tokyo City (東京市) into Tokyo Metropolis (東京都, Toukyou-to, the sole 'to' in Japan), 都内 refers specifically to 'within Tokyo Metropolis'.

history.meaning: within the imperial capital city
within Tokyo Metropolis (東京都)

morphemes.meaning: metropolis, capital (specifically Tokyo Metropolis, 東京都)

都内.notes: In Japanese news reports and real estate listings, 都内某所 (tonai bousho) is the classic phrase for 'an undisclosed location in Tokyo'.

rootFamily.gloss: heart of the metropolis, central Tokyo

都合.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read with Go-on pronunciations tsugou, combining 都 (tsu, from Middle Chinese tu, which in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese developed the adverbial sense 'all, altogether, in total') and 合 (gou, from Middle Chinese hop, 'to join, combine, add up'). In medieval Japanese documents, tsugou was an accounting term meaning 'sum total, in all'; during the Edo period it evolved from 'how figures add up' to 'how circumstances fit together', yielding modern 'circumstances, convenience, arrangement'.

history.meaning: sum total, altogether, in all (accounting and administrative usage)
financial arrangement, coordination of affairs, convenience, circumstances

morphemes.meaning: altogether, all, in total (medieval vernacular Chinese sense of 都)
combine, add up, fit together, match

都合.notes: Preserves both its modern noun sense in 都合がいい ('convenient / works for my schedule') and its medieval adverbial sense in 都合三日間 (tsugou mikkakan, 'three days in total').

rootFamily.gloss: inconvenience, bad timing, awkward flaw in a plan
opportunism; at one's own convenience (in ご都合主義)
rootFamily.word: ご都合主義 (ごつごうしゅぎ)

rootFamily.gloss: sum total, grand total (shares 合 'add up')

配る.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) transitive godan verb attested since Old Japanese (found in the Nihon Shoki and Man'yoshu) as kubaru ('to divide and hand out, allot, distribute'), plausibly derived from an ancient root kub- ('to share out, place into') extended with the transitive/distributive verbal suffix -aru. Written with the kanji 配 ('apportion, distribute, match').

history.meaning: to divide into shares, allot, distribute among people
to distribute, hand out, deal (cards), deploy (attention/care)

morphemes.meaning: distribute, allot, hand out in shares

配る.notes: Beyond physically handing out flyers or dealing cards, 配る forms expressive idioms of vigilance: 気を配る (ki o kubaru, 'pay close attention to everyone's needs') and 目を配る (me o kubaru, 'keep a watchful eye on everything').

rootFamily.gloss: worry, anxiety, concern (Sino-Japanese compound literally 'distributing the mind')

配線.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun and suru-verb ('wiring, electrical cabling layout'), formed from 配 (はい 'distribute, arrange, allocate') + 線 (せん 'wire, line').

history.meaning: electrical wiring; wire layout

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 配線

配送先.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the Sino-Japanese (*kango*) noun 配送 (*haisō*, 'delivery, distribution'), formed from Middle Chinese 配 (*phwojH*, 'to apportion, match, distribute') and 送 (*suwngH*, 'to send off, escort, deliver'), with the native Yamato (*wago*) suffixal noun 先 (*saki*, from Old Japanese *saki*, 'tip, point ahead, destination'). Literally 'the point ahead to which goods are apportioned and sent'.

history.meaning: distribution + point ahead / destination
delivery address, shipping destination

配送先.notes: As a productive suffix on action nouns, 先 (*-saki*) marks the target location or counterparty (compare 連絡先 'contact address', 勤務先 'workplace').

配達.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 配 ('distribute, allot') and 達 ('reach, deliver to a destination'), coined for modern postal and goods delivery.

酒.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) noun descending from Old Japanese *sake2* ('fermented rice beverage'), with combining form *saka-* (as in 酒屋 *sakaya*, 酒場 *sakaba*), pointing to Proto-Japonic *saka-i. Further origin outside Japonic is debated; some linguists propose a connection to verb *sakayu* ('to flourish, become spirited'), though internal reconstruction treats *saka-* as a primary root written logographically with Chinese 酒 ('fermented millet or rice liquor').

history.meaning: fermented grain liquor
rice beer, ritual and festive fermented drink
alcoholic beverage in general; brewed rice sake

酒.notes: In Japanese, 酒 (*sake*, often polite お酒 *osake*) refers to any alcoholic beverage in general, whereas English 'sake' specifically translates 日本酒 (*nihonshu*). In compounds where 酒 is the first element, the older vowel *a* surfaces (*saka-*), and when second, rendaku yields *-zake* (e.g., 甘酒 *amazake*).

cognates.meaning: to release from custody, to set free

釈放.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) legal compound from Classical Chinese 釋放 (reformed in post-war Japanese shinjitai to 釈放), composed of Middle Chinese 釋 (*syek*, 'to untie, loosen, explain, release') and 放 (*pjangH*, 'to let go, banish, set free'). Adopted into Meiji-era penal and procedural jurisprudence for discharging a detainee from physical custody.

history.meaning: to untie and let go; to release a captive or animal
formal release from arrest or penal detention

釈放.notes: Used specifically for physical release from police detention or prison; compare 保釈 (*hoshaku*, 'release on bail') and 解放 (*kaihō*, 'emancipation, general liberation').

重い.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('heavy, weighty; serious, grave, sluggish'), continuing Old Japanese *omosi* (stem *omo-*), attested in the Man'yōshū.

history.meaning: heavy; weighty; grave; important
heavy; serious; sluggish

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 重い

重なる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) intransitive verb from Old Japanese *kasanaru* ('to be piled up in layers, to occur repeatedly'), derived from the base *kasana-* (seen also in the transitive counterpart 重ねる *kasaneru*, 'to pile up, layer') plus the intransitive verbalizer *-ru* (from Proto-Japonic *-ra-). Written logographically with the kanji 重 ('heavy; layer, fold').

history.meaning: to be piled in layers, to be doubled
to pile up, overlap, coincide (of events or layers)

重なる.notes: Forms a classic transitivity pair with 重ねる (*kasaneru*, transitive 'to pile up, repeat'): 不幸が重なる means 'misfortunes pile up / happen one after another'.

rootFamily.gloss: pile, layer; counter for layers of clothing

重役会議.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (*kango*) corporate compound combining 重役 (*jūyaku*, originally an Edo-period term for a senior feudal magistrate or high official, from 重 *jū* 'heavy, senior, weighty' + 役 *yaku* 'official duty, post', repurposed in the Meiji era for corporate directors) with 会議 (*kaigi*, 'council, conference', from 会 *kai* 'meet, assemble' + 議 *gi* 'deliberate, discuss').

history.meaning: high-ranking feudal official, senior councillor in a clan domain
board of directors meeting, executive conference

重役会議.notes: Notice that 重 uses its go-on reading *jū* here (重役 *jūyaku*), whereas in 重要 (*jūyō*) it also reads *jū*, contrasting with its kan-on reading *chō* in 重複 (*chōfuku*). In modern statutory law, 取締役会 (*torishimariyakukai*) is the formal legal term for a board of directors, while 重役会議 is standard in everyday business and drama dialogue.

重病患者.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) medical compound joining 重病 (*jūbyō*, 'severe or critical illness', from Middle Chinese 重 *drjowngX* 'heavy, grave' + 病 *bjaengH* 'sickness, disease') and 患者 (*kanja*, 'sufferer, medical patient', from 患 *hwanH* 'affliction, worry, suffer from illness' + agentive particle 者 *tsyaeX* 'one who').

history.meaning: grave sickness + one afflicted with illness
critically ill patient, patient with a serious disease

重病患者.notes: Notice the rendaku voicing in 患者 (*kanja*, not *kansha*, which avoids homophony with 感謝 'gratitude'!), contrasting with 医者 (*isha*) or 読者 (*dokusha*).

重要.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) adjectival noun (*keiyōdōshi*) borrowed from Classical Chinese 重要, a coordination of two near-synonymous morphemes: Middle Chinese 重 (*drjowngX*, 'heavy, weighty, serious') and 要 (*'jewH*, 'essential, pivotal, waist of the body, summary point'). Literally 'weighty and pivotal'.

history.meaning: weighty and essential; a strategic or crucial point
important, vital, of major consequence

重要.notes: Functions as a *na*-adjective (重要な *jūyō na*) and relates closely to 要 (*kaname*, literally the pivot-pin of a folding fan, hence 'linchpin, vital point').

野球賭博.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound combining 野球 (*yakyū*, 'baseball', coined in 1894 by Chūma Kanoe as a translation of English *baseball* using 野 *ya* 'open field' + 球 *kyū* 'ball', playing on the homophonous 棒球 / native ball-in-field concept) with 賭博 (*tobaku*, 'gambling, wagering', from Classical Chinese 賭 *tuX* 'to wager, bet' + 博 *pak* 'ancient board game Liubo, dice/gaming').

history.meaning: wagering at board and dice games
field-ball (Meiji neologism for baseball, 1894)
illegal betting on professional or high-school baseball games

野球賭博.notes: In Japanese cultural and legal contexts, 野球賭博 evokes high-profile postwar scandals involving yakuza bookmaking rings and professional baseball (NPB) players (such as the infamous 1969–1970 ''Black Mist Scandal'').

野菜.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('vegetable, greens'), composed of 野 (や 'field, open country') + 菜 (さい 'edible greens, side dish'). Originally denoting wild edible herbs gathered in the fields, in Modern Japanese it generalized to all cultivated culinary vegetables.

history.meaning: wild edible greens gathered from fields
vegetables; culinary greens

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 野菜

野菜スープ.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Japanese and Western loanword compound ('vegetable soup'), combining 野菜 (やさい 'vegetable') + スープ (borrowed from English *soup*).

history.form: 野菜スープ (やさいスープ)
history.meaning: vegetable soup

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 野菜

野蛮.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) adjectival noun from Classical Chinese 野蠻 (reformed in Japanese shinjitai to 野蛮), combining Middle Chinese 野 (*yaeX*, 'open wilderness, rustic, untamed, outside the court') and 蠻 (*maen*, originally an ethnonym for non-Sinitic southern peoples in the Zhou–Han sinocentric worldview, extended to mean 'uncivilized, fierce, uncultivated'). Repurposed in Meiji Japan to translate European 'barbarous / savage' in contrast to 文明 (*bunmei*, 'civilization').

history.meaning: untamed wilderness tribes beyond imperial administration; rustic and uncultivated
barbaric, uncivilized, uncouth, rough-mannered

morphemes.meaning: southern non-Han peoples; uncivilized, fierce (shinjitai of 蠻)

野蛮.notes: Functions as a *na*-adjective (野蛮な *yaban na*) and takes the suffix -人 in 野蛮人 (*yabanjin*, 'barbarian, brute'); in everyday speech it often means simply 'boorish, uncouth, crude'.

量産.etymology: Modern Sino-Japanese (*kango*) clipped compound (*ryakugo*) shortened from 大量生産 (*tairyō seisan*, 'large-quantity production'), preserving 量 (*ryō*, from Middle Chinese *ljangH*, 'measured quantity, volume, capacity') and 産 (*san*, from Middle Chinese *srjenX*, 'to give birth, produce, yield'). Coined during Japan's twentieth-century industrial expansion and re-borrowed into Chinese and Korean.

history.meaning: large-volume industrial manufacturing
mass production, serial manufacturing (clipped compound)

量産.notes: A classic 2-kanji abbreviation of a 4-kanji compound (大量生産 → 量産); used both for industrial manufacturing and figuratively in media/pop-culture (e.g., 量産型 *ryōsangata*, 'mass-produced model; cookie-cutter style').

金.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) noun *kane* (often prefixed with polite *o-* as お金 *okane*), descending from Old Japanese *kane* (combining form *kana-* as in 金物 *kanamono*, 金槌 *kanazuchi*), from Proto-Japonic *kana-i ('metal, ore, bronze/iron'). As metallic coinage circulated from the Asuka and Nara periods onward (and expanded in the Edo monetized economy), the sense 'metal' narrowed in everyday speech to 'coin, money', while the Sino-Japanese readings *kin* ('gold; money') and *kon* come from Middle Chinese 金 (*kim*, 'metal, bronze, gold').

history.meaning: metal, ore, cast bronze or iron implement (bell, gong)
metal; metallic coin, currency, money
money, cash (kane); gold, Friday, money in compounds (kin)

金.notes: Reading determines meaning and register: bare 金 (*kane*) means 'money, cash' (slightly blunt or rough compared to polite お金 *okane*,fitting the gritty world of *The Naked Director*), whereas 金 (*kin*) means 'gold' (or 'money' in kango compounds like 金額 *kingaku*). In native compounds, watch for the archaic vowel *a* in *kana-* (金物 *kanamono* 'hardware').

金具.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Japanese compound noun ('metal fittings, hardware, metal clasp or bracket'), formed from native 金 (かな-, bound combining form of *kane* 'metal') + Sino-Japanese 具 (ぐ 'implement, fitting, tool').

history.meaning: metal fittings; hardware

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 金具

金属.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('metal'), borrowed from Classical Chinese 金属 ('substances belonging to the category of metal'), composed of 金 (きん 'gold, metal') + 属 (ぞく 'class, category, belong to').

history.meaning: the class of metals
metal

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 金属

金庫.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound from Classical Chinese 金庫, composed of Middle Chinese 金 (*kim*, 'metal, gold, money, bullion') and 庫 (*khuoH*, 'storehouse, arsenal, treasury', originally a carriage shed under a roof 广 + 車). Historically denoted a state or clan treasury before coming to designate modern fireproof iron safes and bank vaults in the Meiji period.

history.meaning: imperial or state treasury for storing gold and coin
strongbox, iron safe, bank vault; credit treasury (as in 信用金庫)

金庫.notes: Also appears in 金庫番 (*kinkoban*, 'keeper of the safe; trusted treasurer/bagman') and 信用金庫 (*shin'yō kinko*, 'shinkin bank / cooperative regional credit association').

金曜.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('Friday', often short for 金曜日), from Classical Chinese and Buddhist astrological 金曜 ('the planet Venus, Metal-star'), composed of 金 (きん 'metal, Venus') + 曜 (よう 'celestial luminary, day of the week').

history.meaning: planet Venus (Metal-luminary); day of Venus
Friday

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 金曜

金曜日.etymology: Compound of 金曜 ('Venus day', linked to the Five Phases element 金 'metal/gold') and 日 ('day') in the seven-day planetary week.

金物屋.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('hardware store, ironmonger'), formed from 金物 (かなもの 'metalware, hardware, ironware', from *kana-* 'metal' + 物 'thing, goods') + shop suffix -屋 (-や).

history.meaning: hardware store; metalware shop

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 金物屋

金策.etymology: Japanese-coined Sino-Japanese (*wasei-kango*) compound combining 金 (*kin*, from Middle Chinese *kim*, 'metal, gold, money') and 策 (*saku*, from Middle Chinese *tsrhaek*, originally 'bamboo slip, riding whip', extended in Classical Chinese to 'written plan, stratagem, scheme'). Attested from the Edo period for devising means to procure or scrape together needed cash.

history.meaning: stratagem or scheme for procuring money; financial maneuvering
raising funds, scrambling for cash (e.g. 金策に走る)

金策.notes: Almost always used when someone is hard-pressed and hustling to raise money from lenders or backers—most famously in the idiom 金策に走る (*kinsaku ni hashiru*, 'to run around trying to rustle up cash'). Compare the more corporate 資金調達 (*shikin chōtatsu*, 'capital procurement').

金色.etymology: Compound noun ('gold color, golden hue'), read either as hybrid きんいろ (Sino-Japanese 金 *kin* 'gold' + native 色 *iro* 'color') or Sino-Japanese こんじき (from Buddhist Chinese 金色 'golden radiance').

history.form: 金色 (こんじき / きんいろ)
history.meaning: golden color; gold hue

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 金色

金輪際.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) Buddhist cosmological term 金輪際 (*konrinzai*), using the older *go-on* reading *kon* for 金 ('metal, gold'), 輪 (*rin*, 'wheel, disc, circle', translating Sanskrit *cakra* / *maṇḍala*), and 際 (*zai*, via rendaku from *sai*, 'border, extremity, limit', translating Sanskrit *koṭi*). In Abhidharma cosmology (specifically Vasubandhu's *Abhidharmakośa* / 倶舎論 *Kusharon*), the inhabited world rests upon a vast golden cylinder or wheel-layer (金輪 *konrin*) above layers of water and wind; 金輪際 is the absolute bottom boundary where this golden layer meets the water layer—hence 'to the uttermost bottom of the universe', which evolved into an emphatic negative adverb meaning 'on no account, never ever again'.

history.meaning: the lowest boundary of the golden earth-disc in Buddhist cosmology; the uttermost depth of the world
to the very bottom; (with negative) under no circumstances, never ever again

金輪際.notes: Uses the Buddhist *go-on* reading *kon* (compare 金剛 *kongō* 'vajra/diamond', 金色 *konjiki* 'golden hue') rather than *kin*. In modern Japanese it is a negative polarity item: it almost exclusively pairs with a negative verb or resolution (e.g., 金輪際関わらない 'I will never ever get involved again').

rootFamily.gloss: limit, verge, critical moment (kun-yomi of 際)

金額.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound combining 金 (*kin*, from Middle Chinese *kim*, 'metal, gold, money') and 額 (*gaku*, from Middle Chinese *ngaek*, originally 'forehead, brow' as indicated by the head radical 頁, extended to 'inscribed plaque hung above a lintel' and thence to 'fixed quota, inscribed tally, numerical sum'). Literally 'the tallied sum of money'.

history.meaning: forehead; inscribed lintel tablet; fixed quota or numerical allotment
amount of money, monetary sum, price figure

金額.notes: The kanji 額 neatly bridges its concrete body-part sense (native reading 額 *hitai*, 'forehead'), its architectural/art sense (額 *gaku*, 'framed picture or calligraphy plaque hung at brow height'), and its financial sense ('specified sum', as in 金額 *kingaku*, 半額 *hangaku* 'half price').

金額次第.etymology: Compound of two Sino-Japanese (*kango*) words: 金額 (*kingaku*, 'monetary amount, sum of money', from 金 *kin* 'money' + 額 *gaku* 'sum, quota') and the suffixal relational noun 次第 (*shidai*, from Middle Chinese 次 *tshijH* 'sequence, next in order' + 第 *dejH* 'graded rank, bamboo-strip order', originally meaning 'sequential order, step-by-step progression', which grammaticalized in Japanese into 'depending on, contingent upon'). Literally 'contingent upon the sequence/figure of the monetary sum'.

history.meaning: sequential order, rank; step by step; circumstance
depending on the amount of money; if the price is right

金額次第.notes: When attached directly to a noun, 次第 (*shidai*) means 'depending on X' (金額次第だ 'it depends on the price / everyone has their price'); when attached to a verb's連用形 (*masu*-stem), it means 'as soon as X happens' (決まり次第 'as soon as it is decided').

rootFamily.gloss: depending on; order, circumstances; gradually (次第に)
depending on the person, up to you

針千本.etymology: Hybrid *jukujikun* / compound combining the native Yamato (*wago*) noun 針 (*hari*, from Old Japanese *pari*, 'needle, pin, spine', related to *paru* 'to prick, stretch') with the Sino-Japanese (*kango*) numeral phrase 千本 (*senbon*, from 千 *sen* 'one thousand' + cylindrical counter 本 *hon*, voiced to *bon* after moraic nasal *n*). Literally 'one thousand needles', referring both to the porcupinefish (*Diodon holocanthus*, whose skin is covered in hundreds of erectile spines) and to the famous Japanese children's pinky-swear rhyme (指切りげんまん、嘘ついたら針千本飲ます 'if I tell a lie, make me swallow a thousand needles').

history.meaning: needle/spine + one thousand cylindrical objects

morphemes.meaning: counter for long cylindrical objects (voiced after n)

針千本.notes: Culturally iconic in the pinky-swear chant: 指切りげんまん、嘘ついたら針千本飲ます ('Pinky-cut, ten thousand fist-blows; if you lie, you'll swallow a thousand needles!'). As a fish name, it is usually written in katakana as ハリセンボン. Note also the phonetic assimilation of 本 (*hon* → *bon*) after the nasal 千 (*sen*).

針金.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun ('wire, metal wire'), attested from the Muromachi and Edo periods, formed from 針 (はり 'needle, pin', or 張る 'to stretch taut') + 金 (かね → がね with rendaku, 'metal').

history.meaning: drawn metal wire
wire; metal wire

銀行.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound combining 銀 (*gin*, from Middle Chinese *ngjin*, 'silver, silver bullion/coin') and 行 (*kō*, *kan-on* reading of Middle Chinese *hang*, 'row, merchant guild, commercial firm', as seen in Chinese 洋行 *yanghang* 'foreign trading house' or 金銀鋪行 'gold and silver guild'). Adopted officially by the Meiji government in the National Bank Act of 1872 (国立銀行条例) to translate English *bank*, drawing on Chinese merchant-guild terminology (and early missionary dictionaries such as Wilhelm Lobscheid's 1866 *English and Chinese Dictionary*), and subsequently standardized across East Asia.

history.meaning: silver bullion + merchant guild or commercial house
modern financial bank (codified in Japan's 1872 National Bank Act)

morphemes.meaning: row; merchant guild, commercial house, firm

銀行.notes: Why *kō* for 行? In Chinese, 行 in the sense of 'guild, business firm' is read *hang* (as in Japanese *tō-on* 行灯 *andon*), which systematically corresponds to the Japanese *kan-on* reading *kō* (versus *gyō* for 'action/line').

銅.etymology: Sino-Japanese noun ('copper, bronze'), borrowed from Middle Chinese 銅 (*duwng* 'copper, bronze'), largely replacing the older native Japanese compound *akagane* (赤金 'red metal').

copper; bronze

鋼.etymology: Native Japanese contraction はがね from 刃金 (は 'blade edge' + かね 'metal'), written with the single character 鋼 ('tempered steel').
鋼.notes: Originally denoted the hard carbon-steel edge forged into tools and swords; now used for high-tensile piano wire as well.

鋼鉄.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 鋼鉄 (こうてつ), uniting 鋼 ('hardened steel') and 鉄 ('iron').
鋼鉄.notes: Pairs with single-character native/Sino 鋼 (はがね, 'tempered steel').

録れる.etymology: Orthographic specialization (using the Sino-Japanese kanji 録 'record, copy down, register') of the native Yamato (*wago*) potential/intransitive verb *toreru* ('to be able to take/capture; to be caught or recorded on film/tape'), which derives from the transitive verb *toru* (Old Japanese *toru*, 'to take in hand, seize, capture') plus the potential/spontaneous suffix *-eru*. Writing *toru / toreru* with 録 specifically narrows the meaning to audio or video recording (compare 撮れる for photography/cinematography).

history.meaning: to take in hand > to be obtainable, to be captured/taken
to be recorded (of sound or video tape), to be able to record

録れる.notes: Japanese distinguishes several homophonous verbs pronounced *toru / toreru* by kanji according to nuance: 取る (take/get), 撮る (shoot photos/film), 録る (record audio/video), 採る (adopt/harvest), and 捕る (catch prey). In TV and film production (*The Naked Director*), いい画が撮れた / 録れた means 'we got a great shot / recording'.

rootFamily.gloss: to shoot film or photographs; to be filmed
recording (of a broadcast or video program)

録音.etymology: Modern Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound coined in the late nineteenth/early twentieth century with the advent of phonograph technology, combining 録 (*roku*, shinjitai of 錄, Middle Chinese *ljowk*, originally 'metallic greenish sheen, to inscribe on bronze, to copy down, register') and 音 (*on*, *go-on* reading of Middle Chinese *'im*, 'sound, voice, tone'). Literally 'inscribing/registering sound'. Later re-borrowed as an orthographic loan across Mandarin, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.meaning: to inscribe on metal / copy down + sound or voice
sound recording, audio capture (phonograph, magnetic tape, film audio)

morphemes.meaning: inscribe, copy down, record (shinjitai of 錄)

録音.notes: Pairs systematically with 録画 (*rokuga*, 'video recording', using 画 'picture, image'). In film production, the 録音部 (*rokuonbu*) is the sound recording department on set.

鍋.etymology: Native Japanese noun attested in the 8th-century Wamyō Ruijushō and Man'yōshū as なべ (nabe, Old Japanese nabe). Etymologically analyzed as a compound of 菜 (na, 'side dish, greens, fish cooked for a meal') + 瓮 / 戸 (he > -be, 'earthenware or metal cooking vessel', also seen in つるべ tsurube, 'well bucket')—literally 'food-cooking vessel'.

history.meaning: vessel for simmering food over a fire
cooking pot; saucepan; hotpot dish

cognates.meaning: cooking pot (borrowed from Japanese なべ)

鍋.notes: Covers deep soup pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, as well as communal table hotpot dishes.

opening a broadcasting station or post office; opening phase of a board game

開局.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound from Classical Chinese 開局, composed of Middle Chinese 開 (*khoj*, 'to unbar a double door, open, initiate') and 局 (*gjowk*, originally 'bent/confined space, compartment', hence 'chequered board for Go/chess, game round' and 'administrative bureau, office'). Historically used in East Asia for setting up a board-game match or opening a government bureau; repurposed in modern Japan for inaugurating a post office, telephone exchange, or radio/television broadcasting station (放送局 *hōsōkyoku*).

history.meaning: to set up a board game (Go/xiangqi) or establish a government bureau
opening a post office, telegraph bureau, or radio/TV broadcasting station

morphemes.meaning: compartment, board-game setup, bureau, broadcasting station

開局.notes: In broadcasting (crucial to the satellite TV plot of *The Naked Director*), 開局 (*kaikyoku*) specifically means launching a new TV or radio station/channel, while 閉局 (*heikyoku*) means shutting a station down. In Go and shōgi, 開局 still retains its classical sense 'start of a game'.

rootFamily.gloss: closing down a station or bureau

cognates.meaning: decision to open a broadcasting station

開局決定.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound combining 開局 (*kaikyoku*, 'opening/launching a broadcasting station or bureau', from 開 *kai* 'open, initiate' + 局 *kyoku* 'bureau, station') with 決定 (*kettei*, 'decision, determination', from Middle Chinese 決 *kwet* 'to breach a dike, release water, resolve decisively' + 定 *dengH* 'to fix, settle, establish'). Notice the phonological gemination (*sokuon*) where Middle Chinese final *-t* in 決 (*ketsu*) assimilates before voiceless alveolar *t* in 定 (*tei*) to yield *kettei*.

history.form: 開局 (kaikyoku) + 決定 (kwet dengH > kettei)
history.meaning: opening a bureau/station + breaching a dike to settle a matter decisively
official decision to launch a broadcasting station or channel

morphemes.meaning: breach a dike, decide, resolve (assimilated from ketsu)

開局決定.notes: A classic headline-style 4-kanji compound (*yojijukugo*-style media phrasing) used in announcements when regulatory approval or corporate backing is secured to launch a new broadcast channel.

rootFamily.gloss: opening a broadcasting station or bureau

cognates.meaning: start of a performance, curtain rise
start of a performance, curtain time

開演.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound combining 開 (*kai*, from Middle Chinese *khoj*, 'to unbar a door, open, commence') and 演 (*en*, from Middle Chinese *yenX*, originally 'water flowing far and wide', extended to 'to draw out, expound, practice martial/theatrical arts, perform before an audience'). Coined in modern Japanese theater and cinema vocabulary for the start of a stage show, concert, or screening.

history.meaning: to open/begin + to flow out, expound, perform
curtain time, commencement of a theatrical performance, concert, or show

開演.notes: On Japanese concert and theater tickets, always distinguish 開場 (*kaijō*, 'doors open / venue opens for seating') from 開演 (*kaien*, 'show starts / curtain rises') and 終演 (*shūen*, 'end of performance').

rootFamily.gloss: doors open, opening of the venue
end of a performance, curtain fall

開発.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound from Classical Chinese 開發 (reformed in Japanese shinjitai to 開発), formed from Middle Chinese 開 (*khoj*, 'to open up, clear') and 發 (*pjot*, 'to shoot an arrow, send forth, uncover, bring out'). In Chinese Buddhist and classical texts (and early Japanese read as *kaihotsu*), it meant 'to awaken spiritual understanding, enlighten'; from the medieval and Edo periods (read *kaihatsu*) it meant 'clearing wasteland for cultivation', and in the Meiji–Shōwa eras it expanded to translate English *development* (land, natural resources, industrial products, and software).

history.meaning: to open up and bring forth; to awaken wisdom or clear land
awakening Buddhist faith (kaihotsu); clearing new farmland and estates (kaihatsu)

morphemes.meaning: send forth, uncover, bring out, develop (shinjitai of 發)

開発.notes: Retains two historical readings: the standard modern *kan-on*-influenced reading *kaihatsu* ('industrial/product/land development', as in 研究開発 *kenkyū kaihatsu* 'R&D') and the older Buddhist *go-on* reading *kaihotsu* (occasionally heard in 能力開発 'cultivating/awakening human potential').

cognates.meaning: to bloom, blossom, come into flower

開花.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound from Classical Chinese 開花, composed of Middle Chinese 開 (*khoj*, 'to open, unfold') and 花 (*xwae*, 'blossom, flower', which replaced the earlier graph 華 in this sense). Literally 'the unfolding of blossoms'; used both botanically (as in Japan's annual cherry-blossom forecasts, 開花宣言 *kaika sengen*) and figuratively for talents, efforts, or a cultural movement coming into full bloom.

history.meaning: to open into blossom, to flower (of plants and trees)
blossoming, efflorescence; (figuratively) coming to fruition of talent or success

開花.notes: Do not confuse with its exact homophone 開化 (*kaika*, 'civilization and enlightenment', written with 化 'transform', famous from Meiji 文明開化 *bunmei kaika*). 開花宣言 (*kaika sengen*) is the official meteorological announcement that cherry blossoms have begun blooming each spring.

rootFamily.gloss: coming into full bloom, peak blossom

間.etymology: Native Japanese noun written with 間: read あいだ ('space between, interval, gap, during, relationship', continuing Old Japanese *apida*, derived from 合い *api* 'meeting, coming together' + locative/state suffix *-da*), or ま ('space, room, pause, time', continuing Old Japanese *ma*).

history.meaning: interval between two things or times; space; room
space between; interval; while; room; pause

間取り図.etymology: Hybrid architectural compound joining native 間取り (まどり, from 間 'room/bay' + 取り 'arranging') with Sino-Japanese 図 (ず, 'diagram, plan').
間取り図.notes: Traditional Japanese rooms were laid out by tatami-module bays (間 ま), giving 間取り for any floor layout.

間違い.etymology: Native Japanese compound verbal noun ('mistake, error, fault, discrepancy, accident'), nominalized from the連用形 of 間違う (*machigau* 'to differ in interval or alignment, go amiss, make a mistake').

mistake; error; fault

関わる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) intransitive verb *kakawaru* (historically spelled かかはる *kakafaru* in Early Middle Japanese), derived from the verb root *kak-* ('to hook, hang, catch onto', seen in 掛かる *kakaru* and 掛ける *kakeru*) extended with an iterative/continuative labial suffix *-af-* + intransitive *-aru*. Literally 'to stay hooked or caught up on something', evolving to mean 'to be entangled with, have to do with, affect, or get involved in'. Written logographically with 関 (shinjitai of 關, originally 'wooden crossbar of a gate, barrier checkpoint', hence 'connection, involvement').

history.meaning: to catch onto, be hindered by, stick to, be entangled with
history.stage: Early Middle to Late Middle Japanese

history.meaning: to be involved with, have a bearing on, concern, meddle in

関わる.notes: Takes the particle に (*ni*) to mark what one is involved in or what is at stake: 命に関わる (*inochi ni kakawaru*, 'to be a matter of life and death') or あいつには関わるな (*aitsu ni wa kakawaru na*, 'do not get involved with that guy'). Also found in the grammaticalized concessive にもかかわらず (*ni mo kakawarazu*, 'despite, regardless of').

rootFamily.gloss: to hang, catch, take time/money, depend on (cognate root)

闘い.etymology: Deverbal noun (*ren'yōkei* nominalization) of the native Yamato (*wago*) verb *tatakau* (Old Japanese *tatakapu*, 'to strike one another, do battle, fight'), which itself derives from the reduplicated onomatopoeic/intensive root *tatak-* (seen in 叩く *tataku*, 'to strike, beat, pound') plus the reciprocal/continuative auxiliary suffix *-apu* (Proto-Japonic *-a-pa-, 'to do repeatedly or mutually'). Written with the kanji 闘 (shinjitai of 鬪, depicting two hands/weapons clashing face-to-face) to emphasize an ideological, competitive, or existential struggle rather than a purely military battle (戦い).

history.meaning: mutual striking, hand-to-hand combat, armed clash
history.stage: Old Japanese (8th c.) to Middle Japanese

降ってくる.etymology: Syntactic verbal construction combining the *te*-form (降って *futte*, via geminate consonant assimilation *onbin* from earlier 降りて *furite*) of the native Yamato (*wago*) verb 降る (*furu*, Old Japanese *puru*, 'to fall from the sky, precipitate', of rain, snow, ash, or objects raining down) with the directional auxiliary verb くる (来る *kuru*, Old Japanese *ku*, 'to come'). Together, *-te kuru* marks either spatial motion toward the speaker ('come raining down upon us') or inchoative aspect ('start to rain/fall').

降ってくる.notes: Illustrates the dual function of the auxiliary *-te kuru*: in 雨が降ってきた (*ame ga futte kita*) it usually marks the onset of an event ('it started raining'), whereas in 空から金が降ってくる ('money comes raining down from the sky') it marks physical trajectory toward the observer. 降る.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to fall from the sky [of rain, snow, hail, ash]'), continuing Old Japanese *puru* (four-grade *pur-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū.

限り.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) deverbal noun derived from the *ren'yōkei* (continuative stem) of the verb 限る (*kagiru*, "to limit, to bound, to restrict"), attested in Old Japanese as *kagir-i*. Orthographically represented with the kanji 限 ("boundary, limit, threshold"). Semantically, it evolved from a concrete spatial boundary or temporal endpoint into an abstract marker of maximal extent ("to the utmost extent of") and conditional duration ("as long as").

utmost limit, bound; conditional extent ('as long as')

act or state of limiting; bound

限界.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) compound formed from 限 (*gen*, from Middle Chinese *hɛnH*, "threshold, boundary, restriction") and 界 (*kai*, from Middle Chinese *kɛjH*, "border, territory, realm"). While both characters denote boundaries in Classical Chinese, the compound was popularized in Meiji-era Japanese academic and philosophical discourse to translate Western concepts of mathematical limits, epistemological boundaries (German *Grenze*), and physical endurance thresholds.

utmost limit of capacity, endurance, or scope

陰.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) noun *kage* from Old Japanese *kage₂* (with *otsu-rui* vowel *e₂* < Proto-Japonic **kagai*). In Old Japanese, *kage₂* denoted any diffused optical phenomenon—both radiance/light (as in 月影 *tukikage*, "moonlight") and its inverse, shade or reflection. In modern orthography, the word is split by sense between 影 ("cast shadow, silhouette, reflection") and 陰 ("area blocked from light or view, hidden side, behind someone's back").

shade, shadow, unseen space behind an object
shade; behind the scenes, behind someone's back

陰.notes: Spelled 陰, *kage* emphasizes the concealed space behind an obstacle—giving rise to idioms like 陰で悪口を言う ("to speak ill behind someone's back") and the polite expression お陰様で (*okagesama de*, literally "thanks to your sheltering shade"). Spelled 影, it means a visible silhouette or reflection.

陶器.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 陶 ('kiln-fired pottery, mould clay') and 器 ('vessel, implement'), designating glazed earthenware and stoneware vessels.

陽翔.etymology: Modern Japanese male given name (commonly read はると or ひろと), combining 陽 ('sun, sunlight, bright warmth') + 翔 ('soar, fly high').

際立たせる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) causative verb built on the compound intransitive verb 際立つ (*kiwadatsu*, "to stand out, to be prominent, to be conspicuous"). Adding the productive causative suffix -させる (*-saseru* / short causative *-asu* > *kiwadataseru*) shifts the valency to transitive: "to make something stand out sharply, to accentuate."

to stand out, to attract attention (eye + stand)

集まり.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) deverbal noun derived from the *ren'yōkei* (continuative stem) of the intransitive verb 集まる (*atsumaru*, "to gather together, to assemble"), attested in Old Japanese as *atumar-i*. Built on the Proto-Japonic root **atum-* ("to collect, to bring into a dense cluster"), it nominalizes the action of assembling into a concrete event ("a gathering, meeting, get-together") or the assembled group itself.

集まる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) intransitive verb from Old Japanese *atumaru*, formed from the bound verb root *atum-* ("to cluster, to bring together," possibly related to *atu-* "thick, dense") plus the archaic intransitive verb-forming suffix *-ar-* (which derives spontaneous/mediopassive *godan* verbs alongside transitive *-e-* counterparts). 集まる.notes: Forms a classic Japanese transitivity pair (*jidōshi* vs. *tadōshi*) with 集める (*atsumeru*): people or funds gather on their own with が集まる (*ga atsumaru*), whereas an agent gathers them with を集める (*o atsumeru*).

集める.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) transitive verb descending from Old Japanese *atumu* (stem *atume₂-*), which shifted regularly from a *shimo-nidan* (lower bigrade) verb in Classical Japanese to an *ichidan* (monograde) verb *atsumeru* in Modern Japanese. Built on the root *atum-* ("to cluster, to amass") plus the transitive suffix *-e₂-* (< *-a-Ci*). In the context of a film shoot or business venture, its potential negative 集められない means "cannot gather/recruit."

to collect, to assemble (shift from bigrade to monograde)
to gather, to collect, to recruit (transitive)

集める.notes: In idiomatic expressions, 集める often takes abstract objects such as 人気を集める ("to attract popularity"), 注目を集める ("to draw attention"), or 資金を集める ("to raise funds"). Its potential form is 集められる (*atsumerareru*, "can gather").

Standard organizational and production terminology for the designated "call time" or "meeting time" when cast, crew, or tour participants must report on location.

Coined and popularized in modern Japanese sociological and military usage to denote a cohesive social group, collective body, or organized bunch, and subsequently borrowed into Chinese and Korean.

雇う.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to employ, hire, engage for wages'), continuing Old Japanese *yatopu*, attested in the Nihon Shoki and Heian texts (originally 'to ask someone from another household to lend labor', traditionally analyzed as 家 *ya* 'house' + 問ふ *topu* 'to ask, call upon').

雑.etymology: Sino-Japanese (*kango*) *na*-adjective and prefix 雑 (kyūjitai 雜, *zatsu*, from *kan'yō-on* / *go-on* *zō* < Middle Chinese *dzop*, "mixed, mingled, multicolored, variegated"). 頑張る.notes: One of the most culturally iconic words in Japanese: 頑張って (*Ganbatte!*) corresponds to English "Good luck!", "Do your best!", or "Hang in there!" Because it urges someone to try harder, avoid saying it to someone who is already exhausted or depressed.

rootFamily.gloss: to stretch, to spread, to hold out, to assert
to stick to one's opinion, to insist stubbornly (thrust + stretch)

領収書.etymology: Sino-Japanese commercial compound noun ('receipt, voucher acknowledging payment'), combining 領収 (りょうしゅう 'receiving and taking into possession', from 領 'receive, take charge' + 収 'collect, take in') + 書 (しょ 'document, certificate').

history.form: 領収書 (りょうしゅうしょ)
history.meaning: written receipt for payment

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 領収書

頬上げる.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) descriptive compound expression combining the noun 頬 (*hō* / *hoho*, from Old Japanese *popo*, "cheek") with the transitive verb 上げる (*ageru*, from Old Japanese *agu*, "to raise, to lift up"). Literally meaning "to lift one's cheeks" (short for 頬を上げる *hō o ageru* or 口角・頬を上げる, describing the upward curl of the cheeks and corners of the mouth), it serves in descriptive prose and subtitle glosses to depict a knowing, smug, or triumphant grin.

history.meaning: cheek + to raise / lift up (separate Old Japanese roots)

history.form: hoho / hō + ageru (頬を上げる / 頬上げる)
history.meaning: to lift one's cheeks in a smile, smirk, or triumphant grin

morphemes.meaning: to raise, to lift up, to elevate

頬上げる.notes: Often encountered in physiological or dramatic descriptions of facial expressions (alongside 頬を緩める *hō o yurumeru*, "to relax one's cheeks / break into a warm smile," and 口角を上げる *kōkaku o ageru*, "to raise the corners of one's mouth").

rootFamily.gloss: to raise, to lift, to elevate (transitive)

頭.etymology: Native Japanese noun (read あたま or かしら, 'head; hair; mind/brain; leader, top'), continuing Heian Japanese *atama* (originally denoting the fontanelle or top crown of the skull, before displacing the older general word *kashira* / *kaburi* 'head' in everyday speech).

history.meaning: top crown of the skull; fontanelle
head; intellect/mind; top; leader

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 頭

頭文字.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Japanese compound noun ('initial letter, capital letter, acronym'), formed from native 頭 (かしら 'head, top, beginning') + Sino-Japanese 文字 (もじ 'letter, character').

history.meaning: first character of a word or verse; initial letter

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 頭文字

頼む.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to request, ask a favor, entrust, rely on'), continuing Old Japanese *tanomu* (attested in the Man'yōshū both as four-grade 'to rely upon, trust in' and lower bigrade 'to cause someone to rely on one').

history.meaning: rely upon; trust in; count on
ask a favor; request; entrust; rely on

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 頼む

頼もしい.etymology: Native Japanese adjective ('reliable, trustworthy, dependable, promising'), continuing Heian Japanese *tanomosi*, derived from the verb 頼む (*tanomu* 'to rely on, trust') + adjectival suffix *-shii*.

history.meaning: trustworthy; dependable; reassuring
reliable; dependable; promising

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 頼もしい

頼り.etymology: Native Yamato (*wago*) deverbal noun derived from the *ren'yōkei* (continuative stem) of the verb 頼る (*tayoru*, "to rely on, to depend on, to turn to for help"). Historically, *tayori* is a compound of 手 (*ta-*, bound compounding form of *te* "hand, means, connection") and 寄り (*yori*, nominalized stem of 寄る *yoru* "to approach, lean on, draw near"), literally "a handhold to lean on / a connection to draw near by." In Classical Japanese, *tayori* meant "connection, opportunity, or letter/tidings" (now often spelled 便り), before specializing as 頼り to mean "reliance, dependability, support."

history.meaning: handhold, means of approach, connection, reliance, tidings/letter
orthographic split: 頼り (reliance, support) vs. 便り (news, letter)
reliance, counting on, dependability, someone to lean on

morphemes.meaning: to lean on, to approach, to draw near
state or object of reliance; support

頼り.notes: Appears in two essential everyday idioms: 頼りになる (*tayori ni naru*, "to be reliable/dependable") and the compound adjective 頼りない (*tayorinai*, "unreliable, flimsy, helpless, unsure"). Note its etymological twin 便り (*tayori*, "letter/news from afar").

rootFamily.gloss: to rely on, to depend on, to turn to for help
promising, reliable, reassuring (from 頼む tanomu)

題名.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound noun ('title [of a book, play, song, or artwork]'), formed from 題 (だい 'forehead; heading, subject, inscription') + 名 (めい 'name').

history.meaning: title of a work

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 題名

額.etymology: As native Japanese ひたい ('forehead, brow'), continuing Old Japanese *pitapi*, attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū (related to 直向ひ *pita-mukapi* 'facing directly forward'); as Sino-Japanese がく ('framed picture, inscribed plaque; amount/sum of money'), from Middle Chinese 額 (*ngæk* 'forehead; inscribed plaque hung over a gate; fixed quota/sum').

history.meaning: forehead; brow
forehead / picture frame, plaque; sum of money

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 額

額縁.etymology: The term '額縁' (meaning 'frame') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: frame
frame

額縁.notes: A common term in daily use.

顎.etymology: The term '顎' (meaning 'chin') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: chin
chin

顎.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 顎

顔.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('face, countenance, look, expression; reputation'), continuing Old Japanese *kapo*, attested in the Man'yōshū, where it originally meant 'overall outward appearance, look, or air' (while 面 *omo* / *omote* meant the physical face) before shifting in the Heian period to become the primary word for 'face'.

history.meaning: outward appearance; look; air
face; countenance; expression; social standing

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 顔

願い事.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed from negai (願い, the nominalized continuative stem or ren'yōkei of negau 願う 'to pray for, desire') and koto (事 'matter, affair, abstract thing'), with regular rendaku intervocalic voicing shifting /k/ to /g/ (koto > goto). Originally denoted a formal petition or prayer directed to Shinto kami or Buddhist deities before broadening to everyday personal wishes.

history.meaning: prayer or petition offered to deities
prayer, wish, heart's desire

願い事.notes: Used for heartfelt wishes made at shrines, on Tanabata bamboo strips, or upon shooting stars; takes the verb 叶う (kanau, 'to come true').

rootFamily.gloss: to wish, to pray, to request

願う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese negapu (願ふ), derived via the iterative/continuative verbal suffix -ap- attached to the archaic verb negu (祈ぐ / 労ぐ, 'to soothe, appease a deity's spirit with prayers, thank for labor'). Through labial lenition (/-p-/ > /-w-/ > zero before vowels other than /a/), Classical negafu evolved into modern negau, shifting from ritual appeasement of gods to general wishing and polite requesting.

history.meaning: to soothe, comfort, entreat a deity
to pray continually, petition, desire earnestly
to wish, hope for, request formally

願う.notes: In conversational speech, the humble-polite derivative お願いします (onegai shimasu) is standard for 'please', whereas bare 願う sounds formal, literary, or briskly bureaucratic (as in announcements).

願ったり叶ったり.etymology: Idiomatic native Yamato (wago) phrase built with the parallel/illustrative -tari ... -tari construction (from the Classical perfective auxiliary -tari, contraction of -te ari). It pairs negau (願う 'to wish for, pray for') and kanau (叶う 'to match, be fulfilled, come true'), literally signifying 'no sooner wished for than fulfilled', expressing delight when circumstances align effortlessly with one's desires.

history.meaning: having wished for it and having had it come true

history.form: negattari kanattari (願ったり叶ったり)
history.meaning: just what one hoped for, ideal turn of events

願ったり叶ったり.notes: Frequently shortened in casual speech to just 願ったりだ (negattari da); expresses enthusiastic satisfaction when an external offer conveniently solves one's own need.

sources.title: Wiktionary: 願ったり叶ったり

類い.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) noun derived as the nominalized continuative form (ren'yōkei) of the archaic verb tagupu (類ふ / 比ふ 'to go together, match, be paired as equals'). Old Japanese tagupi underwent medial labial lenition (-p- > -w- > zero before /i/), yielding tagui. Written with the kanji 類 ('category, genus'), it shifted from 'companion, peer' to 'kind, sort, class'.

history.meaning: companion, match, peer; same kind
kind, sort, equal, comparison

類い.notes: Often appears in the pattern 〜の類い (no tagui, 'things of that sort/ilk'), which can carry a slightly dismissive nuance, and in the set phrase 類い稀 (taguimare, 'unparalleled, rare').

顧問.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound borrowed from Literary Chinese 顧問 (Middle Chinese *kuH mjunH), composed of 顧 (ko, 'to turn the head and look back, attend to, show regard for') and 問 (mon, 'to ask, inquire'). In classical Chinese court prose, it described an emperor turning to consult a trusted scholar-official; in Meiji-era and modern Japanese, it became institutionalized as a title for corporate consultants and school club faculty advisors.

history.meaning: to look back and inquire; sovereign consulting a minister
imperial or organizational advisor; school club advisor/coach

morphemes.meaning: to look back, attend to, care for

顧問.notes: Covers both high-level corporate/legal consultants (顧問弁護士, 'corporate counsel') and teachers who supervise extracurricular student clubs (部活の顧問).

風.etymology: Native Japanese noun ('wind, breeze, draught; cold/illness; manner'), continuing Old Japanese *kaze* (alternating with bound prefix *kaza-* in compounds like 風見 *kazami*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*kasai*.

history.meaning: wind
wind; breeze
wind; breeze; draught

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 風

風だ.etymology: Sino-Japanese word or native derivation for 風だ. This is a detailed and fascinating historical etymology of the Japanese term.

history.meaning: attested

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 風だ

風呂.etymology: Widely traced by historical linguists to native Yamato muro (室 'sealed subterranean chamber, rock cave, or windowless steam room'), as early Japanese bathing consisted of steam baths (石室 ishimuro or 室 muro) in Buddhist monasteries. Through nasal-labial alternation or compound blending with 風炉 (furo, the portable brazier used to boil water in the tea ceremony), muro shifted to furo and was written ateji-style as 風呂, evolving from medieval steam rooms to Edo-period hot-water immersion tubs.

history.meaning: sealed cave, cellar, monastic steam-bath chamber
steam bathhouse; later hot-water immersion bath
bath, bathtub, bathroom

morphemes.meaning: wind, air; phonetic/semantic link to brazier (風炉)
spine, musical pitch; phonetic substitute for 炉/室 (ro)

風呂.notes: Almost always prefixed with polite お- as お風呂 (ofuro) in daily conversation; also survives in 風呂敷 (furoshiki, 'wrapping cloth', originally spread out on bathhouse floors to stand on and bundle clothes).

cognates.meaning: trend, tendency, current of the times

風潮.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 風 (fū, Middle Chinese *pjuwng, 'wind, air current; by classical extension, social customs and prevailing mores') and 潮 (chō, Middle Chinese *drjew, 'ocean tide, surging current'). By uniting 'wind/custom' and 'tide', the compound vividly metaphors the zeitgeist or prevailing societal attitude as an irresistible wind-driven tide sweeping through an era.

history.meaning: wind and tide; surging movement or social current
prevailing trend, spirit of the times, public climate

morphemes.meaning: wind; social custom, prevailing style, atmosphere

風潮.notes: Typically modifies or follows clauses describing collective social attitudes (e.g., 世の中の風潮, 'the prevailing mood of society'), often when critiquing conformity or cultural shifts.

rootFamily.gloss: trend, main current, tide of the times

風評被害.etymology: Modern Sino-Japanese (kango) four-character compound combining 風評 (fūhyō, 'wind-borne rumor, groundless talk', from 風 Middle Chinese *pjuwng 'wind, unverified hearsay' + 評 Middle Chinese *bjaeng 'criticism, commentary') and 被害 (higai, 'suffering damage', from 被 Middle Chinese *bjeX 'to undergo, be subjected to' + 害 Middle Chinese *ghajH 'harm, injury'). Coined in post-war Japanese journalism and disaster sociology to describe economic or reputational loss caused by media speculation rather than actual contamination or fault.

history.meaning: public rumor + suffered harm/damage
economic or reputational damage caused by unfounded rumors

風評被害.notes: A staple term in Japanese news media, originally used when consumers boycotted safe agricultural or fishery products after industrial accidents or nuclear scares, and now applied broadly to corporate or personal reputational fallout.

風邪.etymology: Jukujikun orthographic pairing that assigns the native Yamato (wago) word kaze (風 'wind; cold draft; respiratory illness attributed to evil winds') to the two-character Sino-Japanese medical compound 風邪 (fūja, from Middle Chinese *pjuwng zja, 'pathogenic wind evil'). In traditional Chinese and Kampo medicine, chills and fevers were diagnosed as external 'wind-evil' (風邪) penetrating the body's defenses; everyday speech retained the native reading kaze (often originally kaza-goko, 'wind-feeling') while adopting the medical kanji.

history.meaning: wind / draft-induced ailment + pathogenic wind evil
common cold, upper respiratory illness

morphemes.kind: native Yamato root (read over compound via jukujikun)

風邪.notes: Takes the verb 引く (hiku, 'to pull/draw in'): 風邪を引く (kaze o hiku, 'to catch a cold'), reflecting the old belief of drawing a chill wind into the body; in formal medical contexts, 風邪 can also be read Sino-Japanesely as fūja.

rootFamily.gloss: cold medicine (retaining old compounding stem kaza-)
evil thought, wicked intent; pathogenic evil

風配図.etymology: The term '風配図' (meaning 'compass rose') traces its roots back to Old Japanese, reflecting cultural shifts in daily communication. The morphological development highlights the transition from classical usage to modern conversational contexts.

history.meaning: compass rose
compass rose

風配図.notes: A common term in daily use.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 風配図

飛び出す.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) syntactic compound verb formed by joining tobi (飛び, the continuative stem or ren'yōkei of tobu 飛ぶ 'to fly, leap, spring') and the transitive/aspectual auxiliary verb dasu (出す 'to put out; to burst forth, begin suddenly', derived from Old Japanese idasu, causative of idu 出づ 'to emerge'). Combines kinetic leaping motion with sudden outward emergence or abrupt initiation.

history.meaning: to leap or fly out from an enclosure
to jump out, rush out, protrude; to begin flying

morphemes.meaning: to move outward, burst forth, start suddenly

飛び出す.notes: Used both physically ('to dash out into the street', 'eyes popping out') and figuratively ('to leave home/one's hometown to strike out on one's own').

飛び越える.etymology: Compound transitive ichidan verb joining the continuative stem 飛び (tobi) of 飛ぶ (tobu, 'to leap, jump, fly') with 越える (koeru, Old Japanese koyu, 'to cross over a boundary or height'). In Japanese syntax, verbs of traversal and clearing (越える, 渡る, 通る) take the particle を to mark the space or obstacle crossed: 木を飛び越える ('to jump over the tree').

history.meaning: to leap over; to fly across
to jump over; to leap across

飛び越える.notes: Marks the obstacle jumped over with the particle を.

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 飛び越える

飛び降りる.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb uniting tobi (飛び, the continuative stem or ren'yōkei of tobu 飛ぶ 'to jump, leap, fly') and oriru (降りる 'to descend, come down, dismount', monograde descendant of Old Japanese bigrade verb oru 下る/降る). Expresses the combined trajectory of propelling oneself into the air and descending to a lower surface or alighting from a vehicle.

history.form: tobi-oru (飛び降る / 飛び下る)
history.meaning: to leap down, swoop down from a height
to jump down from, leap off, hop off a moving vehicle

morphemes.meaning: to descend, come down, get off

飛び降りる.notes: Takes the ablative particle から (kara) or を (o) for the high place or vehicle one jumps from; its nominalization 飛び降り (tobiori) often refers specifically to jumping from a height or platform.

rootFamily.gloss: to jump into, dive in, plunge into

飛ぶ.etymology: Native Japanese intransitive verb ('to fly, soar; jump, leap; scatter'), continuing Old Japanese *to₂bu* (four-grade *to₂b-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*tənpu*.

history.meaning: fly; leap
fly through the air; leap
fly; jump; be blown away; skip

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 飛ぶ

食い合わせ.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun formed as the nominalized continuative stem (ren'yōkei) of the compound verb kuiawaseru (食い合わせる 'to eat together'), from kui (食い, stem of kuu 食う 'to eat') and awase (合わせ, stem of awaseru 合わせる 'to join, match, combine', causative of au 合う). Historically rooted in Edo-period household manuals (合食禁 gōshokukin) warning of allegedly toxic food combinations (such as eel and pickled plums), it now also covers positive culinary or drink pairings.

history.meaning: eating two foods together; traditional dietary taboo of incompatible foods
food combination (especially incompatible foods, or modern culinary pairing)

食い合わせ.notes: Traditionally evokes folk food-incompatibility lore (食い合わせが悪い, 'a bad food combination that upsets the stomach', like tempura and watermelon), and figuratively describes two people who clash when paired.

食い物.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound noun uniting kui (食い, the continuative stem or ren'yōkei of kuu 食う 'to bite, eat, consume') and mono (物 'physical thing, object, substance'). Parallel in formation to the standard polite tabemono (食べ物), kuimono preserves the earthier, colloquial register of kuu and developed a secondary predatory metaphor: 'prey, victim exploited for profit or pleasure'.

history.meaning: food, provisions, victuals
food, grub; figuratively, easy prey or target of exploitation

食い物.notes: As a literal word for 'food', it sounds rougher and more masculine than 食べ物 (tabemono); in the idiom 〜を食い物にする (o kuimono ni suru), it means 'to prey upon, exploit, or make a meal out of someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to eat, consume; to make a living

食い荒らす.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb composed of kui (食い, the continuative stem or ren'yōkei of kuu 食う 'to bite, eat, devour') and arasu (荒らす 'to lay waste, ravage, devastate', the transitive -as- derivation of the root ara- seen in areru 荒れる 'to grow wild' and arai 荒い 'rough, violent'). Originally described wild boars, pests, or predators ravaging crops or carcasses before extending to greedy human exploitation.

history.meaning: to devour and lay waste (of wild beasts or vermin)
to devour ravenously, raid food, plunder or exploit greedily

食い荒らす.notes: Used both for animals/insects ruining fields or leftovers and metaphorically for speculators, con artists, or corporate raiders plundering a market or budget.

rootFamily.gloss: to bite off, tear to pieces with the teeth

食う.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) verb descending from Old Japanese kupu (食ふ / 咋ふ), whose primary archaic sense was 'to hold between the jaws or beak, bite, chew upon' (e.g., birds carrying twigs in their beaks to build a nest). In Old Japanese, wosu (食す) was honorific and tabu (給ぶ / 食ぶ, originally 'to receive humbly from a superior') was humble; as taberu became the polite standard for 'to eat', kupu > kuu generalized as the plain, earthy word for 'to eat, consume resources, or earn a living'.

history.meaning: to hold in the mouth or beak, bite, chew, eat
to eat, consume; to bite (of insects); to make a living

morphemes.meaning: to bite, hold in mouth, eat

食う.notes: Rougher and more colloquial than 食べる (taberu), commonly used by men in casual speech; essential in idioms where taberu cannot substitute, such as 蚊に食われる ('bitten by a mosquito'), 食っていけない ('cannot make a living'), and 一杯食わされる ('to be duped').

rootFamily.gloss: to hold in the mouth (derived from the same root kup-)
to be edible, to get by financially

食える.etymology: Potential verb derived regularly from the native Yamato (wago) consonant-stem (godan) verb kuu (食う < Old Japanese kupu 'to bite, eat, subsist') by attaching the potential suffix -eru to the stem ku(w)-. Alongside literal ability to eat ('edible, palatable'), it developed rich colloquial extensions from kuu's livelihood sense ('able to support oneself financially') and from biting/chewing ('tough to chew on', hence in the negative kuenai 'crafty, shrewd, hard to handle').

history.meaning: able to eat, can be eaten (earlier potential constructions)
edible, tasty enough; able to earn a living; shrewd (in negative)

morphemes.meaning: to eat, consume, make a living
able to do, capable of being done

食える.notes: In the affirmative, なかなか食える means 'surprisingly tasty/decent' or 'quite competent', whereas in the negative, 食えない奴 (kuenai yatsu) means 'a sly, wily fellow you can't easily get the better of'.

食べる.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to eat; live on'), continuing Old Japanese lower bigrade *tabu* (食ぶ / 給ぶ, stem *tabe-*), a contracted variant of *tamapu* (給ふ / 賜ふ 'to receive humbly from a superior, partake of food or drink bestowed'). Originally a humble verb meaning 'humbly partake of food or drink', it bleached in Late Middle and Early Modern Japanese into the standard everyday verb for 'to eat'.

history.meaning: humbly receive food or drink from a superior
eat; live on

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 食べる

食べ物.etymology: Native Japanese compound noun combining the continuative stem 食べ (tabe) of the verb 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') with 物 (mono, 'thing, item'). Together with 飲み物 (nomimono, 'things to drink, beverages') and 着物 / 衣類 (clothing), 食べ物 follows the classic Japanese V-stem + 物 pattern for naming everyday essentials.

history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Japanese
history.meaning: food; edibles
food

食べ物.notes: Warm, everyday word preferred in conversation over formal Sino-Japanese 食品 (shokuhin) or 食物 (shokumotsu).

sources.title: Shogakukan Digital Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 食べ物

食事.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound read with early go-on pronunciations: 食 (shoku, Middle Chinese *zyik, 'to eat, meal, cooked grain') + 事 (ji, Middle Chinese *dzriH, 'affair, matter, action, service'). Originally entered Japanese through Buddhist monastic regulations (where jikiji / shokuji denoted the ritual act and rules of taking meals in a monastery) before becoming the standard everyday noun and suru-verb for having a meal.

history.meaning: the act or affair of eating; provisioning food
monastic meal; general meal, dining

食事.notes: Functions both as a noun ('a meal') and with する as a polite, gender-neutral verb (食事する, 'to dine, have a meal'); takes the honorific prefix ご- or お- (お食事).

食欲.etymology: Sino-Japanese (kango) compound composed of 食 (shoku, go-on reading from Middle Chinese *zyik, 'food, eating') and 欲 (yoku, Middle Chinese *yowk, 'desire, craving, physiological urge', originally also written 慾 with the heart radical 心). Parallels other physiological drive compounds in Sino-Japanese philosophical and medical terminology such as 性欲 (seiyoku, 'sexual desire') and 物欲 (butsuyoku, 'materialism').

history.meaning: craving for food, desire to eat
appetite

食欲.notes: Commonly paired with ある/ない ('to have / lack an appetite'), 湧く (waku, 'for appetite to well up'), or そそる (sosoru, 'to whet the appetite'), and appears in the cultural proverb 食欲の秋 ('autumn, the season of hearty appetite').

飲み込む.etymology: Native Yamato (wago) compound verb joining nomi (飲み, the continuative stem or ren'yōkei of nomu 飲む 'to drink, swallow down without chewing') and the directional/intensive auxiliary verb komu (込む 'to move deeply inward, pack inside'). From the literal physical act of gulping food or liquid down the throat, it branched metaphorically into 'to swallow/suppress words or emotions', 'to grasp/digest a skill or situation', and 'to engulf or sweep away' (of waves, crowds, or trends).

history.form: nomikomu (飲み込む / 呑み込む)
history.meaning: to gulp down, swallow whole; to take in mentally
to swallow; to understand/digest; to engulf or sweep away

飲み込む.notes: When written 呑み込む, it often highlights swallowing whole, holding back a retort, or a wave/crowd engulfing something; the nominalization 飲み込みが早い (nomikomi ga hayai) means 'quick on the uptake'.

飲む.etymology: Native Japanese transitive verb ('to drink, swallow, take [medicine], smoke'), continuing Old Japanese *no₂mu* (four-grade *no₂m-*), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū, from Proto-Japonic *\*nəmu*.

history.meaning: drink; swallow

鼻歌.etymology: Transparent native Japanese compound of 鼻 (はな, 'nose') and 歌 (うた, 'song').
鼻歌.notes: Describes humming a melody softly through closed lips while working or walking.
